# Set up with your AI assistant

You can let an AI coding assistant install Regia Engine for you: open the engine folder (or paste the repository's
URL, https://github.com/Regia-Engine/Regia-Engine) in any assistant that can read files and run commands, and say
*"Set Regia up for me."* This page says what happens then, what the assistant will and will not do, and how to do
it by hand instead.

The assistant reads `AGENTS.md` at the root of the engine folder, the instructions Regia ships for assistants. Any
assistant works, including one that runs a local model; Claude Code also picks up the project skills in
`.claude/skills/`. Regia itself always runs on your machine and needs no account.

## What happens

1. **Introduction.** The assistant says in a few sentences what Regia is, names the three ways of working with
   it, and says it will ask about six questions.
2. **Two questions before anything is downloaded**: whether to set Regia up on this machine (it names the OS, CPU,
   memory, GPU and free disk it sees), and whether to get the engine as a git clone or a release archive, and into
   which folder. Either way Regia is built from source on your machine.
3. **Prerequisites.** A C/C++ compiler and some system libraries with a Vulkan driver (Linux), the Visual Studio
   Build Tools (Windows) or the Xcode command-line tools (macOS). These need administrator rights, so the assistant
   shows you the exact command and why, and you run it.
4. **Rust and Regia.** With your consent for each download, and after telling you its size and where it comes
   from, the assistant installs Rust for your user account (checking the installer against its published hash),
   gets the engine source, and builds the `regia` tool and the editor. The first build downloads about 150 MB of
   crates, uses about 10 GB of disk and takes 20 to 60 minutes.
5. **The check.** `regia doctor` checks the toolchains and the GPU driver; the assistant shows you the fix for
   anything it reports.
6. **Four more questions**: which platforms to build games for, how you want to work with the assistant (below),
   which template to start from, and the project's name and folder.
7. **Your first project.** It creates the project from the template, builds it, runs it once and opens the editor.

Each question is asked once and labeled, for example "(Question 3 of 6 · targets)". Say "you decide" to any
question and the assistant takes the default and tells you which. If you stop part-way, nothing breaks: say
"continue Regia setup" later and it picks up from what is already built.

| Question | Default |
|---|---|
| (Question 1 of 6 · machine) set Regia up on this machine | yes |
| (Question 2 of 6 · install_from) git clone or release archive, and the engine folder | a git clone in `~/Regia/regia-engine` |
| (Question 3 of 6 · targets) platforms to build games for | this machine only |
| (Question 4 of 6 · mode) how you want to work | 1, local-first |
| (Question 5 of 6 · template) the first project's template | `first_person` |
| (Question 6 of 6 · project) project name and folder | `My Game` in `~/RegiaProjects` |

## How you work together

| Mode | Who drives | What the assistant does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Local-first (default) | you | installs, explains what is on screen, points at the manual, runs the commands you ask for; does not connect to the editor or change your project unasked |
| 2 Co-pilot | you | also connects to your running editor over MCP to look, take screenshots, play-test and make the edits you ask for |
| 3 Assistant builds | the assistant | builds the game through the editor (code, content, tests, screenshots) and asks you only for decisions; keeps a short decision log in your project |

In modes 2 and 3 every edit the assistant makes goes onto the editor's undo stack and shows in the Agent Changes
panel, so you can see and revert it. Golden images stay yours: only you accept one, with `regia golden accept` at a
terminal. Switch modes at any time by saying so ("connect to my editor", "take over", "stop touching my project").

Connecting (modes 2 and 3) writes one entry into your project's MCP file (for Claude Code, `<project>/.mcp.json`)
and nothing into your assistant's own settings. Your assistant then asks you to start a new session in the project
folder and to approve the `regia` server there.

## What the assistant will and will not do

It will:

- ask before every download, saying what, from where and how large;
- show you every command that needs administrator rights, with the reason, for you to run;
- change files only in the engine folder and your projects folder, and ask separately before anything else (the
  `PATH` line in your shell profile, the project's MCP file);
- check the Rust installer against its published hash before running it.

It will not:

- accept any license or terms for you (Regia's own license, the Mozilla Public License 2.0, needs no acceptance to
  use or build it), or click Regia's windows for you;
- run `sudo` or any other elevation, or pipe a downloaded script into a shell;
- edit the engine's own source unless you ask.

## Privacy

Regia sends nothing anywhere on its own: no telemetry service, no update check, no account. (A game you make can
upload its crash reports to your own server, but only when you turn that on for it:
[Crash reports](book/agents/crash-reports.md).) The only network traffic setup makes is the downloads you agreed to (the repository, the Rust distribution server, crates.io during the
first build, and the Android SDK repository if you chose Android).

What you type to your assistant, and what it reads (including `regia doctor` output), goes wherever your assistant
sends it; an assistant running a local model keeps it on your machine. The `regia` MCP server listens on your
machine only ([MCP over HTTP](book/agents/mcp-http.md)).

## Uninstall

Setup puts nothing outside the folders you chose and the changes you agreed to. Delete the engine folder to remove
Regia (your projects stay, but they need the engine folder to build), remove the `PATH` line from your shell profile
if you let the assistant add one, and delete the `regia` entry from a project's MCP file. Rust (`rustup self
uninstall`) and system packages are yours to keep or remove.

## Doing it by hand

Everything the assistant does is in [Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md), then
[Your first project](book/getting-started.md). For assistants and the curious, the full flow, the consents and the
fixes for common failures are in [Onboarding: setting Regia up (agents)](book/agents/onboarding.md).

<!-- source: book/start/install.md -->
# Installing Regia Engine

> **Rather let an AI assistant do it?** Open the engine folder in an assistant that can run commands and say
> *"Set Regia up for me."* It follows the same steps and asks you before every download and every administrator
> command: [Set up with your AI assistant](book/start/assistant-setup.md).

Regia Engine is open source (MPL-2.0, see [Licensing](book/user-guide/licensing.md)) and distributed as source. You build the command-line tool and the editor
from your engine checkout, and every project you create path-depends on that checkout. This
chapter sets up a machine for desktop development and, optionally, for Android.

## 0. Get the engine

An engine release arrives as one archive, `regia-engine-<version>.tar.gz` (made with
`regia engine package`, [Distribution and upgrades](book/agents/distribution-upgrade.md)). Unpack it
where it will stay, because every project you create refers to that folder by path, and work inside
it for the rest of this chapter. In a terminal, in the folder that holds the archive:

```sh,walkthrough=install
tar -xzf regia-engine-<version>.tar.gz
cd regia-engine-<version>
```

Replace `<version>` with the version in the archive's name. If you work from a git checkout of the
engine instead, `cd` into the checkout; everything below is the same.

## 1. Rust

The engine pins one stable compiler in `rust-toolchain.toml` at the repository root (currently
Rust 1.99.0, with `rustfmt`, `clippy` and `rust-src`, and the Linux, Windows and Android targets).
Install Rust with [rustup](https://rustup.rs): it reads that file and fetches the right toolchain
the first time you run `cargo` inside the checkout. Rustup also adds the Android targets later.
A distribution `rustc` builds the desktop targets if its version matches, but cannot add
Android targets.

## 2. A GPU driver with Vulkan (or DX12 on Windows)

The renderer uses Vulkan on Linux and Android, and DX12 or Vulkan on Windows. It never falls back
to OpenGL. On Linux, install your distribution's Vulkan driver (Mesa's RADV/ANV, or the NVIDIA
driver) and `vulkan-tools` so `vulkaninfo` can confirm it. Without a GPU, Mesa's `lavapipe`
software driver runs every headless test, slowly; it is what the engine's golden images are
recorded on.

On Linux the build also needs `pkg-config` and the development headers of ALSA, udev, D-Bus,
xkbcommon and Wayland (the same set the engine's CI installs):

| Distribution | Command |
|---|---|
| Debian, Ubuntu | `sudo apt install pkg-config libasound2-dev libudev-dev libdbus-1-dev libxkbcommon-dev libwayland-dev mesa-vulkan-drivers vulkan-tools` |
| Fedora | `sudo dnf install pkgconf-pkg-config alsa-lib-devel systemd-devel dbus-devel libxkbcommon-devel wayland-devel mesa-vulkan-drivers vulkan-tools` |
| Arch | `sudo pacman -S pkgconf alsa-lib systemd-libs dbus libxkbcommon wayland vulkan-icd-loader vulkan-tools` |

To run a game without a display (a server, CI), also install `xvfb` and start it under `xvfb-run`.

## 3. Build the tools

From the engine folder:

```sh,walkthrough=install
cargo build --release -p regia_cli -p regia_editor
export PATH="$PWD/target/release:$PATH"
```

The first build takes a while (the whole engine, optimized). The `export` line only lasts for this
terminal: add it to your shell profile (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`) with the absolute path of the
engine folder in place of `$PWD`, so every new terminal finds `regia`. If you set
`CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, the programs are in `$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/release` instead of `target/release`.

On Windows, in PowerShell, the same steps are (Windows 10 and later include `tar`):

```powershell
tar -xzf regia-engine-<version>.tar.gz
cd regia-engine-<version>
cargo build --release -p regia_cli -p regia_editor
$env:Path = "$PWD\target\release;$env:Path"
```

and the folder goes into the user `Path` (Settings → System → About → Advanced system settings →
Environment Variables) to last.

This produces the two programs you use (plus `regia-hot-host`, a scripted hot-reload host the
engine's own tests drive, and `regia-ext-host`, a scripted extension host for the dynamic-extension
tests):

| Program | What it is |
|---|---|
| `regia` | The command-line tool: create projects, cook, package, preview assets, run the MCP server, call the agent protocol ([CLI reference](book/reference/cli.md)) |
| `regia-editor` | The editor ([Editor tour](book/start/editor-tour.md)) |

Check that the engine folder is complete and unmodified against the release manifest
(`regia-engine.release.ron`; a git checkout has none, so skip this there):

```sh,walkthrough=verify
regia engine verify .
```

It reports a missing or changed file as an error and an extra file (your own notes, say) as a
warning; `target/` is ignored.

## 4. Check the machine

For desktop development on Linux (on Windows, `--platform windows`):

```sh,walkthrough=doctor
regia doctor --platform linux
```

Plain `regia doctor` also checks the Android tools of § 5, so on a machine without them it reports
those as failures; run it once you have set up Android.

`regia doctor` checks Rust, cargo, rustup, `cargo-ndk`, Vulkan and, for Android, the SDK, the
NDK, a JDK 17+, Gradle, `adb` and the Rust Android targets. Each failed check prints the command
that fixes it. `--platform linux|windows|android|macos|deck|gpu|all` narrows or widens the check
(`windows` on Linux checks the cross-build tools: cargo-xwin, the MSVC target, clang-cl; `deck` checks
cargo-zigbuild and zig); `--project DIR` uses that project's `rust-toolchain.toml`; `--json` prints the checks
for scripts and agents ([Toolchain doctor](book/agents/doctor.md)). Run it again after each fix until it reports no
failures.

## 5. Android (optional)

You only need this to ship on Android. The editor itself is desktop-only.

1. Add the Rust targets: `rustup target add aarch64-linux-android x86_64-linux-android`.
2. Install the Android SDK command-line tools and set `ANDROID_HOME`; install an NDK (r27 or
   newer) with `sdkmanager` and set `ANDROID_NDK_HOME` if it is not under the SDK.
3. Install a JDK 17+ and Gradle (the packager generates a small Gradle project around your game's
   `cdylib`).
4. `cargo install cargo-ndk`.
5. Connect a device with USB debugging on; `adb devices` should list it.

`regia doctor --platform android` verifies all of it. Packaging and installing on a device are
covered in [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md).

## 6. Windows notes

Windows builds need the MSVC toolchain (Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload). The
engine is developed on Linux and verified on Windows in a virtual machine; both are supported
targets, and every change is built for Windows.

## 7. Optional tools

| Tool | Used for |
|---|---|
| `mdbook` | Building this manual as a multi-page website (`cargo xtask manual`) |
| Tracy | The `tracy` feature of `regia_core` streams profiling spans to it ([Profiling](book/systems/profiling.md)) |
| `steamcmd` | `regia steam upload` ([Steam](book/user-guide/steam.md)) |
| `jq` | Handy for scripting `regia agent call` output |

Next: [create your first project](book/getting-started.md).

# Your first project

<!-- Steps 1 to 5 run as written in crates/regia_cli/tests/getting_started_walkthrough.rs: keep every command, the Cargo.toml fence and the lib.rs fence runnable. -->

Two shorter paths sit beside this walkthrough. [Quickstart for a person](book/start/quickstart-human.md)
goes from a built toolchain to a running game. [Quickstart for an agent](book/start/quickstart-agent.md)
connects to a project and makes one call. This chapter is the longer tour, and its commands are
the ones the engine's test runs.

This chapter creates a project, runs it, puts something on screen, makes it move, opens it in
the editor and takes a screenshot through the agent protocol. It assumes the tools from
[Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md) are on your `PATH`.

## 1. Create the project

Open a terminal in the folder that should hold your projects (your home folder will do; not inside
the engine folder) and run:

```sh,walkthrough=new,template=blank
regia new "My Game"
```

`regia new <name>` writes a Cargo workspace in a new directory named after the snake_case form
of the name, here `my_game`, and prints its path (`--path DIR` chooses the parent directory; an
existing empty folder of that name is used, one with anything in it is refused). Letters and digits
are kept, spaces and dashes become `_`, other characters are dropped. A name that starts with a
digit, is a Rust or Java reserved word (the name is also the Android application id), or is a
Windows device name (`con`, `nul`, `com1`, `lpt1`...) is refused; the editor's project browser uses
the same rule. Pick a template with `--template`:

| Template | What you get |
|---|---|
| `blank` (default; `empty` is the same template) | An empty game plugin and a startup level with two entities. |
| `third_person` | A playable third-person game: rapier character movement, a boom camera, a procedural walking body with foot placement, coins, a three-hit sword combo against three enemies, death and respawn, a title screen with a settings menu, an Esc pause menu, procedural sound, quicksave on F5 and quickload on F9, and agent-protocol smoke tests. [A tour of the template](book/user-guide/third-person-template.md). |
| `first_person` | A first-person starter: WASD and mouse look, a crosshair, a gate and a button you use with E (with a prompt), a pause menu with a settings panel, a controls screen, quicksave, and agent-protocol smoke tests. [A tour of the template](book/user-guide/first-person-template.md). |
| `top_down` | A top-down starter: click or stick movement, a fixed-angle overhead camera (Q and E turn it), an enemy that walks a navmesh under a behavior tree with a health bar, an attack, quicksave on F5 and quickload on F9, and agent-protocol smoke tests. [A tour of the template](book/user-guide/top-down-template.md). |
| `quick` | One crate and one `main.rs`: the shortest start ([Quick start](book/user-guide/quick-start.md)). |
| `net-game` | A networked game: a dedicated server and a client of one shared simulation ([Networked game](book/tutorials/networked-game.md)). |

[Which template shows what](book/user-guide/project-templates.md) compares them side by side.

For example, a first-person and a top-down starter:

```sh,walkthrough=new,template=first_person
regia new "Rooftop Run" --template first_person
```

```sh,walkthrough=new,template=top_down
regia new "Garden Patrol" --template top_down
```

The editor's project browser and the `editor.new_project` agent method create the same
templates except `quick`.

The generated `game/Cargo.toml` depends on the engine by path (the engine checkout your
`regia` binary runs from), so `cargo` always builds your game against exactly that engine. If you move
the engine, update the path. [Project structure](book/user-guide/project-structure.md) describes every
file; the ones you need now are:

- `game/src/lib.rs`: your gameplay, a `Plugin` named `Game`;
- `launcher/src/main.rs`: the desktop entry point, which calls `regia::run_with(my_game::Game, ...)`
  (with `--exit-after-frames N` it quits after N frames, for smoke runs);
- `Regia.toml`: the project manifest;
- `assets/levels/main.level.ron`: the startup level the editor opens.

## 2. Run it

```console
$ cd my_game
$ regia run
```

`regia run` cooks the assets, builds the launcher and starts it (`regia run --dev` also reloads
assets you save while it runs); `cargo run -p my_game_launcher` builds and runs it without the
cook. The `<name>_launcher` crate comes with the `blank`, `first_person`, `third_person` and
`top_down` templates; a `quick` app has none (use plain `cargo build` and `cargo run`), and a
`net_game` project builds with plain `cargo build` and runs its `<name>_server` and `<name>_client`
crates as its `README.md` says.

The first build compiles the engine, which takes a few minutes; later builds only compile your
crates. A window opens. It is empty: the blank `Game` plugin adds no systems, there is no camera
and nothing to draw. `regia::run` has already set up logging, the window, input, the renderer,
the asset server, the runtime UI and the agent-protocol server (`DefaultPlugins`); everything
else comes from your plugin.

## 3. Put something on screen

To see anything you need three things: a camera, something to draw and some light. The renderer
reads them from components on entities. Add the engine crates the game will use to
`game/Cargo.toml`, next to the existing `regia` line. The paths below are an example: copy the path
prefix (everything before `/crates/regia`) from the `regia` line `regia new` wrote, which points at
your engine folder:

```toml
[dependencies]
regia = { path = "../../regia/crates/regia" }
regia_core = { path = "../../regia/crates/regia_core" }
regia_render = { path = "../../regia/crates/regia_render" }
regia_scene = { path = "../../regia/crates/regia_scene" }
```

Then replace `game/src/lib.rs` with:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_render::{Camera, CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, DirectionalLight, MeshRenderer, box_mesh};
use regia_scene::Transform;

/// The game plugin the launcher runs.
pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        // Transform propagation, levels and prefabs. `DefaultPlugins` does not add it.
        app.add_plugins(regia_scene::ScenePlugin)
            .add_systems(Startup, setup);
    }
}

/// Spawns a camera, a sun and a box.
fn setup(mut commands: Commands) {
    // The camera looks down its local -Z axis: stand back and tilt down a little.
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Camera"),
        Transform {
            translation: Vec3::new(0.0, 1.5, 5.0),
            rotation: Quat::from_rotation_x(-0.25),
            ..Transform::default()
        },
        Camera::default(),
    ));

    // A noon sun: 100 000 lux, travelling down and slightly forward.
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Sun"),
        DirectionalLight {
            direction: [0.3, -1.0, -0.4],
            color: [1.0, 0.98, 0.95],
            illuminance: 100_000.0,
            cast_shadows: true,
            static_shadow: false,
        },
    ));

    // A one-meter box with an orange material.
    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Box"),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 0.5, 0.0)),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.9, 0.45, 0.15, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.6,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));
}
```

Close the window and run it again:

```console
$ regia run
```

You see an orange box under a blue procedural sky. The sky also lights
the scene (image-based lighting); the sun adds direct light and casts the box's shadow (this
scene has no ground, so there is nothing for the shadow to fall on yet); auto exposure picks the
brightness. [Rendering](book/user-guide/rendering.md) and [The default look](book/user-guide/default-look.md)
explain each part.

A few things to notice:

- **Systems are plain functions.** `setup` takes `Commands`, a queue of world changes that apply
  after the system runs. Registering it in `Startup` runs it once before the first frame.
- **Components are plain structs.** `Transform`, `Camera`, `DirectionalLight` and
  `MeshRenderer` are components; an entity is the tuple you spawn.
- **`Transform` brings `GlobalTransform` with it** (a required component), which the renderer
  reads; `ScenePlugin` keeps it up to date every frame.
- **`Name`** here is the ECS name from `regia::prelude`, the one the agent protocol searches
  (step 5). Level files store `regia_scene::components::Name`; see
  [Scenes](book/user-guide/scenes.md#two-name-components).
- **Meshes and materials are shared.** `MeshRenderer` holds `Arc`s; the GPU upload is cached by
  the `Arc`'s identity, so a thousand boxes sharing one mesh upload it once.

## 4. Make it move

Add a component that marks things to spin, and a system that runs every frame:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::Quat;
use regia_scene::Transform;

/// Spins its entity around the vertical axis.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct Spin {
    /// Radians per second.
    pub speed: f32,
}

fn spin(time: Res<Time>, mut query: Query<(&Spin, &mut Transform)>) {
    for (spin, mut transform) in &mut query {
        transform.rotation = Quat::from_rotation_y(spin.speed * time.delta_secs()) * transform.rotation;
    }
}

pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(regia_scene::ScenePlugin)
            .register_type::<Spin>()
            .add_systems(Update, spin);
    }
}
```

Insert `Spin { speed: 1.0 }` into the box's tuple in `setup`. `Query<(&Spin, &mut Transform)>`
visits every entity that has both components; `Res<Time>` is the frame clock. Deriving `Reflect`
and calling `register_type` makes `Spin` visible to the editor's inspector, to save games, to hot
reload and to the agent protocol. [The ECS](book/fundamentals/ecs.md) and
[Reflection](book/fundamentals/reflection.md) cover these in depth.

## 5. Look at it from an agent

While the launcher runs, open a second terminal in the project directory:

```console
$ regia agent call agent.hello
$ regia agent call scene.query_entities '{"name":"Box"}'
$ regia agent call seeing.screenshot --out shot.png
$ regia agent call quit.request
```

The last call closes the game as closing its window would, and `regia run` returns.

A dev build of every Regia Engine game runs the agent-protocol server. The game writes its endpoint
and a bearer token to `.regia/agent/` in the project, and `regia agent call` reads them. The
same calls are what an AI agent makes through `regia mcp`. See
[Agent protocol and MCP](book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md).

## 6. Open it in the editor

```console
$ regia-editor --project .
```

The editor opens the startup level from `Regia.toml` (`levels/main.level.ron`) in its own
edit world: a ground and a marker entity with transforms. The [editor tour](book/start/editor-tour.md)
walks through the panels. Your `setup` system spawns its entities at runtime, so they are not in
the level file; to author content in the editor, create entities there and save the level, then
load that level from your game ([Scenes](book/user-guide/scenes.md)).

## 7. Package it

From the project folder:

```sh,walkthrough=package
regia package --platform linux
```

`regia package` cooks the project's assets into `.fpak` archives, builds the launcher and
writes `dist/linux/<id>-linux.tar.gz`, a self-contained build that runs from any directory.
`--platform windows` and `--platform android` work the same way. See
[Running and iterating](book/start/running.md) and [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md).

## Where next

- [Editor tour](book/start/editor-tour.md) and [Running and iterating](book/start/running.md) finish the
  getting-started section; [Checking your game with an agent](book/start/first-agent-check.md) runs a
  First Person project and checks it from a second terminal.
- [Fundamentals](book/fundamentals/ecs.md) explains the concepts this chapter used.
- [Tutorial: a third-person game](book/tutorials/third-person.md) builds a playable game.

# Introduction

The Regia Engine Manual. It covers making a game with Regia Engine, from installing the tools to shipping
a packaged build. It starts with the ideas the engine is built on, walks through a first project,
explains each fundamental concept and every engine system in turn, then builds a small 3D game
step by step. The reference chapters at the end list the command-line tools, the content formats,
the render settings and every agent-protocol method.

## Where to start

<!-- index: Where to start -->

Three doors. Each one is a short list. The [feature catalog](book/manual/catalog.md) says whether a
feature is in this version. The [glossary](book/manual/glossary.md) and the [index](book/manual/index.md)
are the map of terms.

- **A person making a game.** [Install the tools](book/start/install.md), follow the
  [quickstart](book/start/quickstart-human.md) through a running game, then the longer
  [first project](book/getting-started.md) and the [editor tour](book/start/editor-tour.md).
- **A programmer linking the crates.** The crate table under
  [What Regia Engine is](#what-regia-engine-is), then
  [App, plugins and schedules](book/fundamentals/app-and-plugins.md) and
  [The ECS](book/fundamentals/ecs.md). A game is a Rust crate that path-depends on this checkout.
- **An agent driving a project.** The [agent quickstart](book/start/quickstart-agent.md) (stdio MCP,
  the HTTP option, and one worked call), then
  [Agent protocol and MCP](book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md) and the
  [method reference](book/reference/agent-methods.md).

## What Regia Engine is

Regia Engine is a 3D game engine written entirely in Rust. A game is a Rust crate: you write your
gameplay as ECS systems and components, author levels, prefabs, materials and UI as text files,
and the engine supplies the rest: a window and input on every platform, a physically based
renderer, physics, animation, audio, runtime UI, navigation, a gameplay framework, an editor with
play-in-editor and code hot reload, and the tooling to cook and package the result.

The engine is built as a set of crates around an Entity Component System (`bevy_ecs`, behind
Regia Engine's own `regia_ecs` facade). The pieces you will meet most often:

| Crate | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| `regia` | The umbrella: `regia::run`, `DefaultPlugins`, the prelude |
| `regia_app` | `App`, `Plugin`, schedules, time, the fixed timestep |
| `regia_scene` | `Transform`, hierarchy, levels and prefabs |
| `regia_render` | The renderer, cameras, lights, render profiles |
| `regia_asset` | The asset server, cooked data, `.fpak` archives |
| `regia_framework` | Players, characters, cameras, game rules, scripts, settings, save games, the sim bridge |
| `regia_physics` | Rigid bodies, colliders, queries (rapier underneath) |
| `regia_animation`, `regia_audio`, `regia_ui`, `regia_input` | Animation, audio, runtime UI, input |
| `regia_terrain`, `regia_vfx`, `regia_matgraph` | Terrain and scatter, particles and decals, material graphs |
| `regia_nav`, `regia_ai` | Navmeshes and pathfinding, behavior trees |
| `regia_agent` | The agent protocol server |
| `regia_editor`, `regia_cli` | The editor (`regia-editor`) and the command-line tool (`regia`) |

## Design goals

- **Agent-native.** Every capability a human has in the editor is also available to an AI agent
  through a typed, documented, testable protocol (JSON-RPC, and MCP through `regia mcp`).
  Agents query and edit the scene, load assets, take screenshots, step the simulation, inject
  input and assert on the result. Every agent change is undoable, attributed and audited.
  Everything the engine stores is diffable text, so agent edits review like code. See
  [Agent protocol and MCP](book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md).
- **Rust first.** Engine, editor, tools and gameplay are all Rust: behavior is Rust code that
  hot reloads into the running editor ([Hot reload](book/user-guide/hot-reload.md)). The one scripting
  option is opt-in: sandboxed Lua 5.1 mods behind the `lua` feature, for games that want
  player-made content ([Lua mods](book/agents/lua-mods.md)). Shaders are WGSL.
- **Data you can read.** Levels, prefabs, materials, UI, animation graphs, VFX and audio cues are
  canonical RON. Saving an unchanged file is byte-identical, so `git diff` shows exactly what
  changed. These formats are versioned and frozen: a format only changes together with a
  migrator ([Content formats](book/reference/formats.md)).
- **One architecture from phones to high-end desktops.** Quality scales through render
  profiles, from Mobile Low to Desktop Ultra plus a Steam Deck profile, not through separate
  renderers ([Render profiles](book/reference/render-profiles.md)).
- **Physically based by default.** Lights are in lux and candela, the camera is exposed in EV100,
  the display transform is AgX. Get the light levels right and the image follows
  ([The default look](book/user-guide/default-look.md)).
- **Deterministic when you need it.** A fixed timestep, manual time stepping and an offscreen
  renderer make two runs produce byte-identical screenshots, which is how the engine's own
  golden-image tests and your game's agent tests work.
- **Ships a real game.** Regia Engine's first title is *Direct Order 27*, which drives a large part of
  the feature set and its priorities: terrain, atmosphere and the sim bridge exist because that
  game needs them.

## Platforms

| Platform | Runtime | Editor | Graphics backend |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linux x86_64 (Wayland and X11), including Steam Deck | yes | yes | Vulkan |
| Windows 10/11 x86_64 | yes | yes | DX12 or Vulkan |
| Android arm64-v8a | yes | no | Vulkan |
| macOS | builds and tests on Metal, testing only: no release build ([macOS](book/user-guide/macos.md)) | not verified | Metal |

The renderer runs on `wgpu`; it never falls back to OpenGL. Every engine change is built for
Linux, Windows and Android. Packaging produces a Linux `tar.gz`, a Windows `zip`, and an Android
APK or AAB, plus a Steam depot layout ([Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md)).

## How this manual is organized

1. **Getting started**: install the tools, create a project, tour the editor, run and package
   your game. The two quickstarts are the short paths; the first-project chapter is the longer tour.
2. **Using this manual**: the [feature catalog](book/manual/catalog.md), the
   [glossary](book/manual/glossary.md), the [index](book/manual/index.md),
   [troubleshooting](book/manual/troubleshooting.md), the [FAQ](book/manual/faq.md),
   [known limits](book/manual/known-issues.md), [upgrade notes](book/manual/upgrade.md), and
   [how to print](book/manual/print.md).
3. **Fundamentals**: the ECS, apps and plugins, scenes, assets and the cook, reflection, input.
   Read these in order; every later chapter assumes them.
4. **Engine systems**: one chapter per system: rendering, materials, terrain, lighting, VFX,
   physics, animation, audio, UI, navigation and AI, the gameplay framework, the sim bridge, hot
   reload, the editor, the agent protocol, packaging, and profiling.
5. **Tutorials**: build a small third-person game from the template, then study the arena sample
   (bots, weapons, match rules) and test it through the agent protocol.
6. **Reference**: CLI, content formats with their versions and migrators, render settings, and
   every agent method.
7. **Agent guide**: task-oriented pages for AI agents driving the protocol. The same pages are
   the exact method parameters and examples.

Every code block marked `rust` in this book is compiled against the engine by
`cargo xtask book-check`, and every RON block that names a format (`ron,material`, `ron,ui`, …)
is parsed by that format's real loader. The same check runs `agent-coverage`: every method the
agent dispatcher registers has a schema entry, a bundled guide topic, a row in the coverage map,
a mention on its guide page, and a test that calls it. Features that are specified but not built yet are marked
**planned** with the specification section that describes them.

## Conventions used here

- `console` blocks show shell commands, with `$` before each command you type.
- Paths such as `docs/specs/13-renderer.md` refer to the engine repository; `book/` pages link to
  each other.
- Component names are nouns (`RigidBody`, `PointLight`), systems are verb phrases
  (`propagate_transforms`), plugins end in `Plugin`.
- Units are SI: meters, seconds, kilograms, radians in code (degrees only where a field says so),
  lux for illuminance, EV100 for exposure.

## Getting help

The engine's specifications live under `docs/specs/`, design decisions in `docs/decisions.md`,
and the rationale for each algorithm, with its public source, in `docs/provenance.md`. When the
manual and the code disagree, the code wins. File the page.

# Quickstart for a person

<!-- index: Quickstart -->

Install the tools, create a project, and run it. The longer tour, with a moving object, the editor
and a screenshot, is [Your first project](book/getting-started.md). Installing Rust, a GPU driver and
the system packages is [Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md). An assistant that can run commands
can follow [Set up with your AI assistant](book/start/assistant-setup.md) instead of typing these steps.

## 1. Build the tools

From the engine folder (the unpacked release, or a git checkout):

```console
$ cargo build --release -p regia_cli -p regia_editor
$ export PATH="$PWD/target/release:$PATH"
```

The first build compiles the engine. It takes a while. The `export` line lasts for this terminal.
To keep `regia` on your `PATH`, put the absolute path of `target/release` in your shell profile.
If `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` is set, the programs are in `$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/release`.

On Windows, in PowerShell, the path line is `$env:Path = "$PWD\target\release;$env:Path"`. The
rest of [Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md) covers the toolchain pin, Vulkan or DX12, and the
Linux packages.

## 2. Create a project

In the folder that should hold your projects (not inside the engine folder):

```console
$ regia new "My Game"
$ cd my_game
```

`regia new` writes a Cargo workspace in `my_game/` and prints that path. The default template is
`blank`: an empty game plugin and a startup level with two entities. Other templates are
`--template first_person`, `third_person`, `top_down`, `quick` and `net-game`. The table and the
naming rules are in [Your first project](book/getting-started.md).

## 3. Run it

```console
$ regia run
```

`regia run` cooks the project's assets and starts the game in a window. Leave that terminal alone
until you close the window. The command returns when the game exits.

To open the same project in the editor, from the parent of `my_game`:

```console
$ regia-editor --project my_game
```

## Finished check

The game window opens on the startup level. Closing the window ends `regia run` with status 0.
If the window never appears, use [Troubleshooting](book/manual/troubleshooting.md) and
[Checking your machine (doctor)](book/user-guide/doctor.md).

## Where next

- [Your first project](book/getting-started.md): put something on screen, move it, open the editor,
  take a screenshot.
- [Editor tour](book/start/editor-tour.md) and [Running and iterating](book/start/running.md).
- [Feature catalog](book/manual/catalog.md): whether a feature is in this version.

# Quickstart for an agent

<!-- index: agent.hello -->
<!-- index: MCP -->

Connect to a project and make one call. The tools have to be on your `PATH`
([Quickstart for a person](book/start/quickstart-human.md), [Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md)). The longer
checked loop (a first-person project, a condition, a screenshot, quit) is
[Checking your game with an agent](book/start/first-agent-check.md). The protocol itself is
[Agent protocol and MCP](book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md).

A running app writes its endpoint and a per-run token under `<project>/.regia/agent/`.
`regia agent call` and `regia mcp` read those files. Nothing here sends a credential to a third
party.

## Stdio MCP

Start the game (`regia run` in the project) or the editor, and leave it running. In another
terminal:

```console
$ regia mcp --project my_game --attach
```

`regia mcp` speaks MCP on standard input and output: one tool per protocol method, plus `regia://`
resources. `--attach` uses the app that is already running.

When no app is running, a headless editor (no window, offscreen views) is enough for scene edits:

```console
$ regia editor --headless --project my_game
$ regia mcp --headless --project my_game
```

`regia editor --headless` prints a `{"event":"ready"}` line when it listens.
`regia mcp --headless` starts that editor if nothing answers, and stops it when the MCP process
ends. See [Headless editor](book/agents/headless-editor.md).

## HTTP

A client that cannot spawn a process uses the same tools over loopback HTTP:

```console
$ regia mcp --project my_game --http
$ regia mcp token --project my_game
$ regia mcp token --project my_game --url
```

The token command prints the bearer token, then the loopback URL. Read them that way. Do not parse
`.regia/agent/mcp_http.json` yourself: a project folder is not trusted. The worked HTTP session
(initialize, `protocolVersion` `2025-06-18`, the session header) is
[MCP over HTTP](book/agents/mcp-http.md). Bind stays on `127.0.0.1` unless you pass `--allow-remote`.

## One worked call

With `regia run` or the editor still running, from a second terminal in the project directory:

```console
$ regia agent call agent.hello
```

`agent.hello` is the connect check. The result names the protocol version (`protocol`), the
engine version, the app, the operating system, the process id, and the methods the app answers.
The project path and the token's permission list are `project.info`. A line that says it cannot
connect means the app is not listening yet:
wait and run the same command again.

The same call is an MCP tool once `regia mcp` is attached. The tool name is the method's MCP name
from [Agent methods](book/reference/agent-methods.md).

## Finished check

`agent.hello` returns a result and does not say it cannot connect. If the code in
`error.data.code` is set, the meaning and the fix are on
[Errors](book/agents/protocol.md#errors) and in the method's row of
[Agent methods](book/reference/agent-methods.md). `errors.explain` returns the long form. Do not
invent a code: the schema is the list.

## Where next

- [Checking your game with an agent](book/start/first-agent-check.md): `play.wait_until`, `play.expect`,
  `seeing.screenshot`, `quit.request`.
- [Safety](book/agents/safety.md): which methods mutate, and `.regia/agent.toml`.
- [Feature catalog](book/manual/catalog.md) before calling a method for a feature this version
  marks partial.

# Crates and imports

A quick map of where things live, for when you know what you want and need the `use` line. The
concepts behind it are in [The ECS](book/fundamentals/ecs.md) and
[App, plugins and schedules](book/fundamentals/app-and-plugins.md).

## The shape of a Regia Engine game

A game is a Rust plugin registered into the engine's `App`:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

struct MyGame;

impl Plugin for MyGame {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_systems(Startup, spawn_player)
            .add_systems(Update, move_camera);
    }
}

// Your systems: `spawn_player` runs once at startup, `move_camera` every frame.
fn spawn_player() {}
fn move_camera() {}

fn main() {
    regia::run(MyGame);
}
```

`regia::run` adds `DefaultPlugins` — platform (window, lifecycle, input messages), renderer,
assets, audio, telemetry, and (with the `ui`/`agent` features) the runtime UI and the agent
protocol server — before your plugin. Everything else is components, resources, systems and assets.

## Imports

`regia::prelude` re-exports the app, ECS, reflection and platform preludes (`App`, `Plugin`,
`Commands`, `Query`, `Res`, schedules, `Time`, window and input message types, the VFS, `tracing`
macros) and, with the `ui` feature, the runtime UI prelude. The umbrella crate also re-exports
some crates as modules: `regia::app`, `regia::core`, `regia::ecs`, `regia::framework`,
`regia::physics`, `regia::platform` and `regia::world`; with the `client` feature (on by default)
`regia::audio`, `regia::render`, `regia::telemetry` and `regia::two_d`; with the `server` feature
`regia::ai` and `regia::nav`; and with their own features `regia::agent`, `regia::crash`,
`regia::fluid`, `regia::lua`, `regia::media`, `regia::net`, `regia::procgen`, `regia::quick`,
`regia::steam`, `regia::ui` and `regia::xr`. Every other area is its own crate that your game depends on by
path (as the templates do), most with a prelude:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;         // App, Plugin, Commands, Query, Res, schedules, platform, tracing
use regia_scene::prelude::*;   // Transform, Name, LevelManager, PrefabCommands, …
use regia_render::{MeshRenderer, PointLight, Camera};   // renderer has no prelude
use regia_framework::prelude::*;   // GamePlugin, PlayerManager, Character, GameRules, Script, …
use regia_input::prelude::*;   // InputConfig, InputPlugin, Actions
use regia_audio::prelude::*;   // AudioPlugin, Audio, …
use regia_animation::prelude::*;   // Animator, AnimationClip, …
use regia_physics::{RigidBody, ColliderShape, PhysicsQuery};   // physics has no prelude
use regia_vfx::{VfxPlugin, VfxRuntimePlugin, SpawnEffect};       // particles, decals
use regia_nav::{NavPlugin, NavMesh, NavAgent};                   // navigation
use regia_ai::{AiPlugin, BehaviorTree, Blackboard};              // behavior trees
use regia_matgraph::{MaterialGraph, MaterialGraphPlugin};        // material graphs
```

## The model

- **Entity** — a handle to a bundle of **components** (data). `Transform`, `Name`, `MeshRenderer`,
  `PointLight`, `RigidBody`, `Character`…
- **System** — a function that runs each frame (or on a schedule) and reads/writes components.
- **Resource** — singleton state (`Time`, `GameSettings`, `AssetServer`, `ClearColor`).
- **Asset** — a cooked file loaded through the `AssetServer` (mesh, texture, material, level,
  prefab, audio…).
- **Level / Prefab** — saved scenes as canonical RON (`.level.ron`, `.prefab.ron`).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/quick-start.md -->
# Quick start: a game in one file

*Prerequisites: a built engine checkout ([getting started](book/getting-started.md)). Reading time:
8 minutes.*

`regia::quick` is the shortest path from nothing to something on screen: one crate, one
`main.rs`, three functions. It runs on the full engine (the same renderer, input, agent protocol
and hot reload), so a quick app can grow into a full project without a rewrite
([Sketch → App → systems → project](book/user-guide/sketch-to-project.md)).

## Create it

From the folder that holds your projects:

```sh,walkthrough=new,template=quick
regia new "Paddle Ball" --template quick
cd paddle_ball
```

Then build and run it:

```console
$ cargo run
```

The template is a small paddle game. Its `src/main.rs` is the whole game. In a script or without a
display (under `xvfb-run -a`), let it run five frames and exit:

```sh,walkthrough=smoke,template=quick
cargo run -- --exit-after-frames 5
```

A quick app is one Cargo crate with no `Regia.toml`, no `launcher/` and no assets to cook:
`regia run` and `regia package` need a project folder and stop with an error, and `regia cook` and
`regia upgrade-project` run but have nothing to do. A build you can hand to someone is the release
binary:

```sh,walkthrough=package,template=quick
cargo build --release
```

It is `target/release/paddle_ball` (or under `$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/release` when you set it), and it
runs from any folder. When you want packaging, cooked assets or Android, move to a full project
([Sketch → App → systems → project](book/user-guide/sketch-to-project.md)).

## The three functions

```rust
use regia::quick::prelude::*;

#[derive(Reflect, Default)]
struct Model {
    ball: Vec2,
    velocity: Vec2,
}

fn main() {
    regia::quick::app(model).update(update).view(view).title("Bounce").run();
}

/// Runs once, when the app is built. Returns the state.
fn model(_q: &Quick) -> Model {
    Model { velocity: Vec2::new(200.0, 150.0), ..Model::default() }
}

/// Runs every frame: input and time in, state out.
fn update(q: &Quick, m: &mut Model) {
    let half = q.window_size() / 2.0;
    m.ball += m.velocity * q.delta();
    if m.ball.x.abs() > half.x {
        m.velocity.x = -m.velocity.x;
    }
    if m.ball.y.abs() > half.y {
        m.velocity.y = -m.velocity.y;
    }
    if q.key_pressed("Space") {
        m.velocity *= 1.2;
    }
}

/// Runs every frame after `update`: draws the state.
fn view(q: &Quick, m: &Model) {
    let draw = q.draw();
    draw.background().color(Color::BLACK);
    draw.ellipse().xy(m.ball).radius(12.0).color(Color::WHITE);
    draw.text(&format!("speed {:.0}", m.velocity.length())).y(q.window_size().y / 2.0 - 30.0);
}
```

- **`model`** builds the state. The model is a plain struct with `#[derive(Reflect)]`: the engine
  stores it as the resource `Model<YourModel>`, hot reload carries it across code edits, and agents
  can read it (`QuickModel`, see the [agent guide](book/agents/quick-app.md)). Fields that cannot be
  reflected (a random generator, a cache) take `#[reflect(ignore)]` and a `Default`.
- **`update`** changes the state. It gets the model mutably and the `Quick` handle read-only.
- **`view`** draws the state. It only reads the model.
- Any of the three may be a closure: `.update(|q: &Quick, m: &mut Model| m.ball.x += 1.0)`.

No model at all? Use a sketch: `regia::quick::sketch(|q: &Quick| { /* draw */ }).run()`.

## The `Quick` handle

| Call | Gives |
|---|---|
| `q.time()`, `q.delta()`, `q.frame()` | Seconds since start, seconds since the last frame, frame number |
| `q.key_down("ArrowLeft")`, `q.key_pressed("Space")`, `q.key_released(..)` | Keys by physical name (`KeyW`, `Space`, `ArrowUp`, `Enter`, `Digit1`, `ShiftLeft`, …) |
| `q.mouse()`, `q.mouse_down(MouseButton::Left)`, `q.mouse_delta()`, `q.mouse_wheel()` | The cursor in drawing coordinates, buttons, raw motion, wheel lines |
| `q.touches()` | Fingers in drawing coordinates with their phase (Android, touch screens) |
| `q.window_rect()`, `q.window_size()` | The window in drawing coordinates (center origin) |
| `q.draw()` | 2D drawing over the frame: `rect`, `ellipse`, `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `tri`, `quad`, `arrow`, `mesh`, `text` ([quick draw](book/agents/quick-draw.md)) |
| `q.draw_3d()`, `q.camera_3d(eye, target)` | Lit 3D primitives (`cube`, `sphere`, `cylinder`, `cone`, `plane`, `grid`, `line`, `cube_wires`) and the camera that looks at them |
| `q.grab_cursor(true)` | Lock and hide the cursor for mouse look |
| `q.save_frame("shots/frame.png")` | Save the next presented frame as a PNG |
| `q.load_bytes("levels/one.txt")` | Read a file through the VFS on the IO pool; poll the request in later frames (works for Android APK assets too) |
| `q.set_run_mode(..)`, `q.quit()` | Change the loop, exit |
| `q.commands(f)` | Anything else: `f` gets `Commands` to spawn entities or insert resources |

**Coordinates.** Drawing uses logical units with the origin at the window center, +X right and +Y
up. `q.mouse()` and `q.touches()` are already converted; `q.screen_to_world(..)` and
`q.world_to_screen(..)` convert raw window pixels.

## Run modes

| Mode | Builder | `update`/`view` run |
|---|---|---|
| `RunMode::Loop` (default) | — | Every frame |
| `RunMode::Wait` | `.wait()` | On the first frame and on frames with input or a resize; the last drawing stays on screen in between and the loop idles at 30 fps |
| `RunMode::LoopNTimes(n)` | `.loop_once()`, `.loop_ntimes(n)` | `n` times, then the drawing is frozen on screen and the loop idles at 10 fps; the window stays closable |

`LoopNTimes` suits generated images: draw once, `q.save_frame(..)`, look at it.

## Examples

`examples/quick/` has nine single-file games and demos (ported from macroquad's examples):

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| `basic_shapes` | A sketch: line, rectangle, circle, text |
| `input_touch` | Touches by phase (mouse on desktop) |
| `snake` | Grid game, key steering, restart |
| `arkanoid` | A playfield in its own units scaled to the window |
| `asteroids` | Frame-rate-independent motion, wrap-around, outlines |
| `life` | Conway's Game of Life on a cell grid |
| `platformer` | Tile collision with pixel-stepped movement and a moving platform |
| `first_person` | `draw_3d`, `camera_3d`, mouse look, a 2D HUD over 3D |
| `destruction` | A brick wall and a plank bridge broken by a hit script (run with `--features quick`) |

Run one with `cargo run -p regia --example snake`.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/sketch-to-project.md -->
# Sketch → App → systems → project

*Prerequisites: [quick start](book/user-guide/quick-start.md). Reading time: 7 minutes.*

A Regia Engine game can start as ten lines and grow into a full project. There are four rungs, and each
one keeps the code of the rung before it. Move up when the current rung starts to hurt, not before.

| Rung | You write | Move up when |
|---|---|---|
| **Sketch** | One `view` function | You need state that lasts between frames |
| **App** | `model`, `update`, `view` | `update` is long and does unrelated things, or you want engine features (physics, audio, scenes) |
| **Systems** | Ordinary ECS systems, still using `Quick` | You want levels made in the editor, several crates, Android packaging, or a team |
| **Project** | A `GamePlugin` in a project from `regia new` | — |

## 1. Sketch

A drawing that reacts to time and input, with no state of its own:

```rust
use regia::quick::prelude::*;

fn main() {
    regia::quick::sketch(|q: &Quick| {
        let draw = q.draw();
        draw.background().color(Color::BLACK);
        draw.ellipse().xy(q.mouse()).radius(20.0 + 10.0 * q.time().sin()).color(Color::WHITE);
    })
    .run();
}
```

## 2. App

State goes into a reflected model; `update` changes it and `view` draws it:

```rust
use regia::quick::prelude::*;

#[derive(Reflect, Default)]
struct Trail {
    points: Vec<Vec2>,
}

fn main() {
    regia::quick::app(|_q: &Quick| Trail::default())
        .update(|q: &Quick, t: &mut Trail| {
            t.points.push(q.mouse());
            if t.points.len() > 120 {
                t.points.remove(0);
            }
        })
        .view(|q: &Quick, t: &Trail| {
            q.draw().background().color(Color::BLACK);
            q.draw().polyline().weight(3.0).color(Color::WHITE).points(t.points.iter().copied());
        })
        .run();
}
```

The model is the resource `regia::quick::Model<Trail>`, so it is visible to the inspector and
agents and survives hot reload.

## 3. Systems

`Quick` is an ordinary system parameter. The functions you wrote for the app can be called from
normal systems, and normal systems can sit next to the quick app's `update` and `view`. Split
`update` into systems when it does several unrelated jobs:

```rust
use regia::quick::prelude::*;

#[derive(Reflect, Default)]
struct Game {
    score: u32,
    paused: bool,
}

/// The same signature as a quick `update`: usable from the app and from a system.
fn tick_score(q: &Quick, game: &mut Game) {
    if !game.paused && q.key_pressed("Space") {
        game.score += 1;
    }
}

/// A plain system that reads the quick model and runs after the quick app's chain.
fn pause_on_p(q: Quick, mut game: ResMut<Model<Game>>) {
    if q.key_pressed("KeyP") {
        game.model.paused = !game.model.paused;
    }
}

fn main() {
    regia::quick::app(|_q: &Quick| Game::default())
        .update(tick_score)
        .view(|q: &Quick, g: &Game| {
            q.draw().text(&format!("score {}", g.score));
        })
        .run();
}

/// To add the extra system, build the app yourself instead of calling `.run()`.
fn main_with_systems() {
    regia::run_with(regia::quick::QuickEngine, |app| {
        app.add_plugins(regia::quick::app(|_q: &Quick| Game::default()).update(tick_score))
            .add_systems(Update, pause_on_p.after(QuickSet));
    });
}
```

- The quick app's own systems are in `QuickSet` (in `Update`): plan the frame → `update` → `view`.
  Order your systems against it.
- `QuickEngine` adds what `.run()` adds around a quick app: the input layer and the quick draw layer.
- A test can drive the same function through a quick app and through a plain system and compare
  the results (`crates/regia_quick/tests/quick_in_system.rs`).

## 4. Project

When you want the editor, levels, hot reload while playing, several crates or an Android build,
create a project and move the code into its game crate:

```console
$ regia new "My Game" --template blank
```

Register the quick app from the game plugin. Everything else (editor play, hot reload, the Android
shell) loads the plugin the same way:

```rust
use regia::quick::prelude::*;
use regia_framework::game::GamePlugin;

#[derive(Reflect, Default)]
struct Game {
    score: u32,
}

pub struct MyGame;

impl GamePlugin for MyGame {
    fn register(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(
            regia::quick::app(|_q: &Quick| Game::default())
                .update(|q: &Quick, g: &mut Game| g.score += u32::from(q.key_pressed("Space")))
                .view(|q: &Quick, g: &Game| {
                    q.draw().text(&format!("score {}", g.score));
                }),
        );
    }
}
```

Export it with `regia_framework::export_game!(MyGame);` in the game crate (see
[hot reload](book/user-guide/hot-reload.md)). On a reload the model is snapshotted, the game library is swapped, the
builder runs `model` again, and the snapshot is applied over it, so the state carries over and the
new `update`/`view` code runs. A field you add to the model starts at its type's `Default`.

From here, entities, scenes, physics and the rest of the engine are available next to the quick
app. The quick app can shrink over time as systems take over its jobs.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/project-structure.md -->
# Project structure

<!-- index: Regia.toml | see: Project -->
<!-- index: Project -->
<!-- index: startup_level | see: Level -->

`regia new "My Game"` writes a Cargo workspace. This page describes what each part is for and the
files you will touch.

## Layout

```
my_game/
  Regia.toml                 project manifest (name, id, startup level, platforms)
  Cargo.toml                   workspace root (members: game, editor, launcher, android)
  game/                        your gameplay crate
    Cargo.toml                 path-depends on the engine checkout
    src/lib.rs                 the game plugin + `// REGIA:SCRIPTS` marker
    src/scripts/               project scripts (registered at the marker)
  launcher/                    desktop entry point (calls regia::run_with)
    build.rs                   Windows exe icon and version info (packaging guide)
  editor/                      hot-reload feature anchor (regia-editor uses it)
  android/                     the Android cdylib (regia::android_main!)
  assets/                      source assets, levels, prefabs, materials…
  config/                      engine config (physics layers, …)
  generators/                  procedural-content generators (specs/23 § 6)
```

`Regia.toml` is the manifest:

```toml
[project]
name = "My Game"
id = "com.regiaengine.my_game"
version = "0.1.0"
build_number = 1
engine = "0.2"
startup_level = "levels/main.level.ron"

[platforms.android]
min_sdk = 29
target_sdk = 35
abis = ["arm64-v8a"]
```

The `quick` template is different: one crate with a `src/main.rs`, no editor, launcher or android
crates ([Quick start](book/user-guide/quick-start.md)).

`startup_level` is the level the editor opens with the project. A running game loads its levels
itself (see [Scenes](book/user-guide/scenes.md#loading-a-level-from-your-game)); a running game does not read
`startup_level`. `regia run --level L` starts a dev run in level `L`.

## The game plugin

`game/src/lib.rs` is your gameplay. `Game` implements `Plugin`; scripts are registered at the
`// REGIA:SCRIPTS` marker (the editor's `editor.create_script` writes there):

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

struct MySystems;

impl Plugin for MySystems {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_systems(Update, tick);
    }
}

fn tick() {}

pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(MySystems);
    }
}

// REGIA:SCRIPTS
```

For hot reload, the game is a `GamePlugin` (not just a `Plugin`). Export the game type with
`regia_framework::export_game!(MyGame)`: the macro emits the two dylib symbols the editor
resolves — `regia_game_entry()`, the address of a `#[repr(C)]` table of the plugin's
`register` / `on_unload` / `on_load`, and the `REGIA_ABI_HASH: u64` static — so the editor can
hot-reload the game. A plain launcher runs the same plugin through the `GamePluginEntry(MyGame)`
adapter; see [Hot reload](book/user-guide/hot-reload.md) and `samples/hot_fixture`.

## Upgrading the engine

A project names the engine it targets in two places: `Regia.toml [project] engine` holds the release line (`"0.2"`,
or `"0.2.5"` for at least that patch), and the Cargo dependencies on `regia` and `regia_*` name one source. Run
`regia engine info --project my_game` to see both. Pick the source when you create the project:
`regia new my_game --engine-source path:/opt/regia-engine-0.2.5` (also `path:vendor/regia-engine-0.2.5` for a copy
inside the project, `git:<url>#<tag>` and `registry:<name>[@<version>]`).

To move to a new release, use that release's `regia`. Without `--write` it only lists what it would do:

```console
$ regia upgrade-project --project my_game --engine path:/opt/regia-engine-0.3.0
$ regia upgrade-project --project my_game --engine path:/opt/regia-engine-0.3.0 --write
```

This runs the registered migrators and rewrites assets in place (specs/12 § 4a), moves every engine dependency to
the new source and stamps the new line, with a `.bak` of every file it rewrites (a later run keeps it and writes
`.bak.2`). Every format change ships with its
migrator, so an older project upgrades cleanly. Run it after every engine update, patch releases too: it changes
nothing when nothing is needed. It refuses, and writes nothing, when the project needs a newer engine or is older
than the oldest line this `regia` still upgrades. Then read the Upgrade section of the release notes of each line
it lists; API changes in your own code are yours to make. The policy and every status code are in
[Distribution and upgrade (agents)](book/agents/distribution-upgrade.md).

## What is `assets://`

Assets are addressed by project-relative paths (`assets/levels/main.level.ron`, written
`levels/main.level.ron`). The `AssetServer` resolves them through the dev cook cache in development
and through mounted `.fpak` archives in a packaged build — the same `assets://` namespace either
way.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/display-calibration.md -->
# Display calibration

<!-- index: Display calibration -->
<!-- index: Paper white -->
<!-- index: HDR10 -->

Regia Engine's look is judged on a good monitor in a dim room. Players see it on dim laptop panels, TVs
that crush their first code values, phones in daylight and HDR TVs. Display calibration lets the
player correct for their screen without changing the content, the way a TV's picture settings do.
Vsync and the window's present mode are display settings (`GameSettings.display.vsync`,
`PresentMode::{Vsync, VsyncRelaxed, Immediate}`), documented on
[Rendering](book/user-guide/rendering.md#present-modes). Calibration does not change them.

## What it changes

Calibration runs as a **display stage** on the finished frame: scene, VFX and UI, after the
tonemap, just before present. The calibration screen's own test patterns go through the same
curve they measure.

| Setting | Range (neutral) | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `black_level` | −1 … 1 (0) | Shadow curve on the lower half of the range. For `v < 0.5`, `v' = ½(x + a·x·(1 − x)²)` with `x = 2v` (equivalently `v' = v + a·v·(1 − 2v)²`; `a = 2.5·s` lifting, `0.9·s` deepening). Black stays black, mid gray and everything brighter never move, slope 1 at mid gray. It is a curve, not a gain: the slope at black is up to 3.5×, and code 3 rises by about 3.38× at full lift. Code 120 barely moves. |
| `gamma` | 1.8 … 2.6 (2.2) | SDR only: `v' = v^(g / 2.2)`, the picture as a display decoding with gamma `g` would show it. Higher is darker mid-tones. |
| `paper_white_nits` | 80 … 500 (203) | HDR: luminance of UI and diffuse white (ITU-R BT.2408 reference white by default). |
| `peak_nits` | 200 … 10 000 (1000, or what the display reports) | HDR: the brightest highlight. The post blit expands tonemapped highlights above half of paper white up to `peak / paper` (C¹ quadratic). |
| `min_nits` | 0 … 1 (0) | HDR: the display's black; output is `min + n·(1 − min/peak)`. |

HDR output encodes in the stage: Rec.709 → Rec.2020 (ITU-R BT.2087) and SMPTE ST 2084 (PQ) for
HDR10, or linear ÷ 80 cd/m² for scRGB.

`DisplayCalibration::NEUTRAL` is the identity. On an SDR surface the stage does not run at all
at neutral, and a GPU test (`neutral_stage_is_byte_identical`) proves every 8-bit code value
comes back unchanged when it does run. Goldens and neutral screenshots are therefore unaffected.

## Defaults per platform

| Platform | Out of the box |
|---|---|
| Desktop | neutral |
| Android (phone/tablet) | `black_level` 0.3: outdoor-friendly shadow lift |
| Steam Deck (`SteamDeck=1` or the Deck render profile) | `black_level` 0.15: LCD panel, ~1000:1 |

Android reports the panel's HDR luminance (`Display.getHdrCapabilities`, API 24+); while the
calibration is still the platform default, its peak and minimum are taken from there. Desktop
winit exposes no display luminance yet (Windows DXGI `IDXGIOutput6::GetDesc1` is the follow-up).

## Persistence

The player's values live in `GameSettings.graphics.calibration` (`settings.ron`), with an `hdr`
flag (request HDR10) and `peak_nits: None` meaning "what the display reports". `None` for the
whole section means the platform default. Older settings files load unchanged.

## The calibration screen

```rust,wrap
use regia_framework::prelude::*;
# use regia_app::prelude::App;
# use regia_ecs::prelude::MessageReader;
# let mut app = App::new();

app.add_plugins(CalibrationScreenPlugin { open_on_first_launch: true });
// From the options menu:
app.world_mut().resource_mut::<CalibrationScreen>().open();
// React when it closes:
fn on_closed(mut closed: MessageReader<CalibrationScreenClosed>) { /* … */ }
```

Pages:

1. **Brightness**: two logos on true black, the left at code ≈ 9, the right at code ≈ 3.
   "Adjust until the logo on the left is barely visible and the logo on the right is not."
   On HDR this page also has the HDR black slider.
2. **Contrast** (SDR): a solid square at the 2.2 mid-gray code value inside 1-pixel black/white
   lines (50 % of white on any display). Matched, the screen decodes like the mastering display.
3. **HDR paper white**: a white card next to an 18 % gray card.
4. **HDR peak brightness**: the display stage draws a ring at the chosen peak on a
   10 000 cd/m² background. The background clips to the panel's real maximum, so the ring
   disappears once the peak reaches it.

Each page leaves a transparent strip along the bottom, so the live scene shows while the
player adjusts. Values preview live. **Done** saves, **Cancel** (or Back on the first page)
restores the previous calibration, **Reset** returns the page to the platform default.

Input: mouse and touch drive the sliders and buttons. Arrows and the d-pad move focus
(up/down) and step the focused slider (left/right). Enter or gamepad A activates, Escape or
gamepad B goes back.

Strings: a game overrides any `calibration-*` key in its own
`assets://localization/<locale>/*.ftl`. Otherwise the bundled strings are used (English, German,
French, Spanish; `crates/regia_framework/locales/`).

## Evidence

`docs/evidence/calibration/2026-10-08/` shows the DO27 GI sheet shots (Mars close, Europa trench)
through three simulated problem displays, at default and calibrated values. Regenerate with
`cargo run -p regia_render --example calibration_sheet -- <out> <shot.png>...`.
`DisplayModel` simulates a display as gain-offset-gamma plus a crush threshold and reflected
ambient light. `DisplayModel::solve` emulates a player running the screen.

Agents: see [Display calibration (agents)](book/agents/display-calibration.md).
