# Android

<!-- index: Android -->
<!-- index: API 29 -->
<!-- index: APK -->
<!-- index: Android App Bundle -->

Regia Engine runs on Android phones (aarch64, API 29+, Vulkan). This page is the state of that port as
of batch v020 (v0.1.21) and the steps to re-run the real-device pass on your own phone. Numbers are from the
Pixel 6 (GrapheneOS, Mali-G78) on 2026-10-08 unless a row says otherwise.

`min_sdk` in `Regia.toml` defaults to 29. The manifest check refuses a value under 24
([Android device bring-up](book/user-guide/android-bringup.md)). The package is an APK or an AAB
([Package a game](book/how-to/platforms/package-a-game.md)). Google Play
services are parked and are not part of that package. A dedicated server is not an Android target
(`server_platform_unsupported`, exit 2). The game renderer uses Vulkan. It does not fall back to
OpenGL. The browser [product viewer](book/agents/web-player.md) is a different program: its WebGL2
path is for that viewer, not for a packaged game.

Surfaces drop on suspend and are created again on resume. That is what the code specifies (the table
below). `docs/versions.md` (2026-11-08) still recorded a failed lifecycle acceptance, and this page
does not re-run that pass. Treat a lifecycle claim beyond the specified suspend and resume behavior
as not accepted here.

Phone setup from a bare machine is [Android device bring-up](book/user-guide/android-bringup.md). The desktop host
is [Linux](book/user-guide/linux.md).

## Build, install, attach

```sh
regia install-android --project <game>     # build the APK, install, launch, forward the agent port
```

`install-android` needs the Android SDK and NDK r27+, `cargo-ndk` and rustup-managed Android
targets (`regia doctor` checks them). It grants `INTERNET` to debug builds (GrapheneOS leaves it
off for adb installs), so `regia agent call ...` works over `adb forward` like on desktop.

Options: `--device <serial>` picks the phone when several are attached; `--abi <abi>` (repeatable)
builds only those ABIs (default: the device's primary ABI when `[platforms.android] abis` lists it);
`--no-build` installs the APK from the last `regia package`; `--no-logcat` returns after the launch
instead of streaming the app's logcat; `--attach` only forwards the agent port of the app that is
already running and writes `.regia/agent/endpoint.json` (no build, install or launch).

## What the engine does on Android

| Android event | Engine behavior |
|---|---|
| Window created / destroyed (`onStart`/`onStop` side) | `Resumed` / `Suspended`. Surfaces drop on suspend and are created again on resume; the `Device` and every GPU resource survive. The audio output stream is freed and rebuilt. |
| `onPause` (batch v020) | `ActivityState.paused`. The audio output gate pauses at once, instead of waiting for the window to be torn down. |
| `onDestroy` (batch v020) | `ActivityState.destroyed` writes `AppExit`, so the same clean exit as a desktop quit runs (ADR-188): final `summary.json`, pipeline cache, ordered GPU shutdown. winit does not forward `onDestroy`, so the generated `RegiaActivity` reports it. |
| Rotation / resize | The swapchain is reconfigured on the next frame; the safe area is re-read. |
| Memory pressure | `LowMemory` message (any state; it never changes `AppLifecycle.state`). The renderer frees idle GPU memory at the next frame. |

Files go to app storage: `user://` is the app's internal files directory and `logs://` is
`user://logs`, so logs, `summary.json`, partial summaries and crash bundles are there. Pull them with
`adb exec-out run-as <package> tar c -C files logs | tar x` (debug builds).

**Defaults.** Mobile High is the platform default preset. Textures are cooked to ASTC for Android
(ADR-144); BC textures are decoded on the CPU only for content that was not cooked for Android.
Several Mali driver bugs are worked around in the shaders (no texture arguments to functions,
no dynamic indexing of vectors; both have tests that fail on a regression).

## TalkBack

With the `accesskit` feature the same screen-reader bridge as on desktop attaches to the activity's
surface view and talks to TalkBack (ADR-3454). Build the game with that feature; it stays off by
default. `REGIA_ACCESSKIT=0` keeps the OS adapter off without a rebuild.

TalkBack connecting is the activation: the next update is the whole tree, and later frames send only
what changed. A double-tap runs through the same action path as a click (`click` on a button). The
bridge does not learn that TalkBack was turned off; it keeps sending until the process ends or an
agent calls `ui.a11y_platform_connect` with `false`. Window focus is not forwarded (TalkBack uses the
view). The Java delegate class is loaded from the crate, so the generated activity does not need a
new class.

TalkBack reads a control's label only, so the Android adapter adds each control's description to its
label: a toggle labelled `Invert Y` with the description `Move, gamepad` is read as "Invert Y, Move,
gamepad" (ADR-4932). Give controls that share a label a description that tells them apart.

**Touch size and scale.** A UI scaled to a 1920x1080 reference is about UI scale 1.0 on a landscape
phone, far below the screen's density: a 44 px control is about 20 dp there. Lay touch screens out with
`ScaleMode::ConstantPhysicalSize` (1 UI px = 1 dp) and let long lists scroll. The First Person
template's controls screen does this on Android (`ControlsLayout::Touch`), with an on-screen
**Controls** button. While that screen is open, Back closes it instead of the game. The `touch` profile
of `ui.a11y_audit` measures targets in dp, so it catches this on the device. Android's font size setting
(`Configuration.fontScale`) multiplies the game's own `text_scale` (`regia_platform::SystemTextScale`, read at
start, on resume and on every configuration change), within the 0.5 to 3.0 text scale range.

`ui.a11y_platform_tree` and `ui.a11y_platform_connect` include `android`: `os`, `registered`,
`attached`, `status` (`pending`, `attached`, `disabled`, or `not_android` on a desktop build) and
`detail`. A JNI failure is logged and the bridge is disabled (`status` `disabled`, `adapter_error`
set); it does not panic. A shipping build still aborts if AccessKit unwraps internally after that
check.

## Frame pacing

On a phone each frame starts on a display vsync and stays on screen for the same number of vsyncs, so
frames arrive evenly and do not pile up in the swapchain (ADR-1942). The swap interval is chosen for
you: a 60 Hz panel with 20 ms frames runs at 30 fps, a 120 Hz panel with the same frames at 40. A rare
spike leaves it alone. `FramePacing::target_fps` still caps the rate, as a whole number of vsyncs.
Agents read and set all this with `pacing.get` and `pacing.set`
([Frame pacing](book/agents/frame-pacing.md)); `pacing.trace` shows the last frames one by one. To return
to the old path, insert `FramePacingSettings { mode: PacingMode::Off, ..Default::default() }`.

## Thermal governor (batch v020)

Phones throttle hard: Mobile High on the Pixel 6 reached the OS's *severe* thermal status after
seven minutes and the frame time rose by a fifth. The engine now reads `PowerManager`'s thermal
status and its 10-second headroom forecast (`ThermalState`, polled every 2 s) and steps the render
scale down before the device gets there:

| Level | Asked for when | Render scale (× the preset's) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | status none/light and headroom under 0.8 | 1.00 |
| 1 | status moderate, or headroom ≥ 0.8 | 0.85 |
| 2 | status severe, or headroom ≥ 0.92 | 0.70 |
| 3 | status critical or worse, or headroom ≥ 1.0 | 0.55 (never under 0.5) |

It steps down at once and back up one level after 30 s of being cooler. The scale the player or the
preset asked for stays the base: if anything else changes the render scale while the governor is
holding it down, that value becomes the new base. Hosts turn the policy off with
`ThermalGovernor { enabled: false, ..default() }` (a resource, changeable at run time; the field
takes effect on the next frame and restores the base scale). On desktop the platform reports no
thermal state and the governor does nothing. `render.get_profile` shows `thermal` (see the
[agent page](book/agents/render-profile.md)). The factors and the 0.8 / 0.92 / 1.0 thresholds are a first
guess; the 20-minute pass below measures them.

## Crash capture

The panic hook writes a bundle to `logs://` on Android as on desktop. A *native* crash (a driver
SIGSEGV) cannot use the desktop crash monitor (ADR-158: Android forbids the ptrace-based dump and
the monitor re-exec), so the crashing process writes a small record itself (ADR-328): the next
launch logs `native crash record from the last run: SIGSEGV ...`, writes a
`logs://crash-<time>-native.txt` report with the stack, and, with `FeedbackPlugin`, a crash bundle
(no minidump). See [Crash reports](book/agents/crash-reports.md#android-native-crash-records). The
engine also logs why the earlier run ended, read from Android's `ApplicationExitInfo` (API 30+):
`previous run ended: native-crash (status 11) ...` as a warning. The OS tombstone itself is in
`adb logcat -b crash` (and `adb bugreport`); the pass script below saves the Regia Engine log lines, and
`--crash-test` checks the record on the device.

## Re-running the Pixel 6 pass

Plug the phone in (USB debugging on), keep it unlocked or use `--screen-suspend`, and run from the
repo root:

```sh
cargo xtask android-pass --package <app id> --project <game> \
    [--device <serial>] [--thermal-minutes 20] [--screen-suspend] \
    [--do27-chase <aarch64 do27_chase> --do27-content <content dir> --do27-map bore_twelve]
```

It installs the app, then runs, in order: the lifecycle check (50 suspend/resume cycles and 10
rotations, PSS leak check), the Mobile Low and Mobile High presets (frame and GPU p50/p99 with per-pass
GPU times, memory report), the DO27 map if you pass the binary and content (build the binary with
`cargo ndk -t arm64-v8a build --release -p lookdev --bin do27_chase`), and a 20-minute Mobile High
run sampled every 15 s. Everything is written to `target/android-pass/<timestamp>/`:
`summary.txt` (read this first), `lifecycle.json`, `presets.jsonl`, `thermal.tsv`
(elapsed, frame p50/p99, GPU p50, render scale, thermal status, skin and SoC °C, RSS),
`do27-*.txt` and `logcat-regia.txt`. Send that folder back. In `thermal.tsv`, a falling
`render_scale` column with `thermal_status` staying at 0–2 is the governor working; status 3 for
long stretches means the thresholds need to be lower.

Tuning options: `--thermal-preset` is the render preset of the thermal run (default `mobile_high`;
`mobile_low` on a phone whose GPU times out at Mobile High), `--sample-secs` the seconds between thermal
samples (default 15) and `--window-secs` how long each `play.hitch_report` window lasts, for the presets and
the thermal samples (default 8). `--crash-test` runs only the native crash record check, and
`--crash-delay-secs` (default 8) is how long after startup its worker thread faults.

### Budget verdicts

A run ends with one verdict per budget instead of a number to compare by hand (ADR-1942): the
`budget ...` lines of `summary.txt`, and `budgets.json` and `budgets.tsv` beside it.

| Budget | Limit (reference tier) | Read from |
|---|---|---|
| `frame_p99` | 16.6 ms at Mobile High: the frame's work, per frame the larger of CPU and GPU frame time | `play.hitch_report` `work.p99_ms`, in `presets.jsonl` |
| `presented_p99` | 1.05 × the refresh interval of the panel (unit `x refresh`; the summary line gives ms and Hz) | `play.hitch_report` `p99_ms` and `pacing.get` `refresh_hz`, in `presets.jsonl` |
| `cpu_main_p99` | 8 ms | `presets.jsonl` |
| `longest_frame` | 50 ms | `presets.jsonl` |
| `memory_pss` | 700 MB | `dumpsys meminfo` after the preset's window, in `presets.jsonl` |
| `cold_start` | 5000 ms (median, first engine frame) | `startup.tsv` |
| `thermal_status` | status 2 at worst | `thermal.tsv` |
| `thermal_p50_growth` | 25 % from the first sample to the last | `thermal.tsv` |
| `pacing_late` | 5 % of the frames in the preset's window | `pacing.get`, in `presets.jsonl` |

Each row is `pass`, `fail`, or `not_measured` when a step was skipped or the phone reported nothing.
A frame shown on a 60 Hz panel is on screen for at least 16.67 ms however little it cost, so
`frame_p99` reads what the frame cost and `presented_p99` checks that the frames keep their display
slot (ADR-4947). A run from a build without `work` leaves `frame_p99` not measured.
A phone's GPU memory is system memory, so the GPU allocator's free space counts in PSS: on Android the
engine asks wgpu for small allocator blocks (4-32 MiB, ADR-5423), and `seeing.memory_report`'s
`reserved_bytes` minus `allocated_bytes` is the part of PSS the allocator holds free.
The limits are `budgets/android-reference.ron`; a low-end phone uses `--budgets budgets/android-low.ron`
(Mobile Low at 30 fps). `docs/06-testing-and-ci.md` § 4 is where the numbers come from.

These budgets are not a gate yet: a failed row is reported and the pass keeps its own verdict. With
`--enforce-budgets` a row that fails or was not measured fails the pass.

To judge a finished run again, for instance against a changed budget file:

```sh
cargo xtask android-budgets --run target/android-pass/<timestamp> [--budgets <file>]
```

It rewrites `budgets.json` and `budgets.tsv` in that folder and exits 1 when a row fails.

## Gamepads

Pads connect through `InputManager` (polled every 30 frames). Buttons arrive as key events: the
`BUTTON_*` family maps to the pad buttons; the D-pad arrives as arrow keys. The left
stick works; the right stick, hat axes and analog triggers are not reachable through winit 0.30 and
need the Java-shim observer hook (not built). Device check: a physical pad's D-pad on the Pixel.

## Known limits

- The emulator (gfxstream) is for checking behavior, not speed. The per-frame surface capability
  query that froze it after the first frame is gone (batch v020), so interactive checks work there.
- Mobile High is 60–67 ms on the Pixel 6 at 2400×1080 and is GPU-bound (the opaque forward pass is
  56 ms). The lite forward shader for the Mobile tiers is in this tree (ADR-1874,
  [Mobile forward path](book/agents/mobile-forward.md)); that figure was measured before it, and the
  fused post and pooled object uniforms from the same work are not confirmed here; see the lane report.
- macOS and the Steam Deck are separate pages and passes.

## Package size, texture formats and lifecycle checks (v0.1.28)

- **Package size.** `regia package --platform android` prints a size report on stderr after
  the build. stdout still prints only the archive path. `regia apk-size <apk|aab>` prints the
  same report for any built archive: stored and extracted bytes per category (native libraries
  per ABI, paks, other assets, dex, resources, manifest, signature) and the largest entries.
  `--json` gives the machine form, `--top N` sets how many entries to list, and `--budget-mb 150`
  exits 1 when the archive is larger. For the native code inside the archive, `cargo xtask binary-size` splits the `.so` by crate (see [Binary size](book/user-guide/binary-size.md)). Two problems are warned about. `pak_compressed` means a
  `.fpak` was stored deflated: the generated Gradle project marks paks `noCompress` so the
  runtime can map them. `unexpected_abi` means the archive has native libraries for an ABI that
  `[platforms.android] abis` does not list.
- **Texture formats.** `regia cook --platform android --stats` ends with the cooked textures
  per format: ASTC by block size, BC, uncompressed. It warns
  `textures_cooked_for_other_platform` when BC textures are in the Android cache: phones decode
  BC to RGBA8 on the CPU. `--stats --json` prints only that report as JSON.
- **Lifecycle without a phone.** `lifecycle.drill { "cycles": 50 }` runs suspend/resume cycles
  on a desktop through the same transitions a home press takes. The surface audit
  (`lifecycle.get`) checks that every surface is dropped on suspend and recreated on resume. On a
  phone, `cargo xtask android-lifecycle` reads the audit's `regia surface audit:` logcat line
  and fails the run on a violation. See [Mobile lifecycle, thermal and touch](book/agents/mobile-lifecycle.md).
- **Thermal hooks.** `ThermalLevelChanged` is written on every governor level change. A game reads it to
  shed its own load. `ThermalGovernor::max_fps` adds an optional frame cap per level; it is off by
  default. `thermal.set_override` forces a reading to test both.
- **Touch controls.** `regia_input::TouchControls` maps screen zones (button, floating stick)
  and gestures to actions, without UI widgets.

## ETC2 for GPUs without ASTC (ADR-1379)

The Android cook writes ASTC. For a GPU without ASTC (some older or low-end parts; ETC2 is part of OpenGL ES 3.0
and most Vulkan Android drivers expose it) the asset pipeline can also write ETC2 / EAC:

| Usage | ETC2 / EAC format | Bits a texel |
|---|---|---|
| sRGB colour, UI | ETC2 RGB8 sRGB, or ETC2 RGBA8 sRGB when the base level has alpha | 4 / 8 |
| linear data (ORM) | ETC2 RGB8 or RGBA8 | 4 / 8 |
| one-channel mask | EAC R11 | 4 |
| normal map | EAC RG11 (X, Y; the shader rebuilds Z, as for BC5) | 8 |

The renderer uploads these as they are (`compressed_texture.rs` maps every ETC2 and EAC format). From code:
`regia_asset_pipeline::cook_texture_rgba8_android(width, height, rgba, usage, quality, AndroidTextureFormat::Etc2)`.
A whole project switches with `Regia.toml` (ADR-2063):

```toml
[cook.textures.android]
format = "etc2"              # or "astc" (the default)
astc_profile = "per_texture" # "high" (4x4 everywhere) or "low" (6x6 / 8x8) for an ASTC cook
```

`regia cook --size-report` compares every image as BC, ASTC and ETC2 before you switch, and a device that cannot
sample what was cooked decodes it to RGBA8 on the CPU instead of drawing the slot white; see
[Android texture compression](book/agents/texture-compression.md).

**Size report.** Compare the two families on your own textures before choosing:

```console
$ cargo run --release -p regia_asset_pipeline --example etc2_survey -- assets/textures/*.png
$ cargo run --release -p regia_asset_pipeline --example etc2_survey -- --json --low assets/textures/*.png
```

Each row gives the full mip chain's bytes as ASTC (the block the cook picks; `--low` for the larger blocks) and as
ETC2 / EAC, with the level-0 PSNR of both, then the totals with the RGBA8 size. ETC2 RGB8 is half the size of
ASTC 4×4 on opaque colour, at a lower quality on detailed content; with alpha, and for normal maps, both are 8 bits
a texel. `regia cook --stats` reports the ETC2 family of a cooked cache.

## Device pass from a host that does not build (ADR-1749)

The phones may sit on a machine that only runs `adb` (the owner's desktop). Build the APK and the two host
tools on a build machine, copy them over, and run the pass with the prebuilt pieces:

```sh
# build machine (repo root; Android SDK, NDK r27+, JDK 17, cargo-ndk)
cargo build -p regia_cli -p xtask
cargo run -p regia_cli -- package --platform android --abi arm64-v8a --project samples/arena
#   -> samples/arena/dist/android/com.regiaengine.samples.arena-debug.apk, target/debug/{regia,xtask}

# phone host (repo checkout for samples/arena/Regia.toml; adb on PATH; phone on USB, USB debugging on)
adb devices -l                     # pick the USB serial (a phone may also show up over wireless adb)
xtask android-pass --package com.regiaengine.samples.arena --project samples/arena \
    --device <serial> --apk <arena debug apk> --regia <prebuilt regia> \
    --screen-suspend --thermal-minutes 10 --uninstall --out <results dir>
```

On top of the steps above the pass now runs:

| Step | What it checks | Files |
|---|---|---|
| startup (`--start-runs 3`) | three cold starts (`am force-stop`, `am start -W`) and three warm starts (suspend, `am start -W`): `TotalTime` and the engine's first presented frame after the system's `START` line | `startup.tsv` |
| screenshots | `screencap` after each preset and after the thermal run | `screen-*.png` |
| touch | a finger held 6 s low in the middle of the screen (`input touchscreen swipe x y x y 6000`; clear of the system's one-time "Viewing full screen" notice, in case a phone shows it anyway) shows in `input.touch_controls` and is gone after release | `checks.json` |
| trim memory | `am send-trim-memory <package> RUNNING_CRITICAL` reaches the engine as `regia lifecycle: LowMemory` and the app keeps its pid | `checks.json` |
| ASTC | `render.get_capabilities` reports ASTC; `assets.cooked_pack` shows no non-ASTC texture and no CPU decode | `checks.json` |
| surface audit | `lifecycle.get` after the lifecycle cycles: every surface dropped on suspend and recreated on resume | `checks.json` |
| gamepads | the gamepads `dumpsys input` lists (none attached is reported, not failed) | `checks.json` |
| back button | `KEYCODE_BACK` suspends the app (Android 12+ keeps a root activity alive) or ends it cleanly, with no crash, and a relaunch renders; when another window has input focus before the key (a system notice or dialog), the line names it (`focus before the key <window>`) | `summary.txt` |
| crash scan | every line of the whole run (`logcat -b main,system,crash`, streamed from the start) through the lifecycle tool's crash attribution | `logcat-all.txt`, `crash-scan.txt` |

The pass keeps the screen on while the phone is plugged in (`settings put global stay_on_while_plugged_in 7`) and
marks the system's one-time "Viewing full screen" notice as seen (`settings put secure immersive_mode_confirmations
confirmed`; otherwise the notice can take input focus from the app part way through the pass, and the back key goes to
it). It puts both old values back at the end; if it is interrupted, or the phone drops off adb before the end, it prints
the commands that restore them. `--uninstall` removes the app at the end, also after a failed step; the summary's
`uninstall:` line reads `pm list packages` and says `UNKNOWN` when adb no longer reaches the phone. The debug APK shows over the lock screen, so a PIN-locked phone needs
nobody to unlock it. The pass wakes the phone and asks it to drop the keyguard; when `dumpsys window` still reports
`isKeyguardShowing=true` (a PIN or pattern lock) it switches to `--screen-suspend` by itself and says so in
`summary.txt` (HOME on the lock screen stops backgrounding the app part way through the lifecycle cycles).
With the screen key, a phone sometimes wakes itself right after `KEYCODE_SLEEP` and the screen never goes off; when
`Suspended` has not arrived after 4 s and `dumpsys power` reads `mWakefulness=Awake`, the cycle sends the key again (at
most twice) and prints a line saying so. The cycle still fails unless the app reports `Suspended`.

An adb transport reset (a USB blip, or the phone's wireless adb transport flapping) ends the streamed logcat and
closes the forwarded agent socket while the app keeps running. The pass restarts `adb logcat` from the last complete
line's time (`-T`, so `logcat-all.txt` keeps every line; `summary.txt` counts the restarts), and the thermal run
re-attaches the agent once per failed sample (`agent reconnects` in the thermal line); a second failure in a row
ends the run.

**ASTC on the phone.** The arena APK carries no textures, so the ASTC step only proves the device exposes ASTC and
that nothing is decoded on the CPU. To see an ASTC map drawn, build the device compression test for the phone and run
it from `/data/local/tmp` (it skips on an adapter without ASTC):

```sh
# build machine
cargo ndk -t arm64-v8a -P 29 test -p regia_render --test device_compression --no-run
#   -> target/aarch64-linux-android/debug/deps/device_compression-<hash>
# phone host
adb -s <serial> shell mkdir -p /data/local/tmp/regia-test
adb -s <serial> push device_compression-<hash> /data/local/tmp/regia-test/device_compression
adb -s <serial> shell 'cd /data/local/tmp/regia-test && ./device_compression --test-threads 1'
adb -s <serial> shell rm -rf /data/local/tmp/regia-test
```

<!-- source: book/user-guide/doctor.md -->
# Checking your machine with `regia doctor`

<!-- index: regia doctor -->
<!-- index: Doctor -->
<!-- index: verify-paks -->

`regia doctor` looks for everything a build needs and prints, for each problem, the command that fixes it.

```console
$ regia doctor                      # Rust, this host's desktop, the GPU probe, Android
$ regia doctor --platform android   # SDK, NDK, JDK, Gradle, adb, cargo-ndk, Rust targets
$ regia doctor --platform windows   # cross builds from Linux: cargo-xwin, MSVC target, clang-cl
$ regia doctor --platform all --json
```

## What each platform checks

| Platform | Checks |
|---|---|
| (every platform but `gpu`) | `rustc`, `cargo`, `rustup`, free disk space where `--project` builds |
| linux | Vulkan driver and devices, `spirv-val` |
| windows | On Windows: the Vulkan loader. From Linux: `cargo-xwin`, the `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` target, `clang-cl` |
| android | SDK path (`ANDROID_HOME`), SDK platform and build tools, NDK r27 or newer, JDK 17+, Gradle, `adb` and attached devices, `cargo-ndk`, the Android Rust targets |
| deck | `cargo-zigbuild` and zig 0.14+ |
| macos | Xcode command-line tools and `spirv-val` (on the Mac only; testing only) |
| gpu | Every adapter and its ray-tracing support (information only) |

Each line is `ok`, `WARN` (some workflows need it), `FAIL` (this platform cannot build) or blank (a fact).
Run the `fix:` commands, then run the doctor again.

## Disk space

The doctor warns under 15 GiB free (`disk_low`) and fails under 2 GiB (`disk_full`) on the volume that holds the
project. A cold engine build and an Android package take many GiB: `cargo clean`, or set `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` on a
larger volume.

## Exit codes

`0` nothing failed (warnings are fine), `1` a check failed, `2` bad arguments. `--json` prints the same checks for
tools; the schema, every code and the pak-verification form are in [Toolchain doctor (agents)](book/agents/doctor.md).

## Pak integrity (`--verify-paks`)

```console
$ regia doctor --verify-paks dist/linux/<slug>/content
$ regia doctor --verify-paks dist/linux/<slug>/content --json
```

This checks the whole-file content hash of every `.fpak` in that directory and runs no other doctor
check. A matching hash is `[ok]`. A pak with no content hash is `[--]` (unhashed) and is not a
failure. A mismatch is `[FAIL]`. One or more corrupt paks is a non-zero exit, with a count. `--json`
prints schema 1, `kind` `regia_doctor_paks`, `ok`, `corrupt`, and `paks`.

Related: [Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md), [Linux](book/user-guide/linux.md), [Android](book/user-guide/android.md),
[Package a game](book/how-to/platforms/package-a-game.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/macos.md -->
# macOS (testing only)

<!-- index: macOS -->
<!-- index: Metal -->
<!-- index: Cursor grab -->

Regia Engine builds and runs its test suite on macOS with Metal. This is a bring-up for testing
(ADR-264, which amends ADR-009), not a supported release target: there is no macOS release build,
packaging, signing or notarization, and macOS tests never gate a merge.

There is no dedicated-server package. `regia package --server` is Linux and Windows, and any other
platform exits 2 with `server_platform_unsupported`. `--format app` is rejected on every platform:
the macOS app-bundle format is not built. An iOS release is parked and is not this testing build.
DLSS is never linked on macOS. The graphics backend here is Metal.

`CursorGrab::Confined` is not available, so a Confined request is sent as Locked and logged once
per process. Locked stays Locked. Spec 11: only the primary window becomes an operating-system
window (ADR-2252).

Install and day-to-day development on Linux are [Linux](book/user-guide/linux.md) and
[Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md). `regia doctor --platform macos` runs on the Mac
(Xcode command-line tools and `spirv-val`).

State recorded for v0.1.22, on an Apple M5 (32 GB, macOS 26.6, Metal 4) with Homebrew `rustc` 1.99.1:
the whole workspace builds, and 4979 of 5006 test cases pass (472 test binaries, 38 ignored).

## What is macOS-specific

- **Platform services** live in `regia_platform::platform::macos` (`crates/regia_platform/src/platform/macos.rs`):
  opening a URL through `/usr/bin/open` (not waited for), the locale from the environment and then
  the user's `AppleLanguages` and `AppleLocale` defaults (GUI launches carry no `LANG`), OS information from `sw_vers` and
  `sysctl`, and `_exit` for the clean-exit watchdog. The Linux module, which used Wayland and X11
  window attributes, no longer compiles for macOS, and `with_app_id` does nothing there.
- **Graphics backend.** `instance_backends()` is Metal on macOS. wgpu's Vulkan backend needs a loader
  a Mac does not have.
- **Metal workarounds**, none of which change Linux, Windows or Android output:
  - The exposure histogram uses one workgroup array instead of 64 scalar workgroup variables
    (`HIST_WORKGROUP_ARRAY`), because Metal allows 31 threadgroup arguments.
  - The frame GPU timer is off where `TIMESTAMP_QUERY_INSIDE_ENCODERS` is missing: Apple GPUs sample
    timestamps at pass boundaries only. Frame timing reports the `fallback_no_timestamps` notice.
  - The terrain impostor shader no longer needs `SHADER_EARLY_DEPTH_TEST`.
- **Pipeline cache.** wgpu 30 has no pipeline cache on Metal, so every launch compiles its pipelines
  (62 boot pipelines took 485 ms and 48 game pipelines 377 ms in `boot_probe` on the M5).
- **Paths.** `host_platform()` is `macos`, so dev cooks land in `.regia/cooked/macos`. The source
  watcher reports changed paths under the root it was given (FSEvents reports real paths; `/var` is
  `/private/var`), and the soak memory probe reads `ps -o rss=`.

## Build and test

```sh
cargo check --workspace
cargo test --workspace
```

Install Rust with Homebrew or rustup; the repository pins 1.99.0 and the Homebrew 1.99.1 compiler
works. Install SPIRV-Tools (`spirv-val`) if you want the SPIR-V validation tests to run.

## Known failures

The 27 failing cases are not gated, and none is hidden or re-blessed:

- Golden images that differ on Metal. Goldens are lavapipe images; they are not re-blessed for Metal.
- Tests that encode a Vulkan capability set: timestamps inside encoders, allocator reports,
  `MULTI_DRAW_INDIRECT_COUNT`, forced early depth tests.
- Tests that need `spirv-val`, which is not installed on the test Mac (8 tests fail with "No such
  file").
- The editor hot-reload fixture test `hot_fixture_edits_keep_reflected_state`: the baseline load is
  refused with "engine changed". Hot reload is not verified on macOS.

## Not verified on macOS

Frame-rate budgets, Vulkan SPIR-V validation, native crash capture (`native_crash.rs` is Linux and
Windows only), SpaceMouse (the `hid` backend has no macOS implementation), Steam, audio devices,
the Android and Windows builds from a Mac.

For the rest of the platform story see [Android](book/user-guide/android.md) and [Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md); the
CI and device matrix is in `docs/06-testing-and-ci.md` § 8.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/windows.md -->
# Windows

<!-- index: Windows -->
<!-- index: DX12 -->
<!-- index: Direct3D 12 -->
<!-- index: Cursor grab -->

The v0.2.17 Windows pass exercised Vulkan and DX12 on the owner's a test machine, including
native crash capture, deliberate device-loss exit and clean quits; the N150 laptop also had
a native pass. See the v0217 notes, `docs/releases/v0.1.28-windows-pass-v0217.md`.
That evidence belongs to its recorded source revision. **The v0.2.20 candidate still needs
its own native Windows acceptance**; its handoff, `docs/evidence/windows/v02020-acceptance-b.md`,
records the frozen source and exact commands. Windows is verified on the owner's machines
only (ADR-009); there are no hosted Windows runners.

## What a Windows package is

`regia package --platform windows` writes `dist/windows/<slug>-windows.zip`. On Linux the same command cross-compiles with cargo-xwin when [regia doctor](book/user-guide/doctor.md) `--platform windows` is clean, and it does not run the exe on the Linux host. A dedicated server is `regia package --server --platform windows`. The procedure is [Package a game](book/how-to/platforms/package-a-game.md). [Linux](book/user-guide/linux.md) is the other desktop shipping target.

Vulkan is the default adapter. DX12 is in the same adapter list after the Vulkan entries. `REGIA_GPU_INDEX` or `REGIA_GPU_NAME` selects a DX12 adapter when the machine has one. A pass on a machine with no DX12 hardware adapter still records that run as `unreachable` (`BLOCKED`). The sections below are the acceptance history and the checks that do not need the Windows machine.

`CursorGrab::Locked` is requested as Confined on Windows, because that is the grab winit applies there. Confined stays Confined. Spec 11: only the primary window becomes an operating-system window (ADR-2252).

## What is checked without a Windows machine

- **Compile and lint.** The `windows-cross` CI job runs `cargo xwin clippy --workspace --all-targets
  --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -- -D warnings` on Linux (ADR-295). It is allowed to fail until it
  has been seen green once.
- **Shaders for DX12.** A Linux test writes every engine shader and permutation as HLSL Shader Model 6.0
  with naga and fails on any naga error; another keeps the three loops ADR-201 rewrote (16 and 12
  shadow taps, 16 parallax steps) free of `break` and `continue` so FXC can unroll them. A second
  check (ADR-367) covers every module of every engine crate, terrain, VFX, UI, 2D and the path tracer
  included: HLSL for Shader Model 5.1 (FXC) and 6.0 (DXC), the Direct3D 12 compute limits (32 KiB of
  workgroup memory, 1024 threads per group), and no `textureSample`, `textureSampleCompare` or
  `dpdx`/`fwidth` inside a loop of a fragment shader (FXC has to unroll such a loop). `cargo xtask
  check-shaders` runs it too. None of this proves FXC or DXC accepts the text.
- **The pass itself.** Its summary schema and verdict logic are unit tested against fixture JSON.

## Running native acceptance

On the Windows machine, with Rust (the `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` host toolchain), the Visual Studio
Build Tools (C++ workload) and a GPU driver with Vulkan installed:

```
cargo xtask windows-pass
```

Allow time for a cold native build: compilation can take hours on a small Windows machine.
Use low build concurrency and distinguish completed builds from executed tests. In order it:

1. checks the toolchain and lists every GPU adapter with its backend and driver;
2. runs the Windows test subset: platform, native crash capture (the bundle, and a real fault in a
   child process), the deliberate exit, paths and Saved Games, adapter selection. One log per step in
   `tests/`. Each step is compiled first (`--no-run`, up to 3 hours) and then run (up to 30 minutes),
   so a slow cold build shows as `build_timeout` or `build_fail` rather than as a hung test (ADR-4050);
   `summary.json` records `build_secs` and `secs` per step;
3. builds `vfx_lab` in release and runs it per backend: a 3 s cold and a 3 s warm start on a fresh
   pipeline cache (the pipeline-compile gap, measured and not fixed), then a 60 s measured run
   (`--run-secs`) whose engine `summary.json` is read back. Vulkan goes through the default pick, so
   it tests ADR-201 itself. DX12 runs only when a variable can reach it; see below;
4. starts and quits the windowed sample five times (`--quits`) and checks that each exit code is 0.

Leave the machine alone while it runs and keep the screen awake: a run with a hidden window is
reported as invalid. The results land in `docs/evidence/windows/<UTC date>/`; `summary.json` is the
one file that matters. Send back that whole folder.

Options: `--out <dir>`, `--run-secs <n>`, `--quits <n>`, `--skip-tests`, `--skip-runs`.

### Reading a result (no Windows needed)

```
cargo xtask windows-pass --read docs/evidence/windows/<date>/summary.json
```

prints `PASS`, `BLOCKED` or `FAIL` with the reasons, and exits 0, 2 or 1. `BLOCKED` means nothing
failed but something could not run.

### Known limits of the pass

- **DX12 needs a DX12 hardware adapter.** The adapter list holds every adapter, Vulkan first and
  then DX12 (ADR-326), so the pass forces DX12 with `REGIA_GPU_INDEX` of a DX12 adapter
  (ADR-201). On a machine with no DX12 hardware adapter the pass records the DX12 run as
  `unreachable` (verdict `BLOCKED`, ADR-296).
- **A step that skipped is not a pass.** A test step whose program prints `<program>: skipped ...` (the native
  crash driver is Linux only; `device_lost_exit` without a GPU) is recorded as `skipped` with its line, and the
  verdict is `BLOCKED` (ADR-5806).
- **Cold means a cold engine cache.** The operating system's own shader cache is not cleared.
- Frame times and compile times are reported, not judged against budgets.

## Paths

`user://` is `%APPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>` and `cache://` is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>`.
`regia_platform::paths::saved_games_dir()` returns the `Saved Games` known folder for games that
keep saves there. The persistent pipeline cache is `cache://pipelines` (`%LOCALAPPDATA%`, never
roaming); it is Vulkan-only in wgpu 30, so on DX12 only the GPU driver's own shader cache helps a
second start. Feedback bundles, crash bundles and native-crash minidumps go to
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>\feedback`, not the roaming `%APPDATA%` (ADR-525). Panic text reports
stay in `logs://`. The agent method `platform.paths` prints all of these on the running machine.

## Swapchain, HDR and the DX12 workflow

The swapchain plan (ADR-525, `render.swapchain`, see [Swapchain](book/agents/swapchain.md)) has three
rules for Windows:

- An HDR request on a display that is not in HDR mode (Windows HDR off) is configured as SDR,
  because DX12 lists HDR color spaces either way and Windows would tone-map the frame back down.
  The display is read again every 120 frames while HDR is requested, so switching Windows HDR on
  or off while the game runs reconfigures the swapchain.
- VRR on DX12 presents with tearing allowed (`Immediate`), the present that variable refresh needs on
  DXGI; without tearing support it uses `Mailbox`.
- The display's peak and minimum nits from DXGI fill the display calibration's defaults.

`.github/workflows/windows-dx12.yml` is defined for the owner's self-hosted runners and has not run:
the `policy` job (no GPU, `WINDOWS_RUNNER=true`) runs these rules' tests and compiles the FXC and
DXC paths; the `gpu` job (`WINDOWS_GPU_RUNNER=true`, a runner labeled `ferrite-gpu`) runs
`cargo xtask windows-pass` and keeps the evidence folder, crash bundles and minidumps as an artifact.

## Native crash capture

Native crash capture is opt-in on Windows: set `REGIA_NATIVE_CRASH=1` or
`FeedbackConfig::native_crashes_windows`. See the [Feedback](book/user-guide/feedback.md) chapter. The pass turns it
on for its runs.

## File names

VFS paths (`user://`, `assets://`, ...) refuse names Windows cannot store, on every platform, so
content made on Linux works on Windows: the device names `CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM1`-`COM9`
and `LPT1`-`LPT9` (any case, with or without an extension), names ending in `.` or a space, and the
characters `< > " | ? *`. `regia_platform::open_path` shows a directory or file in the OS file
manager (`explorer` on Windows).

See also [macOS](book/user-guide/macos.md), [Android](book/user-guide/android.md) and `docs/06-testing-and-ci.md` § 8 for the
verification matrix.

## DX12 readiness (verified on Linux)

Everything in this section runs in the Linux test suite (ADR-326, ADR-327). Keep these compile and policy
results separate from a native Windows pass, and record the source revision for both.

- **Every shader translates to HLSL for both DX12 compilers.** The HLSL test writes every engine shader and permutation at
  Shader Model 6.0 (DXC: the `static-dxc` feature or a `dxcompiler.dll`) and at Shader Model 5.1 (FXC: what wgpu uses when no
  DXC is available, which is the default build on most machines). The 5.1 text is scanned for Shader Model 6 constructs that
  naga writes but FXC rejects (wave intrinsics, 16- and 64-bit integer types). The v0.1.27 gate runs of the Shader Model 6.0
  test found no failing shader, so no shader was changed. There is no allow-list.
- **DX12 can be forced.** The adapter list now holds the DX12 adapters after the Vulkan ones (the Vulkan numbering is
  unchanged), so `REGIA_GPU_INDEX=<n>` or `REGIA_GPU_NAME=<substring>` of a DX12 entry selects DX12 even when Vulkan works.
  The "DX12 cannot be forced" limit above no longer applies, and `cargo xtask windows-pass` runs its DX12 section instead of
  recording it as `unreachable`. The default pick is unchanged: Vulkan first, DX12 only without a Vulkan hardware adapter.
- **Resource Binding Tier from limits.** Each DX12 adapter in the list shows its D3D12 Resource Binding Tier, read from the
  per-stage limits wgpu derives from Microsoft's binding-tier table (Tier 3 is what bindless resource arrays need). wgpu does
  not expose Tier 1 adapters; a `Tier 1` reading means the limits were clamped below Tier 2.
- **Backend decisions in one place.** Which backends open per OS, the adapter order, the Vulkan-only pipeline cache, the
  DX12-only binding tier and the FXC rules are pure functions in `regia_render::backend_policy`, unit tested for Vulkan,
  DX12, Metal and GL.
- **Pipeline count per profile is pinned.** On DX12 the engine has no pipeline cache of its own (wgpu's is Vulkan only), so a
  cold start compiles every pipeline the profile warms. A test pins that count per shipped profile, so a jump in the number of
  shader variants fails CI.

Not proven here: that FXC or DXC accepts the HLSL, whether FXC unrolls the shadow and parallax loops once wgpu's loop bounding
wraps them, the binding tier a real DX12 adapter or WARP reports, and DX12 frame and compile times. The owner's
`windows-pass` run covers those.

# Linux

<!-- index: Linux -->
<!-- index: Vulkan -->
<!-- index: lavapipe -->
<!-- index: Wayland -->
<!-- index: X11 -->
<!-- index: xdg-open -->
<!-- index: Cursor grab -->

Linux is a development host and a shipping target. The editor, the command-line tool, games, and dedicated servers build and run here. The game renderer uses Vulkan. Install steps, package names, and the first `cargo build` live on [Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md). This page is what the engine does on Linux after that install.

The [Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md) runs the same native Linux package inside Steam Linux Runtime. [Windows](book/user-guide/windows.md), [macOS (testing only)](book/user-guide/macos.md), and [Android](book/user-guide/android.md) are separate targets. [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md) and [Package a game](book/how-to/platforms/package-a-game.md) cover the archives.

## Graphics

Vulkan is the Linux backend: Mesa's RADV or ANV, or the NVIDIA driver. There is no OpenGL fallback. Without a GPU, Mesa's lavapipe software driver runs headless tests. Golden images are recorded on lavapipe.

A desktop session needs a running display, or `xvfb-run` when there is none (a server or CI). `regia doctor --platform linux` checks that a Vulkan driver and `spirv-val` are present. `regia doctor --platform gpu` lists adapters and ray-tracing support and does not fail the build.

Vendor upscalers are not part of a Linux install. DLSS links when the optional `sdk` feature and an external SDK are both present. That SDK is not in the repository. Android and macOS do not link it. The quality page is [Automatic quality detection](book/user-guide/auto-quality.md).

## Paths and platform services

`regia_platform::platform::linux` is the Linux service module.

| Service | What it does |
|---|---|
| Open a URL | `xdg-open`, started and not waited on |
| Locale | `LC_ALL`, then `LC_MESSAGES`, then `LANG` |
| OS information | `/etc/os-release` (or `/usr/lib/os-release`), the kernel release, DMI vendor and product, RAM from `/proc/meminfo` |
| Window name | Wayland `app_id` and X11 `WM_CLASS`, both set from the application's id |
| Clean-exit watchdog | `_exit`, so a stuck driver teardown cannot block process exit |

Dev cooks land in `.regia/cooked/linux` (`host_platform()` is `linux`).

| VFS | Host path |
|---|---|
| `user://` | `~/.local/share/RegiaEngine/<exe name>` |
| `cache://` | `~/.cache/RegiaEngine/<exe name>` |
| `logs://` | `user://logs` |

On Linux the local (non-roaming) data directory is the same folder as `user://`. The agent method `platform.paths` prints the paths of the machine you are on. Names Windows cannot store are refused on every platform, including Linux, so content authored here still packs for Windows. See [Windows](book/user-guide/windows.md).

## Cursor grab

`CursorGrab::Locked` and `CursorGrab::Confined` both work on Wayland. On X11 and Xwayland, winit 0.30.13 does not implement `Locked`, so a Locked request is sent as Confined and logged once per process. Confined on X11 stays Confined. See `regia_platform::window_os`.

## Windows of the game

Spec 11: a `Window` component updates the operating-system window in `PostUpdate`. In this version only the primary window becomes an operating-system window (ADR-2252). Extra `Window` entities with no handle are skipped. Runtime games normally use one window. The same limit holds on Windows and macOS.

## What you can ship

`regia package --platform linux` writes `dist/linux/<slug>-linux.tar.gz` by default. `--format dir` leaves the staged directory for inspection. `--format appimage` needs `appimagetool` on `PATH` (or `REGIA_APPIMAGETOOL`); the tool is not bundled. A shipping profile links against glibc 2.31 so the binary starts in Steam Linux Runtime, including on a Deck. `--glibc host` keeps this machine's glibc and does not start on older distributions.

`--container steam-sniper` or `--container debian12` compiles that binary inside a pinned toolchain image. The file you ship is still the tar, the directory, or the AppImage. It is not an image of the game. Details, error codes, and the dedicated-server package are on [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md).

A dedicated server is `regia package --server --platform linux`. Android and macOS refuse that flag with `server_platform_unsupported` (exit code 2).

From Linux, `regia package --platform windows` cross-compiles with cargo-xwin when `regia doctor --platform windows` is clean. The resulting exe is not run on the Linux host. Android packages are built from Linux as well; [Android device bring-up](book/user-guide/android-bringup.md) is the phone-side procedure.

## Check the machine

```sh
regia doctor --platform linux
regia doctor --verify-paks dist/linux/<slug>/content
```

Doctor exit codes, the Android and Deck checks, and `--verify-paks` are on [Checking your machine](book/user-guide/doctor.md). Warnings do not fail the command. A failed check does.

## What this version does not do

- No OpenGL renderer, and no general web game. The browser program is the [product viewer](book/agents/web-player.md) (WebGPU and WebGL2), which is a different target.
- No OpenXR loader. The simulator runs; `OpenXr` and `Auto` stay off with `xr_no_loader`. See [XR](book/agents/xr.md).
- No macOS or iOS package from this host. macOS is a testing build. An iOS release is parked.
- No console package.

Licenses written into every package are on [Licensing](book/user-guide/licensing.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/performance-overlay.md -->
# Performance overlay

Every Regia Engine game has a built-in performance overlay. It is a small panel in the top-left
corner that lets players and alpha testers see how the game runs and report it. It works in any
game that adds `regia::DefaultPlugins` (with the default `ui` feature). There is nothing else
to set up, and it costs nothing while it is hidden.

## What it shows

**Compact**

| Line | Meaning | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `144 FPS   6.9 ms   DesktopHigh` | Average FPS, median frame time of the last 5 s, and the render profile preset (`Custom` when the game changed the profile) | `Diagnostics`, the overlay's 5 s window, `RenderSettings::preset` |
| Graph | Frame time over the last ~5 s, newest on the right. Thin lines mark 16.7 ms (60 fps) and 33.3 ms (30 fps). Bars are green up to 16.7 ms, yellow up to 33.3 ms, orange-red above that, and **red** when a frame took more than twice the median (a stutter). The top of the graph is 50 ms. | `RealTime` delta, the same interval `play.hitch_report` records |
| Render CPU / GPU | The renderer's CPU time for the frame and the GPU frame time. The CPU number covers `FrameRenderer::render_into` only (cull, record, submit): not the game's simulation, extract, the swapchain acquire or the present, so it can be far below the frame time on a CPU-bound game. `GPU-bound` or `CPU-bound` appears when one of them is at least 90 % of the frame. `n/a` means the device has no timestamp queries. | `FrameRenderer::cpu_timings().total_ms`, `GpuTimings::frame_ms` |
| GPU top | The three most expensive GPU passes | `GpuTimings::passes` |
| Textures | Resident material textures against the texture budget. The line turns yellow above 90 % and red above 100 %. | `FrameRenderer::texture_memory_summary` (the same report as `assets.texture_memory`) |
| Stutters | Frames over 2 × median in the last 5 s, and in total since warm-up while the overlay was visible | `HitchReport` over the window |
| Creates | Pipelines and bind groups created after warm-up (the first 300 frames, and 60 frames after each level warm). Anything above 0 is a hitch source, so report it. | frame-path counters |
| Lighting | The lighting option (`Depth` or `Balanced`) and the frame's GI mode | `RenderSettings::effective_gi_look`, `FrameQuality::gi` |
| Resolution | Output size, internal render size, render scale and upscaler (`native`, `TAAU`, `TSR`, `FSR 3`, `SGSR`, `bilinear`) of the last view drawn | `FrameRenderer::last_extent` |

**Detailed** has everything in Compact, plus p50/p99/longest frame time, GPU memory (the
device memory the allocator reserves, and its sub-allocated part; Vulkan and D3D12), the process RSS, the overlay's own CPU time, and the full per-pass
GPU table: shadows, clusters, GI probes, prepass, cull, SSAO, contact shadows, forward, SSGI,
SSR, atmosphere, clouds, fog, TAAU, post, scene and frame.

The GPU memory and RSS lines are refreshed every 2 s by a short-lived worker thread
(`regia-perf-memory`, v0.1.14). The report walks the allocator's block list, which took
milliseconds on the frame thread before; now the frame never waits for it, and the lines show the
new numbers at the next refresh after the report finishes (up to 0.25 s later).

GPU timestamps are switched on while the overlay is visible and switched off again when it is
hidden, unless something else had already switched them on.

## Turning it on

The overlay is a **setting**, `GameSettings::performance_overlay`, saved with the other settings
in `user://settings.ron`:

- `None` (the default) follows the host's default.
- `Some(Off)`, `Some(Compact)` or `Some(Detailed)` is the player's choice. The player's choice
  always wins over the host's default.

**Add the option to your settings menu.** You can drop in the ready-made row, which is a label
and a dropdown that writes the player's choice:

```rust
use regia_app::prelude::*;
use regia_framework::perf_overlay::spawn_settings_entry;

fn build_graphics_page(world: &mut World, page: Entity) {
    spawn_settings_entry(world, Some(page)); // "Performance overlay  [Off | Compact | Detailed]"
}
```

To build your own control instead, use the descriptor `settings_menu_entry()`. It gives the
settings path, the label, the options and the help text. Write the choice with
`set_player_mode(world, mode)`, or set `GameSettings::performance_overlay = Some(mode)` yourself.

**Host default.** The engine's default is `Off`. A game can ship with the overlay on (DO27's
alpha uses `Compact`):

```rust
use regia_app::prelude::*;
use regia_framework::perf_overlay::{PerformanceOverlay, PerformanceOverlayMode};

fn configure(app: &mut App) {
    app.insert_resource(PerformanceOverlay::default_mode(PerformanceOverlayMode::Compact));
}
```

This only sets the default. A player who picks `Off` in the menu keeps `Off`.

**An optional key.** The overlay has no default key binding, because games use the F-keys for
their own controls. To add one, declare the `PERF_OVERLAY_ACTION` action
(`"PerformanceOverlay"`) in your `InputConfig` and bind it. Each press then cycles Off →
Compact → Detailed and saves the result as the player's choice. Players can rebind it like any
other action.

```rust
use regia_input::prelude::*;

fn input_config() -> InputConfig {
    InputConfig::new()
        .action("PerformanceOverlay", ActionKind::Button)
        .binding(Binding::new("PerformanceOverlay", InputSource::key("Backquote")))
}
```

**Agents** call `perf_overlay.toggle` and `perf_overlay.get`. See
[Performance overlay (agents)](book/agents/perf-overlay.md).

## Cost

| | CPU | GPU |
|---|---|---|
| Hidden | a few comparisons per frame | none (it draws nothing) |
| Visible | ≤ 0.1 ms per frame (release build) | ≤ 0.1 ms (one instanced UI draw of a few hundred quads) |

The graph redraws at 20 Hz and the text at 4 Hz. Changing the graph redraws only the overlay's
own UI subtree and never runs layout again. The window's boot warm builds the runtime UI's pipeline on a warm worker (job "overlay layers").
It does this for the window format and both display-stage formats, and the UI also compiles it on
the first frame it draws, even with nothing to draw. Showing the overlay later therefore creates
no pipelines and no bind groups. The test `crates/regia_framework/tests/perf_overlay.rs` checks
both bounds, the zero-create toggle, and that the panel is drawn in the corner and nowhere else.

## Hosts with their own renderer

A host that drives its own `FrameRenderer` instead of the runtime's `RuntimeRenderer` (such as the
lookdev chase) feeds the overlay after each frame:

```rust
use regia_app::prelude::*;
use regia_framework::perf_overlay::{PerfOverlayRendererSample, RendererSample};

fn after_frame(world: &mut World, renderer: &regia_render::FrameRenderer) {
    world.insert_resource(PerfOverlayRendererSample(RendererSample::of(renderer)));
}
```

`cargo run --release -p lookdev --features overlay --bin perf_overlay_shot` draws the overlay over
DO27's chase this way.

## Reporting performance (testers)

1. Turn on **Settings → Performance overlay → Detailed**.
2. Play the scene that feels slow until the graph shows it.
3. Take a screenshot that includes the overlay. Note the map, what was on screen, and the
   **Stutters** and **Creates** lines. A non-zero **Creates** count is always a bug.

# 2D: sprites, tilemaps, 2D physics

<!-- index: Sprite -->
<!-- index: Sprite atlas -->
<!-- index: Tilemap -->
<!-- index: Platformer -->
<!-- index: Physics 2D -->

Regia Engine's 2D toolkit ([spec 22](docs/specs/22-tier2.md) § T2.10 and
[spec 86](docs/specs/86-2d-toolkit.md)) draws sprites from packed atlases, plays sprite-sheet
animations, renders Tiled maps, gives you a pixel-perfect orthographic camera and two kinds of 2D
physics: a pixel-exact platformer model and rapier2d rigid bodies. The editor's 2D mode is a
separate editor-guide page. This chapter is the runtime and the data.

## Set up

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::two_d::{Sprite, Sprite2dPlugin, TileMap};
use regia_core::math::{UVec2, Vec3};
use regia_scene::Transform;
use regia_framework::camera::ortho::{Camera2d, Camera2dFollow, Camera2dPlugin};

fn build(app: &mut App) {
    app.add_plugins((Sprite2dPlugin, Camera2dPlugin));
    app.add_systems(Startup, |mut commands: Commands| {
        // A 320×180 pixel-perfect view, scaled by the largest whole number that fits the window.
        commands.spawn(Camera2d {
            pixel_perfect: Some(UVec2::new(320, 180)),
            clear: Some([0.12, 0.16, 0.22, 1.0]),
            ..Default::default()
        });
        commands.spawn(TileMap::new("assets/maps/level1.tmx"));
        commands.spawn((
            Sprite::named("assets/sprites/hero.atlas.ron", "hero"),
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(40.0, 16.0, 1.0)),
        ));
    });
}
```

The 2D world is **+X right, +Y up**; one world unit is one source pixel at zoom 1. A sprite's
world pose is its `GlobalTransform` (the `Transform` composed with its parents', after `TransformPropagate`; equal to `Transform` without a parent); its z is its draw order (higher in front); a tilemap's layers stack above its z. Sprites
draw over the 3D scene (after tonemapping) and under the runtime UI.

## Sprite atlases (`.atlas.ron`)

List your images in an `.atlas.ron` next to them; `regia cook` packs them into pages
(`texture_packer`'s skyline packer, deterministic) and keeps the pixels exact (no compression).

```ron
(
    version: 1,
    padding: 1,
    extrude: 1,          // repeat edge pixels: no bleeding when zoomed
    trim: true,          // pack only the opaque part; pivots still refer to the full image
    sprites: [
        (name: "hero", image: "hero.png", pivot: (0.5, 0.0)),                 // feet at the origin
        (name: "run", image: "hero_run.png", grid: Some((16, 16))),          // run_0, run_1, …
        (name: "panel", image: "ui/panel.png", nine_slice: Some((4, 4, 4, 4))),
    ],
)
```

- **Pivot**: `(0, 0)` bottom-left, `(1, 1)` top-right; `Sprite::anchor` overrides it per entity.
- **9-slice**: give the sprite a `size`; the corners keep their size, edges and center stretch. When the
  `size` is smaller than the borders added together, the two borders on that axis shrink
  proportionally (the center collapses to nothing).
- `Sprite::flip_x` / `flip_y`, `color` (tint), `visible`.

Format reference: `docs/formats/atlas-ron.md`.

## Sprite-sheet animation

```rust,wrap
use regia::two_d::{AnimatedSprite, Animation};
use regia::two_d::Sprite;
# use regia_ecs::prelude::Commands;
fn spawn_hero(mut commands: Commands) {
commands.spawn((
    Sprite::rect("assets/sprites/hero.atlas.ron", [0, 0, 16, 16]),
    AnimatedSprite::new(16, 16, &[
        Animation::new("idle", 0, 4, 8.0),
        Animation::new("run", 1, 6, 12.0),
        Animation::new("jump", 2, 3, 10.0).once(),   // holds its last frame
    ], true),
));
}
// later: animated.play("run");
```

One row per animation; the frame clock keeps its remainder, so playback speed does not depend on
the frame rate. `sheet_offset` is the pixel offset of tile (0, 0) inside the atlas rect; animated
sprites always sample atlas page 0 for now, so keep the run sheet on the first page.
`play(name)` restarts that animation unless it is already the current one and not finished (a paused
clip resumes where it stopped); once an animation is `finished`, `playing` is ignored.

## Tilemaps (Tiled)

Save maps from [Tiled](https://www.mapeditor.org) as `.tmx` (XML) or `.tmj` (JSON), with tilesets
embedded or as `.tsx`/`.tsj` files. `regia cook` imports them into the `.tilemap.ron` structure
(`docs/formats/tilemap-ron.md`) and embeds the tileset pixels. You can also write `.tilemap.ron`
yourself. Supported: finite maps in every Tiled orientation, CSV/base64 (zlib/gzip) layers, group layers
(flattened), flips (including diagonal), animated tiles, object layers, custom properties.

Collision for the platformer comes from tile properties in Tiled: set a string property
`collision` to `solid` or `one_way` (or a bool `solid` / `one_way`, or the tile's class), or draw a
collision shape on the tile.

At run time `SpriteAssets::tilemap(path)?.map` gives you the `TileMapAsset` for queries:
`tile_at(layer, x, y)`, `cell_at_world` and `collision_grid_all()`. `SpriteAssets::tilemap_mut(path)?`
returns it mutably to edit tiles (the renderer picks the edit up next frame). Saving the `.tmx` or
`.tmj` itself while `regia run --dev` or the editor is watching recooks that map and reloads it.
An external tileset (`.tsx` / `.tsj`) or its PNG does not pull the map in: cook the map again, then
restart the game, to see that change.

### Orientations

A map is `Orthogonal` (square grid), `Isometric` (diamond), `Staggered` (diamonds in offset rows or
columns) or `Hexagonal` (pointy or flat, with Tiled's stagger axis, stagger index and side length).
The importer reads Tiled's `orientation`, `staggeraxis`, `staggerindex` and `hexsidelength`. Cell
`(x, y)` is still the column and row of the layer data; `TileMapAsset::cell_at_world`,
`tile_world_rect` (the cell's bounding box), `tile_world_outline` and `tile_world_center` convert
between cells and the world for every orientation, and the sprite pass draws tiles back to front.
Tile images draw from the bottom-left of the cell's box, so taller tiles (trees, walls) overlap the
cells behind them.

Auto-tiling rules read the cells that touch a cell on screen: on staggered and hexagonal maps the
neighbors depend on the row (or column) being shifted, and a hexagon has six (pointy: no north or
south; flat: no west or east); the table is in `docs/specs/86-2d-toolkit.md` § 13. Use `Rules`
terrains on hexagons. Tiled stores object positions in map pixels, except on isometric maps, where
they are grid units scaled by the tile height; `TileMapAsset::object_world_position` converts either to
the map's world space (+Y up). Tiled 1.0 `<terraintypes>` import as corner Wang sets
(`regia tiled-autotile`).

## Auto-tiling

An `.autotile.ron` (`docs/formats/autotile-ron.md`) turns "this cell is grass" into the right edge,
corner or inner tile of a tileset. Each terrain picks its tile from its neighbours with one of four
layouts:

- `Edge16([..16 ids..])`: walls, pipes, fences. The index is N 1 + E 2 + S 4 + W 8.
- `Blob47([..47 ids..])`: ground, water, anything with inner corners. Entry *i* is drawn for the
  *i*-th of the 47 neighbour masks listed in the format page.
- `WangCorner([..16 ids..])`: corner-based sets. The index is which corners of the cell lie inside
  the terrain: TL 1 + TR 2 + BR 4 + BL 8; a corner counts when the cell and the three neighbours
  touching it are all the terrain. Tiled's corner, edge and mixed Wang sets (and Tiled 1.0
  terrains) import as `WangCorner`, `Edge16` and `Blob47` terrains with
  `regia tiled-autotile <tileset-or-map> [--out-dir DIR]` (a mask without a tile borrows the
  nearest mask's tile and the import warns).
- `Rules([(pattern: "?#? / ### / ?.?", tile: 12), …])`: your own 3×3 patterns, first match wins
  (`#` this terrain, `.` not, `?` either).

`variants` swaps a resolved tile for a weighted pick (flowers in the grass) that depends only on
the cell, so repainting never reshuffles them. The result is an ordinary tile layer: painting is an
authoring step, nothing changes at draw time.

`regia cook` turns each `.autotile.ron` into a binary payload stored with the other 2D assets, so a
shipped game loads its rules from the pak: `AutoTiles::load_from_server(name, path, &mut server)`
(or `tilemap.autotile_register` with `path`) gives the same rule set the raw file parses to.

```rust,ignore
use regia::two_d::autotile::{AutoTileSet, TerrainBrush};

let rules = AutoTileSet::from_ron(include_str!("../assets/maps/terrain.autotile.ron"))?;
let mut assets = world.resource_mut::<SpriteAssets>();
if let Some(map) = assets.tilemap_mut("assets/maps/level1.tilemap.ron") {
    let bound = rules.bind(map)?;
    let grass = rules.terrain_index("grass").unwrap_or(0);
    let layer = map.layer_index("ground").unwrap_or(0);
    // Paint a 10×3 patch; its border and the cells around it re-resolve.
    let cells: Vec<(u32, u32)> = (0..3).flat_map(|y| (0..10).map(move |x| (x, y))).collect();
    bound.paint(map, layer, TerrainBrush::Terrain(grass), &cells)?;
}
```

The result does not depend on the order you paint cells in. `apply_layer` re-resolves a whole layer
after hand edits. Register rule sets in `regia::two_d::AutoTiles` to make them available to agents
(`tilemap.paint`, `book/agents/2d.md`).

## The 2D editor mode

Press `B` in the editor viewport (or `editor.mode2d_set`, `book/agents/editor-2d.md`). The mode
loads the `.tilemap.ron` your level shows and switches to the front view, which looks at the 2D
plane (+X right, +Y up), and frames the map. When the level shows no such map, the **2D** tab opens:
use Open map… there. Open rules… loads an `.autotile.ron`.

Pick the brush in the 2D tab: a tile from the palette (with its flips), a terrain of the rule set, or
Erase. Left-drag paints; hold Shift to erase. Ctrl-drag copies a rectangle of cells into a
**stamp**; the stamp brush then pastes it centered on every painted cell, and the tab's Rotate and
Flip buttons turn it (the tiles' flips turn with it). Picking and the grid follow the map's
orientation. A stroke is one undo step. `,` `.` change the layer and
`[` `]` the terrain. The viewport shows the map's tiles as Play does, with the map bounds, the tile
grid, the cell under the pointer and a preview of the tile. Animated tiles show their first tile. Save
map writes the `.tilemap.ron`, as does saving the level, and the asset watcher re-cooks it. Tiled
sources are edited in Tiled.

### Tools, random brush, patterns, layers and guides

The **Tool** row of the 2D tab picks how a press paints: **Paint** (freehand), **Line** and
**Rectangle** (drag from one end or corner to the other; the cells show while you drag and land when
you let go; Rectangle has a **Filled** option), **Bucket** (fills the cells around the pressed one
that hold the same tile; turn **Contiguous** off to fill every such cell of the layer) and **Pick**
(click takes a cell's tile as the brush, drag takes a rectangle as the stamp; Ctrl does the same with
any tool). A right-click erases the cell under the pointer in every tool, or the bucket's region; a
right drag still pans the view. With the stamp brush, Line, Rectangle and Bucket repeat the stamp
over their cells.

**Random brush** paints one of several tiles per cell: turn it on, click palette tiles to add them,
set each tile's weight and the **Chance of nothing** (cells left alone). With a rule set loaded,
**Connect** joins a terrain to every neighbor of the same terrain, and **Path** joins only the cells
of the same stroke, so a path can run next to another without merging with it.

**Patterns** keeps stamps by name: type a name and **Save stamp as pattern**; click a pattern to make
it the stamp again. They are stored with the tileset in a `.tilepatterns.ron` next to its image, so
every map that uses the tileset sees them.

**Layers** lists the map's tile and object layers, top first, with their depth; **Raise** and
**Lower** change the drawing order. Pick a tile layer to paint it, or an object layer to edit its
objects: add, select, rename, move and delete them in the tab, or drag them in the view.

**Rulers and guides**: the view shows rulers along its top and left edges in level units. Drag from a
ruler to pull out a guide; drop it back on a ruler to remove it. Dragged objects snap to guides and
line up with the edges and centers of nearby objects, or space evenly between their neighbors, with
lines showing what they snapped to; hold Alt to place freely. Guides are saved with the editor's view
state for the level, not in the level.

## The camera

`Camera2d` (in `regia_framework::camera::ortho`) sets the zoom (`pixels_per_unit`), the optional
pixel-perfect virtual resolution with letterbox bars (`bar_color`), `snap` (round the center to
whole pixels so scrolling never shimmers) and the 2D clear color. `Camera2dFollow` follows an
entity with a deadzone and exponential lag. Mouse/touch to world:
`camera.screen_to_world(&transform, window_size, cursor)` (returns `None` on the bars).

## Platformer physics

`regia_physics::platformer2d` is the "actors and solids" model of pixel platformers (ported from
macroquad): actors move one whole pixel at a time with a sub-pixel remainder and stop at the first
pixel that would overlap; solids push actors and carry the ones standing on them; one-way tiles
only block a fall.

```rust,wrap
use regia::physics::platformer2d::*;
use regia::two_d::TileCollision;
# use regia_app::App;
# use regia_ecs::prelude::{Commands, Res, ResMut};
# use regia::two_d::SpriteAssets;
# use regia_core::math::{IVec2, Vec2};
# use regia_scene::Transform;
fn install_platformer(app: &mut App) {
    app.add_plugins(PlatformerPlugin);
}
fn add_tile_layer(
    mut world: ResMut<PlatformerWorld>,
    assets: Res<SpriteAssets>,
    mut commands: Commands,
) {
    // Static tiles from the map (rows bottom first).
    let Some(loaded) = assets.tilemap("assets/maps/level1.tmx") else { return; };
    let map = &loaded.map;
    let grid = map.collision_grid_all().iter().map(|c| match c {
        TileCollision::Solid => Tile::Solid,
        TileCollision::OneWay => Tile::JumpThrough,
        TileCollision::Empty => Tile::Empty,
    }).collect();
    world.add_static_tiled_layer(grid, 8, 8, map.width as usize, IVec2::ZERO, 1);
    commands.spawn((PlatformerActor { size: IVec2::new(8, 12), gravity: 600.0, ..Default::default() }, Transform::default()));
    commands.spawn((PlatformerSolid { size: IVec2::new(32, 8), velocity: Vec2::new(20.0, 0.0) }, Transform::default()));
}
```

Each fixed step moves solids, then actors (gravity, horizontal, vertical) and writes
`PlatformerContacts { grounded, hit_wall, hit_ceiling, squished }`. Set `drop_through` to fall
through a one-way platform.

## Rigid bodies (rapier2d)

Enable the `physics2d` feature (`regia = { features = ["physics2d"] }`) and add
`Physics2dPlugin`: `RigidBody2d` (dynamic/kinematic/static), `Collider2d` (ball, box, capsule,
segment, convex polygon, polyline), `Velocity2d`, `Collision2d` messages, and
`PhysicsWorld2d::raycast` / `entities_at`. Set `set_length_unit` to your typical object size when
you work in pixels.

## Limits

Not yet: 2D lights, and sprites other than the map's tiles inside the editor viewport (animated
tiles play there; Play shows the rest).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/clip-compression.md -->
# Animation clip compression

`regia_animation::clip_compress` cooks an `AnimationClip`'s skeletal tracks into a smaller
quantised form under an object-space error bound, checked at every key time, the midpoints between
keys and a uniform grid (the report shows the measured maximum). It is a cook-time tool: the
runtime only pays for interpolation.

## API

```rust,wrap
use regia_animation::clip_compress::{compress, CompressOptions};
# use regia_animation::{AnimationClip, Skeleton};
# let clip = AnimationClip::empty("wave", 1.0);
# let skeleton = Skeleton::default();

let options = CompressOptions::new(0.01); // 1 cm maximum object-space error per bone
let cooked = compress(&clip, &skeleton, &options)?;

let mut pose = skeleton.bind_pose_pose();
cooked.sample(0.25, &mut pose);

let report = cooked.report();
assert!(report.max_error <= options.tolerance);
println!("{} -> {} bytes", report.original_bytes, report.compressed_bytes);
```

`compress` returns a `CompressError` for invalid input (NaN or infinite key times or values,
a degenerate quaternion, duplicate or out-of-range tracks, a non-positive tolerance) instead of
panicking. `CompressedClip::sample` is a pure function of the stored data and the sample time,
so decompression is bit-deterministic. Start from the bind pose: channels that reproduce the
bind pose within tolerance are dropped, and sampling leaves those joints untouched.

## How it works

Error is measured where it is seen. Each bone carries probe points — its origin plus six points
at its _shell distance_ (`shell_radius`, default 1 unit; per bone via `per_bone_shell`), standing
in for its farthest skinned vertices. A candidate approximation is charged for the displacement
of those probes in model space after forward kinematics, for the bone itself **and every
descendant**, so a small root rotation error that swings a distant hand counts as the large error
it is.

Bones are reduced root-first. Each channel gets an equal share of every descendant's tolerance
(`tolerance`, overridable per bone via `per_bone_tolerance`), so the whole-clip error stays
within tolerance by the triangle inequality; a final verification pass measures the real error
and restores full key sets on any chain that overruns. Per channel the compressor tries, in
order: dropping the track (bind value), collapsing it to a constant, then iterative
least-error key removal on the quantised keys — repeatedly removing the interior key whose
removal causes the least object-space error while the budget holds. End keys are never removed.

## Storage formats

| Channel | Format |
|---|---|
| Rotations | Smallest-three packing: 48 bits (2-bit dropped index + 3×15-bit) or 32 bits (2 + 3×10-bit), chosen per track by its packed error (`RotationFormatPreference`) |
| Translations, scales | Per-track range-normalised 16-bit keys (per-axis min/max stored once) |
| Constant tracks | One stored value |
| Bind-pose tracks | Dropped (no keys) |

Decompression lerps translations and scales and uses normalised lerp for rotations.

## The report

`CompressionReport` records `original_bytes` and `compressed_bytes` under a stated size model
(raw `f32` storage versus the quantised layout, both excluding serde framing), key counts
before and after, and `max_error_per_bone` — the measured maximum probe displacement per bone.
If an extremely small tolerance is below what quantisation alone can represent, the report says
so (`max_error` above tolerance) rather than failing.

Only skeletal TRS tracks are carried. Morph tracks, notifies, named curves and property tracks
are not part of this format; cook those through `regia_animation::compress`.
