# Montages, sync groups and motion warping

<!-- index: Montage -->
<!-- index: Sync group -->
<!-- index: Motion warping -->
<!-- index: Anim slot -->

A **montage** is a one-shot action (an attack, a reload, a vault, an emote) that gameplay starts on a character and
that plays over the character's anim graph. **Sync groups** keep locomotion cycles of different lengths in step while
they blend. **Motion warping** bends a montage's root motion at runtime so the character lands where the game needs
it (on the enemy it lunges at, on the ledge it vaults onto). Spec: [spec 17](docs/specs/17-animation.md) § 4b
and [spec 34](docs/specs/34-montage-extensions.md). A combat procedure that starts a montage from a hit is
[Combat and abilities](book/how-to/play/combat-abilities.md).

## The montage asset (`.montage.ron`)

```ron
(
    format_version: 1,
    name: "attack",
    tracks: [
        (slot: "full_body", segments: [(clip: "Windup"), (clip: "Swing", rate: 1.2), (clip: "Recover", end: Some(0.6))]),
    ],
    sections: [
        (name: "windup", start: 0.0),
        (name: "swing", start: 0.5, next: Jump("recover")),
        (name: "combo", start: 1.1, next: Stop),
        (name: "recover", start: 1.6, next: Stop),
    ],
    notifies: [
        (name: "combo_input", time: 0.9, branch: true),
        (name: "hitbox", time: 0.6, duration: 0.25, payload: Some("(damage: 20)")),
        (name: "swoosh", time: 0.55),
    ],
    blend_in: (time: 0.15, curve: Smooth),
    blend_out: (time: 0.25, curve: Smooth),
    warps: [(target: "enemy", start: 0.2, end: 0.6, rotation: true)],
)
```

- **Tracks**: one per slot. A track's segments play back to back from time 0 (`start`/`end` trim the clip, `rate`
  speeds it up, `loops` repeats it). Track 0 is the main track: it gives the root motion and decides the slot group.
- **Sections** split the timeline. `next` is `Continue` (default: play on into the next section), `Stop` (the montage
  ends at this section's end) or `Jump("name")`; a section that jumps to itself loops. The first section starts at 0;
  without sections the montage has one section, `main`.
- **Notifies**: `duration: 0` fires once; `duration > 0` is a window with a begin and an end event. `branch: true` is a
  branching point: playback stops exactly at that time inside the frame, so a decision made in advance applies at the
  right moment whatever the frame rate.
- `blend_in`, `blend_out`, `blend_out_lead` (seconds before the end the blend-out starts; default the blend-out time),
  `auto_blend_out: false` (hold the last pose until stopped), `root_motion: false` (the montage does not move the
  character), `root_motion_off: [(start, end)]` (windows where gameplay steers instead), `warps` (below),
  `sync_group: Some("gait")` (while the montage blends out, its clip leads that sync group, so the locomotion the
  character returns to is already in step).

`Montage::from_ron_str` loads and validates a file; `regia upgrade-project` knows the format.

## Slots

Slots are the named places montages play into. Define them on the rig's `MontagePlayer`:

```rust,wrap
use regia_animation::prelude::*;
# use regia_ecs::prelude::World;
# let mut world = World::new();
# let rig = world.spawn_empty().id();
let player = MontagePlayer::new(
    vec![
        SlotDef::full_body("full_body", "body"),
        SlotDef::masked("upper_body", "upper", &["spine_01"]), // spine_01 and its children
    ],
    ClipLibrary::default(), // the clips montages use (the animator's library is searched after it)
);
world.entity_mut(rig).insert(player);
```

A montage track blends over the graph's pose through its slot's mask, by the montage's blend weight. An upper-body
reload therefore leaves the legs to the locomotion graph, and adds no root motion (the mask does not cover the
skeleton root). Playing a montage whose main slot is in the same **group** as a playing one interrupts it: the old
one blends out over the new one's blend-in time.

## Playing from game code

```rust,wrap
# use regia_animation::*;
# use regia_animation::montage::SectionNext;
# use regia_animation::montage_player::BranchAction;
# let mut player: MontagePlayer = todo!();
# let (attack, recover): (std::sync::Arc<Montage>, std::sync::Arc<Montage>) = todo!();
# let enemy_position = regia_core::math::Vec3::ZERO;
let id = player.play(attack.clone(), PlayOptions { rate: 1.0, ..PlayOptions::default() });
player.on_branch(Some(id), "combo_input", BranchAction::JumpTo("combo".into())); // the player pressed attack again
player.set_warp_target("enemy", WarpTarget::at(enemy_position));
player.queue(recover.clone(), PlayOptions::default());    // after this one
player.jump_to_section(None, "recover");
player.set_next_section(None, "swing", SectionNext::Stop);
player.stop(None, Some(0.1));
```

Read `MontageEvent` messages for what happened: `Started`, `Section { from, to }`, `Notify { name, payload }`,
`WindowBegin` / `WindowEnd`, `BranchPoint`, `BlendingOut { interrupted }` and `Ended { interrupted }`
(`interrupted: false` means it completed). Clip notifies inside the montage's clips still arrive as `AnimNotify`
while the montage dominates the pose (weight at least one half). `player.instances()` shows section, time, weight and
phase of every playing montage.

## Motion warping

A warp window names a target. While montage time is inside the window and the target is set
(`set_warp_target`), every frame's root motion is corrected so the character's origin reaches the target at the
window's end: the remaining motion of the window is turned and scaled onto the remaining distance, so the move
keeps its shape (a lunge stays a lunge, only longer or angled). `rotation: true` also turns the character to the
target's `facing`, or toward the target. Turning toward the target assumes the rig faces −Z in its object space;
a rig authored facing another axis should pass `facing`. `vertical: true` adjusts the height too (for a vault). The target can move
during the window; the rest of the window re-aims. The character must be root-motion driven
(`regia_framework::character::RootMotionDriven`) for the warped motion to move it.

Only montage time inside the window is warped. A frame that crosses the window's start or end is split there: the
authored motion before the start and after the end plays as authored, so the character lands on the target exactly
at the window end even when no frame ends there, then carries on with the montage's own motion (spec 34 § 4a). A
scripted warp splits the frame it ends in the same way.

## Sync groups (`.sync.ron`)

```ron
(
    format_version: 1,
    groups: [(name: "gait", roles: [("StartWalk", AlwaysLead)])],
    markers: [
        (clip: "Walk", markers: [(name: "left", time: 0.0), (name: "right", time: 0.52)]),
        (clip: "Run", markers: [(name: "left", time: 0.05), (name: "right", time: 0.33)]),
    ],
)
```

Load it with `SyncSetup::from_ron_str` and set it on the animator with
`animator.set_sync_setup(Some(Arc::new(setup)))`. Every graph `Clip` node whose `sync_group` names a declared group
joins it. The heaviest clip leads (`AlwaysLead` clips lead whenever they play, `NeverLead` clips never do); the
others follow its clock and stay quiet (no notifies). With at least two marker names shared by both clips, a follower
matches the leader's position between markers (a 4-step run lines its foot plants up with a 2-step walk); otherwise
it matches the leader's normalised phase. Groups that are not declared keep the old behaviour, so existing graphs are
unchanged. A synced blend space in a declared group joins it as one member (its weighted cycle, by normalised phase),
so an idle clip and a walk/run space cross-fade in step.

## Reverse, time-stretch and editing (ADR-1870)

`PlayOptions { reverse: true, .. }` plays a montage backward, from its end (or the end of `section`, minus
`start_time`) to 0; `MontagePlayer::set_reverse(id, on)` turns a playing montage around. Sections are crossed
backward (their forward links are not taken), notifies fire when crossed, and the rig moves back along the
authored root motion. Warp windows are off in reverse. `PlayOptions { duration: Some(0.8), .. }` sets the play rate
so the montage (rate curve included) takes 0.8 s; `MontagePlayer::stretch_to(id, seconds)` does the same for the
rest of a playing montage.

`Montage::edit_segment(track, segment, start, end)` trims a segment and moves the notifies and sections linked to it
with `follow` (`KeepTime`, `ShiftWithStart`, `ScaleWithLength`); `Montage::apply_edit(&MontageEdit, lengths)` covers
the other edits (add, reorder or remove segments, sections, links, notifies, blends, warp windows). Edits are
atomic: an edit that would leave the montage invalid changes nothing.

## Montages inside the anim graph

A `Slot { name, source, eval_idle_source }` node (`.animgraph.ron` v3) plays slot `name`'s montages at that point of
the graph: `source` plays while nothing is in the slot, and the montage pose is blended over it while something is.
Nodes above the slot node (IK, layers, look-at) then work on the montage pose, so a two-bone IK on top keeps a hand
on a ledge during a vault. Slots no node names keep blending after the whole graph, as before.

The `anim_lab` sample plays one end to end (`samples/anim_lab/src/slot_graph.rs`). Its graph holds a `Grip` layer over
a Slot node, so the hand keeps its grip while a wave montage moves the arm:

```ron
(
    format_version: 3,
    parameters: [("Grip", Float(1.0))],
    root: Layer((
        base: Slot((
            name: "upper",
            source: Clip((clip: "Idle", looping: true, speed: 1.0, sync_group: None)),
        )),
        layers: [(
            graph: Clip((clip: "Grip", looping: true, speed: 1.0, sync_group: None)),
            mask: (joints: ["hand"], include_children: true),
            mode: Override,
            weight_param: "Grip",
        )],
    )),
)
```

The same wave then plays backward in half its length (`PlayOptions { reverse: true, duration: Some(0.5), .. }`) and as
a child montage (`assets/wave_short.montagevar.ron`, which swaps the clip and keeps the timing). Run its checks with
`cargo test -p anim_lab`; `cargo run -p anim_lab` prints the `slot_graph:` line with the measured heights.

## Limits

- Montages play forward or in reverse with `rate >= 0`; a negative rate is refused.
- Motion warping is computed along the timeline as authored: a section jump during a warp window skips warping for
  that frame.
- Blend spaces join named groups by normalised phase only (no marker sync for spaces).
- The editor's Montage timeline panel (spec 34 M10, `book/agents/editor-data-panels.md`) edits montages; you can
  also author the RON by hand, through `Montage::apply_edit`, or through the agent protocol (`anim.montage_edit`,
  `book/agents/montages.md`).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/inertialization.md -->
# Inertialized transitions

A state-machine transition can **cross-fade** (the default) or **inertialize**. A cross-fade
evaluates the old and the new state for the whole `duration` and blends them. A short cross-fade
between two different poses still pops: the blend moves the pose, and its velocity, too fast. An
inertialized transition switches to the new state at once and evaluates only that state, at full
weight. At the switch it records, per joint, how far the shown pose is from the new state's pose
and how fast that gap is changing. It adds this offset back on top of the new state and decays it
to zero over `duration`. Nothing jumps, the motion keeps its momentum, and while the transition
runs it costs one state evaluation instead of two.

## Turning it on

Set `blend` on a transition. `duration` becomes the decay time:

```ron,animgraph
(
    format_version: 2,
    parameters: [("Air", Bool(false)), ("Dead", Bool(false)), ("FireWeight", Float(0.0))],
    root: Layer((
        base: StateMachine((
            initial: "Loco",
            states: [
                ("Loco", Clip((clip: "run", looping: true, speed: 1.0, sync_group: None))),
                ("Air", Clip((clip: "jetpack_hover", looping: true, speed: 1.0, sync_group: None))),
                ("Land", Clip((clip: "land", looping: false, speed: 1.0, sync_group: None))),
                ("Death", Clip((clip: "death", looping: false, speed: 1.0, sync_group: None))),
            ],
            transitions: [
                (from: Some("Loco"), to: "Air", conditions: [Bool(param: "Air", value: true)],
                 duration: 0.15, curve: Smooth, interruptible: true, blend: Inertialize),
                (from: Some("Air"), to: "Land", conditions: [Bool(param: "Air", value: false)],
                 duration: 0.15, curve: Linear, interruptible: true, blend: Inertialize),
                (from: Some("Land"), to: "Loco", conditions: [ClipFinished],
                 duration: 0.2, curve: Smooth, interruptible: false),
                (from: None, to: "Death", conditions: [Bool(param: "Dead", value: true)],
                 duration: 0.2, curve: Linear, interruptible: true, blend: InertializeSpring),
            ],
        )),
        layers: [(
            graph: Clip((clip: "aim_fire", looping: true, speed: 1.0, sync_group: None)),
            mask: (joints: ["spine_01"], include_children: true),
            mode: Override,
            weight_param: "FireWeight",
            weight_inertialize: 0.15,
        )],
    )),
)
```

| `blend` | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Crossfade` (default; also what an omitted `blend` means) | Blends both states with `curve` over `duration`. |
| `Inertialize` | Only the target state plays. The offset decays with a quintic polynomial (David Bollo, GDC 2018). It ends exactly at `duration` and never overshoots. If the old pose was moving *away* from the new one, that part of its velocity is dropped, so the pose never swings further out than either state. |
| `InertializeSpring` | Only the target state plays. The offset decays as a critically damped spring (Daniel Holden's spring inertialization). Velocity carries over completely, even when it points away. The spring can overshoot a little and leaves < 0.5 % of the offset at `duration`, which is dropped. |

`curve` is ignored by the inertialized modes. Good starting points are 0.15–0.3 s. An
inertialized transition can be longer than the cross-fade it replaces, because the new state is
already fully in charge from the first frame.

**Interruptions.** When another transition fires while one is running, an inertialized
transition starts again from the pose that is on screen and from its velocity, so an interrupted
transition does not pop either. A cross-fade that interrupts an inertialized transition keeps the
old offset decaying on top. A cross-fade that interrupts a cross-fade still drops the old source
state (the v1 behaviour).

**Layer weights.** `weight_inertialize` (seconds, default 0) on a layer eases weight changes the
same way. When gameplay snaps `FireWeight` from 0 to 1, the upper body moves into the aim pose
over 0.15 s, continuing whatever motion it had, instead of snapping. With 0 the weight follows the
parameter directly.

## What else to know

- **Everything after the state machine still applies.** The offset is added to the state
  machine's output, so layers with bone masks, two-bone IK, foot IK, look-at and root motion work
  unchanged. A `BlendSpace2D` with a sync group can be a target state.
- **Only the target state runs during the transition.** It fires the notifies and curves and
  supplies the root motion from the first frame. The old state stops at the switch.
- **Old files load unchanged.** Version 1 files have no `blend`, so they load as cross-fades
  through the 1 → 2 migrator. Regia Engine writes `blend` and `weight_inertialize` only when they are
  not the default.
- **Cost.** A machine that has at least one inertialized transition copies its output pose once a
  frame (the velocity history). On the switch frame the target state is evaluated twice, once as
  a side-effect-free probe one frame back, to get its velocity. While the transition runs, only
  one state is evaluated.

## In the editor and for agents

The graph editor's transition inspector has a **Blend** row (Crossfade / Inertialize /
Inertialize (spring)). The state-machine canvas labels inertialized arrows `inertial`, and spring
ones `inertial~`. Layers have a **Weight inertialize (s)** slider. During play-in-editor, the debug
overlay and `anim.get_state` show the running transition's mode and the offset still decaying
(`book/agents/inertialization.md`).

Method and sources: `docs/provenance.md` ("Inertialized state-machine transitions"), ADR-203.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/character-rig.md -->
# Character rigs: twist bones, drivers, pose-space correctives, skeleton profiles

Four pieces that make a skinned character hold up at the joints. All run on the CPU in `regia_animation`, after the
animator evaluates and before the pose is written to the joints. They are data driven by two RON files:
`docs/formats/drivers-ron.md` and `docs/formats/skelprofile-ron.md`.

## Twist and helper bones (C5)

A hand that rolls 90 degrees on one forearm joint pinches the skin at the wrist. Put twist joints along the forearm and let
each carry a share of the roll:

```ron
twists: [(
    name: "forearm_twist", source: "hand", axis: (0.0, 1.0, 0.0),
    driven: [(joint: "twist1", weight: 0.3333), (joint: "twist2", weight: 0.6667)],
)],
```

The roll is measured as the twist of the source's rotation away from its bind rotation about `axis`. Each driven joint
turns about its own copy of the axis by `weight * roll`. The largest step between neighbouring rings drops from the full
roll to a third. If the twist joints are *parents* of the source, set `source_keep` below 1 so the source's own roll shrinks
by the share the chain now carries.

A **helper** joint follows a fraction of another joint's rotation and can slide along a path keyed on that rotation
(shoulder pads, kneecaps). `follow: 0.5` bisects the source's motion.

## Drivers (C4)

A driver reads one channel, maps it through a curve, and writes another. Inputs: an animator parameter, a morph weight,
or a joint's roll, swing or total rotation. Outputs: a morph weight, a material parameter (wrinkle maps), or a joint's
rotation, translation or scale. Drivers run in file order and see each other's morph writes, so one can feed another.

```ron
drivers: [(
    name: "elbow_bulge",
    input: JointAngle(joint: "fore", axis: (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)),
    curve: (keys: [(location: 0.0, value: 0.0, kind: Linear), (location: 100.0, value: 1.0, kind: Linear)]),
    output: Morph("elbow_bulge"),
)],
```

## Pose-space correctives (C4)

Sculpt a corrective morph target at the pose where the mesh collapses (an elbow at 140 degrees) and list the pose
with the weights wanted there. Between listed poses the weights blend smoothly with radial basis functions (Lewis, Cordner &
Fong, SIGGRAPH 2000); at rest the correction is zero and at each listed pose it equals what you authored. These are
authored examples, not learned pose features.

## Attach to a rig

```rust,wrap
use std::sync::Arc;
use regia_animation::{DriverSet, NamedMorphs, RigDrivers, Skeleton};
# use regia_ecs::prelude::World;
# let skeleton = Skeleton::default();
# let mut world = World::new();
# let rig = world.spawn_empty().id();

let set = DriverSet::from_ron_str(&std::fs::read_to_string("hero.drivers.ron")?)?;
// The names of your morph bank, in bank order. NamedMorphs::from_set(&set) is the default
// order (first appearance in the file). Any type can implement `MorphNames`.
let morphs = NamedMorphs::from_set(&set);
let compiled = set.compile(&skeleton, &morphs)?;     // reports every unresolved name at once
world.entity_mut(rig).insert(RigDrivers::new(Arc::new(compiled)));
```

The result lands in the rig's `MorphWeights` (indexed like your names), its joint transforms and skin palette, and
`RigDrivers::state` (driver inputs and outputs, material values). The animator's own pose is not modified.
The morph names are a trait (`MorphNames`) because naming the morph bank is the morph-target lane's job: hand your names in.

## Skeleton profiles (C7)

A `SkeletonProfile` is the canonical joint list of a rig family: names, hierarchy, retarget roles, import aliases, rest
pose rule. Use it to validate imports and to feed the retargeter:

```rust,wrap
# let skeleton: regia_animation::Skeleton = todo!();
use regia_animation::SkeletonProfile;

let profile = SkeletonProfile::vrm_humanoid();       // or generic_humanoid(), or from_ron_str(..)
let report = profile.check_skeleton(&skeleton);      // missing / extra joints, hierarchy, arm elevation
assert!(report.ok(), "{report:?}");
let roles = profile.retarget_profile(&skeleton);     // role -> this skeleton's joint name
// A-pose rig into a T-pose bind: the pose to preview or bake against.
let t_pose = profile.rest_pose_normalization(&skeleton, regia_animation::RestPoseRule::TPose { tolerance_deg: 5.0 });
```

Built-ins: `generic-humanoid` (22 roles, Mixamo aliases) and `vrm` (adds eyes, jaw and finger bones, T-pose within 10
degrees). DO27's 67-joint profile is a `.skelprofile.ron` the DO27 repo owns.

## Agent surface

`anim.rig_attach`, `anim.rig_state` and `anim.profile_check`: see [Character rigs (agents)](book/agents/character-rig.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/morph-targets.md -->
# Morph targets and skinned meshes

Faces, visemes, correctives and a character creator's body sliders are **morph targets** (blend
shapes): per-vertex offsets the renderer adds to a mesh, scaled by a weight per target. Regia Engine
applies them on the GPU, per instance, under skinning, and drives the weights from animation clips,
anim graphs, expression layers, game code and the agent protocol.

## Drawing a morphed mesh

A cooked mesh (cooked mesh format v2 and later; v3 is current) carries its sparse targets. Pack them once per mesh and put
them, with the weights, on the entity that draws the mesh:

```rust,wrap
use std::sync::Arc;
use regia_render::{CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, MeshMorphTargets, MeshRenderer, MorphTargets};
use regia_scene::components::MorphWeights;
# use regia_ecs::prelude::World;
# let bytes: &[u8] = &[];
# let material = Arc::new(CpuMaterial::default());
# let mut world = World::new();

let cooked = regia_asset::load_mesh_bytes(&bytes)?.mesh;          // regia_asset::CpuMesh
let mesh = Arc::new(CpuMesh::from_cooked(&cooked)?);
let targets = MorphTargets::from_cooked(&mesh, &cooked)?;           // None without targets
let mut entity = world.spawn(MeshRenderer::new(mesh, material));
if let Some(targets) = targets {
    let count = targets.len();
    entity.insert((MeshMorphTargets::new(targets), MorphWeights(vec![0.0; count])));
}
```

- `MeshMorphTargets` holds the packed targets (shared by every instance of the mesh through the
  `Arc`) and the **mode**: `MorphMode::Game` (the default) applies the 16 largest weights,
  `MorphMode::Creator` applies every weight (hundreds of sliders).
- `MorphWeights` (one weight per target, target order) is the instance's weights. Without it the
  mesh draws undeformed.
- The render plugin gives the entity a `MorphTargetNames` (the target names) on its own, so weights
  can be set by name.
- `spawn_gltf_hierarchy` (editor and tools) does all of this for glTF meshes with targets, with the
  file's default weights and `extras.targetNames`.

How it works: when an instance's weights change, a compute pass writes its deformed vertices into
the instance's own copy of the mesh, and every pass (shadows, depth, colour, motion vectors,
instancing) draws that copy. Instances whose weights did not change cost nothing; weight changes
create no GPU buffers. Skinning deforms the morphed vertices, so faces animate on skinned
characters. `RenderOverride` (tint, ghost, x-ray) and mask recolor work on morphed instances as on
any other.

Limits:

- A morphed instance does not batch with other instances of the same mesh (its vertices are its
  own). A crowd with identical expressions is cheaper with the weights left at zero.
- A rigid morphed instance writes motion vectors on frames its weights change (ADR-2652), so TAA
  reprojects it. A skinned morph writes its skinning motion only, so a fast expression change on a
  skinned face can ghost slightly under TAA.
- A mesh whose vertex count differs from the targets' (another LOD), and a shadow-only LOD draw,
  draw undeformed.
- Mid-play, the first frame that needs the morph pass may draw undeformed while the pass compiles
  in the background. A warmed level (`warm_extracted` with the morphed instances in the frame) has
  it ready.

## Weights from animation

Clips carry morph weight tracks (`MorphTrack`, from glTF `weights` channels). An `Animator` on a rig
with a `SkinnedMesh` blends them like joint tracks and writes `MorphWeights` every frame.

On top of the animator, `MorphLayers` composes expression layers, in order:

```rust,wrap
use regia_animation::prelude::*;
# use regia_ecs::prelude::World;
# let mut world = World::new();
# let rig = world.spawn_empty().id();

let layers = MorphLayers {
    layers: vec![
        // Visemes from the dialogue system replace the clip's mouth shapes.
        MorphLayer::new("visemes", MorphLayerMode::Override).with("aa", 0.7),
        // A smile on top of whatever plays, as strong as the graph's "Smile" parameter.
        MorphLayer {
            weight_param: Some("Smile".into()),
            ..MorphLayer::new("smile", MorphLayerMode::Additive).with("mouthSmile", 1.0)
        },
    ],
    // Every weight is clamped to 0..=1 (the default), then each set is normalized: one mouth
    // shape at a time.
    normalized_sets: vec![MorphSet {
        name: "visemes".into(),
        targets: vec!["aa".into(), "oh".into(), "ee".into()],
    }],
    ..MorphLayers::default()
};
world.entity_mut(rig).insert(layers);
```

- **Override** moves a weight toward the layer's value by the layer weight; **Additive** adds
  `value × weight`.
- `weight_param` multiplies the layer weight by a float graph parameter (`animator.set("Smile", 0.5)`).
- Targets are named by index or by name (resolved through `MorphTargetNames`).
- With `MorphLayers`, `MorphWeights` is an output, rewritten every frame. Without an animator the
  layers compose over zero.
- Without either, `MorphWeights` is yours: set it from game code
  (`weights.set_named(&names, "blink", 1.0)`).

## Skinned meshes

`SkinnedMesh { skeleton, joints }` binds a mesh entity to a `Skeleton` and its joint entities (it
replaces `SkeletonBinding`, which is now a deprecated alias of the same type). Add
`regia_framework::skinning::SkinnedMeshPlugin` and the renderer gets the joint palette without
any glue:

- with an `Animator`, the palette the animation publishes (`SkinPalette`);
- without one, the palette of the joint entities' world transforms, so joints posed by a glTF
  hierarchy, a pose sampler or physics deform the mesh.

The plugin inserts `SkinJoints` when it is missing. Hosts that fill `SkinJoints` themselves (an
external simulation's poses) leave the plugin out.

## Agents

`anim.morph_weights` and `anim.set_morph_weights` read and set weights by name or index
([Morph weights](book/agents/morph-weights.md)).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/eyes-and-bind-poses.md -->
# Eye gaze and per-instance bind poses

Two components for characters: `Gaze` makes the eyes follow a target with limits and eyelid follow, and
`InstanceBindPose` gives one avatar its own proportions over a shared skeleton and clip set. Both are added
to the rig entity (the one with `Animator` and `SkinnedMesh`). Neither changes a rig that does not have it.

## Eye gaze

```rust,wrap
use regia_animation::prelude::*;
# use regia_animation::gaze::{Gaze, GazeRig, GazeTarget, LidMorphMap};
# use regia_ecs::prelude::World;
# let skeleton = Skeleton::default();
# let morph_names: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
# let mut world = World::new();
# let player = world.spawn_empty().id();
# let character = world.spawn_empty().id();
let mut rig = GazeRig::from_skeleton(&skeleton)
    .ok_or_else(|| std::io::Error::other("eye joints by name"))?;
rig.convergence = 1.0;       // each eye aims at the target; 0 = parallel eyes
rig.saccade_speed = 9.0;     // radians per second; 0 = instant
let mut gaze = Gaze::new(rig);
gaze.morphs = LidMorphMap::from_arkit_names(&morph_names); // optional: eyeLookUpLeft, ...
gaze.target = GazeTarget::Entity(player);                   // or Point(world), or None
world.entity_mut(character).insert(gaze);
```

- The eyes turn to the target inside per-eye limits (`EyeLimits`, default 35° in, 40° out, 26° up, 31° down). A
  target outside the limits pins the eye at the limit; `result().saturated` says so.
- A new target is reached by a fast turn (a saccade, 9 rad/s by default), not a snap.
- Targets nearer than `min_distance` (0.25 m) are pushed out so the eyes never cross absurdly.
- Lids: add `LidSpec` entries (`upper ≈ 0.7`, `lower ≈ 0.2` of the eye's pitch). They turn on top of the clip's lid
  rotation, so blinks keep working. `GazeRig::from_skeleton` finds `upper_lid`/`lower_lid` joints by name.
- Morphs: the four channels per eye (`eyeLookUp`, `eyeLookDown`, `eyeLookIn`, `eyeLookOut`, 0..1 of the eye limit) go
  to a `GazeMorphSink`. `LidMorphMap` maps them to morph target indices of the rig's `MorphWeights`.
- Head: set `rig.head = Some(HeadFollow { chain, weight })` and the head turns first; the eyes cover the rest.
- `weight` blends the whole effect with the animation (0 = untouched).

## Per-instance bind poses

```rust,wrap
# use regia::prelude::*;
# use regia_core::math::{Vec3, Quat};
# use regia_scene::Transform;
# let mut commands: Commands = todo!();
# let world: &mut World = todo!();
# let app: &mut App = todo!();
# use regia_animation::InstanceBindPose;
# let (skeleton, bone_scales, joint_positions, baked_inverse_binds): (regia_animation::Skeleton, std::collections::HashMap<String, f32>, Vec<Vec3>, Vec<regia_core::math::Mat4>) = todo!();
# let character: Entity = todo!();
let tall = InstanceBindPose::uniform(&skeleton, 1.12)?;
let long_legs = InstanceBindPose::from_bone_scales(&skeleton, &bone_scales)?;
let refit = InstanceBindPose::from_joint_positions(&skeleton, &joint_positions)?
    .with_inverse_binds(baked_inverse_binds)?; // the frame the baked mesh was skinned in
commands.entity(character).insert(tall);
```

The clips and graph stay as authored for the shared skeleton. The final pose moves onto the instance's rest pose:
rotations keep their offset from rest, translations keep their offset scaled by the bone length, so hip bobs and
strides scale with the legs. Joint transforms, sockets, joint globals and the skin palette all follow the instance.
The shared `Skeleton` asset is never edited. Root motion is not scaled; a body whose legs differ from the shared
skeleton at the same character speed slides a little, which `foot_ik` corrects. 100 avatars of 60 joints retarget and
build palettes in well under the 2 ms budget (see the agent page for the measurement).

<!-- source: book/start/editor-tour.md -->
# Editor tour

`regia-editor` is a docking editor built on the engine's own ECS: the panels edit the same
world data your game runs, and every edit goes through one undo stack.
[Editor](book/user-guide/editor.md) is the full chapter. The
[agent guide's editor page](book/agents/editor.md) lists the `editor.*` methods that drive every
panel action from a script or an AI agent.

## Opening a project

```console
$ regia-editor --project my_game
```

Without `--project` the editor starts on the **project browser**: recent projects, a Blank
quick-create, and Open folder. With `--project` it opens the folder that holds `Regia.toml` and
loads its `startup_level`. `--game <crate>` names the game crate to host for code hot reload
([Hot reload](book/user-guide/hot-reload.md)).

## The window

The default layout docks these panels; drag a tab to rearrange them.

| Panel | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Viewport** | The 3D scene: procedural sky, your entities, a reference grid, the transform gizmo and selection labels. |
| **Outliner** | The entity hierarchy of the open level. Drag an entity onto another to reparent it. |
| **Inspector** | The reflected components of the selection. Every registered `Reflect` field is editable, with ranges, units and tooltips from its editor attributes ([Reflection](book/fundamentals/reflection.md)). |
| **Content Browser** | The project's `assets/` folder: search, Import…, New (material, prefab, level, folder), and per-asset Copy path, Show in file manager, Reimport, Delete (which warns about files that still reference the asset). Double-click a level to open it, a material to edit it, a prefab to enter prefab mode; drag a mesh or a prefab into the viewport to place it. |
| **Output Log** | The engine log, filterable. |
| **Material** | The `.material.ron` editor: base color, metallic, roughness and the alpha mode, saved to the file. |
| **Project Settings** | `Regia.toml`'s general fields: name, id, version, build number, startup level. |

The menu bar has **File** (New level, Open level…, Open kit…, Save level, Save level as…, Create
entity), **Create** (Shape), **Edit** (Undo and Redo, labeled with the action they revert;
Preferences…, Project settings…, World settings…) and **View** (grid, selection labels, Frame
selection, and saving or resetting the layout).

## Moving around the viewport

| Input | Action |
|---|---|
| Right mouse button + `W` `A` `S` `D` | Fly forward, left, back, right |
| Right mouse button + `E` / `Q` | Fly up / down |
| `Alt` + left drag | Orbit |
| Middle drag | Pan |
| Left drag on empty space | Box select |
| `Alt` + right drag, or the mouse wheel | Zoom |
| Left click | Select (picking) |
| `W` / `E` / `R` | Gizmo: translate / rotate / scale |
| `F` | Frame the selection |
| `G` | Toggle game view (hides every editor helper) |

The editor viewport renders with a stable editing profile: native resolution, no temporal jitter,
so a still frame stays still. Your game's render profile applies in Play.

## Editing

- Select an entity in the Outliner or the viewport; its components appear in the Inspector.
- Drag the gizmo, or type values into the Inspector. Each drag or edit is one undo entry.
- File → Create entity adds an empty entity; add components from the Inspector.
- Prefabs: double-click a prefab in the Content Browser (or `editor.open_prefab`) to edit it in
  prefab mode; Save & Close re-bakes the template and updates every live instance.
- File → Save level writes canonical `.level.ron`: re-saving an unchanged level is byte-identical,
  so diffs show only what you changed.

While a level has unsaved changes the editor autosaves it every five minutes to
`.regia/autosave/<stem>.level.ron`. If the editor closes without saving, the next launch offers
to restore it.

## Play in editor

The toolbar's **▶ Play** copies the edit world into a separate play world and runs it; Pause and
Step (one frame) let you inspect a moment; Stop drops the play world. Play never writes to your
edit world, so nothing you do while playing changes the level. When a game crate is open, the play
world runs your hot-reloaded game plugin; otherwise it runs the engine's built-in systems. If the
game panics during play, the status bar shows the panic message and the editor keeps running.

## Scripts from the editor

`editor.create_script` (and the matching editor action) writes `game/src/scripts/<name>.rs` and
registers it at the `// REGIA:SCRIPTS` marker in `game/src/lib.rs`. The next play or hot reload
picks it up. Scripts are covered in [Gameplay framework](book/user-guide/gameplay.md).

## The editor is agent-controllable

The editor runs the same agent-protocol server as a game, extended with `editor.*` methods.
Selection, gizmo mode, transforms, undo and redo, saving, play-in-editor, imports, asset creation,
prefab editing and project creation are all calls. Agent edits and your edits share the undo
stack, so you can undo what an agent did. See [Agent protocol and MCP](book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md).

<!-- source: book/start/running.md -->
# Running and iterating

How to run a Regia Engine game during development, read its logs, configure the window, iterate
quickly, try it on Android and turn it into a build you can hand to someone.

## The development loop

```console
$ regia run            # cook, build the launcher and run it
$ regia run --dev      # the same, re-cooking saved assets and reloading them while it runs
$ cargo run -p my_game_launcher   # just build and run (cook with `regia cook` first)
```

`regia run` and `regia run --dev` need the `launcher/` crate (`<name>_launcher`) that the `blank`,
`first_person`, `third_person` and `top_down` templates have; in a [quick app](book/user-guide/quick-start.md)
use plain `cargo build` and `cargo run`, and in a `net_game` project plain `cargo build`, then
`cargo run -p <name>_server` and `cargo run -p <name>_client` as its `README.md` says. Run in either kind of
project, `regia run` says so and prints what to run instead. To cook without running (after you
change assets, before a `cargo run`), from the project folder:

```sh,walkthrough=cook
regia cook
```

`regia run` takes `--level PATH` to start in another level, `--release` to build with the release
profile and `--project DIR` (default `.`), and passes everything after `--` to the game ([CLI reference](book/reference/cli.md)). A development run reads assets from the project's dev cook cache (`.regia/cooked/<platform>/`)
and raw files from `assets/`. The asset server finds the project by looking for `Regia.toml`
above the working directory (or `$REGIA_PROJECT`), so run from the project root or set that
variable. `cargo build --release` gives you representative frame rates. The `quick` and `net-game`
templates build their dependencies at `opt-level = 2` in the `dev` profile so debug runs stay playable;
the other templates use Cargo's default `dev` profile, so add a `[profile.dev.package."*"]` section to
the project's `Cargo.toml` if debug runs are too slow.

Three ways to iterate faster than restart-and-rebuild:

- **Asset changes**: re-cook the changed source (`regia cook`, or Reimport in the editor's
  Content Browser). Processes built with `regia_asset`'s `dev-assets` feature, the editor
  among them, watch the cook cache and reload the changed mesh, texture or material in place
  ([Assets and the cook](book/fundamentals/assets.md)).
- **Code changes**: open the project in the editor with `--game <crate>` and rebuild the game
  crate; the editor swaps it in and keeps the world state
  ([Hot reload](book/user-guide/hot-reload.md)).
- **Agent checks**: script `regia agent call` to set up a situation, step frames and take a
  screenshot, instead of playing to it by hand ([Agent protocol and MCP](book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md)).

## Checking that it starts

A script or a CI job cannot close the window by hand. Every game `regia new` writes accepts
`--exit-after-frames N`: it renders N frames, then exits with the game's exit code. From the project
folder:

```sh,walkthrough=smoke
regia run -- --exit-after-frames 5
```

Without a display (a server, a CI runner), start it under `xvfb-run -a`. The packaged binary
accepts the same flag.

## Logs

`regia::run` installs `tracing` logging to the console, to a session log file, and on Android to
logcat. Filter with the `REGIA_LOG` environment variable (the same syntax as `RUST_LOG`):

```console
$ REGIA_LOG=info,regia_render=debug,my_game=trace cargo run -p my_game_launcher
```

The default is `info` for the engine with noisy GPU crates at `warn`. Log from your own code with
the `tracing` macros the prelude re-exports (`info!`, `warn!`, `error!`, `debug!`, `trace!`).

Session logs go to `logs://`: `<data dir>/RegiaEngine/<exe name>/logs` on desktop (for example
`~/.local/share/RegiaEngine/my_game_launcher/logs` on Linux, `%APPDATA%\RegiaEngine\…` on Windows) and the
app's internal storage on Android. The agent protocol's `logs.read` returns the same lines.

When a game panics, the platform writes a crash report next to the logs
(`logs://crash-<timestamp>.txt`): the panic message and backtrace, build identity, OS and GPU, the
active level, the frame count and the last 200 log lines ([Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md)
covers crash upload and symbols).

## Environment variables

Every engine environment variable in this book is named `REGIA_*`. The engine still reads each
one under its name from before the rename (`FERRITE_*`) when the `REGIA_*` one is unset, and logs <!-- rename-keep -->
a one-time warning that names the replacement; set the `REGIA_*` names in new scripts
([Renaming to Regia Engine](book/user-guide/rename-regia.md)).

## Configuring the app before it runs

`regia::run(game)` is `regia::run_with(game, |_| {})`. Use `run_with` to change resources
before the first frame, for example the window:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, _app: &mut App) {}
}

fn main() {
    let _exit = regia::run_with(Game, |app| {
        app.insert_resource(WindowSettings {
            window: Window {
                title: "My Game".into(),
                logical_size: (1600.0, 900.0),
                ..Default::default()
            },
        });
    });
}
```

`Window` also carries the fullscreen mode (`WindowMode`), the present mode (`PresentMode`:
`Vsync`, `VsyncRelaxed` or `Immediate`), resizability, decorations, cursor visibility and grab, and IME. The
player-facing settings (graphics preset, resolution, audio volumes, language) live in
`GameSettings`, which the framework loads from `user://settings.ron` and applies live
([Gameplay framework](book/user-guide/gameplay.md)).

`run_with` (and `run`) returns the `AppExit` value. A system ends the app by writing
`AppExit::Success` (or `AppExit::Error(code)`) through a `MessageWriter<AppExit>`. The launcher
`regia new` generates ignores the value, so its process exits with 0 either way; when a CI job or
a script must see a failure, make the launcher return it:

<!-- ignore-reason: `my_game::Game` is the reader's own crate -->
```rust,ignore
use regia::app::AppExit;

fn main() -> std::process::ExitCode {
    match regia::run(my_game::Game) {
        AppExit::Success => std::process::ExitCode::SUCCESS,
        AppExit::Error(code) => std::process::ExitCode::from(code.get()),
    }
}
```

## Command-line flags of the samples

The engine's samples share a few flags that are convenient for automated runs; your launcher can
copy the pattern (they are ordinary argument parsing in each sample's `main.rs`):

| Flag | Samples | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `--exit-after-frames N` | most samples, and every project `regia new` writes | Quit after N frames (smoke tests, soak runs) |
| `--screenshot PATH` | `third_person` | Write a PNG a few frames before exiting |
| `--seed N`, `--bots N`, `--no-local-player`, `--bench` | `arena` | Deterministic matches and the bot benchmark |

## Running on Android

```console
$ regia install-android --project my_game
```

`install-android` packages a debug APK, installs it with `adb`, launches it and streams the app's
logcat (`--device SERIAL` picks one of several devices, `--no-build` reinstalls the last package,
`--no-logcat` returns after launch). The game's `android/` crate is the `cdylib` entry point; it
calls `regia::android_main!`, which runs the same `Game` plugin. Android drops the window
surface when the app is paused and recreates it on resume; the engine handles this, and your
game sees `LifecycleEvent::Suspended` / `Resumed` messages if it wants to pause audio or
gameplay ([App, plugins and schedules](book/fundamentals/app-and-plugins.md)).

To check that the Android crate compiles without a device or the Gradle tools (the
[Android setup](book/start/install.md#5-android-optional) without step 5 is enough), from the `my_game`
project folder:

```sh,walkthrough=android,template=blank
cargo ndk -t arm64-v8a check -p my_game_android
```

## Making a build

```console
$ regia package --platform linux
$ regia package --platform windows
$ regia package --platform android --format apk
```

Packaging cooks the assets into `.fpak` archives, builds the launcher, and writes a
self-contained archive under `dist/<platform>/`. The default profile is `dev`; `--profile shipping`
builds the optimized, stripped release with separate debug symbols. The agent-protocol server is
part of the `regia` crate's default `agent` feature, so it is compiled into shipping builds too
unless every crate of the build depends on `regia` with `default-features = false` (keep `"ui"`
if you use the runtime UI). It listens on loopback only and requires the per-run token. Details, signing
and Steam: [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md) and [Steam](book/user-guide/steam.md).

## After an engine update

Projects record the engine release line they target (`Regia.toml [project] engine`). After you
build the tools of a newer engine release, run this in each project folder:

```sh,walkthrough=upgrade
regia upgrade-project
```

It lists what would change: content-format migrations, the engine dependency paths and the release
line. Nothing is written until you add `--write` (it keeps a backup of every file it rewrites); on a
project that is already current it changes nothing. `--engine path:<engine folder>` moves the
project to another engine folder ([Distribution and upgrades](book/agents/distribution-upgrade.md)).

<!-- source: book/start/first-agent-check.md -->
# Checking your game with an agent

This page makes a First Person project, builds and runs it, then checks it from a second terminal
through the agent protocol: wait for the game to be ready, assert what is on screen, take a
screenshot and quit. It is the shortest complete loop an AI agent (or a CI script) runs against a
game, and it needs nothing beyond the tools from [Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md).

The commands on this page are the ones the engine's own test runs, in this order
(`crates/regia_cli/tests/getting_started_walkthrough.rs`), so they stay correct.

## 1. Create, build and run

```console
$ regia new "My Game" --template first_person
$ cd my_game
$ cargo build -p my_game_launcher
$ regia run
```

`regia new` writes the project into `my_game/` ([A tour of the template](book/user-guide/first-person-template.md)).
`cargo build` compiles the engine and the game; the first build takes a few minutes, later builds
only compile your crates. `my_game_launcher` is the template's desktop launcher crate: `blank`,
`first_person`, `third_person` and `top_down` have one, `quick` and `net_game` do not (build those with
plain `cargo build`). `regia run` cooks the assets and starts the launcher in a window. It
keeps running until the game quits, so leave this terminal alone.

## 2. Check it from a second terminal

Open a second terminal in the `my_game` directory:

```console
$ regia agent call agent.hello
$ regia agent call play.wait_until '{"condition":{"entity":{"name":"Gate"},"component":"Door","path":"open","op":"eq","value":false},"timeout_ms":60000}'
$ regia agent call play.expect '{"assertions":[{"name":"gate shut","condition":{"entity":{"name":"Gate"},"component":"Door","path":"open","op":"eq","value":false}},{"name":"nothing in reach","condition":{"entity":{"name":"hud-prompt"},"component":"PromptLabel","path":"text","op":"eq","value":""}}]}'
$ regia agent call seeing.screenshot --out shot.png
$ regia agent call quit.request
```

What each one does, and what to look for in its output:

- **`agent.hello`** connects. The game writes its endpoint and a per-run token to `.regia/agent/` in the
  project, and `regia agent call` reads them. If it says it cannot connect to a running app, the game is
  still starting: run it again.
- **`play.wait_until`** blocks until the condition holds, checked once per frame, or until `timeout_ms`
  passes. Here it waits until the level has spawned its gate, closed. Look for `"satisfied": true`; on a
  timeout it is `false` and `detail` says what it last saw.
- **`play.expect`** checks a list of named conditions against the world as it is now, without waiting.
  Look for `"pass": true`; `results` has one entry per assertion, so a failure names the one that broke.
  "Nothing in reach" holds because the player starts 8 m from the gate and the prompt shows only within
  2.6 m.
- **`seeing.screenshot --out shot.png`** writes the window's last frame to `shot.png` and prints its size.
- **`quit.request`** asks the game to quit as if its window were closed. `"will_exit": true` means it
  exits at the end of the frame.

Back in the first terminal, `regia run` returns with exit status 0.

Conditions name an entity by `name` (or by id), a reflected component, a field path and a comparison; the
template's [agent-readable state](book/user-guide/first-person-template.md#what-agents-can-read) lists what
this game exposes. [Playtest](book/agents/testing.md) has the full condition grammar, and
[Agent protocol and MCP](book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md) shows the same calls from an AI agent through
`regia mcp`.

## Where next

- Put these calls in a test that runs without a window: the template's `game/tests/agent_smoke.rs`
  drives the same game headless (`cargo test -p my_game`).
- [Running and iterating](book/start/running.md) covers logs, the live asset loop and packaging.
