# The ECS: entities, components, systems

<!-- index: Entity -->
<!-- index: Component -->
<!-- index: System -->
<!-- index: Resource -->
<!-- index: Message -->
<!-- index: ECS | see: Entity -->

Everything in a running Regia Engine game lives in one **world** organized as an Entity Component
System. Spec: `docs/specs/10-core.md`. Regia Engine uses `bevy_ecs` for this, through its own facade crate `regia_ecs`: game code
imports from `regia::prelude` (or `regia_ecs::prelude`) and never names `bevy_ecs` directly,
which lets the engine pin and upgrade it in one place.

| Concept | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Entity** | An id. It has no data of its own. | the player, a crate, a camera |
| **Component** | A plain Rust struct or enum attached to an entity | `Transform`, `MeshRenderer`, `RigidBody`, your `Health` |
| **System** | A Rust function that reads and writes components and resources | `propagate_transforms`, your `move_player` |
| **Resource** | A singleton value in the world | `Time`, `RenderSettings`, `AssetServer`, your `Score` |
| **Message** | A buffered event that systems write and read | `KeyboardInput`, `CollisionStarted`, your `Explosion` |

An entity *is* whatever its components say it is: an entity with a `Transform`, a `MeshRenderer`
and a `RigidBody` is a visible physics object; remove the `RigidBody` and it stops simulating.

## Components

Derive `Component`. Also derive `Reflect` and register the type when you want the editor, saves,
hot reload or agents to see it ([Reflection](book/fundamentals/reflection.md)); that is almost always.

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// Hit points.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Debug, Clone, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct Health {
    /// Current hit points.
    pub current: f32,
    /// Maximum hit points.
    pub max: f32,
}

/// Marks the entity the local player controls.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct Player;

fn register(app: &mut App) {
    app.register_type::<Health>().register_type::<Player>();
}
```

Empty structs like `Player` are **marker components**: they carry no data and exist to be
filtered on. Components can declare **required components** with `#[require(...)]`; spawning one
adds the others with their defaults. `Transform` requires `GlobalTransform`, for example.

## Spawning and changing entities

`Commands` queue structural changes (spawn, despawn, insert, remove) which apply after the system
that queued them, at the next sync point:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::Vec3;
use regia_scene::Transform;
// Scene files and the editor store this `Name`; the prelude's `Name` is the plain ECS one.
use regia_scene::components::Name;

#[derive(Component, Default)]
struct Health(f32);

#[derive(Component)]
struct Burning;

fn spawn_enemy(mut commands: Commands) -> Entity {
    commands
        .spawn((
            Name::new("Enemy"),
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(4.0, 0.0, -2.0)),
            Health(100.0),
        ))
        .id()
}

fn ignite(mut commands: Commands, enemy: Entity) {
    commands.entity(enemy).insert(Burning);
}

fn extinguish(mut commands: Commands, enemy: Entity) {
    commands.entity(enemy).remove::<Burning>();
}

fn kill(mut commands: Commands, enemy: Entity) {
    commands.entity(enemy).despawn();
}
```

Despawning an entity also despawns its children.

## Systems and queries

A system is a function whose parameters say what it accesses. The scheduler runs systems in
parallel when their accesses do not conflict, so declare only what you need: `&T` for reading,
`&mut T` for writing.

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::Vec3;
use regia_scene::Transform;

#[derive(Component)]
struct Velocity(Vec3);

#[derive(Component)]
struct Frozen;

#[derive(Component)]
struct Player;

/// Moves everything that has a velocity, except frozen things.
fn integrate(time: Res<Time>, mut query: Query<(&Velocity, &mut Transform), Without<Frozen>>) {
    let dt = time.delta_secs();
    for (velocity, mut transform) in &mut query {
        transform.translation += velocity.0 * dt;
    }
}

/// Reads one entity: the player.
fn report(players: Query<&Transform, With<Player>>) {
    for transform in &players {
        info!("player at {:?}", transform.translation);
    }
}

/// Reacts only to entities whose velocity changed (or was added) since this system last ran.
fn on_velocity_change(changed: Query<(Entity, &Velocity), Changed<Velocity>>) {
    for (entity, velocity) in &changed {
        debug!("{entity:?} now moves at {:?}", velocity.0);
    }
}
```

- **Filters**: `With<T>` and `Without<T>` restrict a query without reading `T`; `Changed<T>` and
  `Added<T>` select entities whose `T` changed or was added since the system last ran.
- **Single entities**: `query.get(entity)` / `get_mut(entity)` look one entity up and return a
  `Result`; prefer `let Ok(x) = … else { return };` to unwrapping.
- **Resources**: `Res<T>` reads and `ResMut<T>` writes a resource; `Option<Res<T>>` tolerates
  its absence.
- **Local state**: `Local<T>` is per-system state that persists between runs.

## Resources

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// The current score.
#[derive(Resource, Reflect, Default)]
#[reflect(Resource, Default)]
pub struct Score(pub u32);

fn add_point(mut score: ResMut<Score>) {
    score.0 += 1;
}

fn setup(app: &mut App) {
    app.init_resource::<Score>()            // Default::default()
        .register_type::<Score>()
        .add_systems(Update, add_point);
}
```

`insert_resource(value)` inserts a specific value; `init_resource::<T>()` uses `Default` (or
`FromWorld`).

## Messages

Messages decouple the system that notices something from the systems that react. Writers and
readers never block each other. Messages live for two frames (the buffer swaps once per frame),
so a reader sees each message once only if it runs at least once in that window; a system held
back by `run_if` (a paused or loading state) can miss messages.

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// Something exploded.
#[derive(Message, Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Explosion {
    /// World position.
    pub at: [f32; 3],
    /// Damage at the center.
    pub damage: f32,
}

fn detonate(mut writer: MessageWriter<Explosion>) {
    writer.write(Explosion { at: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], damage: 50.0 });
}

fn shake_camera(mut reader: MessageReader<Explosion>) {
    for explosion in reader.read() {
        debug!("boom at {:?}", explosion.at);
    }
}

fn setup(app: &mut App) {
    app.add_message::<Explosion>()
        .add_systems(Update, (detonate, shake_camera).chain());
}
```

The engine reports input (`KeyboardInput`, `MouseMotion`, `TouchInput`, …), lifecycle
(`LifecycleEvent`), physics contacts (`CollisionStarted`, `TriggerEnter`), level loading
(`LevelLoaded`) and more as messages.

## Ordering systems

Systems in the same schedule run in parallel unless you order them:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

#[derive(SystemSet, Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
enum GameSet {
    Input,
    Simulation,
    Presentation,
}

fn read_input() {}
fn steer() {}
fn shoot() {}
fn update_hud() {}

fn setup(app: &mut App) {
    app.configure_sets(Update, (GameSet::Input, GameSet::Simulation, GameSet::Presentation).chain())
        .add_systems(Update, read_input.in_set(GameSet::Input))
        .add_systems(Update, (steer, shoot).chain().in_set(GameSet::Simulation))
        .add_systems(Update, update_hud.in_set(GameSet::Presentation));
}
```

`.chain()` runs a tuple in order; `.before(x)` / `.after(x)` order against a system or set;
`.run_if(condition)` gates a system. Engine plugins expose sets to order against, for example
`regia_framework::script::ScriptsSet::Update` and `PostUpdateSet::TransformPropagate`.

## Exclusive systems

A system that takes `&mut World` has the whole world to itself: it can spawn and read
immediately, run queries, and call engine functions that need the world (loading a level,
saving a game). It cannot run in parallel with anything, so keep these for setup and rare work.

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

#[derive(Component)]
struct Pickup;

fn count_pickups(world: &mut World) {
    let count = world.query_filtered::<Entity, With<Pickup>>().iter(world).count();
    info!("{count} pickups left");
}
```

## Parents and children

The hierarchy uses the ECS's `ChildOf` / `Children` relationship; a child's `Transform` is
relative to its parent and `ScenePlugin` propagates `GlobalTransform` down the tree every frame.
`regia_scene::HierarchyCommands` adds `set_parent`, `remove_parent`, and
`*_keep_world_transform` variants that keep the entity where it is on screen:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_scene::prelude::*;

fn attach(mut commands: Commands, turret: Entity, tank: Entity) {
    commands.entity(turret).set_parent_keep_world_transform(tank);
}
```

## Where systems run

Systems go into **schedules** (`Startup`, `PreUpdate`, `FixedUpdate`, `Update`, `PostUpdate`,
`Last`, …) that the app runs every frame in a fixed order. Which schedule to use, and how plugins
package systems, is the next chapter: [App, plugins and schedules](book/fundamentals/app-and-plugins.md).

<!-- source: book/fundamentals/app-and-plugins.md -->
# App, plugins and schedules

<!-- index: Plugin -->
<!-- index: Schedule -->
<!-- index: Fixed timestep | see: Schedule -->
<!-- index: DefaultPlugins | see: Plugin -->

An `App` owns one ECS world, the frame schedules and the plugins that configured them.
Spec: `docs/specs/10-core.md`. A runner
drives it: the platform's window runner for games, `run_headless` for tests, servers and tools.
Everything is configured through **plugins**, including the engine itself.

## Plugins

A plugin is a type that implements `Plugin`. `build` adds systems, resources, messages, types and
other plugins to the app:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// Everything about the player.
pub struct PlayerPlugin;

#[derive(Resource, Default)]
struct PlayerStats {
    jumps: u32,
}

impl Plugin for PlayerPlugin {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.init_resource::<PlayerStats>()
            .add_systems(Startup, spawn_player)
            .add_systems(Update, (read_input, move_player).chain());
    }
}

fn spawn_player(mut commands: Commands) {}
fn read_input() {}
fn move_player() {}

/// The game: a plugin made of plugins.
pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins((regia_scene::ScenePlugin, PlayerPlugin));
    }
}
```

Split a game into one plugin per feature, the way the engine is split. `add_plugins` takes one
plugin or a tuple. A plugin can also implement `finish` (runs once every plugin has been built)
and `cleanup`. `App::has_plugin` asks whether one was added, by name.

## `regia::run` and `DefaultPlugins`

`regia::run(game)` does four things: starts logging, creates an `App`, adds `DefaultPlugins` and
then your game plugin, and hands the app to the platform runner. `DefaultPlugins` contains:

| Plugin | Gives you |
|---|---|
| `DiagnosticsPlugin` | Frame timing and the process frame profiler (`Profiler` resource) |
| `PlatformPlugin` | The window, the lifecycle, raw input messages, the VFS, platform services (clipboard, haptics, safe area, locale) |
| `RenderPlugin` | The renderer: cameras, meshes, lights, post, shadows, atmosphere |
| `AssetPlugin` | The `AssetServer`: dev cook cache in development, `.fpak` archives in a package |
| `AudioPlugin` | Audio output: sounds, music, buses, the default output device (`REGIA_AUDIO=off` runs it headless) |
| `TelemetryPlugin`, `ResidencyPlugin` | Structured telemetry (`REGIA_TELEMETRY`) and keeping frame-critical data paged in |
| `UiPlugin` (feature `ui`, on by default) | The runtime UI |
| `AgentPlugin` (feature `agent`, on by default) | The agent-protocol server |

It also adds framework helpers that stay idle until a level uses them (start level, baked GI and
lightmap installs, world streaming, exposure zones, content chunks, the performance overlay,
captions and conversations).

Everything else is opt-in, because games differ in what they need. A typical game adds some of:

| Plugin | Crate | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| `ScenePlugin` | `regia_scene` | [Scenes](book/user-guide/scenes.md) (transform propagation, levels, prefabs) |
| `InputPlugin::new(config)` | `regia_input` | [Input](book/user-guide/input.md) |
| `PhysicsPlugin` | `regia_physics` | [Physics](book/user-guide/physics.md) |
| `AnimationPlugin` | `regia_animation` | [Animation](book/user-guide/animation.md) |
| `VfxPlugin` | `regia_vfx` | [VFX and decals](book/systems/vfx.md) |
| `NavPlugin`, `AiPlugin` | `regia_nav`, `regia_ai` | [Navigation and AI](book/user-guide/navigation-ai.md) |
| `CharacterPlugin`, `CameraPlugin`, `PlayerPlugin`, `RulesPlugin`, `ScriptPlugin`, `SavePlugin`, `SettingsPlugin`, `TimerPlugin`, `TweenPlugin`, `SimBridgePlugin` | `regia_framework` | [Gameplay framework](book/user-guide/gameplay.md) |

## The frame

Each frame runs the schedules in this order:

| Schedule | Runs | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `StateTransition` | once, before `Startup` on the first frame | applies the initial states, so every `OnEnter` for them runs before `Startup` |
| `Startup` | once, after that first `StateTransition` | spawning the initial world |
| `First` | every frame | clocks, frame counters, message buffers (engine) |
| `PreUpdate` | every frame | platform events → input state, asset completions, hot-reload swaps (engine) |
| `StateTransition` | every frame, between `PreUpdate` and `FixedUpdate` | applies `NextState` values written earlier in the frame, runs `OnExit`/`OnEnter` |
| `FixedUpdate` | 0…N times per frame at `FixedTime::hz` | simulation that must not depend on frame rate: physics, AI, match logic |
| `Update` | every frame | most gameplay |
| `PostUpdate` | every frame | late scripts, physics interpolation, animation, transform propagation, visibility, audio and UI layout, in that order (`PostUpdateSet`) |
| `Extract` | every frame | copying render data out of the world (engine) |
| `Render` | every frame | render graph and present (engine) |
| `Last` | every frame | diagnostics, frame-end cleanup |

Two more run outside the frame: `Lifecycle`, synchronously on every application lifecycle
transition (for work that must finish before the OS callback returns), and `OnLevelLoaded` /
`OnLevelUnloading` when the scene system loads or unloads a level.

Systems that touch an OS window must stay on the main thread. The window setters winit exposes
(`set_title`, `request_inner_size`, `set_cursor_grab`, …) post to the event-loop thread and block
when called from a task-pool thread; on Windows that deadlocks the frame loop, because the main
thread is inside `App::update` waiting for the very system that is waiting on it. Add a
`NonSendMarker` system parameter to pin such a system to the main thread:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// `PostUpdate`: applies changed `Window` components to the OS window.
fn apply_window_changes(
    _main: NonSendMarker, // forces this system onto the main thread
    windows: Query<&Window>,
) {
    // …call os.set_title(…), os.set_cursor_grab(…), etc.
}
```

(`NonSendMarker` is a `!Send` marker. `CursorGrab::Locked` falls back to `Confined` on Windows
and on X11, where winit does not support `Locked`. `CursorGrab::Confined` falls back to `Locked`
on macOS. A grab the OS rejects is retried on a later frame.)

Anything that writes `Transform` should run before `PostUpdateSet::TransformPropagate` (anything in
`Update` does) so the renderer sees the new position in the same frame.

## Time and the fixed timestep

`Res<Time>` is the game clock: `delta_secs()`, `elapsed_secs()`, `frame_count()`, plus `paused`
and `time_scale` fields that the game, the editor and the agent protocol's `play.pause` /
`play.set_time_scale` use. `RealTime` is the unscaled wall clock.

`FixedUpdate` runs at `FixedTime::hz` (default 60), as many times per frame as the accumulated
time requires, at most `max_substeps` (default 5, hard cap `MAX_SUBSTEPS_LIMIT` = 64) so a slow frame cannot
spiral. Inside `FixedUpdate`, `Time` is swapped for the step: `Time::delta` and `Time::sim_delta`
are one step, and `Time::elapsed` and `Time::sim_elapsed` are the fixed clock; the frame's values
are restored after the last step. `FixedTime::step()` gives the same length. `FixedTime::overstep_fraction()` is how far the clock is
into the next step, for interpolating what you draw.

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

fn configure(app: &mut App) {
    // A 120 Hz simulation.
    let mut fixed = FixedTime::default();
    fixed.hz = 120.0;
    app.insert_resource(fixed);
}

/// A fixed-step system: integrate with the step length, not the frame delta.
fn simulate(fixed: Res<FixedTime>) {
    let dt = fixed.step().as_secs_f32();
    let _ = dt;
}
```

For tests and deterministic captures, `enable_fixed_step(app, hz)` pins
`TimeUpdateStrategy::ManualDuration` to one step at `hz` (`hz` sanitized to `1..=1000000000`;
`0` becomes 1 Hz and a non-finite value becomes 60) and sets `FixedTime.max_substeps` to 1, so
the frame does not follow the wall clock. One `App::update` runs one `FixedUpdate` when the
simulation delta is at least one step: `time_scale` is 1, no shorter `SimStep` is installed, and
the app is not paused or suspended. `Time::advance` multiplies that manual delta by `time_scale`.
A scale below 1 banks time and a step runs only once the bank reaches `1/hz`. Scale `0.5` at 1 Hz
runs a step on every second update, because a half step is an exact number of nanoseconds. Scale
`0` runs none. At 60 Hz the stored step is 16,666,667 ns and half of that frame is 8,333,333 ns,
so the first step lands on the third update. A scale above 1 still runs at most one
step and drops the rest. Pause and suspend are a zero gameplay delta, so no `FixedUpdate` runs.
That pinning is how two runs on the same machine produce byte-identical screenshots. The manual
duration is not clamped to `MAX_DELTA`; that clamp is only for the wall clock (`RealTime::tick`).
`Time.paused` is a zero gameplay delta, not a schedule gate: `Update` still runs every frame, so
gate gameplay systems on `Time::delta()` or a run condition, and UI systems keep running. `paused`
changes only when the game sets it; suspend does not write `paused`. The agent protocol's
`play.step` does not use `enable_fixed_step`: it unpauses `Time` for the requested number of
frames and pauses again.

Frame-rate caps live in `FramePacing { target_fps }`; render profiles can install one (the Steam
Deck profile caps at 40 fps).

## Headless apps

Tools, servers and tests run the same app without a window:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

#[derive(Resource, Default)]
struct Ticks(u32);

fn tick(mut ticks: ResMut<Ticks>, mut exit: MessageWriter<AppExit>) {
    ticks.0 += 1;
    if ticks.0 == 10 {
        exit.write(AppExit::Success);
    }
}

fn main() {
    let mut app = App::new();
    app.add_plugins(MinimalPlugins)
        .init_resource::<Ticks>()
        .add_systems(Update, tick);
    let _exit = regia::app::run_headless(app);
}
```

In a test you can also call `app.update()` yourself, one frame at a time, and inspect
`app.world()` between frames. The renderer has an offscreen mode for the same purpose
(`RenderPlugin { headless: true }`, see [Rendering](book/user-guide/rendering.md)).

## Platform lifecycle

On Android the OS takes the window away when the app goes to the background and gives it back on
resume. The engine drops the GPU surface on `Suspended` and recreates it on `Resumed`; the device
and every GPU resource survive. Games see the transitions as `LifecycleEvent` messages
(`Started`, `Suspended`, `Resumed`, `LowMemory`, …) and as the `AppLifecycle` resource:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

fn pause_on_suspend(mut events: MessageReader<LifecycleEvent>, mut time: ResMut<Time>) {
    for event in events.read() {
        match event {
            LifecycleEvent::Suspended => time.paused = true,
            LifecycleEvent::Resumed => time.paused = false,
            _ => {}
        }
    }
}
```

On desktop the window stays alive while minimized: the runner throttles frames and the renderer
skips presenting until the window is visible again, so a desktop game sees `Started` and
`Resumed` once and nothing more. Code written against the messages works on every platform.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/scenes.md -->
# Scenes: entities, levels and prefabs

<!-- index: Level -->
<!-- index: Prefab -->
<!-- index: Level directory | see: Level -->
<!-- index: Persistent | see: Level -->

A **level** is a saved scene — a list of entities, each a set of components with values — stored as
canonical RON (`.level.ron`). A **prefab** (`.prefab.ron`) is the same idea for a reusable subtree:
spawn it, then override individual properties per instance.

## Entities and components

An entity is a plain handle. Everything it *is* comes from components. Spawn in a system:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_scene::components::Name;
use regia_scene::prelude::*;

fn spawn_player(mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Player"),
        Transform::from_translation(regia::core::math::Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)),
        // … a mesh, a collider, a controller …
    ));
}
```

Components are nouns (`RigidBody`, `PointLight`, `MeshRenderer`); systems are verb phrases
(`propagate_transforms`); plugins end in `Plugin`. The full glossary is in
`docs/04-conventions.md` § 3.

For blocking out a level before the art exists, `regia_render::Primitive` is a graybox shape
component: add it next to a `Transform` and the renderer meshes it (cuboid, sphere, capsule,
cylinder, cone, conical frustum, plane, torus, tetrahedron, ramp, prism).

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::render::{Primitive, PrimitiveShape};
use regia_scene::components::Name;
use regia_scene::prelude::*;

fn block_out(mut commands: Commands) {
    let ramp = PrimitiveShape::Ramp { size: regia::core::math::Vec3::new(6.0, 1.5, 3.0) };
    commands.spawn((Name::new("Ramp"), Transform::default(), Primitive::new(ramp)));
}
```

It is stored in level files like any component, with a `format_version` (currently 1; see
`docs/formats/primitive-v1.md`).

### Two `Name` components

There are two name components, and it matters which one you use:

- `regia_scene::components::Name` is the name stored in level and prefab files (the `name:`
  field of each entity) and set when a level or prefab spawns.
- `Name` from `regia::prelude` (the ECS's own name type) is what the agent protocol's
  name-based entity references (`scene.query_entities { "name": … }`, `{"name": glob}` entity
  selectors) and the editor's outliner read.

The editor copies scene names onto the ECS `Name` for the entities it shows. In a running game,
give entities you want to find from the agent protocol the prelude `Name` (for example
`commands.spawn((Name::new("Player"), …))`); add the scene `Name` too when the entity should be
saved into a level.

## Levels

A level file is what the editor saves and the game loads:

```ron
(
    format_version: 1,
    entities: [
        (
            guid: "8b6f2a11-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
            name: "Ground",
            components: {
                "regia_scene::transform::Transform": (
                    translation: (0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
                    rotation: (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0),
                    scale: (4.0, 0.2, 4.0),
                ),
            },
        ),
    ],
)
```

Entities have a stable `guid`, a `name`, an optional `parent`, and a map of reflected components
keyed by type path. This example shows the Ground entity from the `blank` template's startup level; the full
template also contains a Marker entity. The template is written at format
version 1; the current scene format is version 14 (`regia_scene::format::SCENE_FORMAT_VERSION`),
and the loader migrates every older version in memory. `regia upgrade-project --write` rewrites
the file. Version 2 added the per-level atmosphere, version 3 the look (exposure meter and color
grade), and later versions further per-level settings; see [Content formats](book/reference/formats.md)
and `docs/formats/scene-files.md`.

A level can also carry `LevelSettings` (a reflected resource stored with the level): gravity,
game-rules name, ambient audio, the acoustic medium (how sound travels: Earth air, thin Mars air
or none, see [Audio](book/user-guide/audio.md)), the planet atmosphere preset with time of day and sky body, and
the map's look. [Rendering](book/user-guide/rendering.md) shows the atmosphere block.

Spec: `docs/specs/14-scene-and-framework.md`. The task steps are in
[Make a level and a prefab](book/how-to/create/levels-and-prefabs.md).

## One file or a directory

A level is one `.level.ron` or a directory `<name>.level.d/` with one file per entity
(spec 37, format `level-dir` v1,
[`docs/formats/level-dir.md`](docs/formats/level-dir.md)). The directory is for
authoring, so version control can merge one entity. A package does not ship it. A level
may exist in only one of the two forms. Both siblings at once is `ambiguous_level_form`.

```console
$ regia level split assets/levels/room.level.ron
$ regia level merge assets/levels/room.level.d
$ regia level validate assets/levels/room.level.ron
```

`split` and `merge` remove the source after a successful conversion. `--keep` leaves it.
`--out` names another destination. `validate` checks layer bindings and memberships and
exits 1 when it finds one. The directory wrapper stays at `level-dir` v1. A new split
writes entity records at the current scene format version (14). Older scene versions still
load through the same in-memory migrators as a single file.

## Despawning a hierarchy

`commands.entity(root).despawn_recursive()` (from `regia_scene::prelude::HierarchyCommands`) and
`regia_scene::hierarchy::despawn_tree(world, root)` remove an entity and its whole `Children` subtree
with an explicit stack, leaves first, so a hierarchy of any depth cannot overflow the stack. Plain
`world.despawn(root)` also removes the children, but recursively, one set of stack frames per level:
a chain of a few thousand links overflowed a 2 MiB Windows thread. Level unload, prefab pruning and the
agent's `scene.despawn` use the iterative walk (ADR-2306).

```rust
use regia_app::prelude::*;
use regia_scene::hierarchy::despawn_tree;

/// Removes `root` and everything under it; false when `root` was already gone.
fn clear_subtree(world: &mut World, root: Entity) -> bool {
    despawn_tree(world, root)
}
```

## Loading a level from your game

The `LevelManager` resource (from `ScenePlugin`) owns the level lifecycle: which level is current,
which are loading, and the load and unload operations. `LoadMode::Replace` despawns the current
level's entities (except those marked `Persistent`) and loads the new one; `LoadMode::Additive`
keeps everything and loads on top, for streamed regions. `LevelLoading`, `LevelLoaded` and
`LevelUnloading` messages fire on the transitions, and the `OnLevelLoaded` / `OnLevelUnloading`
schedules run once each.

`open_level` loads the level's data from the `LevelLibrary` resource. Today a game puts the
parsed level there itself; having the asset server fill the library from `.level.ron` files is
**planned** (`docs/specs/12-assets.md` § 3). The editor opens `Regia.toml`'s `startup_level`
for you, but a running game does not read that field. `regia run --level L` starts the game in
level `L` (the path travels in `REGIA_START_LEVEL`; `StartLevelPlugin`, part of `DefaultPlugins`,
opens it after the game's `Startup` systems and re-opens it when the file is saved in a `--dev`
run). To load your first level from code, do it in a `Startup` system:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::core::id::Guid;
use regia_scene::level::{Level, LevelId, LevelLibrary, LoadMode, open_level};

/// The id this game uses for its main level.
const MAIN_LEVEL: LevelId = LevelId(Guid::from_u128(0x6d61_696e_0000_4000_8000_0000_0000_0001));

fn load_main_level(world: &mut World) {
    let Ok(path) = VfsPath::parse("assets://levels/main.level.ron") else { return };
    let bytes = match world.resource::<Vfs>().read_sync(&path) {
        Ok(bytes) => bytes,
        Err(err) => {
            error!("cannot read the main level: {err}");
            return;
        }
    };
    let level = match Level::from_ron_str(MAIN_LEVEL, &String::from_utf8_lossy(&bytes)) {
        Ok(level) => level,
        Err(err) => {
            error!("main level does not parse: {err}");
            return;
        }
    };
    world.get_resource_or_insert_with(LevelLibrary::new).insert(level);
    if let Err(err) = open_level(world, MAIN_LEVEL, LoadMode::Replace) {
        error!("cannot open the main level: {err}");
    }
}

fn setup(app: &mut App) {
    app.add_plugins(regia_scene::ScenePlugin)
        .add_systems(Startup, load_main_level);
}
```

Mark entities that should survive a `Replace` load (the player, a music manager) with the
`Persistent` component. An agent reads and edits the loaded level through the `scene.*` methods
([agent guide's scene page](book/agents/scene.md)); switching levels from the protocol is not a
method yet.

## Prefabs

A prefab is an entity subtree saved for reuse. Spawn an instance and override fields without
touching the template:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_scene::prelude::*;

fn spawn_pickup(mut commands: Commands) {
    // `guid` is the prefab's asset id, registered from `prefabs/pickup.prefab.ron`.
    let guid = regia::core::id::Guid::from_u128(0x8b6f_2a11_0000_4000_8000_0000_0000_0002);
    // The caller owns the instance root's guid: draw it from the sim RNG so lockstep peers
    // derive the same prefab-internal guids (never `Guid::NIL`, never reused).
    let root_guid = regia::core::id::Guid::from_u128(0x8b6f_2a11_0000_4000_8000_0000_0000_0003);
    commands.spawn_prefab(guid, None, &SpawnOptions::default(), root_guid);
}
```

Instance overrides apply on top of the template's defaults (`PrefabInstance` keeps the authored
overrides as raw RON). Nesting and override merging follow `docs/specs/14-scene-and-framework.md`
(the scene spec).

Like levels, prefab templates live in a library resource (`PrefabLibrary`). A template is baked
from its scene file with `PrefabTemplate::from_scene_file(asset_id, &scene_file, &registry)` and
inserted there; `spawn_prefab` of a template that is not in the library yet spawns a
`PendingPrefab` placeholder that fills in when the template arrives. The editor's prefab mode and
`editor.spawn_prefab` handle all of this for you while authoring.

## Everything is text

Levels and prefabs are diffable RON. Re-saving an unchanged level is byte-identical (canonical
serialization: sorted keys, stable entity order, shortest round-trip floats) — which is what makes
agent edits and `git diff` work. See the [agent guide's scene page](book/agents/scene.md) for how the
protocol reads and edits this same state at runtime.

<!-- source: book/fundamentals/assets.md -->
# Assets and the cook

<!-- index: Cook -->
<!-- index: AssetServer | see: Cook -->
<!-- index: VFS | see: Cook -->
<!-- index: .meta | see: Asset id -->

Source assets (glTF models, PNG and JPEG textures, materials, levels, sounds) live in your
project's `assets/` folder in neutral, editable formats. The **cook** turns the ones the runtime
should not parse itself into compact, platform-specific cooked data. In development the game
reads the cooked cache directly; a packaged game reads the same data from `.fpak` archives. The
code that loads an asset is the same either way.

## Where files live: the VFS

Every engine file access goes through the virtual file system (the `Vfs` resource, from
`PlatformPlugin`) with paths such as `assets://textures/rock.png` or `user://saves/slot1.sav`:

| Mount | Desktop (development) | Packaged desktop | Android |
|---|---|---|---|
| `assets://` | `$REGIA_ASSETS`, else `<exe dir>/assets`, else the crate's `assets/` | `<exe dir>/assets` (raw files copied by the packager) | the APK's assets |
| `config://` | `<assets>/config` | `<assets>/config` | APK `assets/config` |
| `user://` | `<data dir>/RegiaEngine/<exe name>` | same | app internal storage |
| `cache://` | `<cache dir>/RegiaEngine/<exe name>` | same | app cache directory |
| `logs://` | `user://logs` | same | same |

Only `user://` and `cache://` are writable. `Vfs::write_atomic` writes through a temporary file
and a rename, so a crash never leaves a half-written save or settings file.

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// Reads a text file shipped with the game.
fn read_credits(vfs: Res<Vfs>) {
    let Ok(path) = VfsPath::parse("assets://credits.txt") else { return };
    match vfs.read_sync(&path) {
        Ok(bytes) => info!("credits: {} bytes", bytes.len()),
        Err(err) => warn!("no credits file: {err}"),
    }
}
```

## What the cook does

```console
$ regia cook --project my_game
$ regia cook --project my_game --platform android --quality fast
```

| Source | Cooked into |
|---|---|
| `.glb` / `.gltf` | meshes (one per primitive, LODs from `_LOD0…n` naming), materials, textures, skeletons and animation clips |
| `.fbx`, `.obj` | the same outputs, after conversion to an in-memory glTF. FBX and OBJ settings are on [Importing assets](book/user-guide/importing-assets.md) |
| `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg` | textures: KTX2 with block compression for larger maps (BC on Linux, Windows, and macOS; ASTC on Android), RGBA8 for small ones |
| `.exr`, `.hdr` | HDR textures (linear float): KTX2 with BC6H on Linux, Windows, and macOS, and RGBA16F on Android, a full mip chain, optionally a cube map ([HDR images](#hdr-images)) |
| `.material.ron` | a cooked standard material that references cooked textures |
| `.scatter.ron` | the cooked terrain scatter set |
| `.matgraph.ron`, `.matinst.ron` | the cooked material graph / instance |
| `.atlas.ron`, `.tilemap.ron`, `.tmx`, `.tmj`, `.fgiv` | the cooked atlas, tilemap and probe-volume data |

### HDR images

An OpenEXR (`.exr`) or Radiance (`.hdr`) file cooks as a linear float texture, so an HDR sky ships in a
pak and loads like any other texture. The cook:

- replaces NaN and infinite samples with 0 and reports them as one cook warning per file
  (`sky.exr: 3 NaN or infinite sample(s) replaced with 0`); negative samples clamp to 0 and samples
  above 65504 (the largest finite half float) clamp to it; alpha clamps to 0 to 1;
- builds the whole mip chain, each level a 2×2 box filter in linear float;
- stores BC6H unsigned float on Linux, Windows, and macOS (a BC6H texel of a smooth sky stays within 6 % of the texel's
  brightest channel), and uncompressed RGBA16F on Android, where BC6H is not available and ASTC HDR
  is not on every phone.

The image's `.meta` `settings` (RON, the same ones PNG textures use; `usage` does not apply, an HDR
source is always linear) add:

```ron
(hdr_encoding: Some(bc6h), cube_face_px: Some(512), max_size: Some(4096))
```

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| `hdr_encoding` | `auto` (default: BC6H, RGBA16F on Android), `bc6h`, `rgba16f` or `astc_hdr` (ASTC 4×4 HDR, for devices that report it) on every platform. `compress: Some(false)` means `rgba16f`. |
| `cube_face_px` | An equirect sky is converted at cook time to a six-face cube of this face size, 4 to 8192 (`+X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z`). Every cube texel averages a grid of bilinear equirect samples over its footprint, so the faces meet without seams and a small sun does not alias. Unset keeps the 2D equirect image. |
| `max_size` | Larger sources are box-filtered down a level at a time first. |

Errors start with a code: `hdr_decode` (not an image the decoder reads), `hdr_size` (empty, or more
than 64 Mi texels), `hdr_settings` (a `cube_face_px` out of range), `hdr_ktx2` (the writer or an
encoder refused). The cooked file is read on the CPU by `regia_asset::hdr_texture::decode_hdr_ktx2`; the
studio environment takes it by path or id ([Studio environment](book/agents/studio-environment.md)).

Terrain heightfields and their layer textures have their own cook path
([Terrain data: cook and stream](book/user-guide/terrain-data.md)). Everything else under `assets/`
(levels, prefabs, UI, audio, fonts, config) is read as-is through the VFS and is copied verbatim
into a package. Fonts are the exception to "verbatim": a package carries each TrueType font subset to the
characters your shipped locales use ([Font subsetting](book/agents/font-subset.md)).

The cook is **incremental**: each output is keyed by a hash of the source bytes, the import
settings and the importer version, and only stale outputs are rebuilt. `--clean` rebuilds
everything; `--quality fast` turns off pak lz4 compression for quick iteration (textures cook at the quality their `.meta` sets); `--stats`
prints terrain budget statistics. Output goes to `.regia/cooked/<platform>/` with a manifest
that maps project paths to asset ids. `regia preview <asset>` cooks the project incrementally and shows that asset in a
window, the quickest way to check an import.

## `.meta` sidecars and asset ids

The first import of a source writes a `.meta` file next to it. It holds the asset's **id** (a
GUID that never changes, even when the file moves), the import settings, the format versions it
was imported with, and, for content an agent made, **provenance**: which tool, client and session
created it and who reviewed it. Commit `.meta` files with their sources. Levels and prefabs refer
to assets by id, so renaming a texture in the editor does not break the materials that use it.

The provenance policy is set in `Regia.toml` under `[provenance]`; `regia cook --quality
final` can refuse assets that no human has reviewed ([Agent protocol and MCP](../user-guide/agent-protocol.md)).

## Loading cooked assets

The `AssetServer` resource loads cooked assets by project path or id, from mounted `.fpak`
archives first and then from the cook cache:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_asset::AssetServer;
use regia_render::{CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, LabVertex, MeshRenderer};
use regia_scene::Transform;

/// Converts a cooked mesh into the renderer's vertex layout.
fn render_mesh(cooked: &regia_asset::CpuMesh) -> CpuMesh {
    let vertices = (0..cooked.positions.len())
        .map(|i| LabVertex {
            position: cooked.positions[i],
            normal: cooked.normals.get(i).copied().unwrap_or([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]),
            uv: cooked.uvs.get(i).copied().unwrap_or([0.0, 0.0]),
            tangent: cooked.tangents.get(i).copied().unwrap_or([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]),
            color: [1.0; 4],
            joints: [0; 4],
            weights: [0.0; 4],
        })
        .collect();
    CpuMesh { vertices, indices: cooked.indices.clone() }
}

/// Spawns the helmet once its cooked mesh is available.
fn spawn_helmet(mut server: ResMut<AssetServer>, mut commands: Commands, mut done: Local<bool>) {
    if *done {
        return;
    }
    let handle = match server.load_mesh_path("models/DamagedHelmet.glb") {
        Ok(handle) => handle,
        Err(err) => {
            warn!("helmet not cooked yet: {err}");
            *done = true;
            return;
        }
    };
    if let Some(mesh) = server.meshes().get(&handle) {
        commands.spawn((
            Transform::default(),
            MeshRenderer::new(Arc::new(render_mesh(mesh)), Arc::new(CpuMaterial::default())),
        ));
        *done = true;
    }
}
```

- `load_mesh_path`, `load_material_path` and the id-based `load_mesh`, `load_texture`,
  `load_image`, `load_material` return a typed `Handle<T>`; the data is in `server.meshes()`,
  `textures()`, `images()` and `materials()`.
- `server.state(id)` reports `NotLoaded`, `Loading`, `Loaded` or a failure; `server.source_of(id)`
  says whether the bytes came from a pak or the dev cache.
- Every load returns a `Result`. Never unwrap one: a missing or corrupt asset should degrade the
  game, not crash it.

Loads complete synchronously today. Turning a cooked mesh into a `MeshRenderer` is the explicit
conversion above (the cooked mesh is a structure-of-arrays, the renderer's an interleaved vertex
buffer). `regia_render::cooked_model::load_cooked_model` loads the LOD 0 parts of one cooked
glTF by asset id (meshes and materials). Spawning those parts as entities is still your system.
The samples show complete versions: `regia preview` (`crates/regia_cli/src/commands/preview.rs`)
for a static mesh, `samples/third_person/src/assets.rs` for a skinned, animated character.

`regia export usda --glb FILE.glb --out FILE.usda` writes one USDA stage from a glTF binary.
That stage is an exchange file, not a cooked format. The command, its limits, and its error
codes are on [Importing assets](book/user-guide/importing-assets.md).

## glTF conventions

glTF is the interchange format for meshes. The importer understands a few naming conventions so
artists can author engine features in their DCC tool: `_LOD0`, `_LOD1`, `_LOD2` suffixes form an
LOD group when `_LOD0` and another level share a stem, `socket_<name>` empties become attachment
sockets, ORM textures are packed occlusion / roughness / metallic, and `KHR_materials_transmission`,
`_volume`, `_ior` and `_emissive_strength` map onto material v3 fields. A file whose meshes are all
`_LODn` with `n > 0` still cooks; the lowest index is the primary. The full list is
[glTF conventions](book/agents/gltf-conventions.md).

## Hot reload of assets

Processes built with `regia_asset`'s `dev-assets` feature (the editor, and any dev build that
enables it) watch the cook cache. When `regia cook` or the editor's Reimport rewrites a cooked
file, the server reloads it in place and the next frame uses it.

## Packaging

`regia package` runs the cook when the archives are missing or stale and writes the cooked data
into `content/*.fpak` next to the executable; `AssetPlugin` mounts them automatically on startup
(on Android it extracts them from the APK first). Your loading code does not change. See
[Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md) and the pak format in `docs/formats/pak.md`.

## Upgrading content

Content formats are versioned. When the engine moves a format forward, its loader still reads
the old version and migrates it in memory, and `regia upgrade-project --write` rewrites your
files on disk for every format with a registered migrator (material, level, prefab, terrain, UI,
theme, VFX and the rest; keeping a `.bak` of each). It finds a file by the same name the cook and
the loader use: a terrain layer stack is any file whose name ends in `terrain.layers.ron`, in any
letter case, so a plain `textures/terrain.layers.ron` is upgraded too. The [Content formats](book/reference/formats.md) reference
lists every format, its current version and its migrators.

<!-- source: book/fundamentals/reflection.md -->
# Reflection

<!-- index: Reflection -->
<!-- index: Canonical RON | see: Reflection -->

Reflection lets the engine look inside your types at runtime: list a component's fields, read and
write them by name, and turn them into text and back. Regia Engine uses `bevy_reflect` for this
(through `regia_ecs`), and almost every tool in the engine depends on it:

| Feature | Uses reflection to |
|---|---|
| Levels and prefabs | save and load components as canonical RON keyed by type path |
| Editor inspector | show and edit every field, with ranges, units and tooltips |
| Agent protocol | describe types (`types.describe`), read entities, `scene.set_property`, `play.expect` on field values |
| Save games | serialize `Saveable` entities and saveable resources |
| Hot reload | snapshot the world before swapping the game library and restore it after |
| Runtime UI | bind a label to a field (`bind: (source: "Score.value", …)`) |

A component that is not reflected and registered still works in your systems, but none of the
above can see it.

## Making a type reflectable

Derive `Reflect`, list the reflected traits the engine should be able to call, and register the
type with the app:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// A door that opens toward a target angle.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Debug, Clone, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct Door {
    /// Current opening angle, radians.
    pub angle: f32,
    /// Whether the door is locked.
    pub locked: bool,
    /// Opening speed, radians per second.
    pub speed: f32,
}

/// Global door settings.
#[derive(Resource, Reflect, Debug, Clone, Default)]
#[reflect(Resource, Default)]
pub struct DoorRules {
    /// Doors close themselves after this many seconds.
    pub auto_close_secs: f32,
}

fn register(app: &mut App) {
    app.register_type::<Door>().register_type::<DoorRules>();
}
```

- `#[reflect(Component)]` lets the engine insert, read and remove the component by type;
  `#[reflect(Resource)]` does the same for resources.
- `#[reflect(Default)]` lets the engine construct the type when a file or an agent names it.
- Doc comments become field descriptions in the inspector and in `types.describe`; write them.
- Nested structs, enums, `Vec`, `Option`, maps and the math types (`Vec3`, `Quat`) reflect too,
  as long as each nested type derives `Reflect`.
- Fields you do not want saved or shown can be skipped with `#[reflect(ignore)]`.

Engine types are registered by their plugins. A game type you forget to register shows up in
the agent protocol's `errors.explain` and the editor as unknown; register every type in the
plugin that owns it.

## Editor attributes

Attributes attach editing metadata to fields. The inspector and the agent schema read them; the
runtime ignores them:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_ecs::attrs::{Category, Range, Step, Tooltip, Units};

/// A spotlight-like door lamp.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct DoorLamp {
    /// Brightness of the lamp.
    #[reflect(@Range(0.0..=2000.0), @Step(10.0), @Units("lm"), @Tooltip("Luminous flux"))]
    pub intensity: f32,
    /// Opening angle that switches the lamp on.
    #[reflect(@Range(0.0..=180.0), @Units("deg"), @Category("Trigger"))]
    pub trigger_angle: f32,
}
```

| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `@Range(a..=b)` | Sliders clamp to it; `types.describe` emits `minimum`/`maximum` on that field's schema (`attrs.range` is only the attribute on the type itself) |
| `@Step(x)` | Drag and step increment; `types.describe` emits `multipleOf` on a field's schema and `attrs.step` on the type |
| `@Units("m")` | Display units (`"m"`, `"deg"`, `"s"`, `"dB"`, `"lm"`, …) |
| `@Tooltip("…")` | Hover help |
| `@DisplayName("…")` | Label instead of the field name |
| `@Category("…")` | Groups fields under a collapsible Inspector header |
| `@Hidden` | Not shown in the inspector (still saved) |
| `@ReadOnly` | Shown, not editable |
| `@Multiline` | Multi-line text box |
| `@ColorHdr` | Color picker that allows values above 1 |
| `@AssetFilter("mesh")` | Asset picker filter |
| `@EditCondition("expr")` | Greys the field while `expr` over its sibling fields is false (`"cast_shadows"`, `"kind == Spot"`); see [the Inspector agent page](book/agents/inspector.md) for the grammar |
| `@EditConditionHides` | With `@EditCondition`: hide instead of grey |
| `@Toggle` | On a struct field with `enabled: bool`: a header checkbox; the body greys while off |

`regia_ecs::describe::field_attrs::<T>("field")` reads them back in code.

## Canonical text

`regia_ecs::serialize` turns any reflected value into **canonical RON**, the form levels,
prefabs and save files use: struct fields in declaration order, map keys sorted, floats written
in their shortest round-trip form, a fixed indentation. Writing the same value twice produces the
same bytes, which is why re-saving an unchanged level leaves `git diff` empty and why agent edits
review cleanly. `to_postcard` / `from_postcard` give the compact binary form cooked data uses.

## Reflection and the agent protocol

The agent protocol's discovery methods are reflection made visible:

```console
$ regia agent call types.list '{"component":true}'
$ regia agent call types.describe '{"type":"my_game::Door"}'
$ regia agent call scene.set_property '{"entity":42,"component":"my_game::Door","path":"angle","value":1.2}'
```

`types.describe` returns the fields with their types, doc comments and editor attributes, so an
agent can edit a type it has never seen. The exact parameters are in the
[agent guide's protocol](book/agents/protocol.md) and [scene](book/agents/scene.md) pages.

## Who registered what

Every registration made while a game plugin is building is recorded with its owner
(`regia_ecs::owner`). Hot reload uses this to remove exactly the game's types, systems and
observers before loading the new library, so the engine's own registrations are never touched
([Hot reload](book/user-guide/hot-reload.md)).

# Input

<!-- index: Input action -->
<!-- index: Input binding -->
<!-- index: Input rebinding -->
<!-- index: Input context -->
<!-- index: Cursor grab -->
<!-- index: Virtual stick -->
<!-- index: Touch controls -->

`regia_input` turns platform input into two things you use: **messages** (raw events) and
**actions** (named, mapped inputs). Actions are the portable form: the same gameplay code runs on
keyboard and mouse, gamepads and touch, and the bindings can be changed by the player at runtime.
What an agent can inject and read is mapped on [Input (agents)](book/agents/input.md).

## Raw messages

Keyboard, mouse, touch, IME and back-button events arrive as messages from `PlatformPlugin`:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

fn on_key(mut keys: MessageReader<KeyboardInput>) {
    for e in keys.read() {
        if e.state == ButtonState::Pressed {
            // e.physical_key / e.logical_key
        }
    }
}
```

Raw events are platform-shaped; use them for text entry and debug keys, and actions for gameplay.

## Defining actions

An action has a name and a kind (`Button`, `Axis1D`, `Axis2D` or `Axis3D`). Bindings map a source
(`InputSource`: a key, a 2D key set, mouse motion or a button, a gamepad button, stick or axis) to
an action. Build the configuration in code and hand it to `InputPlugin`:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_input::prelude::*;

fn input_config() -> InputConfig {
    InputConfig::new()
        .action("Move", ActionKind::Axis2D)
        .action("Look", ActionKind::Axis2D)
        .action("Jump", ActionKind::Button)
        .action("Fire", ActionKind::Button)
        .binding(Binding::new("Move", InputSource::keys2d("KeyW", "KeyS", "KeyA", "KeyD")))
        .binding(Binding::new("Move", InputSource::gamepad_stick(Stick::Left)))
        .binding(Binding::new("Look", InputSource::MouseDelta))
        .binding(Binding::new("Look", InputSource::gamepad_stick(Stick::Right)))
        .binding(Binding::new("Jump", InputSource::key("Space")))
        .binding(Binding::new(
            "Jump",
            InputSource::gamepad_button(regia::platform::GamepadButton::South),
        ))
        .binding(Binding::new("Fire", InputSource::mouse_button(MouseButton::Left)))
}

pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(InputPlugin::new(input_config()));
    }
}
```

Keys are named by their physical position (`"KeyW"`, `"Space"`, `"ShiftLeft"`), so WASD stays
WASD on an AZERTY keyboard. The configuration also round-trips through RON
(`InputConfig::from_ron` / `to_ron`) if you prefer to keep it in a file under `config/`.

## Reading actions

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_input::prelude::*;

fn drive_player(actions: Res<Actions>) {
    let move_axis = actions.axis2d("Move"); // Vec2, x right, y forward
    let jumping = actions.pressed("Jump"); // held this frame
    let jumped = actions.just_pressed("Jump"); // went down this frame
    let _ = (move_axis, jumping, jumped);
}
```

`value(name)` returns the raw `Vec3`, `axis1d` a scalar, `axis2d` a `Vec2`; `phase(name)` and
`triggered(name)` report the trigger state (below); `elapsed(name)` how long it has been held.
`actions.player(n)` reads local player `n` in split-screen: each player's devices are assigned
through `DeviceAssignment` in the `PlayerInputs` resource.

Actions are evaluated once per **fixed step** in `FixedUpdate` (and once per frame with a zero
delta when the frame runs no fixed step), so a `FixedUpdate` system reading actions orders itself
`after(InputSet::Evaluation)`. `just_pressed` is the per-step edge (use it in simulation); a
system that runs once per frame (`Update`, quicksave, agent polling) uses
`just_pressed_this_frame`, which stays true for the whole frame even when a multi-step frame
consumed the step-level edge on its first step. Mouse motion (`InputSource::MouseDelta`) is per
frame: a frame that runs several fixed steps applies it once, on its last step, so a `FixedUpdate`
reader sees it once and an `Update` mouse look sees the whole frame's motion.

## Modifiers and triggers

A binding can process its value before the action sees it. Triggers run per binding: each binding's
trigger list runs on that binding's own value, and an empty list is `Down`. The action takes the
strongest phase of its bindings, so a `Pressed` on one binding and an empty list on a sibling means
holding the sibling holds the action, and a press of the `Pressed` key still fires while the sibling is
down; an action that was already active reports `Ongoing`, not a second `Started`. A `Hold` or `Tap` on
one binding sees only that binding's key and times that key's own press. The action's value combines its
bindings: a button keeps the last non-zero value and axes add, and a zero value contributes nothing. An
injected value, or an assist that changes whether the action is down, is one value for the whole action:
every binding's triggers then see that value.

| Modifier | Effect |
|---|---|
| `DeadZone(DeadZone::radial(lo, hi))` / `axial(lo, hi)` | Ignore stick noise, rescale the rest |
| `Scale(v)`, `Negate { .. }`, `Swizzle(..)`, `InvertY(bool)` | Shape and remap axes |
| `Smooth(t)` | Exponential smoothing |
| `ResponseCurve(..)` | `Linear`, `Square`, `Cubic`, `SquareRoot`, `SmoothStep` |
| `ScaleByDelta` | Multiply by the frame delta |

| Trigger | Fires |
|---|---|
| `Down` (default) | while actuated |
| `Pressed` / `Released` | on the frame it goes down / up |
| `Hold(secs)` | once held this long |
| `Tap(secs)` | when released within this time |
| `Pulse(secs)` | immediately, then repeatedly while held |
| `Chord(action)` | while the named action's previous-frame `actuated` flag is set (`Started`, `Ongoing` or `Triggered`, and non-zero). A `Pressed` partner only chords on the following frame. Losing the partner ends as `Idle`, not `Completed`. Bind the partner with the default `Down` |

Use them with `Binding::new(..).with_modifier(..).with_trigger(..)`.

## Contexts

Group bindings into **contexts** (`InputConfig::context(name, InputContext::consuming(priority))` and
`binding_in(context, binding)`), then enable and disable them at runtime through the
`InputContexts` resource: a vehicle context while driving, a menu context while paused. Higher
priority contexts evaluate first; a context built with `InputContext::consuming` also hides its
actuated inputs from lower ones (so it wins a shared input), while `InputContext::new` lets both fire.

## Rebinding

`InputRebinder` listens for the next raw input and turns it into a new binding for an action
(the classic "press a key for Jump" screen), detecting conflicts. The result is stored in
`InputOverrides`, merged over the project configuration at startup and saved to
`user://input_overrides.ron` immediately after every change, so a rebind survives restarts.

A capture can be limited to one device (`RebindSlot::KeyboardMouse`, `RebindSlot::Gamepad`), which
keeps the bindings on the other devices. `set_axis_tuning` sets a dead zone and invert on an action's
axes, and `save_profile` and `load_profile` keep named copies in `user://input_profiles/`.
`regia_ui::RebindPanel` with `RebindPanelOptions` is the screen for all of this; the First Person
template has one working in `game/src/controls.rs` (F10). See
[the agent guide page](book/agents/input-rebind.md).

## Touch and Android

Touch arrives as `TouchInput` messages, and the `Touches` state tracks every active touch point
(`centroid`, per-touch displacement) for gestures and virtual sticks; `samples/sim_bridge` has
on-screen touch controls. Without UI widgets, the `TouchControls` resource maps screen zones (a
button or a floating stick) and recognized gestures to actions through `InputInjection`, so they
run the same triggers as a key; agents read it with `input.touch_controls` (see
[Android](book/user-guide/android.md)). On Android, gamepads come through the activity's input events (there
is no `gilrs` on Android, so `regia_input` has a separate Android backend); the action layer
is identical. The Android back button arrives as `BackPressed`.

The `regia_ui` widgets `VirtualStick { action: "Move", .. }` and `VirtualButton { action: "Jump" }`
write to their actions with no glue code: while a finger is on the stick, `Move` holds the stick's
deflection (x right, y up), and while the button is pressed, `Jump` holds `1.0`. Both go through
`InputInjection::hold`, so triggers and phases work as they do for a key, and lifting the finger
hands the action back to its device bindings. While a finger rests on the stick, the stick wins
over the keyboard for that action. `TouchControls` (screen zones and gestures without widgets) uses
the same path.

## Cursor grab

A look-driven game writes `cursor_grab` on the `Window` component: `CursorGrab::Locked` while
playing, `CursorGrab::None` while a menu is open, `CursorGrab::Confined` when the cursor should
stay inside the window and remain visible. Apply the change on the main thread. A system that
calls the OS setter from a worker pool deadlocks the frame on Windows. Take `NonSendMarker` so
the system stays on the main thread. The same rule covers `set_title` and `request_inner_size`.

winit 0.30 does not implement every grab on every backend. Regia rewrites the request before it
is sent, and logs the rewrite once per process:

| Request | Windows | X11 and Xwayland | Wayland | macOS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Locked` | requested as `Confined` | requested as `Confined` | `Locked` | `Locked` |
| `Confined` | `Confined` | `Confined` | `Confined` | requested as `Locked` |
| `None` | `None` | `None` | `None` | `None` |

A grab the OS still rejects is retried on a later frame. The component keeps the mode you asked
for. The fallback is only the mode sent to the window. Tell players who read a settings label
that "locked" on Windows and X11 confines the cursor to the window. On macOS, "confined" hides
and locks it, because that platform has no confine.

The behavior is [spec 11](docs/specs/11-platform-and-input.md) §§ 5–7, implemented in
`regia_platform::window_os`.

## Testing input

The agent protocol can inject raw events and scheduled action values (`play.inject_input`), and
`InputInjection` does the same from a test, so input-driven behavior runs deterministically in
CI. See the [agent guide's testing page](book/agents/testing.md). Input specification:
[spec 11](docs/specs/11-platform-and-input.md) §§ 5–7.
