# Rendering

<!-- index: Vulkan -->
<!-- index: DX12 -->
<!-- index: Metal -->
<!-- index: WebGPU -->
<!-- index: WebGL2 -->
<!-- index: Quality tier -->
<!-- index: VeryLow -->
<!-- index: Cinematic -->
<!-- index: Upscale quality -->
<!-- index: TAAU -->
<!-- index: TSR -->
<!-- index: FSR 3 -->
<!-- index: DLSS -->
<!-- index: XeSS -->
<!-- index: Frame generation -->
<!-- index: Present mode -->
<!-- index: Vsync -->
<!-- index: VsyncRelaxed -->

The renderer is a forward+ renderer behind `regia_render::RenderPlugin` (added by
`DefaultPlugins`). It covers PBR materials, sun and local lights, shadows, an IBL sky, post
processing (AgX tonemap, bloom, TAA), and — for the high tiers — temporal upscaling and atmosphere
(`docs/specs/13`, `docs/specs/26`).

The frame runs on the graphics API the platform opens (`regia_render::backend_policy`):

| Platform | APIs the instance opens | What the default pick uses |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | Vulkan and DX12 | A Vulkan hardware adapter when one exists. DX12 is the fallback, or the adapter `REGIA_GPU_INDEX` or `REGIA_GPU_NAME` names. |
| macOS (testing builds) | Metal | wgpu's adapter pick. Metal is the testing backend (ADR-009, ADR-264). macOS is not a dedicated-server package target. |
| Linux, Android | Vulkan | Vulkan. |

GL is never opened. A persistent pipeline cache (`.fpc`) applies on Vulkan. DX12 and Metal rely
on the driver's own disk cache. The product viewer (`regia_web`) is a separate path: it draws on
a page canvas with WebGPU, or with WebGL2 when WebGPU is missing or the page asks for
`backend: "webgl2"`. That viewer is not a general web game. A general web game target stays on
the version ladder.

DLSS and XeSS are optional link crates (`regia_dlss`, `regia_xess`) against SDKs that are not in
this repository. A build without the SDK falls back to the built-in upscalers. See
[Vendor upscalers](#vendor-upscalers) below.

Task procedures: [Quality and upscalers](book/how-to/picture/quality-and-upscalers.md),
[Light a level](book/how-to/picture/light-a-level.md),
[Materials](book/how-to/picture/materials.md).

Related chapters: [The default look](book/user-guide/default-look.md) (what a frame looks like before you touch
anything, and how to tune it), [Lighting, shadows and GI](book/systems/lighting.md),
[Automatic quality detection](book/user-guide/auto-quality.md),
[Dynamic resolution](book/user-guide/dynamic-resolution.md), and the
generated [render profile table](book/reference/render-profiles.md). That table lists the six
real-time presets. It omits the VeryLow tier and the Cinematic profile.

## Render profiles

A profile is a named bundle of quality settings:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::render::{RenderProfilePreset, RenderSettings};

fn configure(app: &mut App) {
    app.insert_resource(RenderSettings::from_profile(RenderProfilePreset::DesktopHigh));
}
```

Real-time presets (`RenderProfilePreset::ALL`): `MobileLow`, `MobileHigh`, `DesktopLow`,
`DesktopHigh`, `DesktopUltra`, and the Steam Deck `Deck`. `Cinematic` is a seventh preset
(`RenderProfilePreset::WITH_OFFLINE`). It is Desktop Ultra with native scale, 8192² sun cascades,
every cloud texel marched, the light caps at their maximum, and mesh LOD held toward LOD 0
(ADR-1403). No menu and no detector pick it. `regia_render::cinematic::gate_preset` runs it on a
desktop whose detected tier is High or Ultra. On Android the applied preset is Mobile High
(`cinematic_needs_desktop`). On a detected tier below High the applied preset is that tier's own
(`cinematic_tier_too_low`) unless the caller passes `force`. Hosts read `--render-profile`, then
`REGIA_RENDER_PROFILE`, then `render_profile.txt` in the scene directory.

Desktop High and Ultra render at native resolution with temporal AA. A game may set Desktop
High's `render_scale` to 0.67 for a temporally upsampled (TAAU) performance budget, which ADR-041
introduced and the default stopped using on 2026-10-07 because that TAAU loses thin geometry and
floor reflections. The Medium quality tier is that 0.67 scale with Balanced lighting. Deck and
Mobile Low render at 70%, upsampled. The [render profile table](book/reference/render-profiles.md)
is generated from the six real-time presets and lists the main values; not every `RenderProfile`
field has a row (for example `gi_probes`, `texture_streaming`, `contact_shadows` and
`emissive_lights` do not), so read the rustdoc for the rest.

The user-facing ladder is `QualityTier`: `MobileLow`, `MobileHigh`, `Deck`, `VeryLow`, `Low`,
`Medium`, `High`, `Ultra`. `VeryLow` is not its own preset. It is Desktop Low at render scale
1/3 with the SGSR 1 spatial upscaler and a 384 MiB lazy texture budget (ADR-7882). Content
budgets stay on Low, and `RenderSettings::preset` still answers Desktop Low. The saved menu
value is `GraphicsPreset` (`Low`, `Medium`, `High`, `Ultra`, `Clean`, `Deck`, `VeryLow`).
`Clean` renders as High. On Android, Low and VeryLow become Mobile Low and every other menu
preset becomes Mobile High. Individual profile fields can still override the preset. See
[Automatic quality detection](book/user-guide/auto-quality.md) and the
[agent guide](book/agents/framework.md).

## Upscale quality

<!-- index: Native -->
<!-- index: Ultra Performance -->

`RenderProfile::upscale_quality` is `None` on every preset, so `render_scale` applies.
`Some(UpscaleQuality)` replaces that scale. The ratio is display size divided by render size,
as an exact fraction, rounded to the nearest integer (halves up, at least 1):

| Mode | Ratio | Permille |
|---|---|---|
| `Native` | 1/1 | 1000 |
| `Quality` | 3/2 | 667 |
| `Balanced` | 17/10 | 588 |
| `Performance` | 2/1 | 500 |
| `UltraPerformance` | 3/1 | 333 |

The mode sets the size. On a TAA frame the upscaler is still `temporal_upscaler`. On any other
frame it is `spatial_upscaler` (`Bilinear`, or `Sgsr` on VeryLow). Dynamic resolution, when a
host applies it, stays inside the mode's permille range (`DynResConfig::within_quality`).

## Temporal upscalers

`temporal_upscaler` is consulted when anti-aliasing is TAA. The default on every preset is
`Taau` (neighbourhood clamp, bilinear history). `Tsr` is the reconstruction upscaler
(depth-dilated motion, disocclusion, variance clipping, thin-feature locks, a reactive mask).
`Fsr3` is the FSR 3.1 upscaler ported from the AMD FidelityFX SDK v1.1.4. All three are compiled
into every build. The opt-in example under [Renderer features](#renderer-features-and-opt-ins)
sets `Tsr`.

## Vendor upscalers

`VendorUpscaler` is separate from `TemporalUpscaler` so a host's exhaustive match on the built-in
enum keeps compiling. `FrameRenderer::set_vendor_upscaler` tries DLSS or XeSS on a single-sample
TAA frame and falls back to `temporal_upscaler` when the vendor cannot run.
`vendor_upscaler_report` records the reason. Agents read the same facts from `render.get_upscalers`.

- **DLSS** (`regia_dlss`). Optional `sdk` feature plus an external `DLSS_SDK` path. NGX on Vulkan,
  Linux and Windows. Android and macOS never link. A missing runtime, a non-NVIDIA adapter, or a
  DX12 device (`dlss_needs_vulkan`) uses the built-in upscaler.
- **XeSS** (`regia_xess`). Optional `sdk` feature plus an external `XESS_SDK` path. Windows
  Vulkan. Other targets are not linked. Without the SDK the runtime answer is `not_linked`.

The SDK binaries are not in the repository. Refusal codes live in `regia_render::upscaler::reason`
and on [Upscalers (agents)](book/agents/upscalers.md).

## Frame generation

Frame generation presents one interpolated frame between two rendered frames. It is a WGSL port
of the FidelityFX SDK v1.1.4 interpolation and optical-flow shaders, paced on Regia's wgpu
surfaces. No vendor binary is involved. It stays off until `FrameGenSettings.enabled` is set, and
the cargo feature `frame-gen` has to be compiled in (`not_compiled` otherwise). A headless app
reports `headless`. A device without the storage-texture and storage-buffer counts, or a GL
device, reports `needs_desktop_gpu`. The default pauses generation when the rendered rate is
under 55 fps. The HUD is redrawn on the generated image. It is not interpolated. The agent method
is `render.frame_gen`. See [Frame generation (agents)](book/agents/frame-gen.md).

## Present modes

<!-- index: Immediate -->

`PresentMode` on the primary window is `Vsync` (wait for vertical blank; the default),
`VsyncRelaxed` (vsync, and a late frame may tear), or `Immediate` (no wait; the image may tear).
`GameSettings.display.vsync` applies live: on selects `Vsync`, or keeps `VsyncRelaxed` when that
was already the window's mode; off selects `Immediate`. When the window asks for `Immediate`,
the swapchain takes the first unsynced mode the surface offers (`Immediate`, then `Mailbox`),
and FIFO when the surface has none. `Mailbox` and FIFO are surface modes, not `PresentMode`
variants. `DisplayApplied` reports the window mode that stuck and the swapchain summary.
On Android, off is refused (`android_display_paced`): frames stay on the display's vsync grid,
and the rate comes from `display.frame_cap`. A surface with no unsynced mode keeps FIFO
(`no_unsynced_mode_offered`). A host variable-refresh policy picks its own mode
(`host_vrr_policy`).

## Renderer features and opt-ins

Two profile fields are off in every preset, because turning them on changes frames (ADR-041:
look or performance changes are opt-in). A game turns them on per profile:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::render::{RenderProfilePreset, RenderSettings, TemporalUpscaler};

fn configure(app: &mut App) {
    let mut settings = RenderSettings::from_profile(RenderProfilePreset::DesktopHigh);
    settings.profile.temporal_upscaler = TemporalUpscaler::Tsr;
    settings.profile.visibility_buffer = true;
    app.insert_resource(settings);
}
```

- `temporal_upscaler`: `Taau` (the default), `Tsr`, or `Fsr3`. `Tsr` is a reconstruction upscaler
  with depth-dilated motion, disocclusion handling, variance clipping, thin-feature locks and a
  reactive mask. `Fsr3` is a port of AMD's FSR 3.1 upscaler, kept as the comparison baseline for
  `Tsr`. They only apply when the profile's anti-aliasing is TAA.
- `visibility_buffer`: rigid opaque meshes that have meshlets draw through a visibility buffer
  with cluster LOD (GPU culling against a Hi-Z pyramid). It is meant for dense scatter; frames
  change by the LOD cut.

Texture streaming is already on in every preset, with a resident budget from
`TextureStreaming::for_preset` (Desktop High: 4096 px cap, 2 GiB, eager). Standard-surface
materials upload low mips first, step up as the screen needs them inside a per-frame upload
budget, and fade each level in. Material-graph materials stay fully resident. To override, set
`settings.profile.texture_streaming` to another value (for example `TextureStreaming::OFF`, or
`TextureStreaming::DECK` for a 2048 px cap); `TextureStreaming::DESKTOP` is an unbudgeted
low-mips-first ramp and drops the preset's cap.

### Mip streaming metadata

The cook looks at each texture's mip chain and records the largest size at which a level still adds
visible detail: a flat roughness map is capped at 16 px, a photo is not capped at all (ADR-1942). The
streamer keeps levels above that size out of memory when no map of the material needs them, so a flat
map costs what a small one costs and looks the same. Every map of a material drops the same number of
levels from its own top, so one detailed map keeps the levels of the whole material. The check is on the
single worst texel, so a small logo on a flat field keeps every level. A material with one map cooked
before this keeps all its levels.

Two `.meta` settings override the streamer per texture:

```ron
(stream: Some(false), stream_min_px: Some(512))
```

- `stream: Some(false)` keeps the texture at the tier's cap: a menu backdrop, or a texture that must
  never show a low mip. The whole material follows, since a material's maps stream together.
- `stream_min_px` raises the smallest size the texture drops to. A value below the tier's own floor
  changes nothing.

Check a build with `assets.cooked_pack { "inspect": true }`, which counts `mip_metadata_textures`,
`mip_capped_textures` and `unstreamed_textures` per pak.

## Local lights and interiors

Desktop High uploads 256 point and spot lights per view, Desktop Ultra 512, Deck 96. The lab
tools stay at 64. A larger set is ranked and the drop is logged; lights are not
cut off in silence. Spot lights that cast shadows come from the same local-light
atlas as point lights. A point light uses six tiles, so not every point can cast
a shadow at once.

A cockpit or a tunnel needs an interior volume (or an `EnclosureScene` shell) and
an exposure around EV 8. The ambient floor is 40 lux, a floor under the lights,
not a flat fill. At a sunny EV 15 that floor is tonemapped to black, which is the
pure-black console. `build_interior_lighting` places the probe grid and traces one
bounce of the local lights (a miss stays black). Bind that field and one reflection
probe. Auto-exposure lifts a fully indoor view. A view that also contains the sun
stays at the outdoor exposure unless the volume forces the interior shade.

## More than one directional light

A frame draws up to four `DirectionalLight`s: the sun (the lowest entity, with the cascaded
shadow map) and three more, unshadowed. Meshes, terrain and grass, the probe GI and reference
traces of the frame all take the extra lights. A `.bake.ron` bake description lists up to
four suns since format v3 (`suns: [..]`), and every bake set up from it takes them all; the
level export and the editor's bake panel still write one sun. The agent method `render.lights` lists which paths take them
(`extra_directional_paths`) and which do not (`sun_only_paths`); see
[Render lights](book/agents/render-lights.md).

## Fog

Distance and height fog lives on `RenderSettings.fog` (exponential height fog per Hoffman &
Preetham, GDC 2002):

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::render::{FogSettings, RenderProfilePreset, RenderSettings};

fn configure(app: &mut App) {
    // Desktop Low: no LUT sky, so `FogSettings` reaches the meshes. On Desktop High and
    // Ultra the atmosphere's aerial LUT supplies the haze; tune `VolumetricFogSettings` there.
    let mut settings = RenderSettings::from_profile(RenderProfilePreset::DesktopLow);
    settings.fog = FogSettings::outdoor_haze();
    app.insert_resource(settings);
}
```

See the [agent guide's fog page](book/agents/fog.md) for the formula and how goldens verify it.

Desktop High and Ultra also run a physically based atmosphere, froxel fog and a volumetric
cloud layer. Mobile, Desktop Low and Deck stay on the analytic sky plus this height fog.
Put a `TimeOfDay` resource in the world for the sun, `VolumetricFogSettings` and `FogVolumes`
for participating media, and `CloudSettings` for the cloud layer. `gpu_timings().report()`
prints every pass, including `atmosphere`, `clouds` and `fog`. See the
agent pages for the controls.

### Planet presets (per map)

Each level picks its planet in `LevelSettings.atmosphere` (scene format v2; older levels load
as Earth):

```ron
"regia_scene::level::LevelSettings": (
    gravity: (0.0, -1.31, 0.0),
    atmosphere: (
        preset: Airless,                 // Earth | Mars | Airless
        time_of_day: Some((hour: 9.0, day_of_year: 172, latitude_deg: 10.0)),
        sun_illuminance_lux: None,       // None: the preset's (Earth 120 klx, Mars 52 klx, Jupiter 4.4 klx)
        cloud_coverage: 0.0,             // ignored when Airless
        cloud_type: 0.5,                 // 0 stratus, 0.5 cumulus, 1 towering
        sky_body: Some((                 // Jupiter from Europa
            direction: (-0.55, 0.42, -0.72),
            angular_diameter_deg: 12.0,
            tint: (0.62, 0.55, 0.47),
            bands: 1.0,
            fill_lux: None,              // planet-shine; None: physical at the current phase
        )),
    ),
),
```

- **Earth** — blue sky, orange sunsets, aerial haze.
- **Mars** — thin CO₂ and dust: a butterscotch day sky, a blue glow around a low sun, dust haze.
- **Airless** — a black sky with stars, a small hard sun, no haze, no clouds, no fog unless you
  author a fog volume. Ambient light is the ground bounce, so shadows are deep.

The sky body is lit by the sun, so its phase changes with the time of day.

It also lights the ground. **Planet-shine** is a shadowless directional fill from the body
(Jupiter-shine on Europa). Meshes, terrain and scatter all take it as Lambert diffuse, so faces
in the sun's shadow that face the body are not black.

- With `fill_lux: None` the engine uses the physical value: sun illuminance × the body's albedo
  × sin²(half its apparent diameter) × the Lambert phase law. That is about 30 lx for Jupiter
  at full phase under Europa's 4.4 klx sun.
- `Some(lux)` sets an authored value (DO27's Bore Twelve uses 1600 lx).
- The fill is tinted by the body's `tint`. Mars and Airless use
the physical sky on every profile that renders HDR; Earth uses it on Desktop High and Ultra.
`regia upgrade-project --write` rewrites v1 levels with the Earth block spelled out.
`render_lab planets` renders the five reference shots in `docs/evidence/m15c/`.

## Cameras

A camera is an entity with a camera component and a rig (see [Gameplay](book/user-guide/gameplay.md)). Exposure,
field of view and post settings are reflected fields; pin `Camera.exposure_ev` and turn off
auto-exposure when you need deterministic screenshots.

Auto exposure reads a luminance histogram on the GPU and applies it two frames later, blended
in log space, so a frame never waits for that read. The image adapts over a few frames instead
of stepping. Goldens and byte-identical captures leave auto exposure off. Metering, the EV100
clamp and the default grade are described in [The default look](book/user-guide/default-look.md).

### Lens effects and bloom

A camera with a `PhysicalCamera` asks for motion blur and depth of field; the quality preset must
allow each (Desktop High, Ultra and Deck). What the passes guarantee (ADR-1152):

- **Bloom** keeps a highlight's energy and position. Each bloom level is half the one above,
  rounded up, and its texels cover exactly 2 × 2 texels of the level above, so a bright point away
  from the frame border glows with the same total energy, centred on itself, wherever it sits and
  at any frame size. A small light moving by a pixel moves its glow by a pixel; the glow does not
  pulse or jump. A flat image stays flat up to the border.
- **Motion blur** is capped at `MotionBlur::MAX_BLUR_FRACTION` (1/8) of the frame height: a
  teleported object, a hitch frame or a spinning prop blurs over at most that length around itself.
  A long blur takes more samples than `samples` asks for (up to `MotionBlur::MAX_SAMPLES` per
  direction), so its taps stay about 4 px apart and the trail is continuous. Motion vectors that
  are NaN or infinite read as no motion.
- **Depth of field** caps the largest circle of confusion at
  `DepthOfField::MAX_CIRCLE_OF_CONFUSION_DIAMETER` (128 px): the blur loops are as long as the
  radius, so an unbounded value hung the GPU. A blurred foreground spreads its full radius over
  the sharp background behind it, for any circle up to the cap. An infinite far plane is supported.
- NaN or infinite colour texels (a broken material) are skipped by the blur taps, so they stay one
  pixel and do not spread over a trail or a circle of confusion.

## Headless and deterministic capture

The renderer runs **offscreen** — no window, no compositor — with `RenderPlugin { headless: true }`.
Combined with a fixed timestep and the agent protocol's `play.step`, two runs produce
byte-identical PNGs on lavapipe. That is the golden-image and CI path; see
[the agent guide's headless-capture page](book/agents/headless-capture.md).

## Profiling

- `regia_core`'s `tracy` feature enables the Tracy profiler.
- Per-frame systems carry `tracing` spans; the `Profiler` resource holds the process-wide frame
  profiler, and `play.get_diagnostics` reports fps, frame times and draw calls.
- GPU passes record timestamp queries named after the render-graph node (`docs/06` § 2).
  `render_lab outdoor` prints atmosphere, cloud and froxel-fog times on a Desktop High frame.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/dynamic-resolution.md -->
# Dynamic resolution

<!-- index: Dynamic resolution -->
<!-- index: Upscale quality -->

`regia_render::DynResController` chooses an internal render scale in permille (`1000` is
native, `500` is half) from GPU time. It is a pure function of the samples you give it: it does
not read the device, it does not change `RenderSettings`, and it does not write the settings
file. Apply the permille it returns to the frame you are about to draw, and keep that value in
the controller. Writing `render_scale` on every step fsyncs on the main thread.

DO27 can adopt this controller or keep its own. Either way the decision keys on GPU time against
the wall frame. A frame whose GPU time is well under the wall time holds or raises the scale,
even when the GPU time itself is over the frame budget. The bug this closes is a CPU-bound scene
(about 31 ms of GPU time inside a 66 ms wall frame, near 15 fps) whose scale fell from 1000 to
500 because the controller only compared GPU time with the budget.

The Android thermal governor is a different policy. It scales for heat, not for frame time. This
page does not change it.

## What one frame means

Pass two clocks, both in milliseconds:

- `gpu_ms` is [`GpuTimings::frame_ms`](book/agents/renderer.md): the GPU's busy time for the frame
  encoder. Timestamps land two frames late. Until the first one arrives the value is `0`, and the
  controller ignores `0`.
- `frame_ms` is the wall interval between presented frames (the interval the performance overlay
  graphs). `FrameCpuTimings::total_ms` covers `render_into` only; pass the present interval here.

`classify_bound` classifies that pair:

| GPU time / wall time | Bound |
|---|---|
| strictly under 60% | `CpuBound` |
| strictly over 90% | `GpuBound` |
| from 60% through 90%, or a non-finite / non-positive input | `Balanced` |

The 90% line is the same "GPU-bound" idea the performance overlay prints. The 60% line is
stricter: a frame that is only somewhat busy on the GPU is `Balanced`, and a balanced frame does
not step the scale down.

## When the scale moves

The controller keeps a rolling median of the accepted `gpu_ms` samples
(`DynResConfig::window_frames`, default 30). It does not move until that window is full, so one
spike cannot change the scale. Defaults:

| Knob | Default |
|---|---|
| `budget_ms` | 16.6 ms of GPU time |
| `min_permille` / `max_permille` | 500 / 1000 |
| `step_down_permille` / `step_up_permille` | 50 / 25 |
| `window_frames` | 30 |
| `hysteresis` | 0.1 (a deadband of ±10% around the budget) |
| `cooldown_frames` | 60 accepted samples between changes |

On a full window, after the cooldown:

- **Down** when the median is strictly over `budget_ms * (1 + hysteresis)` and the current frame
  is `GpuBound`. A `CpuBound` or `Balanced` frame never steps down.
- **Up** when the median is strictly under `budget_ms * (1 - hysteresis)`, whatever the bound is.
  A scale that was pushed down comes back up once the GPU work drops, including while the frame
  is still CPU-bound.
- **Hold** inside the deadband, on the edges, and while the cooldown is running.

After a change, the next `cooldown_frames` accepted samples keep the new permille. The sample
after those may change again. A non-finite or non-positive sample is dropped whole: it does not
enter the median, it does not tick the cooldown, and it does not change the last bound. The same
inputs always produce the same permille trace.

`min_permille` greater than `max_permille` is clamped down to `max_permille` (the range becomes
that one value). A non-finite or non-positive budget becomes 16.6 ms. `hysteresis` is clamped to 0.0..=0.99 (non-finite becomes 0.1). A window of 0 becomes 1,
and a window above 4096 is capped. The starting permille is clamped into the sanitized range.

## Calling it

```rust
use regia_render::{DynResConfig, DynResController, FrameQuality};

fn start() -> DynResController {
    DynResController::new(DynResConfig::default(), 1_000)
}

fn apply(
    controller: &mut DynResController,
    quality: &mut FrameQuality,
    gpu_ms: f32,
    frame_ms: f32,
) {
    let permille = controller.update(gpu_ms, frame_ms);
    let capped = permille.min(u32::from(u16::MAX));
    quality.render_scale_permille = u16::try_from(capped).unwrap_or(u16::MAX);
}
```

`FrameQuality::render_scale_permille` is a `u16`. The default range 500..=1000 fits. A host that
raises `max_permille` past 65535 has to clamp before that assignment; the controller itself
returns a `u32`.

Read `permille()`, `bound()` (`FrameBound::label` is `"cpu"`, `"gpu"` or `"balanced"`) and
`median_gpu_ms()` for a HUD or a log. This crate does not emit a telemetry event. A later
telemetry row can use the names `dynres_permille`, `dynres_bound` and `dynres_median_gpu_ms`.
`median_gpu_ms()` is `0` until the first accepted sample.

The owner's case, as a unit test in `dynamic_res`: GPU 31 ms, wall 66 ms, budget 16.6 ms, three
minutes at about 15 fps, permille stays 1000. A GPU-bound overload steps down by 50 to 500 and
stops there, then steps up by 25 when the load drops.

## Inside an upscale quality mode

When `RenderProfile::upscale_quality` is set, the frame's top size is that mode's render size,
not the profile's `render_scale`. Build the controller's range from the mode so a step cannot
leave it:

```rust
use regia_render::{DynResConfig, DynResController, UpscaleQuality};

fn controller_for(mode: UpscaleQuality) -> DynResController {
    let config = DynResConfig::default().within_quality(mode);
    DynResController::new(config, mode.permille())
}
```

`UpscaleQuality::permille_range` is Native 667–1000, Quality 588–667, Balanced 500–588,
Performance 333–500. Ultra Performance holds 333. A vendor runtime that publishes its own range
uses `DynResConfig::within_preferred` instead. The quality modes and the present modes are in
[Quality and upscalers](book/how-to/picture/quality-and-upscalers.md).

# The default look

<!-- index: AgX -->
<!-- index: Auto exposure -->
<!-- index: Default look -->

What a frame looks like before a game touches any lighting or post setting, why, and which
knobs move it. The defaults are physically based: a ~100 000 lux sun, a sky in cd/m², a
camera exposed in EV100. Get the light levels right and the look follows; most "it looks
flat" or "it looks washed out" problems are a light level, not a post setting.

The reference shots are `cargo run --release -p lookdev --bin default_look -- --out <dir>`
(props on snow, a vehicle in the air, a cockpit, a wide vista); their lavapipe goldens live in
`samples/lookdev/goldens/` and before/after frames in `docs/evidence/default-look/`.

## What you get by default

`RenderSettings::default()` is the Desktop High profile on a desktop (on a Steam Deck it is `Deck`, on Android
Mobile High; see [Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md)). VeryLow, Medium, Low, Ultra, and the offline
Cinematic profile are choices a game or the detector makes later. They are not this default.
With Desktop High:

| Stage | Default | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| Display transform | AgX, then the default look grade (contrast 1.2, saturation 1.4) | `PostSettings::tonemap`, `contrast`, `saturation` |
| Exposure | Histogram auto exposure, keyed to middle gray, EV100 clamped to −2…15 | `PostSettings::auto_exposure`, `auto_exposure_min_ev100`, `auto_exposure_max_ev100`, `exposure_compensation` |
| Bloom | Energy-conserving blend toward the blurred image, 4 %; the blur keeps a highlight's energy and centre at any frame size | `PostSettings::bloom`, `bloom_mips`, `bloom_intensity` |
| Anti-aliasing | Temporal AA at native resolution (Desktop High and Ultra); 0.67 render scale with temporal upscaling (TAAU) is an opt-in budget | profile `render_scale`, `anti_aliasing` |
| Sun shadows | 4 cascades, PCSS (1° sun, 12 search + 16 filter taps; 6+8 only in the opt-in 0.67 budget), blended cascade seams, fade at the shadow distance | profile `shadow_filter`, `csm_*` |
| Ambient occlusion | View-space AO at half resolution, 1.2 m radius, multi-bounce, also occludes sky reflections. The forward pass samples that half-resolution texture directly | profile `ssao` |
| Diffuse GI | GPU irradiance probes (DDGI, on by default in Desktop High and Ultra; a CPU `GiField` is optional) + a screen-space bounce (half resolution only in the opt-in 0.67 budget), upsampled with a depth-aware filter. A held camera reuses the previous bounce | profile `gi`, `screen_space_gi` |
| Sky | Procedural sky behind geometry, with a sun disc and aureole; it is also the IBL | `Environment::ibl` |
| Haze | Aerial perspective: distance recedes into the horizon sky color. With the LUT sky (`physical_atmosphere`, Desktop High and Ultra) the atmosphere's aerial LUT supplies it and `FogSettings` is forced off for meshes; `FogSettings` applies when the LUT sky is off | `RenderSettings::fog` (`FogSettings::aerial()`), `VolumetricFogSettings` |

### Display transform

AgX maps middle gray (0.18 after exposure) to ≈ 0.5 on screen and rolls highlights off over
about four stops instead of clipping, so a sunlit snowfield stays white with detail and a
shadowed interior keeps its dark grays. Very bright saturated colors (a muzzle-flash core,
an overexposed red) desaturate toward white on purpose — that is AgX's "path to white". Base
AgX is muted; the default look adds an S-curve around mid gray and a saturation boost in
display space. Set `contrast` and `saturation` to 1.0 for the bare transform. `TonemapOperator::AcesFitted`
gives the punchier, hue-shifting filmic curve many games are used to; `Neutral` is near-linear.

The no-post forward path and the terrain shaders print with the same transform and the same
default grade, so meshes, terrain and water agree.

### Exposure

Auto exposure meters the log-average luminance of the frame between the 40th and 95th
percentile (deep shadow and specular glints do not drag it) and keys it to middle gray. The
clamp is what keeps snow white: a frame of sunlit snow meters around EV100 16, and the
ceiling of 15 (the photographer's "sunny 16") stops it from being printed gray. Lower the
ceiling for a darker, moodier daylight; raise `exposure_compensation` (in stops) to brighten
everything. A camera with `Camera::exposure_ev` pins the exposure instead.

If you pin the exposure yourself, meter it: EV100 ≈ 15 under a 100 klx sun, ≈ 14 in open
shade, ≈ 9–12 indoors. Values tuned before the 2026-10-06 transform fix (which printed middle
gray at 0.17) are 1–3 stops too bright now.

### Shadows

The sun uses percentage-closer soft shadows: a blocker search, then a filter whose width is
the gap between receiver and blocker times the sun's angular radius (1°), so contact shadows
are crisp and long shadows soften with distance from the caster. Cascade seams are blended
over the last 15 % of each cascade and the last cascade fades out instead of cutting off.
The kernels rotate per pixel and per frame; TAA accumulates them. Shadow bias is applied on
the receiver (normal offset plus a slope term), identically on every GPU.

### Ambient, AO and GI

Without probes, indirect light is the procedural sky's irradiance: blue from above, a neutral
ground bounce from below. With an irradiance field (`RuntimeRenderer::set_gi_field`, filled by
`update_irradiance` from an `SdfScene`), the probes *replace* the sky term inside the probe
box and fade back to it one cell outside: they already contain the open sky, the bounce off
sunlit ground, and the occlusion of roofs and walls. Call `update_irradiance` a few times
(or every frame with hysteresis) — each update adds a bounce. Put probes where the camera
spends time: around bases, inside cockpits, along trenches.

Screen-space AO darkens contact and creases (radius 1.2 m) and also darkens sky reflections
in crevices. The screen-space bounce adds light from nearby surfaces that face each other.

### Sky and haze

The sky is drawn wherever no geometry was, when IBL is on and the view is not composited over
an earlier one. The default fog is aerial perspective: an exponential height fog whose color
is the horizon sky radiance in the view direction plus a forward-scattering glow toward the
sun, integrated along the ray. About 10 % of the contrast is gone at 500 m and 35 % at 2 km
near the ground; it thins with altitude. `FogSettings::aerial()` is the starting point;
`density` scales the distance, `height_falloff` the altitude, `color` tints it. Set
`fog.enabled = false` for clear air, or `sky_inscatter = false` for the flat-color fog.
This module is a stand-in for the M15c atmosphere and is replaced by it.

## Tuning for a game

1. **Light levels first.** Keep the sun around 100 klx at noon (50 klx at low sun), the
   procedural sky as is, and let auto exposure work. Check a gray card (albedo 0.18) prints
   mid gray in sun.
2. **Give the probes a volume** around every place players look closely. Interiors without
   probes are lit by the open sky — bright and flat.
3. **Then grade.** `contrast` / `saturation` for the mood; `exposure_compensation` for
   brightness; `bloom_intensity` for glow; `auto_exposure_max_ev100` for how bright a sunny
   frame may be.
4. **Albedo matters.** Real snow is 0.8, concrete 0.4, asphalt 0.1. Albedos above 0.9 or
   below 0.03 read as fake under a physically correct transform.

The terrain renderer has its own `TimeOfDay` (sun, sky ambient in exposed units) and its own
flat-color fog; its default sky ambient is a clear sky (≈ 1 : 4 against the sun).

<!-- source: book/systems/lighting.md -->
# Lighting, shadows and global illumination

<!-- index: Directional light -->
<!-- index: Point light -->
<!-- index: Spot light -->
<!-- index: GiLook -->
<!-- index: DDGI -->
<!-- index: Baked GI -->
<!-- index: Lightmap -->
<!-- index: Path tracer -->
<!-- index: Screen-space GI -->
<!-- index: Reflection probe -->

Regia Engine lights scenes in physical units: the sun in lux, point lights in lumens, spot lights in
candela, the sky in candela per square meter, and the camera exposed in EV100. This chapter covers
the light types, shadows, indirect light (sky, ambient occlusion, irradiance probes, screen-space
GI), reflections and interiors. What the defaults look like, and the order to tune them in, is in
[The default look](book/user-guide/default-look.md). The task order (sun, a GI look, an interior,
a bake) is [Light a level](book/how-to/picture/light-a-level.md).

## Light components

| Component | Units | Position and direction |
|---|---|---|
| `DirectionalLight` (the sun) | `illuminance` in lux | `direction` field: the way the light travels. Up to four per frame: the lowest entity is the sun and owns the cascaded shadow map; the other three are unshadowed. |
| `PointLight` | `intensity` in lumens, `radius` cutoff in meters | the entity's `GlobalTransform` |
| `SpotLight` | `intensity` in candela, `inner_angle` / `outer_angle` half-angles in radians, `range` | position from the transform; aims along the entity's −Z axis (rotate the entity to aim) |
| `LightSourceSize` (optional, next to a `PointLight` or `SpotLight`) | `radius_m`: radius of the emitting sphere in meters (default 0.45) | sets the light's shadow softness and highlight size (see below) |
| `LightProfile` (optional, next to a `PointLight` or `SpotLight`) | `profile`: an IES profile's name in the `LightProfileLibrary`; `file_intensity`, `scale`, `rotation` | shapes the light with the IES distribution; nadir = a spot's direction or a point light's rotated −Y (see below) |
| `RectLight` | `intensity` in lumens per face, `width` / `height` in meters, `two_sided`, `range` | a rectangle on the entity's X (width) and Y (height), emitting toward its −Z |
| `TubeLight` | `intensity` in lumens, `length` and `radius` in meters, `range` | a cylinder along the entity's X axis |
| `LightSourceLtc` | a marker next to `LightSourceSize` | shades the sphere through the LTC tables with the path tracer's `1 / d²`: correct below the horizon, brighter near the light than the default form |

All three have `color` (linear RGB) and `cast_shadows`. Reference levels: a clear noon sun is
about 100 000 lux (50 000 at a low sun), an overcast day 10 000, a lit office 500. A 60 W-class
bulb is about 800 lumens.

**Light size.** A point or spot light without `LightSourceSize` has a 45 cm shadow source and a
pinpoint highlight. Add `LightSourceSize { radius_m }` to give it a physical size. A 2 cm LED
casts sharp shadows and a small, bright highlight on gloss. A 30 cm floodlight lens casts soft
shadows and a broad highlight. The shadow penumbra scales with the radius (up to the filter's
10-texel cap). The highlight on glossy surfaces widens and dims so that its total energy stays
the same. Diffuse light does not change. `radius_m: 0.0` is a true point. Agents edit the size
with `editor.set_property` (see [Light source size](book/agents/light-source-size.md)).

**IES profiles and area lights.** Add a `LightProfile` to shape a point or spot light with a
measured IES LM-63 distribution (cooked from an `.ies` file by the asset pipeline, or added by
the `render.set_light_profile` agent method). `RectLight` and `TubeLight` are area lights shaded
like glowing panels and tubes. Their shadow is a soft, static distance probe traced from the
light, not a shadow map. Profiles shade on Desktop only; see
[IES light profiles and area lights](book/agents/light-profiles.md).

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_render::{PointLight, SpotLight};
use regia_scene::Transform;

fn spawn_lamps(mut commands: Commands) {
    // A warm bulb, 800 lm, reaching 8 m.
    commands.spawn((
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 2.5, 0.0)),
        PointLight {
            position: [0.0; 3], // the runtime reads the transform
            color: [1.0, 0.85, 0.7],
            intensity: 800.0,
            radius: 8.0,
            cast_shadows: true,
        },
    ));
    // A floodlight pointing down at 45°, 20 000 cd.
    commands.spawn((
        Transform {
            translation: Vec3::new(4.0, 6.0, 0.0),
            rotation: Quat::from_rotation_x(-std::f32::consts::FRAC_PI_4),
            ..Transform::default()
        },
        SpotLight {
            position: [0.0; 3],
            direction: [0.0, 0.0, -1.0], // ignored as a component: the entity's −Z aims
            color: [1.0; 3],
            intensity: 20_000.0,
            outer_angle: 0.6,
            inner_angle: 0.45,
            range: 30.0,
            cast_shadows: true,
        },
    ));
}
```

**How many lights.** A view uploads up to `max_visible_lights` point and spot lights (Desktop
High 256, Ultra 512, Deck 96, Mobile Low 32; see [Render profiles](book/reference/render-profiles.md)).
With more in view, the dimmest by screen importance are dropped and a warning is logged, never
silently. Lights are assigned to froxel clusters (forward+), at most `max_lights_per_cluster` per
cluster.

## Shadows

- **Sun**: cascaded shadow maps. Desktop High uses four cascades with PCSS-lite soft shadows: a
  blocker search, then a filter as wide as the gap between receiver and blocker times the sun's
  angular radius (0.27°, the real sun's), so contact shadows are crisp and long shadows soften.
  Cascade seams blend over the last 15 % of each cascade and the last one fades out. Every preset
  keeps each cascade on a fixed texel lattice: its center snaps to its own texel grid and its size
  steps on a ladder 2.2 % apart, so turning, moving or zooming the camera does not make static
  shadows shimmer (`FrameQuality::stable_sun_cascades`, ADR-1236; check with
  [`render.shadow_stability`](book/agents/shadow-stability.md)). With `paged_sun_shadows`, each
  cascade is cached as pages that only redraw where a caster moved.
- **Local lights**: one shadow atlas (64 tiles). A shadowed spot takes one tile, a point light
  six (a cube), up to the profile's `local_shadow_max_lights`. When the casters do not all fit,
  the nearest win. Each light's penumbra follows its `LightSourceSize` (45 cm without one).
- **Translucent casters** (alpha-blended and transmissive materials: glass, canopies, visors)
  shadow by what they let through. They draw into a second, coarser map beside the opaque one
  (half the cascade edge; a quarter of the local atlas edge) holding the RGB transmittance product
  and the nearest translucent depth, and a receiver behind them takes that light: `1 − alpha` for a
  blended surface, `transmission × base color` for transmissive glass. Additive materials and
  meshes with `ShadowCast::Off` do not cast. Opaque shadowing is unchanged, and a frame without a
  translucent caster renders exactly as without the feature. The profile sets
  `translucent_shadow_cascades` (Mobile Low 0, Mobile High 1, Desktop Low and Deck 2, Desktop
  High and Ultra 4) and `translucent_local_shadows` (off on both Mobile tiers). The shadow report
  (`FrameRenderer::shadow_cache_report`) counts `translucent_casters`, `translucent_passes` and
  `translucent_draws`. A receiver between two translucent layers gets both layers' tint (one depth
  per texel); glass is not tinted by other glass; terrain and volumetric fog ignore translucent
  casters.
- **Bias** is applied on the receiver (normal offset plus a slope term), identically on every GPU.

The profile picks cascade count, resolution and filter (`csm_cascade_count`, `csm_resolution`,
`shadow_filter`). Shadows are the main lever on Mobile and Deck cost.

## Indirect light

`RenderSettings.gi_look` picks the player-facing indirect light. `None` keeps the profile default.

| `GiLook` | Light | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| `Balanced` | Sky irradiance, a sunlit-wall bounce, a mesh ground bounce. An installed baked volume is ignored. | Every platform. Medium forces the profile's probe column off and lands here unless the player chose another look. |
| `Depth` | GPU irradiance probes (DDGI). | Desktop. `GiLook::depth_available` is false on Android. |
| `Baked` | The map's `.fgiv` volume. With no volume installed, the frame shades as Balanced. | Any tier. A map that names a volume also uses it under Depth and under the preset default, including Low, with DDGI and screen-space GI off. |

**Sky and ambient.** With `Environment::ibl` on (the default), the procedural sky lights
everything that sees it: blue from above, a neutral ground bounce from below, plus reflections.
With it off, `Environment::ambient_lux` is a flat fill.

**Ambient occlusion.** The profile's `ssao` mode darkens creases and contacts (half resolution
on Desktop High, 1.2 m radius, multi-bounce) and also occludes sky reflections in crevices.

**Irradiance probes** (`GiMode::Probes`, Desktop High and Ultra). A `GiField` is a grid of probes
that store the light arriving from every direction: open sky, sunlit ground bouncing into
shadow, the darkness under a roof. Inside the grid the probes *replace* the sky term, fading
back to it one cell outside outdoors. Indoors, up-facing surfaces (`n.y` near 1) keep full probe
confidence for one extra cell and return to the sky at two cells. You fill the field by tracing it against a signed-distance
description of the scene (`SdfScene`: boxes, spheres, voxelized meshes, the terrain
heightfield), on the CPU, and hand it to the renderer:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_render::{GiField, ProbeSun, RuntimeRenderer, SdfScene, SdfShape, update_irradiance};

/// Builds an 8×3×8 probe grid over a courtyard and installs it.
fn bake_courtyard_gi(mut renderer: ResMut<RuntimeRenderer>) {
    let Ok(mut field) = GiField::new([-14.0, 0.5, -14.0], [4.0, 2.0, 4.0], [8, 3, 8]) else {
        return;
    };
    let scene = SdfScene {
        shapes: vec![
            // Ground.
            SdfShape::Box { center: [0.0, -0.5, 0.0], half: [30.0, 0.5, 30.0], albedo: [0.35; 3], emissive: [0.0; 3] },
            // A red wall that should tint its surroundings.
            SdfShape::Box { center: [0.0, 2.0, -6.0], half: [6.0, 2.0, 0.3], albedo: [0.6, 0.1, 0.08], emissive: [0.0; 3] },
        ],
    };
    let sun = ProbeSun { direction: [0.3, -1.0, -0.4], color: [1.0, 0.98, 0.95], illuminance: 100_000.0 };
    // Each update adds a bounce; a few updates converge.
    for _ in 0..4 {
        update_irradiance(&mut field, &scene, sun, 64, 0.5);
    }
    renderer.set_gi_field(Some(field));
}
```

A grid holds at most `MAX_PROBES` (256) probes: cover the places the camera spends time (a base,
a courtyard, a cockpit) rather than the whole map. `update_irradiance_with_lights` adds local
lights to the trace and can treat misses as black for closed interiors;
`update_irradiance_with_sky` takes the radiance an escaping ray sees from the atmosphere tables,
for daylit interiors whose openings let the real sky in. `rays` is clamped to 8..=128.
`hysteresis` is clamped to 0.0..=0.99, so an update every frame near 1 keeps 99 % of the
previous spherical harmonics and takes 1 % of the new trace. Depth moments are replaced
every update, and a probe whose centre is inside a solid is cleared.

**Screen-space GI** (`screen_space_gi`). A half-resolution gather of light from nearby on-screen
surfaces, the cheaper tier. A held camera reuses the previous result.

**Planet-shine.** A level's sky body (Jupiter seen from Europa, for example) lights the ground as
a shadowless directional fill; see [Rendering](book/user-guide/rendering.md).

## Reflections

Screen-space reflections march the depth buffer for floors and wet surfaces, scaled by roughness
and fall back to
reflection probes on a miss. A probe is captured by the renderer
(`FrameRenderer::capture_reflection_probe`) and installed with
`RuntimeRenderer::set_reflection_probes`; the renderer picks one list of probes by distance from the
camera (hard-capped at 4 uploaded), then weights them per pixel with box projection.

Two SSR paths exist. The stock Desktop High and Ultra presets run stochastic SSR: roughness
cutoff 0.55 with a fade starting 0.15 below it, and a miss takes a probe whenever the reflection
ray points below the horizon (no floor-only test). The linear march (lab, editor, probe capture)
scales by roughness (a 0.35-rough floor stays a mirror, zero at 0.7) and gives a probe only to
floors with `normal.y` at least 0.72.

## Interiors

A cockpit or a tunnel lit only by local lights reads as black at an outdoor exposure. Two pieces
fix that:

1. An `InteriorVolume { center, half_extent, ambient_lux }` around the room. Surfaces inside it
   drop the sky term and take a neutral 40 lux floor (or `ambient_lux`) plus probe bounce; the
   sunlit exterior seen through a door keeps the sky. Fit the box to the room's inner faces: a wall,
   floor or roof that lies on a face (or within 2 cm outside it) counts as inside, so it takes the
   interior shade on every pixel. Auto exposure lifts a fully indoor view; for
   a fixed exposure, EV 8 is the interior reference. Without a volume, an `EnclosureScene` (a hollow SDF shell)
   lets the renderer detect enclosure itself.
2. `build_interior_lighting` places a probe grid that covers the room and traces one bounce of the
   local lights (misses stay black, so the mouth of a tunnel is not painted with sky). Bind it
   with `set_gi_field` and capture one reflection probe at its center.

The [agent guide's high-end lighting page](book/agents/high-end-lighting.md) has the exact numbers
and the checks.

## Seeing what the lighting does

- Turn features off one at a time in `RenderSettings::profile` (`gi`, `ssr`, `ssao`,
  `screen_space_gi`) and compare screenshots; the agent protocol's `seeing.compare_images` gives
  a numeric difference.
- `RuntimeRenderer`'s frame renderer reports per-pass GPU times (`gpu_timings()`), including
  `ssgi_ms` and `ssr_ms`; probe tracing is CPU time (`gi_cpu_ms`).
- `render_lab` and `samples/lookdev` render reference scenes and print timings
  ([Look-dev harness](book/user-guide/lookdev.md)).

A ground-truth path tracer (`regia_pt`) renders the same scenes for comparison; renderer
changes are measured against it (`docs/specs/27-renderer-excellence.md`). The tracer is offline.
It does not ship in a game build, and runtime crates do not depend on it. It also writes the
baked volumes (`regia bake-gi`) and the lightmaps (`regia bake-lightmaps`). A lightmap
(`.flmap`, `look.lightmap`) stores irradiance per texel for static meshes and replaces diffuse
indirect light on `LightmapReceiver` entities. The profile caps that lookup: bilinear on Mobile
Low, bilinear plus directions on Mobile High, and the full bicubic-and-directions settings on
the other presets (`RenderProfile::lightmap_tier`). Derived LOW and ULTRA_LOW lightmaps still
miss their original seam and dark-point checks. The agent page is
[Lightmaps](book/agents/lightmaps.md). The editor's one-box probe bake is
[The Bake panel](book/user-guide/bake-panel.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/gizmos.md -->
# Gizmos: debug lines and shapes

Gizmos are immediate-mode debug drawings: call a method from any system and the line or shape
is drawn for that frame. They render in their own pass after the scene (and the post stack and
translucent effects), before the UI, at every quality preset and on Android. The API is a port of
Bevy's `bevy_gizmos` (MIT OR Apache-2.0; see `docs/ported-sources.toml`).

```rust
use regia_core::math::{Color, Quat, UVec2, Vec2, Vec3};
use regia_render::gizmos::Gizmos;

fn debug_draw(mut gizmos: Gizmos) {
    gizmos.line(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::Y * 2.0, Color::RED);
    gizmos.arrow(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::X, Color::GREEN).with_tip_length(0.2);
    gizmos.sphere(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, -3.0), 0.5, Color::BLUE).resolution(48);
    gizmos.grid(
        Quat::from_rotation_x(-std::f32::consts::FRAC_PI_2),
        UVec2::new(10, 10),
        Vec2::splat(1.0),
        Color::GRAY,
    );
    gizmos.text(Vec3::new(0.0, 2.5, 0.0), "spawn", 0.3, Vec2::ZERO, Color::WHITE);
}
```

Draw every frame to keep something visible. Draw from `Update` or `PostUpdate`: gizmos drawn in
`FixedUpdate` show only in frames where a fixed step ran.

## What you can draw

| Call | Shape |
|---|---|
| `line`, `line_gradient`, `ray`, `ray_gradient` | One segment |
| `linestrip`, `linestrip_gradient`, `lineloop` | Connected segments |
| `arrow` (`.with_double_end()`, `.with_tip_length()`), `axes`, `cross` | Pointers and markers |
| `circle`, `ellipse`, `sphere`, `arc_3d`, `short_arc_3d_between`, `long_arc_3d_between` | Round shapes (`.resolution(n)`) |
| `rect`, `rounded_rect`, `cube`, `cuboid`, `rounded_cuboid`, `aabb_3d` | Boxes |
| `capsule`, `cylinder`, `cone`, `conical_frustum`, `torus`, `tetrahedron`, `triangle`, `plane` | Primitives (axis along local +Y) |
| `grid`, `grid_3d` (`.outer_edges()`, `.skew()`) | Line grids |
| `frustum(view_projection)` | A camera's view volume |
| `curve_3d`, `curve_fn_3d`, `curve_gradient_3d` | Sampled curves |
| `text`, `text_sections` | ASCII stroke text (Simplex Hershey font) |

Placement arguments take anything that is an isometry: a `Vec3` (position), a `Quat`
(rotation), `(Vec3, Quat)`, an `Isometry`, a `Transform` or a `GlobalTransform`.

## Groups and styling

Every gizmo belongs to a config group. `Gizmos` (no type argument) is the `default` group;
`Gizmos<MyGroup>` draws into your own group. The `GizmoConfigStore` resource holds each group's
`GizmoConfig`:

- `enabled` — draw the group at all;
- `line.width` (pixels), `line.perspective` (width shrinks with distance), `line.style`
  (`Solid`, `Dotted`, `Dashed { gap_scale, line_scale }`), `line.joints` (`None`, `Miter`,
  `Bevel`, `Round(n)`) and `line.animation_offset` (march dashes);
- `depth_bias` in `-1..=1` — negative values pull lines towards the camera (use a small negative
  value for outlines lying on a surface);
- `on_top` — ignore scene depth so the lines show through walls.

```rust
use regia_app::App;
use regia_render::gizmos::{AppGizmoBuilder, GizmoConfigGroup, GizmoConfigStore};

#[derive(Default)]
struct PathGizmos;

impl GizmoConfigGroup for PathGizmos {
    const NAME: &'static str = "paths";
}

fn setup(app: &mut App) {
    app.init_gizmo_group::<PathGizmos>();
    let mut store = app.world_mut().resource_mut::<GizmoConfigStore>();
    if let Some((config, _)) = store.config_mut::<PathGizmos>() {
        config.line.width = 4.0;
        config.on_top = true;
    }
}
```

Guard expensive drawing systems with `.run_if(gizmo_group_enabled::<PathGizmos>)`.

## Retained gizmos

For geometry that does not change, build a `GizmoAsset` once and attach it with the `Gizmo`
component; it is drawn every frame at the entity's `GlobalTransform` with the component's own
line settings, depth bias and on-top flag.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia_core::math::{Color, Vec3};
use regia_app::prelude::Commands;
use regia_render::gizmos::{Gizmo, GizmoAsset};
use regia_scene::Transform;

fn spawn_marker(mut commands: Commands) {
    let mut asset = GizmoAsset::new();
    asset.circle(Vec3::ZERO, 2.0, Color::YELLOW).resolution(64);
    commands.spawn((
        Gizmo::new(Arc::new(asset)),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 0.1, 0.0)),
    ));
}
```

## Debug overlays

These groups ship disabled; enable them from code (`store.set_enabled("physics", true)`) or from
an agent (`debug.set_gizmos`, see the [agent page](book/agents/gizmos.md)):

| Group | Draws | Drawn by |
|---|---|---|
| `physics` | Collider wireframes (sensors yellow) | `regia_framework::debug_gizmos::DebugGizmosPlugin` |
| `nav_mesh` | Nav-mesh polygon outlines, off-mesh links | `DebugGizmosPlugin` |
| `audio` | Emitter full-volume and silence spheres, cones | `DebugGizmosPlugin` |
| `motion_matching` | Desired and matched trajectories, foot positions | `DebugGizmosPlugin` |
| `ai_perception` | Sight fans and hearing rings | `regia_ai::AiPlugin` |
| `smart_object` | Slots by state, facing rays, entrances | `regia_ai::SmartObjectPlugin` (feature `debug_draw`) |
| `camera_rig` | Camera rig frustums, boom, collision probe, aim point | `regia_framework::camera::CameraPlugin` |
| `post_volumes` | Post volume shapes and blend bands | `regia_render::gizmos::GizmoPlugin` |

`DefaultPlugins` installs `DebugGizmosPlugin`; an overlay costs nothing while its group is off.

## Notes

- `DebugDraw` (the old single-method line queue) still works: insert it as a resource and push
  lines; they draw through the default group.
- Mirrors, UI preview cameras and reflection-probe captures never show gizmos.
- Colors are linear RGBA; lines are alpha-blended over the tonemapped image, so they are not
  affected by exposure, bloom or fog.
