# Volumetric terrain: dual contouring chunks

<!-- index: Dual contouring -->
<!-- index: Signed-distance field -->
<!-- index: Volume mesh -->
<!-- index: Voxel terrain -->
<!-- index: Mesh layer -->

`regia_terrain::volume_mesh` meshes signed-distance fields — caves, overhangs, tunnels and
other volumes a heightfield cannot express — by dual contouring (Ju, Losasso, Schaefer &
Warren, SIGGRAPH 2002). It complements the CDLOD heightfield path: use heightfields for
ordinary ground, and volume chunks where the surface folds over itself.
The heightfield chapter is [Terrain, tunnels and scatter](book/user-guide/terrain-vfx.md).

## What is built, and what spec 122 is not

This page is the mesher and the volume source on a terrain mesh layer (ADR-10071). You supply
a signed-distance field. The cook meshes it and clips it to the ground. That is in the tree.

`docs/specs/122-voxel-core.md` is a different feature: an integer voxel core,
`regia_voxel_core`, with a fixed-point field, an operation log that replays bit for bit,
integer queries, a `.voxfield` file, and a plug-in on `regia_world_geom`. That crate is not in
this tree. There is no runtime voxel edit, no operation-log replay, and no `.voxfield` load.
The catalog status for voxel terrain stays partial until that crate exists and this page
describes it. Do not treat the sections below as that core.

What you can do today:

- Mesh a field you implement as `SdfField` (a cave, a carve, a heightfield adapted by
  `TerrainMapField`).
- Weld chunks and step LOD by 2× without skirts.
- Cook a volume as one terrain mesh layer. The layer names an `sdf` string. The host passes
  the field to `cook_mesh_layers_with_volumes`. There is no volume file format.

What you cannot do in this version:

- Dig or fill a stored voxel field at run time, on the simulation, with a replayable log.
- Read a voxel volume from the world-geometry queries (`support`, `segment`, `push_disc`). Those
  calls exist for the heightfield and for mesh layers. They do not read a voxel core, because
  that core is not in the tree.
- Load a `.voxfield`. The name `.fvox` is the cooked far proxy (`docs/formats/voxel-far.md`). It is not the voxel-core file.
- Author a volume by dropping a file in the project. A `Volume` layer with no host-supplied field is refused with `cook_not_built`.

A crater or a berm on the heightfield is a terrain edit, not a voxel volume. An overhang that
stands above the ground is not a volume layer either: the cook clips the mesh to the ground.
Author that overhang as a `Gltf` or `Collision` mesh layer.

## Defining a field

Implement `SdfField` (`sample` is required; `gradient` defaults to a central finite
difference, override it with an analytic gradient for crisp sharp features or fields far
from unit scale). The sign convention is the usual SDF one: negative inside the solid,
positive outside. Closures `Fn([f32; 3]) -> f32` implement the trait automatically, and
`TerrainMapField` adapts a heightfield `TerrainMap` (solid below the surface), so a cave
field combined with the heightfield by `min`/`max` in your own `SdfField` meshes through
the same path.

```rust
use regia_terrain::volume_mesh::{
    mesh_chunk, MeshParams, NeighborLod, NeighborLods, SdfField,
};

struct Cave {
    center: [f32; 3],
    radius: f32,
}

impl SdfField for Cave {
    fn sample(&self, p: [f32; 3]) -> f32 {
        let d = [p[0] - self.center[0], p[1] - self.center[1], p[2] - self.center[2]];
        // Solid everywhere except a spherical hollow: the negation of a sphere SDF.
        self.radius - (d[0] * d[0] + d[1] * d[1] + d[2] * d[2]).sqrt()
    }
}
```

## Meshing a chunk

```rust,wrap
# use regia_terrain::volume_mesh::{mesh_chunk, MeshParams, NeighborLod, NeighborLods, SdfField};
# struct Cave { center: [f32; 3], radius: f32 }
# impl SdfField for Cave {
#     fn sample(&self, p: [f32; 3]) -> f32 {
#         let d = [p[0] - self.center[0], p[1] - self.center[1], p[2] - self.center[2]];
#         self.radius - (d[0] * d[0] + d[1] * d[1] + d[2] * d[2]).sqrt()
#     }
# }
let field = Cave { center: [8.0, 4.0, 8.0], radius: 3.0 };
let mut neighbors = NeighborLods::same();
neighbors.pos_x = NeighborLod::Coarser; // the +x chunk runs at half resolution
let mesh = mesh_chunk(
    &field,
    [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], // world position of the minimum grid corner
    0.5,             // cell size (meters)
    [32, 16, 32],    // cells per axis
    neighbors,
    &MeshParams::default(),
)?;
// mesh.positions / mesh.normals / mesh.indices: an indexed, outward-wound triangle mesh.
```

Each cell the surface passes through contributes one vertex. The quadratic error
function of the cell's Hermite data (crossing points and normals on the cell edges) is
minimized with a pseudo-inverse. When that minimizer falls outside the cell,
`mesh_chunk` replaces it with the mass point of the crossings. It does not clamp the
minimizer onto the cell boundary: that would glue mirror-image cells together. With
the default `MeshParams`, two Newton steps then project the vertex onto the surface
and clamp those steps into the cell, so the stored vertex is the projected point, not
the raw minimizer and not the mass point, unless the projection stays put. Sharp
edges and corners of the field survive because the vertex starts from the
least-squares intersection of the tangent planes. `solve_qef` is that pseudo-inverse
alone: it clamps the minimizer into the box you pass and does not project onto a
field.

## Stitching and LOD

Chunks stitch without skirts. A border vertex is a pure function of its cell's world box,
so neighboring chunks compute bit-identical copies, and each surface face is emitted by
exactly one chunk (the one whose half-open domain contains the midpoint of the primal
edge the face is dual to). Weld chunk meshes by exact vertex position to join them; the
union is the manifold mesh a single big chunk would have produced.

A neighbor at half resolution (`NeighborLod::Coarser` here, `NeighborLod::Finer` from the
other side) is stitched the same way on a graded grid: faces crossing the shared plane
join fine vertices to the coarse grid's dual vertices (triangles where one coarse cell
stands in for two fine ones), so no T-junction ever appears. Rules: LOD may step by at
most 2x across a face (`NeighborLods::from_neighbor_levels` converts absolute levels and
rejects bigger jumps), every `cells` entry must be even when a step exists, and
neighbors must share tangential origins so the coarse lattice is a sublattice of the
fine one.

Coarse cells that touch a finer neighbor take their Hermite data from every half-size
segment of their boundary (edge halves and the segments through each face center), so a
feature only the fine side samples still gets a coarse vertex. The rest of a coarse chunk
meshes exactly as it would without the finer neighbor, so it still welds to its
same-LOD neighbors.

Where LOD steps meet along a chunk edge or at a corner (every corner of a finer region),
describe the edge and corner neighbors too, or the diagonal chunk cannot know about the
finer chunk and the seam cracks along that edge. The simplest way is to build every
chunk's `NeighborLods` from the absolute LOD levels of its 3x3x3 neighborhood:

```rust,wrap
# use regia_terrain::volume_mesh::*;
# let own_lod = 0u32;
# let levels = Default::default();
// levels[dx + 1][dy + 1][dz + 1]: absolute LOD of the chunk at that offset, None = no chunk.
let lods = NeighborLods::from_region_levels(own_lod, levels)?;
```

`NeighborLods::set_region([dx, dy, dz], lod)` sets one face, edge or corner entry;
unset edge and corner entries are derived from the touching faces.

Exact welding needs chunk origins and cell sizes whose sums are exact in floating point
(for example powers of two, or integer chunk coordinates times a dyadic chunk size). With
values such as an origin of `0.1 + 8 * 0.3`, neighboring chunks compute border vertices
that differ in the last bits and do not weld by exact position.

Two consequences to budget for: a chunk mesh can contain vertices up to one
neighbor-sized cell outside its nominal box (halo vertices of the border faces it owns),
and a lone chunk is open where the surface exits it.

## Errors and determinism

Invalid input is an error, never a panic: non-positive cell size, zero or over-limit cell
counts, non-finite origin or parameters, misaligned LOD steps, and the first non-finite
field sample or gradient all return `MeshError`. An all-air or all-solid chunk returns an
empty mesh. Output is deterministic: fixed iteration order and exact arithmetic in `f64`
mean repeated calls are bit-identical on the same platform.

## Volumes as terrain mesh layers (ADR-10071)

A cave authored as a signed-distance volume becomes a terrain mesh layer through the same seam,
streaming and query contract as an authored mesh. The `<map>.meshlayers.ron` layer names the
volume:

```text
(id: "cave", source: Volume(sdf: "cave", iso: 0.0, cell_m: 0.5), fills: ["cave_mouth"])
```

There is no volume file format yet, so the host passes the field to the cook:
`regia_asset_pipeline::terrain_mesh_layers::cook_mesh_layers_with_volumes(&request, &volumes)`,
where each `VolumeSource { sdf, field, bounds, fingerprint }` gives the `SdfField` for one `sdf`
name, the world box to mesh, and bytes that identify the field for the cook's input hash. A
`Volume` layer without a source is refused with `cook_not_built`.

The cook meshes the field (minus `iso`) with `mesh_chunk` on one grid of `cell_m` cells, then
keeps only what lies under the LOD-0 ground: a triangle that crosses the ground is split where
its height over the ground changes sign, and the new vertices sit on the ground. A cave that
breaks the surface therefore loses its dome everywhere, and the cut edges form closed loops on
the ground. Each filled hole is one loop (`fills` take the loops in `(z, x)` order), and the
loop's outline is the hole's footprint: the ground opens inside it and the cook's zipper joins
the loop to the ring. A loop the layer does not fill stays under whole ground, which closes the
cave. The clipped mesh is the layer's query mesh (`surface_at` answers its floor inside the
mouth), and its chunks and LODs are cut and locked like any layer's.

Use a power-of-two `cell_m` so the meshing blocks weld exactly. An overhang that stands above
the ground is not a volume layer (the clip removes it): author it as a `Gltf` or `Collision`
source. Errors: `meshlayers_volume_mesh` (the mesher refused the field),
`meshlayers_volume_grid` (empty box, bad `cell_m` or `iso`), `meshlayers_volume_mouths` (the
loops do not match `fills`, do not close inside the box, or a loop is not star-shaped from its
mean point).

<!-- source: book/systems/vfx.md -->
# VFX and decals

<!-- index: Particles -->
<!-- index: Decal -->
<!-- index: Trail -->
<!-- index: VFX -->

`regia_vfx` provides GPU particles, projected decals, ribbon trails and camera shake. Particles
are simulated and sorted in compute shaders; decals are box-projected volumes binned into screen
tiles; everything draws in the frame's translucent pass. Specification:
`docs/specs/26-terrain-vfx-highend.md` § 3. Precipitation and ambient particle counts follow
`QualityTier::content_tier`: VeryLow uses Low's counts. The surface a decal lands on is a
material ([Materials](book/how-to/picture/materials.md)). Translucent particles draw after the
upscaler resolve, so they do not write the upscaler's reactive mask
([Upscalers](book/agents/upscalers.md)).

## Setting it up

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_vfx::scene::VfxLibrary;
use regia_vfx::{VfxPlugin, VfxRuntimePlugin, VfxScene};

pub struct Effects;

impl Plugin for Effects {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        // VfxPlugin: effect requests, decals, shake, the CPU scheduler.
        // VfxRuntimePlugin: the GPU side, drawn through the renderer's translucent layer.
        app.add_plugins((VfxPlugin, VfxRuntimePlugin));

        // The effect library: the built-in showcase set (muzzle_flash, impact, explosion, …).
        let mut library = VfxLibrary::new();
        for effect in regia_vfx::showcase_effects() {
            if let Err(err) = library.add(effect) {
                warn!("effect rejected: {err}");
            }
        }
        app.insert_resource(VfxScene::new(library));
    }
}
```

`VfxPlugin` alone runs the deterministic CPU side (spawn scheduling, budgets, decal pool,
shake); add `VfxRuntimePlugin` after it to draw. Your own `.vfx.ron` files load with
`VfxLibrary::load_dir(path)`, or set `VfxSettings::library_dir` and the plugin scans that
directory at startup. `VfxSettings::profile` (`VfxProfile`) sets pool sizes, sorting and the
particle-light budget per quality tier.

## Spawning effects

Effects are requested with messages, so any system (or a script, or the sim bridge) can trigger
them without holding the VFX state:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::Vec3;
use regia_vfx::{CameraShakeRequest, SpawnEffect};

fn on_explosion(mut effects: MessageWriter<SpawnEffect>, mut shake: MessageWriter<CameraShakeRequest>) {
    let at = Vec3::new(3.0, 0.0, -6.0);
    effects.write(SpawnEffect {
        effect: "explosion".into(),
        position: at,
        forward: Vec3::Y,
        seed: None,
    });
    shake.write(CameraShakeRequest { position: at, strength: 0.6, radius: 12.0 });
}
```

`forward` is the effect's local +Z (the direction a muzzle flash fires). `seed: None` takes the
next value of a per-run counter, so a replay with the same inputs spawns identical particles.
Camera shake accumulates trauma that decays over time (`VfxSettings::shake_decay`,
`shake_amplitude`, `shake_roll`); `CameraShake` holds the current offset for your camera rig.

## Authoring a particle system

A `.vfx.ron` file describes one named system of one or more emitters, each a stack of Spawn,
Init, Update and Render modules. The current format is version 5 (`docs/formats/vfx-ron.md`);
older files load and migrate in memory. This version-1 muzzle flash still loads, with the newer
fields at their defaults:

```ron,vfx
(
    version: 1,
    name: "muzzle_flash",
    system: (budget: 256),
    emitters: [
        (
            name: "flash",
            delay: 0.0,
            spawn: (
                mode: Burst(24),
                lifetime: (min: 0.05, max: 0.12),
            ),
            init: (
                shape: Cone(angle: 12.0, length: (min: 0.2, max: 0.8)),
                velocity: (mode: Directional(
                    dir: (0.0, 0.0, -1.0),
                    spread: 8.0,
                    speed: (min: 8.0, max: 20.0),
                )),
                size: (min: 0.1, max: 0.4),
                color: [(t: 0.0, color: "#fff2c8")],
            ),
            update: (drag: 6.0),
            render: (
                mode: Billboard,
                sprite: Flare,
                blend: Additive,
                stretch: (velocity_scale: 0.02),
            ),
        ),
    ],
)
```

| Module | Controls |
|---|---|
| `spawn` | `Burst(n)`, `Rate(per_second)` or `PerDistance` (trails of puffs behind a mover), particle lifetime range |
| `init` | emission shape (`Point`, `Sphere`, `Box`, `Cone`), velocity (including the `Radial` mode), size, color gradient |
| `update` | gravity, drag, curl noise, vortex, attractor, size / color / alpha / rotation over life, depth collision against the scene |
| `render` | `Billboard`, stretched or mesh particles; sprite or flipbook; `Additive` or `Alpha` blend; soft-particle `softness`; `lit` smoke with `self_shadow`; HDR `emissive`; `screen_floor_px` so distant sparks never vanish below a pixel |

Version 2 added lit smoke, emissive, flipbook blending and the screen-size floor; version 3 the
animated fire sheet (`FireAnim`); version 4 the fireball body sheet (`FireballAnim`) and
`heat_haze` cards; version 5 `Planar` velocity. The [agent guide's VFX page](book/agents/vfx.md) has a full version-5 smoke
example and the look rules (fire hue in linear light, bloom on HDR frames only, alpha emitters
sorted back to front).

Effects can also emit **particle lights**: a fireball lights the ground under it through the
renderer's local lights. `vfx.get_look` / `vfx.set_look` (or the `VfxLook` resource) toggle heat
haze and fire light and scale them.

## Decals

A decal is a box that projects albedo (and optionally normal, roughness and emissive) onto
whatever is inside it. Prefabs are `.decal.ron` files (`docs/formats/decal-ron.md`, version 1);
the engine ships `scorch`, `pad_marking`, `rut` and `grime`, and a level adds more by placing
`*.decal.ron` files in the VFX library directory.

- **On a hit**: write a `SpawnDecal` message, or call `vfx.spawn_decal` with a position and a
  surface normal; the decal's local +Z aligns with the normal.
- **Along a path**: `vfx.place_rut` stamps overlapping decals along points (a quadratic curve
  with `curve: true`), for tire ruts.
- **Static markings**: put a `StaticDecal { prefab, yaw, receiver_mask }` component on a level
  entity; the plugin copies it into the pool when it appears.

Each decal has a **receiver mask**: bit 0 terrain, bit 1 static meshes, bit 2 characters. The
built-in prefabs use `3`, so scorch marks land on the ground and walls but never on a character.
The renderer writes a receiver buffer each frame (terrain as layer 0, rigid meshes as 1, skinned
meshes as 2, or `MeshRenderer::decal_layer` when set) that the decal pass reads. Desktop High
keeps 256 visible decals and Desktop Ultra 512; when more are visible the highest priority win.
`vfx.decal_budget` reports the live count and culling.

## Trails

`TrailRig::new(TrailStyle { width, lifetime, color, min_segment })` records an entity's path as a
ribbon that fades from head to tail: tracer rounds, vehicle wakes, sword swipes. `VfxTrails`
holds the live trails for the runtime.

## Checking effects

Particles move, so a single screenshot rarely tells you much. `seeing.capture_sequence` returns a
strip of frames and `seeing.contact_sheet` tiles them into one image for review.
`samples/vfx_lab` renders the showcase set in a window or, with `--evidence <dir>`, offscreen to
PNGs; `regia_vfx::measure_effect` and `assert_effect_plausible` are the not-empty, not-black,
not-blown-out checks its tests use.

# Physics

<!-- index: Physics -->
<!-- index: Rigid body -->
<!-- index: Collider -->
<!-- index: Physics material -->
<!-- index: Physics query -->
<!-- index: Character controller -->
<!-- index: Ragdoll -->
<!-- index: Destruction level 2 -->
<!-- index: Destruction level 3 | see: Known issues -->
<!-- index: Continuous collision detection | see: Swept CCD -->

`regia_physics` is a thin Rust layer over the rapier3d solver, driven by ECS components and synced
both ways. Add `regia::physics::PhysicsPlugin` yourself (`DefaultPlugins` does not install it; the dedicated server does) and give entities rigid bodies and colliders.

The behavior is [spec 15](docs/specs/15-physics.md). That file still opens on the early
milestone (cosmetic debris only). The rest of the spec, and this chapter, are what ships:
bodies, events, queries, joints, the character controller, CCD, and destruction level 2.
Character capsule rules are [spec 93](docs/specs/93-character-physics.md). Continuous
sweeps are [Continuous collision detection](book/systems/physics-ccd.md).

## Bodies and colliders

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_scene::prelude::*;
use regia::physics::{Collider, ColliderShape, RigidBody};
use regia::core::math::Vec3;

fn spawn_crate(mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 4.0, 0.0)),
        RigidBody::dynamic(),
        Collider {
            shape: ColliderShape::Box { half_extents: Vec3::new(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) },
            ..Collider::default()
        },
    ));
}
```

`RigidBody` is static (`RigidBody::static_body()`), dynamic (`RigidBody::dynamic()`) or kinematic
(`RigidBody::kinematic()`); a `Collider` (friction, restitution, density, layer, `active_events`) whose
`shape` is a `ColliderShape` gives it a `Box`, `Sphere`, `Capsule`, `Cylinder`,
`Cone`, `ConvexHull`, `TriMesh`, `HeightField` or `Compound` shape. The engine syncs transforms
ECS→physics for kinematically driven bodies and physics→ECS for dynamic ones.

## Queries

Query the live world without driving it — raycasts, overlaps, closest points:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::physics::{PhysicsQuery, QueryFilter};
use regia::core::math::Vec3;

fn has_clear_shot(queries: PhysicsQuery) -> bool {
    queries.raycast(Vec3::ZERO, Vec3::Y, 100.0, QueryFilter::new().exclude_sensors()).is_none()
}
```

`PhysicsQuery` is the `SystemParam` behind the protocol's
[`physics.raycast` / `overlap` / `closest_point`](book/agents/physics.md) — the same API the
character controller builds on. `overlap(shape, pose, filter)` lists entities inside a shape;
`closest_point(point, max_distance, filter)` finds the nearest collider surface.

## Collision events

Collisions and sensor triggers surface as messages, for colliders whose
`active_events` has `collision: true` (the default is off; `ActiveEvents::ALL` turns both kinds on):

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::physics::CollisionStarted;

fn on_collision(mut reader: MessageReader<CollisionStarted>) {
    for e in reader.read() {
        // e.entity_a, e.entity_b — the two entities that started touching.
    }
}
```

When an entity is despawned (or loses its `Collider`) while it touches something, the pair
still gets its `CollisionEnded`, or `TriggerExit` for a sensor, on the next fixed step. The entity
in that message may already be despawned, so look it up with `get`, not `[]`.

## Stacking, joints and sleeping

- **Solver settings.** `PhysicsSettings::solver_iterations` (default 4) trades solver time for
  stiffer stacks, chains and large mass ratios. `ccd_substeps` (default 1) lets a fast CCD body
  keep moving after its first hit in a step. Insert `PhysicsSettings` before or after
  `PhysicsPlugin`: the plugin keeps yours.

  ```rust,wrap
  # use regia::prelude::*;
  # use regia_physics::PhysicsSettings;
  # let app: &mut App = todo!();
  app.insert_resource(PhysicsSettings { solver_iterations: 8, ..Default::default() });
  ```
- **Fast bodies.** Set `RigidBody { ccd: true, .. }` on bullets and other bodies that move more
  than their own size in a step (at 60 Hz, 6 m/s for a 10 cm ball).
- **Joints come back with their bodies.** If a jointed body loses its `RigidBody` and gets it back,
  or the `connected` entity gets a body only later, the joint is created then. A joint broken by
  `break_force` stays broken until you edit its `Joint` component (`JointBroken` reports it).
- **Breaking by torque.** Put a `JointBreakTorque(n)` component (newton-metres) beside the `Joint` to break it when
  its torque goes over `n`, in addition to `break_force`. It counts a load hanging to the side of the joint.
- **Materials.** A `.physmat.ron` (`docs/formats/physmat.md`) names friction, restitution, density and the combine
  rules; register it in `PhysicsMaterials` and put `PhysicsMaterialRef("name")` beside a `Collider` to give the
  collider those numbers. The default material is the collider default, so unreferenced colliders are unchanged.
- **Debug draw.** The agent's `physics.debug_draw` shows contact points and normals, joints and centers of mass in the
  `physics` gizmo group (see [Physics: debug draw, materials](book/agents/physics-spec15.md)). It costs nothing off.
- **Sleeping.** Bodies at rest go to sleep after half a second and cost no solver time.
  Impulses, `Velocity` writes, `ExternalForce` edits, teleports and a removed floor wake them.
  A steady `ExternalForce` does not keep a body awake. Removing the component stops the force.
  `RigidBody { can_sleep: false, .. }` keeps a body awake.
- **Counting.** `PhysicsWorld::stats()` (agent `physics.stats`) reports awake and sleeping
  bodies, contact pairs and the last step's cost. Its `non_finite_inputs` counts non-finite
  poses, body fields, velocities, forces and impulses that were dropped before reaching the
  simulation (ADR-1507): zero in a healthy app, and a growing count points at a script, scene
  or networked value writing NaN — one bad value cannot poison the contacts of everything a
  body touches, but the guard does not make the value meaningful either; fix the writer.

## Characters

A **character** is a capsule driven through the physics world with movement modes (walk, crouch,
jump, fly) — the foundation for the player and AI controllers. See [Gameplay](book/user-guide/gameplay.md) and
`docs/specs/15-physics.md`.

Crouching shrinks the capsule from the top (the entity's transform stays at the standing centre)
and stands up only when there is headroom; a ceiling ends a jump at once; jumping off a moving
platform keeps its velocity; the reported velocity is the motion achieved. Ragdolls get joint
limits from the bind pose (`RagdollProfile::humanoid_limited`, `.ragdoll.ron`), report when they
have settled (face up or down) and stay within a per-tier budget (`RagdollSettings`). See
`docs/specs/93-character-physics.md` and [character physics (agents)](book/agents/character-physics.md).

## Destruction level 2

Level 2 breaks a structure that was fractured ahead of time. Chunks, masses, and bonds live in a
`.destructible.ron` (version 2; version 1 migrates). Cook it from a `.fracture.ron` with
`regia fracture`, or build a box grid. The format is `docs/formats/destructible.md`. Level 1
cosmetic debris (`DebrisSpawner`) is unchanged and is not this system.

At runtime `DestructionWorld` applies hits (explosion, projectile, impulse) once per fixed tick,
in queue order. A chunk shares the impulse across intact bonds. Bonds at their threshold break,
up to `max_breaks_per_tick`. A chunk with no intact path to a support chunk collapses. Those
decisions use only exact `f32` operations on plain arrays, so the same hits produce the same
`structure_hash` on every platform. They do not read the rapier solver. Debris motion after a
chunk detaches is cosmetic: a pooled dynamic body, capped by `max_spawns_per_tick` and
`max_active_chunks`.

Place one in a level as a `DestructibleSource { asset, seed }` entity. `DestructionPlugin`
defines it at play, outside the fixed tick. The server decides breaks. Replicas replay the break
events to the same hash. Agent methods are `physics.destruction_define`,
`physics.destruction_damage`, `physics.destruction_state`, and `physics.destruction_budget`.
The call shapes, error strings (`destruction_invalid_asset`, `destruction_replica`, and the
rest), and the wall-and-bridge sample are on
[Destruction level 2 (agents)](book/agents/destruction.md).

Support chunks are marked in the Fracture editor panel (clicks, a box, or `support_below_y` on
the asset meta). A test break there uses the same `DestructionWorld` as the game.

Structural load, a falling section as one piece, and contact-driven impact damage are opt-in.
Without `load` settings, a structure that is still connected to a support does not fail under its
own weight. Without `falling` settings, a collapsing section breaks into chunks. Impact damage
reads rapier contacts, so it matches the rapier step on one platform and never runs on a replica.
Those limits are spelled out on the agent page.

**Destruction level 3 is not in this version.** Runtime fracture, carving, and deformation, with
collider, navmesh, and network sync, are parked for a later release (`docs/versions.md`, the v1.2
rung). Do not document them as available.

A lockstep game does not read rapier, and it does not treat destruction debris as simulated
gameplay. Break decisions can still be replayed from `BreakEvent`s. The pose of a debris body
cannot.

## Determinism

On one platform and build, the same inputs give the same simulation, bit for bit, whatever the
thread count. `PhysicsWorld::state_digest()` hashes every body's pose, velocities and sleep flag.
Compare it between two runs at the same step to check a replay (the agent's `physics.stats`
returns it too).

`regia_physics`'s `physics-cross-platform-determinism` feature enables rapier's
`enhanced-determinism`, which makes a measured subset of rapier bit-identical across the CPU
architectures measured so far. It costs speed, so it is off by default. It is not a promise for
lockstep games: Regia does not promise rigid bodies on a lockstep simulation, and a lockstep
simulation never reads a rapier pose, contact or event (ADR-8841). Lockstep games move their units
with the `regia_detsim` models; see [Movement models](book/user-guide/movement-models.md).

Collision layers come from `config/physics.ron` when the project installs `PhysicsLayers`; a
collider on a layer nothing may query is invisible to queries that set `QueryFilter::from_layer`
(a query without `from_layer` is not filtered by the query matrix and still hits it).

<!-- source: book/systems/physics-ccd.md -->
# Continuous collision detection (CCD queries)

<!-- index: Continuous collision detection -->
<!-- index: Swept CCD -->
<!-- index: Time of impact -->

`regia_physics::ccd` answers one question without a physics world: two convex shapes
move from pose A to pose B over one step — do they touch, and if so, when and where?
Use it for projectiles and other fast movers that a discrete overlap test would let
tunnel through thin geometry, for kinematic sweeps, and for placement or probe checks
in tools. For simulated bodies, rapier's own CCD (`RigidBody::ccd`) still applies,
and the opt-in `SweptCcd` component runs this module's angular sweep inside the step
(see "Swept CCD in the step" below).

The module is part of [spec 15](docs/specs/15-physics.md). Rapier's own CCD
(`RigidBody { ccd: true, .. }`) sweeps a fast body against the other bodies' end-of-step
poses. Two fast bodies closing on each other can still pass through (spec 15 records this
limit). `SweptCcd` is the opt-in that sweeps both sides of a pair, including two bullets.
The agent method `physics.time_of_impact` runs the same convex sweep on demand
([Physics: time of impact](book/agents/physics-time-of-impact.md)). Error strings from
`ToiFailure::code()` are lowercase words such as `non_finite_input` and `degenerate_motion`.

## The query

Shapes are `ConvexInput` values (point, sphere, box, capsule, cylinder, cone, segment,
or a convex hull from points). `ConvexInput::from_collider_shape` converts the convex
`ColliderShape` variants; `TriMesh`, `HeightField` and `Compound` return `None` (query
a compound's convex children one by one). Poses are `regia_core::math::Isometry`
(rotation + translation, no scale — bake scale into the shape sizes).

```rust,wrap
use regia_core::math::{Isometry, Vec3};
use regia_physics::ccd::{time_of_impact, ConvexInput, ToiResult};

// A 10 cm sphere flying 10 m in one step (500 m/s at 50 Hz) at a 1 cm wall.
let ball = ConvexInput::sphere(0.1);
let wall = ConvexInput::cuboid(Vec3::new(0.005, 2.0, 2.0));
let result = time_of_impact(
    &ball,
    Isometry::from_translation(Vec3::new(-5.0, 0.0, 0.0)),
    Isometry::from_translation(Vec3::new(5.0, 0.0, 0.0)),
    &wall,
    Isometry::IDENTITY,
    Isometry::IDENTITY,
    0.0,   // target_gap: stop at surface contact
    1e-4,  // tolerance on the separation at the reported t, metres
    64,    // max conservative-advancement iterations
);
match result {
    ToiResult::Hit { t, normal, point } => {
        // t is normalised to the step: impact time is t * dt.
        // normal points from shape A (the ball) toward shape B (the wall);
        // point is the witness point on shape A.
    }
    ToiResult::Separated => { /* never within target_gap this step */ }
    ToiResult::OverlappedAtStart => { /* already interpenetrating at t = 0 */ }
    ToiResult::Failed(reason) => { /* bad input or iteration budget; see ToiFailure */ }
}
```

Translation is interpolated linearly and rotation by slerp between the endpoint
poses. Rotation is accounted for conservatively (its swept angle times the shape's
bounding radius bounds how fast the gap can close), so spinning shapes cannot tunnel
either. `time_of_impact_angular` is the same query with caller-supplied swept-angle
bounds per shape (for example `|angular_velocity| * dt`); a larger bound only makes
the steps smaller, never the answer wrong. It does not model multi-turn spins whose
intermediate orientations leave the slerp path — subdivide the step for those.

`target_gap` is a skin width: the sweep stops when the shapes are that far apart.
`tolerance` is how accurate that stopping separation must be, in metres. Touching, or
already being within `target_gap`, at `t = 0` is a `Hit` with `t = 0`; only actual
interpenetration is `OverlappedAtStart`. Degenerate shapes (zero radius, zero
half-extent, points, segments) are legal. No input panics: NaN or infinite numbers,
negative sizes, empty hulls, zero quaternions, negative gap/tolerance and a zero
iteration budget all return `Failed` with a `ToiFailure` reason.

Two helpers cover the common cases: `sphere_sweep` (a sphere between two centres
against a sweeping convex shape) and `swept_box_vs_thin_wall` (a moving box against a
static box wall). `convex_distance` exposes the underlying GJK distance query
(distance, witness points, normal, overlap flag) at fixed poses — handy for proximity
checks and for verifying a TOI result.

## Choosing parameters and costs

32–128 iterations cover ordinary gameplay sweeps. Grazing near-misses with a very
small tolerance may need more and return `Failed(MaxIterations)` rather than guess;
raise the budget or the tolerance, or subdivide the step. The queries make a few small
heap allocations per distance query (the working simplex), run no broad phase, and are
deterministic: same inputs, bit-identical outputs on one platform (fixed iteration order,
no hash maps, no clock).

`convex_distance` is accurate to about 1e-6 m when its iteration converges; on curved
shapes f32 noise sometimes stops it first, and it then reports a proven lower bound (at
most a few 1e-4 m low, never high), which keeps the time of impact conservative.

## How it works

Distance is Gilbert–Johnson–Keerthi (GJK) on the Minkowski difference of the two
shapes. Time of impact is conservative advancement: each step advances time by
`(separation − target_gap) / closing-speed-bound` along the current witness normal,
which provably cannot jump past the target separation. Papers and provenance are
recorded in `docs/provenance.md` under "Physics / CCD".

## Rigid motions: the true angular sweep

`time_of_impact_motion` sweeps two shapes along constant-velocity rigid motions instead
of between two endpoint poses. A `RigidMotion` is a start pose, a rotation centre in the
shape's local frame (usually the centre of mass), the centre's displacement over the
interval, and a rotation vector (world axis times radians, any size). That is the motion
a physics step integrates, so a body that turns more than half a turn per step, or turns
about a centre other than its pose origin, is swept along its real path. An endpoint
slerp cannot see either: three whole turns have identical endpoint poses.

```rust,wrap
use regia_core::math::{Isometry, Vec3};
use regia_physics::ccd::{time_of_impact_motion, ConvexInput, RigidMotion, ToiOptions, ToiResult};

// A 1 m bar spinning 30 rad/s about its centre, thrown at 120 m/s, over one 60 Hz step.
let bar = ConvexInput::cuboid(Vec3::new(0.5, 0.02, 0.02));
let motion = RigidMotion::from_velocities(
    Isometry::from_translation(Vec3::new(4.0, 0.0, 0.0)),
    Vec3::ZERO,                    // rotation centre, local
    Vec3::new(120.0, 0.0, 0.0),    // m/s
    Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 30.0),     // rad/s, world
    1.0 / 60.0,
);
let wall = RigidMotion::stationary(Isometry::from_translation(Vec3::new(5.0, 0.0, 0.0)));
let result = time_of_impact_motion(
    &bar, &motion,
    &ConvexInput::cuboid(Vec3::new(0.005, 3.0, 3.0)), &wall,
    ToiOptions::default(),        // gap 0, tolerance 0.1 mm, 128 advances
);
if let ToiResult::Hit { t, .. } = result {
    let pose_at_impact = motion.pose_at(t);
}
```

The advance bound is directional: along the fixed witness normal `n`, a point at radius
`r` from a centre spinning at `ω` moves at most `|n × ω| r` toward the other shape. A spin
about the contact normal therefore costs no extra steps; a spin across it costs
`|ω| R` like the endpoint query.

Refusals, never loops. NaN or infinite numbers anywhere return
`Failed(NonFiniteInput)`. A closing-speed bound that is not finite (velocities whose
difference overflows f32, or an angular speed whose bound overflows) or so large that an
advance no longer moves `t` returns `Failed(DegenerateMotion)`. Otherwise the work is
bounded by `max_iterations` advances plus at most 48 bisection steps. A zero closing
speed is a proof that the shapes stay apart, so it returns `Separated`.
`ToiFailure::code()` gives the stable lowercase code (`non_finite_input`,
`degenerate_motion`, ...). The endpoint query `time_of_impact` now refuses overflowing
motion the same way: it used to read a NaN closing speed as "no motion".

## Swept CCD in the step

Add `SweptCcd` to a dynamic body to sweep its whole step motion, rotation included,
against the colliders near its path. If something is reached first, the body goes back
to the time of impact, `skin` short of contact, and an inelastic contact impulse at the
impact point (with the pair's average restitution) removes the closing velocity. The
solver's speculative contacts hold the contact from the next step, so the rest of the
step's motion is dropped.

```rust,wrap
use regia_core::math::Vec3;
use regia_physics::{Collider, ColliderShape, RigidBody, SweptCcd, Velocity};
use regia_scene::Transform;
# use regia_ecs::prelude::Commands;
fn spawn_fast_body(mut commands: Commands) {
commands.spawn((
    Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.5, 0.0)),
    RigidBody::dynamic(),
    Collider { shape: ColliderShape::Box { half_extents: Vec3::new(1.0, 0.02, 0.02) }, ..Default::default() },
    Velocity { linear: Vec3::new(40.0, 0.0, 0.0), angular: Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 70.0) },
    SweptCcd::default(),          // skin 5 mm, 64 advances per pair
));
}
```

- It is opt-in and off by default. Without any `SweptCcd` body the step does no extra
  work, and the simulation is bit-identical to a build without the hook. A `SweptCcd`
  body that never hits anything also leaves the world bit-identical.
- `hits`, `failures` and `last_toi` on the component report what the step did.
- It sweeps against every non-sensor collider whose collision and solver groups interact
  with the body. A moving body is swept along its own step motion (exactly, when it is a
  `SweptCcd` body too; otherwise traced back from its pose and velocity), so two fast
  bodies fired at each other meet instead of passing through. Fixed and resting bodies
  are held where they are. Spheres, boxes, capsules, cylinders, cones,
  convex hulls, triangles, segments and compounds of them work on both sides. Triangle
  meshes and heightfields work as the other side: at most 256 of their triangles inside
  the swept bounds per pair. Rounded shapes, half-spaces, polylines and voxels are skipped.
- A pair already within the solver's prediction distance (2 cm by default) at the start
  of the step is left to the solver, which holds that contact. The exception is a body
  part that swings deeper than that distance through the starting contact plane, like
  the far end of a bar pivoting on its tip into a wall. The first such crossing, when it
  is a real overlap, counts as the impact, up to that depth inside the other shape (the
  solver pushes it out).
- What rapier already does: with rapier 0.36 every fast body is swept against *fixed*
  colliders, and bullets (`RigidBody::ccd`) against all bodies except other bullets.
  `SweptCcd` matters for thin *kinematic* or *dynamic* geometry (doors, platforms,
  vehicle panels, debris) hit by bodies that are not bullets, and for two bullets.
  Rapier also caps one step's rotation at an eighth of a turn (pi/4).
- The impulse acts on the swept body only. The other body is treated as immovable for
  that impulse, and the solver resolves both from the next step.
- It is independent of `RigidBody::ccd`, rapier's own CCD. A body may use both.
- Cost: one sweep per nearby pair, from about a microsecond (boxes, translation) to tens
  of microseconds (fast spins against hulls). Use it for a few fast movers (projectiles, thrown props, debris
  shards), not for every body in a pile.

The agent method `physics.time_of_impact` runs the same sweep on demand
(`book/agents/physics-time-of-impact.md`).
