rates, so a sim that accidentally ties itself to rendering fails a test
([agent guide: gameplay](book/agents/gameplay.md)).

## A threaded host

`ExternalSim` leaves threading to the sim. When the sim is a plain fixed-step simulation, let
`regia_framework::sim_host::ThreadedSimHost` run it: it steps the sim on its own thread and
publishes the last **two** frames as one pair, so the presentation never waits for a tick and can
blend between them. Implement `FixedStepSim` and hand the host to the bridge:

<!-- ignore-reason: a sketch over the game's own MySim and MySnapshot types and an app built elsewhere; the compiled end-to-end example is sim_host::tests::a_threaded_host_drives_the_sim_bridge -->
```rust,ignore
use regia_framework::sim_bridge::{BridgeInput, SimBridgePlugin};
use regia_framework::sim_host::{FixedStepSim, SimHostSettings, ThreadedSimHost};

impl FixedStepSim for MySim {
    type Frame = MySnapshot; // implements SimSnapshot + Clone for the bridge
    type Event = MyEvent;
    fn step(&mut self, input: &BridgeInput) { /* one fixed tick */ }
    fn tick(&self) -> u64 { self.tick }
    fn write_frame(&self, out: &mut MySnapshot) { /* overwrite every field */ }
    fn drain_events(&mut self, out: &mut Vec<MyEvent>) { out.append(&mut self.events) }
}

let host = ThreadedSimHost::start(MySim::new(), SimHostSettings::default())?; // 60 Hz
app.insert_resource(host.handle()); // sim.host_status, sim.host_hold, sim.host_step
app.add_plugins(SimBridgePlugin::new(host));
```

- **The pair.** `host.published()` returns `prev`, `curr`, both ticks, both publish times and a
  sequence, always from the same publish. While the sim steps, `curr_tick` is `prev_tick + 1`;
  `alpha(now, delay)` places a frame drawn `delay` behind the clock between them (one tick is the
  usual delay). The bridge reads the pair through `read_pair` and blends by each kind's policy
  ([Handedness and blending](#handedness-and-blending)); `read_snapshot` copies `curr`.
- **Holding.** `handle.set_held(true)` pauses: the host publishes a *still* pair (`prev` and
  `curr` the same frame), drops the input it is offered and keeps its grants for later.
  `SimHostSettings::start_held` boots held (a lobby preloading a match).
- **Clocks.** `HostPacing::Realtime { tick, catch_up }` steps on the wall clock. A host that falls
  behind runs at most `catch_up` late ticks back to back, then drops the rest of the debt (counted
  as `debt_drops` and `ticks_dropped`), so a hitch never bursts the sim forward. `HostPacing::Manual`
  steps only ticks granted with `handle.grant_ticks(n)`: tests and render-outs step exactly.
- **A stale presentation.** With `client_stale_after: Some(d)`, the host steps only while
  `handle.stamp_client()` was called within `d` (call it once per presented frame), so a loading
  stall does not run the match unseen.
- **Input and events.** Axes replace, edges queue in order until the next tick. Events go to a
  bounded queue (`event_cap`, oldest dropped and counted).
- **Stopping.** Dropping the host stops and joins its thread; `into_sim()` also hands the sim
  back, for a hot-reload unload that keeps the sim's state. A sim that panics stops the host;
  waiters get `SimHostError::SimPanicked` instead of hanging.

Agents read and drive the host with `sim.host_status`, `sim.host_hold`, `sim.host_step`,
`sim.host_snapshot` and `sim.host_restore` ([agent guide: framework](book/agents/framework.md)).

### Lockstep pacing

A lockstep game must step exact agreed frames, never merged input. Implement `LockstepSim` (one
`step_inputs(tick, &inputs)` per agreed tick) and `regia_detsim::state::DetState` for the sim, and
start the host with `HostPacing::Lockstep`:

<!-- ignore-reason: a sketch over the game's MySim and a net seat built elsewhere; the compiled end-to-end test is sim_host::tests::lockstep_pacing_steps_each_frame_once_in_order -->
```rust,ignore
use regia_framework::sim_host::{HostPacing, LockstepSim, SimHostSettings, ThreadedSimHost};

impl LockstepSim for MySim {
    type Inputs = MyFrame; // what one agreed tick carries, such as N224's LockstepFrame<I>
    fn step_inputs(&mut self, tick: u64, inputs: &MyFrame) { /* exactly one tick */ }
}

let settings = SimHostSettings {
    pacing: HostPacing::Lockstep { tick: Some(regia_framework::sim_host::DEFAULT_TICK) },
    ..SimHostSettings::default()
};
let (host, feed) = ThreadedSimHost::start_lockstep(MySim::new(), settings)?;
// On the net seat's thread, for every agreed frame:
feed.push_frame(tick, frame)?;
```

The host steps the frame for the next tick only, each once and in order. A missing frame stalls
the host until it arrives (`frame_stalls`); a duplicate or an old frame is refused with
`SimHostError::FrameOutOfOrder`, and one more than `frame_queue_cap` ticks ahead with
`FrameQueueFull`. Bridge input offered to a lockstep host is dropped (counted in `edges_dropped`):
the frames carry the input. With `tick: None` the host wakes once per grant instead of on the
clock, which tests and replays use to step exactly.

`handle.catch_up(n)` lets each wake step up to `n` queued frames back to back: a late joiner or a
resynced seat reaches the live tick faster than real time, but never more than `n` ticks per wake
(spec 120 § 7.4). Each caught-up tick is still published. When the host reaches a tick whose frame
has not arrived it is at the live edge, and it returns to one tick per wake on its own.

### Snapshots and restore

A host started with `start_lockstep`, or `start_with_snapshots` for a merged-input sim that
implements `DetState`, saves and loads the sim **on its own thread**, between two steps:

<!-- ignore-reason: `handle`, `send_to_seat` and `bytes` are the game's; the compiled test is sim_host::tests::snapshot_then_restore_republishes_and_resumes_bit_identically -->
```rust,ignore
// Now, or when the sim reaches a tick (answered right after that tick's step).
let snapshot = handle.request_snapshot(tick)?.wait()?;
send_to_seat(seat, &snapshot.bytes);

// On the seat: load the bytes, then push the frames after snapshot.tick.
let restored_tick = handle.restore(bytes)?.wait()?;
```

`restore` goes through `regia_detsim::state::restore_with`, so the sim resumes bit for bit; it
replaces the sim, drops queued frames up to the restored tick and publishes a *still* pair at the
restored tick (the presentation snaps there instead of blending from the old timeline). Damaged or
foreign bytes are refused (`SimHostError::RestoreFailed`) and the sim keeps running as it was. A
held host stays held. `HostReply::wait_timeout` bounds the wait.

### FP environment

A lockstep sim must step under the IEEE default floating-point environment on every peer. A thread
inherits its creator's environment, and an audio or video library may have turned on flush-to-zero
there. The host thread therefore calls `regia_detsim::fpu::ensure_default_fp_env()` before the first
step (`SimHostStatus::fp_env_reset` says whether it had to), and again every `fp_check_every` steps
(every step in debug builds, `DEFAULT_FP_CHECK_EVERY` = 600 in release builds) in case foreign code
running on the sim thread changed it; each change is put back and counted (`fp_env_changed`).

### Suspend

`SimBridgePlugin` adds `hold_sim_host_on_suspend` to the `Lifecycle` schedule: when the OS suspends
the app (Android: home button, screen off) a `SimHostHandle` resource is held, so the sim never
steps unseen, and `Resumed` releases it unless the game had held the host itself. An app that hosts
a sim without the bridge adds the system and `init_resource::<SuspendHold>()` itself.

## Handedness and blending

`SimBridgeSettings` (insert it, or build the plugin with `.settings(...)`) sets how the bridge turns
the sim's frames into poses (ADR-8456). The default changes nothing: a right-handed sim that
publishes one snapshot is drawn exactly as read, bit for bit.

<!-- ignore-reason: a sketch over the game's own sim, kinds file and app; the compiled end-to-end tests are sim_blend::bridge_tests -->
```rust,ignore
use std::time::Duration;
use regia_framework::sim_blend::SimBridgeSettings;
use regia_framework::sim_coords::SimHandedness;

app.add_plugins(
    SimBridgePlugin::new(host)
        .kinds(KindRegistry::load(Path::new("config/kinds.ron"))?)
        .settings(SimBridgeSettings {
            handedness: SimHandedness::LeftHandedReflectX, // the sim is left-handed
            teleport_distance: Some(10.0),                 // a 10 m jump in one tick snaps
            presentation_delay: Duration::from_nanos(16_666_667), // draw one tick behind
        }),
);
```

- **Handedness.** A sim whose world is left-handed (+X east, +Y up, +Z north) draws mirrored when
  placed unchanged. `SimHandedness::LeftHandedReflectX` reflects X once at the boundary, for every
  snapshot pose and every `EventPlace::At`: positions `(−x, y, z)`, rotations by quaternion
  conjugation `(w, x, y, z) → (w, x, −y, −z)` (a proper rotation, never a negative scale) and yaw
  `θ → −θ`. The sim must not convert again. Picking rays go back with the same function (the
  reflection is its own inverse: `SimHandedness::inv`). The helpers are in
  `regia_framework::sim_coords` (`pos`, `dir`, `quat`, `yaw`, `rendered_xz`, `seat_delta`).
- **The winding flip.** Placed meshes (glTF, cooked) are right-handed already and are not mirrored;
  only their placement is converted. A mesh the sim authors in its own coordinates and draws with an
  identity transform (baked world geometry) goes through `handedness.mirror_mesh(&mut cpu_mesh)`:
  positions, normals and tangents are reflected, the tangent sign flips and every triangle's winding
  is reversed (`mirror_mesh_winding`), so back-face culling and lighting stay right.
- **Blend policy per kind.** A sim that publishes its last two frames (`ExternalSim::read_pair`;
  `ThreadedSimHost` does) is drawn between them. Each kind in `config/kinds.ron` picks a `blend`
  (optional; `Lerp` when left out):

  ```ron
  (kinds: {
      "hull": (prefab: Some("prefabs/hull.prefab.ron"), presentation_scripts: []),
      "door": (prefab: None, presentation_scripts: [], blend: Hold),
      "marker": (prefab: None, presentation_scripts: [], blend: Snap),
  })
  ```

  `Lerp` lerps the position and slerps the rotation, and snaps to the newest pose past
  `teleport_distance`. `Snap` always draws the newest pose. `Hold` draws the older frame until the
  blend reaches the newest one: no in-between poses, but in time with the lerped kinds.
- **The delay.** The blend weight places a frame drawn `presentation_delay` behind the newest
  publish between the two frames (`PublishedFrames::alpha`). A still pair (a held host), and a
  manually paced host, draw the newest frame.

Agents read and change these with `sim.bridge_settings` and `sim.set_bridge_settings`
([agent guide: framework](book/agents/framework.md#sim-bridge-presentation)).

## Presentation physics

Debris, ragdolls and explosion pushes are presentation: they run on the engine's physics next to
the sim and never feed back into it. The engine piece is
`regia_framework::sim_bridge::presentation` (ADR-8356). It is not on the lockstep closure.

- **Units are kinematic hulls.** `PresentationPhysicsPlugin { hulls, debris_lifetime_s }` and
  `HullShapes` map a sim kind to any `ColliderShape`, not only a box. The bridge writes the
  snapshot pose into `Transform` in `PreUpdate`; physics pushes a kinematic body's `Transform` as
  its next pose in every `FixedUpdate`, so the hull moves exactly where the sim says, with the
  velocity of that move. Debris resting on a deck rides along through friction. Physics never
  writes a kinematic body's `Transform` back.
- **A dynamic body with a sim id is refused.** Before the physics step the module removes that
  body, logs a warning, and increments `PresentationPhysicsStats::refused_writes`. The snapshot
  `Transform` stays. A hull kind is attached again as kinematic. Debris without a sim id stays
  dynamic.
- **The ground is the drawn ground.** With the `client` feature (it links `regia_terrain`),
  `PresentationGround::from_terrain(&TerrainMap, Option<&HolesMask>)` builds the collider from
  `TerrainMap::collision_heightfield` and lists the hole cells the draw skips. Insert the resource
  before `Startup`. The collider sits at the map's origin.
- **Debris has no sim id.** A `DebrisBurst` message spawns chunks through `DebrisSpawner`. The
  lifetime is `debris_lifetime_s` (30 simulated seconds unless you set it). The bridge only
  rewrites entities in its `SimEntityMap`, so the chunks stay dynamic.

Agents read `sim_bridge.presentation_stats` (hull bodies, debris alive, refused writes, and the
spawn counters). See [Presentation physics (agents)](book/agents/presentation-physics.md).

Keep anything that must agree across machines out of this layer: physics is deterministic per
platform, but presentation bodies are not part of the sim's state, so two clients may scatter
debris differently. A sim event (`"explosion"`) is the usual trigger; route it to a system that
writes a `DebrisBurst` at `ExternalSim::event_place`.

`samples/sim_bridge` keeps the windowed demo (`PresentationPhysicsDemo`, the sample terrain
constants, `build_cube_mesh`) and calls the engine plugin (`sim_bridge --presentation-physics`).
The three promises live in `crates/regia_framework/tests/presentation_physics.rs`: a chunk dropped
on a bridged hull rests on its deck and rides with it when the snapshot pose moves, a chunk over a
hole falls through while one beside it rests, and the bridge never writes the `Transform` of an
entity without a sim id. `a_dynamic_body_with_a_sim_id_is_refused` holds the refusal rule.

## Recording input

`regia_framework::input_recording::InputRecordingPlugin` records and replays the per-frame input
of deterministic games; `samples/arena` uses it so a seeded bot match replays identically. That
is the building block for replays and lockstep tests.

## Hot reload and the sim

The sim lives in a library that is **not** hot reloaded: editing it needs an editor restart, like
engine code. The presentation side (scripts, systems) reloads normally
([Hot reload](book/user-guide/hot-reload.md)).

The complete reference is `samples/sim_bridge`: three hover discs from a mock sim, presentation
scripts reading extras, chase/overhead/free cameras, timers, tweens, live settings, touch controls
on Android, a sound on the first sim event, and (with `--presentation-physics`) the presentation
physics above.

<!-- source: book/systems/snapshot-delta.md -->
# Snapshot delta codec

<!-- index: Snapshot delta -->
<!-- index: Quantization -->

`regia_net::snapshot_delta` is a standalone, schema-driven codec for sending world state as
quantized snapshots: a full snapshot first, then per-entity deltas against the last snapshot the
receiver acknowledged. It is a generic engine feature, independent of the ECS replication in
`regia_net::replication`: use it when you already have (or want) plain snapshot values — replay
streams, state-sync prototypes, tools, lockstep-adjacent state broadcasts — and do not want to
mark components for replication. When to choose it over lockstep or ECS replication is
[Lockstep and rollback](book/how-to/online/lockstep-and-rollback.md).

The Rust type is spelled `Vec3Quantised`. The error helper is spelled
`FieldKind::max_quantisation_error`. Prose on this page uses the US spelling.

You describe the per-entity state once as a `SnapshotSchema`, hand whole `WorldSnapshot`s to a
`SnapshotEncoder`, and get back one self-framing packet per call. The peer feeds packets to a
`SnapshotDecoder` and reads the reconstructed snapshot out of each `DecodedSnapshot`.

## The schema

Both peers must build the identical schema. Every packet carries a 32-bit layout hash (field
names, kinds, ranges, widths, variant counts), so a mismatch decodes as `SnapshotError::SchemaMismatch`,
never as silent corruption.

| `FieldKind` | `FieldValue` | Wire cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Bool` | `Bool(bool)` | 1 bit | exact |
| `U8` / `U16` / `U32` | `U8` / `U16` / `U32` | 8 / 16 / 32 bits | exact |
| `I32` | `I32(i32)` | 8–40 bits | zig-zag varint; small magnitudes stay small |
| `Float { min, max, bits }` | `F32(f32)` | `bits` (1–32) | uniform quantization over `[min, max]`; error at most half a step plus `f32` rounding (`FieldKind::max_quantisation_error`) |
| `Vec3Quantised { min, max, bits }` | `Vec3(Vec3)` | 3 × `bits` | each axis quantized over its own range |
| `QuatSmallestThree { bits }` | `Quat(Quat)` | 2 + 3 × `bits` | dropped largest component rebuilt from the unit norm |
| `Enum { variants }` | `Enum(u32)` | smallest width holding all variants | discriminants must be below `variants` |

Values are quantized **before** comparison, so a change smaller than one quantization step is not
a change: the per-entity change mask only names fields whose wire bits differ. Non-finite floats
clamp to the nearer end of their range and a zero or non-finite quaternion travels as the identity,
matching the crate's replication codec — degenerate input is defined behavior, never an error and
never a panic. `SnapshotSchema::quantize_snapshot` (and `quantize_value`) show exactly what a
receiver will reconstruct, which is what tests should compare against.

## Sending and receiving

```rust,wrap
use regia_net::{
    EntitySnapshot, FieldDef, FieldKind, FieldValue, NetId, NetTick, SnapshotDecoder,
    SnapshotEncoder, SnapshotSchema, WorldSnapshot,
};

let schema = SnapshotSchema::new(vec![
    FieldDef::new("alive", FieldKind::Bool),
    FieldDef::new("score", FieldKind::U32),
    FieldDef::new(
        "health",
        FieldKind::Float { min: 0.0, max: 100.0, bits: 12 },
    ),
    FieldDef::new("team", FieldKind::Enum { variants: 4 }),
])?;

let mut encoder = SnapshotEncoder::new(schema.clone());
let mut decoder = SnapshotDecoder::new(schema);

let world = WorldSnapshot::new(vec![EntitySnapshot::new(
    NetId(1),
    vec![
        FieldValue::Bool(true),
        FieldValue::U32(40),
        FieldValue::F32(87.5),
        FieldValue::Enum(2),
    ],
)]);

// Each tick: delta against whatever the client last acknowledged.
let (packet, report) =
    encoder.encode_with_report(NetTick(1), &world, decoder.latest_baseline(), 1200)?;
let decoded = decoder.decode(&packet)?;
assert_eq!(decoded.snapshot.len(), 1);
// Send `decoder.latest_baseline()` back to the server as the ack for the next encode.
let _ack = decoder.latest_baseline();
let _sent_some = !report.included.is_empty();
```

`SnapshotEncoder::encode(tick, &world, ack, budget_bytes)` is the same call without the
`EncodeReport`. The decoder's answer reports the packet's sequence, tick and baseline, the
reconstructed `snapshot` (entities sorted by id), and which entities were `added`, `updated` or
`removed`. Priorities are encoder-local and do not travel; reconstructed entities report priority 0.

## Baselines, loss and the ring buffer

Every packet gets a sequence number (`Seq`, from 1) and names the baseline it was encoded
against: the last sequence the client acknowledged. Both sides keep a ring buffer of recent
baselines keyed by that sequence (`DEFAULT_BASELINE_CAPACITY` = 64; size it with
`with_capacity` to your worst round trip in send ticks).

- **Lost packet:** costs nothing. The client keeps acknowledging the older sequence, so the next
  packet is a delta against the state the client still holds.
- **Baseline evicted at the encoder:** the next encode is a full snapshot (`EncodeReport::is_full`).
- **Baseline evicted at the decoder:** `decode` returns `SnapshotError::BaselineMissing` and
  leaves the decoder's state untouched; keep acknowledging `latest_baseline()` and the server
  will re-base or go full.

Always acknowledge `SnapshotDecoder::latest_baseline()`: the newest packet held as a baseline.
On the server, keep the newest ack you have seen (acks can arrive out of order too).

### Reordered and repeated packets

Packets may arrive late, twice or out of order (any unreliable channel does this on Wi-Fi and
mobile links). Only a packet newer than `SnapshotDecoder::last_seq()` (serial-number order, so
sequences may wrap) moves `current()` forward. An older or repeated packet still decodes and is
stored as a baseline, because the server may already have encoded a delta against it, but it
never moves the shown world back: its `DecodedSnapshot` carries the packet's own `seq`, `tick`
and `baseline`, the unchanged `current()` as `snapshot`, and empty `added`, `updated` and `removed`
lists. Tell a late packet apart with `decoded.seq != decoder.last_seq()`.

A *full* packet more than `capacity()` sequences behind the newest one is taken as a restarted
stream (a new server process starts again at `Seq(1)`) and resets the decoder. When you know the
stream restarted (a reconnect), call `SnapshotDecoder::reset()` instead of relying on that.

### Re-basing after the encoder lost the client's baseline

When the client's acks stop reaching the server for longer than the ring (a stall, an uplink
outage), the encoder's acknowledged baseline falls out of its ring and it sends full packets. Under
a byte budget smaller than the world, such a full packet carries only the highest-priority
entities. The decoder never lets that wipe the world: a full packet cut short by the budget is
*merged* into the shown world, and entities it did not carry stay shown at their last known state.
`SnapshotDecoder::is_rebasing()` is true while the shown world holds such entities; once acks flow
again the stream re-sends every entity over a few packets (each acknowledged packet is progress)
and the first complete packet settles the world exactly. While re-basing, an entity the server
removed meanwhile stays shown until that complete packet.

### Memory: shared baselines

Every packet is a baseline, so both sides keep up to `capacity()` of them. Baselines share their
storage copy-on-write: a baseline is a root of shared leaves of about 16 entities, and a packet
that changes `k` entities copies the root's pointer list, at most `k` leaves and the `k` new
values. 64 baselines of a mostly static 4,000-entity world hold less than twice what one does, and
an encode allocates in proportion to the records it writes, not to the world (the
`snapshot_delta_alloc` tests count both).

## Byte budgets

`budget_bytes` is a hard cap: a returned packet never exceeds it. Entity records pack by
descending `EntitySnapshot::priority` (ties break on the lower id; removals pack first). What
does not fit is listed in `EncodeReport::omitted` and the packet is marked *incomplete*.

Both sides store every packet, complete or not, as a baseline holding exactly what it carried:
the acknowledged baseline with the included records applied, omitted entities left at their
baseline state (or absent, for an omitted add). An overflow therefore defers an update but never
corrupts reconstructed state, and acknowledging an incomplete packet is progress: the next delta
carries only what is still missing, so a world larger than one packet converges over a few
packets. Priorities are taken as given; if high-priority entities change every tick and fill
every packet, low-priority ones wait, so raise a waiting entity's priority over time (a priority
accumulator) when that matters. A budget too small for even an empty packet returns
`SnapshotError::BudgetTooSmall` and consumes no sequence number.

## Wire format and failure behavior

```text
packet  := magic u8 | version u8 | total_len u32le | crc32 u32le | body
body    := schema_hash u32 | flags u8 | seq varint | tick varint
           | baseline varint (0 = full snapshot) | count varint | record*
record  := kind u2 | id varint | payload        (kind: 0 add, 1 update, 2 remove)
add     := every field, in schema order
update  := change mask (one bit per field) | the changed fields, in schema order
```

The body is bit-packed least-significant-bit first (the crate's `bits::BitWriter`); the outer
header is byte-aligned. `total_len` makes every truncation a `LengthMismatch`, and the IEEE
CRC-32 over the body catches corruption before any field is read. Decoding untrusted bytes never
panics: short, truncated, corrupt, schema-mismatched or baseline-less packets return a
`SnapshotError` and leave the decoder exactly as it was. Encoding validates the snapshot against
the schema and reports duplicates, type mismatches and out-of-range enum discriminants as errors.

Encoding is deterministic: the same schema, world, tick, ack and budget produce the same bytes on
every platform, and the order of entities in the input snapshot does not matter.

## Limits

- up to `MAX_FIELDS` (128) fields per schema, `MAX_ENTITIES` (65 536) entities per snapshot;
- entity ids are the crate's `NetId`, ticks are `NetTick`; sequence numbers are this module's `Seq`;
- this layer does no transport, ordering, interpolation or relevance filtering — feed it packets
  from whatever channel you like, one packet per `decode` call.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/lookdev.md -->
# Look-dev harness

<!-- index: Look-dev -->
<!-- index: Shot list -->

`samples/lookdev` is the measured feedback loop for the DO27 alpha maps. It builds two
procedural stand-ins in the terrain data shape, renders a fixed shot list offscreen, and
writes `shots.json`. After a render or terrain merge, `lookdev --compare` prints the deltas.

## Stand-ins

Europa is Bore Twelve: snow, wind-packed snow, blue ice, dirty ice, frosted basalt, regolith.
Mars is The Switchbacks: sandstone strata, scree, dust, gravel, bedrock, dune sand.

Each scene carries:

- a 16-bit eroded heightfield (baseline edge 4096, world width 4096 m)
- six material layers, each with an authored height map
- a macro-variation map (evidence edge 2048; `--macro 8192` is the 8K target and a CPU test
  checks that 8192 allocates). The evidence run stays at 2048: the terrain shader does not
  sample the map yet, and an 8192² `f32` image is 256 MiB before row padding
- a road trench with a shoulder lip, a tunnel mouth (heightfield notch plus the portal mesh
  drawn by the harness), and rock scatter. Scatter is still the terrain pyramid mesh until
  a rock mesh exists

Thermal erosion follows Musgrave, Kolb and Mace, SIGGRAPH 1989. Hydraulic erosion follows
the particle form of Mei, Decaudin and Hu, Pacific Graphics 2007. Both rows are in
`docs/provenance.md`.

## Shot list

Eight cameras per planet: close (1 m), mid (50 m), far (2 km), low sun, noon, tunnel mouth,
road bend, sky-heavy. Three profiles: Ultra (`DesktopUltra`), High (`DesktopHigh`), and
Deck-Medium. Deck-Medium selects the engine preset `Deck` (the profile table has one Deck
row). That is 48 shots. The list does not include the VeryLow tier or the offline Cinematic
profile. Render those with `RenderProfilePreset` (Cinematic through
`regia_render::cinematic::gate_preset`) when the comparison needs them. Each shot renders 30
frames so temporal stability has a real window.

```sh
cargo run -p lookdev --release -- --shots /tmp/lookdev \
  --width 1920 --height 1080 --heightfield 4096 --macro 2048 \
  --frames 30 --png-width 960
```

`--planet europa` or `--planet mars` restricts the list. With no arguments the binary prints
help and exits 1.

## What a frame contains

The heightfield is drawn through the terrain hook that is on main: one sun cascade, exponential
height fog, CDLOD, slope and altitude layers, scatter, and the tunnel hole. The harness also
draws `MeshTunnel::render_mesh` with the same EV100 / AgX lighting, because the hook punches
the hole and does not submit the mesh. Desktop High and Ultra request GTAO, PCSS-lite, four
cascades, the probe budget, and TAA. `shots.json` records those requests next to
`applied_terrain_cascades: 1`. Detecting SSR or GI does not mean those passes ran.

`build.rs` sets a cfg when a named item appears. On this tree that is `fn ssr_roughness_weight`,
`struct ReflectionProbe`, `struct GiField`, and `struct GpuGiGrid`. Atmosphere, clouds,
streaming, and macro sampling stay on their own needles (`struct AtmosphereModel`,
`struct VolumetricClouds`, `struct TerrainStreamer`, `struct MacroVariation`). The flag lands
in `shots.json`, so `--compare` shows that the lane merged. A new draw API still needs a
harness edit before its pixels are in the shot. The harness uploads each layer height map and
the macro map as `R32Float` and records the byte counts. The terrain shader samples them only
when the macro-lane probe flips. Behavior that arrives through `TerrainFrame`, `LayerDesc`,
fog, or CDLOD is picked up on the next build, because the frame is built with
`TerrainFrame::from_camera` and the layers start from `LayerDesc::ground`.

## Measurements

`shots.json` (version 1) stores, per shot, mean BT.709 luminance, contrast (luminance standard
deviation), percent near-black (Y < 8) and blown (Y > 250), saturation, the strongest
secondary autocorrelation peak after the lag-0 lobe (a smooth gradient is 0), RMS Laplacian
sharpness, temporal stability over the frame count, mean luminance of the bottom 45% of the
frame (`ground_luminance`), and mean GPU milliseconds for shadow, sky, terrain, scatter, and
water. Noon and low sun are tuned so Europa snow stays under the AgX shoulder and a low sun
still lights the ground.

Numbers come from the full framebuffer. The PNG is the last frame, box-downscaled to
`--png-width` when the frame is wider. Deck's render scale produces a smaller framebuffer, so
those PNGs stay at their native size when that size is already under the cap.

GPU times need `TIMESTAMP_QUERY` and `TIMESTAMP_QUERY_INSIDE_ENCODERS`. Otherwise every pass
is 0 and `gpu_timing` is false. A failed timestamp read drops timing and keeps the image.

```sh
cargo run -p lookdev -- --compare old/shots.json new/shots.json
```

The table is `new − old` for luminance, contrast, clipping, saturation, tiling, sharpness,
stability, ground luminance (`d_gnd`), and total GPU time, plus a line for each feature flag
or upload byte-count that changed.

## Default-look shots

`cargo run --release -p lookdev --bin default_look -- --out <dir>` renders four DO27-like
frames through the mesh renderer with nothing but the runtime defaults: props on snow, a
vehicle in the air, an enclosed cockpit, and a wide vista. `--fixed-ev <ev100>` pins the
exposure, `--side-by-side <before> <after> <out>` builds comparison images, and `LOOK_DEBUG_*`
environment variables switch single features off for A/B reviews (listed in
`lookdev::default_look`). The 320×180 lavapipe goldens are `samples/lookdev/goldens/`. See
[The default look](book/user-guide/default-look.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/host-look-checklist.md -->
# Host look checklist

The look-dev harness renders DO27's content the way the parity sheets show it
(`docs/evidence/parity/2026-10-07/ferrite-do27-sheet.png`, made before the rename). This page lists every setting a host
(a game shell driving `FrameRenderer` directly) must make to get the same frame. It was written
from the harness's code: `samples/lookdev/src/look_r2.rs` (`render_shot`, `do27_level`), its
content loader `samples/lookdev/src/do27.rs` and the chase bench `samples/lookdev/src/chase.rs`
(`do27_chase`).

**Check a running host in one call.** `FrameRenderer::host_checklist_report(&frame_scene)`
returns a `HostChecklist`. Hosts that load a level call
`host_checklist_report_for_level(&frame_scene, &level_settings)`: it also checks the exposure band,
the sun strength and the sky body against the level. Print the report (`println!("{report}")`) once
per session after the first frame. Frame-breaking items print first as `ERROR` (`report.errors()`),
for example MSAA with terrain. Every other difference from the harness prints as `DIFF`.
`FrameRenderer::frame_problems()` (agent: `render.problems`) says what broke the last frame drawn.
It also carries the device's **capability fallbacks** (`fallback_*` codes, one per optional feature
the adapter lacks — no timestamps, no BC decompression, RGBA16F HDR, CPU indirect counts, …): those
are informational (the frame is correct, a named fast path is off) and appear in the checklist as
the `device capability fallbacks` item, never as `ERROR`. The harness prints its
own report with `LOOK_R2_CHECKLIST=1` (`look_r2` and `do27_chase`), so a shell can diff the two
texts.

## 1. Profile and frame quality

`RenderSettings::default()` (Desktop High on a desktop; on a Steam Deck it is `Deck`, so use
`RenderSettings::from_profile(RenderProfilePreset::DesktopHigh)` there), then `settings.quality()`
(`FrameQuality::from_profile`). Do not edit the result. The report checks each field:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `msaa_samples` | `1` (anti-aliasing is TAA in post) |
| `hdr_target` | `Rgba16f` |
| `render_scale_permille` | `1000` (native) |
| `taau` | `true` |
| `physical_atmosphere`, `volumetric_fog`, `volumetric_clouds` | `true` |
| `paged_sun_shadows` | `true`; `csm_cascade_count` `4`; `csm_resolution` `2048`; `shadow_filter` `PcssLite` |
| `stable_sun_cascades` | `true` (cascades on a fixed texel lattice, so sun shadows do not shimmer; see [shadow stability](book/agents/shadow-stability.md)) |
| `ssao` | `GtaoHalfRes` |
| `gi` / `screen_space_gi` / `ssr` / `reflection_probes` | `Probes` / `true` / `true` / `true` |
| `parallax_occlusion`, `gpu_driven` | `true` |
| `terrain_budget` | `TerrainBudget::OFF` (the default look) |

## 2. HDR, post and exposure

- `let mut post = settings.resolve_post();` then `post.auto_exposure = true;`.
- Apply the map's look with `regia_render::apply_level_look(&mut post, &level.look)`. That sets
  the bias, the EV100 clamp band, the meter, contrast, saturation and grade.
- If `level.look.lut` is set, load it with `ColorLut::load(path)` into `post.lut`.
- Pass the post settings in the frame (`FrameScene::post = Some(&post)`; `LabScene::post` in the
  lab types). The frame renders to the profile's linear HDR target and the post stack applies
  exposure, bloom, AgX (`post.tonemap = AgX`), the grade and the LUT once, at the end.
- Target: `render_into(device, &frame, FrameTarget::full(&view, Rgba8UnormSrgb, w, h))`, or
  `render_offscreen` (`Rgba8Unorm`).
- DO27 content exposure bands (`do27_level`) are EV100 11.1–11.3 for the Switchbacks and 11.9–12.1
  for Bore Twelve. Put them in the level's `look.min_ev100` / `look.max_ev100`
  ([Map look](book/agents/look.md)).

## 3. Frame scene

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `near` / `far` | `0.1` / `12000.0` (the sun cascades stop at 4 km by themselves) |
| `depth_prepass` | `settings.profile.depth_prepass` (`true`) |
| `directional_shadows` | `true` |
| `ibl` | `true` |
| `fog` | `FogSettings::default()` (**disabled**; the planet sky and the froxel haze do the aerial perspective) |
| `directional` | `DirectionalLightUniform::new(travel, color, lux)` with physical lux (DO27: 45 000 Mars, 18 000 Europa) |
| `ambient_lux` | `Environment::default().ambient_lux` (only used without a planet sky) |
| `double_sided` | `false` |
| `meshes` | set pieces, scatter rocks (section 6) and vehicles, as `FrameMesh`es |

The sun direction is the map's authored light. With a level clock (`atmosphere.time_of_day`),
the renderer replaces it with the atmosphere's transmitted sun.

## 4. Level: atmosphere, sky body, fog

- Load the `.level.ron` with `SceneFile::from_ron_str` then `regia_scene::format::migrate_to_latest`.
  Read `LevelSettings` from the `"regia_scene::level::LevelSettings"` resource
  (`LevelSettings::from_ron`).
- Build the outdoor state with `let mut outdoor = OutdoorParams { fog: VolumetricFogSettings::default(), ..Default::default() };`
  then `outdoor.apply_level(&level.atmosphere, false)`, then `renderer.set_outdoor(outdoor)`.
- `atmosphere.preset` is `Mars` or `Airless`. `sun_illuminance_lux` is the map's.
  `haze` is the Switchbacks dust (`density 1.2e-5`, `scale_height_m 600`; it becomes the froxel
  fog) ([Atmosphere](book/agents/atmosphere.md), [Volumetric fog](book/agents/volumetric-fog.md)).
- Bore Twelve: `atmosphere.sky_body = Some(SkyBody { direction, fill_lux: Some(1600.0), ..SkyBody::jupiter_from_europa() })`
  and `moons = vec![SkyBody::io_from_europa() at its direction]`.
  - `fill_lux` is the Jupiter-shine, a shadowless fill on meshes, terrain and scatter.
  - Do not draw a Jupiter card of your own.
- Textured moons (alpha rc2): the sky bodies above stay tint-only unless the shell passes
  albedo maps. Load each moon's equirectangular image (longitude across, north pole at the top,
  sRGB RGBA8) into a `SkyBodyTexture` and set `outdoor.moon_albedo[i] = Some(Arc::new(tex))`
  before `renderer.set_outdoor` — `moon_albedo[i]` textures `moons[i]`, `None` keeps the tint
  byte-identical to today. The body's map is `outdoor.sky_body_albedo` (same format). Do not
  set a map without the matching `moons`/`sky_body` entry; an unset slot is the shipped look.
- Tunnels and interiors: `renderer.set_interior_scene(Some(EnclosureScene))` and
  `OutdoorParams::interiors` ([Tunnels](book/agents/tunnels.md)).

## 5. Terrain: the shared draw and the renderer's three hooks

<!-- ignore-reason: requires a GPU device and queue to create the terrain draw and contact map; names `wgpu::TextureFormat`, and wgpu is not a dependency of the book's snippet crate -->
```rust,ignore
let mut draw = TerrainSharedDraw::new(device, map, &layers, CdlodConfig::default(), root_level)?;
draw.set_material_cooked(&cooked, params, macro_tiles, &[])?; // the cooked BC7/BC5/BC4 pack
draw.set_relief(TerrainRelief::default());                     // strata, near/mid relief
let contact = ContactMap::new(&device.device);
draw.set_contact_map(Some(&contact));
draw.prewarm(wgpu::TextureFormat::Rgba16Float);
let surface = draw.surface();                                   // for scatter (section 6)
renderer.set_shared_draw(Some(Box::new(draw)));
```

- Use a block-compressed device for cooked terrain (`regia_terrain::gpu::headless_bcn_device`
  headless, or request `TEXTURE_COMPRESSION_BC` on your device).
- Root level: 7 for a 1280 m map at 4096² (0.31 m cells at the default 32-cell grid).
- The renderer's three hooks are `set_shared_draw`, `set_outdoor` and `set_interior_scene`.
  - The renderer then calls the draw's `prepare`, `set_engine_csm`, `set_engine_ao` and
    `finish_prepare` itself.
  - The terrain receives the engine's sun cascades, SSAO, hemisphere sky ambient, planet-shine
    and canyon sky occlusion with no further host work.

See [Photoreal terrain](book/user-guide/terrain-photoreal.md) and [Terrain data](book/user-guide/terrain-data.md).

## 6. Scatter

Set-up, once:

```rust,wrap
# use std::sync::Arc;
# use regia_terrain::{
#     DensityMaps, RenderedSurface, ScatterField, ScatterLibrary, ScatterSet, ScatterSource, TerrainLayers, TerrainMap,
# };
# let (text, map, layers, library): (String, TerrainMap, TerrainLayers, ScatterLibrary) = todo!();
# let surface: RenderedSurface = todo!();
let set = ScatterSet::from_ron(&text, Some(&layers))?;
let source = ScatterSource { map: Arc::new(map.clone()), holes: None, layers: Some(layers.clone()), density_maps: DensityMaps::new() };
let mut field = ScatterField::new(&set, source, &library, set.seed)?;
field.set_rendered_surface(Some(surface)); // rocks sit on the drawn CDLOD surface
```

Per frame, before `render_into`:

```rust,wrap
# use regia_render::{FrameMesh, FrameScene, RenderDevice};
# use regia_terrain::{ContactMap, ScatterField, ScatterView};
# let device: &RenderDevice = todo!();
# let mut field: ScatterField = todo!();
# let mut contact: ContactMap = todo!();
# let (eye, target): ([f32; 3], [f32; 3]) = todo!();
# let (fov_y, aspect, near, far): (f32, f32, f32, f32) = todo!();
# let mut rocks: Vec<FrameMesh<'_>> = Vec::new();
# let mut frame: FrameScene<'_> = todo!();
field.update(eye);                          // tile streaming
contact.update(&device.queue, &field, eye); // rock contact pools the terrain samples
let view = ScatterView::look_at(eye, target, fov_y, aspect, near, far);
field.collect(&view, &mut rocks);           // culled, LOD-picked rock FrameMeshes
frame.meshes.extend(rocks);
```

See [Terrain scatter](book/agents/terrain-scatter.md).

## 7. Materials and shadows

- **Set pieces (glTF).** Map them as follows (`do27::load_gltf`):
  - `baseColorTexture` → `LabMaterial::albedo`, uploaded as sRGB bytes, not linearised.
  - `normalTexture` → `normal_map`.
  - `occlusionTexture` (ORM R) → `occlusion_map`.
  - `baseColorFactor` → `base_color`; the metallic and roughness factors carry over.
  - Compute tangents from the UVs.
- **Terrain** takes its material only from the cooked pack and `MaterialParams`. Do not tint it in
  the host.
- **Shadow casting** (`FrameMesh::shadow`):
  - Set pieces and vehicles: `ShadowCast::All`.
  - Rocks: whatever `ScatterField::collect` sets. That is `ShadowCast::Local` within the class's
    `shadow_distance` and `shadow_max_lod` when the class casts shadows, otherwise no shadow.
  - `ShadowCast::Local { .. }` is only for short props.

## 8. Do not

- **Do not use MSAA** (`msaa_samples ≥ 4`). On an MSAA frame the renderer skips the shared terrain
  draw and the planet sky (sky bodies, moons, airless sky). Auto exposure then meters a black frame
  and blows every mesh out. The renderer warns once when this happens.
- **Do not pre-expose.** Lights are physical lux and materials are albedo. Do not scale the sun, the
  ambient or the materials by an exposure. Exposure happens once, in post (the report flags a sun
  under 1000 lux).
- **Do not draw a host sky, sky dome, skybox, Jupiter card or forward fog on top.** The planet LUT
  sky, the aerial composite and the froxel haze already draw them. `FrameScene::fog.enabled` must be
  `false`.
- **Do not ship lab settings.** That means `FrameQuality::LAB` / `EDITOR`, `post.enabled = false`, a
  fixed `exposure_ev` without the map's band, or a `render_scale` below native.
- **Do not set a level clock** (`time_of_day`) if the map authors its sun. The clock replaces the
  authored light.
- **Do not hash texture bytes every frame.** Build the frame scene once and update only the camera
  and meshes (`do27_chase` does this).

## 9. Characters, vehicles and other dynamic meshes

Skinned and rigid meshes are lit by the same forward path as every set piece. No extra call is
needed beyond the items above. That path is:

- the sun with its cascades;
- the planet's sky irradiance, whose lower half is the planet's ground lit by the sun;
- the sky body's planet-shine fill;
- the terrain's wall bounce (`GroundBounce`);
- the terrain's horizon, which takes the sky hidden by canyon walls and mesas out of a mesh's sky
  light, as the terrain does for itself.

`lookdev dyn_light` measures this against the reference path tracer at the same pose. It renders
a skinned 0.18 gray mannequin, a 0.05 charcoal one and a hull at 1, 3 and 5 m on both maps.

The lighting holds only when the host frame has all of the following:

- **`ibl: true`, `msaa_samples` 1 and the HDR post stack.** The atmosphere IBL, which carries the
  ground bounce onto a mesh's shaded side and underside, exists only on single-sample linear-HDR
  frames. With MSAA the terrain and the sky are not drawn at all (`ERROR`, `render.problems`
  `msaa_skips_terrain`).
- **The sky body on airless maps.** DO27's exported Bore Twelve `level.ron` has
  `sky_body: None`. Set `atmosphere.sky_body = Some(SkyBody { direction, fill_lux: Some(1600.0),
  ..SkyBody::jupiter_from_europa() })` before `outdoor.apply_level`. Without it, a mesh's shaded
  side gets only the ice's bounce: 2.4 klx instead of 3.8 klx. The gray mannequin then prints at
  55/255 instead of 82, the charcoal one at 28 instead of 44.
- **One sun.** `directional.illuminance` must equal `outdoor.planet.sun_illuminance` (the level's
  `sun_illuminance_lux`: 18 000 Europa, 45 000 Mars). The sky and ground light on the shaded side
  come from the planet's value, and the sunlit side from the directional light.
- **The level's exposure band** (`apply_level_look`). DO27's raw look prints the same frame darker
  than the harness's band.
- **Skinned palettes in world space with an identity model matrix**, or a model matrix with
  palettes in model space, never both. The renderer skins normals with the same palette.

**Large meshes need a proxy.** A parked hull, crate or vehicle shades its own surroundings in a
way the sky light above cannot know about:

- the ground under its skirt lies in its own shadow (without a proxy, down-facing faces print
  about 2× the tracer);
- the ground in its shadow sees the hull instead of the sky: its bounce, and on Mars a darker
  contact under it.

Add `OcclusionProxy::default()` next to the hull's `MeshRenderer` (albedo from the material,
ground at the bounds' lowest corner; set `ground_y` when the box starts above the ground). A host
that drives `FrameRenderer` itself calls `set_mesh_occluders` with `MeshOccluder::from_positions`
or `from_local_bounds` each frame. Up to 32 proxies, nearest to the eye first, get the full shade;
frames without proxies are unchanged. With more hulls (a 32-40 player match plus AI units and
structures), set `OcclusionProxy { far_band: true, .. }` (or `MeshOccluder::with_far_band(true)`):
the next 128 opted-in proxies each get a coarse ground-contact blob (sky and fill darkened under
the footprint, no sun shadow), and a hull near the 32nd fades from one to the other over 5 m, so
nothing pops. The band costs 2.5 KiB of the occluder uniform and a short sorted-list walk per
pixel; it is off by default, and frames with 32 proxies or fewer are byte-identical either way.
`render.mesh_occluders` lists them, with `bands { near, far, dropped }`. Skip characters: a
mannequin's shadow is too thin to matter.

On airless maps, consider `TerrainSharedDraw::set_fill_canyon_scope` (ADR-8412): where it applies,
the sky body's fill on the ground takes canyon-scale and contact occlusion only, as meshes take it.
With the default occlusion stack, Europa's shadowed ground reads 0.57–0.67× the tracer; with it,
0.81–0.94×. `FillCanyonScope::Off` (the default) applies it nowhere. `MapWide` (the old
`set_fill_canyon_visibility(true)`) applies it to every fill-lit pixel, so it lifts every trench and
canyon floor on the map too. `NearOccluders` applies it only in the sun shade of the mesh occluders
(the hull boxes above): 1 inside a box's sun-shadow polygon, fading out a quarter of the polygon's
radius past its edge and one to two box heights above or below its ground. The ground under and
beside the hulls then gets the fill's color, and the rest of the map keeps the full stack. For
Europa, use `NearOccluders` with hull proxies. With the sun under about 3°, a box casts no polygon,
and `NearOccluders` then lifts nothing. `terrain.get_ground_look` reports the scope as
`fill_canyon_scope` when the host has inserted `TerrainGroundLookControl`.

What the engine cannot fix is albedo: a 0.05 charcoal suit is 28–44/255 on Europa even when its
irradiance matches the tracer within 3 %. Mars light is orange. The sun is authored
1.0/0.72/0.48 and the ground is red, so a neutral suit there reads brown in the tracer too
(shaded side rgb 1.65/0.89/0.45). Push it back with the grade, not the light.

## 10. Baked GI (ships with v0.2.0)

A map baked with `regia bake-gi` ships a `.fgiv` volume (`docs/formats/baked-gi.md`). At level
load, read it (`regia_asset::baked_gi::BakedGiVolume::from_bytes` on the pak entry, or `read` on
a file) and install it with `RuntimeRenderer::set_baked_gi(Some(Arc::new(volume)))`; install `None`
when the next map has no bake. Do this once per map, like `set_gi_field`. A stand-in renderer for a
warm worker gets it too. The volume uploads on the next frame. Its size is printed in the log and in
`render.get_gi_mode`.

While it lights the frame, it replaces DDGI. That frame needs linear HDR, the single-sample depth
prepass and a desktop build. SSGI is off, and full-resolution GTAO drops to half resolution. The sun,
its shadows and the paged cache stay as they are. Every preset uses it, Low included. Only a player
who chose `LightingMode::Balanced` keeps the analytic terms.

- **Light levels:** the sun-bounce term follows the frame's sun (illuminance × color over the baked
  sun). The fill term follows the frame's sky-body fill. Sky and emissive take
  `BakedGiSettings::{sky_scale, emissive_scale}`, relative to the bake. Change those with
  `set_baked_gi_settings` when `apply_level_look` changes the sky. The bake is valid for its sun
  direction only. A sun more than 3° off logs a warning once.
- **Fill:** the bake holds the sky-body fill shadowed, so where the volume covers it replaces the
  forward and terrain passes' live, unshadowed fill. Set `replace_live_fill: false` to go back to
  the live fill (the baked fill is then dropped).
- **Coverage:** outside the volume (more than one column spacing beyond the outermost columns, or
  more than twice the top level above the ground), the frame keeps its analytic terms.
- **Check:** `render.get_gi_mode` → `baked.active` is `true` and `baked.scales` are near 1 at the
  baked look; `sun_mismatch_deg` is near 0.

Related agent pages: [Renderer](book/agents/renderer.md), [Map look](book/agents/look.md),
[Atmosphere](book/agents/atmosphere.md), [Look-dev](book/agents/lookdev.md), [Baked GI](book/agents/baked-gi.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/do27-host-checklist.md -->
# DO27 host checklist

The base frame (Desktop High, the planet sky, the shared terrain draw, exposure, scatter) is
[Host look checklist](book/user-guide/host-look-checklist.md). This page is the rest of what the DO27 shell opts
into or copies into a level. Each section is one feature: what it does, the field or call that
exists in the engine, the setting to ship, and the agent call that checks it.

Numbers are from the integrated tree (ADR-109 and later) and the DO27 plates. A difference the
host checklist prints as `DIFF` is a choice; an `ERROR` breaks the frame. `render.problems`
(`FrameRenderer::frame_problems`) is the last frame's errors.

The look grades below are the values `do27_level` writes onto DO27's own `level.ron` (cooked
albedos, 45 klx Mars / 18 klx Europa). That function is crate-private in `lookdev::look_r2`;
`MarsGrade` and `LOOK_R2_MARS_GRADE` exist only in that harness. Copy the fields into
`LevelSettings.look`. The runtime applies them
(`apply_level_look` inside extract). A host that builds `PostSettings` itself calls
`regia_render::apply_level_look(&mut post, &level.look)`.

## Boot: branding under 1 s, first game frame without a hitch

Alpha smoke #1 wants boot → branding < 1 s, and no frame may compile a pipeline after warm-up
(`specs/27` § 2.4). A cold first game frame compiles everything its configuration uses — post
stack, shadow cascades, sky and clouds, volumetric fog, SSAO/SSGI/SSR, TAAU/TSR, material graphs:
about 5.5 s on the RTX 5080 for a DO27 map. The engine moves that compile onto warm workers while
the branding frame is on screen.

**Windowed runtime (`regia::run`, `RenderPlugin`): one resource, one call.**

1. Insert a `regia_render::BootSplash` before the app runs (logo, text, background). It is
   presented from the lifecycle event that creates the window, before any game frame (≈ 20 ms after
   the device on the 5080).
2. Call `splash.finish()` once the first scene is spawned (camera, level meshes, lights, the
   `RenderSettings` you ship). That is the warm trigger: `GameFrameWarm` (on by default) moves the
   `RuntimeRenderer` onto a `PipelineWarmQueue` worker, renders the extracted frame there at
   64×64 in the window's draw format (and once at the window's size, so the first visible frame
   allocates nothing), and gives it back; the splash holds until then, but never past 1.5 s after
   process start (next section), and fades into a first game frame that compiles nothing.
3. Each later level load: `world.resource_mut::<regia_render::GameFrameWarm>().request()` once the
   level is spawned. Until the warm is back the window shows the clear color and the UI overlay
   (the loading screen), not the scene.

**A map behind a UI-only menu warms by itself (v0.1.8, ADR-190).** When a window that drew no
scene on its last tick (the UI-only main menu, a lobby, a loading screen) gets a frame with at least
32 MiB or 256 meshes the runtime renderer has not uploaded, the engine warms that frame on a worker
before drawing it, exactly like `request()`. The window keeps presenting the clear color and the
UI meanwhile, so the menu stays interactive instead of freezing for seconds while the frame thread
compiles the map's pipelines and uploads it (v0.1.6 testers: a 4.7 s frame, 72 pipelines, 1 GB).
The map then appears and its first frame compiles nothing. This needs no call from DO27. It
runs at most once per scene-less stretch, never hides a scene already on screen, and is bounded by
`timeout`. Knobs: `GameFrameWarm::on_new_scene` (default `true`; `REGIA_SCENE_WARM=0`),
`new_scene_min_bytes`, `new_scene_min_meshes`; `scene_warms()` counts them, and the boot mark
`scene_warm_request` marks each one. A level swap under a scene that stays visible still needs
`request()` behind its loading screen (step 3).

**First-frame compiles overlap (v0.1.8, ADR-190).** A frame that builds its forward pipelines also
compiles the GPU-driven forward variants in parallel with them, instead of after them: about a
quarter less wall time for a cold map warm (RTX 5080). No call from DO27; `REGIA_FORWARD_OVERLAP=0`
turns it off for A/B timing. For a slow first run on a tester's machine, the log has
`wgpu instance flags: ..` after the `GPU:` line and, after `pipeline cache saved`, a line
`pipeline creation this run: N pipelines, X ms on the creating threads, Y ms each`: the per-pipeline
cost on that machine.

Configure the renderer before the trigger: while it is on the worker, systems that touch
`RuntimeRenderer` see a stand-in. The stand-in starts with copies of the renderer's VFX layers, GI
field and reflection probes. Translucent layers (VFX) and the shared pass draw (terrain) set on the
stand-in are moved over when the warm comes back. Since v0.1.8 so are a GI field, reflection
probes, an interior scene, DDGI settings and switch, and `reserve_instances` set on it (the last
call wins), because the engine can now start a warm by itself (previous paragraph).

Call order cannot blank or hang the window (ADR-166). The splash's warm runs only while the splash
still covers the window. A `finish()` before any scene exists queues the request; if the splash has
faded before a frame with a camera and a mesh arrives, the request is dropped and the scene draws
unwarmed, with no blank frames (a large scene on a scene-less window takes the new-scene warm
above instead; it shows nothing less than the window already showed). Only an explicit
`GameFrameWarm::request()` may hold a renderer whose scene is on screen, so call it behind a
loading screen. A request with no renderable frame expires after
`request_grace` (10 s). A watchdog (`GameFrameWarm::timeout`, 15 s by default,
`REGIA_GAME_WARM_TIMEOUT_S` overrides it) gives up on a warm that has not come back in that time.
If the job is still queued, it is canceled and the renderer comes back unwarmed. If it is running
and still building pipelines (one within `progress_grace`, 8 s), it is slow, not hung: since
v0.1.10 the watchdog lets it finish, up to `max_timeout` (30 s, `REGIA_GAME_WARM_MAX_S`). A
running warm that has built nothing for `progress_grace` past its timeout, or reaches
`max_timeout`, is abandoned and the stand-in takes over, compiling what it needs on its first frames. It already
has the GI field and reflection probes; the terrain shared draw comes back to it when the abandoned
job returns, unless you set or cleared the shared draw on it in the meantime. Both cases
log a `warn` with the warm queue's state. A host that replaces the
`RenderDevice` resource must also recreate the `PipelineWarmQueue`; otherwise the game warm is
skipped with a warning, because the queue's workers stay on the first device.

The persistent pipeline cache is on by default in the windowed runtime (`cache://pipelines`,
keyed by adapter, driver, wgpu and shader set); a second boot creates its pipelines from it.
`REGIA_PIPELINE_CACHE_DIR` moves it, `REGIA_PIPELINE_CACHE=0` turns it off.

**Ship pipeline caches for the test GPUs.** Before `regia package`, run each render profile you ship once on
every test machine (RTX 5090, RTX 5080, RTX 3080 Ti, GTX 1080) with `REGIA_PIPELINE_CACHE_DIR=<dir>` and copy
the `pipelines-vulkan-*.fpc` files into `<project>/pipeline-caches/`; `regia package --platform linux|windows`
(or `--pipeline-caches <dir>`) then ships them in `content/pipelines/`. A tester with the same GPU and driver then
starts from a filled cache (first launch ≈ a second launch); anyone else compiles behind the splash as before.
Redo it after a shader change or a driver update on a test machine (the key changes; a stale file is ignored,
never used). Book: Instant load → Shipped pipeline caches.

**A shell that drives `FrameRenderer` itself** does the same in two calls:

```rust,ignore
// Before the device: where the persistent cache lives.
regia_render::pipeline_cache::set_directory(Some(cache_dir));
// After the device: present the splash every frame (`BootSplash::record` into the swapchain view),
// then move the renderer onto a worker with the first frame it will draw.
let queue = regia_render::PipelineWarmQueue::default();
queue.start(&device);
let handle = queue.warm_renderer(WarmTier::Map, "map:switchbacks", renderer, move |r, device| {
    let scene = level.frame_scene(width, height); // owned data, built on the worker
    r.warm_scene(device, &scene, surface_format, false).map_err(|e| e.to_string())
});
// Each frame: keep presenting the splash until the renderer is back.
if let Some(done) = handle.take() { renderer = done.renderer.unwrap_or_else(FrameRenderer::new); }
```

A quit during a warm stops it between compiles: `warm_scene`, `warm_extracted` and `prewarm`
return an error once the queue shuts down. A warm job of your own that builds many pipelines in a
loop should check `regia_render::warm_cancelled()` between them and return early, or the quit
waits for the loop (up to 30 s, then the exit hook's 30 s; 250 ms after a device loss, ADR-276).

`warm_scene` alone (synchronous) is what `do27_chase` and `cargo xtask smoke` use inside their
prewarm span. Check: agent `render.pipeline_warm` → `game_frame.first_frame_ms` and
`pipelines_outside` unchanged after the `game_warm_done` mark (`render.boot_timeline`). Since
v0.5.1 (ADR-7883) do not gate the game on these counters: call `SceneReadiness::prepare(map_id)`
once the map is spawned and wait for the `SceneReady` message (below, "Scene ready").

**Effects, decals and glass (v0.1.5).** A map warm `frame_job` renders on a throwaway renderer
with no effect layer, so it cannot build what the first explosion, scorch decal or canopy needs.
Those pipelines live on your own objects; warm them there, next to the map's frame jobs:

```rust,ignore
// The VfxGpu you gave to `translucent_layer` (or `VfxGpuHandle::warm_job` on the ECS path).
// Billboards (haze, additive, sorted alpha, soft smoke), mesh particles, decals, trails and the
// soft-layer composite, for the window format and the HDR pass (`Rgba16Float`).
queue.push(WarmTier::Map, "vfx", regia_vfx::vfx_warm_job(vfx.clone(), VfxGpu::warm_formats(surface_format)));
// Your FrameRenderer, in the warm closure that already renders the map (`warm_renderer`):
r.warm_scene(device, &scene, surface_format, false)?;
r.prewarm_decals(device)?;           // the decal receiver's stamp variants
r.prewarm_glass_instances(device)?;  // GLASS sets for every target the warm drew (own canopy, cracks)
```

`vfx_warm_job` compiles outside the `VfxGpu` lock (frames keep drawing), stops between compiles
when the queue shuts down (the job then ends with `canceled at shutdown`), and goes through the
installed and shipped pipeline caches. `VfxGpu::warm(&formats)` does the same in place behind a
loading screen. The engine's own game-frame warm (`GameFrameWarm`, `warm_extracted`) now also
builds the decal receiver when translucent layers are installed and the glass-instance sets when
the frame has a transmissive standard material, and its frame already draws the effect layer, so
an ECS host needs no extra call. Check: after the map warm, `render.pipeline_warm` →
`outside_sites` lists no `regia_vfx/src/gpu/*`, `decal_receiver.rs` or `glass_gpu.rs` site when
the first effects, decals and canopies appear.

**Warm coverage (v0.1.10).** The v0.1.8 smoke still logged pipelines "created outside the warm
queue" after START: terrain sets, material graphs, forward sets, the translucent shadow and effects.
What the engine now does by itself, and the calls that are new:

- **Terrain pipelines are the device's** (`RenderDevice::shared_pipelines`). A terrain built on
  your thread (a map loaded behind the menu, the next map's terrain), its `prewarm` and its first
  hole cut compile nothing once any terrain or the terrain warm job built them. `TerrainPlugin`
  queues that job (`regia_terrain::terrain_warm_job`, map tier) once the device exists; turn it
  off (`app.world_mut().resource_mut::<TerrainWarm>().enabled = false`) only if you queue it yourself. Without
  `TerrainPlugin`, queue it at boot:
  `queue.push(WarmTier::Map, "terrain", terrain_warm_job(terrain_warm_formats(&profile, &device)))`.
  It warms the HDR format of your `RenderSettings`; apply saved settings before the first `Update`
  if you can (a later format change queues the new format too, but the first job was wasted).
- **Hole cuts mid-play:** `TerrainSharedDraw::prewarm` and the game-frame warm now also build the
  hole-cut sets (`SharedPassDraw::warm_pipelines`), so a crater or a tunnel mouth cut after START
  compiles nothing.
- **Effects (ECS):** `VfxRuntimePlugin` builds the `VfxGpu` (simulation, sort and radix-sort compute
  pipelines) and its render sets for the window and HDR formats on a map-tier warm worker
  (`VfxGpu::new_warmed`) and installs the layer when it is back (a few frames after boot).
  A host that owns its `VfxGpu`: build it with `VfxGpu::new_warmed` inside a warm job (it returns
  `Ok(None)` when the app quit mid-build), and call `FrameRenderer::set_warm_decals(true)` if a
  game-frame warm can run before its layer is installed.
- **Material graphs:** hand over every graph the level can draw, spawned units included, before the
  warm: `RuntimeRenderer::set_level_material_graphs(graphs)` (new). The game-frame warm starts
  their sets for the targets it drew. The graph worker threads now count as warm builders (map
  tier), not "outside": they never ran on the frame thread.
- **Double-sided meshes:** the game-frame warm builds the cull-none twin of every forward set it
  drew (`prewarm_double_sided`), so the first wreck or foliage card compiles nothing.

Check: `render.pipeline_warm` → `pipelines_outside` does not grow after `first_game_frame`.
Still compiled on the frame thread (unchanged, ADR-166): a window's first scene that the engine
does not warm (the splash's warm expired and the scene is under the new-scene thresholds). Prepare
the scene once the map is spawned, behind the loading screen, to cover it (next paragraph).

**Prepare maps at first launch (v0.5.1, ADR-8453): a cold driver cache never costs play time.**

| Do | Instead of |
|---|---|
| At launch, before the menu: `regia_render::prepare::host_status(&request, &device.adapter.get_info())` with one `PrepareMap` per map (from your loader's `ExtractedFrame`) and your render targets. When `needed`, show a "Preparing shaders" page and run `prepare::run_on(&device, &request, ..)` on a background thread (bar: `fraction()`, `eta`). Or run `regia prepare --cache-dir <cache> --scene <map>...` from the launcher or installer step; `regia package --prepare-scene <map>` records the list in `build_info.json` (`prepare_maps`). | Shipping driver caches for every GPU and driver, or letting the first match compile its pipelines (tester B: 225 pipelines, 83 s of thread time on a cold cache). |

**Scene ready (v0.5.1, ADR-7883): one event for the loading page, audio and player control.**

| Do | Instead of |
|---|---|
| Behind the loading page, once the map is spawned: `world.resource_mut::<SceneReadiness>().prepare("switchbacks")`. Keep the loading page, game audio and player input off until a `SceneReady` message arrives (`MessageReader<SceneReady>`, or `SceneReadiness::is_ready()`); then drop the page, unmute and hand over control. | Polling `render.pipeline_warm` counters, `BootBackground::warm_done()` or the `first_game_frame` mark: those say "no warm pending" or give a CPU time, not "the map is resident and on screen". |

From the prepare until `SceneReady` the window keeps presenting your UI and does not draw the scene;
the engine uploads every mesh and texture the frame references and creates the pipelines of its
draw keys on a warm worker, and warms again when more of the map spawns while it runs (tester A1's
340 MB second batch, tester A2's map that arrived after a warm of an empty frame). `SceneReady` is
sent once per prepare, after the present of the first frame that drew the map (frame generation:
after its present thread presented it). A warm the watchdog cancels or abandons still ends in
`SceneReady { timed_out: true }`: never wait without it. Agents: `render.scene_ready` (wait until
`state` is `presented`). Telemetry: `scene_load_end` has `map` and `complete`, and `scene_ready`
has `first_present_ms`.

**Warm coverage (v0.1.11).** The v0.1.10 smoke still logged ~14 pipelines "outside the warm queue"
per map at the start of play. All but one came from `do27.apply_lighting`'s
`capture_reflection_probe`, which ran on the main thread before the game-frame warm. A probe face
has no post stack, so it draws the forward set and the terrain (plain and hole-cut) into the
`Rgba8Unorm` readback target. No game frame and no warm used that target. The last one was the
glass sets. They compiled on the frame thread for the first glass canopy, a transmissive mesh with a
`GlassInstance` that was not in the warm's frame (its vehicle spawned after the warm started).

- **Glass:** the game-frame warm now always builds the glass sets. Nothing to call.
- **Probe captures after the warm** compile nothing. A frame warm renders one probe face when the
  renderer has reflection probes installed, has captured one, or was told to with
  `RuntimeRenderer::set_warm_probe_capture(true)` (new). The terrain's warm then builds its plain
  and hole-cut sets for every format it was drawn into, so a hole cut after a capture is covered.
- **The first capture of a map** still compiles where you call it if it runs before the
  game-frame warm, which is DO27's order today: about 14 pipelines on the main thread behind the
  loading screen, before `first_game_frame`. To move them onto the warm worker, call
  `set_warm_probe_capture(true)` at level load and capture once the warm is done
  (`GameFrameWarm::is_pending()` and `is_warming()` both false, with `last_report()` set).
  Otherwise leave the order as it is. Nothing compiles after `first_game_frame` either way.
- Still worth doing: `set_level_material_graphs`. Without it, graph sets for units spawned
  mid-play build on the graph workers. That is not "outside", but those units draw the standard
  surface until the build lands; the v0.1.10 smoke showed `graph forward` builds 45 s into play.

**Warm coverage (v0.1.15).** Rehearsal B on v0.1.11 still logged pipelines outside the warm queue
after `first_game_frame`. The engine side is fixed, and there is nothing new to call.
- **Renderer pipelines built by a stand-in:** the cluster build, the page clear and the translucent
  casters (`frame.rs`, `translucent_shadow.rs`) are now built once per device. A stand-in renderer
  (what `GameFrameWarm` leaves while the warm runs; a graph material that resolves then is
  prewarmed on it) or a second renderer compiles none of them.
- **TSR and the depth match:** the game-frame warm now builds TSR and the depth match whatever
  upscaler and scale the warm frame used. Applying the 0.67 + TSR lever after the preset's
  `SettingsChanged` (§ FSR 3, TSR, SGSR and 4K render scale), a fullscreen toggle and switching
  back to TAAU compile nothing. So does the half-resolution SSGI upsample at exactly 0.67.
- **A second map's sky:** the warm builds the sky, aerial perspective, froxel fog and cloud
  pipelines for its HDR target even when the warm frame's map has no clouds or fog.
- Still request `GameFrameWarm::request()` for each map, behind its loading screen (DO27's
  WARM_PER_MAP). The engine covers the switches above, but a new map's own forward sets, terrain
  formats and probe faces come from that map's warm frame.
- MSAA switched on mid-play, a render-to-texture camera or a second window: register each target's format and
  sample count with `pipeline_warm::register_warm_target(format, samples)` (or `PipelineWarmQueue::warm_target`)
  before the game-frame warm, and the warm builds them (ADR-7885; for a target made later, register it and call
  `GameFrameWarm::request()`). A late pipeline in your log now names its format, sample count, thread and the key axis
  that was new ([Targets and late pipelines](book/agents/instant-load.md#targets-and-late-pipelines)).
- Not covered: FSR 3 switched on mid-play.

## Splash and lobby: the splash is gone by 1.5 s

The splash leads into the lobby, and gameplay is seconds to minutes away, so since v0.1.0
(ADR-173) the splash is gone **1.5 s after process start at the latest**, fade-out included.
Whatever the engine has not finished by then carries on in the background behind the lobby.

What DO27 does:

1. Call `splash.finish()` as soon as the lobby can draw. DO27 already does this at sim boot. The
   cap only cuts engine holds (a running game-frame warm, `min_duration`). It never fades a splash
   the host has not finished, because `finish()` is the host's "my first screen can draw" signal.
2. Keep the default cap, or set it: `BootSplash::with_max_duration(Some(Duration::from_millis(1500)))`
   (`None` = no cap, the pre-v0.1.0 behavior). `REGIA_SPLASH_MAX_MS=<ms>` overrides it for a
   test run (`0` = no cap).
3. The lobby's UI draws from its first frame. The overlay layers (runtime UI, quick draw, 2D) are
   the first job in the warm queue's boot tier, so their pipelines are built before the cap.
4. If the lobby has a 3D backdrop, spawn it before `finish()`, so the splash's game-frame warm
   covers it. If the warm is still running when the splash goes (a cold first launch: 2–4 s on an
   RTX 5080 without a matching shipped cache), the window shows the clear color plus the UI until
   the renderer is back. The backdrop then appears, and nothing compiles on the frame path. A
   backdrop spawned after the splash has gone draws unwarmed (ADR-166).
5. Entering a match: call `GameFrameWarm::request()` once the map is spawned, behind the loading
   screen, as for any level load (§ Boot, step 3). If the splash's warm is still running, the
   map's warm starts as soon as it is back. Until then the window shows the loading path (clear
   color + UI), never a frame that compiles.

What tells DO27 the background work is done: the `regia_render::BootBackground` resource,
refreshed every `PreUpdate`:

```rust,ignore
fn lobby_ready(bg: Res<regia_render::BootBackground>) {
    if bg.is_changed() && bg.warm_done() { /* game-frame warm back: the scene draws warmed */ }
    if bg.probe_done() { /* first-launch quality probe finished (or never ran) */ }
    // bg.splash_done, bg.splash_capped, bg.game_warm_running, bg.deferred_pending, bg.is_idle()
}
```

`GameFrameWarm::is_pending()` / `last_report()` and the boot marks `game_warm_done`,
`splash_capped` and `boot_background_idle` (`render.boot_timeline`) say the same thing.

**First launch is table-only in v0.1.0; the player's preset menu is the correction path.** DO27's first
launch takes the GPU table's pick and saves it as `Detected`: measured rows for the RTX 5090/5080 (Ultra),
RTX 3080 Ti (High) and GTX 1080 (Low), estimated rows for the rest of the Steam survey's top 40. A GPU
in no row gets the fallback: integrated, virtual and software GPUs get Low, an unknown discrete GPU with
15 GB or more gets Medium, anything less (or unknown VRAM on DX12) gets Low. It never picks Ultra, nor
High for an unknown or integrated GPU. A player who finds the pick too high or too low changes the preset
in the options menu; that choice is saved as the player's and never overridden. The menu's
Auto-detect button runs the table again. The confirmation probe is off by default, because its GPU
timings were not trustworthy on the RTX 5080 when v0.1.0 shipped (ADR-173).
`AutoQuality::with_confirm(true)` opts in. When on, it no longer runs behind the splash. Once the splash is gone and
the game-frame warm is back, a probe renderer on a warm worker draws the lobby's scene offscreen at
the window's size, back to back, for about 3–4 s (30+ frames of warm-up, then GPU timestamps), so the
GPU is at its clocks. The visible lobby frames are not touched; each can wait at most one probe frame
on the GPU. A step-down applies in the lobby, before the first match. A match
started before the probe has finished aborts it, and the table's pick (ADR-157) stays. A lobby
with no 3D scene gives it nothing to draw: after 15 s it ends with no frames and keeps the table
pick. It gets the runtime renderer's VFX layers, GI field and reflection probes, but not
the terrain shared draw. A saved preset skips the probe. It never steps up, never steps down on the wall clock or
when the GPU was busy under half the time, and needs the median near the budget too, not just
the p95.

**The `SettingsChanged` contract is unchanged.** Detection on the first `Update`, and a probe
step-down later in the lobby, each change `graphics.preset` and send one `SettingsChanged`. The
preset re-seeds `RenderSettings.profile`, so DO27 re-applies its 4K render scale 0.67 + TSR on
that message (§ FSR 3, TSR, SGSR and 4K render scale), exactly as before. The only difference is
when it can arrive: a step-down now comes a few seconds into the lobby, not under the splash.

## Performance overlay: on (Compact) for the alpha, option in the settings menu

Alpha testers report performance from the in-game overlay ([Performance overlay](book/user-guide/performance-overlay.md)).
It is a top-left panel showing FPS, a 5 s frame-time graph, renderer CPU against GPU time, the top GPU
passes, texture memory against the budget, stutters, creates after warm-up, preset, GI mode and
resolution. **Detailed** adds the full per-pass GPU table. `DefaultPlugins` already includes it.

1. **Add the Performance overlay option to your settings menu.** Use
   `regia_framework::perf_overlay::spawn_settings_entry(world, Some(graphics_page))` for a
   ready-made label and Off / Compact / Detailed dropdown. Or build your own control from
   `settings_menu_entry()` and write the choice with `set_player_mode`. The choice is
   `GameSettings.performance_overlay`, saved with the other settings.
2. **Ship it on for the alpha.** Insert
   `PerformanceOverlay::default_mode(PerformanceOverlayMode::Compact)`. That is the host
   default; the engine default is Off. A player's saved choice (`Some(Off)` included) always
   wins over the host default, and `None` follows it.
3. **No default key.** DO27 uses the F-keys, so the overlay binds none. To add a key, declare
   and bind the `"PerformanceOverlay"` action (`PERF_OVERLAY_ACTION`) in your `InputConfig`.
   Each press cycles the mode.

Check: `perf_overlay.get` shows `mode: Compact, source: host_default` on a fresh install, and
`source: player` once the menu was used. Showing the overlay costs ≤ 0.1 ms CPU and ≤ 0.1 ms
GPU, and the toggle creates no pipelines. Guide: [Performance overlay (agents)](book/agents/perf-overlay.md).

## Mars look: `ue`, `nasa`, `nasa_dark`

One grade on the Switchbacks `look` block. `ue` matches the UE v13 plates. `nasa` matches NASA's
white-balanced rover photographs. `nasa_dark` is that grade 0.35 EV darker, the darkest step that
still keeps shadow detail on a dim laptop.

All three share the meter and the band. Haze is `LevelAtmosphere.haze` (`LevelHaze`): `density`
`1.2e-5`, `scale_height_m` `600`, `base_height_m` `0`.

| Field | `ue` | `nasa` | `nasa_dark` (ship this) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `exposure_bias_ev` | `0.7` | `0.8` | `0.45` |
| `min_ev100` / `max_ev100` | `9.0` / `12.0` | same | same |
| `meter.low_percentile` | `0.35` | same | same |
| `meter.high_percentile` | `0.97` | same | same |
| `meter.center_weight` | `0.4` | same | same |
| `contrast` | `1.5` | `1.65` | `1.65` |
| `saturation` | `1.5` | `1.15` | `1.15` |
| `grade.white_balance_kelvin` | `6200` | `5200` | `5200` |
| `grade.tint` | `0.3` | `0.3` | `0.3` |
| `grade.lift` | `[0.010, 0.003, 0.0]` | `[0.0, 0.03, 0.02]` | `[0.0, 0.03, 0.02]` |
| `grade.gamma` / `grade.gain` | `[1, 1, 1]` / `[1, 1, 1]` | same | same |

`nasa_dark`'s bias is `switchbacks_nasa_grade`'s `0.8` plus `NASA_DARK_EV` (`-0.35`).

Ship `nasa_dark`. On DO27 content at 960×540, sunlit landscape saturation is 0.26–0.30 against
0.23 on the white-balanced Mastcam set, while `ue` is 0.43–0.65 (the rust-brown complaint).
`switchbacks_close` luma p50 is 158 on `nasa` and 154 on `ue` (UE 155). Darkening `nasa` by 0.5 EV
drops shadow-band steps on `DisplayModel::DIM_LAPTOP` to 81 % (`switchbacks_mid`) and 83 %
(`tunnel_interior`). −0.35 EV keeps every shot at or above 85 % (mid 89 %, tunnel 85 %, close 96 %,
wide 97 %; those were measured before the green-blue lift, which takes `switchbacks_mid` to 97 %). Shade stays warm; the natural-color photographs do too.

Check: `level.get_look`, then `seeing.screenshot` (`offscreen`) after a few frames so the meter
settles. `level.set_look` deep-merges a partial object if you are tuning live. Guide:
[Map look](book/agents/look.md).

## Europa grade

Bore Twelve. Neutral ice is the path tracer; the blue-white print is this grade. Snow compensation
is on: a frame of sunlit ice (from 250 cd/m²) takes up to +1 EV.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `exposure_bias_ev` | `0.0` |
| `min_ev100` / `max_ev100` | `10.5` / `13.6` |
| `meter.low_percentile` / `high_percentile` / `center_weight` | `0.45` / `0.98` / `0.3` |
| `meter.bright_threshold_cd_m2` | `250` |
| `meter.bright_bias_ev` | `1.0` |
| `contrast` | `1.05` |
| `saturation` | `1.15` |
| `grade.white_balance_kelvin` | `6200` |
| `grade.tint` | `0.1` |
| `grade.lift` | `[0, 0, 0]` |
| `grade.gamma` | `[0.87, 0.88, 0.95]` |
| `grade.gain` | `[1.15, 1.15, 1.15]` |
| `PostSettings::band_bounds_final_exposure` (host, not the level file) | `true` |

Turn `band_bounds_final_exposure` on (in code, or `render.set_exposure_settings
{"band_bounds_final_exposure": true}`) when the band is meant as the range the frame may print at:
the snow bias and the compensation then apply before the band clamp, so DO27's `min_ev100` /
`max_ev100` is the final exposure and sunlit ice no longer settles 1 EV under the floor (ADR-7969;
a level look keeps the switch, and the level file gains the field with the v0.6 scene-format bump).

The cool gamma (blue above red and green) moves lit ice from about 214° to 224–228° hue without
lifting the black sky. Contrast 1.05 opens trench shadows: visible shadow steps on
`bore_twelve_wide` go from 42 % to about 65 % on the dim laptop, and `set_piece_borehole` p50 stays
near the UE plate (about 139 vs 135).

Jupiter and Io stay as in the host look checklist (`SkyBody::jupiter_from_europa`,
`SkyBody::io_from_europa`, the map's `fill_lux`). Do not add a second Jupiter card.

Check: `level.get_look` shows `bright_bias_ev` `1` and the 6200 K grade, then
