## Windows

<!-- index: OS window -->

A game has one primary OS window. `docs/specs/11-platform-and-input.md`: a `Window` component on another entity does not become an OS window. `apply_window_changes` skips a window entity that has no handle (ADR-2252). Closing the primary window asks the app to exit unless the game handles `WindowCloseRequested` itself. Runtime games normally use that one window.

The editor's dock is separate from that limit. Drag a tab out of the dock to float its group. Preference `ui.floating_windows` is `os` or `in_window`. `os` is the default on Linux and Windows and makes the float its own OS window. `in_window` (the default elsewhere, and single-window mode) keeps the float inside the main editor window. A headless editor has no OS windows for floats. A floated window shares the editor's device, theme and worlds. Closing it docks the panels back. A window whose monitor is gone docks back. Where the window system gives no positions (Wayland), the compositor places the window. Details: [Floated panels and OS windows](book/agents/editor-os-windows.md).

The Outliner, Content Browser and Inspector can each open further copies: **Window ▸ New Outliner**, **New Content Browser** and **New Inspector**, up to seven besides the original. The tab id is `outliner#1` through `outliner#7`, and the same shape for `content` and `inspector`. Each copy keeps its own search, columns, folder or lock. They are not extra entries in the built-in panel list. The panel ids stay `outliner`, `content` and `inspector`.

**⧉ Play in window** is a second OS window for the game picture during play. It is not a second game `Window` entity. See [Play window](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-window.md).

## DCC scene feed

The live scene feed (spec `docs/specs/60-dcc-scene-feed.md`) lets a content tool stream meshes, transforms and clips into the editor. Cargo feature `dcc-feed` on the `regia` crate is off by default and is not part of a shipping profile. The editor links the feed through `regia_agent`'s `dcc-feed-assets` feature, so the **DCC Feed** tab (panel id `dcc_feed`) is in the editor. The listener still stays off until the project sets `[dcc_feed]` with `enabled = true` in `Regia.toml`. A build compiled without the feature shows "The DCC feed is not in this build." Bake, sessions and the record file are on [DCC Feed](book/user-guide/editor-guide/dcc-feed.md).

## Source plugins

An extension is a versioned bundle described by `regia-plugin.toml` (spec `docs/specs/57-plugin-extension-api.md`). Source plugins are built: Rust and content the project compiles in, discovered, ordered and enabled from the [Extensions](book/user-guide/editor-guide/extensions.md) tab (panel id `extensions`) or with `plugin.enable`. Enabling changes `Regia.toml`. Code takes effect at the next start. In-process extension code is trusted native code with the editor's privileges. Capabilities are a review aid, not a sandbox.

Dynamic extensions (a library the editor reloads in a development build, **Reload** on that tab) are not what a shipping player loads. This version has no setting that turns them on in a shipped game, and it has no extension registry or marketplace. The manifest can carry publisher and licence fields. Hosting a registry is out of scope for this version.

The keymap, every built-in panel and the chords you can change are in the [editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/viewports.md -->
# Independent viewports

The editor's main viewport keeps its camera, layout and display settings in three world
resources: `EditorCamera`, `ViewportLayout` and `ViewportSettings`. A tool built on the Regia Engine
editor crates often needs more views of the same world: a workspace view, a review lightbox, a
before/after toggle, a concept side-by-side. Each needs its own camera, show flags and quality
preset. `ViewportInstance` holds its own copy of all three.

```rust,ignore
use regia_editor::viewport::{viewport_panel_with, ViewportPanelState};
use regia_editor::viewport_instance::{CameraLinkGroup, ViewportInstance};
use regia_editor::views::ViewportQuality;

struct Compare {
    left: ViewportInstance,
    right: ViewportInstance,
    states: [ViewportPanelState; 2],
}

impl Compare {
    fn new() -> Self {
        let group = CameraLinkGroup::new(1);
        let mut left = ViewportInstance::new(10);
        let mut right = ViewportInstance::new(11);
        right.layout.quality = ViewportQuality::Game;
        left.link_to(&group);
        right.link_to(&group); // adopts the left camera
        Self { left, right, states: Default::default() }
    }

    fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, world: &mut World, device: Option<&RenderDevice>) {
        let [a, b] = &mut self.states;
        ui.columns(2, |cols| {
            viewport_panel_with(&mut cols[0], world, device, a, &mut self.left);
            viewport_panel_with(&mut cols[1], world, device, b, &mut self.right);
        });
    }
}
```

`viewport_panel_with` is the full viewport panel: the panes, overlays, GPU picking, box select,
gizmos, hotkeys and toolbar. It reads and writes only the instance it is given. The world still
holds what every view shares: the selection, the gizmo mode, camera bookmarks and the undo
stack. `viewport_panel` (the main viewport) is the same panel over the world resources, and it
behaves as before.

- **One `ViewportPanelState` per instance.** It holds the gizmo drag state and the box-select
  drag. Set `state.toolbar = false` to hide the toolbar (a lightbox tile, say) and drive
  `instance.layout` from your own UI.
- **Ids.** Keep `ViewportInstance::id` unique per world. It keys the instance's egui widgets, its
  renderer and its entry in the `ViewportInstances` registry.
- **Linking.** `CameraLinkGroup` is a shared handle. Every member's perspective camera follows the
  member that moved last. Your own camera code (a SpaceMouse through `nav::step`, a "match
  concept view" button) just writes `instance.camera`, and the group follows on the next draw.
  `unlink()` leaves the group. Groups work across worlds too, so a before/after over two worlds
  can still orbit together.
- **Headless.** `regia_editor::render::capture_instance(device, world, &instance, kind, [w, h])`
  renders one instance with its overlays, with no egui. `render_instance_pane` and
  `capture_instance_pane` take a full `PaneRequest`.
- **Closing a view.** Call `ViewportInstances::remove(world, id)` to free its registry entry and
  its renderers. An instance you just stop drawing keeps its renderer cached until then.
- **Agent.** Every drawn instance shows up in `editor.viewport_instances`. Agents can edit, link
  and capture instances; the panel picks up their edits on its next draw. See
  [Independent viewports (agents)](book/agents/viewports.md).

Cost: in a world without its own `RuntimeRenderer`, each instance pane owns a frame renderer
(render targets at the pane size, pipelines, IBL maps), the same as one main-viewport pane. In
a world with a `RuntimeRenderer`, all views share it, and TAAU is off while more than one view
draws in a frame.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/hot-reload.md -->
# Hot reload

Hot reload recompiles your **game crate** and swaps it into the running editor without restarting —
state survives. It is the core of the Regia Engine iteration loop.

## How it works

The game is a dylib (`regia_dylib`), linked once and swapped per reload. Because Rust dylibs
cannot be safely unloaded (TLS destructors), each reload copies the game dylib to a **unique
filename** and never unloads the old one. The editor snapshots the reflected world state before the
swap and restores it after (`docs/specs/20-hot-reload.md`).

## Making a game reloadable

Implement `GamePlugin` (not just `Plugin`) and export it:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_framework::prelude::*;

struct MySystems;

impl Plugin for MySystems {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_systems(Update, tick);
    }
}

fn tick() {}

struct MyGame;

impl GamePlugin for MyGame {
    fn register(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(MySystems);
    }

    fn on_unload(&self, world: &mut World) {
        // join game threads, write their state into reflected resources
    }

    fn on_load(&self, world: &mut World) {
        // restart those threads from the restored resources
    }
}

// A plain launcher (or test app) runs the game plugin through the adapter:
//   app.add_plugins(GamePluginEntry(MyGame));
```

The hot-reload host resolves two dylib symbols, `regia_game_entry` and `REGIA_ABI_HASH`. A
game library exports both with `regia_framework::export_game!(MyGame);` — it generates
`regia_game_entry()`, which returns the address of a static `#[repr(C)]` table
(`regia_framework::GameExports`) whose `register` / `on_unload` / `on_load` call your
`GamePlugin`, and the `REGIA_ABI_HASH` static (a `const` computation, so it works in a static
initializer; the editor pins it per build through the `REGIA_ABI_HASH` environment variable). A plain launcher or test runs the same plugin
through `GamePluginEntry(MyGame)` (above), which adapts any `GamePlugin` to an app `Plugin`.

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_framework::prelude::*;

struct ExportedGame;

impl GamePlugin for ExportedGame {
    fn register(&self, _app: &mut App) {}
}

regia_framework::export_game!(ExportedGame);
```

The editor rebuilds the game when a file under `src/` changes (500 ms after the last change) or
when you press **⚙ Compile** in the toolbar (Ctrl+Alt+F11). The build runs in the background;
the toolbar shows `code: compiling 3.2 s`, then `code: Reloaded in 1.3 s (12 types, 340
instances)` or `code: error — …` (the old code keeps running on an error).

State that should survive lives in **reflected** components and resources. `on_unload`
runs before the snapshot, `on_load` after the restore.

Scripts (`#[derive(Script, Reflect, Default, Clone)]`, registered with `app.register_script`) are
rebuilt on every reload: the editor saves each script slot's reflected fields, drops the old
instance, builds the script again from the new code and puts the fields back, so the next tick
runs your edited `update` with the state it had. `start` does not run again. If you delete or stop
registering a script type, its slots are removed and the log says how many. A script whose
`ReflectScript` you implement by hand (without the derive) comes back with default fields.

## Running

```console
$ regia-editor --project my_game --game my_game
```

`--game <crate>` names the game dylib to host. Rebuild the game crate and the editor picks it up:
state survives, a small edit is back in under a second. Play-in-editor runs the reloaded game;
`docs/specs/20` § 3 walks the exact reload sequence (pause → snapshot → swap → restore → resume).

## What survives a reload, and what does not

- State that should survive lives in **reflected** components and resources
  (`Reflect + Default`). After the swap each value is restored field by field through the new
  library's types: a new field takes its `Default`, a removed field is dropped, a field whose type
  changed takes its `Default` (with a warning in the log), and a type that no longer exists is
  dropped (the warning gives the count).
- Game **scripts** are not snapshotted: a script slot survives a reload still running the old
  library's code (a known issue; see the hot-reload fragment's
  Known issues, `docs/releases/v0.1.28-spec-08-20-hot-reload.md`).
- Raw statics, thread-locals and closures stored in engine resources are **gone** after a reload:
  the old library's systems, observers and registrations are torn down before the new one registers.
- A thread your game spawns must be joined in `on_unload` (write its state into a reflected
  resource first) and started again from that resource in `on_load`. Engine task pools are fine.
- An external simulation does not live in the reloaded library: build it as its own dylib that
  links `regia_dylib`, and keep its handle in an engine-owned resource
  (`docs/specs/25-sim-bridge-and-do27.md` § 3). Editing that simulation means restarting the editor.
- Changing **engine** code means restarting the editor: rebuild the editor and the game together.
  The editor fingerprints the engine dylib when it starts and refuses every reload once that dylib
  was relinked ("engine changed — restart the editor"), whether the game build or another cargo run
  on the same target directory relinked it.

## When a reload fails

- **Build error**: nothing is swapped and the old code keeps running; the compiler output is in the
  output log and on the toolbar (`code: error — …`).
- **Refused** (engine changed, ABI hash mismatch, an editor without `hot-dylib`, an identity clash):
  the old code keeps running. An identity clash is found after the new library registered; the
  previous plugin is registered again with its state.
- **Panic during restore**: there is no rollback after teardown. The editor logs the panic, leaves
  the world without game types and keeps the snapshot at `.regia/hot/last_snapshot.bin`. Fix the
  code and compile again: the retry restores from that snapshot. The level itself is safe on disk
  and in the autosave.

Each reload maps a new copy of the library and never unloads the old one (Rust dylibs cannot be
unloaded safely), about 2.2 MB each. From the 50th reload on, the toast suggests a restart.

Agents drive the same loop with `agent.hot_reload` and `editor.code_status`
([Game-code hot reload (agents)](book/agents/hot-reload.md)).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/live-asset-reload.md -->
# Live asset reload

Save a file, see it in the running game or editor, no restart. This is the rapid-prototyping loop
of `docs/specs/12-assets.md` § 8.

## Where it runs

| Host | How to start it | What watches |
|---|---|---|
| Editor | opening a project (on unless `REGIA_ASSET_WATCH=0`) | `assets/` and, in a source checkout, the engine's WGSL |
| Dev game | `regia run --dev` | `regia run` cooks; the game watches the cooked cache and the files it reads itself |
| Shipping game | never | the `dev-assets` feature is off in `regia package` builds |

```console
$ regia run --dev
regia run: live asset reload on (/home/me/mygame/assets); save a file under assets/ to see it in the game
regia run: reloaded assets/props/crate.material.ron in 41 ms
regia run: cook error in assets/props/crate.material.ron: 7:5: expected `)`
```

`--level L` starts the game in `L` (a `.level.ron`, relative to the project or to `assets/`)
instead of the level its code opens: the engine opens it after the game's `Startup` systems.

```console
$ regia run --dev --level levels/test_arena.level.ron
regia run: starting in /home/me/mygame/assets/levels/test_arena.level.ron
```

## What reloads

Each edit is debounced (120 ms after the last write, so an editor's write-and-rename save counts
once), then only that file and the sources that embed it are re-cooked, on a background thread.

| Kind | Files | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Meshes | `.glb`, `.gltf` (+ its `.bin` and images) | re-imported; the asset server replaces the mesh in place — every handle stays valid |
| Textures | `.png`, `.jpg` | re-compressed; replaced in place |
| Materials | `.material.ron` (v3) | re-cooked; replaced in place |
| Material graphs | `.matgraph.ron`, `.matinst.ron`, `.matfunc.ron` | re-cooked (a function or image re-cooks the graphs that use it, a graph its instances); every `MaterialGraphRef` entity swaps to the new material and its pipelines build on the renderer's workers, never on the frame — meshes draw with the standard surface for the few frames until they are ready |
| Engine shaders | `crates/regia_render/shaders/*.wgsl` (dev checkout) | recomposed and validated for every entry shader that imports the file; renderers rebuild their pipelines on the next frame |
| Levels | `.level.ron`, `.level.d/` | the editor reloads the open level and keeps the camera; with unsaved edits it asks first (status bar: **Reload from disk** / **Keep mine**; agents answer with `editor.level_reload_resolve`). A `regia run --dev --level L` game re-opens `L` on save (`Persistent` entities stay) |
| Prefabs | `.prefab.ron` | re-baked; every placed instance is re-instantiated with its transform and overrides |
| Terrain | `*terrain.layers.ron` (any letter case; `terrain.layers.ron` itself too), `.scatter.ron` | tiles re-cook; a `Terrain` with a `TerrainLayersSource` re-reads its layer stack; `ScatterSets` entries are replaced |
| Decals, VFX | `.decal.ron`, `.vfx.ron` | the prefab/system is replaced by name; running effects continue with the new parameters; placed static decals are rewritten |
| Audio | `.wav`, `.ogg`, `.flac`, `.mp3` | sounds registered with `SoundAssets::add_file` re-decode in place (handles stay valid); the next play uses the new sound |
| UI layouts | `.ui.ron` | the template is re-parsed and every root spawned from it is respawned |

**Errors never break the running app.** A file that does not parse, a material graph that does
not compile or a shader that does not validate keeps the previous version live; the status bar
shows `cook error in <file>: <reason>` and the log has the full message.

## Status

The editor's status bar shows the latest line: `reloaded assets/rock.png in 120 ms` or
`cook error in …`. Agents read the same through `assets.watch_status`
([Assets](book/agents/assets.md#live-reload-status)).

## Making your own system reloadable

Systems that cache data derived from an asset listen for the two messages `regia_asset` sends:

- `AssetReloaded { id, kind }` — a cooked asset was replaced in place (rebuild GPU uploads,
  colliders, …);
- `SourceAssetChanged { path, kind }` — a source file your system reads changed (re-read it).

Record the outcome in `AssetWatchStatus` so the status line and the agent see it:

```rust,ignore
fn reload_my_tables(
    mut changes: MessageReader<SourceAssetChanged>,
    mut tables: ResMut<MyTables>,
    mut status: Option<ResMut<AssetWatchStatus>>,
) {
    for change in changes.read().filter(|c| c.path.extension().is_some_and(|e| e == "csv")) {
        let outcome = match tables.reload(&change.path) {
            Ok(()) => WatchOutcome::Reloaded,
            Err(err) => WatchOutcome::Error(err.to_string()), // keep the old table
        };
        if let Some(status) = status.as_deref_mut() {
            status.record(WatchEntry { path: change.path.display().to_string(), kind: change.kind, millis: 0, outcome });
        }
    }
}
```

## Game code

Code reload is separate: see [Hot reload](book/user-guide/hot-reload.md) (the toolbar's **⚙ Compile**,
Ctrl+Alt+F11, 500 ms after the last `src/` save).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md -->
# Agent protocol

Regia Engine's defining feature: every capability a human has in the editor is available to an AI agent
through a typed, documented, testable API (`docs/specs/23-agent-native.md`). Agents are first-class
users.

## The idea

A dev build of any Regia Engine game runs a small server. An agent (or a script, or CI) connects and
inspects and drives the running app — query the world, edit entities, capture screenshots, play and
step deterministically, assert results, build and reload. Everything an agent authors is diffable
text (RON), and every agent action is observable, undoable and attributable.

## Driving it yourself

```console
$ regia agent call agent.hello --project my_game
$ regia agent call scene.query_entities '{"name":"Player*"}' --project my_game
```

`regia agent call <method> [json]` calls one method and prints the result. The app writes its
endpoint to `<project>/.regia/agent/endpoint.json` and a bearer token next to it.

## MCP

```console
$ regia mcp --project my_game --attach
```

`regia mcp` runs an MCP server over stdio (one MCP tool per protocol method, plus `regia://`
resources), so Claude Code and other MCP clients drive the game directly. It attaches to the
project's running app (a game or the editor). For CI and cloud agents, `regia mcp --headless
--project DIR` starts a **headless editor** when no app answers (no window, offscreen views), waits
until it listens, and takes it down again when the adapter ends, so nothing is left running; see
[Headless editor](book/agents/headless-editor.md). You can also start one yourself with `regia editor
--headless --project DIR` (it prints a `{"event":"ready"}` line when it listens) and attach.

Golden images stay yours: an agent can run a golden's test and propose a new image with a reason, and
only you accept it, at a terminal, with `regia golden accept <id>`. See [Golden images](book/agents/goldens.md).

### Connecting Claude Code

Register the server once per project, then start the game (or the editor) and ask the agent to
work with it:

```console
$ claude mcp add my-game -- regia mcp --project /path/to/my_game
```

The agent sees one tool per method (`query_entities`, `spawn`, `screenshot`, `step`, `expect`, …),
can read the agent guide through the `guide` tool, and acts with the permissions in
`.regia/agent.toml`. Other MCP clients take the same command line.

A client that cannot spawn a process connects over HTTP instead: `regia mcp --project my_game
--http` serves the same tools on a loopback port with a bearer token (see
[MCP over HTTP](book/agents/mcp-http.md)). Long operations answer a job id that `job_status` polls
([Jobs and test runs](book/agents/jobs.md)), and an agent can propose file changes for your review
in the editor's Agent Changes panel ([Staged review](book/agents/staged-review.md)).

### A typical agent loop

1. **Discover**: `agent.hello` (project, protocol version, permissions), `agent.guide` (the
   agent pages of this book), `types.list` and `types.describe` (the reflected types).
2. **Look**: `scene.query_entities`, `scene.get_entity`, `seeing.screenshot`.
3. **Change**: `scene.spawn`, `scene.set_property` or a batch with `scene.apply_edits`
   (`dry_run` previews it); in the editor, `editor.*` methods that land on the undo stack.
4. **Verify**: `play.pause`, `play.inject_input`, `play.step`, then `play.expect` assertions and
   another screenshot; `seeing.compare_images` against a reference.
5. **Report**: `agent.changes` lists everything it changed, stamped with provenance, for a human
   to review.

## The surface

The protocol is described by one schema table (`agent.schema` returns it; the MCP tool list is
generated from it). Methods group into:

- **Discovery** — `agent.hello`, `types.describe`, `resources.list`, `errors.explain`, …
- **Scene** — `scene.query_entities`, `scene.get_entity`, `scene.set_property`, `scene.spawn`, …
- **Assets** — `assets.list`, `assets.describe`, `assets.load`, …
- **Seeing** — `seeing.screenshot`, `seeing.compare_images`, …
- **Play & test** — `play.step`, `play.inject_input`, `play.wait_until`, `play.expect`, …
- **Logs & events** — `logs.read`, `events.read`, …
- **Framework** — `scripts.*`, `camera.*`, `settings.*`, `sim.*`
- **Physics** — `physics.raycast`, `physics.overlap`, `physics.closest_point`
- **Gameplay** — `players.*`, `scene.possess`, `save.*`

Every method has parameters, a result shape, a mutating flag and a permission. The
[agent methods reference](book/reference/agent-methods.md) lists all of them, generated from the
schema; the [agent guide](book/agents/protocol.md) has example calls and results.

## Safety

The project gates the protocol with `.regia/agent.toml` permission profiles (`read`, `edit_scene`,
`assets`, `play`, …); every call lands in an audit log, and every agent-made change is stamped with
provenance and listed for review. Granting `build`/`play` amounts to code execution — grant them
only to agents you trust like a developer with a shell. See the
[agent guide's safety page](book/agents/safety.md).

## Where the pages live

The agent guide — task-oriented pages an agent reads through the `agent.guide` method — is under
[`book/agents/`](book/agents/protocol.md), one page per feature area. The
[coverage map](book/COVERAGE.md) maps every method, feature, command and format to its page.

# Packaging

<!-- index: Package -->
<!-- index: Cook -->
<!-- index: pak -->
<!-- index: AppImage -->
<!-- index: Dedicated server -->
<!-- index: Build container -->
<!-- index: Container image | see: Build container -->
<!-- index: sbom.json -->
<!-- index: Engine credit -->

Packaging cooks your assets, builds the launcher and assembles a distributable. The pipeline is
`docs/specs/21-tooling-and-packaging.md`. The step-by-step with a finished check is
[Package a game](book/how-to/platforms/package-a-game.md). Platforms are Linux, Windows, and Android.
macOS is testing-only and is not a package target ([macOS](book/user-guide/macos.md)).

## Cook

```console
$ regia cook --project my_game --platform linux
$ regia cook --project my_game --platform android --quality fast
```

`cook` converts source assets to per-platform cooked data. `--quality fast` turns off pak lz4 compression;
`--clean` rebuilds from scratch. Cooked output is archived into `.fpak` files (`docs/formats/pak.md`),
the packed content archive the packaged build mounts.

### Texture quality

`[cook] texture_quality` in `Regia.toml` sets the quality every texture cooks at when its `.meta` names no
`quality` of its own:

```toml
[cook]
texture_quality = "draft"   # "final" (default) or "draft"
```

`"final"` cooks colour textures as BC7 on desktop and ASTC 4×4 on Android. `"draft"` cooks them at the low
quality (BC1 for opaque colour, BC3 with alpha, the 6×6 / 8×8 ASTC ladder): it encodes faster and writes smaller
paks while you iterate, and switching back recooks the affected sources. A texture whose `.meta` says
`quality: Some(high)` or `Some(low)` keeps it either way. Terrain layers keep their own fixed quality. Any other
value fails the cook and `regia package` with the message ``[cook] texture_quality `<value>` is not `final` or `draft` ``.

### Machine-readable output (`--json`)

`regia cook`, `regia package` and `regia run` take `--json` for CI, the editor and agents. Stdout then holds
exactly one JSON object on one line, printed when the command ends; every other line goes to stderr: the
cook summary (`cook: …`, `pak: …`), cargo's output and, for `run`, the game's own stdout. A failure still prints
one object, `{"ok": false, "error": {"code": …, "message": …}}`, after the usual `error:` line, and the exit
code is non-zero.

| Command | Keys of the object |
|---|---|
| `regia cook --json` | `ok`, `platform`, `quality`, `texture_quality`, `pak_dir`, `paks` (absolute paths), `cooked`, `skipped`, `imports_skipped`, `warnings` (count), `elapsed_ms` |
| `regia package --json` | `ok`, `artifact` (absolute path of the package: archive, APK/AAB or directory; the output directory for `--dry-run`), `platform`, `profile`, `server`, `dry_run`, `symbols` and `build_info` (paths, or `null` when absent) |
| `regia run --json` | `ok` (the game exited 0), `artifact` (the launcher binary cargo built), `artifact_exists`, `exit_code` (`null` when a signal ended the game), `package`, `profile` (`debug` or `release`), `level`, `cooked`, `cook_skipped` |

Error codes: `cook_failed`, `package_failed`, `run_failed`, and `server_platform_unsupported` (exit code 2) for
`regia package --server --platform android`. Arguments clap rejects (an unknown `--platform`) print clap's usage
error, not an object.

`--json` on `regia cook` with `--stats`, `--size-report` or `--lightmap-tiers`, and `regia cook cache … --json`,
print those reports as before (pretty-printed).

Paks count as fresh for `regia package` only when the last pack finished and was made from the
current project manifest (`Regia.toml`, or `Ferrite.toml` in a project that has only that one), the
current asset database, and compressed. `build/paks/<platform>/package-pack.stamp` records that; it
never ships. So the paks of `regia cook --quality fast` are packed again by `regia package`, while
those of `regia cook --quality final` (or `--ship`, GPU-ready meshes included) are staged as they are.
When the environment asks the package for GPU-ready meshes (`REGIA_PAK_GPU_MESHES=1`), paks with
cooked meshes are packed again (ADR-7612).

A pack fails with `chunk_asset_unwritten` when the chunk rules put assets in a chunk whose cooked
file is missing (a cook that skipped or failed them with only a warning): they would ship in no pak.
Fix the cook's warnings and cook again, or set `REGIA_ALLOW_UNWRITTEN_ASSETS=1` for a deliberate
partial pack. A cooked cache without `asset_manifest.bin` (no cook finished there) has no content to
name a build id after, so packing from it fails too.

## What ships in a package

A packaged build is self-contained: the game binary, its `content/*.fpak` archives, and everything it
reads through the VFS.

- **Cooked assets** (`.gltf`/`.glb` meshes, textures, materials, …) are cooked into `content/*.fpak`
  and mounted automatically. The launcher finds its paks **relative to its own path**
  (`<exe dir>/content`), so the extracted package runs from any directory — no `--content` flag.
- **Raw assets** — anything under `assets/` that is not a cookable source (`about.txt`, config files,
  fonts, notes) — are copied verbatim next to the binary into `assets/`, where the `assets://` VFS
  mount resolves them.
- **Notices**: `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` is copied from the workspace root into the package root, with the
  workspace's own `LICENSE.md` when the game has one. Every package also gets the engine's MPL-2.0 notice
  with the source-location line (`REGIA-ENGINE-NOTICE.txt`), the MPL text (`REGIA-ENGINE-LICENSE.txt`) and
  `CREDITS.txt` with the default "Made with Regia Engine" line; `--no-engine-credit` or
  `[package] engine_credit = false` leaves the credit out ([Licensing](book/user-guide/licensing.md), ADR-10225).
- **Software bill of materials**: `sbom.json` sits beside the notices. It records the resolved Cargo
  packages' names, versions and license identifiers (or license-file labels), sorted by name. Its
  `format_version` is `1`; missing license metadata is recorded as `unknown`. The list is the packages the
  package's platform resolves (`cargo metadata --filter-platform <target>`: the build's target triple, or the
  host's for a host build; every ABI for Android), so another platform's crates are not listed, and a host
  that only ever built this platform needs nothing more downloaded (`--frozen`).

## Package

```console
$ regia package --platform linux                              # → dist/linux/<slug>-linux.tar.gz
$ regia package --platform windows                            # → dist/windows/<slug>-windows.zip
$ regia package --platform android --format apk               # → dist/android/<slug>-debug.apk (Dev)
$ regia package --platform android --format apk --profile shipping  # → dist/android/<slug>-release.apk
$ regia package --platform android --format aab               # → dist/android/<slug>.aab (Play Store)
```

`--format dir` on Linux leaves the staged directory and does not write an archive. `--format app`
is rejected on every platform (the macOS app bundle is not built, ADR-264). An AAB is a store
bundle of the game. It does not include Google Play services; those services are parked.

Linux also builds an AppImage (`--format appimage`, or `formats = ["tar", "appimage"]` under
`[platforms.linux]` in `Regia.toml`; see [Linux AppImage](#linux-appimage)). `[platforms.<p>]
render_profile = "MobileHigh"` (any render profile preset: `MobileLow`, `MobileHigh`, `DesktopLow`,
`DesktopHigh`, `DesktopUltra`, `Deck`, or the offline `Cinematic`; or, since v0.7, a quality tier with no preset row:
`VeryLow`, the integrated-GPU floor, or `Medium`, ADR-8844) is written to the package's `build_info.json` as
`render_profile` (canonical spelling); Android packages carry that file in the APK assets. A name that is neither
fails the manifest with `render_profile_unknown` (`Low`, `High` and `Ultra` are not names: use `DesktopLow`,
`DesktopHigh`, `DesktopUltra`). A packaged tier starts as the tier, as Auto would apply it.

At startup the runtime reads that file beside the executable, even when launched from another
working directory; Android reads it from the APK assets root. `AutoQualityPlugin` (included in
`DefaultPlugins`) and `SettingsPlugin` apply the exact preset before `Startup`, including when
the game has no settings file. The order is **player settings > packaged profile > saved or
first-launch Auto detection > runtime default**. Per-setting player overrides still apply. A
package profile is never saved as a player choice. An explicit Auto-detect request replaces it
for this launch; on the next launch the package profile wins again unless the player saved a
preset. Games can still customize `RenderSettings` in their startup systems.

`regia package` also carries the optional `[boot]` table in `build_info.json`, including APK
assets. `BootMoviesPlugin` uses it when no loose `Regia.toml` exists. Explicit `BootMovies` or
plugin configuration wins over a loose manifest, which wins over package metadata. An empty
loose list deliberately disables the packaged movies. Add the media and boot plugins as described
in [Boot movies](book/agents/video-boot-and-cues.md); the package does not install plugins for the
game. Named shipping profiles must include their boot media in the asset closure or `include`.

Missing metadata keeps the older startup behavior. Invalid metadata is logged and ignored; an
invalid loose manifest never silently falls back to a different packaged list. Read
`render.get_profile` or `quality.get_detected` → `configuration` for the configured profile's
origin, and `media.boot_state` → `configuration` for the boot list's origin (ADR-7893).

`<slug>` is the slugified project `id` from `Regia.toml`. `regia package` runs the cook
automatically when paks are missing or stale, builds the launcher, and lays out the package
(`content/*.fpak` next to the binary, the `.desktop` file and icon on Linux, the Gradle project on
Android). The default build profile is `Dev` (cargo `dev`, debug-signed); pass `--profile shipping`
for a release build (release-signed). `--out DIR` overrides the output directory. On Android,
`--abi <abi>` (repeatable) builds only the listed ABIs from `[platforms.android] abis`.

On desktop, `--pipeline-caches PATH` (default `<project>/pipeline-caches` when it exists) accepts
loose `.fpc` files, stored feedback ZIPs, or a directory containing either recursively and ships
the selected caches in `content/pipelines/`, so a tester whose GPU and driver
match skips the first-launch shader compile. `regia prepare` warms the same pipelines on the
player's machine before the first start (see [Instant load](book/agents/instant-load.md)).
For harvested feedback, repeatable `--pipeline-cache-reference PATH` selects the current game's
shader/wgpu build, including a content salt. Without a reference, feedback caches must match
this engine's unsalted build. See [Pipeline cache harvest](book/agents/pipeline-cache-harvest.md)
for limits, integrity checks and exact GPU/driver matching.

## Shipping builds and the agent server

The `regia` crate's default features are `client`, `agent`, `functional-tests`, `ui`, `quick` and
`procgen`, and packaging does not change a
crate's features, so a game that keeps the defaults links the agent-protocol server. A shipping
package built with a named profile **fails `ship_check`** if it contains the server (see "Build profiles" below); the plain `shipping` profile only warns. It
listens on loopback only and requires the per-run token, but a release should not carry
it: depend on `regia` with `default-features = false, features = ["ui"]` for the builds you ship,
in every crate of the build that depends on `regia` (game, launcher, Android crate). Cargo
unifies features, so one crate that keeps the defaults turns the server back on.

## Build profiles

A `[profiles.<name>]` table in `Regia.toml` ships only what its entry levels need:

```toml
[profiles.demo]
entry_levels = ["levels/main.level.ron"]
exclude = ["levels/debug*"]
```

`regia package --platform linux --profile demo --dry-run` cooks if needed and prints exactly the files
the package would hold (cooked assets with sizes, raw files, the totals and what was left out) without
building. Without `--dry-run` the package gets its own `content/base.fpak` with that closure only, and only
the raw files the levels reference. The closure follows each cooked asset's dependency list and the quoted
strings in raw files (`"materials/rock.material.ron"`, `"assets://levels/b.level.ron"`, an asset id). The
keys are `base`, `entry_levels`, `include`, `exclude`, `features`, `no_default_features`, `allow_agent` and
`target` (`"server"` makes it a dedicated-server profile; spec 21 § 4, spec 76 § 3). The closure scan is heuristic: an asset that code loads through a computed path is not
found, so list it in `include`. Each run restages from scratch (`content/` and `assets/` are cleared).

**This is not obfuscation.** Profiles shrink the package; they do not hide or encrypt anything, and anyone
can unpack a `.fpak`.

Every shipping package (built-in `shipping` or a profile) is checked: it fails with a stray `.fpak`
(anything but `content/base.fpak`) or editor content (a root-level `editor/`, `.regia/` or
`assets/editor/`, `*.editor.ron`, autosaves). Packages from a named profile also fail with the agent
server, editor code or the dev asset watcher in the binary, or those features in the game's `Cargo.toml`. A playtest profile can keep the agent
with `allow_agent = true`.

## Compare a dev run with the package (`regia package parity`)

<!-- index: Package parity -->
<!-- index: regia package parity -->

`regia package parity` (ADR-8428) compares asset opens from a development run with asset opens from
an extracted package. It is not a clap subcommand of `regia package`: the binary handles the two
words before clap, so `regia package --help` does not list it. `regia package parity --help` prints
the usage.

Two traces you already recorded:

```console
$ regia package parity --dev-trace dev.log --dev-root . --package-trace pkg.log --package-root out/pkg
```

Or two programs. The tool sets `REGIA_ASSET_TRACE` and `REGIA_PARITY_ROOT` on each child and runs it. There is no `regia play` subcommand. Pass the dev launcher and the packaged binary:

```console
$ regia package parity --dev-command 'regia run' --package-command './my_game' \
    --dev-root . --package-root out/pkg --json
```

`regia run` opens a window. `--script FILE` checks that the file exists and sets `REGIA_PARITY_SCRIPT` on the child. No engine system reads that variable, so the file does not drive input by itself.

| Exit | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | The package accounts for every dev open |
| 1 | A dev open is missing. Drift is listed and does not fail the run unless `--strict-drift` |
| 2 | A usage error, `parity_script_missing` (the `--script` path is not a file), or `parity_run_failed` |

`parity_script_missing` and `parity_run_failed` are exits of this command. They are not
agent-protocol error codes. `--report-md PATH` and `--report-json PATH` write the report beside
the terminal. `--json` prints one JSON object on stdout instead of the markdown. The object has
`ok`, `missing`, `drift`, `dieted`, `cooked`, `never_touched`, and `exit_code`. `never_touched`
does not fail the run.

`--classify` reads strace open traces instead (`--trace FILE`, repeatable, or a directory;
`--root DIR`; optional `--manifest`; `--json` or `--markdown`). Exit 0 prints the classification.
Exit 2 is a usage error or an unreadable trace, root, or manifest. `regia package parity
--classify --help` prints that form.

The line format of `REGIA_ASSET_TRACE` is [Asset access trace](book/agents/asset-access-trace.md).
The agent method `package.parity` reads the same four paths and does not launch a process. Its
error codes (`parity_bad_params`, `parity_not_a_directory`, `parity_trace_missing`) are on
[Package parity (agents)](book/agents/package-parity.md). It does not accept `--strict-drift`.
Hygiene, which rejects bytes inside staged files, is a different check
([Package hygiene](book/user-guide/package-hygiene.md)).

## Dedicated servers

`regia package --server --platform linux` (or `windows`) packages the game with no window, renderer or audio: the
game's `server` feature, a content filter that removes presentation assets, a default `server.toml`, an empty `bans.ron`
and a `README-server.txt`. Any other platform, including Android, exits 2 with
`server_platform_unsupported`. macOS is not a package platform. The game declares the feature and builds `regia` without its defaults:

```toml
[dependencies]
regia = { path = "...", default-features = false }

[features]
default = ["client"]
client = ["regia/client", "regia/agent", "regia/ui"]
server = ["regia/server"]
```

Add `--dry-run` to see what is kept and what the filter removes. `regia server` runs the same build from the dev cache,
and `regia server --clients 2` adds two headless clients. `samples/dedicated_server` is a complete small example;
[Net dedicated server (agents)](book/agents/net-dedicated-server.md) has the details.

## Android

```console
$ regia install-android --device <serial>
```

`install-android` packages, installs via adb, launches, and streams logcat. Android packaging is the
Gradle shim from `docs/specs/21` § 4: a debug-signed APK for dev, and (with signing keys in
`Regia.toml`) a release APK/AAB for stores. The Android surface is recreated on suspend and
resume — the packaged build is tested through the suspend/resume cycle every milestone.

### Android release signing

Release builds (`--profile shipping`) sign with a keystore configured under `[platforms.android]` in
`Regia.toml`. Secrets are `env:` references so they are never committed:

```toml
[platforms.android]
keystore = "env:REGIA_ANDROID_KEYSTORE"          # path to the .jks/.keystore
keystore_password = "env:REGIA_ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD"
key_alias = "env:REGIA_ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS"
key_password = "env:REGIA_ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD"  # defaults to the keystore password
```

With those set, build the Play-Store bundle (the lead's NDK run):

```console
$ REGIA_ANDROID_KEYSTORE=/secure/upload.jks \
  REGIA_ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD=… \
  REGIA_ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS=upload \
  REGIA_ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD=… \
  regia package --platform android --format aab --profile shipping --project samples/sim_bridge
```

Without a keystore, `--profile shipping` fails with an error: AGP 8 does not fall back to the debug
keystore for release builds, so the APK/AAB would be unsigned (and uninstallable). Build with
`--profile dev` for a debug-signed APK, or configure the keystore above.

## Crash reports and symbols

When a game panics, the platform writes a self-contained crash report to `logs://crash-<timestamp>.txt`
(panic message + backtrace, build identity, OS/GPU facts, the active level and frame count, and the
last 200 log lines). An opt-in `regia_crash::CrashReporter` (`regia::crash`, umbrella `crash`
feature) uploads pending reports — and a game-provided match log — to a configured endpoint on the
next start (retry/backoff, size cap, a consent flag; nothing is sent unless the game opts in).
`https://` endpoints need `regia_crash`'s `tls` feature (ureq + rustls); without it `https://` is
refused. A remote `http://` endpoint leaves uploads off unless the game sets `allow_cleartext`. See [Crash reports](book/agents/crash-reports.md) for the
`diagnostics.crash_reports` method that lists/reads the local copies.

Shipping builds strip the shipped binary but keep the debug symbols separately: `--profile shipping`
writes `dist/<p>/symbols/` next to the package — on Linux `<name>.debug`, extracted with
`objcopy --only-keep-debug` from the (unstripped) build and address-resolvable, on Windows the
MSVC linker's `<name>.pdb` (stored as `symbols/<name>.pdb`; the Windows exe is not stripped because
MSVC writes all debug info into the `.pdb`, leaving nothing embedded in the exe). Symbolicate a
shipped backtrace on Linux with `addr2line -C -e symbols/<name>.debug -f <address>`; on Windows load
the `.pdb` in WinDbg or Visual Studio.

### Android symbols

Android shipping builds keep the unstripped libraries before Gradle runs (AGP strips the copy inside
the APK or AAB). `--profile shipping` copies each ABI's `lib<name>.so` from the cargo-ndk output into

```text
dist/android/symbols/
  symbols.json              # format_version 1: version, build_number, per library abi/file/build_id/size
  arm64-v8a/libmain.so      # unstripped
  x86_64/libmain.so
```

Keep this folder with the release it belongs to: `symbols.json` records each library's GNU build id,
which matches the build id of the library in the shipped APK (`readelf -n`). The step fails with
`android_symbols_missing` (an ABI has no library), `android_symbols_not_elf` or
`android_symbols_stripped` (no symbol table or debug info: keep `strip = "none"` in the shipping
profile). A library without a build id is recorded as `null` and warned about.

Symbolicate a native crash from the Android NDK (the `ndk-stack` and `llvm-addr2line` tools live in
`$ANDROID_NDK_HOME/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/<host>/bin`, and `ndk-stack` in the NDK root):

```console
$ adb logcat -d | ndk-stack -sym dist/android/symbols/arm64-v8a            # a tombstone or logcat crash
$ llvm-addr2line -C -f -e dist/android/symbols/arm64-v8a/libmain.so 0x1a2b3c   # one pc offset
```

`ndk-stack` picks the library by name from the `-sym` directory; use the `symbols/` of the release
that crashed (compare the `Build ID` line in the tombstone with `symbols.json`).

## Linux AppImage

```console
$ regia package --platform linux --format appimage       # → dist/linux/<slug>-<arch>.AppImage
```

The package is laid out as an AppDir and handed to `appimagetool`:

```text
<slug>.AppDir/
  AppRun                  # sh script, mode 0755: runs usr/bin/<binary>
  <slug>.desktop          # Type, Name, Exec=<binary>, Icon=<slug>, Categories=Game;
  <slug>.png              # the project icon (assets/branding/icon.png), required
  .DirIcon -> <slug>.png
  usr/bin/<binary>        # the game, with content/, assets/ and build_info.json beside it
```

Regia Engine does not bundle or download `appimagetool`. It uses the file named by
`REGIA_APPIMAGETOOL`, otherwise `appimagetool` on `PATH`; with neither the package fails before
the build starts with `appimagetool_missing`. Get the tool from the appimagetool releases page
(`appimagetool-<arch>.AppImage`), `chmod +x` it, and put it on `PATH` as `appimagetool`. Other
errors: `appimage_icon_missing` (no PNG icon) and `appimage_failed` (the tool exited with an error
or wrote no file). The tool runs with `APPIMAGE_EXTRACT_AND_RUN=1`, so FUSE is not needed to build.
An AppImage is for direct downloads; Steam depots keep the tarball layout (`--steam` needs no AppImage).

## Clean

```console
$ regia clean --dry-run            # list what the default level would remove
$ regia clean                      # the cook and asset-database caches
$ regia clean --cache              # also the shader and pipeline caches
$ regia clean --all                # also build/, dist/ and target/
$ regia clean --all --dry-run --json   # the plan as one JSON object (scripts, CI)
```

`--json` prints one object on stdout instead of the text lines, after the removal:
`{ "dry_run", "level": "default" | "cache" | "all", "removed", "paths": [{ "path", "kind": "dir" | "file" |
"symlink", "bytes" }], "bytes" }`, with project-relative `/`-separated paths. A failure prints no object; the
error and its code go to stderr as usual.

| Level | Removes (relative to the project root) |
|---|---|
| default | `.regia/cooked`, `.regia/assetdb` |
| `--cache` | the default set, `.regia/shader-cache`, `.regia/pipeline-cache` |
| `--all` | the `--cache` set, `build/`, `dist/`, `target/` |

Never removed: sources, `assets/`, `Regia.toml`, `pipeline-caches/` (the caches a package ships) and the rest of
`.regia/` (agent tokens, autosaves, review state). `regia clean` runs only in a project root (a directory with
`Regia.toml`; `--project DIR` selects another), checks the whole plan before the first deletion, refuses a target
whose parent resolves outside the project, and removes a symlink as the link only, never the folder it points to.

Exit codes: 0 (also when there is nothing to remove), 2 for `clean_not_a_project` and for
conflicting flags (`--cache` with `--all`), 1 for `clean_outside_project` (nothing is removed) and `clean_failed`.

## Windows shipping builds: no console window

A Windows program is either a console program, which opens a console window when it starts outside a
terminal, or a GUI program. A game should be a GUI program. New projects' game mains (the launcher,
the quick app, the net client) start with

```rust,ignore
#![cfg_attr(all(windows, not(debug_assertions)), windows_subsystem = "windows")]
```

so release and shipping builds are GUI programs and debug builds keep the console for logs. A project
made before v0.2.13 can add that line at the top of `launcher/src/main.rs` (after the `//!` doc
comment). The dedicated server of the net template stays a console program.

`regia package --platform windows --profile shipping` reads the staged exe's PE header: a console
exe is a warning on the plain `shipping` profile and fails a named `[profiles.<name>]` build profile
(ADR-2306).

## Windows icon and version info

Explorer, the taskbar and the exe's Properties > Details tab read two resources from the exe: an
icon and the version info. New projects embed both from a build script beside each game main:
`launcher/build.rs` (the `quick` template: `build.rs`; the net template: `client/build.rs` and
`server/build.rs`). It does
nothing on other targets. On a Windows target it reads `Regia.toml`:

```toml
[project]
name = "Night Train"            # ProductName and FileDescription
version = "1.4.2"               # FileVersion, ProductVersion and the binary file version
organization = "Example Studio" # CompanyName

[platforms.windows]
icon = "assets/branding/icon.png"
```

The icon is a PNG, square and 256 pixels or larger for the sharpest result. The build script turns
it into an `.ico` with 16, 32, 48 and 256 pixel images (a smaller or non-square PNG is scaled and
centred). Without `[platforms.windows] icon` it uses `assets/branding/icon.png` or `assets/icon.png`.
With none of these the exe gets a placeholder icon and release builds print a cargo warning. The
`winresource` crate compiles the resources. That needs the Windows SDK's `rc.exe` (installed with the
MSVC build tools) or, when cross-compiling from Linux, `llvm-rc` on `PATH` (set `RC_PATH` to use
another one). Without a resource compiler the build prints a warning and continues, and the exe has
no icon and no version info.

`regia package --platform windows` reads the staged exe's resources back. It warns when the icon group
(`RT_GROUP_ICON` with its `RT_ICON` images) or the version info (`RT_VERSION`) is missing, or when
the exe's `FileVersion` differs from `[project] version`. A named `[profiles.<name>]` shipping profile
fails instead (ADR-2645). An older project gets the build script with `regia upgrade-project
--write`. It adds `build.rs` and the `[build-dependencies]` it needs (`winresource`,
`png`, `toml`) and backs up the crate's `Cargo.toml` as `Cargo.toml.bak`. A crate that already has a
build script of its own is left alone: copy the resource code from a new project's `launcher/build.rs`
into it.

To check a build on Windows, open the exe's Properties > Details, or in PowerShell:

```text
(Get-Item .\dist\windows\<slug>\night_train.exe).VersionInfo | Format-List
```

## Linux shipping builds and the Steam runtime

Steam runs native Linux games, on desktops and on the Steam Deck, inside Steam Linux Runtime 3.0
("sniper", Debian 11, glibc 2.31). A binary linked against a newer distro's glibc does not start
there, so `--profile shipping` Linux packages link against glibc 2.31 by default:

```console
$ cargo install --locked cargo-zigbuild        # once; also put zig 0.14+ on PATH
$ regia package --platform linux --profile shipping           # glibc 2.31 (Steam runtime)
$ regia package --platform linux --profile shipping --glibc host   # this machine's glibc
```

After staging, the package step checks the binary and fails on a problem: the newest `GLIBC_x.y`
it imports (read from the binary's version-needed table) must not exceed the floor (`build_info.json` records `glibc_floor` and `glibc_max`),
and a shipping binary must not contain the build machine's repo, home or cargo-home path, nor the
dev asset watcher (do not enable `regia/dev-assets` in shipped builds). Libraries the runtime
lacks are reported as warnings: bundle them next to the binary (shipping builds link an `$ORIGIN`
rpath, which is also how `libsteam_api.so` is found).

### Build containers

<!-- index: steam-sniper -->
<!-- index: debian12 -->

This builds the game binary inside a toolchain image. It does not write an image of the game.
The artifact is still the tar, the directory, or the AppImage from the format you asked for.

cargo-zigbuild relinks the game against an older glibc's symbol list, but C and C++ dependencies
still compile with this machine's headers and `libstdc++`. `--container` builds the whole binary
inside a real older distribution instead (C-26, ADR-8835):

```console
$ regia package --platform linux --profile shipping --container steam-sniper   # glibc 2.31
$ regia package --platform linux --profile shipping --container debian12       # glibc 2.36
```

| Profile | Base image (pinned by digest) | glibc | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `steam-sniper` | Steam Linux Runtime 3.0 "sniper" SDK, `3.0.20261110.268881` | 2.31 | C and C++ build with clang (`CC=clang`, `CXX=clang++`); the depot for Steam and the Steam Deck |
| `debian12` | Debian 12 "bookworm", `bookworm-20261104` | 2.36 | distributions from about 2023 on; not for `--steam` |

- **Container tool.** podman, else docker, found on `PATH` when the command runs;
  `REGIA_CONTAINER_TOOL=podman|docker` picks one. Without either the package fails with
  `container_tool_missing`.
- **Image.** The first run builds a toolchain image `localhost/regia-build-<profile>:<rustc
  version>-<digest>` from the pinned base (pulled once) with the same Rust version as this
  machine, and reuses it afterwards. The Containerfile is written to
  `<target>/container/<profile>/image/`. `--container-image <image>` runs in an image you
  prepared instead (it must have cargo); it must be pinned by digest (`<image>@sha256:<hex>`) or
  be a local image with a version tag (`localhost/<name>:<tag>`), never `latest`.
- **Mounts.** The cargo workspace is mounted read-only at its own path, so the build runs
  `cargo build --locked` (commit `Cargo.lock`). A path dependency outside the workspace needs
  `--container-mount <dir>` (repeatable, read-only). The target directory and cargo home are
  per profile, `<target>/container/<profile>/{target,cargo-home}`, so a container build never
  reuses artifacts linked against another glibc. docker runs the build as the workspace owner;
  rootless podman needs nothing.
- **Check.** `--glibc` is optional and must equal the profile's glibc. The staged binary passes the
  same floor check as every Linux package, read from its ELF version table (no binutils needed).

Error codes (`regia package --json` prints them as `error.code`): `container_platform_unsupported`,
`container_host_unsupported`, `container_tool_missing`, `container_tool_unknown`,
`container_image_unpinned`, `container_image_missing`, `container_glibc_conflict`,
`container_lockfile_missing`, `container_mount_missing`, `container_build_failed`; see
[Cook and package from the protocol](book/agents/cook-package.md#build-containers).

Test the package inside the runtime itself before uploading. Download
`SteamLinuxRuntime_sniper.tar.xz` from
`https://repo.steampowered.com/steamrt-images-sniper/snapshots/latest-container-runtime-public-beta/`
(check `SHA256SUMS`), extract it, and run the game through it:

```console
$ SteamLinuxRuntime_sniper/run -- ./arena --exit-after-frames 600
```

`cargo test -p regia_cli --test package_e2e packaged_arena -- --ignored` packages `samples/arena`
this way, runs it from a clean directory, and captures the presented frame through the agent
protocol (it must not be black).

Proton: the Windows build prefers a Vulkan adapter, which Proton forwards to the host driver, so no
DXVK translation is involved. Ship the native Linux depot; Proton is the player's override.

## Steam packaging

`regia package --steam` additionally stages the Steam depot layout and steamcmd VDFs
(`steam_appid.txt`, the Steamworks redistributable, `steamcloud.md`, `app_build_<appid>.vdf`,
`depot_build_<depotid>.vdf`, and `game_actions_<appid>.vdf` when the project has
`config/input.ron`) under `<out>/steam`. Publish with `regia steam upload` — see
[Steam](book/user-guide/steam.md).

## Steam Deck

The Deck runs the same native Linux package as any Steam Linux machine (glibc 2.31 floor, tested
in Steam Linux Runtime 3.0). Before uploading a build for it:

- **Controller configuration.** Ship a default Steam Input template (gamepad, with the D-pad and
  left stick on menu navigation, A confirm, B back) and let Steam show your glyphs. The engine's
  UI takes its navigation from the gamepad and keyboard, so either template works.
- **Launch option.** Set the Linux depot launch option to the binary; nothing else is needed.
  `SteamDeck=1` in the environment turns on the Deck's UI text floor
  (`UiDevicePolicy::detect`); `regia_steam` detects the Deck through Steam and selects the
  `Deck` render profile and the frame-cap setting.
- **Deck Verified checklist.** Run through the table in [Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md): controller
  operation of every screen, text legibility, on-screen keyboard for text entry, default
  resolution, no mouse-only launcher or prompt, sleep and resume, quit.
- **Test on the device.** [Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md) has the one-command measurement run and the
  sleep, cap and quit checks. Proton (the Windows build) is a fallback only; test the native build
  first.

## Lightmap seams

If the project ships baked lightmaps (`.flmap`), a shipping `regia package` reads the chart-seam figures stored in each
one and fails with `lightmap_seam_budget`, naming the entries, when one passes the budget. Set it in `Regia.toml`:

```toml
[lightmaps]
seam_budget = 0.25 # the default: the seam p95, as a relative luminance step
```

A project with no lightmaps never meets this. A file baked before format version 3 has no figures: a warning, not a
failure. See [Lightmaps](book/agents/lightmaps.md).

## Smoke-test a package before shipping

The 60-second timer begins after startup and all recorded input steps complete; shader warmup is excluded.
`cargo xtask package-smoke` packages `samples/sim_bridge` and a generated third-person project at the dev and
shipping profiles, extracts each archive, and runs the game for 60 seconds with a scripted input recording. The
game exits itself (`REGIA_SMOKE_SECONDS`) so the session can write `summary.json`. The run fails when the JSON
log has an `ERROR` record, when playback never starts, when `summary.json` is missing or not a clean exit, or
when a shipping APK is over 150 MiB.

On Linux the games run under `xvfb` with lavapipe. `--android` also builds the sim_bridge APK and AAB (the
manifest ABIs, arm64-v8a and x86_64) and records their sizes. `--android-emulator` boots an x86_64 API 35 image
when `/dev/kvm` can be opened read-write, installs the dev APK, and fails on a crash or an error line in that
process's logcat. Without a usable KVM device the same command prints the emulator command lines and still
finishes the rest of the run. `--dry-run` prints those commands and does not boot.

```sh
cargo xtask package-smoke
cargo xtask package-smoke --android
cargo xtask package-smoke --android-emulator --dry-run
```

The report is `target/package-smoke/package-smoke.json` (`format_version` 1). It is a CI report, not a content
format. The size table is also printed.

Windows zip smoke runs on Windows:

```sh
cargo xtask package-smoke --windows
```

## When a package audit stops early

A shipping package check can fail in two different ways.

A **policy failure** means the audit finished. The package contains a forbidden string, a deny term, or a recognized secret signature. The report lists each hit as a path, a rule name, whether it was in the file name or the file bytes, and a byte offset. It does not include the matched text. Fix or review the file, or add a narrow allowance with a reason, then package again.

An **incomplete audit** means the checker stopped before it had looked at every selected byte. The package is not approved and it is not rejected for a specific finding. The report's `complete` field is false and `incomplete_reason` names the ceiling: the file is larger than the memory budget and a pattern cannot be streamed, a pak entry declares more bytes than the audit will decompress, the pak and a decoded entry would have to sit in memory together, a file changed while it was being read, or a byte, entry, or work limit was hit. Raise the matching limit in `[package_hygiene]` only when the package truly needs it. Leaving secret scanning on and raising nothing refuses files larger than 32 MiB, because those signatures are not split across a window.

```toml
[package_hygiene]
max_memory_bytes = 33554432
scan_window_bytes = 1048576
max_matcher_bytes = 8388608
max_work = 1099511627776
```

Project Settings writes these six numbers without changing forbidden strings or allowances. `regia package --audit-dir DIR --json` prints the same `complete` flag, the reason, the limits that were in force, and the peak memory and work the audit actually used.

On Linux that flag prints the commands and does not build. The owner's Windows a test machine is the host for that
run. Re-record the committed playback files with `scripts/write-package-smoke-recordings.sh`. See
[Package smoke](book/agents/package-smoke.md).

## Reviewing package hygiene findings

Audit an extracted, immutable staging directory before publishing:

```sh
regia package --platform linux --project . --audit-dir dist/linux/player --json
```

Configure `[package_hygiene]` in `Regia.toml`; the [package hygiene guide](book/agents/package-hygiene.md)
lists policy rules and error codes. Auditing reads files without rewriting them or starting a cook.
Findings contain a scrubbed `path`, an opaque `location_id`, a rule ID, source and byte offset.
They never include matched snippets. Sensitive filenames are scrubbed in size-limit, IO and
pak errors as well as completed reports; JSON and terminal output use the same safe data.

For example, two synthetic private filenames can both appear as `[redacted]`, with
`location-1` and `location-2` identifying them separately. These IDs are traversal ordinals,
not encoded or hashed filenames. Preserve the staging tree while reviewing; IDs can change
when entries change. Pak entries retain their asset IDs instead of manifest paths.

An authorized local tool can rerun `regia_cli::package_hygiene::audit_tree_with_locations`
to resolve an ID to its original normalized path through an explicit callback. Keep that
callback's values local; they are sensitive and must not be copied into shared logs or agent
responses. Normal CLI/agent reports have no reveal switch or embedded mapping. Invalid names
are not revealed. Use the original path, not `[redacted]` or the ID, for a reviewed allowance.
Redaction recognizes configured values and supported secret shapes; add project rules for
private names it cannot infer. See the guide's synthetic examples and local review contract.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/binary-size.md -->
# Binary size

<!-- index: Binary size -->
<!-- index: apk-size -->

The executable (or the Android `.so`) is the biggest single file of most games. It sets the Steam
download, the install size on a phone and how long the final link takes. `regia apk-size` splits an
Android archive by kind of entry; `cargo xtask binary-size` goes one level deeper and tells you which
crates and which generic functions make the native code large, then keeps a budget so the size does not
grow by accident. A shipped package strips the game binary and keeps symbols beside it
([Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md)). `cargo xtask binary-size` measures the build before that strip.

```console
$ cargo xtask binary-size                       # blank and third_person on this machine
$ cargo xtask binary-size --template quick --json
$ cargo xtask binary-size --target aarch64-linux-android      # needs cargo-ndk and the NDK
$ cargo xtask binary-size --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc     # needs cargo-xwin; sections only
$ cargo xtask binary-size --file path/to/game --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
$ cargo xtask binary-size --check               # fail above docs/ci/size-budgets.toml
$ cargo xtask binary-size --update              # record the budgets again
```

The command generates each template with `regia new`, builds it with the shipping profile (fat LTO, one
codegen unit, `panic = "abort"`, symbol table kept) and reads the result. It builds each template once per
target (two by default), so expect a long run; it is a nightly job, not part of preflight. The generated
projects share one cargo target directory under the temp dir, removed after the run; `--target-dir <dir>`
uses (and keeps) a directory of your own, so a later run reuses its build.

## Reading the report

```text
== blank on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu (elf) ==
file 212.40 MiB | loaded 71.03 MiB | not loaded (symbols, debug info) 141.37 MiB
text 38.10 MiB | rodata 22.00 MiB | data 4.90 MiB | bss 0.40 MiB
```

- **loaded** is what the operating system maps: text (code), rodata (strings, tables, vtables, unwind
  data), data (initialized globals, relocation targets) and bss (zeroed globals, no file bytes). This is the
  number the budget tracks. It does not change when you strip the file.
- **not loaded** is the symbol table and debug line tables. `regia package` extracts them to a
  `symbols/` folder and strips the shipped copy, so they do not reach players.
- **top crates** lists each crate's symbol bytes, biggest first. A symbol belongs to the crate in its path;
  `<A as Trait>::method` belongs to the crate of `A` (or of `Trait` when `A` is a primitive).
- **`(no symbol)`** is every loaded byte no symbol covers: string literals, unwind tables, relocations,
  padding. It is a line of its own and is never spread over the crates, so a crate's number is only what its
  named code and data weigh. When this line is large, the crate numbers understate the real cost of
  everything that carries strings or `Debug` output.
- **`(native)`** is C and C++ libraries linked in (their symbols are not Rust paths).
- **top symbols** are the 30 biggest single functions or statics (`--top N` sets the row count of this
  list and the crate list).
- **generic paths with the most instantiations** counts symbols that have the same path and different type
  parameters. Each copy is separate machine code. A function with dozens of copies is worth turning into a
  thin generic wrapper around a non-generic inner function, or into a trait object.

The Windows report has section sizes only: its symbols are in the PDB, which the tool does not read. Use the
Linux or Android numbers for the crate split, the engine code is the same. A stripped binary reports
nearly everything under `(no symbol)` and says so.

## What usually makes a binary large

- **Generic bloat**: one function instantiated per type, found in the generics list.
- **Crates that should not ship**: an editor, importer or debug-only crate reached through a default feature.
  A crate in the top list that your game never uses is a feature to switch off (`book/user-guide/cargo-features.md`).
- **Duplicated dependency versions**: two versions of one crate show up as two rows with the same prefix.
  `cargo tree -d` lists them.
- **Panic and format machinery**: every `unwrap`, `expect`, `assert!` and `{:?}` carries a message and a
  location string; they land in rodata and in `(no symbol)`.

## Budgets

`docs/ci/size-budgets.toml` (`format_version = 1`) has one `[[budget]]` per template and target with the
loaded total, the biggest crates and a `tolerance_percent` (default 3). `--check` exits 1 when the total or a
crate is above the tolerance (a crate also has 16 KiB of slack, and a crate with no row fails above 64 KiB, or above the smallest
recorded crate plus tolerance when the row holds the full 40 crates),
and prints a hint when the total is far below the budget so you can lock the gain in with `--update`.
Re-record only when the growth is intended, and say why in the commit message. Budgets are only comparable on
the same compiler version and flags.

See also [Android packaging](book/user-guide/android.md) for `regia apk-size`, which splits an APK or AAB by entry kind.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/steam.md -->
# Steam

<!-- index: Steam sockets -->
<!-- index: Steam Input -->
<!-- index: Steam cloud -->
<!-- index: Lobby -->

`regia_steam` integrates Steamworks, and the CLI stages and uploads Steam builds. Steam is opt-in:
without the `steam` feature the engine ships with no Steam code. The owner creates the Steam app.
Credentials for upload come from the environment. This page does not record a completed real match.
The 2026-11-05 versions note (ADR-2828) recorded Steam sockets and lobbies as mock-tested. The owner
procedure is [Steam real run](book/user-guide/steam-real-run.md). Hosting over raw UDP, which does not need Steam, is
[Host a game](book/how-to/online/host-a-game.md).

## Runtime integration

Enable the `steam` feature and use `regia::steam`:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

fn configure(app: &mut App) {
    app.add_plugins(regia::steam::SteamPlugin::default());
}
```

Without the `steamworks` feature (or on Android), the plugin compiles to a graceful no-op:
`SteamState::Unavailable` and every call degrades to `SteamError::Unavailable`, so the game keeps
running. The real `steamworks` backend links Valve's Steamworks SDK at build time
(`STEAM_SDK_LOCATION`), and only on desktop. The SDK and its redistributable are never committed to
this repository (`docs/specs/24-steam.md`, `docs/03` § 5).

## One shared Steam client

The engine owns the one Steam connection. Steam allows a single API instance per process, so a
host (a game shell) must **not** call `steamworks::Client::init` itself; it asks the engine:

<!-- ignore-reason: needs the `steamworks` feature of regia_steam, which the book check does not build -->
```rust,ignore
fn host_system(steam: Res<Steam>) {
    // `None` when Steam is not running (or on the mock backend): degrade, do not init.
    if let Some(client) = steam.client() {
        let _friends = client.friends(); // raw steamworks-rs calls on the shared handle
    }
}
```

- `Steam::client()` returns the shared `steamworks::Client` (a cheap clone). It exists only with
  the `steamworks` feature. The host must depend on the **same `steamworks` version** as
  `regia_steam` (0.13.x, `docs/03` § 5), or the type does not unify.
- The app id comes from project settings (explicit, `SteamSettings`, `Regia.toml` `[steam]`,
  `STEAM_APP_ID`, `steam_appid.txt`); the plugin initializes once, before the first frame.
- The plugin runs `run_callbacks` once per frame in `PreUpdate`. Hosts must not pump callbacks.
- `SteamStatus` (resource): `running`, `offline`, `user_id`, `app_id`, `overlay_open`. Read it for UI
  and gating; it is refreshed every frame.
- Overlay: `OverlayOpened` / `OverlayClosed` messages and `OverlayActive`. Gameplay input contexts
  of local players 0 to 7 are suspended while it is open (player 8 and up keep `Gameplay`; set
  `suspend_contexts` to `None` and handle `OverlayOpened` for more players); set `SteamSettings::pause_on_overlay` to pause game time too.
- Rich presence: `steam.set_presence("status", Some("In a match"))`, `set_presence(key, None)` to
  unset, `steam.clear_presence()` to clear everything (call on disconnect).
- Shutdown: the plugin flushes stats, clears presence and shuts the API down on app termination.
  `Steam::shutdown(&mut self)` does the same earlier; it is idempotent. Clones of the client that
  a host still holds keep the SDK alive until dropped.
- Tests and CI: `SteamPlugin::with_backend(MockSteam::shared())` runs everything with no Steam
  running (`MockSteam::set_offline`, `inject(SteamEvent::OverlayActivated { .. })`, `init_calls`,
  `presence_calls`). The agent method is [`steam.status`](book/agents/steam.md).

## Achievements, stats and invites

- `config/achievements.ron` lists the project's achievements: `(id, display, stat?, threshold?, hidden?)`; the
  `id`s and stat names must match the app on the Steamworks partner site (`SteamSettings::achievements_path`
  picks another file).
- `steam.unlock("FIRST_BLOOD")` unlocks one; `steam.stat_add("kills", 1)` adds to an integer stat and returns the
  new value, and an achievement whose `threshold` the new value crosses unlocks automatically. Both raise
  `AchievementUnlocked { id }`. They reach Steam's servers with `steam.store_stats()` (its result arrives as
  `StatsStored`) or the flush on app exit.
- A friend who joins through the overlay or the friends list arrives as `JoinRequested { friend, connect }`, where
  `connect` is the string the game set as the `connect` rich presence key. It comes from the network: check it
  before dialing or parsing it (at most `MAX_CONNECT_BYTES`, 1024).

## Steam Input

Steam Input is opt-in. Insert `SteamInputSettings { enabled: true, player: 0 }` before the plugin
runs (or flip it at runtime). Off, nothing below runs and controllers come through `gilrs` as
before.

- **Contexts are action sets.** Each context in `config/input.ron` is a Steam Input action set
  (`Gameplay` is `GAMEPLAY`, `Main Menu` is `MAIN_MENU`). The enabled context with the highest
  priority for the player picks the set; it is activated when it changes or a controller connects.
- **Actions.** A Regia Engine action with a gamepad binding in a context becomes the Steam action
  `<context>_<action>` (lower case, `_` for anything else): `Button` is digital, `Axis1D` an analog
  trigger, `Axis2D` an analog stick. `Axis3D` is rejected. The values are held on
  `InputInjection` while non-zero and released at zero, so keyboard and mouse bindings of the same
  action keep working.
- **UI navigation.** Every set also has eight actions, `<context>_ui_up`, `_ui_down`, `_ui_left`,
  `_ui_right`, `_ui_accept`, `_ui_cancel`, `_ui_prev`, `_ui_next`. The bridge reports their edges as
  `GamepadButtonChanged` messages (D-pad, A, B, shoulders) on device `STEAM_INPUT_PAD_DEVICE`, which
  is what `ui_gamepad_navigation` reads, so menus stay navigable when Steam hands the game actions
  instead of a gamepad. Ship a controller configuration that maps the D-pad, left stick, A, B and
  shoulders to them.
- **Manifest.** `regia_steam::action_manifest(&InputConfig)` returns the in-game actions file text
  (a set per context, English titles); the agent method `steam.input_manifest` returns the same
  text for the running app. Upload it with the app's Steam Input configuration on the Steamworks
  partner site.
- **Manifest from the command line.** `regia steam input-manifest` writes the same text from
  `config/input.ron` to `dist/steam/game_actions_<appid>.vdf` (the app id comes from `[steam]` in
  `Regia.toml`). `--out <file>` picks another path and needs no app id; `--stdout` prints it.
  `regia package --steam` writes the file into its `steam/` folder as well. If Steam Input cannot
  express the config, packaging logs a warning and continues.
  During development Steam reads the file from its `controller_config` folder (Valve's Steam Input
  documentation). For release, upload it on the partner site.
- **Sleep and resume.** A suspend or resume (on the Deck, also the pair the engine raises after a
  sleep) releases every action the bridge holds and every UI button it reported down. The next
  frame initializes Steam Input again and re-activates the action set, so a button held when the
  Deck went to sleep is not stuck after it wakes (ADR-526).
- **Prompts.** `regia_steam::action_prompts(&config, context, action, family)` turns an action's
  gamepad bindings into glyph labels and texture keys ([Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md)). Steam's own
  per-origin glyph images are not wired yet.
- **Not done yet:** action set layers, several players on several controllers (player 0 reads the
  first controller), Steam's per-origin glyph images, and the Deck's floating text input. A template
  that also emulates a gamepad makes menus receive each press twice; ship an action-only template.

The agent methods are [`steam.input`](book/agents/steam.md) and `steam.input_manifest`.

## Steam cloud saves

Steam cloud saves back the `SaveGame` system (see [Gameplay](book/user-guide/gameplay.md)): wrap the
Steam backend in `SaveStore::new(SteamRemoteStorage::new(&steam))` (see [Save flow](book/agents/save-flow.md)):
slots are written through Steam Remote Storage as `saves/{slot}.frts`, not through Auto-Cloud.
`--steam` packaging writes `steamcloud.md`, the Auto-Cloud configuration doc for files under
`user://`; a game that only publishes that doc and never uses `SteamRemoteStorage` does not sync
`SaveGame` slots.

## Leaderboards, ownership and timeline markers

Leaderboards go through the framework's `Leaderboard` resource, so the game never touches the SDK and the same code
runs offline (`LeaderboardPlugin::local()`) and in tests (`MockSteam`):

```rust,ignore
use regia_framework::leaderboard::{Leaderboard, LeaderboardDisplay, LeaderboardRange, LeaderboardSpec};

app.add_plugins((SteamPlugin::new(AppId(480)), SteamLeaderboardPlugin));

fn finish_lap(mut boards: ResMut<Leaderboard>, lap: Res<LapTimer>) {
    boards.declare(LeaderboardSpec::new("fastest_lap").ascending().display(LeaderboardDisplay::TimeMilliseconds)).ok();
    boards.submit("fastest_lap", lap.millis, &[]).ok(); // keep-best by default
    boards.request("fastest_lap", LeaderboardRange::AroundUser { before: 4, after: 5 }).ok();
}
```

Answers arrive on later frames as `LeaderboardMessage`s and in `boards.entries("fastest_lap")`. Ownership and the
game-recording timeline are on `Steam`:

```rust,ignore
let soundtrack = steam.dlc_installed(AppId(1_234_560)).unwrap_or(false);
steam.timeline_mode(TimelineMode::Playing).ok();
steam.timeline_event(&TimelineEvent::new("Boss down").icon("steam_achievement").clip(TimelineClip::Featured)).ok();
```

Limits, error codes and the agent methods are on
[Steam leaderboards, ownership and timeline (agents)](book/agents/steam-services.md). With the real client, attaching
UGC to an entry is not available yet (ADR-2340).

## Multiplayer over Steam: lobbies and Steam sockets

The code below is in the tree and is tested against `MockSteam`. ADR-2828 (2026-11-05) recorded that
limit. A two-account session on a real Steam client is
[Steam real run](book/user-guide/steam-real-run.md). Fill `docs/specs/24-steam.md` § 4 from that run. A row stays
`not run` until its step is in both logs and the verdict is `PASS`.

`regia_steam::SteamLobbyPlugin` (add it after `SteamPlugin`) adds `regia_net`'s `LobbyPlugin` when it is not there
yet and, once Steam is ready, gives the `Lobbies` resource the Steam lobby backend (ISteamMatchmaking) and a
