# Steam real run: two accounts, two machines

<!-- index: Steam sockets -->
<!-- index: Lobby -->

One owner session that checks `regia_steam` against a real Steam client (spec 24 § 4). Everything the
SDK side can prove without Steam is already tested against the mock backend (`cargo test -p regia_steam`);
this page is only the part that needs real accounts. Credentials stay on the machines: sign in to the Steam
client yourself, and never put a password, token or Steam Guard code into a file, a log or a command line.

**Status.** The 2026-11-05 versions note (ADR-2828) recorded Steam sockets and lobbies as mock-tested.
This page is the procedure the owner runs. It is not a record that a real match has been played. A row
in `docs/specs/24-steam.md` § 4 stays `not run` unless its step is in both logs and the verdict is
`PASS`. `ignored`, `skipped`, `NOT RUN`, and `INCOMPLETE` are not a pass. Hosting over raw UDP does
not use this page ([Host a game](book/how-to/online/host-a-game.md)).

## What you need

- Two machines (A = host, B = guest), each with a Steam client signed in as a different account, and the two
  accounts friends of each other: both legs create friends-only lobbies, which B joins by id (on the shared test
  app 480, a public lobby would let a stranger take B's slot).
- App 480 (Valve's test app, "Spacewar") or your own app id: set `STEAM_APP_ID=<id>` on both machines.
  App 480 needs no purchase; your own id needs both accounts to own it or be on the app's dev team.
- The Steamworks SDK unpacked outside the repository (`crates/regia_steam/README.md`, `STEAM_SDK_LOCATION`).
- A checkout of the same commit on both machines.

## 1. One-account smoke (each machine)

```
STEAM_SDK_LOCATION=~/sdk/steamworks_1.64 cargo test -p regia_steam --features steamworks \
    --test real_client -- --nocapture steam_client_smoke
```

Expect `test steam_client_smoke ... ok` and no line starting with `skipped:` (a `skipped` line means Steam was
not reachable). It covers init, a lobby create and read-back, ownership, the leaderboard lookup and the
Workshop listing.

## 2. Lobby, Steam sockets match, leave and reconnect, cloud (A and B)

The script is `regia_steam::real_run` (ADR-4896); `real_run_harness.rs` runs the same script on the mock
network, so a failure here is about Steam, not the script. The test is `#[ignore]`d: in an ordinary
`cargo test` it shows as `ignored`. That means not run, never pass. Run it only with `--ignored` and the
setup below; with `--ignored` but no setup it fails with `NOT RUN (<code>)`.

Both machines need the same commit and the same app id. On each, in the checkout:

```
export STEAM_SDK_LOCATION=~/sdk/steamworks_1.64   # where you unpacked the SDK
export STEAM_APP_ID=480                           # or your own app id, the same on both
export REGIA_STEAM_RUN_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
```

On A (host):

```
REGIA_STEAM_TWO_ACCOUNT=host REGIA_STEAM_RUN_LOG=$PWD/host.log \
    cargo test -p regia_steam --features steamworks --test real_client -- \
    --ignored --nocapture --exact two_account_lobby_and_steam_sockets
```

It prints `REGIA_STEAM_LOBBY_ID=<number>`, then waits about 4 minutes for the guest. On B (guest):

```
REGIA_STEAM_TWO_ACCOUNT=guest REGIA_STEAM_LOBBY_ID=<number> REGIA_STEAM_RUN_LOG=$PWD/guest.log \
    cargo test -p regia_steam --features steamworks --test real_client -- \
    --ignored --nocapture --exact two_account_lobby_and_steam_sockets
```

What happens, in order (every step is a `REGIA_RUN` line on the console and a line in the log):

1. A creates a friends-only lobby with its commit and app id in the lobby data (`lobby_created`).
2. B joins by id and checks the lobby advertises the same commit and app id (`lobby_entered`,
   `content_checked status=match`); another build stops B with `content_mismatch`.
3. A sees B join and launches the lobby to its own Steam id (`member_joined join=1`, `server_set`); B
   follows the launch (`server_seen`).
4. B sends `ping.1.<lobby>` over Steam sockets, A answers `pong.1.<lobby>` (`datagram_in`/`datagram_out`).
5. B leaves and joins the same lobby again (`left`, `rejoin`, `lobby_entered round=2`); A logs
   `member_left` and `member_joined join=2`. B reads the launch from the lobby data and runs the echo
   again as round 2: this is the reconnect.
6. B sends `done`, A logs `guest_done` and leaves.
7. Each machine writes `saves/regia_real_run_<role>.frts` through Steam Remote Storage on its own account,
   reads it back, compares, deletes it and checks it is gone (`cloud_round_trip`).
8. Each ends with `result status=complete`, and the test is `ok`. Anything else ends with
   `result status=failed code=<code>` (for example `timeout waiting=<step>`) and the test fails.

The logs hold the app id, the commit, the lobby id and account tags (`acct-<16 hex>`, a fixed hash of
each Steam id so the two logs can be matched without publishing the ids). They never hold a password,
token, Steam Guard code or account name; nothing in the script reads one.

Pass for this section takes both: both tests `ok`, and the verdict in § 4a is `PASS`.

To also see the template's follow branch (`LobbySteamTransport` with `regia::steam::SteamLobbyTransport`
in `follow_lobby`), run your game's client on both machines with the Steam plugin and create/join from its UI or
with the agent method `lobby.create` / `lobby.join`; the link reaches `connected` on B.

## 3. Overlay on Vulkan and DX12

The app is the windowed client of the `net_game` sample built with `--features steamworks`: it runs
`SteamPlugin` (app id from `STEAM_APP_ID`, `steam_appid.txt` or `[steam] app_id` in a `Regia.toml` of the
working directory) and its HUD shows a line in the top-left corner (ADR-7317):

```
STEAM OVERLAY: closed (opened 0, closed 0)
Steam (steamworks): running, app 480
overlay closed (Shift+Tab opens it)
last: no overlay message yet
gpu: <adapter name> (Vulkan)
```

The first row is the one to read (ADR-7349): `STEAM OVERLAY: OPEN (opened 1, closed 0)` while the overlay is up (the
whole block turns yellow), `STEAM OVERLAY: closed (...)` otherwise, with how many `OverlayOpened` and `OverlayClosed`
messages arrived. While the overlay is up the third line reads `overlay OPEN (Shift+Tab closes it)`; the fourth names the last message the
game received, `OverlayOpened` or `OverlayClosed`, with how many of each arrived; the last line is the GPU and backend
the window renders with (`Vulkan` or `Dx12`). `Steam (steamworks): not running` means the client found no Steam
(start Steam and sign in). An agent reads the same state with `steam.status` (`overlay_open`) and the line with
`ui.query {"name": "steam_overlay"}`.

Before you start, on each machine: the Steam client is running and signed in. Then, from the repository root:

```
bash docs/evidence/steam/2026-11-10/steam-owner-session.sh overlay
```

It builds the client (`cargo build -p net_game --features steamworks --bin net_game_client`, in its own cargo
invocation, never together with the server), and puts into `target/steam-session/overlay/` the client, the Steam API
library, `steam_appid.txt` (`480`, or your `STEAM_APP_ID`) and a launcher, `net_game_client.sh`. It ends by listing
the adapters (`adapter <n>: <name> (<backend>, ...)`, the numbering `REGIA_GPU_INDEX` takes). `steam_appid.txt` is
what lets a program Steam did not start pass the plugin's shipping restart check; without it the client logs
`Steam relaunched the app (id 480); exiting this process` and closes.

No server is needed: the client shows its window and HUD while it waits for one. To see avatars as well, start
`cargo run -p net_game --no-default-features --features server --bin net_game_server` in another terminal first.

- **Linux (Vulkan).** Steam draws its overlay in programs it starts, so launch the client from Steam: Steam > Games >
  Add a Non-Steam Game to My Library > Browse, set the file filter to all files, pick
  `target/steam-session/overlay/net_game_client.sh`, add it, and play it from the library (leave Compatibility off).
  Press Shift+Tab once and let go: expect the overlay to draw over the window and stay, the first HUD row to read
  `STEAM OVERLAY: OPEN (opened 1, closed 0)`, and after a second Shift+Tab `STEAM OVERLAY: closed (opened 1, closed 1)`. On a Wayland desktop, run it once more with the launch option
  `WAYLAND_DISPLAY= %command%` (the window then goes through XWayland) and record both. A run from a terminal
  (`... overlay run`) reaches Steam (the line says `running`), but Steam may not draw its overlay there; that is not
  the finding.
- **Windows (DX12).** In Git Bash, run `... overlay` as above; from the adapter list pick a line that says `Dx12`.
  Then start the client with that adapter, either by index or by a part of its name:

  ```
  cd target/steam-session/overlay
  REGIA_GPU_INDEX=<n> ./net_game_client.exe
  REGIA_GPU_NAME=<substring> ./net_game_client.exe
  ```

  The HUD's last line must read `gpu: <name> (Dx12)`; if it says `Vulkan`, the index was not a DX12 entry. Press
  Shift+Tab, same expectation as on Linux. On Windows Steam usually draws its overlay in a game started from a terminal too; if it
  does not, add `net_game_client.exe` as a non-Steam game, set `REGIA_GPU_INDEX` as a user environment variable
  (`setx REGIA_GPU_INDEX <n>`, then restart Steam) and play it from the library.

Record, per backend, whether the overlay draws, flickers or is missing, and what the HUD line said; a missing overlay
on one backend is the finding.

**The overlay trace (ADR-7349).** The launcher sets `REGIA_STEAM_OVERLAY_TRACE`, so every run started from it writes
`overlay-trace-<date>-<time>.txt` (and appends the client's log to `overlay-client-log.txt`) in the overlay folder. Any
game with `SteamPlugin` writes the same trace when you set `REGIA_STEAM_OVERLAY_TRACE=<file>` yourself. The header
says whether Steam injected its overlay (`overlay_renderer_preloaded yes`, `vk_overlay_layer 1`) and which display the
window could use; then one line per event, `t=+<seconds>s frame=<n> ...`:

- `steam callback GameOverlayActivated active=true (edge)` / `(repeat)`: what Steam told the game,
- `game OverlayOpened` / `game OverlayClosed`: what the game acted on,
- `window focus in` / `out`, `key ShiftLeft (Shift) down`, `key Tab (Tab) up`, ...,
- `game asks cursor_grab=... cursor_visible=...`, `cursor hold for the overlay: on/off`, `os set_cursor_grab call #n ...`,
- `renderer surfaces hidden (throttled, not presenting): true/false` (the `net_game` client),
- `heartbeat frames=<n> ...` once a second.

How to read it: no `GameOverlayActivated` line at all means Steam never told the game the overlay opened (what you saw
was not Steam's overlay, or Steam drew it without telling the game); `active=true` on the Shift+Tab press and
`active=false` on the key release means Steam closed it on the release; an `os set_cursor_grab` line between them
means the game took the pointer back. While the overlay is open the engine holds the cursor free and visible
(`SteamSettings::release_cursor_on_overlay`, on by default), so that last line should not appear.

The `net_game` HUD shows its scoreboard while Tab is held; in the Steam build Shift (and an open overlay) keeps it
hidden, so a panel that appears only while Shift+Tab is held is not the scoreboard.

## 4. Cloud round trip across machines

Section 2 already round-trips a file through Steam Remote Storage on each account. The cross-machine
sync needs one account on both machines, which the two-account run cannot do: sign A's account in on B
yourself (the harness never changes accounts), or use one machine and a second install. On A, write a save
with the Steam cloud backend (`SteamRemoteStorage`, or an Auto-Cloud path from `autocloud_document`
configured in the Steamworks partner site), wait for the client to show the sync as done, quit. On B,
start the game and read the save. Pass: the bytes read on B equal what A wrote. Then delete the save on B
and confirm it disappears on A after sync.

## 4a. Judge the two logs

Copy `guest.log` from B next to `host.log` on A (any copy method; the logs hold no secrets) and run:

```
cargo run -p regia_steam --example steam_real_run_verdict -- host.log guest.log
```

It prints one line and exits 0 only for `PASS`:

| Output | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PASS` | Both logs complete and consistent with each other |
| `NOT RUN (setup_absent)`, `NOT RUN (missing_host_log)`, `NOT RUN (missing_guest_log)` | A log is missing: nothing was proven (exit 2) |
| `INCOMPLETE (incomplete_host)` / `(incomplete_guest)`: missing ... | An endpoint stopped early; the missing steps are listed (exit 1) |
| `FAIL (<code>)`: ... | The logs contradict a pass (exit 1) |

`FAIL` codes: `log_unreadable`, `wrong_role` (logs swapped), `app_id_mismatch`, `commit_mismatch`,
`same_account` (both logs from one account), `lobby_mismatch`, `peer_mismatch` (a record names an account
other than the other endpoint), `wrong_payload`, `content_mismatch`, `cloud_mismatch`, `endpoint_failed`.
Setup codes printed by the test itself as `NOT RUN (<code>)`: `setup_absent`, `bad_role`,
`missing_lobby_id`, `bad_lobby_id`, `missing_commit`, `bad_app_id`, `steam_not_ready`, `socket_failed`,
`request_refused`. Endpoint failure codes in a `result status=failed` line: `timeout`,
`lobby_create_failed`, `lobby_join_failed`, `content_mismatch`, `launch_refused`, `host_lost_lobby`,
`wrong_payload`, `socket_failed`, `cloud_write_failed`, `cloud_read_failed`, `cloud_mismatch`,
`cloud_delete_failed`.

### Template match over Steam (N08)

The second leg plays the `net-game` template over the same two accounts (ADR-5375). The driver is
`net_game::steam_leg`; `samples/net_game/tests/steam_leg.rs` runs the same driver on the mock Steam network,
so a failure here is about Steam, not the script. It is `#[ignore]`d like section 2's test. Keep the same
`STEAM_APP_ID` and `REGIA_STEAM_RUN_COMMIT` exports. On A (host):

```
REGIA_STEAM_NET_LEG=host REGIA_STEAM_NET_LOG=$PWD/net-host.log \
    cargo test -p net_game --features steamworks --test steam_leg_real -- --ignored --nocapture
```

It prints `REGIA_STEAM_LOBBY_ID=<number>` (a new lobby, not section 2's) and waits about 4 minutes. On B (guest):

```
REGIA_STEAM_NET_LEG=guest REGIA_STEAM_LOBBY_ID=<number> REGIA_STEAM_NET_LOG=$PWD/net-guest.log \
    cargo test -p net_game --features steamworks --test steam_leg_real -- --ignored --nocapture
```

What happens (each step is a `REGIA_NET` line on the console and a line in the log):

1. A serves the game on a Steam socket and its agent creates a friends-only lobby with `lobby.create`, the commit
   and app id in the lobby data (`agent method=lobby.create lobby=<id>`). B joins by id, so a stranger on app 480
   cannot take the slot; the two accounts must be friends.
2. B's agent joins it with `lobby.join` (`agent method=lobby.join`, `lobby_entered`) and checks the advertised
   commit and app id (`content_checked status=match`). Another build stops B with `content_mismatch`; a wrong or
   expired id, or a full lobby, stops it at once with `lobby_join_failed`.
3. A sees B (`member_joined`) and launches the lobby to its own Steam id (`launch`). B's client follows the
   launch over Steam sockets.
4. B's agent reads `net.status` with the client link `connected` (`net_status endpoint=client state=connected
   server=<tag>`; the tag is the account of the Steam peer the link reached). A's agent reads the server with one
   peer (`net_status endpoint=server peers=1`).
5. B's scripted bot plays 600 fixed steps (10 s) and stands for 120 more. B logs its `netstats` line
   (corrections, resyncs, verify failures, round trip, loss) and leaves; A logs its server `netstats` and leaves.
   A link that drops during the match ends B with `net_disconnected`.
6. Each ends with `result status=complete`, and the test is `ok`.

Copy `net-guest.log` next to `net-host.log` and run the same verdict command; it tells the two legs apart by
the logs' first line:

```
cargo run -p regia_steam --example steam_real_run_verdict -- net-host.log net-guest.log
```

`PASS` takes both logs complete, the guest `connected` to the host's account and still connected at its report,
the server's `datagrams_in` at least 300 (the match was played, not only joined), and every client within the
template's bounds: at most 20 corrections, at most 2 resyncs and no verify failures. The `NOT RUN` and
`INCOMPLETE` lines are as above. `FAIL` codes for this leg: `log_unreadable` (also one log of each leg),
`wrong_role`, `app_id_mismatch`, `commit_mismatch`, `same_account`, `content_mismatch`, `endpoint_failed`,
`lobby_mismatch`, `peer_mismatch`, `net_not_connected`, `net_disconnected`, `net_corrections`, `net_resyncs`,
`net_verify_failed`, `net_too_short`.
Setup codes printed by the test as `NOT RUN (<code>)`: `setup_absent` (`REGIA_STEAM_NET_LEG` is not set),
`bad_role`, `missing_lobby_id`, `bad_lobby_id`, `missing_commit`, `bad_app_id`, `steam_not_ready`,
`socket_failed`, `link_failed`, `request_refused`. Endpoint failure codes: `timeout`, `content_mismatch`,
`lobby_join_failed`, `launch_refused`, `net_disconnected`.

### Owner checklist (two machines, under 30 minutes)

`docs/evidence/steam/2026-11-10/steam-owner-session.sh` runs every command above; each step prints what to do
next. Build first, outside the 30 minutes (a cold build takes a while):

1. Both machines: Steam client running and signed in (A and B on different accounts, friends). Same commit:
   `git rev-parse HEAD` matches. `bash docs/evidence/steam/2026-11-10/steam-owner-session.sh build`.
2. Both (2 min): `... smoke`. Expect `steam_client_smoke ... ok` and no `skipped:` line.
3. A then B (about 5 min): `... echo host` on A; within 4 minutes `... echo guest <id>` on B with the printed id.
4. A then B (about 3 min): `... net host` on A; `... net guest <id>` on B with the new id.
5. Copy `guest.log` and `net-guest.log` from B into A's session folder. On A: `... verdict`. Expect two `PASS`
   lines.
6. Both (5 minutes, manual): `... overlay`, then the overlay check of section 3. Record what you see and what the
   HUD's Steam line said.
7. Fill the table in `docs/specs/24-steam.md` § 4 and keep the session folder (four logs, the verdict lines).

Never type a password, token or Steam Guard code into the script; it asks for none.

## 5. Record the result

Fill the table in `docs/specs/24-steam.md` § 4 ("Real-run results") with the date, the app id, the two
machine descriptions, the commit, and pass, fail or not run per row; keep `host.log`, `guest.log` and the
verdict line with it. A row stays `not run` unless its step is in both logs and the verdict is `PASS`. Report a failure with the full test output only
after removing any account name you do not want published.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/test-bundles.md -->
# Test bundles for Windows and the Steam Deck

<!-- index: Test bundle -->
<!-- index: cargo xtask dist -->

`cargo xtask dist` builds a folder (and a zip or tar of it) that you copy to a Windows PC or a
Steam Deck to run engine binaries there, with no Rust toolchain on that machine. It is for engine
testing: the owner's Windows pass, the Deck test run on [Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md), a tester's
crash report. A game ships with `regia package` instead ([Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md),
[Package a game](book/how-to/platforms/package-a-game.md)).

A bundle holds:

- the binaries, `vfx_lab` by default;
- Windows: a `run-<bin>.cmd` launcher per binary, the DLL set (`--dlls`) and the DXC pair for
  Direct3D 12 (`--dxc`), all next to the exe;
- the engine license and the third-party notices, in `licenses/`;
- optional pre-built pipeline caches, in `content/pipelines/`;
- a `README.txt` that says how to run it and which folders to send back;
- `dist-manifest.json`, which lists every file with its size and BLAKE3 hash.

## Commands

```console
$ cargo xtask dist --target windows --dry-run      # print the plan as JSON; builds and writes nothing
$ cargo xtask dist --target windows --dry-run --manifest-out windows-preview.json   # plus the manifest it would write
$ cargo xtask dist --target windows                # cargo-xwin cross build on Linux, then the zip
$ cargo xtask dist --target deck                   # cargo-zigbuild against glibc 2.31, then the tar
$ cargo xtask dist --verify target/dist/windows/regia-windows-0.1.27.zip
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--target windows\|deck` | The platform. Required, except with `--verify`. |
| `--bin <package>[:<bin>]` | A binary to bundle. Repeat it for more than one, for example `--bin vfx_lab --bin lookdev:do27_chase`. The default is `vfx_lab`. |
| `--profile <name>` | The cargo profile: `release` (the default), `shipping`, `dev` or a custom one. |
| `--out DIR` | The output folder. The default is `target/dist/<target>`. |
| `--from DIR` | Skip the build and bundle binaries that were already built into `DIR`. This works on any host. |
| `--pipeline-caches DIR` | Ship the `.fpc` files in `DIR`. Each file is validated and stored under its key's shipped name. When two files have the same key, the larger one is kept. A corrupt file stops the bundle. |
| `--crt-static` | Windows only: link the C runtime statically, so the exe does not need the Visual C++ Redistributable. It has not been tried with every C dependency yet. If the link fails, drop the flag. |
| `--dlls DIR` | Windows only: copy every `*.dll` of `DIR` next to the exe (for example `steam_api64.dll`). A DLL the exe imports and the bundle ships is classed `bundled`, so the import check passes. Each must be an x64 image. |
| `--dxc DIR` | Windows only: copy `dxcompiler.dll` and `dxil.dll` from `DIR` next to the exe. Both are required (`dxil.dll` signs what `dxcompiler.dll` compiles). See [Direct3D 12 and DXC](#direct3d-12-and-dxc). |
| `--no-launcher` | Windows only: do not write `run-<bin>.cmd`. |
| `--git REV` | The commit the binaries were built from, recorded as the manifest's `git` and in the README. The default is `REGIA_GIT_HASH`, then the repository's HEAD; give it with `--from` when the binaries were built from another commit (ADR-5002). A blank id or one with spaces fails with `dist_git_invalid`. |
| `--readme FILE` | Ship `FILE` as `README.txt` instead of the generated tester README. `demo-package` passes its player README here. |
| `--notices FILE` | Ship `FILE` as `licenses/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` instead of the engine-wide notices. `demo-package` passes the demo's own list (ADR-5419). |
| `--no-default-features`, `--features LIST` | Passed to the cargo build (ignored with `--from`). `demo-package` builds `--no-default-features --features demo`. |
| `--overlay DIR` | Ship every file under `DIR` at the same relative path in the bundle (role `overlay`). A path another plan file already holds fails the plan; `*.sh` files and files with an executable bit keep it. `demo-package` passes the cooked scene and the launchers here. |
| `--no-archive` | Write the folder only. |
| `--dry-run` | Print the plan and stop. |
| `--manifest-out FILE` | With `--dry-run` only: also write the manifest the bundle would get (see [The dry-run manifest](#the-dry-run-manifest)). |
| `--verify PATH` | Check a bundle folder, a `.zip` or a `.tar` against the manifest inside it, then exit. |

Build tools:

- **Windows on Linux:** `cargo install cargo-xwin`. The build runs
  `cargo xwin build --profile <p> --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -p <package> --bin <bin>`.
  On Windows, plain `cargo build` is used.
- **The Deck:** `cargo install cargo-zigbuild` and zig 0.14 or newer on `PATH`. The build runs
  `cargo zigbuild --profile <p> --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.2.31`, which uses the glibc of
  Steam Linux Runtime 3.0. A Deck bundle builds on Linux only. On another host, build there and
  pass `--from`.

## Layout

```text
target/dist/<target>/
  regia-<target>-<version>/          the bundle folder
    vfx_lab.exe (Windows) or vfx_lab (Deck)
    run-vfx_lab.cmd                    Windows launcher, one per binary (not with --no-launcher)
    steam_api64.dll ...                only with --dlls
    dxcompiler.dll, dxil.dll           only with --dxc
    licenses/LICENSE                   the engine's MPL-2.0 text (README.txt names the source location)
    licenses/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md
    content/pipelines/*.fpc            only with --pipeline-caches
    README.txt
    dist-manifest.json
  regia-<target>-<version>.zip|.tar  the same tree under one top-level folder
  symbols/vfx_lab.pdb                  Windows, when the linker wrote one (not in the archive)
```

The archives are written by xtask itself: a stored (uncompressed) zip for Windows, made by the same
writer as feedback bundles, and a ustar tar for the Deck. The tar keeps the executable bit. Neither
needs `zip`, `tar` or PowerShell on the build machine. The same files give the same archive bytes when `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` is set;
without it, the archive timestamp is the build time.

## The launcher

On Windows each binary gets `run-<bin>.cmd` (CRLF line ends). It changes to the bundle folder
wherever it was unzipped, sets `REGIA_NATIVE_CRASH=1` unless the variable is set already, runs the
exe with the arguments it was given, and on a non-zero exit code prints the code and waits for a
key, so a double-clicked window does not vanish with the error. The exit code is passed on.

## Direct3D 12 and DXC

The engine tries Vulkan first and falls back to Direct3D 12 (ADR-201). On Direct3D 12 the shader
compiler is one of three, and the manifest's `dx12` object says which this bundle relies on:

| `dx12.compiler` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `bundled_dxc` | `--dxc` was given. `dxcompiler.dll` and `dxil.dll` sit next to the exe and shaders compile with DXC (Shader Model 6). Keep the two together. |
| `engine` | No DXC files. The exe uses the DXC linked into it when it was built with the `static-dxc` feature, otherwise FXC (Shader Model 5.1). |

The DXC files are not imports of the exe (they are loaded at run time), so the import check does
not need them. The Windows SDK ships a matching pair; take both from the same release.

## Symbols

The linker's `.pdb` is not in the zip. It is copied to `symbols/<bin>.pdb` next to the archive
and listed under `symbols[]` with its size and hash, so a minidump from a tester can be matched to
the exact build.

## The binary checks

`dist` reads the staged binaries before it writes the manifest. A failed check stops the bundle,
leaves the folder without a manifest for you to inspect, and the next run replaces it.

**Windows.** The exe's DLL imports are read from its PE header, so this check also runs on the Linux
machine that cross-built it. Each DLL falls into one class:

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `system` | Part of Windows 10 and 11, including the `api-ms-win-*` API sets and the Universal CRT. |
| `msvc_runtime` | `VCRUNTIME140.dll` and the other Visual C++ runtime DLLs. Most gaming PCs have the redistributable; a fresh Windows install does not. The README says so, and the manifest records `"msvc_runtime": "dynamic"`. `--crt-static` removes the dependency. |
| `gpu_driver` | `vulkan-1.dll`, which the GPU driver installs. |
| `bundled` | A DLL that ships next to the exe in the bundle. |
| `unknown` | Anything else. An unknown import **fails the bundle**, because the exe would not start without that DLL. An unknown delay-loaded DLL is only a note. |

If an `unknown` DLL is in fact part of Windows, add it to `WINDOWS_SYSTEM_DLLS` in
`xtask/src/dist_binary.rs`.

**The Deck.** The ELF's `NEEDED` libraries and the `GLIBC_x.y` versions it requires are read from
its section headers. A binary that needs a glibc newer than 2.31 **fails the bundle**. A library
that the Steam Linux Runtime does not provide is a note: the binary still runs in Desktop Mode
when SteamOS has that library. The runtime's library list is the one `regia package` uses, and a
test keeps the two lists equal.

## Where the program writes

The manifest's `runtime_dirs` and the README list these folders. `<exe>` is the program name
without `.exe`. When something goes wrong, the tester sends back `crash_dumps`, `logs` and the
run's `--out` folder.

| Key | Windows | Steam Deck |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | `%APPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>` | `~/.local/share/RegiaEngine/<exe>` |
| `logs` | `%APPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>\logs` | `~/.local/share/RegiaEngine/<exe>/logs` |
| `crash_dumps` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>\feedback` | `~/.local/share/RegiaEngine/<exe>/feedback` |
| `cache` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>` | `~/.cache/RegiaEngine/<exe>` |
| `pipeline_cache` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>\pipelines` (Vulkan only; Direct3D 12 has no pipeline cache in wgpu 30) | `~/.cache/RegiaEngine/<exe>/pipelines` |
| `shipped_pipeline_caches` | `<bundle>\content\pipelines` | `<bundle>/content/pipelines` |

Notes:

- Native crash capture is opt-in on Windows. Set `REGIA_NATIVE_CRASH=1` before a test run; the
  README shows the command.
- `REGIA_PIPELINE_CACHE_DIR` moves the pipeline cache for one run.

## The manifest

`dist-manifest.json` (schema 1) has these fields:

| Field | What |
|---|---|
| `schema`, `kind` | `1` and `regia_dist`. `--verify` refuses other values. |
| `bundle`, `target`, `triple`, `engine_version`, `git`, `profile` | What was built, and from which revision. |
| `build` | `{tool, command}` (`cargo-xwin`, `cargo-zigbuild` or `cargo`), or `{tool: "prebuilt", from}` with `--from`. |
| `glibc_floor` | `"2.31"` for the Deck, `null` for Windows. |
| `binaries[]` | The binary checks. Windows: `machine`, `subsystem` (`console` or `windows`), `imports[] {dll, class, delay_load}`, `msvc_runtime`. Deck: `machine`, `needed`, `glibc_max`, `glibc_floor`, `outside_runtime`. |
| `dx12` | Windows: `{compiler, files, note}`, see [Direct3D 12 and DXC](#direct3d-12-and-dxc). `null` for the Deck. |
| `files[]` | `{path, role, bytes, blake3, mode}` for every file except the manifest, sorted by path. `role` is one of `binary`, `license`, `readme`, `pipeline_cache`, `dll`, `dxc`, `launcher` or `overlay`. `mode` is `755` or `644`. |
| `licenses` | The license files. |
| `runtime_dirs` | The table above, as `{key: {path, what}}`. |
| `symbols[]` | The `.pdb` files kept next to the bundle, with size and hash. |
| `warnings` | The notes, which the README repeats. |

`--verify` checks the following and lists every problem it finds:

- every listed file is present, with the listed size and hash;
- no file is present that the manifest does not list;
- the Deck binaries are executable;
- the manifest names at least one license;
- for a folder, the binary checks pass again.

## The dry-run manifest

`--dry-run --manifest-out FILE` writes, on any Linux machine and without a build, the manifest a
real bundle of the same plan would get. Use it to review a Windows zip layout before cargo-xwin
runs, or to diff two layouts in review. It has every field of the table above, plus:

| Field | What |
|---|---|
| `dry_run` | `true`. `--verify` refuses a manifest with this field, so a preview is never mistaken for a bundle. |
| `missing` | The bundle paths whose source does not exist yet (usually the binaries). |
| `archive` | The file name the zip or tar would get, or `null` with `--no-archive`. |

Files whose source exists already (the license files) carry their real size and hash, the same
values the staged bundle gets. Binaries not built yet carry `null`. The README hash is the README
without notes: binary checks can add notes (the Visual C++ runtime note, for example), and then
the staged README differs. `binaries[]` and `warnings` stay empty, because the binary checks need
the built files.

The Windows bundle is an installer-less folder. Unzip it anywhere outside `Program Files` and run
the exe; nothing is registered and nothing is written next to the exe. The license and the
third-party notices are always in `licenses\` (`cargo xtask notices` regenerates
`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, and the gate checks that it is current). A game's own Windows package
comes from `regia package --platform windows` ([Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md)), which also puts the
notices next to the exe.

Related: [Windows](book/user-guide/windows.md), [Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md), [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/demo-package.md -->
# Packaging the demo

<!-- index: Demo package -->

`cargo xtask demo-package` turns the showcase's free-camera demo (`showcase --demo`) into something you can hand out or upload. It builds the `shipping` profile (`panic = "abort"`) for Windows and Linux, adds the cooked scene, the credits and the notices, and lays out a Steam depot and plain archives with checksums. It uploads nothing and reads no credential. The owner creates the Steam app. A game you ship yourself uses [Package a game](book/how-to/platforms/package-a-game.md), not this command.

```text
cargo xtask demo-package --scene samples/showcase/example_scene --app-id 1234560
```

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--scene DIR` | The scene to ship (default the generated example scene). It needs an `asset_manifest.json`. |
| `--out DIR` | Output folder (default `target/demo-package`). |
| `--targets windows,linux` | Platforms (default both). Linux is the glibc 2.31 build that also runs on the Steam Deck. |
| `--bin PKG[:BIN]` | The binary to ship, `<package>` or `<package>:<bin>` (default `showcase`). |
| `--app-id N` | Steam app id for the scripts. Without it they carry `REPLACE_WITH_APP_ID`. |
| `--from-windows DIR`, `--from-linux DIR` | Use binaries built elsewhere. |
| `--git-windows REV`, `--git-linux REV` | The commit the `--from-*` binaries were built from; required with them (ADR-5002). Recorded in the bundle manifest, the player README and `demo-package.json`. |
| `--check` | Only run the content and profile checks. |
| `--verify DIR` | Re-check a finished package. |

## What fails the build

The checks run before anything compiles, and every finding is printed:

- `do27_content_path`: a scene path, file name, manifest row or the scene directory's own path names Direct Order 27 content.
- `asset_no_licence`: a scene file has no row in `asset_manifest.json`, or the row's licence is empty, `unknown`, `TBD` or `TODO`.
- `asset_manifest_missing`, `asset_manifest_invalid`, `asset_row_duplicate`, `asset_row_orphan`, `scene_special_file`.
- `shipping_not_abort`: `[profile.shipping]` in the workspace does not set `panic = "abort"`.
- `demo_package_git_unknown`: `--from-windows` / `--from-linux` without `--git-windows` / `--git-linux`, or no git id at all (not a git checkout and no `REGIA_GIT_HASH`). `dist_git_invalid`: a given id is blank or has spaces.

## What you get

```text
depot/content/windows/ , depot/content/linux/   the bundle folders
depot/scripts/                                   app_build_<appid>.vdf, depot_build_<id>.vdf, UPLOAD.txt
archive/                                         regia-demo-<version>-windows.zip, -linux.tar, CHECKSUMS.b3
bundles/<platform>/                              the xtask dist output (dist-manifest.json inside)
DECK-CHECK.md                                    the Steam Deck check steps
WINDOWS-CHECK.md                                 the Windows minimum-spec check steps (ADR-5578)
demo-package.json                                what was built
```

Each bundle holds the binary, `run-demo.sh` or `run-demo.cmd`, `content/scene/`, `CREDITS.txt`, `licenses/`, `dist-manifest.json` and `README.txt`. The binary is `showcase --no-default-features --features demo` (ADR-5419): no agent protocol and no network crate; `dist` gets `--no-default-features --features demo`, and binaries given with `--from-windows`/`--from-linux` must be built the same way (`cargo xtask demo-notices --verify <depot>` refuses a binary with traces of a forbidden crate). `licenses/` holds `LICENSE` (the engine's MPL-2.0 text; `CREDITS.txt` names where the engine's source is), the demo's own `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` (a copy of `docs/demo/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES-demo.md`, given to `dist --notices`) and `EULA.md` (`docs/demo/EULA.md` once the owner's text lands, the draft `docs/demo/EULA-DRAFT.md` until then); `demo-package` stops before building without them (`demo_package_legal_missing`), and `--verify` reports a folder without them (`demo_package_legal`). The bundle is what players install, so it holds no tester files (ADR-5002): `README.txt` is the player README (the demo's name and version, `Build <git>`, how to start it with and without Steam, the controls as the demo's panel shows them, what it does and does not send, and where it writes), and the Windows bundle has no `run-showcase.cmd` (`dist --no-launcher`). The texts are written to `readme/<platform>/README.txt` and passed to `dist --readme`. Check `archive/` with `b3sum --check CHECKSUMS.b3`, or `cargo xtask demo-package --verify target/demo-package`.

## Uploading (your step)

`depot/scripts/UPLOAD.txt` has the command: `steamcmd +login <build account> +run_app_build <path>/depot/scripts/app_build_<appid>.vdf`. `setlive` is empty, so the build waits on the partner site until you set a branch.

## Building the platforms

Windows builds with `cargo xwin` and Linux with `cargo zigbuild` (glibc 2.31) from a Linux host, as for [test bundles](book/user-guide/test-bundles.md). Without them, build elsewhere and pass `--from-windows` / `--from-linux`.

The glibc floor also applies to linked system libraries. A newer host's ALSA,
udev or D-Bus library can prevent a 2.31 build from linking. Use a verified,
isolated build sysroot with compatible versions of those existing dependencies
and set `PKG_CONFIG_SYSROOT_DIR` and `PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR` for the build. Keep these
build libraries out of the package. Do not suppress unresolved-symbol checks or
raise the floor to make a build pass; inspect the resulting ELF and test it in
the target runtime (ADR-4862).

## Complete-package verification

Verification requires `demo-package.json` and every target it names. Each target
needs its shipping-profile bundle, depot content directory, and archive; their
manifests must agree, and the files must match those manifests. The archive
inventory and `CHECKSUMS.b3` must cover exactly the named targets. Empty or
duplicate checksum lists fail. Shipped scene licenses are checked again, and
depot scripts must match the package targets with `setlive` empty (ADR-4862).
Links and special files are refused before opening package artifacts.

Additional diagnostics: `demo_package_invalid` for a missing/invalid summary or
bundle contract; `demo_package_inventory` for missing/unlisted files or checksum
rows; `demo_package_manifest` for differing manifests across copies;
`demo_package_script` for missing/changed depot scripts;
`demo_package_special_file` for links or special files;
`demo_package_git_unknown` for a bundle that records no build id;
`demo_package_git_mismatch` for a bundle whose id differs from the one `demo-package.json` records;
`demo_package_extra_launcher` for a `run-*.cmd` other than `run-demo.cmd`;
`demo_package_readme` for a `README.txt` that is not the player README of the bundle's build. An unreadable artifact
also fails verification. Existing dist and asset-license errors remain errors.

Checksums establish integrity against the provided manifests, not publisher
identity. Keep the separately recorded archive hashes with the handoff. A fixture
package in a unit test is not evidence of a runnable shipping build. Native
Windows/Linux launch, real gamepad input, and Deck acceptance use the exact
archives produced for release. The Linux tar extracts to `regia-deck-<version>/`.

<!-- source: book/systems/profiling.md -->
# Profiling and performance tools

Regia Engine treats frame time as a feature: per-frame engine work carries `tracing` spans, the GPU
passes are timed with timestamp queries, frame statistics are always available to the game and
the agent protocol, and soak runs check budgets that include a **hitch rule** (no frame over
50 ms after the first ten seconds of play). This chapter shows where each number comes from.

## Frame statistics in the game

`DefaultPlugins` installs `DiagnosticsPlugin`, which keeps the `Diagnostics` resource up to date:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// Logs frame statistics and the five most expensive CPU spans every ten seconds at 60 fps.
fn frame_report(time: Res<Time>, diagnostics: Res<Diagnostics>, profiler: Option<Res<Profiler>>) {
    if time.frame_count() % 600 != 0 {
        return;
    }
    info!(
        "{:.1} fps (1% low {:.1}), {:.2} ms avg, {} entities, {} draw calls",
        diagnostics.fps,
        diagnostics.fps_1pct_low,
        diagnostics.frame_time_avg.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0,
        diagnostics.entity_count,
        diagnostics.draw_calls,
    );
    if let Some(profiler) = profiler {
        for (span, cost) in profiler.0.top(5) {
            info!("  {span}: {:.3} ms", cost.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0);
        }
    }
}
```

- `Diagnostics`: fps, average frame time, the 1 % low, entity count, draw calls, and allocated
  bytes when a counting allocator is installed.
- `Profiler` (from `regia::run`): the process-wide frame profiler, fed by the logging layer. It
  keeps per-span-name CPU time for the recent frames: `last_frame()`, `averages(n)`, `top(n)`.
  Spans are free when nobody records them, so instrument your own expensive systems with
  `#[tracing::instrument]` or `info_span!` the same way the engine does.

The agent protocol's `play.get_diagnostics` returns the same numbers, which is how scripts, CI and
soak runs read them from a running game.

## Whole-run span reports in benches

`Profiler` keeps only the recent frames. To see where a whole bench run's CPU time went, wrap a
profiler in `regia_core::profiling::RunTotals`: call `end_frame()` once per measured frame,
`skip_frame()` for warm-up frames, and print `report(n)`. The table lists the `n` span names and
ECS systems with the most **self time** (the span's time minus the child spans entered inside it on
the same thread), with their inclusive time and calls per frame. Times are means per frame summed
over every thread, so a span that runs on four workers at once can exceed the frame time. Work a
span hands to another thread and then waits for counts as the waiting span's self time.

The engine's headless benches print it when `REGIA_SPAN_REPORT` is set (the value is the row
count; any other value prints 30 rows):

```console
$ REGIA_SPAN_REPORT=25 cargo run --release -p arena -- --bench
$ REGIA_SPAN_REPORT=25 cargo run --release -p render_lab -- sponza_1080p_runtime_fps
$ REGIA_SPAN_REPORT=25 cargo run --release -p terrain_lab -- --do27-chase --variants base
```

In your own bench, call `RunTotals::install_from_env()` first thing in `main`: it starts logging
with the profiler installed and returns `None` when the variable is unset. A process that also
runs the telemetry plugin uses `RunTotals::spans_only`, because both would drain the same
per-system counters. The engine's own hotspot history is in `docs/perf-log.md`.

## Flame graph

`Profiler`'s flat totals lose the call hierarchy. Turn on flame capture and read the span call tree
back over a window of frames:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia::core::profiling::FlameGraph;

fn flame_graph(profiler: Res<Profiler>, time: Res<Time>) {
    profiler.0.set_flame_enabled(true); // once, at startup
    if time.frame_count() % 600 == 0 {
        let graph: FlameGraph = profiler.0.flame_graph(120); // mean over the last 120 frames
        info!("{}", graph.folded_stacks());                    // grep-friendly `name;name  <self ms>`
        std::fs::write("frame.svg", graph.to_svg()).ok();      // capture to file
    }
}
```

`flame_graph` returns the engine's span call tree (the `scope!` spans and host sections), each node
with `inclusive`, `self_time`, `calls` and its `children`; `folded_stacks` and `to_svg` are the text and
SVG forms. A span whose nearest timed ancestor is a system or schedule span appears as a root; ECS
systems themselves stay on the flat per-system table (`top`, `take_system_times`). Capture keeps at most
65536 edges per frame; further exits in that frame are dropped and do not allocate a call path. Leave
capture on only while you need it.

## Work on other threads

Every ECS system runs inside its own span (bevy's `trace` feature), but a span covers only the
thread it was entered on. Work a system hands to a pool or a worker thread opens its own span there,
so it is counted too:

| Span | Where it runs | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `par_chunk` | compute pool | one chunk of `regia_core::tasks::par_chunks` / `par_chunks_mut`; `of` names the caller's span, `index` the chunk |
| `async_task` | async compute pool | a future started with `regia_core::tasks::spawn`, on every poll; `of` names the caller's span |
| `io_task` | IO pool | a future started with `regia_core::tasks::spawn_io`, on every poll; `of` names the caller's span |
| `scatter_collect_tiles` | compute pool | one tile range of the scatter cull (`collect`) |
| `finish_segment` | `regia-encode-*` workers (or the render thread) | `CommandEncoder::finish` of one frame segment |
| `finish_join` | render thread | the frame's last `finish` plus the wait for the workers' segments |
| `collect_gpu_timings` | render thread | reading back the timestamp queries of older frames |

Each is a child of the span that was current where the work was handed off, so Tracy and the
`of` field tie it to the system that asked for it. Their times add up over every thread, like
every other span in the tables above. Your own `par_chunks` calls get `par_chunk` spans without any
code; in a `regia_core::tasks::scope`, open a span inside each spawned task (create it before the
spawn and use `span.in_scope(..)`, as the scatter cull does). ADR-1378 records the audit that added
them.

## GPU timings

The renderer times each pass with timestamp queries when the device supports them.
`FrameRenderer::gpu_timings()` (reach it through the `RuntimeRenderer` resource) returns
`GpuTimings`: shadows (and each sun cascade and the local-light atlas separately), light clusters,
depth prepass, GPU culling, SSAO, forward, screen-space GI, SSR, atmosphere, clouds, froxel fog,
post, and the terrain's own share of the forward pass. `report()` formats them as one line:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_render::RuntimeRenderer;

fn gpu_report(time: Res<Time>, renderer: Res<RuntimeRenderer>) {
    if time.frame_count() % 600 == 0 {
        info!("gpu: {}", renderer.0.gpu_timings().report());
    }
}
```

On the window path the values are at least two frames old (the renderer never waits on the
query). Measure with the GPU busy: an idle GPU clocks down and every pass reads longer.

## Tracy

`regia_core` has a `tracy` feature that streams every span to the
[Tracy](https://github.com/wolfpld/tracy) profiler. Enable it in your launcher's `Cargo.toml`
(add `regia_core` with `features = ["tracy"]`), start Tracy, and run the game: CPU spans from
every thread appear on its timeline.

## Picking the GPU

On machines with several adapters, `REGIA_GPU_UUID`, `REGIA_GPU_PCI`, `REGIA_GPU_INDEX` or
`REGIA_GPU_NAME` choose the card for every device the engine creates, and `REGIA_GPU_STRICT=1`
makes an unmatched request an error instead of a fallback.
[Performance and benches](book/user-guide/perf-benches.md) has the details and the adapter list.

## Soak runs and the hitch rule

`cargo xtask soak` runs a built game for minutes at a time, samples it through the agent protocol,
optionally drives it with an input script, and checks the result against a budgets file:

```console
$ cargo build --release -p arena
$ cargo xtask soak --exe target/release/arena --minutes 5 --project-dir samples/arena \
    --input budgets/arena-soak.input.ron -- --bots 4
```

`budgets/default.ron` is the desktop reference budget:

| Budget | Default |
|---|---|
| `frame_p99_ms` | 6.9 ms |
| `frame_max_ms` (the hitch rule) | 50 ms, after `warmup_secs` |
| `warmup_secs` | 10 s |
| `rss_mb` | 1536 MB peak |
| `start_secs` (cold start to first agent answer) | 3 s |
| `errors`, `crashes` | 0 |
| `warns` | 2 |

The soak derives an unclamped frame-time series from the frame counter and the wall clock, so a
frame-rate cap cannot hide a hitch. `--sessions K` repeats the run; reports go to
`docs/evidence/m18/` by default; `cargo xtask budgets check` re-checks a written report.

## Hitch reports

Zero hitches is a hard gate (`docs/specs/27-renderer-excellence.md` § 2.4): after warm-up no
pipeline or bind group is created on the frame path, no frame is over 50 ms and the frame-time
percentiles stay close to the median. The `play.hitch_report` agent method measures a running
app against it:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"play.hitch_report","params":{"seconds":60,"warmup_s":2}}
```

The reply comes after `warmup_s + seconds`, with the frame-interval percentiles (`p50_ms`,
`p99_ms`, `p999_ms`), the hitch counts (`over_2x_p50`, `over_50ms`, `longest_ms`), the renderer's
device calls after warm-up (pipelines, bind groups, buffers, textures, uploads, blocking polls),
the worst spikes, and a `pass` verdict with every missed row in words. The usual fix for creates
on the frame path is `FrameRenderer::prewarm` at level load. The causes, their fixes and the
look-dev soak that drives whole maps are in the agent guide's [Hitches](book/agents/hitches.md)
page.

## Benches

| Tool | What it measures |
|---|---|
| `render_lab` (`samples/render_lab`) | Reference render scenes; `render_lab outdoor` prints atmosphere, cloud and froxel-fog pass times on a Desktop High frame |
| `samples/lookdev` (`look_r2`, `default_look`, `do27_chase`) | The look-dev shots with measurements; `do27_chase` replays a vehicle chase on *Direct Order 27*'s content and prints wall, CPU and per-pass GPU p50/p99 |
| `arena --bench` | The arena's bot simulation without rendering |
| `cargo xtask build-times` | Clean and incremental build times against the workspace budgets |

[Performance and benches](book/user-guide/perf-benches.md) covers the DO27 frame bench in detail.

## Budgets to keep in mind

- **Hot paths do not allocate.** Engine systems reuse buffers frame to frame; do the same in
  yours (keep a `Local<Vec<_>>`).
- **Per-frame work over 0.1 ms gets a span**, so it shows up in `Profiler` and Tracy.
- **Pipelines are built before gameplay.** Material graphs and new render paths compile on first
  use; render a warm-up frame behind a loading screen so the first real frame does not hitch.

<!-- source: book/systems/mesh-queries.md -->
# Mesh queries

`regia_core::mesh_query` answers spatial questions about triangle meshes and point sets on the
CPU: where does a ray hit, what is the closest surface point, which triangles are in this box,
do two meshes touch, is a point inside, how far is it from the surface. It has no engine state:
you build a structure from a mesh once and query it as often as you like, from a game system, a
tool or the asset pipeline (ADR-1461).

| Structure | Built from | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `TriMesh` | positions and index triples (or a flat index buffer) | the validated mesh every other structure uses |
| `TriBvh` | a `TriMesh` | `ray_cast`, `closest_point`, `triangles_in_aabb`, `triangles_in_sphere`, `intersects` and `intersecting_pairs` with another tree (optionally under an `Affine3A`) |
| `WindingNumberTree` | a `TriMesh` or a `TriBvh` | `winding_number`, `is_inside` |
| `SignedDistanceGrid` | a `WindingNumberTree` (or a `TriMesh`) and `SdfParams` | `sample`, `gradient`, `sample_with_gradient`, grid values |
| `PointHash` | a slice of points and a cell size | `within_radius`, `nearest` |

`winding_number_exact` and the `triangle` module (closest point, ray hit, triangle/box and
triangle/triangle overlap, solid angle on one triangle) are there for one-off questions and as
references for tests.

## Example

```rust
use regia_core::glam::Vec3;
use regia_core::math::Ray;
use regia_core::mesh_query::{
    MeshQueryError, SdfParams, SignedDistanceGrid, TriMesh, WindingNumberTree,
};

/// Builds the queries for one mesh and asks it a few questions.
fn mesh_questions(positions: Vec<Vec3>, indices: &[u32]) -> Result<(), MeshQueryError> {
    let mesh = TriMesh::from_indices(positions, indices)?;
    let tree = WindingNumberTree::build(mesh)?;
    let bvh = tree.bvh();
    let down = Ray::new(Vec3::new(0.0, 5.0, 0.0), Vec3::NEG_Y);
    if let Some(hit) = bvh.ray_cast(&down, 100.0) {
        println!("hit triangle {} at {} m", hit.triangle, hit.distance);
    }
    let nearest = bvh.closest_point(Vec3::ZERO, f32::INFINITY);
    let inside = tree.is_inside(Vec3::ZERO);
    let sdf = SignedDistanceGrid::build(&tree, &SdfParams::new(0.05))?;
    println!("{nearest:?} inside={inside} distance={:?}", sdf.sample(Vec3::ZERO));
    Ok(())
}
```

## Meshes and errors

A `TriMesh` checks every index against the vertex count and rejects NaN or infinite positions.
Triangles are counter-clockwise when seen from outside; `TriMesh::flip` reverses them all.
Degenerate (zero-area) triangles are kept: closest-point and overlap tests treat them as segments
or points, rays never hit them, and they add nothing to a winding number.

Every failure is a `MeshQueryError`:

| Variant | When |
|---|---|
| `EmptyMesh` | a tree, winding tree or distance grid is built from a mesh without triangles |
| `IndexCount` | a flat index list's length is not a multiple of three |
| `IndexOutOfRange` | a triangle names a vertex the mesh does not have |
| `NonFinite` | a position or point has a NaN or infinite coordinate |
| `TooLarge` | more elements than a `u32` index can name |
| `InvalidCellSize` | a grid cell size is zero, negative or not finite |
| `GridTooLarge` | a distance grid would exceed `SdfParams::max_points` (2²⁵ by default) |
| `InvalidBeta` | the winding-number `beta` is not finite and positive |

Queries do not fail: a ray with a zero direction, a NaN point or a negative radius simply finds
nothing. The one exception is `winding_number`, which returns NaN for a non-finite point
(`is_inside` is then `false`); filter such points before averaging winding numbers.

## The tree

`TriBvh` is a binary tree of axis-aligned boxes, split at the midpoint of the longest axis of the
triangle centroids, with at most four triangles per leaf. Ray and closest-point searches visit the
nearer child first and skip boxes farther than the best answer so far, so a query near the surface
touches a handful of leaves. The one slow case is a point deep inside a closed, round mesh: from
the center of a sphere every triangle is about equally far, and the search must look at most of
them. All per-triangle math runs in `f64`; results are `f32`.

`intersects` and `intersecting_pairs` walk two trees together. Pass `Some(&other_to_self)` when
the second mesh is placed by a transform; touching (a shared vertex or edge) counts as an
intersection.

## Inside and outside: winding numbers

The generalized winding number is 1 inside a closed mesh and 0 outside. Unlike a ray-parity test
it degrades gracefully: a mesh with a hole gives values a little under 1 inside, a few flipped
triangles disturb only the points close to them, and a triangle soup still gets a sensible answer.
`is_inside` means "winding number above 0.5".

`WindingNumberTree` stores a small far-field expansion on every tree node, so far-away parts of the
mesh are summed in one step. `beta` trades accuracy for speed: the expansion is used once a node is
farther than `beta` times its own size. The default is 2. Measured largest errors against the exact
sum, over points in and around the mesh:

| Mesh | beta 2 | beta 4 | beta 8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| sphere, 2,208 triangles | 0.041 | 0.0089 | 0.00046 |
| torus, 2,304 triangles | 0.020 | 0.0018 | 0.00028 |
| random soup, 1,500 triangles | 0.0024 | 0.00018 | 0.000015 |

The error falls about as `1 / beta³`. For inside/outside tests the default is plenty; raise `beta`
(`set_beta`, no rebuild) when you use the value itself.

## Signed distance grids

`SignedDistanceGrid::build` samples the signed distance to the mesh on a regular grid: negative
inside, positive outside, grid points at `origin() + (i, j, k) * cell_size()`. The grid covers the
mesh's box plus `2 * exact_band` cells and `margin` on every side.

1. Every grid point within `exact_band` cells of a triangle's box gets the exact distance.
2. With `sweep` on (the default), fast sweeping carries the closest triangle outward so every point
   gets the distance to a nearby triangle. Outside the band this is an upper bound that is usually
   exact; with `sweep` off, points outside the band keep a large placeholder distance.
3. The winding number decides each point's sign, so open meshes work. Blocks of 4³ points that lie
   outside every triangle's band (its box grown by `exact_band` cells) are signed with one evaluation;
   blocks that touch a band are signed per point.

`sample` interpolates trilinearly between grid points and `gradient` returns that interpolant's
derivative (about unit length near the surface, pointing outward). Both return `None` outside
`bounds()`. In the tests, every grid point and every sample of a tessellated sphere is within one
cell of the analytic distance.

## Point hash

`PointHash` buckets points in cubic cells. `within_radius(center, r)` returns the indices of all
points within `r` (any radius; a sphere far larger than the cells visits occupied cells instead),
in ascending order. `nearest(center, max_distance)` searches growing shells of cells and falls back
to a scan when the points are too spread out for shells to pay off. Pick a cell size near your
typical query radius.

## Cost

One thread, release build, a 100,000-triangle sphere:

| Operation | Time |
|---|---|
| `TriBvh::build` | 14 ms |
| `closest_point`, points near the surface | 2.3 µs each |
| `closest_point`, points 1 to 2 radii outside | 23 µs each |
| `closest_point`, points deep inside | 380 µs each |
| `ray_cast` | 0.7 µs each |
| `WindingNumberTree::from_bvh` | 9 ms |
| `winding_number` | 2.4 µs each |
| `winding_number_exact` | 2.3 ms each |
| `SignedDistanceGrid`, 45³ points | 0.7 s |
| `SignedDistanceGrid`, 85³ points | 2.9 s |

Distance grids are meant to be built offline or at load, not per frame. The benchmark is the
ignored test `bench_100k_triangles` in `crates/regia_core/tests/mesh_query.rs`:

```sh
cargo test --release -p regia_core --test mesh_query -- --ignored --nocapture bench_100k
```

## Agents

There is no agent-protocol method for this module: it holds no engine state, so there is nothing
for an agent to inspect or change. Features built on it (a distance-field bake, a query method on
the scene) carry their own methods and pages.

## Sources

The tree, winding-number, distance-grid and point-hash code is ported from geometry3Sharp by Ryan
Schmidt (Boost Software License 1.0), with the changes listed in `docs/provenance.md`. The methods
come from A. Jacobson, L. Kavan and O. Sorkine-Hornung, "Robust Inside-Outside Segmentation using
Generalized Winding Numbers" (SIGGRAPH 2013); G. Barill, N. Dickson, R. Schmidt, D. Levin and A.
Jacobson, "Fast Winding Numbers for Soups and Clouds" (SIGGRAPH 2018); H. Zhao, "A fast sweeping
method for Eikonal equations" (2005); and, for the triangle tests, C. Ericson, *Real-Time Collision
Detection*, Möller and Trumbore (1997), Akenine-Möller (2001) and van Oosterom and Strackee (1983).

# Vehicles

<!-- index: Vehicle -->
<!-- index: Wheel -->
<!-- index: Drivetrain -->
<!-- index: Trailer -->
<!-- index: Aircraft -->
<!-- index: Hover craft -->
<!-- index: Bike -->
<!-- index: Tracked vehicle -->

`regia_physics::vehicle` drives wheeled vehicles with rapier's ray-cast vehicle controller. A
vehicle is one dynamic chassis body. Each wheel is a ray cast down its suspension each step, not a
rigid body. The ray finds the ground, a spring and damper push the chassis up, and tire impulses
drive, brake and corner it. This is cheap and stable at game speeds. It does not model tire
deformation. Wheel spin, a gearbox, and differentials are the optional geared drivetrain below.
Trailers, a two-wheel bike, a hover hull, a fixed-wing aircraft, and skid-steer tracks are
separate models under [Other hulls](#other-hulls). The editor's
[Vehicle Tuning](book/user-guide/editor-guide/vehicle-tuning.md) tab edits the car, trailer, aircraft, bike,
and hover hull. Agent calls are
[Vehicles (agents)](book/agents/vehicles.md).

## Axes and units

The engine's axes apply: the chassis' forward is local −Z, right is +X, up is +Y. Every wheel's
suspension points down the chassis' −Y and its axle runs along +X, so model wheel meshes with the
axle on +X. Distances are meters, mass kilograms, forces newtons, angles radians.

## Configure

`VehicleConfig::default()` is a 1,200 kg four-wheel car: a 1.8 m × 0.7 m × 4.2 m box, 2.6 m
wheelbase, 1.6 m track, front-wheel steering, rear-wheel drive and brakes on all four wheels.
Wheels 0 and 1 are front left and right; 2 and 3 are rear left and right.

```rust
use regia_core::math::Vec3;
use regia_physics::vehicle::{VehicleConfig, VehicleError, WheelConfig};

fn all_wheel_drive_car() -> Result<VehicleConfig, VehicleError> {
    let mut config = VehicleConfig::default();
    config.max_engine_force = 4500.0; // per driven wheel at full throttle
    for wheel in &mut config.wheels {
        wheel.drive = true; // all-wheel drive
    }
    config.wheels.push(WheelConfig {
        position: Vec3::new(0.0, -0.2, 2.0), // a trailing fifth wheel
        ..WheelConfig::default()
    });
    config.validate()?;
    Ok(config)
}
```

| `VehicleConfig` field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `chassis_half_extents`, `chassis_mass`, `center_of_mass` | The chassis box, its mass and its center of mass in chassis space. Lower the center of mass to keep the car upright in hard turns. |
| `max_engine_force` | Newtons per driven wheel at full throttle. |
| `max_brake_force` | Newtons per braking wheel at full brake. |
| `rolling_resistance` | Newtons per wheel that is neither driving nor braking, so a coasting car slows down. 0 lets it roll forever. |
| `max_steer_angle` | Steered wheels' angle at full lock, in `[0, π/2)`. |
| `wheels` | 1 to 32 `WheelConfig`s. Their order is the readout order. |

| `WheelConfig` field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `position` | The suspension's top (hard point) in chassis space. It may sit inside the chassis collider: wheel rays ignore the chassis. |
| `radius` | Wheel radius. |
| `suspension_rest_length`, `suspension_travel` | Spring length at rest and how far it may compress or extend from it. The ray reaches `rest length + radius` below the hard point. |
| `suspension_stiffness` | Spring rate **per kilogram of chassis** (1/s²): a wheel pushes with `stiffness · compression · chassis_mass` newtons. `n` equal wheels settle compressed by about `g / (n · stiffness)`. The default 30 compresses each of four wheels by about 8 cm. |
| `suspension_compression_damping`, `suspension_relaxation_damping` | Damping while compressing and extending, per kilogram of chassis. A damping ratio of about 0.3 to 0.6 is `ratio · 2 · sqrt(n · stiffness) / n`. Raise relaxation damping if the car bounces. |
| `max_suspension_force` | Cap on one suspension's force. |
| `friction_slip` | Tire grip: the most tire impulse per step is `suspension force · dt · friction_slip`. Higher values brake and corner harder, and can flip the car. |
| `side_friction_stiffness` | Multiplier on the cornering impulse. |
| `steer`, `drive`, `brake` | Whether the wheel steers, is driven, and brakes. |

`validate` names the first bad field: `VehicleError::InvalidWheel { index, field }`,
`InvalidConfig { field }`, `NoWheels` or `TooManyWheels`. `VehicleError::code()` gives a stable
lowercase identifier (`vehicle_invalid_wheel`, …) for logs and the agent protocol.

## With the ECS

Add `VehiclePlugin` after `PhysicsPlugin` and create vehicles with `spawn_vehicle`. The entity gets
the chassis' `RigidBodyHandle` and `ColliderHandle`, so the physics step writes its `Transform` and
queries and collision events name it. It also gets a `VehicleController` and a `VehicleInput`.

```rust
use regia_app::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_physics::PhysicsPlugin;
use regia_physics::vehicle::{VehicleConfig, VehicleError, VehicleInput, VehiclePlugin, spawn_vehicle};

fn add_car(app: &mut App) -> Result<Entity, VehicleError> {
    app.add_plugins((PhysicsPlugin, VehiclePlugin));
    spawn_vehicle(app.world_mut(), VehicleConfig::default(), Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), Quat::IDENTITY)
}

/// The player's controls, filled by the game's input mapping.
#[derive(Resource, Default)]
struct Controls {
    accelerate: f32,
    reverse: f32,
    brake: f32,
    stick_x: f32,
}

fn drive(mut cars: Query<&mut VehicleInput>, controls: Res<Controls>) {
    for mut input in &mut cars {
        input.throttle = controls.accelerate - controls.reverse; // -1..1
        input.brake = controls.brake; // 0..1
        input.steer = controls.stick_x; // +1 = right
    }
}
```

The plugin updates every vehicle once per `FixedUpdate`, inside the `PhysicsStep` chain after the
velocity sync and before the step, in entity spawn order. Input is clamped; a non-finite value
reads as released. When an update fails (the chassis was removed, say), the error lands in
`VehicleController::last_error` and the vehicle is skipped. Nothing panics. Despawning the entity
removes the chassis from the world.

`throttle` and `brake` interact per wheel: on a wheel that can brake, braking cancels its engine
force. With brakes on every wheel, throttle plus brake holds the car still.

## Without the ECS

`Vehicle` works on a bare `PhysicsWorld`, for tools and tests:

```rust
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_physics::PhysicsWorld;
use regia_physics::vehicle::{Vehicle, VehicleConfig, VehicleError, VehicleInput};

fn make_car(physics: &mut PhysicsWorld) -> Result<Vehicle, VehicleError> {
    Vehicle::spawn(physics, VehicleConfig::default(), Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), Quat::IDENTITY)
}

/// Every fixed step, before the world steps.
fn drive_one_step(
    physics: &mut PhysicsWorld,
    vehicle: &mut Vehicle,
    input: VehicleInput,
    dt: f32,
) -> Result<(), VehicleError> {
    vehicle.update(physics, input, dt)
}
```

`Vehicle::attach` turns an existing dynamic body with mass into a chassis and keeps its colliders.
A vehicle's chassis never sleeps, because its wheels push it every step.

## Wheel poses for rendering

`vehicle.wheel_states(&physics)` returns one `WheelState` per wheel, posed against the chassis'
current pose:

- `local_translation` / `local_rotation`: the wheel in chassis space (the hard point moved down by
  the suspension length; steer about +Y, then spin about +X). Use these when wheel meshes are
  children of the chassis entity.
- `world_translation` / `world_rotation`: the same in world space.
- `steer_angle` (about +Y, a right turn reads negative) and `spin_angle` (grows while rolling
  forward; the mesh turns by `-spin_angle` about +X).
- `grounded`, `compression`, `suspension_length`, `contact_point`, `contact_normal`,
  `ground_collider`, `ground_entity` and `suspension_force` for gameplay: dust, skid marks, sounds.

`vehicle.state(&physics)` adds the chassis pose, `forward` axis, velocities, `forward_speed` and the
grounded-wheel count. Its `linear_velocity` is rapier's end-of-step velocity. A car resting on its
springs reads a small downward vertical velocity (about −0.06 m/s at 60 Hz) while its position
holds still: the suspension impulse lands once per step and gravity acts across the solver's
substeps. `forward_speed` is not affected.

## Reset

`vehicle.reset(&mut physics, position, rotation)` teleports the chassis to a pose at rest (no
velocity, no forces) and clears the wheels. `reset_to_spawn` returns to the pose it was spawned or
attached at. No wheel is grounded until the next update casts the rays.

## A geared drivetrain

`VehicleConfig::drivetrain` picks the drive model. `Drivetrain::Simple`, the default, is `max_engine_force` per driven
wheel. `Drivetrain::Geared` has an engine with a torque curve, a slip clutch, a gearbox (automatic or manual) and open,
locked or limited-slip differentials for rear, front or all-wheel drive. Each wheel has its own spin, the tire force
follows the slip ratio, and `VehicleState` reads `rpm`, `gear`, `speed` and each wheel's `slip_ratio` and `slip_angle`.

```rust
use regia_physics::vehicle::VehicleConfig;
use regia_physics::vehicle_drivetrain::{AbsConfig, AeroConfig, AntiRollBar, Differential, Drivetrain, DrivetrainConfig};

fn limited_slip_car() -> VehicleConfig {
    let mut config = VehicleConfig {
        drivetrain: Drivetrain::Geared(DrivetrainConfig {
            rear_differential: Differential::LimitedSlip { torque_bias: 2.5 },
            ..DrivetrainConfig::default()
        }),
        anti_roll: vec![AntiRollBar { left: 0, right: 1, stiffness: 14_000.0 }],
        aero: Some(AeroConfig::default()),
        ..VehicleConfig::default()
    };
    config.aids.abs = Some(AbsConfig::default());
    config
}
```

`anti_roll` and `aero` work with either model. The aids need `Geared`. Use `Vehicle::request_shift` and
`Vehicle::set_automatic_shifting` to shift in code. In `.vehicle.ron` these are the v2 sections; see
`docs/formats/vehicle.md` for every field. A v1 file loads as `Simple` and drives exactly as before.

A held brake leaves a slow creep on a slope, because a locked tire's force comes from its slip. The speed is
about `peak_slip · tan(slope) / peak_friction`, a little more at a 60 Hz step: with the default tire about 3.4 cm/s on a 15
degree hill, or 2 m a minute.

## Other hulls

These share the engine axes (forward is local −Z, right is +X, up is +Y) and they are not the
ray-cast car. None of them is a lockstep model. A lockstep game uses
`regia_detsim::ground_vehicle` for tracked and wheeled units. See
[Movement models](book/user-guide/movement-models.md).

- **Trailer** (`regia_physics::vehicle_trailer`). A trailer chassis couples to a tow vehicle at a
  hitch, or a tractor couples at a fifth wheel. Brakes, a jackknife stop in reverse, and a
  multi-trailer train are part of the model. The asset is a trailer configuration beside the car.
- **Bike** (`regia_physics::vehicle_bike`, `.bike.ron`). Lean, steer, and speed for two wheels.
  It does not drive the car solver and it does not read a chassis body. The caller passes steer,
  speed, the drive command, and the two wheel-ray lengths each step. Below the upright speed the
  target lean is zero and a spring stands the bike up. Lean past the limit sets `fallen`.
- **Hover hull** (`regia_physics::hover`, `.hoverhull.ron`). A dynamic box held up by ray-cast
  thrusters. Each thruster pushes along the ground normal. Drive, brake, yaw, and lateral-slip
  impulses act only while some thruster has ground. `VehiclePlugin` reads the entity's
  `VehicleInput`. Forward is the same axis as the car.
- **Aircraft** (`regia_physics::aero`, `.aircraft.ron`). One dynamic body, lifting surfaces,
  engines, and landing-gear rays. Positive pitch raises the nose, positive roll lowers the right
  wing, positive yaw turns the nose right. The model has no downwash, no ground effect, no
  propeller wash, no compressibility, and no stall hysteresis. `trim` solves level flight offline.
- **Tracks** (`regia_physics::vehicle_track`). Two track speeds on one rigid body in the XZ plane.
  This is a pure function, not the wheeled solver. Throttle is clamped to −1..=1. Coasting moves
  a track toward zero and does not reverse it. Yaw rate is the speed difference divided by the
  track separation (2 m).

The proving-ground rides for these hulls are editor actions. This chapter is the runtime.

## Determinism

Same build, same platform, same inputs and fixed step: bit-identical runs (the test drives a
scripted 300-step run twice and compares `PhysicsWorld::state_digest` every step). The plugin
updates vehicles in entity spawn order, so several vehicles stay reproducible too.

Two CPU architectures (an x86-64 PC and an aarch64 phone) may compute different bits, so these
vehicles do not belong on a lockstep simulation. A lockstep game uses the kinematic tracked and
wheeled models of `regia_detsim::ground_vehicle` instead (ADR-8841; see
[Movement models](book/user-guide/movement-models.md)).

## Agents

`physics.vehicles`, `physics.vehicle_input` and `physics.vehicle_reset` read, drive and reset
vehicles over the agent protocol, and `physics.vehicle_telemetry` and `physics.vehicle_shift` read the
drivetrain and change gear; see [Vehicles (agents)](book/agents/vehicles.md).
