# Asset creators

Several places in the editor create something new. None of them is a dock tab of its own; each is a
menu or a small form, and each calls the same code as its agent method, so a person and an agent make
the same files. This page lists them: the Content browser's **New** menu (assets), the **Create** menu
(entities in the level), **File ▸ New script…**, and the project browser's template picker.
Depth: [Editor creators](book/agents/editor-creators.md), [Create menu and viewport
helpers](book/agents/create-menu.md).

## New assets: the Content browser's New menu

The **Content** tab has a **New** button next to **Import…**. Each entry creates a file in the folder
the browser is showing, under the first free name `<kind>-<n>.<extension>`, with the kind in snake case (`material-1.material.ron`,
then `material-2.material.ron`; `material_graph-1.matgraph.ron`), selects it and shows `Created <path>` on the toolbar. With no
project open, the toast says `no project is open`.

| New entry | File | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Material | `.material.ron` | |
| Prefab | `.prefab.ron` | |
| Level | `.level.ron` | |
| Anim graph | `.animgraph.ron` | |
| Sound cue | `.cue.ron` | |
| UI layout | `.ui.ron` | |
| Data asset ▸ *type* | `.data.ron` | A submenu of the registered data asset types; the new file opens in the Data Asset panel (the `data-asset.md` page of this guide). With no registered type the submenu says so. |
| Material graph | `.matgraph.ron` | |
| Material function | `.matfunc.ron` | |
| Sequence | `.seq.ron` | |
| Shot list | `.shots.ron` | |
| Attribute set | `.attrs.ron` | |
| Effect | `.effect.ron` | |
| Ability | `.ability.ron` | |
| Material instance ▸ *graph* | `.matinst.ron` | A submenu of the project's `.matgraph.ron` files: the instance has that graph as its parent and no overrides. With no material graph the submenu says so. |
| Folder | none | A folder under `assets/`. |

An agent makes the same files at a path it chooses with `editor.create_asset`:

```json
{"method": "editor.create_asset", "params": {"kind": "sound_cue", "path": "assets/audio/door.cue.ron"}}
```

`kind` is the entry's name in snake case (`anim_graph`, `ui_layout`, `data_asset`, `material_graph`,
`shot_list`, `material_instance`, `folder`, ...). `data_asset` also needs `type`, and `material_instance`
needs `parent`. The path must end with the kind's extension; a path that escapes `assets/`, names a file
that already exists, or omits the extension is refused and nothing is written. The agent page
[Editor creators](book/agents/editor-creators.md) lists what each new file holds and the error codes of
the data asset methods.

## Create menu: entities in the level

**Create ▸ Shape ▸** adds a graybox primitive. Below it are **Player start**, **Trigger volume**,
**Point light**, **Spot light**, **Directional light**, **Camera** and **Reflection capture**. Each adds
one entity at the viewport's focus point, selects it and records one undo step. The agent method is
`editor.create_entity` with the kind (`player_start`, `trigger_volume`, `point_light`, `cuboid`, ...) and an
optional `translation`.

## New script wizard

**File ▸ New script…** opens a small **New script** window: a **Name** field, a **Template** choice
(`empty` or `component`) and **Create**. The window says where the file goes
(`game/src/scripts/<name>.rs`, registered at the `REGIA:SCRIPTS` marker). **Create** is disabled until the
name is valid and a project is open. After a successful Create the name field clears and the window shows
`created <path>`; **Close** hides the window.

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open the wizard | **File ▸ New script…** | `editor.script_wizard` with `open: true` |
| Create the script | **Create** | `editor.create_script` with `name`, `template` |

## Project browser: template picker

Launching the editor without a project shows the project browser. Under **New project**, type a
**Name**, pick a **Folder** (**Browse…**), choose a **Template** (**Blank**, **First Person**, **Third
Person**, **Top Down**) and press **Create project**. **Open folder…** opens an existing project, and
**Recent** lists projects opened before. The agent method is `editor.new_project` with `name`, `path`
and `template` (`blank`, `first_person`, `third_person`, `top_down`).

## Walk-through: a data asset

1. Open the **Content** tab and the folder that should hold it.
2. Press **New ▸ Data asset** and pick a type from the submenu.
3. The file is created as `data_asset-1.data.ron` (or the next free number) and opens in the Data Asset
   panel; edit its fields there and press **Save**.

## Actions

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| New asset in the shown folder | **Content ▸ New ▸ *kind*** | `editor.create_asset` |
| List creatable data asset types | the **Data asset** submenu | `editor.data_asset_types` |
| Add an entity at the focus point | **Create ▸ ...** | `editor.create_entity` |
| New script | **File ▸ New script…** | `editor.script_wizard`, `editor.create_script` |
| New project from a template | the project browser | `editor.new_project` |

None of these has a keyboard shortcut of its own.

## Known limits

- The New menu and the wizards are desktop-editor features; they need an open project.
- A data asset type appears in the New menu only when it is registered as a data asset.
- The project browser offers four templates; the `regia new` command has more (`quick`, `net_game`), which
  need command-line options.

## See also

[Content browser](book/user-guide/editor-guide/content-browser.md), [Project settings](book/user-guide/editor-guide/project-settings.md),
[Editor creators](book/agents/editor-creators.md), [Create menu and viewport
helpers](book/agents/create-menu.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/autosave-recovery.md -->
# Autosave and recovery

The editor saves a copy of your unsaved work in the background, and offers it back after a crash. It
covers the open level and every document panel that has unsaved edits: material graphs, procedural
graphs, UI designs and UI animations, behavior trees, state trees, tables, sound cues, VFX effects,
conversations, animation graphs, sequences, shot lists and prefabs. There is nothing to open: autosave
runs by itself, and the **Crash recovery** window appears at the next launch when something was left
behind. Depth: [Editor autosave and crash recovery](book/agents/editor-autosave.md), [Editor crash
reports](book/agents/editor-crash-reports.md).

## What is saved, and where

Every few minutes the editor writes:

- the open level, when it has unsaved edits, to `.regia/autosave/<name>.level.ron` in the project;
- each document with unsaved edits, to `.regia/autosave/docs/<id>.autosave`, with an index file.

The interval is the **Autosave interval (minutes)** preference (**Edit ▸ Preferences…**, category
**Autosave**): 5 by default, from 0 to 120, and 0 turns autosave off. The snapshot is taken on the main
thread; encoding and writing run on a worker thread, so editing does not wait for the disk.

Autosaves are editor state under `.regia/`: the cook and the packager read `assets/` only, so they are
never cooked or packaged. Saving a document removes its autosave. A normal exit removes every autosave
except the ones still waiting in the recovery window.

## Walk-through: recover after a crash

1. Reopen the project. If the last session did not exit cleanly, a **Crash recovery** window appears over
   the editor. It says `The editor closed unexpectedly.`
2. Under `A previous editor session left unsaved work behind:` each row shows the document's label, its
   kind (`level`, `matgraph`, `sound_cue`, ...), its original path, when it was saved and its size.
3. Press **Restore** on a row to bring it back: a level becomes the open level, and a document opens in
   its own panel at its original path. A restored item stays unsaved (dirty) until you save it, and its
   autosave stays until then.
4. Press **Discard** to throw a row away, or **Restore all** and **Discard all** for every row.
5. If the editor also wrote a crash report, the window shows its first line with **View report**, **Copy to
   clipboard**, **Open folder** and **Dismiss report**.

While a prefab is open, **Restore** of a level row is refused (close the prefab first); document rows
restore normally.

## Closing with unsaved work

Closing the editor with unsaved documents shows an **Unsaved changes** window listing them, with **Save
and exit**, **Discard and exit** and **Cancel**. A close requested by an agent (`quit.request`) exits without a prompt and writes
the dirty level's autosave first, so the next launch offers it.

## Actions

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Change or turn off the interval | **Preferences ▸ Autosave** | `editor.prefs_set` `autosave.interval_minutes` |
| Read autosave state (interval, ticks, dirty documents, last error) | none | `editor.autosave_state` |
| Autosave now | none | `editor.autosave_now` |
| List what is offered for recovery | the **Crash recovery** window | `editor.recovery_list` |
| Restore rows | **Restore**, **Restore all** | `editor.recovery_restore` (`ids`, or none for all) |
| Discard rows | **Discard**, **Discard all** | `editor.recovery_discard` (`ids`, or none for all) |
| Cancel a running game build or import | **Cancel** beside the compiling label (build), **Cancel import** (Content) | `editor.cancel_task` with `game_build` or `import` |

## Version history

Every autosave and every save of a level or an asset document also keeps a version of it in the
project's `.regia/history/` folder. **File ▸ Version history…** lists the versions of the open level (or
pick another level or document), with the time, whether an autosave or a save made it, and its size.
**Preview** shows a version's text read-only (for a level, its entity count too). **Restore** puts the
version back as a new change: nothing is written until you save, and **Edit ▸ Undo** takes it back. A
document's unsaved edits are kept as a "Before restore" version first. Preferences ▸ Autosave sets how many
autosave and save versions stay per file (10 each) and the history's size cap (512 MB); the oldest go first.

**File ▸ Duplicate project…** copies the project's source files to a new folder (no build output, caches or
editor state). On the command line, `regia upgrade-project --write --backup <folder>` makes the same copy to
a dated folder before it migrates anything; it also keeps the settings files directly inside `.regia/` (the
editor layouts it upgrades, `agent.toml`), but not the caches and autosaves in its subfolders.

| Action | Editor | Agent |
|---|---|---|
| List versions | File ▸ Version history… | `editor.versions` |
| Preview a version | **Preview** | `editor.version_preview` |
| Restore a version | **Restore** | `editor.version_restore` |
| Duplicate the project | File ▸ Duplicate project… | `editor.duplicate_project` |

## Keyboard

Autosave and the recovery window have no shortcuts of their own. The buttons are focusable: Tab reaches
them and Space or Enter presses the focused button.

## Known limits

- Only documents that are registered with the autosave registry are covered; a panel that holds
  unsaved state outside it is not.
- A document autosave is dropped when you save it by hand, so an autosave never outlives a save.
- The recovery list reads `.regia/autosave/docs/index.ron`; an index row with a malformed id or a file
  name that is not a plain name is ignored.

## See also

[Editor autosave and crash recovery](book/agents/editor-autosave.md), [Editor crash
reports](book/agents/editor-crash-reports.md), [Editor](book/user-guide/editor.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/panel-timings.md -->
# Panel timings

Panel timings are not a tab you open. The dock times how long every panel takes to draw and keeps
the results; you read them through an agent method, `editor.panel_timings`. They exist to catch a
panel whose draw time grows with the size of the project. This page also describes how the panels
behave in a large project, which is what the timings measure. Depth: [Editor panels at
scale](book/agents/editor-panel-timings.md).

## What the dock records

Each time a panel draws, the dock measures the draw and stores it under the panel's tab title
(`Outliner`, `Output Log`, `Inspector`, ...). Per panel it keeps the last 240 draw times (milliseconds)
and a count of the draws since the editor started or since the last clear. A panel that was never
drawn is not listed. There is no on-screen view, no setting and no keyboard shortcut for the timings.

## Walk-through: find the slow panel

1. Open a large level, or spawn many entities with `scene.spawn` in a loop.
2. Scroll the Outliner, filter the Output Log and edit a few values, so every panel draws for a while.
3. Ask for the timings: `{"method": "editor.panel_timings", "params": {"panel": "Outliner", "last": 30}}`.
   Omit `panel` for every panel; `last` is how many of the newest times to return per panel (1 to 240,
   default 60).
4. Read each panel's `draws`, `last_ms`, `median_ms` and `max_ms`. A panel whose times grow as the
   project grows is the one to look at. Pass `"clear": true` to forget every recorded time after reading.

## Large projects: what the panels do

The Outliner, the Output Log and the Inspector lay out only what is on screen, so their draw time
stays flat as the project grows.

- **Outliner.** The tree is flattened into the listed rows (the search and **Group by category** applied,
  each row's open or closed state respected), and only the rows in view are drawn. The arrow keys work
  on the whole list, on screen or not: **Up** and **Down** move the selection, **Shift+Up** and
  **Shift+Down** extend it, **Left** closes and **Right** opens the selected row. Shift-click selects the
  range between the primary selection and the clicked row. These keys work while the pointer is over the
  Outliner and no text field has focus. A selection made elsewhere (a viewport pick, `editor.select`)
  opens the entity's parents so its row is listed.
- **Output Log.** The panel keeps its own history of the last 100 000 lines, polled from the engine's
  log ring (which keeps 4 096). It has a level choice (**ERROR** to **TRACE**), a target-prefix field and a
  search field. A new line is tested against the filters once. Rows are one line high; click a row to
  show its whole message under the list, and **Close** hides it. Links in a row stay clickable.
- **Inspector.** A list, array, map or set longer than 200 elements shows one page of 100, with buttons
  for the first, previous, next and last page, and an index box with **Go** to jump to the page holding
  an index. An edit on any page records the element's own path.

## Actions

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read draw times | none | `editor.panel_timings` (`panel`, `last`, `clear`) |
| Read the Outliner's listed rows, open, close or reveal rows | Up, Down, Left, Right in the Outliner | `editor.outliner_rows` (`open`, `close`, `reveal`, `offset`, `limit`) |
| Read log lines | the **Output Log** tab | `logs.read` |
| Read or edit an element of a long list | the Inspector pager | `scene.get_entity`, `editor.set_property` with a path such as `values[150]` |

## Known limits

- The timings are read through the agent method only; the editor shows no timings view.
- Times are held in memory: they are lost when the editor exits, and a panel is listed only after it has
  drawn.
- `last` outside 1 to 240, or a `panel` that is not a string, is refused with error code `F0002`
  (`data.param` names the parameter).

## See also

[Editor panels at scale](book/agents/editor-panel-timings.md), [Outliner](book/user-guide/editor-guide/outliner.md),
[Inspector](book/user-guide/editor-guide/inspector.md), [Profiler](book/user-guide/editor-guide/profiler.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

# Vehicle tuning

Panel id: `vehicle_tuning`.

The **Vehicle Tuning** tab tunes a car (`.vehicle.ron`), a trailer (`.trailer.ron`), a fixed-wing
aircraft (`.aircraft.ron`), a two-wheel bike (`.bike.ron`) and a hover hull (`.hoverhull.ron`). It shows each configuration as editable sections, plots the car with the
runtime's own vehicle math, sends the edited car to a running play session without a respawn, and tries
every edit on a proving ground: scripted car runs on a flat plane, a ramp, a slope or a bump strip (towing
the trailer if you like), level flights for the aircraft, and rides for the bike and the hover hull. Depth for agents:
[Vehicles: Vehicle Tuning panel](book/agents/vehicles.md#vehicle-tuning-panel-editor) and
[Vehicle tuning: trailers, aircraft and tracks](book/agents/vehicle-tuning.md).

Open it from the editor's tab list (**Vehicle Tuning**); it docks with the other tool tabs.

## The car

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open a car | the path box, **Open** | `editor.vehicle_tuning_open { path }` |
| Start a new car (the default car, named after the file) | **New** | `editor.vehicle_tuning_open { path, create: true }` |
| Edit a field | the number, checkbox and picker fields of each section | `editor.vehicle_tuning_set { field, value }` |
| Undo, redo | **Undo**, **Redo** | `editor.vehicle_tuning_undo`, `editor.vehicle_tuning_redo` |
| Save | **Save** | `editor.vehicle_tuning_save` |
| Send the car to the play session | **Apply** (while playing) | `editor.vehicle_tuning_apply` |
| Run a script | **Run accel**, **Run skidpad**, the run length | `editor.vehicle_tuning_run { script, seconds }` |
| Pick the proving-ground track | the **track** picker in Runs | `editor.vehicle_tuning_run { track }` |
| Tow the open trailer | **tow the open trailer** in Runs | `editor.vehicle_tuning_run { tow: true }` |
| Read everything | the tab | `editor.vehicle_tuning_state` |

The sections are chassis, wheels (with the tire model), engine and its torque curve, gearbox, clutch,
differentials, anti-roll bars, aero and driver aids. A value the configuration refuses is not applied: the
field shows **refused** and the status line names the reason and its code. Dragging a number is one undo
step however long the drag lasts. **Save** writes the file atomically and keeps the file's comments
whenever it can; if it cannot, the status line says the comments were lost.

The plots show torque and power against engine speed, the force at the wheels in every gear, the selected
wheel's tire side force against slip angle, and its suspension force against travel.

## Proving ground

Every run drives the edited car from rest on a private world with a fixed 60 Hz step, so the same car and
script always give the same numbers. The runs table lists each run side by side: 0 to 100 km/h, top speed,
skid-pad lateral g, upshifts, the track, the wheel contacts and the trailer.

| Track | What is in the car's lane, 20 m ahead |
|---|---|
| flat | Nothing. |
| ramp | A wedge 1.5 m high and 6 m long: the car jumps off its top edge. |
| slope | A 10 % grade rising 6 m, then a long plateau. |
| bump strip | Low ridges every 2 m, alternating left and right: the wheels lose and regain the ground. |

**contacts** shows the fewest and most wheels on the ground during the run and how many steps that number
changed: on the flat plane it never changes; on the bump strip it does, and a car that stays planted over it
has softer, better-damped suspension.

With **tow the open trailer** ticked, the run spawns the open trailer coupled to a tow ball just behind the
car and brakes it with the car; the trailer column shows its mass and its largest articulation angle.

## The trailer

The **Trailer (.trailer.ron)** section has its own path box, **Open**, **New**, **Save**, **Undo** and
**Redo**, and shows the trailer's fields: the chassis (a vehicle configuration whose wheels neither drive
nor steer), the coupling (its kind, point and capture radius), the brakes, the parking brake, the stand and
the rear hitch. Agents use the same methods as for the car with `asset: "trailer"`. To try an edit, tick
**tow the open trailer** in Runs and run the car.

## The aircraft

The **Aircraft (.aircraft.ron)** section works the same way (`asset: "aircraft"`): mass, center of mass,
inertia, fuselage, parasite drag, each lifting surface (span, chord, incidence, airfoil coefficients, stall
and control links), engines and landing gear.

**Fly** takes an airspeed, an altitude and a length: it trims the aircraft for level flight there and flies
that trim on its own. The flights table shows the trim's angle of attack and throttle and how far the flight
drifted in altitude, speed and bank; a well-trimmed aircraft holds its altitude within a meter or two. Agent
method: `editor.vehicle_tuning_fly`.

## The bike and the hover hull

The **Bike (.bike.ron)** and **Hover hull (.hoverhull.ron)** sections work the same way (`asset: "bike"`,
`asset: "hoverhull"`). The bike's fields are its wheelbase, gravity, the lean limit and lean rate, the
upright speed and spring, the lean response and the wheel-contact reach. The hover hull's fields are its
`params`: ride height, thrust and braking, drag, speed limits, yaw and roll rates and the cushion; the
file's limits and flight mode are kept as written.

**Ride 1 s** rides the open bike or hull on the flat proving ground for 60 fixed steps with the held input
beside it (the bike's steer and speed; the hull's throttle, strafe and steer). The first ride spawns it at
rest; each later ride carries on from where the last stopped, so an edit you make between rides reaches the
bike or hull that is already riding, without a respawn. **Respawn** starts it at rest again. The line under
the buttons shows the step count and the lean and speed (bike) or speed, heading and altitude (hull). Agent
method: `editor.vehicle_tuning_ride`.

## Limits

- Trailers and aircraft have no **Apply** to a play session: try them on the proving ground or with **Fly**.
- Bikes and hover hulls have no **Apply** either: try them with **Ride**. The hover form does not edit a
  hull's limits or flight mode.

The tab has no keyboard shortcuts of its own; every control takes focus with Tab.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/accessibility.md -->
# Editor accessibility

What works today for keyboard-only use, screen readers, larger text and color contrast in the
editor, and what does not yet. The review behind this page (November 2026, every finding with
its file and line) is `docs/evidence/editor-a11y-2026-11.md`; findings are numbered **E-n**
(fixed) and **FU-n** (follow-ups). The game-side runtime UI has its own page,
[Accessibility](book/user-guide/accessibility.md).

## Keyboard

- **Every panel of this guide opens from the keyboard**: Ctrl+Shift+P, type `open`, pick **Open
  the … tab** (E-9). Bind any of those commands to a key in **Edit ▸ Preferences… ▸ Keymap**.
- **Tab** and **Shift+Tab** move focus through the buttons, fields, checkboxes and sliders of the
  editor in drawing order: the menu bar, the play toolbar, then each docked panel. **Space** or
  **Enter** presses the focused button; arrow keys change a focused slider.
- The keys each panel handles are listed on its page; [the index](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md#keys-that-work-everywhere)
  has the ones that work everywhere.
- **Play-in-editor** is fully keyboard driven: Alt+P plays, Escape stops, and the toolbar's
  **▶ Resume** (shown while paused, E-1) and **⏭ Step** take focus with Tab.
- **Viewport panes are focusable widgets** ("Viewport pane 1" to "Viewport pane 4"): Tab into a
  pane and it becomes the active pane, so its keys — `W`/`E`/`R` gizmo mode, `F` frame selection,
  `G` game view, the camera bookmarks, the 2D mode keys (`B`, `,` `.` `[` `]`) and the terrain
  tool keys (`T`, `[` `]`, `-` `=`, `0`-`9`, `,` `.`) — act on that pane without a click (FU-9).
  Clicking a pane still activates it. **Space** and **Enter** on a focused pane do nothing: they
  never pick or clear the selection (picking is a mouse click). A focused text field keeps every
  key it types.
- **A focused pane keeps the keys** in the four-pane layout: while a pane holds keyboard focus,
  its keys stay with it even when the pointer is over another pane, so hovering no longer moves
  the keys until you click a pane (a click on another pane takes the keys there and drops the
  focus) or press **Escape**. Meanwhile the hovered pane can be the one reported active: the
  SpaceMouse button actions (camera views) and the `active` pane agents read follow it. Without
  pane focus, the keys follow the pointer as before.
- The **material and procedural graphs**, the **sequence curve and section strip**, and the
  **profiler's flame view and trace timeline** each have a focusable list beside the canvas
  (ADR-7383): add a node wired after the focused one (Ctrl+Shift+A), connect pins by name
  (**Connect…**), delete, move by Alt+arrow or by one frame (Left / Right), and read span times
  without a hover. Each canvas is announced with its role and a count ("Material graph canvas, 12
  nodes"). The keys are on each area's page.
- The **animation graph**, its **state machine**, the **state tree**, the **VFX curves**, the
  **conversation graph**, the **UI animation keys**, the **camera rig graph**, the **blend
  spaces**, the **animation timeline**, the **curve editor** (animation clips and shot curves),
  the **clip notifies** and the **content grid** follow the same pattern (FU-5): Tab reaches the
  list, Up / Down move between items, Enter selects (Enter again opens a state machine or a
  state's sub-graph, or previews a conversation from its node), Left / Right or Alt+arrows move
  the item (Shift: a coarser step), Delete removes it, Ctrl+Shift+A adds one after it, and
  **Ctrl+Shift+C** starts a connection where the canvas has wires (type the target by name,
  Enter connects, Escape cancels). The focused item draws a ring in the theme's focus color on
  the canvas. In the content grid, arrows move the focus and the selection between tiles.
- Not yet: the 2D tile palette, the montage strip, the sequencer timeline rows, the procedural
  curve parameter, the curve table plot and the UI designer canvas still need the mouse for
  some edits; the agent methods on each page do them without a mouse. Shift+arrows extend the
  selection in the Outliner; the content grid has one selected asset, so Shift does not extend
  there yet.

## Screen readers

egui builds an AccessKit tree of the editor's widgets with a role and a name for each; the
editor now names its glyph buttons (**▾**/**▸** in the Outliner, **↻** in Content, **−**/**+**
in the trace timeline, the **x** buttons of the UI designer), its checkboxes and fields whose
visible label is a separate widget (Preferences, the procedural graph's settings, Project
Settings, the Content search) (E-2 to E-8), the Inspector's boolean checkboxes (named after
their field) and its list buttons **+ − ↑ ↓** ("Add element", "Remove element 0", "Move element
0 up", "Move element 0 down") (FU-6), the **⚠** warnings of the material and procedural graphs
(read as text: the label is the warning text, not a button) (FU-7), the fracture panel's half-extent fields ("Half
extent x/y/z") (FU-8) and the viewport panes (FU-9).

The editor window hands that tree to the operating system's screen reader (FU-1, ADR-7746):
Orca on Linux, NVDA or Narrator on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS. Start the reader, then the
editor (or the other way round: the editor notices a reader that starts later). The window is
read as "Regia Engine Editor"; the play toolbar and the viewport toolbar are announced as
toolbars, and each dock panel as a pane named after its tab (Inspector, Content, Outliner, ...).
The Outliner's eye and lock say what they do and to which row ("Hide Rock in the viewport",
"Lock Rock: not pickable in the viewport"); the Outliner's search field is "Search the Outliner",
and the viewport toolbar's menus are "Viewport quality" and "Gizmo pivot".

With a reader you can press buttons, tick checkboxes, open collapsed sections, select rows,
move the focus, and change number fields and sliders (the reader's increase and decrease
commands, or typing a value). To change a text field, focus it and type. Set
`REGIA_ACCESSKIT=0` before starting the editor to keep it off the accessibility bus.

Checked with tests only so far: the runs with Orca, NVDA and VoiceOver on real windows are
listed in the agent page's real-window steps and the evidence file.

## Text size

**Edit ▸ Preferences… ▸ Appearance ▸ UI scale** zooms the whole interface from 50 % to 300 %, so
150 % and 200 % are both available and kept between sessions. **Ctrl+=** (or Ctrl+Plus) and
**Ctrl+-** zoom in and out by 10 % and **View ▸ Reset zoom** (Ctrl+Alt+0) goes back to 100 %;
each changes the **UI scale** preference, so the zoom is kept between sessions. All three are
commands you can rebind in **Edit ▸ Preferences… ▸ Keymap** (`view.zoom_in`, `view.zoom_out`,
`view.reset_zoom`). **Ctrl+0** is only camera bookmark 0 in the viewport; it no longer resets
the zoom (FU-4, ADR-7733).

The UI scale multiplies your display's own scale: at 200 % on a display set to 150 %, text and
controls are three times their 100 %-display size. Before ADR-8589 the editor window reset the zoom to
the display scale every frame, so the preference saved but changed nothing on screen.

Symbols the editor writes (the Content browser's ← and → buttons, the ▸ in menu paths, the ● before a
changed setting, ✓, ⎇) come from fonts that ship with the editor; none draws as an empty box
(ADR-8589).

## Color contrast

`editor.a11y_contrast` measures a theme's colors against WCAG 2.x AA: every text color on every
surface it is drawn on (panels, windows, fields, the ground, and resting, pressed and open
controls) needs 4.5:1, and control outlines, the keyboard focus ring and small marks need 3:1;
[Editor accessibility (agents)](book/agents/editor-a11y.md) documents it. The editor's built-in
looks, **Piercing Graphite** (the default), **AMOLED Night**, **Paper** and **High contrast**
(**Edit ▸ Preferences… ▸ Appearance ▸ Theme**), pass every pair (ADR-8585; FU-2 is closed). The
lowest ratios in the default look are error text on a window (5.8:1), secondary text on a pressed
button (5.7:1) and a control's outline on a window (4.0:1).

Controls at rest have a visible outline, and a control you reach with Tab shows a 2 px ring in the
theme's Signal color (white in the dark looks, black in Paper, yellow in High contrast); a text
field you click into shows the ring too.

The bridged UI themes (**Theme** `regia-dark`, `regia-light`) take their button, field and
dropdown colors and their warning, error, success, unsaved and log colors from the theme's own
roles (ADR-8589): a control at rest has the panel's color and the theme's strong border as its
outline, hovered and open controls a lifted surface, and every text color, every control state and
the audio meters meet WCAG AA on both themes. Before, both kept the default look's dark buttons and
bright accents, which on `regia-light` meant dark buttons, a yellow "unsaved" label and black meter
bars on white panels (FU-3). Pairs that still miss on the full measured list are listed in
`docs/evidence/editor-a11y-2026-11.md`.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/terrain.md -->
# Terrain

Panel id: `terrain`.

The **Terrain** tab shows the terrain the open level names, exports and imports heightmaps, sets
the grass density target and edits scatter rules. The viewport's terrain tool (`T`) sculpts and
paints it; see [Viewport](book/user-guide/editor-guide/viewport.md). Depth: [Terrain editing (agents)](book/agents/terrain-editing.md)
and [Level terrain](book/agents/level-terrain.md).

## Create a terrain

**New terrain…** (in the Terrain tab, or **Content ▸ New ▸ Terrain…**, which starts in the shown
folder) opens the New terrain dialog:

| Field | What it sets |
|---|---|
| Name | The terrain's folder and file name (letters, digits, `_`, `-`) |
| Folder | Where the terrain's folder goes, under `assets/` (default `assets/maps`) |
| Size | 129, 257, 513, 1025, 2049 or 4097 samples a side (one fewer cells) |
| Cell size | 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 or 4 meters between samples; the terrain is `(size − 1) × cell size` meters wide |
| Height range | The heights of the lowest and the highest 16-bit sample; a new terrain is flat at the height nearest 0 m |
| Layers | Layer names, bottom first: grass, rock and dirt when the project has the starter content's terrain layers, else one `ground` layer |
| Start from a 16-bit heightmap | Import as new: the file's samples are kept as they are and its size sets the terrain's |

**Create** writes the terrain by the cook convention (`docs/formats/terrain.md` § 9) into
`assets/<folder>/<name>/`: `<name>.terrain.layers.ron`, `heightfield.png` (16-bit), and
`heightfield.json` (the width). It cooks the terrain in the background (the dialog shows the
progress, and **Cancel** stops it with nothing written), then names it in the level (World
settings ▸ terrain) and builds it, so the terrain tool can sculpt it at once. Save the level to
keep the reference. An unsaved level builds the terrain once it is saved.

**Undo** removes the level's reference and the built terrain. The files stay in the Content
Browser: delete the folder there if you do not want them.

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Create a terrain | **New terrain…** ▸ **Create**, **Content ▸ New ▸ Terrain…** | `editor.terrain_create` |
| Import a heightmap as a new terrain | **Start from a 16-bit heightmap** ▸ **Create** | `editor.terrain_create { heightmap }` |
| Cancel the cook | **Cancel** | `editor.cancel_job { id: "terrain_create:<n>" }` |
| Read the level's terrain | the tab | `terrain.level_terrain` |
| Export or import the heightmap | **Export**, **Import** | `terrain.export_heights`, `terrain.import_heights` |

The dialog's fields take focus with Tab; it has no keyboard shortcuts.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/output-log.md -->
# Output Log

Panel id: `output_log`.

The **Output Log** tab shows the engine's log: every record the editor, the engine and a running
game write, with a level filter, a target filter and a text search. The records are the same ring an
agent reads with `logs.read`, so the tab and an agent see the same lines. A `path:line` or an asset
path in a line is a link you can click. Depth: [Editor panels at scale](book/agents/editor-panel-timings.md)
(how the list handles 100 000 lines), [Viewport tools](book/agents/viewport-tools.md) (the link
methods).

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group, next to **Content**. From the keyboard press
Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the Output Log tab** (command `window.open_output_log`); bind a key to it
in the keymap if you use it often. An agent brings it forward with
`editor.layout_apply {"open": "output_log"}`.

## Read and filter the log

1. Each row shows the level (colored), the target (the part of the engine that logged it) and the
   first line of the message. A multi-line message ends in `…`.
2. Pick the lowest level to show from the drop-down (**ERROR**, **WARN**, **INFO**, **DEBUG**,
   **TRACE**); it starts at **INFO**.
3. Type a target prefix in the first box (hover says "target prefix") and a text in the second (hover
   says "search"). With a filter that matches nothing the tab says "(no records match the filters)".
4. Click a row's text to show the whole message, wrapped, under the list; **Close** hides it. Clicking
   the row again also closes it.
5. New lines keep the view at the bottom.
6. Click a link in a row. A source file opens in your code editor at that line (the `code.editor_command`
   preference, else the project's `.regia/agent.toml`, else `$VISUAL` or `$EDITOR`); an asset path opens
   the way a double-click in Content would. The result shows beside the filters.

The tab keeps the last 100 000 lines in its own history, polled from the log ring (which itself holds
fewer); only the rows on screen are laid out, so a long log does not slow the editor.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read log lines with the same filters | Level, target and search boxes | `logs.read` |
| Find the links in a line | Links in a row | `editor.log_links` |
| Open a link | Click it | `editor.log_open_link` |
| Open the tab | Palette command `window.open_output_log` | `editor.layout_apply` |

## Keyboard

The tab handles no keys of its own. The filter boxes and the level drop-down take Tab focus.

## Known limits

- Agents cannot choose the code editor program: it comes from your preference, the project's agent
  settings or the environment, and it is never started through a shell.
- A link opened by an agent stays inside the project; a click in the tab may open any existing file.
- The tab has no clear button; it shows the engine's log, not a copy you can empty.

See also: [Profiler](book/user-guide/editor-guide/profiler.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/world-settings.md -->
# World Settings

Panel id: `world_settings`.

The **World Settings** tab edits the open level's `LevelSettings`: gravity, the environment asset,
the game rules, the ambient audio bed, streaming, the atmosphere and sky, the look (exposure, color
grade), the audio medium, the terrain and the baked light a level names. The settings are saved with
the level, so an edit marks the level as changed. The fields are drawn by the same reflection
inspector as the [Inspector](book/user-guide/editor-guide/inspector.md). Depth: [Viewport tools](book/agents/viewport-tools.md)
(the `editor.world_settings_*` methods).

## Open it

The tab is not in the default layout. **Edit ▸ World settings…** opens it as a tab; so does the
command palette entry **World settings** (Ctrl+Shift+P, then type `world`). An agent opens it with
`editor.world_settings_panel`, or `editor.layout_apply {"open": "world_settings"}`.

## Change a setting

1. Open a level. With no level the tab says "Open a level to edit its settings."
2. Edit a field. The header shows the level's path (or `(unsaved level)`). A change takes effect at
   once for what reads the settings every frame (gravity in play, the look and the atmosphere in the
   renderer); what a level load applies (the game rules, the baked GI volume, the lightmap) takes
   effect the next time the level opens.
3. The viewport's `editor` quality preset keeps its own sky and exposure, so a look change may not
   show there.
4. If a value is refused (gravity that is not finite, cloud coverage outside 0 to 1, an hour outside
   0 to 24, a day outside 1 to 365, a latitude outside -90 to 90, an exposure bias that is not
   finite) the message appears next to the **Reset to defaults** button and nothing changes.
5. **Reset to defaults** puts every setting back to the engine default.
6. Save the level to keep the change.

Each edit is one undo step; scrubbing a slider on one field merges into one step.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open the tab | **Edit ▸ World settings…**, palette command `window.world_settings` | `editor.world_settings_panel` |
| Read the settings | The tab | `editor.world_settings_get` |
| Change settings | The fields | `editor.world_settings_set` (`settings`, or `reset: true`) |
| Reset to defaults | **Reset to defaults** | `editor.world_settings_set` with `reset: true` |
| Undo, redo | Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y | `editor.undo`, `editor.redo` |

## Keyboard

The tab has no keys of its own beyond the editor-wide ones: Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo, and the
fields take Tab focus like the Inspector's.

## Known limits

- It needs an open level.
- The tab is not part of the default or reset layout; reopen it from the Edit menu.

See also: [Viewport](book/user-guide/editor-guide/viewport.md), [Baked lighting panels](book/user-guide/editor-guide/bake.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/asset-viewer.md -->
# Asset Viewer

Panel id: `asset_viewer`.

The **Asset Viewer** tab previews a mesh, a texture or a sound from the project without putting it in
the level. A mesh is drawn in an orbit render with its LOD chain, parts and materials, and optional
overlays; a texture shows its mip chain and one channel at a time; a sound shows its waveform and
plays. Depth: [Editor surface](book/agents/editor.md) (`editor.view_asset`),
[Import settings panel and mesh viewer overlays](book/agents/import-settings.md).

## Open it

Double-click a mesh (`.gltf` or `.glb`), a texture (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`,
`.tga`, `.bmp`, `.hdr`, `.exr`) or a sound (`.wav`, `.ogg`, `.flac`, `.mp3`) in the **Content** tab.
The tab is in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a closed one.
Until you open something it says "Double-click a mesh, texture or sound in the Content Browser to view
it." An agent brings the tab forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "asset_viewer"}`. There is no
palette command for this tab.

## Look at an asset

1. Double-click the asset in Content. The tab's title row shows its path; a file that cannot be loaded
   shows the reason in red.
2. **Mesh.** The summary gives the parts, triangles, vertices and bounds. Pick **LOD0**, **LOD1** and so
   on to see each level with its triangle count and ratio; the LODs shown are a preview of the cook's
   default chain, not the asset's own cooked ones. Each part lists its material. Drag in the picture to
   orbit. The **Overlays:** toggles **UV0**, **UV1**, **Normals** and **Collision** draw over the render; one that
   cannot be drawn says why in a warning line.
3. **Texture.** The size and mip count show above a **mip** drop-down and a channel selector; pick a mip
   and a channel to isolate it.
4. **Sound.** The sample rate, channels and length show next to **▶ Play**, with the waveform below.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open and render an asset as an image with its info | Double-click in Content | `editor.view_asset` (`path`, `lod`, `yaw`, `pitch`, `mip`, `channel`, `overlay`) |
| Mesh overlays | **UV0**, **UV1**, **Normals**, **Collision** | `editor.view_asset` with `overlay` |
| Play a sound | **▶ Play** | `editor.play_sound` |

## Keyboard

The tab handles no keys of its own; its toggles and buttons take Tab focus. Orbiting a mesh is a mouse
drag.

## Known limits

- The mesh LODs are generated with the cook's default settings for the preview; they show what a
  cook with LOD generation turned on would produce.
- The render needs a GPU device; without one the mesh summary shows but no picture.
- The viewer is read-only: it changes no asset.

See also: [Content browser](book/user-guide/editor-guide/content-browser.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/anim-graph.md -->
# Animation editor: Anim Graph, Clip and Skeleton

Panel ids: `anim_graph`, `anim_clip` and `anim_skeleton`.

Three tabs edit a character's animation: **Anim Graph** builds the blend tree and state machines
(`.animgraph.ron`), **Clip** edits a clip's notifies, curves, property tracks and root-motion mode,
and **Skeleton** adds sockets and IK chains to the rig. Clip and Skeleton write an authoring
sidecar, `<source>.animedit.ron`, next to the imported glTF; the graph's canvas positions go to an
editor-only `.animgraph.layout.ron` next to the graph. Depth:
[Animation editor (agents)](book/agents/animation-editor.md); the runtime side is
[Animation](book/user-guide/animation.md).

## Open it

All three tabs are in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a
closed one. An agent brings one forward with `editor.layout_apply`:

```json
{ "method": "editor.layout_apply", "params": { "open": "anim_graph" } }
```

The ids are `anim_graph`, `anim_clip` and `anim_skeleton`. There is no palette command for these
tabs.

## Build a graph

1. Open the **Anim Graph** tab. Type a path such as `graphs/x.animgraph.ron` into the path field
   and press **Open**, or press **New** for an empty graph.
2. Pick a character in **Rig:** (**Demo biped**, **Selected entity**), or type a `.glb` path and
   press **Load rig**. The preview on the right shows it.
3. In the left panel, add **parameters** (a kind from the drop-down, then **Add**): float, int,
   bool, vec2, vec3 or trigger. A trigger shows a **fire** button; **×** removes a declaration.
4. Right-click empty canvas for **Add node** and a list of node kinds. Drag from a pin to another
   node's input to connect. Right-click a node for **Make output**, **Open states** (state
   machines), **Duplicate** (not for state machines) and **Delete**. A state machine node also
   has an **Open states ›** button that opens its states canvas.
5. Select a node, state or transition to edit it in the inspector under the parameters.
6. Press **Play** in the preview, move parameter values, and watch the active state. **Restart**
   resets it; **speed** scales time; **Apply root motion** moves the preview character.
7. Press **Save**. It refuses an invalid graph and drops nodes no output reaches.

While a play-in-editor session runs, the preview shows the play world's animator running this
graph (an orange `PIE: debugging ...` line) with its live parameter values and active node
([Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md)).

## Edit a clip

1. Open the **Clip** tab and pick a clip in the clip drop-down; **Play** runs it and the readout
   shows the time and the clip length.
2. Click or drag the ruler to scrub. Double-click the ruler to add a notify; drag a notify marker
   to move it. Select a notify to edit its **Name**, **Time** and **Payload (RON)** or press
   **Delete**.
3. In **Curves** and **Property tracks**, pick one to edit its keys, or type a name (a property
   track takes a path such as `Component.path`) and press **+ curve** or **+ property track**.
4. Choose a **Root motion** mode: None, XZ, XYZ or Yaw.
5. Type a `.animedit.ron` path if the rig has none and press **Save edits**.

The first edit of an imported clip copies its imported notifies into the sidecar, so they are kept.

## Edit a skeleton

1. Open the **Skeleton** tab. The header counts joints, sockets and IK chains.
2. Select a joint in the tree (arrows fold branches) or click it in the preview.
3. **Add socket here** adds a socket on that joint; **Add IK chain ending here** adds a two-bone
   chain (the joint needs a parent and a grandparent, or a message says so).
4. Edit sockets (name, joint, offset, rotation) and IK chains (name, joints, pole parameter) in
   their lists; **Delete socket** and **Delete chain** remove them.
5. Save the sidecar with **Save edits** on the **Clip** tab.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| New, open, save a graph | **New**, **Open**, **Save** | `editor.anim_open`, `editor.anim_save` |
| Undo, redo | **Undo**, **Redo** buttons, Ctrl+Z | `editor.undo`, `editor.redo` |
| Declare a parameter | The parameter list, **Add** | `editor.anim_param` |
| Add, edit, remove a node | Canvas menu, inspector, **Delete** | `editor.anim_add_node`, `editor.anim_set_node`, `editor.anim_remove_node` |
| Connect, disconnect, set the output | Drag pins, **Make output** | `editor.anim_connect`, `editor.anim_disconnect` |
| States and transitions | The states canvas | `editor.anim_state`, `editor.anim_transition` |
| Read the graph with its validation | The inspector | `editor.anim_graph` |
| Choose the preview character | **Rig:**, **Load rig** | `editor.anim_rig` |
| Set preview parameters and advance | The preview | `editor.anim_preview` |
| Read the play world's animator | The PIE line | `editor.anim_debug` |
| Edit a clip (notifies, curves, root motion) | **Clip** tab | `editor.anim_clip` |
| Add sockets and IK chains | **Skeleton** tab | `editor.anim_skeleton` |
| Save the sidecar | **Save edits** | `editor.anim_save_edits` |
| Sample a clip into a scratch rig | none | `editor.sample_into` |
| See a panel as an image | none | `editor.capture_panel` with `anim_graph`, `anim_clip` or `anim_skeleton` |

## Keyboard

Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo graph, clip and skeleton edits in order with level edits (the
shared undo stack). In the **Clip** tab, **F** refits the ruler to the whole clip. The tabs have no
other keys of their own.

## Known limits

- Two documents are open at a time: one graph and one rig's sidecar.
- Graphs are trees: connecting a node that already feeds something moves it.
- A saved graph drops unreachable nodes; the autosave keeps them for recovery.
- The editor-only layout file keeps canvas positions; the runtime ignores it.

See also: [Montage](book/user-guide/editor-guide/montage.md), [Inertialized transitions](book/user-guide/inertialization.md),
[Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/montage.md -->
# Montage

Panel id: `montage`.

The **Montage** tab is the timeline of a `.montage.ron` (or a child `.montagevar.ron`): one lane
per slot track with its clip segments, then lanes for sections, notifies and warp windows, a
playhead, and a pose preview of one section chain or the whole timeline. Every control writes the
same validated, undoable edit an agent sends, so the file is saved by each edit. Depth:
[Editor data panels](book/agents/editor-data-panels.md) (the Montage section), and for the runtime
[Montages, sync groups and motion warping](book/user-guide/montages.md).

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a closed one.
An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "montage"}`. There is no palette
command for this tab.

## Edit a montage

1. Type a project-relative path such as `assets/anim/combo.montage.ron` in the path field and press
   **Open**. The lanes appear; a message under the path field shows the code of a refused edit.
2. Press **Preview on selected rig** with a skinned entity selected to see the pose at the
   playhead in the viewport (the status reads `posed` or `bind pose`). Drag the **Playhead**
   slider, or click or drag the ruler. **Whole timeline** previews every section in order instead
   of one chain; the `plays:` line lists the chain.
3. Add a clip: type its name in the **clip** field and a slot in the **slot** field (a slot no
   track plays starts a new track; empty means the first track), then press **Add to** the slot.
   You can also drop a clip from the Content browser on a track lane: it joins that track at its end.
4. Click a segment to edit its **start**, **rate** and **loops**, or use **◀** and **▶** to
   reorder and **Remove** to delete it.
5. **Section at playhead** adds a section; drag a section marker to move it. With a section
   selected, **Preview from here**, **Jump to** (the target typed beside it), **Continue**,
   **Stop at end**, **Set follow** and **Clear follow** edit how it links. Select a notify or warp
   to **Remove** it.
6. Type a name and press **Add notify at playhead** to add a notify. In the warp row, a target,
   a window and the **translation**, **vertical** and **rotation** checkboxes with **Add warp** add a
   motion-warping window.
7. The blend row (**in**, **out**, **lead**, **auto blend-out**, **Apply blend**) sets the blend times.
8. **Slot table** (a collapsing section) loads a skeleton's `.slots.ron` with **Load slots** and
   adds, renames, deletes (**force delete**) and sets slots (group, joints, **with children**).
9. **Undo** (shown once a montage is open) reverts the last montage edit.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open a montage | Path field, **Open** | `editor.montage_panel_open` |
| Read the timeline, selection and preview | The tab | `editor.montage_panel_get` |
| Any edit above | The controls | `editor.montage_panel_edit` (`anim.montage_edit`) |
| Move the playhead, pick the chain or the rig | **Playhead**, **Whole timeline**, **Preview on selected rig** | `editor.montage_panel_preview` |
| Select a segment, section, notify or warp | Click on the timeline | `editor.montage_panel_select` |
| Slot table edits | **Slot table** | `anim.montage_slot_edit`, `anim.montage_slots` |

## Keyboard

The tab handles no keys of its own; its controls are reached with Tab and pressed with Enter or
Space. To undo a montage edit use **Undo** in the tab (or `{ "op": "undo" }` through
`editor.montage_panel_edit`); the tab's code has no Ctrl+Z handler of its own.

## Known limits

- A segment that plays to the end of a clip no loaded library knows is drawn one second long with
  an amber outline.
- The pose preview samples the first track only; other tracks' slot masks are not applied.
- A child `.montagevar.ron` cannot be previewed (the preview answers
  `montage_panel_preview_variant`).

See also: [Animation editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/anim-graph.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/ragdoll.md -->
# Ragdoll

Panel id: `ragdoll`.

The **Ragdoll** tab edits a character's physics asset, a `.ragdoll.ron` profile: one body per
simulated joint (a capsule, sphere or box with a radius, mass and length) and the swing-twist limits
of each joint to its nearest simulated ancestor. Select a character in the level and the tab checks
joint names against its skeleton, can generate a humanoid profile, draws each body in the viewport,
and runs a **Drop test**. Depth: [Editor data panels](book/agents/editor-data-panels.md) (the
Ragdoll section) and [Active ragdolls](book/agents/ragdoll-active.md).

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a closed one.
An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "ragdoll"}`. There is no palette
command for this tab.

## Author a ragdoll

1. Type a project-relative path such as `assets/chars/hero.ragdoll.ron` in the path field and press
   **Open**, or press **New** to start an empty profile at that path.
2. Select the character in the level (an entity with a skinned mesh) and press **Use selected rig**.
   The line above the table names the rig; **Gizmo** shows or hides the bodies in the viewport.
3. Press **Humanoid from rig** to generate bodies and limits from the skeleton, or add a body by
   typing a joint name and pressing **Add body**.
4. In the table, edit each body's **radius**, **mass** and **length** (auto means it is measured from
   the skeleton), turn **limits** on or off, or press **Remove**. Select a row to choose its shape
   (capsule, sphere or box, with width and depth for a box), to tick **length from skeleton**, and
   to set its limits in degrees (**flexes backward (knee)** for a hinge that bends the other way).
5. Amber lines under the table are findings, such as a joint the skeleton does not have.
6. Press **Drop test**: the ragdoll falls limp onto a floor in a private physics world and the tab
   reports whether it settled, its fastest speed and its lowest body center; the final pose is drawn
   beside the rig. The level is not touched. The line says `(stale)` once the profile changes.
7. Press **Save**. It is enabled while there are unsaved changes and writes the file atomically.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open or start a profile | Path field, **Open**, **New** | `editor.ragdoll_panel_open` (`new: true` to start) |
| Read the profile, findings and preview | The tab | `editor.ragdoll_panel_get` |
| Edit bodies, shapes, limits, the forward axis | The table and row editors, **Add body**, **Humanoid from rig** | `editor.ragdoll_panel_edit` |
| Pick the rig, show the gizmo | **Use selected rig**, **Gizmo** | `editor.ragdoll_panel_set_rig` |
| Drop test | **Drop test** | `editor.ragdoll_panel_preview` |
| Save | **Save** | `editor.ragdoll_panel_save` |
| Undo, redo | **Undo**, **Redo** | `editor.ragdoll_panel_edit` with `op: undo` or `redo` |

## Keyboard

The tab handles no keys of its own; its controls are reached with Tab and pressed with Enter or
Space.

## Known limits

- Edits stay in memory until **Save**; **Undo** and **Redo** keep the last 32 steps.
- **Drop test** needs a rig and an open profile; without a rig the button is disabled.
- A profile that names a joint the rig lacks is flagged; if no body names a joint of the rig, the
  drop test answers `ragdoll_preview_no_bodies`.

See also: [Animation editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/anim-graph.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/cloth.md -->
# Cloth

Panel id: `cloth`.

The **Cloth** tab opens a `.cloth.ron` (or a `.soft.ron` soft body) from the project, edits its
simulation parameters, and paints per-vertex maps on the simulation mesh in the viewport. It edits
the file through its own types and saves it atomically; the level is only touched when you change an
instance's blend or LOD distances. Depth: [Cloth (agents)](book/agents/cloth.md); the solver itself
is described in [Cloth and ropes](book/user-guide/cloth.md).

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a closed one.
An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "cloth"}`. There is no palette command
for this tab.

## Edit and paint a cloth

1. Type a project-relative path such as `cloth/cape.cloth.ron` and press **Open**. The header shows
   the cloth's name, path and kind, and `(edited)` once it has unsaved changes.
2. Select an entity that has a cloth or soft-body simulation component: it becomes the target of
   the instance controls. Without one the tab says to select an entity with a `ClothSimSource`.
3. For a cloth, pick a **starting point** (a preset, or none). Edit any parameter in the grid (a soft
   body shows the parameters it has). For a cloth choose a **self-collision** mode (off, spheres or
   vertex_triangle) and its radius.
4. With a target selected, set its **blend** and its **LOD m** distances; these are saved with the level.
5. Turn on **Paint**, pick a **map**, a **value**, a brush radius **r**, **str**ength and a falloff
   (linear, smooth or hard). Press and drag over the sim mesh in the viewport and release: the
   stroke is painted as one undo step. The viewport colors each vertex on the **ramp m** range.
   Ctrl-click a vertex to select or deselect it for the gizmos.
6. **Simulate preview** steps a private solver with the edited parameters so you can see the result
   without touching the level. **Gizmos** shows the `cloth` gizmo group (body proxies, collision
   shapes, and `reach` and `standoff` for selected vertices).
7. Press **Save** (enabled while there are changes). A file you did not change is never rewritten.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open a file | Path field, **Open** | `editor.cloth_panel_edit` with `path` |
| Read the panel | The tab | `editor.cloth_panel_state` |
| Parameters, preset, self-collision, wind model | The grid and drop-downs | `editor.cloth_panel_edit` |
| Instance blend and LOD distances | **blend**, **LOD m** | `editor.cloth_panel_edit` (`blend`, `lod_distances`) |
| Paint mode and brush | **Paint**, **map**, **value**, **r**, **str**, falloff | `editor.cloth_panel_edit` (`paint`) |
| Paint a stroke | Drag in the viewport | `editor.cloth_paint_stroke` |
| Select vertices | Ctrl-click (Cmd on macOS) in paint mode | `editor.cloth_panel_edit` (`selected`) |
| Simulate preview, gizmos | **Simulate preview**, **Gizmos** | `editor.cloth_panel_edit` (`simulate`, `gizmos`) |
| Save | **Save** | `editor.cloth_panel_edit` (`save: true`) |
| Undo, redo | Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y | `editor.cloth_panel_edit` (`undo`, `redo`) |

## Keyboard

Every change is one entry on the editor's shared undo stack, so Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo
cloth edits and strokes in order with level edits. In paint mode Ctrl-click selects a vertex. The tab
has no other keys of its own.

## Known limits

- Paint needs a sim mesh: the cooked asset of a cloth simulation in the level with the file's name,
  else the file cooked from the project. Without one the tab shows `no sim mesh` and the reason.
- Paint works on cloth files; a soft body has the parameter grid but no paint controls.
- One stroke holds a limited number of points; past the limit the tab says so and the release paints
  the points kept.
- The preview never changes the level.

See also: [Physics](book/user-guide/physics.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/kit.md -->
# Kit

Panel id: `kit`.

The **Kit** tab shows an exported content kit: a folder with a `kit.json` manifest and a model
(`<kit_id>.glb`), optionally with a cockpit model, a rig and sockets list, and a `SHA256SUMS`
file. It lays out the kit's metadata, checksum result, warnings, clips, sockets and budget next to
a render of the model you can orbit and switch between LOD levels. It is a viewer: it never
writes or repackages a kit. The kit folder layout and what the viewer refuses are on [Open
kit](book/user-guide/open-kit.md); the agent call is on [Open kit (agents)](book/agents/open-kit.md).

## Open it

- **File ▸ Open kit…** (also **Open kit…** on the project browser, which needs no project) asks
  for a folder and opens it. The Kit tab comes forward, even if you had closed it.
- Inside the tab, **Open kit…** does the same, and **Reload** (shown once a kit is open) re-reads
  the open folder.
- An agent calls `editor.open_kit {"path": "..."}` or `editor.layout_apply {"open": "kit"}`.
  The command palette has no `open` command for the tab.

## Inspect a kit

1. Pick the kit folder. With nothing open the tab says to open a kit folder with `kit.json`,
   `<kit_id>.glb` and optionally a cockpit, `rig.json`, `sockets.json` and `SHA256SUMS`. If the kit
   cannot open, the tab shows "Kit not opened:" with the reason in red.
2. The left column lists the **manifest** fields (including whether it is a character kit), then
   the `SHA256SUMS` result: green **verified**, red when a file differs, is missing or was refused,
   or gray when there is no list. Expand **Checksums** for each file's result.
3. **Warnings** lists everything that did not stop the kit from opening, one line each.
4. **Budget** measures the model against the limits of a class; the class picker next to it
   changes the class, and **Budget meters** expands one meter per limit.
5. Under **Clips**, a clip from the model plays in the Clip tab when you click it (the model must
   be skinned; the tab then uses it as the preview rig). A clip listed only in `rig.json` is
   disabled and marked "rig.json only".
6. Under **Sockets**, tick **Socket gizmos** to draw the sockets over the render, and click a
   socket to highlight it (click again to clear).
7. The right column is the render. Drag it to orbit the model. The buttons above it switch
   between LOD levels, with each level's triangle count and "generated" when the viewer built
   the level rather than the model supplying it. A line below says where the cockpit is drawn:
   at `socket_cockpit`, or at the origin when the model has no such node.

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open a kit | **File ▸ Open kit…**, **Open kit…** | `editor.open_kit` |
| Re-read the open kit | **Reload** | `editor.open_kit` with the same path |
| Play a clip | click a clip | `editor.open_kit` with `clip` |
| Render a LOD | the LOD buttons | `editor.open_kit` with `render: true` and `lod` |
| Read the budget | **Budget** | `editor.budget` with `source: "kit"` |
| Show the tab | the tab | `editor.layout_apply` with `open: "kit"` |

## Keyboard

The tab has no shortcuts. Its buttons, LOD selectors and list rows take focus with Tab. The
render responds to the mouse only (drag to orbit); an agent gets a rendered frame from
`editor.open_kit` with `render: true`.

## Known limits

- The folder dialog is a native dialog; an agent passes the path instead.
- Without a GPU device the tab says "No GPU device: the render is off." and still shows the
  information columns.
- The viewer does not check a kit against a content contract (scale, budget tables, node and clip
  names) and does not write kits.
- A kit that cannot be read safely (an unsafe path, a file over its size cap, a model without
  embedded data) does not open and the tab says why; every other problem is a warning.

See also: [Content browser](book/user-guide/editor-guide/content-browser.md), [Editor budget
(agents)](book/agents/editor-budget.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/bake.md -->
# Baked lighting panels: Bake, Bake runner and Lightmaps

Panel ids: `bake`, `bake_runner` and `lightmaps`.

Three tabs run the offline lighting bakes from the editor. Each bake runs as a child process
(the `regia` command-line program next to the editor, else `regia` on the `PATH`, or the one named by
the `REGIA_CLI` environment variable), so the editor keeps drawing, **Cancel** stops it at once, and
a crash in a bake cannot take the editor down. One bake runs at a time per tab.

| Tab | Runs | Use it to |
|---|---|---|
| **Bake** | `regia bake-gi` on a description the tab writes | Place one probe volume in the level, choose a quality and bake it |
| **Bake runner** | `regia bake-gi` on a built-in scene or a project `.bake.ron` | Run a hand-written description with progress and cancel |
| **Lightmaps** | `regia bake-lightmaps` | Bake per-mesh lightmaps for the open level or a description, and review the atlas |

The Bake tab is described step by step in [The Bake panel](book/user-guide/bake-panel.md). Depth:
[Baking from the editor](book/agents/baked-gi-editor.md), [Bake runner](book/agents/editor-bake.md),
[Lightmaps](book/agents/lightmaps.md).

## Open them

The three tabs are in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a
closed one. An agent brings one forward with `editor.layout_apply` and the id `bake`, `bake_runner`
or `lightmaps`. There is no palette command for these tabs.

## Run the Bake runner

1. Open **Bake runner**. The **Scene** drop-down lists the built-in scenes (`cornell`, `furnace`,
   `rolling-hills`) and every `.bake.ron` in the project; **Refresh** rescans the project.
2. Leave **Output** empty for the default, or type a `.fgiv` path.
3. Optionally open **Overrides** to set rays per probe, samples, bounces, seed or probes per batch,
   or to skip the visibility filter.
4. **Validate** is a dry run: it checks the description and shows the layout without a GPU. **Bake**
   traces. The bar shows the stage and the probes done; **Cancel** stops it and writes nothing.
5. When it ends the tab shows a summary (probes, bricks, size, device, time) or the failure code,
   and a **Log** section with the bake's last lines.

## Run the Lightmaps tab

1. Open **Lightmaps**. **Source** is the open level by default; the drop-down also lists the
   project's levels and descriptions and the built-in scenes.
2. Set **Texels per metre**, **Samples per texel**, **Bounces**, **Largest atlas side** and
   **Atlas pages at most**, and the checkboxes (**Bake the direct sun**, **Skip the filter**, **Planar
   charts**, **On the GPU** (needs a CLI built with the `lightmap-gpu` feature), **Visibility
   clusters**, **Denoise**, **Crease placement**, **Stitch seams**, **Auto density**) and **Encoding**.
3. **Lay out** is a dry run that lays the atlas out and previews density without baking. **Bake**
   bakes; **Cancel** kills it and leaves the old output.
4. The result shows the atlas size and entry count. **Density** colors each entry by its texel
   density against the density asked for; **Seams** colors by chart-seam error against the
   **Budget**. **Seams in the viewport** draws the worst seams in the scene. **Entries** lists each
   mesh with its texels per meter and seam numbers.
5. A bake that was interrupted may leave a checkpoint: the tab shows its status with **Discard**,
   which deletes it so the next bake starts over.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read, set, start and cancel the Bake tab's volume bake | **Bake**, **Dry run**, **Cancel** | `editor.bake_get`, `editor.bake_set`, `editor.bake_start`, `editor.bake_cancel` |
| Start a Bake runner bake | **Validate**, **Bake** | `editor.bake_gi` |
| Read the runner's progress and summary | The state area | `editor.bake_status` |
| Cancel the runner's bake | **Cancel** | `editor.bake_gi_cancel` |
| Start a lightmap bake or dry run | **Bake**, **Lay out** | `editor.lightmap_bake` |
| Read its progress and the atlas view | The state area and preview | `editor.lightmap_status` |
| Cancel it | **Cancel** | `editor.lightmap_cancel` |
| Density or seam preview, seam budget, seams in the viewport | **Density**, **Seams**, **Budget**, **Seams in the viewport** | `editor.lightmap_preview` |

## Keyboard

None of the three tabs handles keys of its own; reach their controls with Tab and press them with
Enter or Space.

## Known limits

- The CLI program must be found; without it a bake reports `bake_spawn_failed`.
- The Bake tab's volume is one box; for bricks over a whole level, write a `.bake.ron` and use the
  Bake runner.
- The seam **Budget** here is a preview value; a shipping package reads `[lightmaps] seam_budget` in
  `Regia.toml`.

See also: [Look-dev](book/user-guide/editor-guide/lookdev.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/lookdev.md -->
# Look-dev

Panel id: `lookdev`.

The **Look-dev** tab traces the open level with the reference path tracer and shows the result: the
ground truth a real-time frame can be compared against. The trace takes the same inputs the
real-time path uses (the runtime extraction of the level), with the editor camera or the level's own
game camera as the view. Editor-only helpers (the preview sun, proxy cubes, the backdrop) are not
traced, so a level with no sun of its own traces dark where the viewport shows the preview sun. Each
trace runs on its own thread with its own GPU device, so the editor keeps drawing and a device loss
in the trace does not reach the editor. Depth: [Look-dev panel (agents)](book/agents/editor-lookdev.md).

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a closed one.
An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "lookdev"}`. There is no palette
command for this tab.

## Trace a level

1. Open **Look-dev**. Choose a **Scene**: `viewport` (the open level through the editor camera, the
   default), `game` (through the level's game camera), or `cornell` and `furnace` (the tracer's own
   test scenes, which need no level and show that the tracer runs on this machine).
2. Set the image **Size**, a **Preset** (`none`, `draft`, `preview`, `final`, `reference`), the
   **Samples / pixel**, **Max bounces** and **Seed**. A preset uses its own sample count and path
   length unless you changed those fields.
3. Leave **Output dir** empty for the default under the project's `.regia/lookdev/`, or type a folder.
4. Press **Trace**. A bar counts samples per pixel; **Cancel** stops the trace.
5. When it ends the tab shows the sample count and time, the files it wrote (`exr`, `preview_png`,
   `metadata_json`; click a path to copy it) and the preview image.

A failure shows its code and message in red; one trace runs at a time.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Start a trace | **Trace** | `editor.lookdev_trace` |
| Read progress, files and the result | The progress bar and file list | `editor.lookdev_status` |
| Stop a trace | **Cancel** | `editor.lookdev_cancel` |

## Keyboard

The tab handles no keys of its own; reach its controls with Tab and press them with Enter or Space.

## Known limits

- The trace shows the level as a game would render it, not the editor viewport with its helpers.
- A preset that denoises writes a separate `preview.png`, which is never a reference.
- Trace outputs are the layered `reference.exr`, its AgX preview and a metadata file; compare them
  with a real-time frame with `seeing.compare` ([Renderer excellence](book/agents/renderer-excellence.md)).

See also: [Baked lighting panels](book/user-guide/editor-guide/bake.md), [Look-dev harness](book/user-guide/lookdev.md),
[Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/theme.md -->
# Theme

Panel id: `theme`.

The **Theme** tab edits a runtime UI theme, a `.theme.ron` file: the colors, sizes, durations and
other tokens your game's interface is drawn with. Open a built-in theme or a theme file, change
tokens, watch a swatch preview and the lint findings, and save. It edits a working copy (the draft)
and never touches the running game's theme; the file it saves is what a game loads. The editor's own
window stays on the editor's tokens. Depth: [Theme panel (agents)](book/agents/ui-theme-panel.md) and
the theme format in [Runtime UI themes](book/agents/ui-theme.md).

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a closed one.
An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "theme"}`. There is no palette command
for this tab.

## Edit a theme

1. Open the **Open theme…** drop-down and pick a theme, or type a path such as
   `path/to/my.theme.ron` in the path field and press **Open file**.
2. To start your own, pick the theme to extend, type a name in **new theme name** and press
   **New child**. The child sets only the tokens you change and inherits the rest.
3. Choose **Comfortable** or **Compact** density.
4. Edit tokens. Rows are grouped (the **Color** group opens first) and a **filter tokens** box narrows
   them. A color row has a color picker, a number row a drag value, any other row a text box
   (an expression such as `@color.accent` or `lighten(@color.accent, 0.06)`); the edit applies
   when the box loses focus. Hover a row's name to see whether it is set here or inherited; **reset**
   removes your value.
5. An edit that would make the theme invalid is refused and the draft stays as it was; the reason shows
   in red under the path field.
6. The swatches above the token list preview the main roles. Under the list, **Lint** says `clean` or
   lists findings with their code (`contrast`, `touch_target`, `unknown_key`, `resolve_error`) and
   severity color.
7. Type the output path and press **Save**. The line `unsaved changes` shows until you do.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read the draft and its token rows | The tab | `editor.theme_panel_state` |
| Open a built-in theme, a file, or a new child | **Open theme…**, **Open file**, **New child** | `editor.theme_panel_open` |
| Set or reset tokens, rename, set density | Token rows, density buttons | `editor.theme_panel_set` |
| Lint | The lint section | `editor.theme_panel_lint` |
| Save | **Save** | `editor.theme_panel_save` |

## Keyboard

The tab handles no keys of its own; reach its controls with Tab. A token text box applies its edit
when it loses focus.

## Known limits

- The panel changes a draft and a saved file only; to see a theme in a running game, load the file in
  the game.
- The tab shows no Undo of its own; **reset** puts a token back to inherited.

See also: [UI designer](book/user-guide/editor-guide/ui-designer.md), [Editor accessibility](book/user-guide/editor-guide/accessibility.md),
[Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/tools.md -->
# Tools

Panel id: `tools`.

The **Tools** tab runs **editor tools**: separate programs the editor launches from a small
manifest file, such as a review queue, a publishing calendar or an asset checker. Each tool shows
its status, progress bars, a small view it describes itself, its log and the methods it provides.
A tool runs in its own process, in any language, and talks to the editor over a local WebSocket
with a token that can call only what its manifest allows. Depth: [Editor tools
(agents)](book/agents/editor-tools.md), [Tools acceptance](book/agents/tools-acceptance.md).

The **Tools** menu in the menu bar is a different thing: it holds editor commands such as
rebuilding the asset database. This page is about the **Tools** tab.

## Open it

The tab is part of the default layout (the group under the viewport); **View ▸ Reset layout**
brings it back when closed. An agent uses `editor.layout_apply {"open": "tools"}` or
`editor.tool_panel`, which also brings the tab forward when it was closed and can select a tool.
The command palette has no `open` command for it.

## Add and run a tool

1. Put a manifest named `<id>.tool.toml` (the tool's id, then `.tool.toml`) in `<project>/.regia/tools/`, in the editor's user
   `tools` folder, or in a folder listed in `REGIA_TOOL_PATH`. The first manifest of an id wins. The
   manifest names the program to launch, the permissions and methods its token may use, the methods
   it provides, and an optional web panel address.
2. Open the tab and press **Refresh** if the tool was added while the editor ran. The header says
   how many manifests were found. A manifest that does not parse shows as `<id> (invalid)` and
   its error appears when selected; it never stops the editor.
3. Click a tool in the left list. The dot is green while it runs, yellow while it stops, red when
   it failed and gray otherwise, followed by the status name.
4. Press **Launch**. The editor starts the program with a fresh scoped token. **Stop** asks it to
   shut down; if it does not, **Kill** appears. **Open in browser** shows when the manifest has a
   panel address.
5. While it runs the right column shows the tool's tasks as progress bars, then the view the tool
   set (headings, labels, values, progress bars, links and buttons). Buttons are enabled while
   the tool runs; pressing one sends a click event to the tool.
6. Open **Log** to read the tool's last output lines and **Methods** to see the methods it provides,
   each with its permission.
7. A tool whose manifest sets `autostart` launches when a project opens only if its manifest is in
   the user folder or a `REGIA_TOOL_PATH` folder: opening a project never runs a program by
   itself.

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| List manifests and refresh | **Refresh** | `editor.tool_list` (with `refresh: true`) |
| Read a tool's status, tasks, view and log | the right column | `editor.tool_status` |
| Read the methods a tool provides | **Methods** | `editor.tool_methods` |
| Launch a tool | **Launch** | `editor.tool_launch` |
| Stop or kill a tool | **Stop**, **Kill** | `editor.tool_stop` |
| Press a view button | the view's buttons | `editor.tool_click` |
| Call a method a tool provides | none | `editor.tool_call` |
| Bring the tab forward, select a tool | the tab | `editor.tool_panel` |

## Keyboard

The tab has no shortcuts. The tool list, buttons and hyperlinks take focus with Tab.

## Known limits

- A tool's own token never has the `tools` permission and is revoked when the tool exits.
- Unknown keys in a manifest are errors, not ignored settings.
- The tab shows what a tool describes with its own view items; it does not embed a web page, only
  the **Open in browser** link.
