   it, **Per-emitter cost** lists, for each emitter, the live particles, spawn rate, draw list,
   draw calls and GPU time.
7. Change the **budget** number beside the effect name to set the system's particle budget.
8. Press **Save**. It is enabled only while the effect has unsaved edits.

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open an effect | the path box, **Open** | `editor.vfx_open` |
| Read the open effect | the whole panel | `editor.vfx_state` (`sim_steps` runs the CPU reference simulation and returns its hash; `cost_time` returns the cost rows) |
| Add, remove, enable or disable a module; change a parameter | module rows, **Add module**, **Remove**, the A/B box | `editor.vfx_edit` (`add_module`, `remove_module`, `enable_module`, `disable_module`, `set_param`) |
| Add, move, delete a curve or gradient key | the curve and gradient widgets | `editor.vfx_edit` (`curve_add_key`, `curve_move_key`, `curve_delete_key`, `gradient_*`) |
| Add, remove, reorder an emitter; set the budget | **Add emitter**, **Remove**, **Up**, **Down**, **budget** | `editor.vfx_edit` (`add_emitter`, `remove_emitter`, `move_emitter`, `set_budget`) |
| Save | **Save** | `editor.vfx_edit` with `op: "save"` |
| Undo and redo | **Undo**, **Redo** on the tab; Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z | `editor.vfx_edit` (`undo`, `redo`), `editor.undo`, `editor.redo` |
| Render the preview | the **Preview** image | `editor.vfx_preview` (works without a window; `png: true` writes the frame) |

## Keyboard

The tab handles no keys of its own. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work through the shared undo stack
([Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md#keys-that-work-everywhere)). Buttons, boxes and number fields take focus
with Tab. The curve widgets and the gradient bar are drawn shapes that respond to the mouse only;
the selected gradient key also has a time field and a color field you can type into. An agent edits
any key with `editor.vfx_edit` ([Editor accessibility](book/user-guide/editor-guide/accessibility.md)).

## Known limits

- The preview needs a GPU device; without one the panel says so (`editor.vfx_preview` renders
  headless and reports `vfx_editor_no_gpu` when no device exists).
- A curve or an emitter list holds at most 64 keys and 64 emitters.
- The module order inside an emitter is fixed by the file format; only emitters can be reordered.
- The `events` module cannot be added from the list: it needs a child emitter, so write the link in
  the file.
- A module disabled with the A/B switch is not written by **Save**.
- An unsaved effect is covered by the editor's document autosave and offered for recovery after a
  crash.

See also: [Editor surface](book/agents/editor.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/video.md -->
# Video

<!-- index: Video panel -->
<!-- index: media-codecs -->

Panel id: `video`. The **Video** tab opens a `.webm`, `.mkv` or `.video.ron` from the project, shows the decoded
picture, plays, pauses, scrubs and steps single frames, lists the file's streams and decode
counters, and edits the boot movie list of the project's `Regia.toml`. It opens a file the way a game's
video player does, so what the tab shows is what the runtime decodes. Depth:
[Video panel (agents)](book/agents/video-panel.md), [Video playback](book/agents/video-playback.md).

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings back a closed one.
Double-clicking a video file in the **Content** tab opens it here (and brings the tab forward). An
agent brings the tab forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "video"}`. There is no palette command
for this tab.

## Watch a video

1. Type a project-relative path such as `movies/intro.webm` and press **Open**, or double-click the file
   in the Content tab. A project must be open; without one the tab says so.
2. The picture appears with the transport row: **⏮** (previous frame), **Play** or **Pause**, **⏭**
   (next frame), a **frame** slider and the time over the duration.
3. Open **Stream** for the codec, size, frame rate, duration and container, each audio track, and each
   caption or subtitle track with the cues read so far. The line under it reports decode time,
   frames presented, dropped and corrupt, and the decode pool use.
4. A file that cannot play leaves the tab in an error state shown in red (a missing file, a damaged
   container, a refused codec, a full decode pool).

## Edit the boot movies

Under **Boot movies (Regia.toml [boot])** the tab lists the movies a game plays at start, in order.

1. A red code beside an entry means it does not open.
2. **Up** and **Down** reorder, **Remove** deletes an entry.
3. Type a project-relative path in the box (for example `movies/studio.video.ron`) and press **Add**.
4. The `skip_video` line tells where the skip key binding comes from: the project's
   `config/input.ron`, the default keys (Escape, Space, Enter, gamepad South and Start), or an input
   file that cannot be read.
5. **Save** writes the list back to `Regia.toml`.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open a video | Path field, **Open**; double-click in Content | `editor.video_open` |
| Seek, step, play, pause | **⏮**, **⏭**, **Play**, **Pause**, the **frame** slider | `editor.video_seek` |
| Read the player, stream and decode counters | The tab | `editor.video_state` |
| Reorder, remove, add boot movies; save | **Up**, **Down**, **Remove**, **Add**, **Save** | `editor.video_boot` |

## Keyboard

The tab handles no keys of its own; reach its controls with Tab and press them with Enter or Space.

## Known limits

- Compressed codecs are off unless the build turns them on. Cargo feature `media-codecs` (AV1 video, Opus and Vorbis audio) is off by default. Without it the tab refuses those files, the same refusal the runtime uses (`video_panel_codec_unsupported`, and `video_codec_unsupported` on `video.open`). Every build still decodes the reference codecs: uncompressed I420 video (`V_UNCOMPRESSED`) and float PCM audio (`A_PCM/FLOAT/IEEE`). See [Video playback](book/agents/video-playback.md).
- A project must be open to open a video or edit the boot list.
- Caption and subtitle cues are read as the decoder reaches them, so step or play to the end to see
  them all.
- A **Save** that changes the list rewrites the manifest, so its comments and key order are not
  preserved; a list that did not change is never written.

See also: [Content browser](book/user-guide/editor-guide/content-browser.md), [Audio](book/user-guide/audio.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/conversation.md -->
# Conversation

Panel id: `conversation`.

The **Conversation** tab edits a `<id>.conv.ron` conversation as a graph: blocks of lines between labels, branch
nodes for `If` and `Choice` steps, and End nodes, laid out automatically. An inspector edits the selected node, a
findings list shows what the conversation validator reports on the nodes, and a preview runs the conversation from any
node with conditions you set by hand. Depth: [Conversation editor (agents)](book/agents/conversation-editor.md),
[Conversation (agents)](book/agents/conversation.md), [Dialogue](book/user-guide/dialogue.md).

## Opening it

The tab sits in the group under the viewport in the default layout; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings it back if you
closed it. An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "conversation"}`. It has no palette command
and no key.

## Walk-through: add a line and preview it

1. Type a path such as `assets/conversations/guard.conv.ron` in the box and click **Open**. If the file does not
   parse, the tab says **Read-only: the file does not parse** and shows the error; fix the file in a text editor and
   open it again.
2. Click a node in the graph. The inspector on the right (**Node**) shows its id and, for each step in the block,
   its fields: **Speaker**, **Text key** (with the text for that key in the source locale, or a note that there is
   none), **Note**, **Label**, **Goto**, **If** (with its then and else targets), **Prompt key**, options for a
   choice, or **Event**. **Up**, **Down** and **Delete** move or remove a step.
3. Under **Insert after this node:**, type a line id, speaker and text key and click **Line** to add a line after
   the node's last step. Type a label, event or condition name and click **Label**, **Goto**, **If**, **Choice**,
   **Event** or **End** to add that step.
4. To change where a branch goes, drag the branch's port onto another node that has a label. A node with no label
   cannot be a jump target: the tab says to add a **Label** step first.
5. Watch the toolbar: **N error(s), M warning(s)** counts the validator's findings, which are listed under
   **Findings**; hovering a finding shows its fix, and clicking it goes to its node.
6. In **Preview**, tick the conditions the conversation names (the **true** boxes; **Add** adds a condition by name),
   then click **Start** (or select a node and click **From selected**, or double-click a node). **Next** steps past a
   line; for a choice, click an option. **Show node** jumps to the running node, **Stop** ends the run, and **Play
   voice** plays a line's voice clip.
7. Click **Save**.

Every edit is one undo step: **Undo** and **Redo** on the toolbar (their hover text names the step) use the editor's
shared undo stack, so Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y work too. A conversation you did not edit is saved with the bytes that were
read; an edit writes the asset's canonical form.

## The graph

Drag empty space to pan, use the mouse wheel to zoom and drag a node to move it (one undo step; the position is kept
in a layout file under `.regia/conversation_layout/`). **Auto place** in the inspector (shown for a node you moved) returns it to its automatic position,
and **Fit** in the toolbar shows the whole graph. **Search** counts the nodes whose lines, labels, jumps or conditions contain the text, and **Go** selects
the first hit. **Preview from here** in the inspector starts a preview at the selected node.

## Actions

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open a conversation | Path box, **Open** | `editor.conversation_open` |
| Read the graph, findings and layout | The panel | `editor.conversation_graph` |
| Edit steps, labels, jumps, options | The inspector, **Insert after this node:**, drag a port | `editor.conversation_edit` |
| Save | **Save** | `editor.conversation_save` |
| Run the preview a step at a time | **Start**, **Next**, an option button | `editor.conversation_preview_step` |
| Undo, redo | **Undo**, **Redo**, Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y | `editor.undo`, `editor.redo` |

## Keyboard

The panel handles no keys of its own. Tab and Shift+Tab move between its controls, and Space or Enter presses the
focused button ([Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md)). The graph is a pointer canvas; the same edits are available from the
inspector and the findings list, and from `editor.conversation_edit`.

## Known limits

- A file that does not parse opens read-only.
- There is no **New** button: create the `.conv.ron` file first, then open it.
- A jump needs a labeled target node.
- The preview mocks conditions with the check boxes; it does not run game code.

## See also

[Localization](book/user-guide/editor-guide/localization.md), [Dialogue](book/user-guide/dialogue.md), [Conversation editor
(agents)](book/agents/conversation-editor.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/localization.md -->
# Localization

Panel id: `localization`.

The **Localization** tab shows the project's Fluent translation files as a table: one row per key, one column per
locale (the source locale first), each cell colored by its state. Edit a translation in place, gather the keys the
content and code use, find where a key is used, preview pseudo-localization in the viewport, and hand a locale to a
translator as a PO or XLIFF file and read it back. It uses the same library calls as `regia loc`. Depth: [Editor
localization (agents)](book/agents/editor-localization.md), [Localization](book/user-guide/localization.md), [Localization
(agents)](book/agents/localization.md).

## Opening it

The tab sits in the group under the viewport in the default layout; **View ▸ Reset layout** brings it back if you
closed it. An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "localization"}`. It has no palette command
and no key. The locale list itself is not edited here: that is **Project Settings**.

## Walk-through: translate a missing string

1. Open the tab. The header reads the source locale, the number of locales and keys, and each locale has a progress
   bar with its translated, placeholder and stale counts. Click **Reload** to read the files again.
2. Pick **missing** in the first drop-down to list only keys with a missing translation (the others are **all**,
   **untranslated**, **stale** and **long**, for strings longer than the source by a ratio you set with the **ratio**
   box). Pick a locale in the second drop-down, or **every locale**, and use **Search** to narrow by text. **◀** and
   **▶** page through the rows.
3. Click a cell. Its key and locale appear under the table with the source text, and an edit box fills with the
   current text (or the source text when the cell is empty). A cell outlined orange is longer than the source; hover a
   cell to see its state and the file that defines it.
4. Edit the text and click **Apply**. The value is written back into the file that defines it with every other byte
   kept, as one undo step (Ctrl+Z restores the file).
5. Click **Find usages** to list the files that name the key (layouts, scenes, conversations, dialogues, code) and,
   when the editor has an asset registry, the assets that reach them.
6. Click **Gather** to find the keys content and code use and add the missing ones to each locale's `gathered.ftl`;
   a line under the table reports how many keys and entries it found and added. Gathering is one undo step.
7. Tick **Pseudo (viewport)** to preview pseudo-localization of the viewport's runtime localization, in the edit world and
   in play; the label reads **Pseudo (viewport: no runtime localization)** when there is none.

## Walk-through: a translator round trip

1. In the **Exchange** row pick a target locale (not the source), a format (`po` or `xliff`) and a filter (`all`,
   `untranslated` or `stale`). The file box hints `.regia/loc/<locale>.po`; the **…** button picks a file.
2. Click **Export** to write the translator's file.
3. When the file comes back, name it in the box and click **Import…**. The panel shows what would change (added,
   changed, still missing, skipped entries) before it writes anything.
4. Click **Apply (N file(s))** to write the changes as one undo step, or **Cancel**.

## Actions

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read the table | The table, filters, **Search** | `editor.loc_table` |
| Edit one translation | A cell, the edit box, **Apply** | `editor.loc_set` |
| Gather keys | **Gather** | `editor.loc_gather` |
| Find where a key is used | **Find usages** | `editor.loc_usages` |
| Preview pseudo-localization | **Pseudo (viewport)** | `editor.loc_pseudo` |
| Export a locale for a translator | **Export** | `editor.loc_export` |
| Read a returned file | **Import…**, **Apply**, **Cancel** | `editor.loc_import` |
| Read the files again | **Reload** | none (view only) |
| Undo | Ctrl+Z | `editor.undo` |

## Keyboard

The panel handles no keys of its own. Tab and Shift+Tab move between its controls, and Space or Enter presses the
focused button or cell ([Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md)).

## Known limits

- The panel does not edit `localization.ron`: add or remove locales in **Project Settings**.
- Pseudo-localization changes the viewport's runtime localization only, not the files.
- A returned file is planned first; nothing is written until you click **Apply**.

## See also

[Localization](book/user-guide/localization.md), [Conversation](book/user-guide/editor-guide/conversation.md), [Editor localization
(agents)](book/agents/editor-localization.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/data-asset.md -->
# Data Asset

Panel id: `data_asset`.

The **Data Asset** tab edits one `.data.ron` file: a single reflected value of a type your game
registers as a data asset (the game derives `Asset` and registers it with `register_data_asset` or
`#[reflect(Asset)]`). The panel draws the value with the same reflection widgets the
[Inspector](book/user-guide/editor-guide/inspector.md) uses, so numbers, text, lists, maps and nested structs all edit in place.
Every edit is one step on the editor's undo stack. Depth: [Editor creators and the Data Asset
panel (agents)](book/agents/editor-creators.md).

## Open it

- Double-click a `.data.ron` in the [Content browser](book/user-guide/editor-guide/content-browser.md).
- Create one with **New ▸ Data asset** in the Content browser and pick a type from its list. The new file is created in
  the folder shown and opens in the panel at once.
- An agent calls `editor.data_asset_open {"path": "assets/..."}`.

Any of these brings the tab forward, adding it when it was closed. The tab is not in the default
layout and the command palette has no `open` command for it; with nothing open it says to
double-click a `.data.ron` or use **New ▸ Data asset**.

## Edit a data asset

1. Open the file. The header shows its project path (with `*` when it has unsaved edits) and the
   type's name.
2. Change fields in the form. Typing in a field, dragging a number and adding or removing list
   elements each change the value; consecutive edits of one field by dragging merge into a single
   undo step.
3. Press **Save** to write the file (it is enabled only while there are unsaved edits).
4. Press **Revert** to reload the file and drop unsaved edits.

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| List the types New offers | **New ▸ Data asset** in the Content browser | `editor.data_asset_types` |
| Create a data asset | **New ▸ Data asset** and then a type from its list | `editor.create_asset` with `kind: "data_asset"` and `type` |
| Open | double-click the file in the Content browser | `editor.data_asset_open` |
| Edit a field | the form fields | `editor.data_asset_set` (`field` is a reflect path such as `weights[1]`) |
| Undo and redo | Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z | `editor.undo`, `editor.redo` |
| Save | **Save** | `editor.data_asset_save` |
| Revert | **Revert** | `editor.data_asset_open` with `discard: true` and the open path |

## Keyboard

The tab has no shortcuts of its own besides the shared Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z ([Editor
guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md#keys-that-work-everywhere)). Fields, **Save** and **Revert** take focus with Tab.

## Known limits

- Only types registered as data assets can be created or opened; any other type is refused with
  `data_asset_unknown_type`, because the game's loader would refuse the file. The **New** list
  hides standard-library and math types.
- Opening a second file while the open one has unsaved edits is refused (`data_asset_unsaved`);
  save it, revert it, or pass `discard: true`.
- Fields the file leaves out keep the type's defaults.
- Only one data asset is open at a time.

See also: [Data tables](book/user-guide/data-tables.md), [Content browser](book/user-guide/editor-guide/content-browser.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/layouts-workspaces.md -->
# Layouts, workspaces and feature profiles

The editor's dock is yours to arrange: drag a tab to move it, out of the window to float it. This page covers keeping
arrangements, switching between task layouts and trimming the editor down to the features a project uses. Agents have
the same controls ([Editor layouts, workspaces and feature profiles](book/agents/editor-layouts.md)).

## Named layouts

**View ▸ Layouts** saves the current arrangement under a name (tick **Workspace** to also list it in the workspace
switcher), shows a saved one, renames it (type the new name, then **Rename**) and deletes it. Each layout is one file in
your user config folder (`layouts/<name>.editor_layout.ron`), so you can copy it to another machine. **View ▸ Save
layout as my default** makes the current arrangement the one new projects open with, and **View ▸ Reset layout** brings
back the built-in one.

## Workspaces

The **Workspace** list at the right end of the toolbar (also **View ▸ Workspace**, and `Workspace:` entries in the
command palette, Ctrl+Shift+P) switches between task layouts:

| Workspace | Opens |
|---|---|
| Level | the built-in layout |
| Animation | animation graph, clips, skeletons, montages, motion matching, ragdolls |
| Materials | material graph, material instances, look development |
| UI | the UI designer, its animation and inspector panels, theme, localization |
| World | terrain, procedural graphs, the 2D tile mode, layers, world settings |
| Cinematics | shots, sequence curves, cameras, video |
| Debug | log, problems, tests, network, size map, and the profiler window |
| Terrain | terrain tools and viewport, with terrain brushing active |
| 2D tiles | tile tools and viewport, with tile painting active |

Switching never closes a document, and switching back shows the arrangement you left, exactly. Your own workspaces are
the named layouts you saved as workspaces.

Each workspace also selects a **Mode**: World, Terrain, 2D tiles, Animation or UI design.
The mode brings forward its tool palette and shows a strip of related tool-panel buttons.
Change Mode beside the workspace switcher to remember a different mode for this workspace
for the rest of the session. Your documents and brush settings remain open and unchanged.
User mode overrides reset on restart; saved layout files still contain only the arrangement.
Extensions can contribute workspaces, marked **(extension)** in the list.

## Maximize and full screen

**Ctrl+Space** (**View ▸ Maximize panel**, or **Maximize** in a tab's right-click menu) shows the tab under the pointer,
or the focused one, alone in the whole dock area; press it again to put everything back as it was. **F11** (**View ▸
Full-screen viewport**) shows the viewport alone and hides the menus, toolbars and status bar; F11 or Escape brings
them back. While a play session runs, Escape stops play first; the next Escape leaves full screen. Both keys can be
rebound in **Edit ▸ Preferences… ▸ Keymap**.

## Changing a pane

Every tab group has a **+** button at the end of its tab bar. Its list starts with the tabs already in the group (handy
when a crowded tab bar hides some: pick one to bring it forward), then every panel you can add there. Right-click a tab
for **Replace with**, which puts another panel in its place. While you drag an asset or an entity, holding it over a tab
for 30 frames (about half a second) brings that tab forward, so you can drop into a panel that was behind another.

The **+** button is named **Add panel** for screen readers and is reachable with Tab;
Enter opens its menu. Its **Join with neighbor** submenu merges this area's tab stack into
the selected neighboring area. **Swap with** exchanges two areas' tab stacks while keeping
their sizes and positions. Both commands also appear in a tab's right-click menu. These
are view changes and do not enter document undo history.

## Feature profiles

**View ▸ Feature profile** hides whole feature areas the project does not use. **Full** shows everything; **UI only**
keeps the core panels (viewport, outliner, inspector, content, log, settings) and the UI designer's panels. Hidden
panels leave View ▸ Panels, the palette, the `+` list and Replace with, and their tabs close; Create loses the entity
kinds of hidden areas. Pick **Full** to bring everything back. The active profile belongs to the project
(`.regia/editor_profile.ron`); a profile you build with an agent can be saved to your `profiles` folder and shared as a
file.

## The window comes back

When you close the editor, it remembers for this project the window's monitor, size, position and full-screen state,
the open level and the documents open in the Material and animation graph editors. The next time you open the same
project they come back. If that monitor is no longer connected, the window opens centered on your primary display.

## Panels in their own windows

Right-click a tab and pick **Float in own window** to give that panel a window of its own: drag it to another monitor,
resize it, keep a graph editor (material graph, anim graph, sequence curves, montage) beside the level. **Dock back** on
the same menu, or the window's close button, puts its panels back into the main window; nothing closes. Tearing a tab
out of a group with the mouse floats it too. From the keyboard, the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) has **Float the
focused panel in its own window** and **Dock every floated panel back**.

The windows share everything with the main window: the theme, the UI scale, the open level and play. Drag an asset from
the Content Browser in one window and release it over a field in another: the drop lands there (the field does not
light up while you drag across, the window system keeps the pointer in the window the drag started in).

Saved layouts remember where each window was. If its monitor is gone the next time, the window docks back. On Wayland
the compositor decides where a window opens.

**Edit ▸ Preferences ▸ Appearance ▸ Floating windows** picks the mode: `os` (each floated group is its own window; the
default on Linux and Windows) or `in_window` (single-window mode: floated panels stay inside the editor's window).

## More than one Outliner, Content Browser or Inspector

**Window ▸ New Outliner**, **New Content Browser** and **New Inspector** open another copy of the panel beside the
first (up to eight of each; the command palette has the same three commands, so no mouse is needed). The copies are
titled "Outliner 2", "Content 3" and so on, and each keeps its own view: an Outliner its search and columns, a
Content Browser its folder and search, an Inspector its lock. Use two Outliners with different searches to compare
parts of a level, or lock one Inspector on an entity while another follows the selection. The layout remembers every
copy and what it showed, and brings them back when the project opens. Closing a copy forgets its view; the next new
copy starts fresh.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/bulk-edit.md -->
# Bulk Edit

Panel id: `bulk_edit`.

The Bulk Edit panel edits many objects at once as a spreadsheet. Each row is an entity (or a data
asset); each column is a field of one component (or of the asset's type).

## Opening it

- Select entities and choose **View ▸ Bulk Edit**, or right-click a row in the Outliner and choose
  **Edit in grid** (the clicked rows or the selection).
- Right-click a data asset (`.data.ron`) in the Content Browser and choose **Edit in grid**: the
  rows are every data asset of the same type in that folder.

The **Component** list switches to another component the rows share. Nested fields show as their own
columns (`offset.x`, `offset.y`, `offset.z`).

## Working in the grid

- **Edit a cell** with its usual Inspector widget (drag a number, tick a box, pick an enum value), or
  press Enter on the cursor cell and type.
- **Sort**: click a column header (again to reverse, a third time to go back to the opened order).
- **Filter**: type in **Filter rows**; rows whose name or shown cells contain the text stay.
- **Columns**: open **Columns** to search the fields, show or hide them and pin them. Pinned
  columns stay at the left while the others scroll. Right-click a header to pin or hide it.
- **Resize** a column by dragging the right edge of its header, or with Alt+Left and Alt+Right.
- **Copy and paste**: Ctrl+C copies the selected cells as tab-separated text, which a spreadsheet
  pastes as cells; Ctrl+V pastes a block copied from a spreadsheet at the cursor.
- **Fill down**: select a range (Shift+arrows) and press Ctrl+D or **Fill down**: the top row is
  copied into the rows below.

Each paste, fill or cell edit is one step in **Edit ▸ Undo**, however many cells it changes. If one
pasted value does not fit its field (text in a number column), nothing is pasted and the panel says
which cell. Data assets are written to disk with **Save**. **Close** keeps a grid with unsaved asset edits open and says which asset; **Discard and close** drops the edits and closes it.

## Keys

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| Tab (from the toolbar) | Moves into the grid |
| Arrows | Move the cell cursor; with Shift, extend the selection |
| Tab / Shift+Tab | Next / previous cell |
| Enter or F2 | Edit the cell as text; Enter commits, Escape cancels |
| Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V | Copy / paste the selected cells |
| Ctrl+D | Fill down |
| Alt+Left / Alt+Right | Narrow / widen the column |
| Escape | Leave the grid |

Large selections stay fast: only the rows on screen are drawn.

Agents use the same grid through `editor.bulk_edit_open`, `editor.bulk_edit_set`,
`editor.bulk_edit_state`, `editor.bulk_edit_view` and `editor.bulk_edit_save`
([Bulk Edit grid](book/agents/bulk-edit.md)).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/accessibility-rules.md -->
# Accessibility rules for editor panels

These are the rules for people who build editor panels and tools in `regia_editor` (or an editor extension). Each
rule is one the editor's own tests enforce (`regia_editor::a11y_audit`, the agent-parity scan, the theme tests), so a
panel that follows them passes review the first time. The person-facing page is [Editor
accessibility](book/user-guide/editor-guide/accessibility.md); the agent page is [Editor accessibility (agents)](book/agents/editor-a11y.md).

## 1. Every action has a keyboard path

- Draw controls with egui widgets that take focus (buttons, checkboxes, text fields, combo boxes, selectable labels,
  drag values). A person reaches them with Tab and Shift+Tab and activates them with Space or Enter.
- An action that lives on a painted canvas (a graph, a timeline, a curve) also needs a focusable list beside it:
  register it in `regia_editor::canvas_keys`, as the material graph, the procedural graph, the sequencer and the
  profiler do. A drag on a canvas is never the only way.
- A panel that opens from a menu or a toolbar also gets a command palette entry (`window.open_<panel>`), so it opens
  without the pointer.
- No action is mouse-only: no hover-only buttons, no right-click-only menus without a menu bar or palette twin.
- Prove it with a test: feed `egui::Event::Key { key: Tab, .. }` frames into the panel, read the focused AccessKit
  node, and activate it with Enter or typed text (the Theme page's
  `the_accent_is_reachable_and_editable_from_the_keyboard` is a short example).

## 2. Every control has a name

- A button whose visible text is a glyph (`x`, `−`, `↻`, `▾`) uses `a11y_audit::glyph_button(ui, glyph, spoken)`:
  the spoken name is also its hover text.
- A checkbox or field whose label is a separate widget uses `a11y_audit::bare_checkbox` or `a11y_audit::name`.
- A drag value with no label beside it uses `a11y_audit::named_drag_value` ("Half extent x").
- A focusable pane uses `a11y_audit::spoken_only` (a name without a pane-sized tooltip).
- A status glyph whose color or shape carries meaning ("⚠") uses `a11y_audit::warning_glyph`: it stays a label that
  speaks its message.
- Check it in a test: turn AccessKit on (`ctx.enable_accesskit()`), draw the panel, and assert
  `a11y_audit::unnamed_widgets(&update)` is empty.
- Every control is also drawn through an `agent_parity::action_*` helper or listed in `agent-parity-allow.ron` with
  its agent route, so an agent can do what the control does (`agent_parity_scan`).

## 3. Colors come from the theme, in measured pairs

- Never write a literal color (`Color32::from_rgb`, `Color32::RED`) for chrome. Read the theme: `theme::ui_tokens(ctx)`
  in panel code, `theme::tokens(world)` where you have the world. Users switch themes (including the high-contrast
  one) and change the diagnostic colors; literal colors ignore both.
- Draw text only on the surface its token pair names, so the measured contrast is the contrast on screen:

| Foreground token | On | Needs (AA) | High contrast (AAA) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `text`, `strong`, `muted` | `panel` | 4.5:1 | 7:1 |
| `text` | `well` (text fields, recessed fills) | 4.5:1 | 7:1 |
| `widgets.button_text` / `hover_text` / `open_text` | `widgets.idle` / `hover` / `open` | 4.5:1 | 7:1 |
| `on_signal` | `signal` (the selection) | 4.5:1 | 7:1 |
| `widgets.link`, `warn`, `error`, `accents.*` text colors | `panel` | 4.5:1 | 7:1 |
| a control's boundary (`widgets.idle`, or `line` when the fill is the panel color) | `panel` | 3:1 | 3:1 |

- `editor.a11y_contrast` (with `level: "aaa"` for the high-contrast bar) measures these pairs for any theme; a new
  pair your panel needs belongs in `a11y_audit::editor_contrast` with a test.
- Diagnostic colors go through `theme::diagnostic_color(tokens, level)` (or the `accents.log_*` tokens), so the
  user's error, warning, info and success colors apply.

## 4. Color is never the only meaning

- Pair every meaning-carrying color with text or a shape: the log writes `ERROR` and `WARN`, the Problems panel
  writes the severity, a node error has a "⚠" glyph that speaks its message.
- Check a panel under View ▸ Color Vision (Simulate protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia): if two states can no
  longer be told apart, they are relying on hue alone.
- Hues that must stay distinct (gizmo axes, graph pin kinds) come from token sets chosen to survive the simulations
  (`theme::DATA_KIND_DEFAULTS` is a colorblind-safe set).

## 5. Layouts scale

- Sizes are points from egui's spacing and text styles, never pixel constants for text boxes. Users set both the
  whole-UI scale (`appearance.ui_scale`) and the text scale (`appearance.text_scale`, 0.8 to 2.0).
- Let labels wrap or elide (`Label::wrap`, `egui::TextWrapMode`), give fields a desired width rather than an exact
  one, and put long rows in a scroll area.
- Check it with `a11y_audit::clipped_text` on a frame drawn at text scale 2.0: no text may extend past its clip edge
  (`main_panels_at_text_scale_two_clip_no_text` runs the editor's main panels at 1920×1080).

## 6. Text

- US English in every label, hint and message.
- Name things by what they do ("Save theme as…", "Use theme"), not by an internal id.

## 7. Side effects run once

egui may run a panel's UI twice in one frame. A per-frame side effect (a file write, a status message, a counter)
is guarded with `ctx.cumulative_frame_nr()`; actions that follow a click or a key press already run once.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/undo-history.md -->
# Undo History

Panel id: `undo_history`.

The **Undo History** tab lists the editor's shared undo history: every retained edit, oldest first, with the
documents it touched. Click an entry to go back (or forward) to that point; the details under the list say what
the entry changed. It is the same history Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z walk, and the same history an agent reads with
`editor.history`. Depth: [Shared undo history and recovery (agents)](book/agents/undo.md), [Undo and redo in the
editor (agents)](book/agents/undo-redo.md).

## Open it

Choose **Window ▸ Undo History**. From the keyboard press Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the Undo History tab**
(`window.open_undo_history`); bind a key to it in the keymap if you use it often. An agent brings the tab
forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "undo_history"}`.

## Read the history

1. The first line counts the entries: "N applied · M available to redo".
2. The list starts with **0 · Before retained history** (the state before the oldest edit the editor still keeps),
   then one row per edit: its number, its description and the documents it touched (`level` is the open level).
   The last applied edit is marked **Current**; entries after it, which a redo would apply again, are marked
   **Redo**.
3. Hover a row, or move keyboard focus to it, to show its **Change details**: for each thing the edit touched, the
   document and, when the edit reports them, the entity, its guid, the asset and the property. "This command does
   not report detailed changes" means an older kind of edit has not supplied details.
4. While a script or agent transaction is open, a line says "Transaction in progress" with its label, and the rows
   are disabled: jumps wait until the transaction is committed or aborted.

## Jump to a point

Click a row, or Tab to it and press Enter or Space. The editor undoes or redoes one edit at a time until exactly
that many entries are applied: **0** undoes everything retained, the last row redoes everything. Each edit's own
revert or apply runs, so a jump is the same as pressing Ctrl+Z or Ctrl+Shift+Z that many times. A refused jump
shows its error under the details.

Making a new edit after jumping back drops the entries marked **Redo**, as Ctrl+Z followed by an edit does. The
history keeps a bounded number of entries; the oldest fall off, and row numbers always count the retained history.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read the history with its details | The list and **Change details** | `editor.history` |
| Jump to an entry | Click a row, or Tab to it and press Enter or Space | `editor.history_jump {"index": N}` |
| Undo, redo | Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y | `editor.undo`, `editor.redo` |
| Group several edits into one entry | (agents and scripts) | `editor.transaction_begin`, `editor.transaction_commit`, `editor.transaction_abort` |
| Capture the tab as an image | (agents) | `editor.capture_panel {"panel": "undo_history"}` |

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/notes-activity.md -->
# Notes and Activity

Panel ids: `notes` and `activity`.

Two tabs for reviewing a level together. **Notes** holds review notes pinned in the world: a note is a marker in the
open level with a text, its author, replies and a resolved flag, saved with the level and stripped from cooked and
packaged levels. **Activity** is the session's timeline of who changed what: every agent call and every user edit,
undo and redo, in the order they happened. Depth: [Review notes and session Activity
(agents)](book/agents/review-notes.md).

## Open them

Choose **Window ▸ Notes** or **Window ▸ Activity**. From the keyboard press Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the Notes tab** or
**Open the Activity tab** (`window.open_notes`, `window.open_activity`). An agent runs the same commands with `editor.command`.

## Notes

1. The first line shows the author name new notes get: the project's git `user.name`, else the `review.author`
   preference.
2. **Show** filters the list: **all**, **open**, **resolved** or **mine** (notes whose author is you).
3. To add a note, type in **New note** and press **Add note**. The note goes where you placed it in the viewport
   (press **N** over a surface to start a note there), else on the selected entity. Without either, the tab shows an
   error under the list and adds nothing.
4. Each row reads "author: text (N replies)". Click it to frame the note in the viewport and open it: its replies
   are listed, with a **Reply text** box, **Reply**, and **Resolve** (or **Reopen** on a resolved note).
5. Every change is one undo entry and marks the level unsaved; nothing is written until you save the level.

A note badge in the viewport shows how many messages the thread has; clicking it frames the note as well.

## Activity

1. **Source** picks **all**, **agent** (calls an agent made) or **user** (your edits, undos and redos).
2. **Method filter** keeps the rows whose method or command contains the text (case-sensitive).
3. Each row reads "time (Unix milliseconds) · who · method or command · outcome". An agent row names the
   connection's client; a user row names the edit. Below a row, **Select entity N** selects an entity the row touched (disabled once that entity is
   gone), and the asset paths it touched are listed.

The tab keeps the newest 4,000 rows. It also reads the end (the last 1 MiB) of the project's existing agent audit
log, so calls from earlier sessions appear, without their targets (that log did not store them).

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Start a note at the surface under the cursor | **N** in the viewport (command `review.add_note`, rebindable) | `editor.note_add {"text", "position"}` |
| Add a note | **New note**, **Add note** | `editor.note_add` |
| List notes with a filter | **Show** | `editor.note_list {"filter"}` |
| Frame a note | Click its row or its badge | `editor.select`, `editor.focus` |
| Reply | **Reply text**, **Reply** | `editor.note_reply` |
| Resolve or reopen | **Resolve**, **Reopen** | `editor.note_resolve {"resolved"}` |
| Read the activity timeline | **Source**, **Method filter** | `editor.activity {"since", "source", "method"}` |
| Select an entity from a row | **Select entity N** | `editor.select` |

Tab and Shift+Tab reach every filter, text box and button; Space or Enter presses the focused button.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/debug-visual-log.md -->
# Selected Object Debug and Visual Log

Panel ids: `selected_debug` and `visual_log`.

Two debugging tabs for gameplay. **Selected Object Debug** shows what the selected object's gameplay systems are doing
right now: perception, the state-tree path, smart-object claims, navigation waypoints, abilities and effects, as text
in the tab and as a label in the viewport. **Visual Log** replays the lines and text labels a game recorded per
entity, one frame at a time, so you can scrub back to the frame where something went wrong. Both only change what is
drawn: they never edit the level and add nothing to the undo history. Depth: [Selected-object debug overlay and visual
log (agents)](book/agents/visual-log.md).

## Open them

Press Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the Selected Object Debug tab** or **Open the Visual Log tab** (commands
`window.open_selected_debug`, `window.open_visual_log`; bind a key to either in the keymap). An agent brings a tab
forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "selected_debug"}` or `{"open": "visual_log"}`.

## Selected Object Debug

1. Check **Show selected object debug data**. Unchecked, the overlay does no gameplay queries at all.
2. Select an object in the viewport or the Outliner; the tab follows the selection the viewport and Outliner share.
   With nothing selected it says "Select an object in the viewport or Outliner."
3. The tab names the world it reads (the edit world, or the play world while playing) and the entity, then one
   line per piece of data: perception cones and hearing radius, perceived targets, the active state-tree path,
   smart-object claims, the remaining navigation waypoints, running abilities and applied effects. Each list is
   capped at 128 rows. The same text is drawn as a label next to the object in the viewport.
4. If the selected entity is gone (for example, despawned during play), the tab says why instead of showing data.

## Visual Log

A game records shapes with the `debug_log!` macro of `regia_framework` (the `visual-log` feature);
play-in-editor installs the recorder for you. The recorder keeps a ring of recent frames.

1. The first line names the world the recording comes from. With nothing recorded the tab says "No recorded frames.
   Start play with visual logging enabled."
2. Drag **Recorded frame** to pick a frame. The viewport draws exactly that frame's shapes, also while play is paused;
   scrubbing does not rewind the game. A frame that has fallen out of the ring draws nothing ("This frame is not
   retained").
3. Click an **Entity N** row to show or hide that entity's shapes. Entities that are gone keep their recorded rows.
4. Under the list, each shape of the frame is listed: a text label as "entity: text", a line with its two ends.

The tab keeps its last recording after play stops. A closed tab does no work.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Turn the overlay on or off, pick the entity | **Show selected object debug data** (Tab to it, Space) | `editor.debug_overlay {"on", "entity"}` |
| Read the overlay's text | The tab | `editor.debug_overlay {}` |
| Scrub to a frame | **Recorded frame** (Tab to it, Left and Right) | `editor.visual_log {"frame"}` |
| Show an entity's shapes | **Entity N** (Tab to it, Space) | `editor.visual_log {"entities"}` |
| Read the recorded shapes | The tab | `editor.visual_log {}` |

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/project-health.md -->
# Project Health

Panel id: `project_health`.

The **Project Health** tab gathers the checks the project already has into one ranked list: validator findings,
budgets, missing references, large assets nothing uses, cook warnings, toolchain problems from `regia doctor` and
autosaves a crash left behind. Each row says what was found, recommends an action and links to where you fix it.
The pre-commit hook that validates staged assets is set up in **Project Settings ▸ Validation**. Depth: [Project
health, staged validation and the Problems and Output Log lists (agents)](book/agents/project-health.md), the
[Problems](book/user-guide/editor-guide/problems.md) tab.

## Open it

Choose **Tools ▸ Project Health**. From the keyboard press Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the Project Health tab**
(`window.open_project_health`). An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "project_health"}`
and runs the checks with `editor.project_health {"action": "run"}`.

## Run the checks

1. Press **Re-run**. The checks run as an editor job: a spinner shows "running (project_health:N)" and the button
   is disabled until it ends. The job can be cancelled like any editor job; the rows of the checks that ran stay.
2. The header then counts the errors, warnings and notes. "No checks ran yet: use Re-run." means the tab has not run
   in this session; "No problems found." means every check passed.
3. The run also fills the [Problems](book/user-guide/editor-guide/problems.md) tab with the same validator report.

## Read the list

Rows rank errors first, then warnings, then notes; within a severity by category, in this order:

| Category | Comes from |
|---|---|
| Missing reference | the missing-reference and missing-UI-image validators |
| Budget | the texture size, triangle and size budgets of `config/validation.ron` |
| Validation | every other validator: one row per validator and finding, with a count and example assets |
| Toolchain | `regia doctor` checks that warn or fail (a note when the CLI did not run) |
| Cook warning | the cook's import warnings, per source |
| Unreferenced | cooked assets of 1 MiB or more that nothing references and that are not a root |
| Recovery | autosaves left by a crash |

Each row shows its severity, category and title (hover the title for the details) and, under it, **Recommended:**
with the action to take. Click the title to select the row. The button at the end of the row follows the link:

- **Open** opens the asset the way a double-click in the Content Browser does.
- **Show in Problems** filters the Problems tab to the validator and brings it forward.
- **Copy command** copies the fix command (for example, a toolchain install step); it is never run for you.

**Checks**, folded under the list, says which sources ran and which were skipped, and why.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Run every check | **Re-run** | `editor.project_health {"action": "run", "wait"?, "doctor"?}` |
| Cancel a run | the editor job list | `editor.cancel_job` |
| Read the rows and the sources | The list, **Checks** | `editor.project_health {}` |
| Follow a row's link | **Open**, **Show in Problems**, **Copy command** | `editor.project_health {"action": "open", "row": N}` |
| Install or remove the pre-commit hook | **Project Settings ▸ Validation** | `editor.precommit_hook {"action": "install" \| "uninstall"}`, CLI `regia hooks` |

Tab and Shift+Tab reach **Re-run** and every row's link button; Space or Enter presses the focused one.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/world-map.md -->
# World Map

Panel id: `world_map`.

The **World Map** tab edits a large streamed level a few cells at a time. It draws the level's streaming grid; you
pick cells and load their entities into the edit world, where they appear in the Outliner and the Inspector like any
other entity. Saving a cell writes back only that cell's entity files, so the rest of the world keeps its bytes.
Depth: [World Map (agents)](book/agents/world-streaming-editor.md), [World streaming and
HLOD](book/agents/world-streaming.md).

## What it needs

- The level in its **directory form** (`<name>.level.d`, one file per entity). Split a single-file level with
  `regia level split`.
- A **cooked world index**: run `regia cook` first. The cook decides which cell each entity belongs to, so an entity
  you place after the last cook joins a cell at the next cook.

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group (**View ▸ Reset layout** brings it back). From the keyboard press
Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the World Map tab** (`window.open_world_map`). An agent brings it forward with
`editor.layout_apply {"open": "world_map"}`.

## Open a world

Type the streamed level's path in **Streamed level** (absolute or under the project) and press **Open world**. With
no world open the tab says "No world is open. Cook the project, then open a streamed level." You cannot open another
world while cells of this one are loaded.

## Pick cells

The map draws the grid with +X to the right and +Z down. Cells are shaded by their content height; loaded cells are in
the accent color; a cell the runtime would refuse (a missing or damaged cooked cell) is outlined in the error color with
a cross; the editor camera is a dot with its view cone.

- Click a cell to select it; Ctrl-click or Shift-click adds or removes one; drag a box to select every cell it
  touches. **Clear selection** empties the selection.
- From the keyboard, use the cell list beside the map: Tab to a row, Up and Down move between rows, Enter or Space
  selects or deselects the row's cell.

## Load and unload

1. **Load selected** loads the selected cells; **Load around camera** loads every cell within the radius next to it
   (in meters) of the editor camera. Loading runs as an editor job ("Loading (world_load:N)"); **Cancel load** stops it
   before anything is added, and the edit world stays as it was.
2. A cell that fails to read loads nothing and shows the reason; the other cells of the job are not loaded either.
3. **Unload selected** removes the selected cells' entities from the edit world. If you changed any of them, the tab
   asks: **Save and unload** writes each changed entity's file (and removes the files of entities you deleted),
   **Discard and unload** drops the changes, **Keep loaded** cancels.

Entities that were already in the edit world because the whole level was opened with **File ▸ Open level** are not
taken over by a cell: loading skips them and unloading never removes them. Unloading clears the undo history, as
opening a level does.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open a streamed level | **Streamed level**, **Open world** | `editor.world_open {"path"}` |
| Read the grid, the loaded cells and a running load | The map and the cell list | `editor.world_cells` |
| Load cells | **Load selected** | `editor.world_load {"cells": ["0_0"]}` |
| Load the cells around the camera | **Load around camera** | `editor.world_load {"radius_m"}` |
| Cancel a load | **Cancel load** | `editor.cancel_job {"id": "world_load:N"}` |
| Unload cells | **Unload selected**, then **Save and unload** or **Discard and unload** | `editor.world_unload {"cells", "save"}` |

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/agent-panel.md -->
# Agent

Panel id: `agent`.

The **Agent** tab runs an agent program you choose, inside the editor, and lets you talk to it. The editor installs no
agent, no provider and no credentials: you configure the command of an agent you already have, and the panel starts
it in the open project's folder and connects it to the editor's agent protocol. A mode decides what the agent may do:
only read (**Ask only**), propose file changes you review (**Propose**), or edit with the project's normal permissions
(**Act**). Depth: [Hosted Agent panel (agents)](book/agents/agent-panel.md), [Agent Changes](book/user-guide/editor-guide/agent-changes.md).

## Open it

Choose **Window ▸ Agent**. From the keyboard press Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the Agent tab** (`window.open_agent`).
Nothing starts when the tab opens.

## Configure a command

In **Preferences ▸ Agents ▸ Agent commands**, add a name and the program with its arguments, for example the name
"Local assistant" and the command `/path/to/my-agent --regia-stdio`. Each argument is passed as written: there is no
shell, so no variables or wildcards are expanded. Keep the agent's credentials in its own environment or credential
manager: the editor refuses argument names and text that look like credentials. Only an editor user can change this
setting; an agent cannot.

The program runs with your normal operating-system rights in the project folder. The mode limits what it can do through
the editor's agent connection, not what the program itself can do with files or the network: only run commands you
trust with your project.

## Run a session

1. Pick a configured command and press **Start**. Each start is a new session; the session picker switches between
   them, and **Stop** ends the selected one. At most 16 sessions are kept; a stopped one makes room for the next.
2. Pick the mode: **Ask only**, **Propose** or **Act**. Changing the mode never approves a plan.
3. Type in the message field and press **Send** (or Enter in the field). The agent's answers appear in the
   conversation, each marked with the mode it arrived in.
4. When the agent sends a plan, its steps appear as a checklist and the agent cannot make changes until you press
   **Approve plan**; **Reject plan** keeps it blocked. Reading stays allowed meanwhile. A new plan replaces the old
   one.
5. In **Propose**, the agent's file changes wait in [Agent Changes](book/user-guide/editor-guide/agent-changes.md) for you to accept or reject.

Each session's conversation is kept in `.regia/agent_sessions/` (the newest 256 messages). After the editor restarts,
earlier conversations can still be read, but their sessions are not started again.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control / key | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| List commands and sessions | The command and session pickers | `editor.agent_sessions {"action": "list"}` |
| Start a session | **Start** | `editor.agent_sessions {"action": "start", "command", "mode"}` |
| Send a message | Message field, **Send** or Enter | `editor.agent_sessions {"action": "send", "session", "text"}` |
| Change the mode | **Ask only**, **Propose**, **Act** | `editor.agent_sessions {"action": "mode", "session", "mode"}` |
| Approve or reject a plan | **Approve plan**, **Reject plan** | `editor.agent_sessions {"action": "send", "session", "approve_plan"}` |
| Stop a session | **Stop** | `editor.agent_sessions {"action": "stop", "session"}` |

Tab and Shift+Tab move through the command picker, **Start**, the session picker, **Stop**, the mode buttons, the plan
checklist and its decisions, the message field and **Send**. The session methods need the project's `tools`
permission, and a hosted agent can never control sessions or approve its own plan through them.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/retarget.md -->
# Retarget

Panel id: `retarget`.

The **Retarget** tab maps one rig's bones onto another's, so animations made for one character play on another. You
open a source and a target rig, map their bones chain by chain (automatically, then by hand where needed), line the
chains up with a reference pose, watch a clip play on both rigs side by side, save the map as a `.retarget.ron` file
and bake clips for the target. A game that loads the saved map plays what the tab shows. Depth: [Retargeting editor
(agents)](book/agents/retargeting.md), [Retargeting on real content and crowds](book/agents/retarget-crowds.md).

## Open it

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group. From the keyboard press Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the Retarget
tab** (`window.open_retarget`). An agent brings it forward with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "retarget"}`.

## Open two rigs

Type a rig in **Source** and in **Target** and press **Open rigs**. A rig is `demo` (the editor's procedural biped),
`fixture:source` or `fixture:target` (two test rigs: an A-pose rig facing −Z and a T-pose rig facing +Z), or the path of
a `.glb`, `.gltf` or `.bvh` file in the project. The map starts empty.

## Map the bones

1. Press **Auto-map**. It pairs every humanoid role both rigs have (guessed from the joint names) and groups them into
   chains: Root, Spine, Head, the two arms and the two legs. Target joints still unmapped then pair with a source joint
   of the same name (ignoring a `namespace:` prefix, case and punctuation, so `mixamorig:Tail1` matches `tail_1`); those
   are listed under **Other**. The status line says how many it mapped each way.
2. **Bone map** lists each chain with its count of mapped roles; open one to see its rows. In a row, pick the
   **Source joint** and the **Target joint** for the role from their lists, or clear one.
3. Twist, IK, end and helper joints never take a humanoid role.

## Line up the rest pose

When the target should stand in a reference pose rather than copy the source's rest pose, set the chain's **Rest
offset** (X, Y and Z, in degrees), or press **Align to T-pose** or **Align to A-pose**: the editor computes the offset
that points the target's arm, leg, spine or neck bones the reference way while the source stands in its bind pose. Without an offset, the target follows the source's rest pose.

## Preview

Under **Preview**, pick a clip of the source rig, press **Play** (or **Pause**), or drag the time slider. Both rigs are
drawn side by side, the source turned to face the same way as the target.

## Save and bake

- Type a path ending in `.retarget.ron` and press **Save map**. "unsaved" next to the button means the map changed
  since the last save.
- To bake clips for the target, tick the source clips to bake, type an **output folder** and press **Retarget clips…**.
  Each clip is written as `<folder>/<clip>.cooked`. The bake runs as an editor job; **Cancel** stops it, and a cancelled
  or failed bake writes no clip at all.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open the rigs (and a saved map) | **Source**, **Target**, **Open rigs** | `editor.retarget_open {"source", "target", "setup"?}` |
| Map automatically | **Auto-map** | `editor.retarget_auto_map` |
| Set or clear a role's joint | **Source joint**, **Target joint** | `editor.retarget_map_set {"role", "source"?, "target"?}` |
| Set or compute a chain's rest offset | **Rest offset**, **Align to T-pose**, **Align to A-pose** | `editor.retarget_map_set {"chain", "rest_offset_deg" \| "align"}` |
| Preview a clip | **Preview** clip, **Play**, time slider | `editor.retarget_preview {"clip", "time", "playing"?}` |
| Save the map | **Save map** | `editor.retarget_save {"path"?}` |
| Bake clips | **Retarget clips…**, **Cancel** | `editor.retarget_batch {"out_dir", "clips"?, "wait"?}`, `editor.cancel_job` |

Tab and Shift+Tab move between the controls; Space or Enter presses the focused button.

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/biome.md -->
# Biome

Panel id: `biome`.

The **Biome** tab edits a biome definition (`.biome.ron`): what the procedural tools grow in an area and how. It shows
the file as forms: the biome's name, color, map key and priority; its layers (rank, sharing, the candidate source and
its density noise, channels and their rules, child depth); each layer's entries (what spawns, its weight, the channels
it takes, its filters with a small curve of their density window, footprint, placement, render settings and children);
and the grass multipliers. Depth: [Biome editor (agents)](book/agents/biome-editor.md), [Biomes](book/agents/biomes.md)
(what each field does).

## Open it

Choose **Window ▸ Biome**, or press Ctrl+Shift+P and pick **Open the Biome tab** (`window.open_biome`). To make a new
biome, use **Content ▸ New ▸ Biome**: it creates a file named after itself with no layers. The procedural **Area**
tool picks its biome from the project's `.biome.ron` files.

## Edit a biome

1. Pick a `.biome.ron` of the project from the list, or type its path, and press **Open**; type a new path and press
   **New** to start a biome there. A file that breaks a rule still opens, and its issues are listed.
2. Edit the forms: numbers drag, switches toggle, choices are drop-downs, and a text field takes effect when you press
   Enter or leave it. Every list has ▲ and ▼ to reorder, **Remove** and **Add**.
3. An edit that would break a rule (a duplicate name, a negative weight, a filter window whose minimum is above its
   maximum, a child naming no entry of its layer) is refused and changes nothing, so the open biome always stays one
   the game can load. Renaming an entry renames the children that name it; renaming a channel renames it in the
   layer's entries.
4. **Undo** and **Redo** keep 128 steps, one per edit; one drag of a value is one step.
5. **Save** writes the file in its canonical form. RON comments in the opened file are not kept: when the file has
   any, a warning line says how many will be lost. A file with rule issues saves only once they are fixed.

Opening another file or starting a new biome while the open one has unsaved edits is refused first: the tab shows the
refusal with a **Discard edits and open …** (or **… start …**) button, and **Keep editing** keeps your edits. The tab has
no autosave, so save first.

## Actions and agent methods

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Open a biome, or start a new one | **Open**, **New**; **Content ▸ New ▸ Biome** | `editor.biome_panel_open {"path", "new"?, "discard"?}`, `editor.create_asset {"kind": "biome", "path"}` |
| Read the definition, its issues and the undo depth | The forms and the issue list | `editor.biome_panel_get` |
| Change a field, add to or remove from a list, move an item | The forms, **Add**, **Remove**, ▲ ▼ | `editor.biome_panel_edit {"op", "path", "value"?, "index"?, "to"?, "merge"?}` |
| Undo, redo | **Undo**, **Redo** | `editor.biome_panel_edit {"op": "undo"}`, `{"op": "redo"}` |
| Save | **Save** | `editor.biome_panel_save` |

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/cameras.md -->
# Cameras

<!-- index: Camera rig -->
<!-- index: Cameras panel -->

Panel id: `cameras`. The **Cameras** tab is the asset page for every `.camera.ron` in the project, the rig graph of the asset you select, and the camera drivers of a running game. Depth: [Camera framework](book/agents/camera-framework.md), [Gameplay panels](book/agents/editor-gameplay-panels.md).

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group. The Cinematics workspace opens it with shots and video. **View ▸ Reset layout** restores a closed tab. An agent opens it with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "cameras"}`. **Content ▸ New ▸ Camera rig** creates a file (`editor.create_asset` with `kind: "camera"`): one `look` slot and a rig named `follow`.

The page holds the edit world's assets. No driver runs there, so editing does not move a camera in a running game. **Save** writes the file; the asset watcher reloads it in the edit world and in the play world.

## Edit a rig

1. Open the tab. The first time it draws, it scans the project. Pick an asset. The **Asset** section lists status, issues, parameters, variables, input slots and the director.
2. Edit **Parameters**, **Rigs** (rename, duplicate, remove, add a node, tags, blend out) and **Transitions**. Each change is one step of that asset's own history. **Undo** and **Redo** walk it. A drag or a typing session in one field is one step until you let go.
3. Open **Rig graph**. Boxes are laid out from the asset. Click a node for its form (move, duplicate, remove, add after, add inside a group). Green boxes ran, red ones were skipped, gray ones are switched off. Arcs on the left are transitions.
4. **Apply** validates the working copy and, with no errors, makes it the active version. **Save** (Ctrl+S while the pointer is over the panel) applies, writes the canonical file and marks the history saved. **Save\*** means unsaved edits.
5. Press Alt+P. The **Live** section lists drivers: the asset they name, whether they are bound, the primary rig, blend, layers and variables. Pick one to inspect it.

## Actions

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read assets, the page and drivers | The tab | `editor.camera_panel_get` |
| Select an asset or a driver | The lists | `editor.camera_panel_select` |
| Load one file, or scan | Opening the tab, or a path | `editor.camera_panel_load` |
| Read the graph | **Rig graph** | `editor.camera_rig_graph` |
| Edit the working copy | The forms | `editor.camera_panel_edit` |
| Apply, save | **Apply**, **Save** | `editor.camera_panel_apply`, `editor.camera_panel_save` |
| Drive a running camera | **Live** | `editor.camera_panel_driver` |

## Keyboard

Tab moves between the forms. Ctrl+S saves while the pointer is over the panel. The graph is operated by click; the same edits are on the forms.

## Known limits

- A file that changes on disk replaces the working copy. Edits you have not saved are lost. **Apply** alone does not write the file.
- Saving writes the canonical text. Comments in the old file do not survive. The tab says so while the file still has comments.
- A `Hook` director cannot be fully checked in the edit world, which has no game code to ask. The play world checks the name.
- While play runs, a call that changes a driver is queued for the next frame. Read `last_call` on the next `editor.camera_panel_get`. Entity ids from the edit world and the play world are not the same; the selection clears when play starts or stops.
- `play_framework` stays false until the game adds `CameraPlugin`. A play session with no camera drivers says so.

## See also

[Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md), [Sequencer](book/user-guide/editor-guide/sequencer.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/mode-2d.md -->
# 2D

<!-- index: 2D mode -->
<!-- index: Tilemap -->

Panel id: `mode2d`. The **2D** tab paints a `.tilemap.ron` and, when you open one, an `.autotile.ron` rule set. It edits those source files. A running game keeps its own loaded copy until the asset watcher cooks the file you saved. Depth: [2D](book/user-guide/2d.md), [2D editing (agents)](book/agents/editor-2d.md). Spec: `docs/specs/86-2d-toolkit.md`.

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group. **View ▸ Reset layout** restores a closed one. An agent opens it with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "mode2d"}`. The World and 2D tiles workspaces open it with the viewport ([Layouts, workspaces and feature profiles](book/user-guide/editor-guide/layouts-workspaces.md)).

## Paint a map

1. Tick **2D mode**. The viewport switches to the front orthographic pane and frames the map.
2. Press **Open map…** and choose a `.tilemap.ron` under the project. If the map already open has unsaved edits, choose **Save and open**, **Discard and open** or **Cancel**.
3. Press **Open rules…** for an `.autotile.ron` that fits this map, or leave rules clear and paint raw tiles.
4. Under **Layers**, pick the tile layer strokes write into. **Add object** and **Delete object** edit object layers.
5. Under **Tool**, pick paint, line, rectangle, bucket or pick. **Filled** makes the rectangle a fill or an outline. **Contiguous** makes the bucket fill the connected region or every matching cell.
6. Under **Brush**, pick a tile from the palette (arrow keys move the palette focus; Enter or Space paints the map cursor). **Flip X**, **Flip Y** and **Diagonal** flip that tile. With rules open, pick a terrain instead.
7. Paint in the viewport: left-drag paints, Shift erases. One stroke is one undo step (Ctrl+Z).
8. **Save** writes the map. Saving the level also writes the map when it is dirty.

**Grid** draws the cell grid when cells are large enough on screen. **Play animations** advances animated tiles. **Rulers** and **Snap to guides** use the guide list; **Add vertical guide** and **Add horizontal guide** add one. **Paint random tiles** scatters the weighted tiles you list, including a chance of leaving a cell alone.

This tab does not edit `.tmx` or `.tmj` files. Author those elsewhere and import, or work in `.tilemap.ron`.

## Keys while the viewport is painting

These apply when 2D mode is on and no text field has focus. Rebind them from the [keymap](book/user-guide/editor-guide/keymap.md).

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| B | Toggle 2D mode |
| Left-drag | Paint |
| Shift | Erase |
| `,` / `.` | Previous / next layer |
| `[` / `]` | Previous / next terrain |
| Ctrl-drag | Copy a rectangle into the stamp |

The tab's **Rotate**, **Flip** and **Drop** buttons transform the stamp. Arrow keys move the map cursor when it has focus; Enter or Space paints that cell and Delete erases it.

## Actions

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Turn the mode on, open a map or rules, pick a layer | **2D mode**, **Open map…**, **Open rules…**, the layer list | `editor.mode2d_set`, `editor.mode2d_get` |
| Paint or erase | The viewport, or the map cursor | `editor.tile_stroke` |
| Stamp | Ctrl-drag; Rotate, Flip, Drop | `editor.tile_stamp` |
| Save the map | **Save**, or save the level | `editor.tilemap_save` |
| New map, tilesets, layers | The layer and tileset controls | `editor.tilemap_new`, `editor.tilemap_tilesets` |
| Rule set | **Open rules…** and the terrain brush | `editor.autotile_open`, `editor.autotile_edit`, `editor.autotile_save` |

## Known limits

- Opening another map while this one is dirty is refused until you save or discard (`mode2d_unsaved`).
- A rule set that does not fit the map is refused (`mode2d_bad_rules`).
- A missing tileset image draws flat colors. Painting still works. **Reload images** (or `reload_images`) reads the files again.
- An orthogonal map draws at most 200 000 tiles; farther zoom draws every Nth cell. Isometric, staggered and hexagonal maps stop at 200 000 quads instead of skipping cells.
- Paths must stay inside the project.

## See also

[Viewport](book/user-guide/editor-guide/viewport.md), [Content browser](book/user-guide/editor-guide/content-browser.md), [2D](book/user-guide/2d.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/match-rules.md -->
# Match rules

<!-- index: Match rules -->
<!-- index: Rule set -->
<!-- index: Playlist -->

Panel id: `match_rules`. The **Match Rules** tab edits a project's `.rules.ron` rule sets and `.playlist.ron` playlists, and play-in-editor uses those files when a match runs. The level's Game Rules picker lives on [World settings](book/user-guide/editor-guide/world-settings.md) and reads the same library. Depth: [Match rules in the editor](book/agents/editor-match-rules.md), [Authoring modes](book/user-guide/game-modes.md).

The tab is not in the built-in dock. **View ▸ Reset layout** closes it. On [World settings](book/user-guide/editor-guide/world-settings.md), **Edit rules…** opens it. `editor.rules_open` opens the tab and the file. An agent can also add the tab with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "match_rules"}`.

Rule sets and playlists are files. Their edits sit on the editor undo stack and do not mark the level dirty.

## Edit a rule set

1. Under **Rule set**, type a project path that ends in `.rules.ron` and press **Open or create**. Create starts from the file stem, a skeleton (`tdm`, `ffa`, `ctf`, `koth`, `dom` or `custom`) and an optional parent.
2. If the open rule set has unsaved edits, the tab asks you to save or discard before replacing it. An agent passes `discard: true` or gets `match_rules_dirty`.
3. The form lists the file fields (`id`, `name_key`, `skeleton`, `extends`, `teams`, `win_conditions`, `options`) and then each session section (`flow`, `phases`, `objectives`, `teams`, `respawn`, `zones`). An empty field inherits the parent, or the engine default at the root.
4. Problems appear on the rows (`ruleset_option_range`, `ruleset_unknown`, `ruleset_cycle` and the other rule-set codes). **Save** is refused while one is listed (`match_rules_save_blocked`) and writes nothing.
5. **Save** writes the file by a temporary file and a rename, then reloads the project library so the Game Rules picker lists the id. A rule set with no edits is not rewritten, so comments and layout stay.

## Edit a playlist

1. Under **Playlist**, open or create a `.playlist.ron`.
2. **Add row**, remove, and reorder. Each row names a map, a mode and options. A row whose mode names no rule set and no skeleton is a warning (`playlist_mode_unknown`), not a save blocker: that mode belongs to the game.
3. A row option the schema does not declare, or a value out of range, blocks the save (`playlist_save_blocked`). An empty playlist cannot be saved.

## Game Rules on the level

World Settings shows `LevelSettings.game_rules` as a combo: registered rules types (including `DefaultRules` and `MatchSessionRules`, plus a game crate's types after one play session) and the project's rule sets. A name in neither list stays as typed and is marked custom. The warning code is `game_rules_unregistered`. On load, that level uses `DefaultRules`.

## Play

While a play session runs, the match controls start, pause, resume, step and end the match, add or remove a bot seat, and advance the playlist row. With no session the control answers `match_control_not_playing`. The same actions are `editor.match_control`.

## Actions

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read the panel | The tab | `editor.match_rules_state` |
| Open or create a rule set | **Rule set**, **Open or create** | `editor.rules_open` |
| Edit one field | The form | `editor.rules_set_field` |
| Save the rule set | **Save** | `editor.rules_save` |
| Edit the playlist | **Playlist** | `editor.playlist_edit` |
| Drive the match in play | The match strip | `editor.match_control` |

## Keyboard

The path fields and buttons are focusable. Undo is Ctrl+Z, including rule-set and playlist edits.

## Known limits

- A `.rules.ron` over 256 KiB, or a file that does not parse, is left out of the library. `editor.match_rules_state` lists those files under load errors. They do not appear in the picker.
- A field the form cannot represent (`match_rules_field_unsupported`) has to be edited as text.
- Playlist rows stop at 1024. A playlist file over 256 KiB is not opened.
- This tab does not place a public match, a lobby or a relay. It authors the files and drives the match inside play-in-editor.

## See also

[World settings](book/user-guide/editor-guide/world-settings.md), [Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md), [Net](book/user-guide/editor-guide/net.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/keymap.md -->
# Keymap

<!-- index: Keymap -->
<!-- index: Shortcut -->
<!-- index: Command palette -->

The keymap is the list of chords that run editor commands. It is not a dock panel id. You edit it on the **Preferences** tab (`preferences`), under **Keymap**, or from the command palette. The chords the editor ships, and the ones you replace them with, are the same list. Depth: [Editor preferences, keymap, layout](book/agents/editor-preferences.md), [Editor command palette](book/agents/editor-command.md).

Open **Edit ▸ Preferences…**, then **Keymap**. An agent opens that tab with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "preferences"}`.

## Change a chord

1. Find the command in the Keymap list, or press Ctrl+Shift+P, highlight the command and press F2.
2. Press the new chord (**Set…** in the list). The label spells modifiers as `Ctrl`, `Shift` and `Alt`. On macOS, Ctrl in a label is the Command key.
3. The binding is saved at once in the user config file `regia/editor_keymap.ron` (format version 1). A project does not carry this file. Copy it if you want the same chords on another machine.
4. **Default** on a row clears your chord and restores the built-in one. **Reset all shortcuts** clears every user binding. **Import…** and **Export…** read and write the same file shape. A file from a newer editor (`keymap_newer`) is left untouched.

A user chord replaces the built-in chord of that command. If two commands claim one chord, the Keymap tab lists the conflict. The user binding wins while it is set. Bindings for command ids this editor does not know stay in the file and are written back, so a newer editor's chords are not dropped.

## Chords you cannot move

| Chord | Stays |
|---|---|
| Ctrl+Shift+P | Opens the command palette. A binding that uses it is dropped (`reserved`). |
| Escape | Stops play. A safety key: it stays global. |
| Ctrl+S | Save. Safety key. |
| Ctrl+Z | Undo. Safety key. |
| Ctrl+Shift+Z and Ctrl+Y | Redo. Ctrl+Y is also a fixed editor key beside the palette command. Safety keys. |

Binding a safety key in a panel scope is refused (`shortcut_safety_key`).

## Where a chord applies

A binding has a scope. The focused panel's scope is tried first, then the global bindings. While a text field has the keyboard, only text-scope bindings run, so a letter you type into a name does not run a viewport command.

| Scope | When it wins |
|---|---|
| `global` | No more specific scope claimed the chord |
| `viewport` | The viewport has focus. Built-in camera, gizmo, frame and collider chords start here |
| `outliner` | The Outliner has focus. Built-in Outliner chords start here |
| `inspector` | The Inspector has focus |
| `content` | The Content browser has focus |
| `graph` | A graph canvas has focus (material, animation, procedural, behavior, state tree, conversation, VFX) |
| `timeline` | A timeline has focus (sequence curves, shots, clips, montages, UI animation) |
| `text` | A text field has the keyboard |

The same chord may be bound in two different non-global scopes. A clash is reported only inside one scope, or against a global binding.

In the file, a scoped binding's key is `<scope>:<command id>` (for example `viewport:view.toggle_grid`). A global binding's key is the command id alone.

## Presets

The Keymap tab lists presets. **Default** is an empty user file: every command keeps its built-in chord. **Laptop** is for a keyboard without a navigation block: Drop to floor moves from End to Alt+Down in the viewport, and the Outliner's Delete also answers Backspace. Applying a preset replaces the current user keymap at once. You can save your own preset under `regia/keymaps/<name>.editor_keymap.ron`. A built-in preset cannot be overwritten (`preset_builtin`).

## Defaults you will meet first

The built-in chords are listed on [Editor](book/user-guide/editor.md) (viewport and Outliner) and [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md) (undo, redo, the palette, play, zoom).
