F1 runs `help.context` in every scope, including while a text field has focus, and opens the help for the focused panel. **Set…** can move a command off its built-in chord, including undo, save and stop-play. It cannot assign Ctrl+Shift+P, and it cannot give a safety chord to one panel: that chord stays global.

The command id in the Keymap row is the id you pass to `editor.command`. Search the palette for `open` to bind a key that brings one panel forward (`window.open_viewport`, and the same shape for the other tabs).

## Actions

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read bindings and conflicts | The Keymap tab | `editor.keymap_get` |
| Set or clear one chord | **Set…**, **Default**, or F2 in the palette | `editor.keymap_bind` |
| Find which command a chord runs | Press a key in the Keymap search | `editor.keymap_lookup` |
| Import, export, reset | **Import…**, **Export…**, **Reset all shortcuts** | `editor.keymap_import`, `editor.keymap_export`, `editor.keymap_reset` |
| List, apply or save a preset | The preset list | `editor.keymap_preset_list`, `editor.keymap_preset_apply`, `editor.keymap_preset_save` |

## Known limits

- Ctrl+Shift+P is not rebindable.
- Safety keys cannot be scoped to one panel.
- A chord that does not parse is dropped (`bad_chord` in the file report, code `keymap_parse` when the whole file is refused).
- The numpad and the main digit row report as the same key, so a preset cannot bind a numpad view key separately.
- Held fly keys (`camera.fly_*`) are commands. Binding one moves it. They are not dispatched as a tap.

## See also

[Project settings](book/user-guide/editor-guide/project-settings.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md), [Editor](book/user-guide/editor.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/net.md -->
# Net

<!-- index: Net panel -->
<!-- index: Play in editor -->
<!-- index: Listen server -->
<!-- index: Dedicated server -->

Panel id: `net`. The **Net** tab sets how play-in-editor hosts a session, then shows the clients and the bandwidth of that session. It does not open a match on the public network. Depth: [Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md), [PIE with several clients and net stats](book/agents/pie-net.md).

The tab sits in the default layout's bottom group. **View ▸ Reset layout** brings a closed tab back. An agent opens it with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "net"}`.

## Start a session

1. Choose **Mode**: `offline` (no session; play as usual), `listen` (this process is the server and a player) or `dedicated` (this process is a dedicated server).
2. Set **Clients** from 0 to 16. In one process those clients join in memory over the loopback transport. No socket is opened.
3. Choose **Conditions**: `off`, `lan`, `good`, `average`, `bad` or `terrible`. The same preset and seed report the same numbers on every run. The session clock advances 16 ms per editor frame.
4. Leave **Separate processes** off for the in-memory clients, or turn it on to start real processes (below).
5. Press **▶ Play** on the play toolbar (Alt+P). Stop ends the session. Pause holds the session clock.

With a game crate open, a mode other than `offline` and at least one client, the play world is the replication server and each client gets its own world. The main viewport keeps showing the server. **Client worlds** picks a client, and **Focus input on this client** sends keys to that client while the pointer is over its view.

**Overlay lines** adds the plain-text form of the connection rows under the table. Each connection row shows state, round-trip time, jitter, loss, and bytes and packets per second. The bandwidth table is per message kind.

## Separate processes

With **Separate processes** checked, play starts the server and the clients as their own processes on loopback, the same shape as `regia server --clients n`. **dedicated** starts a server process and one process per client. **listen** hosts on a loopback UDP port in the editor's play session and the client processes join it.

The binaries live in `build/server-dev/bin/` (`<game>-server` and `<game>-client`). Run `regia server --clients 1` once so those binaries exist. The editor does not build them.

**Show in a Game tab** opens that process in a dock tab. Those tabs use panel id `game_view` and are described on [Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md#game-tabs).

## Actions

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Mode, client count, conditions, separate processes | The controls at the top of the tab | `editor.pie_net_config` |
| Start or stop with the play toolbar | **▶ Play**, **⏹ Stop** | `editor.play`, `editor.stop` |
| Step the session clock | while paused, or from an agent | `editor.pie_net_run` (`action: "step"`) |
| Read clients and bandwidth | The tables | `editor.pie_net_state`, `editor.pie_net_clients` |
| Separate-process pictures | **Show in a Game tab** | `editor.pie_processes`, `editor.pie_process_view` |

## Keyboard

The tab's own controls are focusable (Tab, then Space or Enter). Play and Stop keep the toolbar keys on [Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md).

## Known limits

- In-memory clients share one process and open no socket. They exercise handshake, join, streams and the conditioner. They are not a match between two machines.
- Separate processes use loopback addresses chosen at start. They are not a proof of a relay, a lobby, or a two-account online session.
- At most 16 clients. A failed client world unloads the client worlds already built; the play world stays as the game made it.
- A step longer than the links' silence timeout drops nobody: clients step as many frames as the play world did.

## See also

[Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md), [Play window](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-window.md), [Networking](book/user-guide/networking.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/smart-objects.md -->
# Smart objects

<!-- index: Smart object -->
<!-- index: Smart object definition -->

Panel ids: `smart_objects` and `smart_object_def`. Two tabs, two jobs. **Smart Objects** (`smart_objects`) lists the smart objects and slots in the world the editor is showing, with claim state, and can switch one off or take a claim back. **Smart Object Definition** (`smart_object_def`) edits a `.smartobject.ron` definition. State trees stay on [State trees](book/user-guide/editor-guide/state-trees.md); that page does not document these tabs. Depth: [Smart objects (agents)](book/agents/smart-objects.md), [Smart-object definition editor](book/agents/smart-object-editor.md), [Gameplay panels](book/agents/editor-gameplay-panels.md). Spec: `docs/specs/39-smart-objects-v2.md`.

**Smart Objects** is in the default layout's bottom group. **View ▸ Reset layout** brings that tab back. **Smart Object Definition** is not in that dock. `editor.layout_apply {"open": "smart_object_def"}` adds it. **Open definition** on a selected object loads that object's file into the definition editor.

## Watch claims

1. Open **Smart Objects**. Each object lists its slots. A slot's state is `free`, `claimed`, `in_use` or `disabled`, with the holder's name, the claim priority and why the slot is off.
2. Select an object or a slot. The viewport draws a marker for each slot (a small cross, larger when selected) and a line to the holder while markers are on.
3. Switch the selected object or slot off, or back on. A second off-reason needs a second enable.
4. **Release** takes a slot's claim back from its holder.
5. The recent claim messages sit under the list. They need the smart-object systems in the world you are watching. The edit world does not run those systems, so it still lists authored objects and it may show no messages until you press Alt+P.

While play runs, a change is applied on the play world on the next frame. Read the outcome from the next panel refresh.

## Edit a definition

1. **Content ▸ New ▸ Smart object** writes a definition with one slot, `slot_0`, at the origin (`editor.create_asset` with `kind: "smart_object"`).
2. Open **Smart Object Definition**, type the project path and press **Open**.
3. Edit activity tags, how those tags combine with a slot (`union` or `slot_first`), the requester rule (`definition_and_slot`, `slot_only` or `slot_else_definition`), the requester query, conditions and behaviors. Then each slot: name, start enabled, position and yaw, pitch and roll, tags, and its entrances.
4. The line under the header is the runtime validator: **valid**, or the message (a bad slot name, too many slots, a non-finite offset, a query that is too deep). The forms still accept the edit. **Save** refuses an invalid definition.
5. With **Slot handles** on, select the preview entity (or a level object whose definition is this file). Drag a slot or an entrance in the viewport. Each drag is one undo step. The handles replace the transform gizmo on that object.

Every form edit is one undo step (Ctrl+Z). A definition you have not edited is never rewritten. **Save** writes the canonical file. A file that still has comments warns you: the first save drops them.

## Actions

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Read objects, slots and messages | **Smart Objects** | `editor.smart_object_panel_get` |
| Select, show markers | The list and the marker switch | `editor.smart_object_panel_set` |
| Enable, disable, release | The row actions | `editor.smart_object_panel_control` |
| Read or edit a definition | **Smart Object Definition** | `editor.smart_object_def_state`, `editor.smart_object_def_edit` |

## Keyboard

Both tabs' buttons and fields are focusable. Ctrl+S with the pointer over **Smart Object Definition** saves, and refuses when the definition is invalid.

## Known limits

- Slot rows in one snapshot stop at 2048. The total count still includes the rest. Messages kept on screen stop at 32.
- Claim messages need `SmartObjectPlugin` in the world you are reading.
- Entity ids do not survive the switch between the edit world and the play world. The selection clears when play starts or stops.
- Definition files are format version 1. This tab does not change that format.

## See also

[State trees](book/user-guide/editor-guide/state-trees.md), [Viewport](book/user-guide/editor-guide/viewport.md), [Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/user-guide/editor-guide/motion-matching.md -->
# Motion matching

<!-- index: Motion matching -->
<!-- index: Motion database -->

Panel id: `motion_matching`. The **Motion Matching** tab is the debug view for one character that has a `MotionMatching` component: what is playing, the latest search, and the database that character uses. The runtime chapter is [Motion matching](book/user-guide/motion-matching.md). The agent methods for this tab are on [Motion matching (agents)](book/agents/motion-matching.md) under the editor panel, and `editor.mm_panel_get`, `editor.mm_panel_select` and `editor.mm_panel_freeze`.

The tab is in the default layout's bottom group. The Animation workspace opens it with the other animation tabs. **View ▸ Reset layout** restores a closed one. An agent opens it with `editor.layout_apply {"open": "motion_matching"}`.

## Read a search

1. Press Alt+P so the character is simulating. The **Character** list names each entity that has the component, the database it uses and the frame count.
2. Pick a character. The line under the list reads the playing clip and time, the search count, the jump count and the search method.
3. The table lists the top candidates (default 8, from 1 to 32). Columns are status, clip, time, frame, total cost and a stacked bar of the cost groups. A bar segment is cheaper or equal (`below`), dearer (`above`) or ignored (the group's weight is 0).
4. **Freeze** holds this report while the game keeps playing. Press it again (**Frozen**) to follow the live search.
5. **Cost parts** lists the same numbers beside the bars. **Contacts and phase** draws one cell per frame and foot when the database has contact labels, with the current frame marked.
6. **Database** shows the asset path, frame count, dimensions, clips and tags. **Sort** orders the clip list and the tag list; selecting the same sort again reverses it. **Edit database** opens that file in the motion database editor.

## The database editor window

**Edit database**, or opening a `.motiondb.ron` from the Content browser, opens the motion database editor. That editor is a window over the dock, not a second dock panel and not a second panel id. It edits the database document (schema, clips, tags) and can rebuild it in memory. Agent methods: `editor.mm_db_open` and the other `editor.mm_db_*` calls ([Motion database editor](book/agents/motion-database-editor.md)). Document autosave keeps an unsaved database (kind recorded with the other editor documents) and offers it after a crash.

## Actions

| Action | Control | Agent method |
|---|---|---|
| Choose the character | **Character** | `editor.mm_panel_select` |
| How many candidates | **top** | `editor.mm_panel_get` (the `candidates` count) |
| Hold the report | **Freeze** | `editor.mm_panel_freeze` |
| Open the database file | **Edit database** | `editor.mm_db_open` |

## Keyboard

The combo box, the candidate count and **Freeze** are focusable. The tab does not take letter keys of its own.

## Known limits

- With no `MotionMatching` entity the character list is empty and the table has nothing to show.
- Freeze keeps the report on screen. It does not pause the game.
- The candidate table stops at 32 rows, which is the matcher's top-k limit.
- The database editor window is not saved as a layout tab. Closing it leaves the **Motion Matching** tab where it was.

## See also

[Animation panels](book/user-guide/editor-guide/anim-graph.md), [Play-in-editor](book/user-guide/editor-guide/play-in-editor.md), [Motion matching](book/user-guide/motion-matching.md), [Editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md).

<!-- source: book/tutorials/third-person.md -->
# Tutorial: a third-person game

In this tutorial you build **Coin Run**, a small third-person game: run and jump around a level,
collect every coin, see your progress on a HUD, save and load, test it automatically through the
agent protocol, and package it. It starts from the `third_person` template and adds one feature
per step. The engine's `samples/third_person` is the finished, larger version of the same idea
(an animated character with foot IK, a pause menu, split-screen); this tutorial points to it
where it goes further.

You need the tools from [Installing Regia Engine](book/start/install.md) and the concepts from
[Fundamentals](book/fundamentals/ecs.md).

## Step 1: create the project

From the folder that holds your projects:

```sh,walkthrough=new,template=third_person
regia new "Coin Run" --template third_person
cd coin_run
```

```console
$ cargo run -p coin_run_launcher
```

You get a window with a gray floor, two blocks and an orange box standing in for the player. WASD
or the left stick moves, Space or the south button jumps, the mouse or right stick orbits the
camera. The camera boom shortens when a wall gets between it and the player.

## Step 2: read the template

Open `game/src/lib.rs`. Condensed to its essentials (the template builds its cube mesh by hand;
this version uses the renderer's `box_mesh` helper), it is:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::physics::{CharacterBody, Collider, ColliderShape, PhysicsPlugin, RigidBody};
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_framework::camera::{CameraMode, CameraPlugin, CameraRig, ChaseCamera, ThirdPerson};
use regia_framework::character::{
    Character, CharacterInput, CharacterMovement, CharacterPlugin, CharacterState,
    use_rapier_character_controller,
};
use regia_framework::script::ScriptPlugin;
use regia_input::prelude::*;
use regia_render::{Camera, CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, Environment, MeshRenderer, box_mesh};
use regia_scene::Transform;

pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        // 1. Input: named actions bound to keyboard, mouse and gamepad.
        let config = InputConfig::new()
            .action("Move", ActionKind::Axis2D)
            .action("Look", ActionKind::Axis2D)
            .action("Jump", ActionKind::Button)
            .binding(Binding::new("Move", InputSource::keys2d("KeyW", "KeyS", "KeyA", "KeyD")))
            .binding(Binding::new("Move", InputSource::gamepad_stick(Stick::Left)))
            .binding(Binding::new("Look", InputSource::MouseDelta))
            .binding(Binding::new("Look", InputSource::gamepad_stick(Stick::Right)))
            .binding(Binding::new("Jump", InputSource::key("Space")))
            .binding(Binding::new("Jump", InputSource::gamepad_button(GamepadButton::South)));

        // 2. The engine systems this game uses.
        app.add_plugins((
            regia_scene::ScenePlugin,
            PhysicsPlugin,
            CharacterPlugin,
            CameraPlugin,
            ScriptPlugin,
            InputPlugin::new(config),
        ));
        // 3. Characters move through rapier's kinematic character controller.
        use_rapier_character_controller(app);

        // 4. Gameplay systems.
        app.init_resource::<Environment>()
            .add_systems(Startup, (setup_level, setup_character, setup_camera).chain())
            .add_systems(Update, (write_character_input, write_camera_look));
    }
}

/// A gray static box with a collider and a mesh.
fn block(commands: &mut Commands, translation: Vec3, half: Vec3) {
    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh(half.to_array());
    commands.spawn((
        Transform::from_translation(translation),
        RigidBody::static_body(),
        Collider { shape: ColliderShape::Box { half_extents: half }, ..Collider::default() },
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial { base_color: [0.55, 0.6, 0.65, 1.0], ..CpuMaterial::default() }),
        ),
    ));
}

fn setup_level(mut commands: Commands) {
    block(&mut commands, Vec3::new(0.0, -0.5, 0.0), Vec3::new(20.0, 0.5, 20.0));
    block(&mut commands, Vec3::new(3.0, 0.5, -2.0), Vec3::new(1.0, 1.0, 1.0));
    block(&mut commands, Vec3::new(-3.0, 1.0, 2.0), Vec3::new(2.0, 2.0, 2.0));
}

/// The player: a character capsule (movement, state, physics body) with a stand-in mesh.
fn setup_character(mut commands: Commands) {
    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([0.3, 0.9, 0.3]);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Player1"),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.2, 5.0)),
        Character,
        CharacterMovement::default(),
        CharacterInput::default(),
        CharacterState::default(),
        CharacterBody::default(),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial { base_color: [0.9, 0.5, 0.2, 1.0], ..CpuMaterial::default() }),
        ),
    ));
}

/// A camera rig in third-person mode chasing the character.
fn setup_camera(mut commands: Commands, characters: Query<Entity, With<Character>>) {
    let Some(target) = characters.iter().next() else { return };
    let mode = ThirdPerson {
        boom_length: 4.5,
        socket_offset: Vec3::new(0.0, 1.6, 0.0),
        target_offset: Vec3::new(0.0, 1.2, 0.0),
        ..ThirdPerson::default()
    };
    commands.spawn((
        Transform::default(),
        CameraRig { mode: CameraMode::ThirdPerson(mode), ..CameraRig::default() },
        ChaseCamera { target },
        Camera::default(),
    ));
}

/// Move input relative to the camera's yaw.
fn write_character_input(
    actions: Res<Actions>,
    rigs: Query<&CameraRig>,
    mut inputs: Query<&mut CharacterInput, With<Character>>,
) {
    let axes = actions.axis2d("Move");
    let yaw = rigs.iter().next().map_or(0.0, |rig| rig.yaw);
    let forward = (Quat::from_rotation_y(yaw) * -Vec3::Z).with_y(0.0).normalize_or_zero();
    let right = (Quat::from_rotation_y(yaw) * Vec3::X).with_y(0.0).normalize_or_zero();
    for mut input in &mut inputs {
        input.move_dir = (forward * axes.y + right * axes.x).clamp_length_max(1.0);
        input.jump = actions.pressed("Jump");
    }
}

/// Mouse / right stick orbits the boom.
fn write_camera_look(actions: Res<Actions>, mut rigs: Query<&mut CameraRig>) {
    let look = actions.axis2d("Look");
    for mut rig in &mut rigs {
        rig.yaw -= look.x * 0.003;
        rig.pitch = (rig.pitch + look.y * 0.003).clamp(-1.2, 1.2);
    }
}
```

The pieces:

1. **Input** ([Input](book/user-guide/input.md)). Gameplay reads `Move`, `Look` and `Jump`, never
   a key code, so the game works the same with a keyboard or a gamepad.
2. **Plugins**. `ScenePlugin` propagates transforms, `PhysicsPlugin` runs rapier, `CharacterPlugin`
   moves `Character` entities from their `CharacterInput`, `CameraPlugin` drives `CameraRig`s.
3. **The character** is data: `CharacterMovement` holds speeds, acceleration, jump height, air
   control and coyote time; `CharacterInput` is what to do this frame; `CharacterState` reports
   back (`grounded`, velocity, movement mode); `CharacterBody` is its physics capsule.
4. **The camera** is a `CameraRig` with a `ThirdPerson` boom chasing the character
   (`ChaseCamera`), plus the render `Camera` on the same entity.

Read [Physics](book/user-guide/physics.md) and [Gameplay framework](book/user-guide/gameplay.md) for
what each component offers.

## Step 3: coins

Add coins the player collects by running through them. A coin is a small spinning box with a
`Coin` component holding its id; a system checks the distance from each character to each coin.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_framework::character::Character;
use regia_render::{CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, MeshRenderer, box_mesh};
use regia_scene::Transform;

/// Where the coins are, in id order.
pub const COIN_SPOTS: [[f32; 3]; 6] = [
    [0.0, 1.0, -3.0],
    [4.0, 1.0, 0.0],
    [3.0, 2.6, -2.0], // on top of block A
    [-3.0, 4.6, 2.0], // on top of block B
    [-6.0, 1.0, -6.0],
    [8.0, 1.0, 6.0],
];

/// A collectible coin.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Debug, Clone, Copy, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct Coin {
    /// Index into [`COIN_SPOTS`].
    pub id: u32,
}

/// Which coins are gone, in collection order.
#[derive(Resource, Reflect, Debug, Clone, Default)]
#[reflect(Resource, Default)]
pub struct CoinProgress {
    /// Collected coin ids.
    pub collected: Vec<u32>,
}

/// Spawns one coin.
pub fn spawn_coin(commands: &mut Commands, id: u32) {
    let [x, y, z] = COIN_SPOTS[id as usize];
    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([0.2, 0.2, 0.05]);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new(format!("Coin{id}")),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(x, y, z)),
        Coin { id },
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [1.0, 0.78, 0.2, 1.0],
                metallic: 1.0,
                roughness: 0.3,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));
}

fn spawn_coins(mut commands: Commands) {
    for id in 0..COIN_SPOTS.len() as u32 {
        spawn_coin(&mut commands, id);
    }
}

/// Collects every coin a character is within 0.9 m of.
fn collect_coins(
    mut commands: Commands,
    mut progress: ResMut<CoinProgress>,
    characters: Query<&Transform, With<Character>>,
    coins: Query<(Entity, &Coin, &Transform)>,
) {
    for character in &characters {
        for (entity, coin, transform) in &coins {
            if character.translation.distance(transform.translation) < 0.9
                && !progress.collected.contains(&coin.id)
            {
                progress.collected.push(coin.id);
                commands.entity(entity).despawn();
                info!("collected coin {}", coin.id);
            }
        }
    }
}

/// Spins the coins (visual only).
fn spin_coins(time: Res<Time>, mut coins: Query<&mut Transform, With<Coin>>) {
    for mut transform in &mut coins {
        transform.rotation = Quat::from_rotation_y(time.elapsed_secs() * 2.0);
    }
}

/// Add this plugin next to the template's: `app.add_plugins(CoinsPlugin)`.
pub struct CoinsPlugin;

impl Plugin for CoinsPlugin {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.register_type::<Coin>()
            .register_type::<CoinProgress>()
            .init_resource::<CoinProgress>()
            .add_systems(Startup, spawn_coins)
            .add_systems(Update, (collect_coins, spin_coins));
    }
}
```

Run it and collect a coin: the log prints `collected coin 0`. A distance check is the simplest
pickup. Physics **sensors** are the other way: a `Collider` with `sensor: true` raises
`TriggerEnter` messages, and a [script](book/user-guide/gameplay.md) can react to them per entity;
`samples/third_person/src/collectible.rs` does it that way.

## Step 4: a HUD

The runtime UI is part of `DefaultPlugins`. Spawn a `UiRoot` with a text node, and update the
text when the progress changes. The counter also lives in a reflected component, so tests can
read it (step 6):

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;

/// Mirrors the coin progress for the HUD and for agent checks.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Debug, Clone, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct CoinCounter {
    /// Coins collected.
    pub collected: u32,
    /// Coins in the level.
    pub total: u32,
}

#[derive(Resource, Default)]
struct CoinProgress {
    collected: Vec<u32>,
}

const TOTAL: u32 = 6;

fn setup_hud(mut commands: Commands) {
    let root = commands
        .spawn((
            UiRoot::default(),
            SafeAreaPadding,
            NodeStyle::new(Style { padding: Edges::px(16.0), ..Default::default() }),
        ))
        .id();
    let label = commands
        .spawn((
            Name::new("hud-coins"),
            UiNode,
            Text {
                spans: vec![TextSpan::lit(format!("Coins: 0 / {TOTAL}")).with_style(TextStyle {
                    font_px: 28.0,
                    color: UiColor([1.0, 0.92, 0.6, 1.0]),
                    ..Default::default()
                })],
                ..Default::default()
            },
            CoinCounter { collected: 0, total: TOTAL },
        ))
        .id();
    commands.entity(root).add_child(label);
}

fn refresh_hud(progress: Res<CoinProgress>, mut labels: Query<(&mut Text, &mut CoinCounter)>) {
    if !progress.is_changed() {
        return;
    }
    let collected = progress.collected.len() as u32;
    for (mut text, mut counter) in &mut labels {
        counter.collected = collected;
        let line = if collected == counter.total {
            "All coins! Well done.".to_string()
        } else {
            format!("Coins: {collected} / {}", counter.total)
        };
        if let Some(span) = text.spans.first_mut() {
            *span = TextSpan::lit(line).with_style(span.style.clone());
        }
    }
}

fn setup(app: &mut App) {
    app.register_type::<CoinCounter>()
        .add_systems(Startup, setup_hud)
        .add_systems(Update, refresh_hud);
}
```

`UiRoot`, `UiNode`, `Text`, `NodeStyle` and the rest come from `regia::prelude` when the `ui`
feature is on (the default). Layout is flexbox: `NodeStyle` holds direction, size, padding and
gaps; `SafeAreaPadding` keeps the HUD clear of notches and rounded corners. The same HUD can be
authored as a `.ui.ron` file with a `bind:` to a reflected field instead of a system
([UI](book/user-guide/ui.md)).

## Step 5: save and load

Make the progress a **saveable resource** and add `SavePlugin`. Save on F5 and load on F9; after a
load, bring the world in line with the loaded progress (despawn collected coins, respawn coins
collected after the save):

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_framework::prelude::{
    RegisterSaveableExt, SaveDirectory, SaveGame, SavePlugin, SaveSpec, SaveableResource,
};

#[derive(Resource, Reflect, Debug, Clone, Default)]
#[reflect(Resource, Default)]
pub struct CoinProgress {
    pub collected: Vec<u32>,
}

impl SaveableResource for CoinProgress {}

#[derive(Component)]
struct Coin {
    id: u32,
}

fn spawn_coin(commands: &mut Commands, id: u32) {
    // as in step 3
}

/// A save or load the player asked for this frame.
#[derive(Resource, Default)]
struct SaveRequest(Option<bool>); // Some(true) = save, Some(false) = load

/// F5 asks for a save, F9 for a load.
fn read_save_keys(mut keys: MessageReader<KeyboardInput>, mut request: ResMut<SaveRequest>) {
    for key in keys.read() {
        if key.state != ButtonState::Pressed || key.repeat {
            continue;
        }
        match key.physical_key.as_str() {
            "F5" => request.0 = Some(true),
            "F9" => request.0 = Some(false),
            _ => {}
        }
    }
}

/// Saving and loading need the whole world, so this is an exclusive system.
fn apply_save_request(world: &mut World) {
    let Some(save) = world.resource_mut::<SaveRequest>().0.take() else { return };
    let dir = world.get_resource::<SaveDirectory>().cloned().unwrap_or_default();
    let slot = SaveGame::slot(&dir, "Coins");
    if save {
        match SaveGame::save(&slot, world, &SaveSpec::default()) {
            Ok(result) => info!("saved {} bytes", result.bytes_written),
            Err(err) => error!("save failed: {err}"),
        }
    } else {
        match SaveGame::load(&slot, world, &SaveSpec::default()) {
            Ok(_) => info!("loaded"),
            Err(err) => error!("load failed: {err}"),
        }
    }
}

/// Makes the live coins match the progress (after a load, or any time).
fn reconcile_coins(mut commands: Commands, progress: Res<CoinProgress>, coins: Query<(Entity, &Coin)>) {
    if !progress.is_changed() {
        return;
    }
    let mut present = Vec::new();
    for (entity, coin) in &coins {
        if progress.collected.contains(&coin.id) {
            commands.entity(entity).despawn();
        } else {
            present.push(coin.id);
        }
    }
    for id in 0..6u32 {
        if !progress.collected.contains(&id) && !present.contains(&id) {
            spawn_coin(&mut commands, id);
        }
    }
}

fn setup(app: &mut App) {
    app.add_plugins(SavePlugin::default())
        .register_saveable_resource::<CoinProgress>()
        .init_resource::<SaveRequest>()
        .add_systems(Update, (read_save_keys, apply_save_request, reconcile_coins).chain());
}
```

Saves are written atomically to `user://saves/` with a CRC check; a corrupt or truncated file
fails to load with an error instead of crashing. `SavePlugin` also autosaves to the `Auto` slot
when the app is suspended (Android going to the background). Entities marked `Saveable` are saved
with all their reflected components; this game only needs the resource. In a larger game, bind
`Save` and `Load` actions instead of reading keys ([Input](book/user-guide/input.md)). The save system is described
in [Gameplay framework](book/user-guide/gameplay.md) and `docs/formats/save-format.md`.

## Step 6: test it through the agent protocol

Leave the game running and drive it from a terminal (or let an AI agent do it through
`regia mcp`). Pause it, walk the player forward for two seconds, and check that a coin was
collected:

```console
$ regia agent call play.pause
$ regia agent call play.inject_input '{"actions":[{"action":"Move","value":[0.0,1.0],"duration_frames":120}]}'
$ regia agent call play.step '{"frames":120}'
$ regia agent call play.expect '{"assertions":[{"name":"a coin was collected","condition":{"entity":{"name":"hud-coins"},"component":"CoinCounter","path":"collected","op":"gte","value":1}}]}'
$ regia agent call seeing.screenshot --out after-run.png
```

From the start position the first coin (`[0, 1, -3]`) is straight ahead, so walking forward
collects it. `play.step` advances exact frames while paused, which makes the check deterministic;
`play.wait_until` waits for a condition instead. Each method is in the
[agent guide's testing page](book/agents/testing.md). The same calls work from Rust tests: build an
`App` with your plugin, run frames with `app.update()`, and assert on the world.

## Step 7: package it

```console
$ regia package --platform linux --profile shipping
$ regia package --platform android --format apk
```

A Linux shipping package is built against glibc 2.31 (the Steam Linux Runtime), which needs
`cargo-zigbuild` and `zig` on `PATH` (`regia doctor --platform deck` checks both); add
`--glibc host` to build against your own system's glibc instead, or leave out `--profile shipping`
for a development package. The Android package needs the
[Android setup](book/start/install.md#5-android-optional).

The result runs from any directory: the cooked assets are in `content/*.fpak` next to the
executable. See [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md).

## Where to go from here

`samples/third_person` takes the same game much further; read its modules in this order:

| Module | What it adds |
|---|---|
| `assets.rs` | Fetching and cooking the Khronos Fox glTF, loading its mesh, skeleton and clips, binding the skin |
| `anim.rs` | An animation graph driven by `CharacterState` (idle, walk, run, jump) and foot IK on stairs and slopes ([Animation](book/user-guide/animation.md)) |
| `character.rs`, `camera.rs` | One character and camera per local player, split-screen viewports |
| `collectible.rs` | Collectibles as sensor colliders with a `CollectScript` |
| `hud.rs` | The counter, health, damage numbers and a pause menu with buttons |
| `save.rs` | Save and load through the save flow (`SaveFlowPlugin`), with a migration for older saves |
| `level.rs` | Stairs, a slope, platforms |
| `enemy.rs` | Two enemy kinds driven by `.bt.ron` behavior trees over a navmesh crowd: patrol, notice, chase, attack, give up |
| `combat.rs`, `melee.rs` | Health and hits through abilities and attributes, a three-hit melee combo timed by a montage, hit detection with a physics shape query |
| `ragdoll_fx.rs`, `checkpoint.rs` | Ragdoll deaths and respawning at the last checkpoint |
| `menu.rs`, `sound.rs` | A title screen and a settings menu that persists; procedural footsteps, hits and an ambient bed |

### Adding enemies and combat

The sample's combat is a good next step for Coin Run, in this order:

1. **Health.** Add `AbilityPlugin` and `HealthBridge`, give the player an `.attrs.ron` with
   `health` and `health_max`, and apply an instant effect with a `Param` amount for each hit
   ([Abilities](book/agents/abilities.md)). The bridge raises `DiedEvent` when health reaches zero.
2. **An enemy brain.** Write the tree as `.bt.ron` (a `sense` service writing blackboard keys, a
   selector of `condition` + leaf sequences) and implement the leaves as `BtTask`s. Re-evaluate the
   selector every tick by making movement leaves finish in one tick; only an attack runs over
   several ticks.
3. **Movement.** Bake a `NavMesh` from the level's static colliders at startup, add each enemy to a
   `NavCrowd`, set targets from the leaves and copy the agent position onto the enemy after
   `NavCrowdStep`.
4. **Death.** Read `DiedEvent`, spawn a limp `Ragdoll`, and respawn the player at a checkpoint.

`samples/third_person/README.md` lists the files, and the agent page
[Third-person demo](book/agents/third-person-demo.md) shows how its tests drive and check all of it.

Then try the [arena tutorial](book/tutorials/arena.md): AI bots, weapons, match rules and navigation.

# Tutorial: the arena

`samples/arena` is a first-person arena shooter against AI bots. Where the
[third-person tutorial](book/tutorials/third-person.md) built a game from nothing, this one takes a complete
sample apart: how a match is structured with **game rules**, how **bots** decide what to do (a
steering brain, or a **behavior tree** on a **navmesh**), how **weapons** use physics queries,
how effects and sound are triggered, and how the whole match is tested and replayed
deterministically. Each section ends with something to change.

## Run it

The arena is one of the engine's samples, so this page works in the engine folder (an engine
release includes `samples/`), not in a project of your own:

```console
$ cargo run --release -p arena
$ cargo run --release -p arena -- --bots 3 --seed 42
$ cargo run --release -p arena -- --no-local-player --bots 8
```

You are a pawn on a square arena with crates, walls and seven bots. WASD and the mouse move and
look, the left button fires (gamepad sticks and the right trigger work too; on a touch screen the
HUD shows a virtual stick and a fire button). The match goes warm-up → round → match over, ending
at the score limit or when the timer runs out; a pawn that dies respawns at a spawn point.

`--seed N` makes the match deterministic: every random decision draws from one seeded generator
(`MatchRng`), so the same seed plays out the same way. `--bench` runs a budget probe (8 bots, 200
rigid bodies, about 20 000 particles) and prints frame-time percentiles.

## The shape of the sample

`samples/arena/src/lib.rs` is the plugin. It adds the engine plugins the game needs (input with a
`Fire` action, scene, physics, camera, input recording, damage, VFX, audio), registers its
reflected types so the agent protocol can inspect them, installs its rules, and orders its
fixed-step simulation in three sets:

| Set | Systems |
|---|---|
| `ArenaSimSet::Bots` | bots steer and decide to fire (`bots.rs`, or the behavior tree in `bot_bt.rs`) |
| `ArenaSimSet::Weapons` | fire requests become hitscan rays or pooled rockets; explosions push crates (`weapons.rs`) |
| `ArenaSimSet::Match` | the match clock, deaths, scores, respawns (`match_flow.rs`) |

All three run in `FixedUpdate`, so the simulation advances at the same rate whatever the frame
rate. Presentation (HUD, camera, sounds) runs in `Update`.

## Game rules

The match flow is a `GameRules` implementation, `ArenaRules` in `match_flow.rs`. The trait's hooks
are the decisions a mode makes: what happens when the level starts (`on_level_start`: spawn the
pawns and the match state), when a player joins (`on_player_joined`: where to spawn them), when
a character dies (`on_character_died`: respawn with full health), every tick (`tick`: advance
warm-up → round → match over), and whether the match is over (`is_match_over`).

The framework calls `on_player_joined` when a local player joins through `PlayerManager`, and
`RulesPlugin` installs the rules a level names in `LevelSettings.game_rules`. The other hooks are
called by the game at the moments it defines, which keeps the timing explicit. The arena's pattern
is to take the rules out of their resource, call a hook with a `RulesCtx`, and put them back:

```rust
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_framework::prelude::{GameRules, GameRulesResource, RulesCtx, RulesPlugin, SpawnRequest};

/// A timed free-for-all: the match ends after `limit_secs`.
#[derive(Default)]
pub struct TimedMatch {
    elapsed: f32,
    limit_secs: f32,
}

impl GameRules for TimedMatch {
    fn on_player_joined(&mut self, ctx: &mut RulesCtx, _player: Entity) -> Option<SpawnRequest> {
        // Spawn at the default spawn logic's position (the first PlayerStart).
        let _ = ctx;
        None
    }

    fn tick(&mut self, ctx: &mut RulesCtx) {
        if let Some(time) = ctx.world.get_resource::<Time>() {
            self.elapsed += time.delta_secs();
        }
    }

    fn is_match_over(&self, _world: &World) -> bool {
        self.elapsed >= self.limit_secs
    }
}

/// `FixedUpdate`: advance the rules' clock and report the end of the match once.
fn tick_rules(world: &mut World, mut announced: Local<bool>) {
    let mut rules = world.remove_resource::<GameRulesResource>().unwrap_or_default();
    {
        let mut ctx = RulesCtx::new(world);
        rules.rules.tick(&mut ctx);
    }
    let over = rules.rules.is_match_over(world);
    world.insert_resource(rules);
    if over && !*announced {
        *announced = true;
        info!("match over");
    }
}

fn setup(app: &mut App) {
    app.add_plugins(RulesPlugin)
        .insert_resource(GameRulesResource { rules: Box::new(TimedMatch { elapsed: 0.0, limit_secs: 180.0 }) })
        .add_systems(FixedUpdate, tick_rules);
}
```

Register rules by name in `GameRulesRegistry` (`register::<TimedMatch>("my_game::TimedMatch")`)
and a level can select them with `LevelSettings.game_rules`.

The arena keeps its live match state (`phase`, `scores`, time) in an `ArenaState` **component** on
an entity named `"match"`, not in a resource, because the agent protocol's `play.expect` reads
reflected component fields on entities (its resource checks cover a fixed set of engine
resources). Keep state you want to test somewhere tests can read it.

**Try it:** change `ArenaConfig::score_limit` and `match_secs` (in `config.rs`) and watch the
phase change in `ArenaState` with `regia agent call scene.query_entities '{"component":"ArenaState"}'`.

## Bots: a steering brain

By default each bot is a `Pawn` driven by `drive_bots` (`bots.rs`), a single fixed-step system:

1. pick the nearest living enemy within 30 m, re-picking every few seconds;
2. steer toward it (or wander with seeded jitter), clamped to the arena;
3. cast a ray from the eye toward the target with `PhysicsQuery`, excluding itself; if the first
   thing hit is the target, the shot is clear;
4. if clear and the cooldown has elapsed, write a `FireRequest` (every fourth shot a rocket).

The raycast is what makes walls matter: a crate or wall between two bots blocks the shot until
one of them moves. `PhysicsQuery` is the same API the [Physics](book/user-guide/physics.md) chapter
describes, and the agent protocol exposes it as `physics.raycast`.

**Try it:** change `ENGAGE_RANGE` or `FIRE_COOLDOWN` in `bots.rs` and compare scores for a fixed
`--seed`.

## Bots: a behavior tree on a navmesh

Insert `ArenaConfig { use_navmesh: true, .. }` before adding the plugin, and the bots switch to
the navigation stack ([Navigation and AI](book/user-guide/navigation-ai.md)):

- `navmesh.rs` builds a navmesh from the arena's static geometry with `NavMeshBuilder`;
- each bot gets a `NavAgent` (radius, max speed), a `NavAgentState`, a `Blackboard` and a compiled
  `BehaviorTree`;
- `bot_bt.rs` defines two leaf tasks, `SeekEnemy` (pick the nearest enemy, write it to the
  blackboard, plan a navmesh path into `NavAgentState`) and `FireAtEnemy` (line-of-sight check and
  cooldown), and composes them under a `Parallel` node so the bot moves and shoots at once;
- `NavPlugin` follows the path with ORCA local avoidance, so bots flow around each other, and
  `AiPlugin` ticks every tree in `FixedUpdate` and publishes a `BehaviorTreeStatus` snapshot the
  agent protocol can read.

The tree is built in code:

```rust
use regia_ai::{BehaviorTreeBuilder, BehaviorTreeDef, BtContext, BtStatus, BtTask, BtTaskRegistration, ParallelPolicy};

#[derive(Default, regia_ai::BtTask)]
struct SeekEnemy;

impl BtTask for SeekEnemy {
    fn tick(&mut self, _ctx: &mut BtContext<'_>) -> BtStatus {
        BtStatus::Running
    }
}

#[derive(Default, regia_ai::BtTask)]
struct FireAtEnemy;

impl BtTask for FireAtEnemy {
    fn tick(&mut self, _ctx: &mut BtContext<'_>) -> BtStatus {
        BtStatus::Running
    }
}

/// A parallel of seek + fire: both leaves run every tick.
fn build_bot_tree() -> BehaviorTreeDef {
    let mut builder = BehaviorTreeBuilder::new();
    let seek = builder.leaf("seek", <SeekEnemy as BtTaskRegistration>::task_type_path());
    let fire = builder.leaf("fire", <FireAtEnemy as BtTaskRegistration>::task_type_path());
    let root = builder.parallel("bot", ParallelPolicy::RequireAll, vec![seek, fire]);
    builder.build(root)
}
```

The leaves are registered in the `BtTaskRegistry`, and `BehaviorTree::compile(&def, &registry)`
turns the definition into the runtime tree each bot carries. A definition can also be saved as
`.bt.ron`.

**Try it:** add a third leaf that retreats when `Health::current` is low, and put it with
`SeekEnemy` under a selector.

## Weapons, damage and physics

`weapons.rs` turns `FireRequest`s into shots:

- **Rifle (hitscan)**: a `PhysicsQuery` raycast from the muzzle; a hit on a pawn applies damage
  through `regia_framework::damage` (`Health`, `DamageEvent`, `DiedEvent`); a hit elsewhere
  spawns an impact effect and a decal.
- **Rocket (projectile)**: taken from a `PrefabPool` (`rocket`) instead of spawned, advanced in
  `FixedUpdate` with a swept check, and on impact an explosion: radial damage, an `overlap` query
  that writes `ExternalImpulse` on dynamic crates so they fly, an explosion effect, a scorch
  decal and a sound.

Pooling (`regia_framework::pool`) keeps frequently spawned entities alive and recycles them,
which avoids per-shot allocation. `match_flow.rs` reads `DiedEvent`s, scores the killer and calls
`on_character_died` to respawn the victim.

## Effects and sound

The arena registers the built-in showcase effects (`muzzle_flash`, `impact`, `explosion`, …) in a
`VfxScene` and triggers them with `SpawnEffect` messages ([VFX and decals](book/systems/vfx.md)).
`audio.rs` builds the sound bank and plays spatial one-shots at the shot's position
([Audio](book/user-guide/audio.md)). The HUD in `hud.rs` shows the score, the match timer, the phase and a crosshair,
plus a pause menu that works with mouse, gamepad focus navigation and touch ([UI](book/user-guide/ui.md)).

## Testing the match

The arena is built to be verified without a human. Its tests show three techniques you can reuse:

- **Agent assertions** (`tests/agent_expect.rs`): the same `play.expect` conditions an agent sends
  over the protocol, for example "a bot is alive" (`Health.current > 0` on any `Pawn`) and "the
  match is in the round" (`ArenaState.phase == Round`). The
  [agent guide's arena page](book/agents/arena.md) lists them.
- **Determinism** (`tests/determinism.rs`): a three-minute bot match is recorded with
  `InputRecording` (the seed plus every fixed-step action value), replayed through
  `InputInjection`, and must end with identical scores.
- **Offscreen screenshots** (`tests/offscreen.rs`): the match renders headless on lavapipe and the
  first-person and overhead frames are checked for content and kept as evidence.

From a terminal, against a running arena:

```console
$ regia agent call play.pause --project samples/arena
$ regia agent call play.step '{"frames":600}' --project samples/arena
$ regia agent call play.expect '{"assertions":[{"name":"round started","condition":{"entity":{"component":"ArenaState"},"component":"ArenaState","path":"phase","op":"eq","value":"Round"}}]}' --project samples/arena
```

(The arena advertises its agent endpoint in its own sample directory, hence `--project
samples/arena`.)

## Soak it

```console
$ cargo build --release -p arena
$ cargo xtask soak --exe target/release/arena --minutes 2 --project-dir samples/arena \
    --input budgets/arena-soak.input.ron -- --bots 16 --no-local-player
```

A soak run plays for minutes and checks frame-time percentiles, the 50 ms hitch rule, memory,
start-up time and log errors against `budgets/default.ron` ([Profiling](book/systems/profiling.md)).

## Where next

The arena runs every gameplay system together. The reference chapters list the exact
shapes: [agent methods](book/reference/agent-methods.md), [content formats](book/reference/formats.md)
and [render profiles](book/reference/render-profiles.md).

# Build a networked game

This tutorial walks through the `net-game` template: a dedicated server and a client of one shared
simulation, over encrypted UDP, with client-side prediction, interpolation, lag compensation and
lobbies. The same code is the workspace sample `samples/net_game`, so everything below is compiled
and tested in CI (ADR-2039).

## 1. Create the project

```sh,walkthrough=new,template=net_game
regia new "Tag Yard" --template net-game
cd tag_yard
```

(`net-game` and `net_game` name the same template.)

| Crate | Package | What |
|---|---|---|
| `game/` | `tag_yard` | The simulation both sides run; its `client` feature adds the presentation (`view`) |
| `server/` | `tag_yard_server` | The headless dedicated server: no window, no renderer, no audio |
| `client/` | `tag_yard_client` | The windowed game |

The server turns on `regia`'s `server` feature (`default-features = false`), so it links no window,
render or audio crate; the client turns on `client`. `regia` needs one of the two, and with both
`regia::run` hosts a dedicated server, so never build the server and the client in one cargo
invocation: `cargo build` and `cargo run` in the project build the workspace's default members (the
game and the client), and the server is built on its own with `cargo build -p tag_yard_server
--release`. Do not use `--workspace`.

## 2. Play it

The quickest way is `regia server --clients 2` in the project folder: it builds the server and the
client crates (each in its own cargo invocation), runs the server with a relay inside it, and starts
two headless bot clients that join by the printed join code. By hand:

```sh
cargo run -p tag_yard_server --release -- --level levels/arena.level.ron --relay local
# listening 0.0.0.0:7777 key 3f1c...e9
# join code ABC123 relay 127.0.0.1:7800
cargo run -p tag_yard_client -- --join ABC123
cargo run -p tag_yard_client -- --join ABC123 --bot
cargo run -p tag_yard_client -- --connect 127.0.0.1:7777 --key 3f1c...e9
```

WASD runs, Space fires at the nearest other player. Each tag adds to your `Score::tags` and the
target's `Score::tagged`.

The server crate always runs under the engine's dedicated-server host, so its flags are the host's
(`--port N`, `--level PATH`, `--relay local|HOST:PORT`, `--console`, `--config PATH`, `--bind ADDR`,
`--max-players N`, `--shared-port`, `--bots N`, ...), its settings are `server.toml` in its directory
(`REGIA_SERVER_DIR`, else the executable's directory), and it keeps its key in `server.key`. Console,
bans, `/health`, signals and exit codes (0, 2 configuration, 3 port, 4 content, 70 crash) are on
[the dedicated server](book/agents/net-dedicated-server.md) page.

| Client flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--connect ADDR` | The server |
| `--join CODE` | Look a join code up on the relay and connect with the server's key pinned |
| `--relay ADDR` | The relay for `--join` (default `127.0.0.1:7800`, the port of a server started with `--relay local`) |
| `--key KEY` | Pin the server's key. Without it (and without `--join`) the client accepts any key: that stops a listener, not an attacker in the middle |
| `--bot`, `--bot-for N` | Play the scripted bot instead of the keyboard (for `N` ticks, then stand still) |
| `--headless --ticks N` | No window; print what the client saw after `N` ticks |
| `--clients N` | With `--headless`: `N` clients in one process, each with its own socket (1 to 64); a load and soak tool |
| `--host` | With `--headless`: also run the dedicated server in this process, on 127.0.0.1 (play-in-editor with N clients, over real encrypted UDP) |
| `--exit-after-frames N` | With a window: close after `N` rendered frames, exit 0 (the smoke flag every template's game takes) |
| `--conditioner SPEC`, `--seed N` | Shape this client's outbound datagrams (a profile such as `wan`, or `delay=40,jitter=10,loss=0.02`; see [net match](book/agents/net-match.md)) |

Client exit codes: 0 done, 2 bad arguments, 3 the port cannot be bound.

To check the whole loop in one process, without a window or a second terminal (a script, CI), let
the client host the server and run a bot for 120 ticks:

```sh,walkthrough=smoke,template=net_game
cargo run -p tag_yard_client -- --headless --host --bot --ticks 120
```

It prints `client 0 connected=true sealed=true` and the avatars it saw. The windowed client also
takes `--exit-after-frames N`.

Packaging: `regia package --platform linux` does not handle this layout yet. It looks for a root
package or a `launcher/` crate and stops with "a project needs a root package or a launcher/
package". Until it does, build the client in release; the binary is
`target/release/tag_yard_client` (under `$CARGO_TARGET_DIR` if you set it), and it runs from any
folder:

```sh,walkthrough=package,template=net_game
cargo build --release -p tag_yard_client
```

The dedicated server has its own `regia package --server` (`docs/specs/76-dedicated-server-package.md`).

## 3. The transport: `NetLink`

`regia::net::NetPlugin` runs replication inside an app: it fills a `NetNode`'s inbox and outbox.
`NetLink` moves those frames over a socket. `NetLinkPlugin` inserts an idle link; the game starts
it:

```rust,ignore
let opts = link_options(LinkClock::Wall, ConditionerConfig::default());
app.world_mut().resource_mut::<NetLink>().host_udp::<NetGameWire>(bind, &opts)?;      // server
app.world_mut().resource_mut::<NetLink>().connect_udp::<NetGameWire>(server, &opts)?; // client
```

`NetGameWire` is the game's `NetGame` identity: its `GAME_ID` and `PROTOCOL_VERSION` are checked at
the handshake, so a client of another game or another wire version is refused. Bump the version on
every wire change.

| Setting (`LinkOptions`) | Template value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `crypto` | `CryptoMode::Required` | Every link sealed, loopback included ([transport encryption](book/agents/net-crypto.md)) |
| `server_key` | the `--key` flag | Pins the server, so an attacker in the middle is refused |
| `conditioner` | off (`--conditioner` on the client; `REGIA_NET_CONDITIONER` for a dev-build server) | Seeded loss, delay, jitter, duplicates and reorders for testing |
| `clock` | `LinkClock::Wall` | Tests use `LinkClock::Manual`: one app update is one fixed step, no sleeps |

Any `DatagramSocket` works with `NetLink::host` and `NetLink::connect`: `UdpTransport`, the in-memory
`LoopbackSocket` of tests, or `regia::steam::SteamSocket`, which carries the same datagrams over
Steam's relay network to a Steam id.

## 4. Replicated state

```rust,ignore
app.replicate::<Avatar>(ReplicateOptions::default())
    .replicate::<Score>(ReplicateOptions::default())
```

Registration order feeds the protocol hash, so register in the same order on both sides:
`NetGamePlugin` does it once for both. When a peer joins, the server's `sync_avatars` spawns an avatar
with `Replicated { transform: PositionOnly }`, `NetOwner(peer)`, `NetPredicted` and `HitShapes`;
when the peer leaves, the avatar goes.

## 5. Prediction

The client predicts its own avatar so movement answers at once:

```rust,ignore
app.add_net_input::<Pad>()
    .predict::<Transform>(Tolerance::position(0.001))
    .add_predicted_systems((move_avatars, judge_shots).chain());
```

`Pad` is the per-tick command (`move_x`, `move_z`, `fire`, `aim`); its `on_missing` keeps running but
never repeats a shot. `move_avatars` runs on the server for every player and in the owner's
prediction for its own avatar; `PredictionCx::simulates` picks which. When the server's state at a
tick differs by more than 1 mm, the client rolls back and re-runs its unacknowledged commands. See
[net prediction](book/agents/net-prediction.md).

## 6. Interpolation

Other players' avatars are proxies: the client shows them between two server states, about one
send interval behind. The template uses `LinkInterpolationPlugin`, which reads the link's clock, so
the manual-clock tests show the same proxies on every run. See
[net interpolation](book/agents/net-interpolation.md).

## 7. Lag compensation

A shot is judged on the server, but against the targets as the shooter saw them: the input stream
carries the shooter's view tick, and `LagCompensation::raycast` rewinds every `HitShapes` to it.
`judge_shots` excludes the shooter's own avatar and counts each command tick once, even when
prediction re-runs it. See [net lag compensation](book/agents/net-lag-compensation.md).

## 8. Lobbies

`lobby.rs` follows a lobby (spec 89) to the dedicated server:

1. One player creates a lobby; the others list and join it.
2. Everyone marks ready (`Lobbies::set_ready(true)`).
3. The owner calls `launch_when_ready(&mut lobbies, server_addr)`, which publishes the address.
4. `follow_lobby` connects every member's idle `NetLink` there, the owner's too.

Insert `Lobbies` with a backend first: `LocalLobbyHub` for tests and LAN builds, the Steam backend
in a Steam build. A launch to a Steam id (`LobbyServer::Steam`) is followed over Steam sockets when
the app holds a `LobbySteamTransport` (in a Steam build, wrapping `regia::steam::SteamLobbyTransport`);
without one it is refused once with a logged `no_transport` and the member leaves the lobby. See
[net lobbies](book/agents/net-lobbies.md).

## 9. The end-to-end test

`game/tests/e2e.rs` (in the sample: `samples/net_game/tests/e2e.rs`):

| Test | What it proves |
|---|---|
| `a_scripted_minute_over_encrypted_udp_agrees` | A server and two bot clients over real UDP on 127.0.0.1, encryption required, key pinned, 2 % loss with jitter, reorders and duplicates, play 3600 ticks. Afterwards every process agrees on every avatar's position (within 1 mm) and score, both links are sealed, the conditioner dropped traffic, at least 90 % of shots hit through lag compensation, every shot was judged in the past, no failed verification, at most 20 corrections and at most 2 lead resyncs (a clock step, not a state divergence) |
| `the_in_memory_minute_replays_bit_for_bit` | The same match over the in-memory network, twice: every position, score, shot count and prediction counter repeats |
| `a_lobby_launch_brings_both_clients_to_the_server` | Create, join, ready, launch: both clients connect through the lobby and see both avatars |
| `a_steam_id_launch_is_followed_through_the_steam_transport` | A launch to a Steam id, with a stand-in lobby transport installed: both clients connect and see both avatars |
| `a_steam_id_launch_without_a_transport_is_refused_once` | The same launch without a transport: the links stay idle and the members leave the lobby instead of retrying every frame |
| `a_player_who_leaves_loses_the_avatar_everywhere` | A client goes silent: after the server's 10 s silence timeout its avatar is gone on the server and on the other client |

The sample has three more tests that the template leaves out: `tests/render_smoke.rs` renders a client headless (lavapipe in CI) and checks that an agent screenshot shows both players' colors, `tests/agent_smoke.rs` reads and steers the link over the agent protocol, and `tests/process_pair.rs` starts the real `net_game_server` and `net_game_client --headless --clients 2 --bot` as two processes, plays a minute over encrypted UDP in real time with the `home` conditioner on the server, and compares what each process printed.

The e2e tests run without a GPU, on a manual link clock: no sleeps, no timing budgets. The process pair needs no GPU either; it takes a real minute, since each binary paces itself, and asserts no durations.

## 10. Watching it with the agent

Run a client or a server built with the `agent` feature and use the agent protocol:

| Method | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `net.status`, `net.peers` | The link's endpoint report, published every frame under the label `server` or `client` |
| `net.crypto` | Whether the link is sealed and the server key |
| `net.conditioner_set` | Changes the link's conditioner live |
| `net.prediction`, `net.input_buffer` | Prediction counters and the server's input buffer |
| `net.interpolation` | Proxy delay and starvation |
| `lagcomp.stats`, `lagcomp.last_queries` | What the shots were judged against |
| `lobby.status`, `lobby.launch` | The lobby and its launch |

See [net link (agents)](book/agents/net-link.md) for the link's own report and error codes.

## 11. Make it yours

- Replace `move_avatars` with your character movement and keep it in the predicted schedule.
- Give `NetGameWire` your own `GAME_ID`.
- Replace the boxes in `game/src/view.rs` (the `client` feature: meshes, camera, light, input) with
  your characters, and add a score HUD.
- The server crate already runs under the supervised production host (health endpoint, console,
  `server.toml`, bans, join codes): the game's `HostedLink` binds the game port, and `--shared-port`
  serves the session layer of spec 77 on the same port. See
  [the dedicated server](book/agents/net-dedicated-server.md) and `regia package --server`.
