# Tutorial: your first scene

[Your first project](book/getting-started.md) put one box on screen. This tutorial builds a small
scene on purpose: a ground, a lamp post made of parts that move together, a row of spheres that
share one mesh, a sun and a point light, and a camera that frames it. Then it checks the result
from outside the game, with the agent protocol, and loads the same kind of content from a level
file. Steps 2 and 3 add functions to the file from the step before (merge the imports at the
top); the page ends with the whole `game/src/lib.rs`, which `cargo xtask book-check` compiles.

You need a project (`regia new "Scene Lab"`, then `cd scene_lab`) and the engine crates in
`game/Cargo.toml` that [Your first project](book/getting-started.md#3-put-something-on-screen) lists:
`regia`, `regia_core`, `regia_render` and `regia_scene`. Run the game after each step with
`cargo run -p scene_lab_launcher`.

## Step 1: a ground and a camera

The renderer reads three kinds of things from the world: a `Camera`, lights, and entities with a
`MeshRenderer`. Positions come from `Transform`. The engine is right-handed with +Y up, and a
camera looks down its own −Z axis, so to look at the origin from the +Z side you stand back and
tilt down.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_render::{Camera, CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, MeshRenderer, box_mesh};
use regia_scene::Transform;

/// The game plugin the launcher runs.
pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(regia_scene::ScenePlugin)
            .add_systems(Startup, spawn_ground_and_camera);
    }
}

/// A flat gray slab and a camera standing back from it.
fn spawn_ground_and_camera(mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Camera"),
        Transform {
            translation: Vec3::new(0.0, 4.0, 12.0),
            rotation: Quat::from_rotation_x(-0.3),
            ..Transform::default()
        },
        Camera::default(),
    ));

    // `box_mesh` takes half extents: this slab is 30 m by 0.2 m by 30 m, its top face at y = 0.
    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([15.0, 0.1, 15.0]);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Ground"),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, -0.1, 0.0)),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.35, 0.33, 0.30, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.9,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));
}
```

You see a gray slab under the default procedural sky. The sky already lights it a little
(image-based lighting), which is why it is not black; there is no sun yet, so there are no
shadows.

## Step 2: a sun, and objects that share a mesh

Add a `DirectionalLight` (the sun) and a row of spheres. The sun's `direction` is the way the
light *travels*, so a sun high in the sky shining down and slightly forward points mostly along
−Y. `illuminance` is in lux: 100 000 is a clear noon.

The row of spheres shows the rule that keeps scenes cheap: **a mesh and a material are shared
through `Arc`**. The GPU copy is cached by the `Arc`'s identity, so five spheres built from one
`Arc<CpuMesh>` upload one mesh.

Add these functions to the file from step 1, merging the imports at the top:

<!-- ignore-reason: fragment: the whole file compiles at the end of the page -->
```rust,ignore
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::Vec3;
use regia_render::{CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, DirectionalLight, MeshRenderer, uv_sphere};
use regia_scene::Transform;

/// A noon sun with shadows.
pub fn spawn_sun(commands: &mut Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Sun"),
        DirectionalLight {
            direction: [-0.4, -1.0, -0.3],
            color: [1.0, 0.97, 0.92],
            illuminance: 100_000.0,
            cast_shadows: true,
            static_shadow: false,
        },
    ));
}

/// Five spheres, one mesh, five materials of increasing roughness.
pub fn spawn_spheres(commands: &mut Commands) {
    let (vertices, indices) = uv_sphere(0.6, 32, 16);
    let mesh = Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices });
    for i in 0..5 {
        let roughness = 0.1 + 0.2 * i as f32;
        commands.spawn((
            Name::new(format!("Sphere {i}")),
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(-4.0 + 2.0 * i as f32, 0.6, 2.0)),
            MeshRenderer::new(
                Arc::clone(&mesh),
                Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                    base_color: [0.8, 0.2, 0.15, 1.0],
                    metallic: 0.0,
                    roughness,
                    ..CpuMaterial::default()
                }),
            ),
        ));
    }
}
```

Call both from the startup system (`spawn_sun(&mut commands); spawn_spheres(&mut commands);`).
Run it: the left sphere is glossy and the right one matte, and every sphere throws a shadow on the
ground. Each material is its own `Arc`, because each differs; only the mesh is shared.

## Step 3: a parent and its children

A lamp post is a pole and a lamp head. If you move the post, the head should come with it. Make
the pole the **parent** and the head a **child**: a child's `Transform` is relative to its parent,
and `ScenePlugin` propagates the result to the child's `GlobalTransform`, which is what the
renderer reads.

Add this function to the file from step 2, merging the imports at the top:

<!-- ignore-reason: fragment: the whole file compiles at the end of the page -->
```rust,ignore
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::Vec3;
use regia_render::{CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, MeshRenderer, PointLight, box_mesh, uv_sphere};
use regia_scene::Transform;
use regia_scene::hierarchy::HierarchyCommands;

/// A lamp post at `base`: a pole, and a glowing head that is a child of the pole.
pub fn spawn_lamp_post(commands: &mut Commands, base: Vec3) {
    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([0.08, 1.5, 0.08]);
    let pole = commands
        .spawn((
            Name::new("Lamp Post"),
            // The pole's origin is its center, so lift it by half its 3 m height.
            Transform::from_translation(base + Vec3::new(0.0, 1.5, 0.0)),
            MeshRenderer::new(
                Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
                Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                    base_color: [0.1, 0.1, 0.12, 1.0],
                    metallic: 0.8,
                    roughness: 0.4,
                    ..CpuMaterial::default()
                }),
            ),
        ))
        .id();

    let (vertices, indices) = uv_sphere(0.2, 16, 8);
    let head = commands
        .spawn((
            Name::new("Lamp Head"),
            // Relative to the pole: at its top.
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.6, 0.0)),
            MeshRenderer::new(
                Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
                Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                    base_color: [1.0, 0.9, 0.7, 1.0],
                    emissive: [1.0, 0.8, 0.5],
                    emissive_intensity: 20.0,
                    ..CpuMaterial::default()
                }),
            ),
        ))
        .id();
    commands.entity(head).set_parent(pole);

    // The light is a second child of the pole, at the head's local position. A point
    // light's position in the world is its entity's `GlobalTransform` — the `position`
    // field is ignored on a component — so parenting the light moves it with the post.
    let light = commands
        .spawn((
            Name::new("Lamp Light"),
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.6, 0.0)),
            PointLight {
                position: [0.0; 3], // unused as a component: the transform carries it
                color: [1.0, 0.8, 0.5],
                intensity: 800.0,
                radius: 12.0,
                cast_shadows: false,
            },
        ))
        .id();
    commands.entity(light).set_parent(pole);
}
```

Two things to notice. First, the head's `Transform` says `y = 1.6` and nothing about where the
pole is; its place in the world is the parent's transform times its own. Change the pole's
translation (in code, in the editor or through the agent) and the head follows. Second, the point
light is a second child of the pole at the same local position, so it follows too: like every
light except the sun, its position in the world comes from its entity's `GlobalTransform`
(the `position` field exists for extracted lights, not for the component). The sun, by
contrast, has no position at all.

Call `spawn_lamp_post(&mut commands, Vec3::new(4.0, 0.0, -2.0))`. Run it: at noon neither the
emissive head (20 units, against a sunlit ground of about 9 000) nor the 800 lm point light (about
7 lux at the ground, 1/15 000 of the sun) shows. `intensity` is lumens, and the auto exposure
(which settles on the new average brightness over a second or so) keys on the sun. Set the sun's
`illuminance` to a deep-twilight 5.0 and rerun: the head glows and the lamp throws a pool of light
around the post.

## Step 4: look at it without looking at it

Leave the game running and, in a second terminal in the project directory, ask the agent protocol
what is in the world. This is how a script (or an AI agent) checks a scene: it does not need to
read pixels to know that a lamp post has a child.

```console
$ regia agent call scene.query_entities '{"name":"Lamp*"}'
$ regia agent call scene.query_entities '{"component":"MeshRenderer","near":{"point":[0,0,2],"radius":5}}'
$ regia agent call seeing.screenshot --out scene.png
```

The first call lists the pole, the head and the light with their translations; the head's and
the light's are local to the pole, so both read `(0, 1.6, 0)`. The second finds **seven**
entities, not five: the Ground, the five spheres and the Lamp Head. A spatial filter compares
each entity's *local* `Transform` translation, not its world position — the Lamp Head is about
6.5 m from `(0, 0, 2)` in the world (its world position is `(4, 3.1, −2)`: the pole's origin plus
the head's 1.6 m local offset), but its local translation is only 2.6 m away, so it
matches (and the Lamp Post, whose local translation is its world position at 5.9 m, does not).
The third writes a PNG of the window.

Move something and see it change, without recompiling. Take the id from the query result:

```console
$ regia agent call scene.set_property '{"entity": 4294967297, "component": "Transform", "path": "translation.x", "value": 7.0}'
```

`scene.set_property` edits the live world. It is a debugging tool: the next run starts from your
code again. [Scene: finding, inspecting and editing entities](book/agents/scene.md) lists the other
calls, including `scene.spawn` and `scene.reparent`.

## Step 5: move the scene into a level file

Everything above is Rust code, which is the right place for gameplay and generated content. Static
content, like this ground and these spheres, belongs in a **level**: a diffable `.level.ron` file
that the editor and the agent protocol can both edit. Open the project in the editor:

```console
$ regia-editor --project .
```

Create entities with the editor's **File → Create entity** menu, give them `Transform`s, and save: the level lands in
`assets/levels/`. A level file is plain text, one entity per record, with a stable `guid`:

```ron
(
    format_version: 13,
    entities: [
        (
            guid: "5c2d7a10-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
            name: "Pedestal",
            components: {
                "regia_scene::transform::Transform": (
                    translation: (0.0, 0.5, 0.0),
                    rotation: (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0),
                    scale: (1.0, 1.0, 1.0),
                ),
            },
        ),
    ],
)
```

To run the level in your game, read it in a `Startup` system and open it, exactly as
[Scenes](book/user-guide/scenes.md#loading-a-level-from-your-game) shows (`Level::from_ron_str`,
`LevelLibrary`, `open_level`). The editor does not run your `Startup` systems, which is why the
code-built scene above is not in the level it opens; the split is the point. Static layout lives
in the level, and code adds what changes.

## The whole file

Replace `game/src/lib.rs` with this. It is checked by `cargo xtask book-check`, so it compiles
against the engine as the book describes it.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_render::{
    Camera, CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, DirectionalLight, MeshRenderer, PointLight, box_mesh, uv_sphere,
};
use regia_scene::Transform;
use regia_scene::hierarchy::HierarchyCommands;

/// The game plugin the launcher runs.
pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(regia_scene::ScenePlugin)
            .add_systems(Startup, spawn_scene);
    }
}

/// The ground, the camera, the sun, the spheres and the lamp post.
fn spawn_scene(mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Camera"),
        Transform {
            translation: Vec3::new(0.0, 4.0, 12.0),
            rotation: Quat::from_rotation_x(-0.3),
            ..Transform::default()
        },
        Camera::default(),
    ));

    // `box_mesh` takes half extents: this slab is 30 m by 0.2 m by 30 m, its top face at y = 0.
    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([15.0, 0.1, 15.0]);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Ground"),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, -0.1, 0.0)),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.35, 0.33, 0.30, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.9,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));

    spawn_sun(&mut commands);
    spawn_spheres(&mut commands);
    spawn_lamp_post(&mut commands, Vec3::new(4.0, 0.0, -2.0));
}

/// A noon sun with shadows.
pub fn spawn_sun(commands: &mut Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Sun"),
        DirectionalLight {
            direction: [-0.4, -1.0, -0.3],
            color: [1.0, 0.97, 0.92],
            illuminance: 100_000.0,
            cast_shadows: true,
            static_shadow: false,
        },
    ));
}

/// Five spheres, one mesh, five materials of increasing roughness.
pub fn spawn_spheres(commands: &mut Commands) {
    let (vertices, indices) = uv_sphere(0.6, 32, 16);
    let mesh = Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices });
    for i in 0..5 {
        let roughness = 0.1 + 0.2 * i as f32;
        commands.spawn((
            Name::new(format!("Sphere {i}")),
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(-4.0 + 2.0 * i as f32, 0.6, 2.0)),
            MeshRenderer::new(
                Arc::clone(&mesh),
                Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                    base_color: [0.8, 0.2, 0.15, 1.0],
                    metallic: 0.0,
                    roughness,
                    ..CpuMaterial::default()
                }),
            ),
        ));
    }
}

/// A lamp post at `base`: a pole, a glowing head, and the light, all moving together.
pub fn spawn_lamp_post(commands: &mut Commands, base: Vec3) {
    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([0.08, 1.5, 0.08]);
    let pole = commands
        .spawn((
            Name::new("Lamp Post"),
            // The pole's origin is its center, so lift it by half its 3 m height.
            Transform::from_translation(base + Vec3::new(0.0, 1.5, 0.0)),
            MeshRenderer::new(
                Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
                Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                    base_color: [0.1, 0.1, 0.12, 1.0],
                    metallic: 0.8,
                    roughness: 0.4,
                    ..CpuMaterial::default()
                }),
            ),
        ))
        .id();

    let (vertices, indices) = uv_sphere(0.2, 16, 8);
    let head = commands
        .spawn((
            Name::new("Lamp Head"),
            // Relative to the pole: at its top.
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.6, 0.0)),
            MeshRenderer::new(
                Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
                Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                    base_color: [1.0, 0.9, 0.7, 1.0],
                    emissive: [1.0, 0.8, 0.5],
                    emissive_intensity: 20.0,
                    ..CpuMaterial::default()
                }),
            ),
        ))
        .id();
    commands.entity(head).set_parent(pole);

    // The light is a second child of the pole, at the head's local position. A point
    // light's position in the world is its entity's `GlobalTransform` — the `position`
    // field is ignored on a component — so parenting the light moves it with the post.
    let light = commands
        .spawn((
            Name::new("Lamp Light"),
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.6, 0.0)),
            PointLight {
                position: [0.0; 3], // unused as a component: the transform carries it
                color: [1.0, 0.8, 0.5],
                intensity: 800.0,
                radius: 12.0,
                cast_shadows: false,
            },
        ))
        .id();
    commands.entity(light).set_parent(pole);
}
```

## What you built, and where next

You used `Transform`, `Camera`, `DirectionalLight`, `PointLight` and `MeshRenderer`; shared one
mesh between several entities; built a parent and a child; checked all of it through the agent
protocol; and met the level file. Next:

- [Tutorial: a game loop with input](book/tutorials/game-loop.md) makes the scene respond to the keyboard.
- [Tutorial: your first baked light](book/tutorials/baked-light.md) lights a scene with path-traced indirect
  light, instead of a flat ambient term.
- [Materials](book/user-guide/materials.md) and [Rendering](book/user-guide/rendering.md) go deeper on
  what you set here.

<!-- source: book/tutorials/game-loop.md -->
# Tutorial: a game loop with input

This tutorial builds **Orb Run**, the smallest thing that is a game: you move a box around an
arena with the keyboard or a gamepad, orbs sit on the floor, touching one collects it, and
collecting them all wins. It is about the *loop*: how input becomes movement, why simulation runs
in `FixedUpdate` and input is read in `Update`, how systems are ordered, how a system tells another
one something happened, and how to test the whole thing without touching a key.

You need a project ([Your first project](book/getting-started.md)) with these crates in
`game/Cargo.toml`: `regia`, `regia_core`, `regia_input`, `regia_render` and
`regia_scene` (the [first-scene tutorial](book/tutorials/first-scene.md) shows the lines). The page ends with the
whole `game/src/lib.rs`; the sections before it explain each part, so you can read first and paste
once.

## The loop, in one picture

A frame runs these schedules in order (see [App, plugins and schedules](book/fundamentals/app-and-plugins.md)):

| Schedule | Orb Run puts here |
|---|---|
| `PreUpdate` | the engine's `InputPlugin` evaluates bindings into `Actions` (its own systems, not yours) |
| `FixedUpdate` | `move_player`, then `collect_orbs`: the simulation, at a fixed 60 Hz |
| `Update` | `read_intent`: read the input actions, store what the player wants; `spin_orbs` (cosmetic) |

Input is evaluated once per frame, before the simulation, and the simulation consumes it zero or
more times per frame. `read_intent` runs in `Update`, *after* that frame's fixed steps, so a key
press reaches `MoveIntent` one frame after it was evaluated — one frame of latency, the same at
any frame rate. The win check lives inside `collect_orbs`, in `FixedUpdate`. That
split keeps the simulation independent of the frame rate: at 30 fps `FixedUpdate` runs twice per
frame and at 240 fps it runs on one frame in four, and the player moves the same distance per
second either way. It also keeps the simulation deterministic, which is what lets you test it.

## Step 1: name your inputs

Gameplay code never asks "is W down". It asks for an **action**, a named input with a kind, and the
bindings (keys, sticks, buttons) are data. Orb Run has one action, `Move`, a 2D axis:

<!-- ignore-reason: fragment: the whole file compiles at the end of the page -->
```rust,ignore
fn input_config() -> InputConfig {
    InputConfig::new()
        .action("Move", ActionKind::Axis2D)
        .binding(Binding::new("Move", InputSource::keys2d("KeyW", "KeyS", "KeyA", "KeyD")))
        .binding(Binding::new("Move", InputSource::gamepad_stick(Stick::Left)))
}
```

`keys2d(up, down, left, right)` turns four keys into one axis whose y is "forward"; the left
stick is a second binding on the same action, so both work at once. Keys are named by physical
position (`KeyW` is the key in W's place on a US layout, wherever your layout puts the letter), so
the controls stay under the same fingers on an AZERTY keyboard. [Input](book/user-guide/input.md)
covers modifiers (dead zones, curves), triggers (hold, tap), contexts and rebinding.

## Step 2: read input in `Update`, simulate in `FixedUpdate`

`read_intent` copies the action into a `MoveIntent` resource. `move_player` reads that resource
at the fixed step:

<!-- ignore-reason: fragment: the whole file compiles at the end of the page -->
```rust,ignore
fn read_intent(actions: Res<Actions>, mut intent: ResMut<MoveIntent>) {
    intent.0 = actions.axis2d("Move").clamp_length_max(1.0);
}

fn move_player(
    intent: Res<MoveIntent>,
    fixed: Res<FixedTime>,
    mut players: Query<&mut Transform, With<Player>>,
) {
    let dt = fixed.step().as_secs_f32();
    for mut transform in &mut players {
        // The axis's y is "forward", which is -Z in the world.
        let step = Vec3::new(intent.0.x, 0.0, -intent.0.y) * PLAYER_SPEED * dt;
        let moved = transform.translation + step;
        transform.translation = Vec3::new(
            moved.x.clamp(-ARENA_LIMIT, ARENA_LIMIT),
            moved.y,
            moved.z.clamp(-ARENA_LIMIT, ARENA_LIMIT),
        );
    }
}
```

Three habits to take from it:

- **Clamp the axis.** `keys2d` already normalizes a diagonal of length √2 to length 1, but
  several bindings on one action (keys plus a gamepad stick pushed past the dead zone) can still
  add past 1; `clamp_length_max(1.0)` keeps combined input from being faster than a single one.
- **Use the step, not the frame delta.** Inside `FixedUpdate`, `Res<Time>` still reports the
  *frame's* delta. The step length is `FixedTime::step()`.
- **Do not read edges in `FixedUpdate`.** `just_pressed` is true for one frame, and a fixed step may
  not run on that frame. Continuous values (held keys, sticks) are safe to read anywhere. For a
  button press, read it in `Update` and store it, as `read_intent` does for the stick.

## Step 3: order the systems

Systems in one schedule may run in parallel, in any order. Orb Run needs `move_player` to finish
before `collect_orbs` checks distances, so they are chained:

<!-- ignore-reason: fragment: the whole file compiles at the end of the page -->
```rust,ignore
app.add_systems(Update, (read_intent, spin_orbs))
    .add_systems(FixedUpdate, (move_player, collect_orbs).chain());
```

`.chain()` runs the tuple in order. [App, plugins and schedules](book/fundamentals/app-and-plugins.md)
shows system sets, which are the tool for ordering across plugins.

## Step 4: tell the rest of the game that something happened

When the player touches an orb, `collect_orbs` despawns it, bumps the score and writes an
`OrbCollected` **message**. A message is a buffered event: the writer does not know who reads it.
Sound, particles and a HUD can each read it without `collect_orbs` changing:

<!-- ignore-reason: fragment: the whole file compiles at the end of the page -->
```rust,ignore
fn collect_orbs(
    mut commands: Commands,
    players: Query<&Transform, With<Player>>,
    orbs: Query<(Entity, &Transform), With<Orb>>,
    mut scores: Query<&mut Score>,
    mut collected: MessageWriter<OrbCollected>,
) {
    let (Ok(player), Ok(mut score)) = (players.single(), scores.single_mut()) else {
        return;
    };
    for (entity, orb) in &orbs {
        if player.translation.distance(orb.translation) < PICKUP_RADIUS {
            commands.entity(entity).despawn();
            score.collected += 1;
            collected.write(OrbCollected { at: orb.translation.to_array() });
        }
    }
    if score.collected == score.total && score.total > 0 {
        info!("all orbs collected");
    }
}
```

`players.single()` returns an error when there is not exactly one player; the `let ... else`
returns quietly instead of panicking. That is the habit for any system that runs before its
entities exist (a level still loading, a player that just died).

The score lives in a **component** on an entity named `Score`, not in a resource. The reason is
testability: the agent protocol's `play.expect` reads reflected component fields on entities, so a
number you want a test to check should live where a test can read it
([the arena tutorial](book/tutorials/arena.md) makes the same choice).

## The whole file

Replace `game/src/lib.rs` with this. It is checked by `cargo xtask book-check`, so it compiles
against the engine as the book describes it.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec2, Vec3};
use regia_input::prelude::*;
use regia_render::{
    Camera, CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, DirectionalLight, MeshRenderer, box_mesh, uv_sphere,
};
use regia_scene::Transform;

/// Player speed, meters per second.
const PLAYER_SPEED: f32 = 6.0;
/// The player stays inside a square this far from the origin, meters.
const ARENA_LIMIT: f32 = 12.0;
/// An orb is collected when the player is closer than this, meters.
const PICKUP_RADIUS: f32 = 1.0;
/// Orbs placed around the arena.
const ORB_COUNT: u32 = 8;

/// Marks the box the player drives.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct Player;

/// Marks a collectible orb.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct Orb;

/// Progress through the level. A component, so `play.expect` can read it.
#[derive(Component, Reflect, Default)]
#[reflect(Component, Default)]
pub struct Score {
    /// Orbs picked up so far.
    pub collected: u32,
    /// Orbs the level started with.
    pub total: u32,
}

/// What the player asked for this frame, written in `Update` and read in `FixedUpdate`.
#[derive(Resource, Default)]
pub struct MoveIntent(pub Vec2);

/// Written when an orb is collected.
#[derive(Message, Debug, Clone)]
pub struct OrbCollected {
    /// Where the orb was.
    pub at: [f32; 3],
}

/// Named actions bound to keyboard and gamepad.
fn input_config() -> InputConfig {
    InputConfig::new()
        .action("Move", ActionKind::Axis2D)
        .binding(Binding::new("Move", InputSource::keys2d("KeyW", "KeyS", "KeyA", "KeyD")))
        .binding(Binding::new("Move", InputSource::gamepad_stick(Stick::Left)))
}

/// The game plugin the launcher runs.
pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(regia_scene::ScenePlugin)
            .add_plugins(InputPlugin::new(input_config()))
            .register_type::<Player>()
            .register_type::<Orb>()
            .register_type::<Score>()
            .init_resource::<MoveIntent>()
            .add_message::<OrbCollected>()
            .add_systems(Startup, spawn_world)
            .add_systems(Update, (read_intent, spin_orbs))
            .add_systems(FixedUpdate, (move_player, collect_orbs).chain());
    }
}

/// Camera, sun, floor, the player, the orbs and the score.
fn spawn_world(mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Camera"),
        Transform {
            translation: Vec3::new(0.0, 22.0, 16.0),
            rotation: Quat::from_rotation_x(-0.95),
            ..Transform::default()
        },
        Camera::default(),
    ));
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Sun"),
        DirectionalLight {
            direction: [-0.4, -1.0, -0.3],
            color: [1.0, 0.97, 0.92],
            illuminance: 100_000.0,
            cast_shadows: true,
            static_shadow: false,
        },
    ));

    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([14.0, 0.1, 14.0]);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Floor"),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, -0.1, 0.0)),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.3, 0.32, 0.35, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.9,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));

    let (vertices, indices) = box_mesh([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Player"),
        Player,
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(0.0, 0.5, 0.0)),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.9, 0.45, 0.15, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.5,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));

    // One mesh and one material, shared by every orb.
    let (vertices, indices) = uv_sphere(0.35, 24, 12);
    let orb_mesh = Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices });
    let orb_material = Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
        base_color: [0.2, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0],
        emissive: [0.2, 0.7, 0.9],
        emissive_intensity: 4.0,
        roughness: 0.3,
        ..CpuMaterial::default()
    });
    for i in 0..ORB_COUNT {
        // A ring of orbs, 8 m from the center. Fixed positions: the same level every run.
        let angle = i as f32 / ORB_COUNT as f32 * std::f32::consts::TAU;
        commands.spawn((
            Name::new(format!("Orb {i}")),
            Orb,
            Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(8.0 * angle.cos(), 0.6, 8.0 * angle.sin())),
            MeshRenderer::new(Arc::clone(&orb_mesh), Arc::clone(&orb_material)),
        ));
    }

    commands.spawn((Name::new("Score"), Score { collected: 0, total: ORB_COUNT }));
}

/// `Update`: store what the player is asking for.
fn read_intent(actions: Res<Actions>, mut intent: ResMut<MoveIntent>) {
    intent.0 = actions.axis2d("Move").clamp_length_max(1.0);
}

/// `FixedUpdate`: move the player by the step length, inside the arena.
fn move_player(
    intent: Res<MoveIntent>,
    fixed: Res<FixedTime>,
    mut players: Query<&mut Transform, With<Player>>,
) {
    let dt = fixed.step().as_secs_f32();
    for mut transform in &mut players {
        // The axis's y is "forward", which is -Z in the world.
        let step = Vec3::new(intent.0.x, 0.0, -intent.0.y) * PLAYER_SPEED * dt;
        let moved = transform.translation + step;
        transform.translation = Vec3::new(
            moved.x.clamp(-ARENA_LIMIT, ARENA_LIMIT),
            moved.y,
            moved.z.clamp(-ARENA_LIMIT, ARENA_LIMIT),
        );
    }
}

/// `FixedUpdate`, after `move_player`: collect orbs the player touches.
fn collect_orbs(
    mut commands: Commands,
    players: Query<&Transform, With<Player>>,
    orbs: Query<(Entity, &Transform), With<Orb>>,
    mut scores: Query<&mut Score>,
    mut collected: MessageWriter<OrbCollected>,
) {
    let (Ok(player), Ok(mut score)) = (players.single(), scores.single_mut()) else {
        return;
    };
    for (entity, orb) in &orbs {
        if player.translation.distance(orb.translation) < PICKUP_RADIUS {
            commands.entity(entity).despawn();
            score.collected += 1;
            collected.write(OrbCollected { at: orb.translation.to_array() });
        }
    }
    if score.collected == score.total && score.total > 0 {
        info!("all orbs collected");
    }
}

/// `Update`: turn the orbs, so they read as pickups. Purely cosmetic.
fn spin_orbs(time: Res<Time>, mut orbs: Query<&mut Transform, With<Orb>>) {
    for mut transform in &mut orbs {
        transform.rotation = Quat::from_rotation_y(2.0 * time.delta_secs()) * transform.rotation;
    }
}
```

Run `cargo run -p orb_run_launcher` (or whatever your project is called). WASD or the left stick
moves the box; touching an orb removes it. The log prints `all orbs collected` once, when
the last one goes. (It prints on every fixed step after that, as written. Making it fire once is
the exercise at the end.)

## Test it without touching a key

A game you can only test by playing is a game you test less. The agent protocol can drive the
loop. Pause the game so time only moves when you say, send the `Move` action, step frames and
assert, all from a second terminal in the project directory:

```console
$ regia agent call play.pause
$ regia agent call play.inject_input '{"actions":[{"action":"Move","value":[1.0,0.0],"duration_frames":1200}]}'
$ regia agent call play.step '{"frames":120}'
$ regia agent call play.expect '{"assertions":[{"name":"player moved right","condition":{"entity":{"name":"Player"},"component":"Transform","path":"translation.x","op":"gt","value":1.0}}]}'
```

Paste the script as one block. The injection window is counted in frames — including paused
ones — so pausing, typing the calls in slowly and only then stepping lets the window expire
while no fixed step runs, and the player never moves. Also, `play.step` advances exact frames,
but a stepped frame still carries its wall-clock time (unless the host pins the clock with
`TimeUpdateStrategy::ManualDuration`), so how many fixed steps a batch of 120 contains depends
on the display's frame rate. On a fast uncapped display one batch may not move the player a
full meter: step another 120 and expect again — a script simply loops the two calls until the
assertion passes. To drive the player to a
specific orb, move along z first, since the ring's orbs sit at fixed angles. When the player is
in range, check the score:

```console
$ regia agent call play.expect '{"assertions":[{"name":"one orb collected","condition":{"entity":{"component":"Score"},"component":"Score","path":"collected","op":"gte","value":1}}]}'
```

(One orb of eight is what this drive collects; `all orbs collected` cannot print until a script
walks the whole ring.)

Action injection needs `InputPlugin` to be installed, which `Game` does. The conditions and the
rest of the grammar are in [Testing gameplay](book/agents/testing.md).

## Exercises

1. **Fire once.** `info!("all orbs collected")` runs every fixed step after the last orb. Add a
   `done: bool` field to `Score` (it derives `Default`, so the spawn needs `..Score::default()`)
   and log only when it flips.
2. **Make the message do something.** Add a system that reads `MessageReader<OrbCollected>` and
   plays a sound or spawns a `Gizmos` marker at `at`; `collect_orbs` does not change. See
   [Audio](book/user-guide/audio.md) and [Gizmos](book/user-guide/gizmos.md).
3. **Add a jump.** Bind a `Jump` button to `Space`, read `just_pressed("Jump")` in `Update` into a
   `JumpRequested` resource, and consume it in `FixedUpdate` (clear it after use). That is the
   edge-input pattern from step 2.
4. **Replace the box with a physics character.** [Tutorial: a third-person game](book/tutorials/third-person.md)
   does the movement with a rapier character controller.

Next: [Tutorial: your first baked light](book/tutorials/baked-light.md).

<!-- source: book/tutorials/baked-light.md -->
# Tutorial: your first baked light

Real-time lighting estimates how light bounces around a scene every frame, with a budget of a
few milliseconds. A **baked** light does that work once, ahead of time, with the reference path
tracer, and stores the answer in a file. At runtime the renderer looks the answer up: path-traced
bounce light, sky light and emitted light at a small fixed cost, with no settling time after a
load or a camera cut. The catch is that the answer is for the scene as it was when you baked it.

This tutorial bakes the light for a small outdoor scene, attaches the result to a level, runs the
game with it, and checks, with the agent protocol, that the bake is really in use. It uses the
`rolling-hills` scene that ships inside the `regia` tool, so you do not need any art.

You need a project ([Your first project](book/getting-started.md)), the crates `regia`,
`regia_core`, `regia_render` and `regia_scene` in `game/Cargo.toml`, and **a GPU**: the bake
runs on the first graphics adapter (`--dry-run` does not). The background and every runtime
control are in [Baked GI volumes](book/agents/baked-gi.md); this page is the guided walk.

## What gets baked

A bake stores a volume of **probes**: points in space where the tracer recorded the light arriving
from every direction, as four terms (bounce of the sun, sky, sky-body fill, and emitted light),
plus distances that tell the lookup which probes can see a surface. The probes are laid out in a
layer that follows the terrain, with optional finer **bricks** around things that need detail.
The file is a `.fgiv`.

What is *not* baked: direct sun light and its shadows (the sun is real-time, as always), and
anything that moves. Moving things are lit from the volume at runtime, and can darken it near them
with capsule occluders ([Dynamic occluders](book/agents/baked-gi.md#dynamic-occluders)).

## Step 1: see what a bake would do

```console
$ regia bake-gi rolling-hills --dry-run
```

`rolling-hills` is a built-in scene: a 256 m procedural heightfield, one boulder, a sun and a
uniform sky. A dry run loads the scene, lays out the probes and prints one JSON object (progress
goes to stderr) without tracing anything. Look at three things in it:

- `layers.terrain`: the terrain layer's origin, spacing and counts. Fewer, wider-spaced probes
  bake faster and smooth the light more.
- `layers.probes`: the total number of probes. This is the number that sets the file size and
  the bake time.
- `ok: true`. A description error prints `{"ok": false, "code": ..., "message": ...}` and exits
  non-zero. The codes are listed in [Baking GI from meshes](book/agents/baked-gi-bake.md#errors).

## Step 2: bake

```console
$ mkdir -p assets/maps
$ regia bake-gi rolling-hills --out assets/maps/hills.fgiv
```

The command traces from every probe on the GPU and writes `assets/maps/hills.fgiv`. It takes
from seconds to a few minutes, depending on the GPU and the settings. The output object adds the
`report`: how many probes are `valid`, how many were `inside_geometry` or `under_terrain` (probes
the bake had to move or throw out), and how many rays were cast. A healthy bake has almost every
probe valid. `--rays`, `--samples`, `--bounces` and `--seed` trade quality for time; a fixed
`--seed` makes the result repeatable.

## Step 3: a scene that matches the bake

Light that was baked for one scene is only right for that scene. Your game must put the same
terrain under the sun, or the lookup will light a surface that is not where the bake thought it
was. The bake's heightfield is a known function, so the game builds the same hills as a mesh.
This step and the next add functions to `game/src/lib.rs`; the page ends with the whole file,
which `cargo xtask book-check` compiles. Start from a fresh `regia new` project, or delete the
`setup` system (and its camera and sun) that [Your first project](book/getting-started.md) put in
`lib.rs` — keeping it would spawn a second camera and a second sun, and the bake's checks would
compare against the wrong light.

<!-- ignore-reason: fragment: the whole file compiles at the end of the page -->
```rust,ignore
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_render::{
    Camera, CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, DirectionalLight, LabVertex, MeshRenderer, uv_sphere,
};
use regia_scene::Transform;

/// Samples per side of the ground mesh: 129 vertices at 2 m is the bake's 256 m square.
const GRID: usize = 129;
/// Meters between ground vertices.
const SPACING: f32 = 2.0;

/// The height of the `rolling-hills` bake scene at (`x`, `z`), meters.
fn hills_height(x: f32, z: f32) -> f32 {
    6.0 * (x * 0.045).sin() * (z * 0.037).cos() + 3.0 * (x * 0.11 + z * 0.07).sin()
}

/// The slope of `hills_height` along x and z, for vertex normals.
fn hills_slope(x: f32, z: f32) -> (f32, f32) {
    let w = x * 0.11 + z * 0.07;
    let dx = 6.0 * 0.045 * (x * 0.045).cos() * (z * 0.037).cos() + 3.0 * 0.11 * w.cos();
    let dz = -6.0 * 0.037 * (x * 0.045).sin() * (z * 0.037).sin() + 3.0 * 0.07 * w.cos();
    (dx, dz)
}

/// A grid mesh over the hills, centered on the origin.
fn hills_mesh() -> CpuMesh {
    let half = (GRID - 1) as f32 * SPACING * 0.5;
    let mut vertices = Vec::with_capacity(GRID * GRID);
    for j in 0..GRID {
        for i in 0..GRID {
            let (x, z) = (i as f32 * SPACING - half, j as f32 * SPACING - half);
            let (dx, dz) = hills_slope(x, z);
            let normal = Vec3::new(-dx, 1.0, -dz).normalize();
            vertices.push(LabVertex {
                position: [x, hills_height(x, z), z],
                normal: normal.to_array(),
                uv: [i as f32 / (GRID - 1) as f32, j as f32 / (GRID - 1) as f32],
                tangent: [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
                color: [1.0; 4],
                joints: [0; 4],
                weights: [0.0; 4],
            });
        }
    }
    let mut indices = Vec::with_capacity((GRID - 1) * (GRID - 1) * 6);
    for j in 0..GRID - 1 {
        for i in 0..GRID - 1 {
            let a = (j * GRID + i) as u32;
            let b = a + 1;
            let d = a + GRID as u32;
            let c = d + 1;
            // Counter-clockwise seen from above (+Y): a -> d -> c, a -> c -> b.
            indices.extend_from_slice(&[a, d, c, a, c, b]);
        }
    }
    CpuMesh { vertices, indices }
}

/// Camera, sun, hills and the bake's boulder.
fn spawn_scene(mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Camera"),
        Transform {
            translation: Vec3::new(-30.0, 6.0, 30.0),
            // Yaw toward +X / -Z, pitch down a little.
            rotation: Quat::from_rotation_y(-0.785) * Quat::from_rotation_x(-0.2),
            ..Transform::default()
        },
        Camera::default(),
    ));

    // The bake's sun is `toward: (0.4, 0.6, 0.3)`, the direction *to* the sun. The light
    // travels the opposite way.
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Sun"),
        DirectionalLight {
            direction: [-0.4, -0.6, -0.3],
            color: [1.0, 0.96, 0.9],
            illuminance: 100_000.0,
            cast_shadows: true,
            static_shadow: false,
        },
    ));

    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Hills"),
        Transform::default(),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(hills_mesh()),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.35, 0.3, 0.26, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.9,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));

    // The bake's boulder: radius 4 m at (10, 2, -6), mostly below the hill.
    let (vertices, indices) = uv_sphere(4.0, 32, 16);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Boulder"),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(10.0, 2.0, -6.0)),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.4, 0.4, 0.4, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.8,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));
}
```

The numbers are not arbitrary. They are the ones in the `rolling-hills` definition: the height
formula, the sun's `toward` vector `(0.4, 0.6, 0.3)` and illuminance 100 000 lux, and the boulder.
The bake grid is 1 m and the mesh 2 m, so the rendered surface is a little coarser than the
traced one; for a tutorial that is invisible. A real project bakes the *same meshes* it renders.
[Baking GI from meshes](book/agents/baked-gi-bake.md) describes how a `.bake.ron` names them.

## Step 4: a level that names its bake

A level carries its bake in its look settings: when the level opens, the framework loads the
volume and installs it in the renderer. Create `assets/levels/hills.level.ron`:

```ron
(
    format_version: 13,
    entities: [],
    resources: {
        "regia_scene::level::LevelSettings": (
            look: (
                baked_gi: Some((
                    volume: "maps/hills.fgiv",
                )),
            ),
        ),
    },
)
```

`volume` is a path under `assets/`. Open the level from `Startup`, next to the scene, with the same
loader as in [Scenes](book/user-guide/scenes.md#loading-a-level-from-your-game). Add this function
to the same file (merging the imports at the top):

<!-- ignore-reason: fragment: the whole file compiles at the end of the page -->
```rust,ignore
use regia::core::id::Guid;
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_scene::level::{Level, LevelId, LevelLibrary, LoadMode, open_level};

/// The id this game uses for the hills level.
const HILLS_LEVEL: LevelId = LevelId(Guid::from_u128(0x6869_6c6c_0000_4000_8000_0000_0000_0001));

/// Reads `levels/hills.level.ron` and opens it. The level names the bake; the framework installs it.
pub fn load_hills_level(world: &mut World) {
    let Ok(path) = VfsPath::parse("assets://levels/hills.level.ron") else {
        return;
    };
    let bytes = match world.resource::<Vfs>().read_sync(&path) {
        Ok(bytes) => bytes,
        Err(err) => {
            error!("cannot read the hills level: {err}");
            return;
        }
    };
    let level = match Level::from_ron_str(HILLS_LEVEL, &String::from_utf8_lossy(&bytes)) {
        Ok(level) => level,
        Err(err) => {
            error!("the hills level does not parse: {err}");
            return;
        }
    };
    world.get_resource_or_insert_with(LevelLibrary::new).insert(level);
    if let Err(err) = open_level(world, HILLS_LEVEL, LoadMode::Replace) {
        error!("cannot open the hills level: {err}");
    }
}
```

## The whole file

Replace `game/src/lib.rs` with this (a fresh project's blank `Game::build` body, or in place of
the getting-started `setup`). It is checked by `cargo xtask book-check`, so it compiles against
the engine as the book describes it.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use regia::core::id::Guid;
use regia::prelude::*;
use regia_core::math::{Quat, Vec3};
use regia_render::{
    Camera, CpuMaterial, CpuMesh, DirectionalLight, LabVertex, MeshRenderer, uv_sphere,
};
use regia_scene::Transform;
use regia_scene::level::{Level, LevelId, LevelLibrary, LoadMode, open_level};

/// Samples per side of the ground mesh: 129 vertices at 2 m is the bake's 256 m square.
const GRID: usize = 129;
/// Meters between ground vertices.
const SPACING: f32 = 2.0;

/// The id this game uses for the hills level.
const HILLS_LEVEL: LevelId = LevelId(Guid::from_u128(0x6869_6c6c_0000_4000_8000_0000_0000_0001));

/// The game plugin the launcher runs.
pub struct Game;

impl Plugin for Game {
    fn build(&self, app: &mut App) {
        app.add_plugins(regia_scene::ScenePlugin)
            .add_systems(Startup, (load_hills_level, spawn_scene));
    }
}

/// The height of the `rolling-hills` bake scene at (`x`, `z`), meters.
fn hills_height(x: f32, z: f32) -> f32 {
    6.0 * (x * 0.045).sin() * (z * 0.037).cos() + 3.0 * (x * 0.11 + z * 0.07).sin()
}

/// The slope of `hills_height` along x and z, for vertex normals.
fn hills_slope(x: f32, z: f32) -> (f32, f32) {
    let w = x * 0.11 + z * 0.07;
    let dx = 6.0 * 0.045 * (x * 0.045).cos() * (z * 0.037).cos() + 3.0 * 0.11 * w.cos();
    let dz = -6.0 * 0.037 * (x * 0.045).sin() * (z * 0.037).sin() + 3.0 * 0.07 * w.cos();
    (dx, dz)
}

/// A grid mesh over the hills, centered on the origin.
fn hills_mesh() -> CpuMesh {
    let half = (GRID - 1) as f32 * SPACING * 0.5;
    let mut vertices = Vec::with_capacity(GRID * GRID);
    for j in 0..GRID {
        for i in 0..GRID {
            let (x, z) = (i as f32 * SPACING - half, j as f32 * SPACING - half);
            let (dx, dz) = hills_slope(x, z);
            let normal = Vec3::new(-dx, 1.0, -dz).normalize();
            vertices.push(LabVertex {
                position: [x, hills_height(x, z), z],
                normal: normal.to_array(),
                uv: [i as f32 / (GRID - 1) as f32, j as f32 / (GRID - 1) as f32],
                tangent: [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
                color: [1.0; 4],
                joints: [0; 4],
                weights: [0.0; 4],
            });
        }
    }
    let mut indices = Vec::with_capacity((GRID - 1) * (GRID - 1) * 6);
    for j in 0..GRID - 1 {
        for i in 0..GRID - 1 {
            let a = (j * GRID + i) as u32;
            let b = a + 1;
            let d = a + GRID as u32;
            let c = d + 1;
            // Counter-clockwise seen from above (+Y): a -> d -> c, a -> c -> b.
            indices.extend_from_slice(&[a, d, c, a, c, b]);
        }
    }
    CpuMesh { vertices, indices }
}

/// Reads `levels/hills.level.ron` and opens it. The level names the bake; the framework installs it.
pub fn load_hills_level(world: &mut World) {
    let Ok(path) = VfsPath::parse("assets://levels/hills.level.ron") else {
        return;
    };
    let bytes = match world.resource::<Vfs>().read_sync(&path) {
        Ok(bytes) => bytes,
        Err(err) => {
            error!("cannot read the hills level: {err}");
            return;
        }
    };
    let level = match Level::from_ron_str(HILLS_LEVEL, &String::from_utf8_lossy(&bytes)) {
        Ok(level) => level,
        Err(err) => {
            error!("the hills level does not parse: {err}");
            return;
        }
    };
    world.get_resource_or_insert_with(LevelLibrary::new).insert(level);
    if let Err(err) = open_level(world, HILLS_LEVEL, LoadMode::Replace) {
        error!("cannot open the hills level: {err}");
    }
}

/// Camera, sun, hills and the bake's boulder.
fn spawn_scene(mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Camera"),
        Transform {
            translation: Vec3::new(-30.0, 6.0, 30.0),
            // Yaw toward +X / -Z, pitch down a little.
            rotation: Quat::from_rotation_y(-0.785) * Quat::from_rotation_x(-0.2),
            ..Transform::default()
        },
        Camera::default(),
    ));

    // The bake's sun is `toward: (0.4, 0.6, 0.3)`, the direction *to* the sun. The light
    // travels the opposite way.
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Sun"),
        DirectionalLight {
            direction: [-0.4, -0.6, -0.3],
            color: [1.0, 0.96, 0.9],
            illuminance: 100_000.0,
            cast_shadows: true,
            static_shadow: false,
        },
    ));

    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Hills"),
        Transform::default(),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(hills_mesh()),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.35, 0.3, 0.26, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.9,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));

    // The bake's boulder: radius 4 m at (10, 2, -6), mostly below the hill.
    let (vertices, indices) = uv_sphere(4.0, 32, 16);
    commands.spawn((
        Name::new("Boulder"),
        Transform::from_translation(Vec3::new(10.0, 2.0, -6.0)),
        MeshRenderer::new(
            Arc::new(CpuMesh { vertices, indices }),
            Arc::new(CpuMaterial {
                base_color: [0.4, 0.4, 0.4, 1.0],
                roughness: 0.8,
                ..CpuMaterial::default()
            }),
        ),
    ));
}
```

Run the game. A missing or unreadable volume logs one warning and changes nothing: the frame keeps
its other indirect light, so a typo in the path costs you the bake, not the game.

## Step 5: prove the bake is in use

A screenshot that "looks lit" proves little. Ask the engine. With the game running:

```console
$ regia agent call level.get_baked_gi
```

The reply you want has `"source": "level"`, `"error": null`, and `probes` equal to the probe count
from the bake. `error_code` is `volume_not_found` when the file is not under `assets/` at that
path, and `volume_unreadable` when it is damaged or from another engine version (rebake). Then
check the renderer:

```console
$ regia agent call play.pause
$ regia agent call play.step '{"frames":2}'
$ regia agent call render.get_gi_mode
```

`baked.active` must be `true`, and `baked.error` `null`. `uses_bake` in the same reply says whether
the current look would use an installed volume at all: a chosen Balanced preset does not, so a
volume can be `installed` and still not `active`. Those are two different questions, and the second
is the one that matters.

## Step 6: compare

Capture a frame with the bake, remove it, step, capture again:

```console
$ regia agent call seeing.screenshot --out with-bake.png
$ regia agent call level.set_look '{"look":{"baked_gi":null}}'
$ regia agent call play.step '{"frames":2}'
$ regia agent call seeing.screenshot --out without-bake.png
```

Compare the two images. The baked frame has path-traced indirect light: shadowed slopes pick up
warm bounce from the sunlit ground and cool light from the sky, and the hollows under the boulder
are darker. The other frame falls back to the analytic or probe-based terms. Neither is "right"
in an absolute sense; the bake is the one that follows the reference tracer, at a lower runtime
cost. [Baked GI volumes](book/agents/baked-gi.md) has the per-preset table of what the bake replaces.

If the colors look wrong rather than merely different, the likeliest cause is the sky: the
built-in scene was baked under a *uniform* sky of fixed radiance, and the game renders a
procedural one. Scale the baked sky term with the level's settings (`settings: (sky_scale:
Some(0.8))` inside `baked_gi`) until it fits, or bake with a description whose sky matches your
look. A sun that moved more than 3 degrees from the baked one logs a warning once; it means the
bounce and shadows no longer agree, and a rebake is due.

## When to rebake

The volume is a snapshot. Rebake after you change: the terrain or any static mesh, a static
light's position or color, the sun's direction, or an interior. You do not rebake for changes to
light *levels*: the sun-bounce term follows the frame's sun intensity and the fill term follows its
sky-body fill, so exposure and brightness changes still apply. Moving objects are never in the
bake; give them capsule occluders if you want them to darken the light next to them.

## What you did, and where next

You inspected a bake with `--dry-run`, baked a volume, built a scene that matches it, attached it
to a level, confirmed through `level.get_baked_gi` and `render.get_gi_mode` that it is installed
*and* active, and compared with and without it. Next:

- [Baking GI from meshes](book/agents/baked-gi-bake.md): your own `.bake.ron` with static meshes,
  interiors and automatic detail bricks.
- [Baked GI from the level](book/agents/baked-gi-maps.md): the level fields, hot reload and the
  failure codes.
- [Lighting, shadows and GI](book/systems/lighting.md): where the bake sits among the other
  lighting terms.

# Tutorial: your first scene in the editor

This tutorial builds a small scene in the editor without writing code: a new project from a
template, a ground, two meshes, a sun and a lamp, a save, and a play-in-editor run. Each step
says what to do with the mouse and keyboard, and gives the agent call that does the same thing,
so an agent (or a CI job) can follow the page too.

The page is a test. `cargo test -p regia_editor --test book_tutorials` reads the `regia agent
call` lines below and runs them, in order, against a headless editor; a step the editor refuses
fails the test with this page's line number. If you change a step, run that test.

For the same scene written as code, see [Your first scene](book/tutorials/first-scene.md).

## Step 1: a new project from a template

In the editor: start it with no project (`regia editor`). The **Projects** window lists recent
projects and has a **New project** row: type `First Scene` in **Name**, the parent folder in
**Folder** (or **Browse…**), and press **Create blank project**. The editor writes the project
from the Blank template and opens its startup level, `assets/levels/main.level.ron`.

From a terminal, `regia new` writes the same files (the editor's `editor.new_project` agent
method does too):

```sh
regia new "First Scene" --template blank
cd first_scene
```

An agent then starts a headless editor on it and waits for its `ready` line
([Headless editor](book/agents/headless-editor.md)):

```text
regia editor --headless --project . > editor.out &
```

Every `regia agent call` below talks to that editor. In the windowed editor the same calls work
while you watch: the editor answers on the endpoint in `.regia/agent/endpoint.json`.

## Step 2: place a ground and two meshes

In the editor: **Create ▸ Shape ▸ Cuboid**, three times. Each shape appears at the point the
viewport camera orbits, selected, so the Inspector shows its parameters (the **Primitive**
section: shape, size, color, roughness). Press **W** in the viewport for the move gizmo (**E**
rotate, **R** scale; hold **Ctrl** to snap), drag the handles, and press **F** to frame the
selection. Rename an entity from its Outliner row: right-click ▸ **Rename…**. Flatten the first
one into a ground (scale 20, 0.2, 20), stand the third up as a pillar.

The agent does the same with the editor's undoable methods: `editor.spawn` makes a named entity
with a transform (one undo step, and the guid a saved level needs), `editor.add_component` adds
the `Primitive` shape (a 1 m box by default) and `editor.set_property` changes one field:

```sh
GROUND=$(regia agent call editor.spawn '{"name":"Ground","translation":[0,-0.1,0],"scale":[20,0.2,20]}' | jq .entity)
regia agent call editor.add_component '{"entity":'"$GROUND"',"component":"Primitive"}'
CRATE=$(regia agent call editor.spawn '{"name":"Crate","translation":[0,0.5,0]}' | jq .entity)
regia agent call editor.add_component '{"entity":'"$CRATE"',"component":"Primitive"}'
regia agent call editor.set_property '{"entity":'"$CRATE"',"component":"Primitive","path":"color","value":[0.8,0.45,0.2,1.0]}'
PILLAR=$(regia agent call editor.spawn '{"name":"Pillar","translation":[2,1,0],"scale":[0.5,2,0.5]}' | jq .entity)
regia agent call editor.add_component '{"entity":'"$PILLAR"',"component":"Primitive"}'
```

Moving the crate with the gizmo is one undoable edit; `editor.set_transform` is the same edit,
and **Ctrl+Z** (`editor.undo`) takes it back:

```sh
regia agent call editor.set_transform '{"entity":'"$CRATE"',"translation":[0,0.5,-1.5]}'
regia agent call editor.undo
regia agent call editor.redo
```

## Step 3: light it

In the editor, create an empty entity (**File ▸ Create entity**, or the agent's
`editor.spawn`), then in the Inspector press **Add component** and pick `DirectionalLight` for a
sun or `PointLight` for a lamp. Its fields (direction, color, illuminance in lux, intensity in
lumens, radius) are edited in place.

```sh
SUN=$(regia agent call editor.spawn '{"name":"Sun"}' | jq .entity)
regia agent call editor.add_component '{"entity":'"$SUN"',"component":"DirectionalLight"}'
regia agent call editor.set_property '{"entity":'"$SUN"',"component":"DirectionalLight","path":"illuminance","value":100000.0}'
LAMP=$(regia agent call editor.spawn '{"name":"Lamp","translation":[-2,2,1]}' | jq .entity)
regia agent call editor.add_component '{"entity":'"$LAMP"',"component":"PointLight"}'
regia agent call editor.set_property '{"entity":'"$LAMP"',"component":"PointLight","path":"color","value":[1.0,0.8,0.6]}'
regia agent call scene.query_entities '{"name":"Lamp"}'
```

## Step 4: save

**File ▸ Save level** (or **Save level as…**) writes the open level. The agent call saves it to its last path (here
`assets/levels/main.level.ron`); pass `path` to save somewhere else:

```sh
regia agent call editor.save_level '{}'
```

## Step 5: play in the editor

Press **▶ Play** on the toolbar (or **Alt+P**). The editor plays a copy of the level; the edit
world is not touched, so whatever happens in play is gone when you stop. **⏸ Pause** pauses,
**⏭ Step** advances one frame while paused, and **⏹ Stop** (or **Escape**) ends the session.
**F8** possesses the game camera and gives it back.

The agent asks for the same, and waits on `editor.play_state` (each call is answered on an
editor frame, so this is a wait on the editor, not on a clock):

```sh
regia agent call editor.play
regia agent call editor.play_state  # until /mode == "playing"
regia agent call editor.pause
regia agent call editor.play_state  # until /mode == "paused"
regia agent call editor.step '{"frames":10}'
regia agent call editor.stop
regia agent call editor.play_state  # until /mode == "stopped"
```

A `# until P == V` comment means: repeat the call until the answer's value at the JSON pointer
`P` is `V`, so it follows only read calls (the page's test refuses an `# until` on a call the
schema marks mutating). A `# expect` comment checks the answer once and may follow any call.

## What you built, and where next

A level with a ground, a crate, a pillar, a sun and a lamp, saved, and played once. Next:

- [Your first material](book/tutorials/editor-first-material.md): a material graph for those shapes.
- [Package a build](book/tutorials/package-a-build.md): turn the project into something you can hand out.
- The [editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/index.md) lists every panel's actions,
  shortcuts and agent methods.

<!-- source: book/tutorials/editor-first-material.md -->
# Tutorial: your first material graph

This tutorial builds a material in the editor's **Material Graph** panel: a tint parameter
multiplied by the mesh's vertex color, wired to the surface's base color, compiled, undone and
redone, and saved as a `.matgraph.ron`. Each step gives the mouse-and-keyboard way and the agent
call that does the same thing.

The page is a test. `cargo test -p regia_editor --test book_tutorials` reads the `regia agent
call` lines below and runs them, in order, against a headless editor; a step the editor refuses,
or a `# expect` that does not hold, fails the test with this page's line number.

The graph format and every node kind are on [Material graphs](book/agents/material-graph.md); the
panel's whole agent surface is on [Material graph editor](book/agents/material-graph-editor.md).

## Step 1: a project and an empty graph

Make a project as in [your first scene](book/tutorials/editor-first-scene.md#step-1-a-new-project-from-a-template),
and start a headless editor on it if an agent is driving:

```sh
regia new "First Material" --template blank
cd first_material
```

```text
regia editor --headless --project . > editor.out &
```

In the editor, open the **Material Graph** tab (it is in the default layout; **View ▸ Reset
layout** brings back a closed tab) and press **New** for an empty, unsaved graph; type
`assets/materials/painted_metal.matgraph.ron` in the path field next to it, which **Save as**
uses at the end. The agent call creates the graph with its path in one step:

```sh
regia agent call editor.matgraph_open '{"create":true,"path":"assets/materials/painted_metal.matgraph.ron"}'
```

## Step 2: a parameter and three nodes

A parameter is a value a material instance can override without recompiling. In the panel's
side column open **Parameters**, write the list as RON
(`[(name: "tint", value: Color((0.8, 0.2, 0.1)))]`, the form of the `.matgraph.ron` file) and
press **Apply**. Then right-click the canvas ▸ **Add
node** for a `Param` node reading `tint`, a `VertexColor` node, a `Swizzle` that keeps its
`rgb`, and a `Mul`. Adding a node has no keyboard shortcut; every node edit is one step on the
editor's undo stack.

```sh
regia agent call editor.matgraph_edit '{"op":"params","params":[{"name":"tint","value":{"Color":[0.8,0.2,0.1]}}]}'
regia agent call editor.matgraph_edit '{"op":"add","name":"tint_value","node":"Param(\"tint\")"}'
regia agent call editor.matgraph_edit '{"op":"add","name":"vcol","kind":"VertexColor"}'
regia agent call editor.matgraph_edit '{"op":"add","name":"rgb","node":{"Swizzle":{"input":"vcol","channels":"rgb"}}}'
regia agent call editor.matgraph_edit '{"op":"add","name":"base","kind":"Mul"}'
```

## Step 3: wire it

Drag from an output pin to an input pin to connect them: `tint_value` into the `a` slot of
`base`, `rgb` into `b`. Then wire `base` into the **Surface** box's `base_color` (or right-click
`base` ▸ **Drive output**). A slot left unwired is a compile error shown on its node.

```sh
regia agent call editor.matgraph_edit '{"op":"connect","from":"tint_value","to":"base","slot":"a"}'
regia agent call editor.matgraph_edit '{"op":"connect","from":"rgb","to":"base","slot":"b"}'
regia agent call editor.matgraph_edit '{"op":"output","slot":"base_color","from":"base"}'
regia agent call editor.matgraph_state  # expect /ok == true
```

## Step 4: compile, undo, redo

The panel compiles after every edit and shows **compiles** or the error count in its header.
`editor.matgraph_compile` runs the full check (the generated shader code is composed into the
forward pass) and answers the shader key and the parameters' slots:

```sh
regia agent call editor.matgraph_compile  # expect /ok == true
```

**Ctrl+Z** undoes the last edit (the base-color wire) and **Ctrl+Shift+Z** (or **Ctrl+Y**)
redoes it, in the panel as everywhere in the editor:

```sh
regia agent call editor.undo
regia agent call editor.matgraph_state  # expect /outputs/base_color == null
regia agent call editor.redo
regia agent call editor.matgraph_state  # expect /outputs/base_color == "base"
```

## Step 5: preview and save

The side column's preview sphere shows the material lit by the panel's light. It needs a GPU;
an agent on a machine with one reads the same image (base64 PNG and its mean color):

```text
regia agent call editor.matgraph_preview '{"width":256,"height":256}'
```

Press **Save as** (the path field's path; later saves use **Save**; the agent's
`editor.matgraph_save`). The graph is written next to a
`.matgraph.layout.ron` sidecar that holds only the canvas positions:

```sh
regia agent call editor.matgraph_save  # expect /ok == true
```

## What you built, and where next

`assets/materials/painted_metal.matgraph.ron`, a compiled graph with one parameter. Next:

- Material instances (`.matinst.ron`) override `tint` per object without a new shader:
  [Material graph editor § Tabs](book/agents/material-graph-editor.md#tabs).
- [Package a build](book/tutorials/package-a-build.md) ships the project with its materials.
- The [Material graph page of the editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/material-graph.md)
  lists every action of the panel.

# Tutorial: package a build

This tutorial takes a project from the editor to a package you can hand out: set the version in
**Project Settings**, check the assets, save, close the editor, and let `regia package` show
what it would ship before it builds anything. The full reference is [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md).

The page is a test, in two halves. `cargo test -p regia_editor --test book_tutorials` runs the
`regia agent call` lines against a headless editor; `cargo test -p regia_cli --test
book_tutorials` runs the `regia new`, `cd` and `regia package` lines through the real `regia`
binary. A step that fails names this page's line.

## Step 1: a project with something in it

```sh
regia new "Ship It" --template blank
cd ship_it
```

```text
regia editor --headless --project . > editor.out &
```

In the editor, place a shape (**Create ▸ Shape ▸ Cuboid**) and save the level
(**File ▸ Save level**):

```sh
regia agent call scene.spawn_primitive '{"shape":"cuboid","name":"Crate","transform":{"translation":[0,0.5,0]}}'
regia agent call editor.save_level '{}'
```

## Step 2: name and version

Open **Edit ▸ Project settings…** (the **Project Settings** tab). The top rows are the project's
**Name**, **Id**, **Version**, **Build number** and **Organization**, and **Default level:**
picks the level a package starts on. Change **Version** to `1.0.0` and **Build number** to `2`,
then press **Save**: the panel writes `Regia.toml` and keeps every key it does not show.

`editor.project_settings_set` is the same edit and the same validation (nothing is written when
a value is refused); `editor.project_settings_get` reads what the panel shows:

```sh
regia agent call editor.project_settings_get  # expect /project/name == "Ship It"
regia agent call editor.project_settings_set '{"project":{"version":"1.0.0","build_number":2}}'
regia agent call editor.project_settings_get  # expect /project/version == "1.0.0"
```

The **Platforms and quality presets** rows of the same panel turn targets on and off and pick
each one's render profile (`editor.project_settings_set` with `platforms`).

## Step 3: check the assets

In the **Content** tab, **Validate project** runs the asset validators (missing references,
naming rules, texture sizes, duplicate ids, orphans, triangle budgets) over the cooked asset
registry and lists each finding. A shipping package refuses some of the same problems, so fix
them here. The agent lists the validators and their limits:

```sh
regia agent call editor.asset_validate '{"list":true}'
```

and, once the project has been cooked (step 5's dry run cooks it, as does `regia cook`), runs
them over the registry. Before the first cook that call answers `registry_not_loaded`:

```text
regia agent call editor.asset_validate '{"source":"registry"}'
```

## Step 4: close the editor

Packaging reads the files on disk, so save and close the editor first. `agent.shutdown` saves
every document with edits and ends a headless editor with exit status 0:

```sh
regia agent call agent.shutdown
```

## Step 5: see what would ship

`--dry-run` cooks the content if it is missing or stale, prints the size report of the files the
profile ships, and stops: no compile, no package. It is the cheap check before a long build:

```sh
regia package --platform linux --dry-run
```

## Step 6: build the package

The real build compiles the game for the platform and writes the package under
`dist/<platform>/` (the test does not run these: they compile the whole game):

```text
regia package --platform linux                       # a dev package (tar, per [platforms.linux] formats)
regia package --platform linux --profile shipping    # no agent server, no dev tools
regia package --platform windows                     # a zip; build it on Windows or with the cross tools
regia package --platform android                     # an APK; needs the Android SDK and NDK (regia doctor)
regia package --platform linux --steam               # adds the Steam depot layout and steamcmd files
```

[Packaging § Smoke-test a package](book/user-guide/packaging.md#smoke-test-a-package-before-shipping)
starts the package and checks it through the agent protocol before you ship it.

## What you did, and where next

A versioned project, checked and dry-run packaged. Next:

- [Build profiles](book/user-guide/packaging.md#build-profiles) ship one level's content only.
- [Steam](book/user-guide/steam.md) and [Steam Deck](book/user-guide/steam-deck.md) for a store build.
- The [Project Settings page of the editor guide](book/user-guide/editor-guide/project-settings.md).
