# Driving a running Regia Engine app (agent protocol 0.2)

Every dev build of a Regia Engine game (feature `agent`, on by default) runs a small server that lets an AI
agent — or a script — inspect and drive it while it runs. This page is written for agents.

## Connecting

The app writes `<project>/.regia/agent/endpoint.json` when it starts:

```json
{ "url": "ws://127.0.0.1:41234", "pid": 4242, "protocol": "0.2", "token_file": ".../token", "app": "hello_window" }
```

- Connect with a WebSocket to `url` (it must be `ws://127.0.0.1:<port>`), sending
  `Authorization: Bearer <contents of the token file next to endpoint.json>` in the
  handshake. The client always reads `<dir>/token`; the `token_file` field is informational and never followed.
  `endpoint.json` is mode 0600 on Unix; on Windows both files get a DACL that names only the
  current account, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` (no inherited entries; ADR-5489). Connections without the token, or with a browser `Origin` header, are refused.
- Send JSON-RPC 2.0 requests as text messages; each gets one response with the same `id`.
  A response of 64 KiB or more (a screenshot) arrives as one text message split into 64 KiB
  frames (RFC 6455 § 5.4 continuation frames, ADR-8848); WebSocket libraries reassemble it.
- Easiest: `regia agent call <method> '<params json>' --project <dir>`, or the MCP server
  `regia mcp --project <dir>` (one MCP tool per protocol method). Attached to an editor
  (or with `--headless`), the tool list also holds the editor's own methods that have a tool
  name, read from the editor's live `agent.schema` each time the client lists tools:
  `save_level`, `undo`, `redo`, `select`, `focus`, `import`, `create_asset`, `create_script`,
  `play`, `stop` and the rest. Where an editor method shares a tool name with a runtime method
  (`pause`, `step`, `set_property`, `list_assets`), the tool calls the runtime method; call
  the editor one by its method name (`editor.pause`) with `regia agent call` (ADR-5628).
- The file disappears when the app exits. If it is missing, start the app (`cargo run -p hello_window`).
- Tell the app who you are: `agent.hello` with `client` and `model` — both land in the audit log and
  on every provenance record of your edits.

Calls take effect at the next frame boundary (usually within 16 ms). If the window is on a hidden
workspace or minimized, the app keeps running at 10 frames per second, so calls still work.

## The surface

The schema is the source of truth: `agent.schema` returns every method with its parameters, result
shape, whether it mutates, and which permission it needs. The MCP tool list is generated from the
same table. Topic pages (also bundled as `agent.guide`): **[scene](book/agents/scene.md)** —
**[testing](book/agents/testing.md)** — **[seeing](book/agents/seeing.md)** — **[assets](book/agents/assets.md)** —
**[events](book/agents/events.md)** — **[gameplay](book/agents/gameplay.md)** — **[framework](book/agents/framework.md)** —
**[physics](book/agents/physics.md)** — **[safety](book/agents/safety.md)** — **[renderer](book/agents/renderer.md)** —
**[high-end lighting](book/agents/high-end-lighting.md)**.

| Area | Methods (MCP tool) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Discovery | `agent.hello` (`hello`), `agent.guide` (`guide`), `agent.schema` (`schema`), `agent.changes` (`changes`), `project.info` (`project_info`), `types.list` (`list_types`), `types.describe` (`describe_type`), `resources.list` (`list_resources`), `errors.explain` (`explain_error`) | What exists and what it means: reflected types with JSON Schema + docs, resources, your own change history, long-form error help |
| Scene | `scene.query_entities` (`query_entities`), `scene.get_entity` (`get_entity`), `scene.set_property` (`set_property`), `scene.spawn` (`spawn`), `scene.spawn_primitive` (`spawn_primitive`), `scene.despawn` (`despawn`), `scene.duplicate` (`duplicate`), `scene.reparent` (`reparent`), `scene.add_component` (`add_component`), `scene.remove_component` (`remove_component`), `scene.apply_edits` (`apply_edits`), `scene.serialize` (`serialize_scene`) | Find, inspect and edit entities through reflection |
| Assets | `assets.list` (`list_assets`), `assets.describe` (`describe_asset`), `assets.load` (`load_asset`), `assets.reload` (`reload_asset`), `assets.skin_check` (`skin_check`), `assets.status` (`asset_status`), `assets.load_progress` (`load_progress`), `assets.watch_status` (`asset_watch_status`), `assets.texture_memory` (`texture_memory`) | The running AssetServer's manifest and load state; load-set residency; live reload status; texture memory against the budget |
| Seeing | `seeing.screenshot` (`screenshot`), `seeing.capture_sequence` (`capture_sequence`), `seeing.contact_sheet` (`contact_sheet`), `seeing.compare_images` (`compare_images`), `seeing.reference_trace` (`reference_trace`), `seeing.compare` (`compare`), `seeing.pick_entity` (`pick_entity`), `seeing.memory_report` (`memory_report`) | Screenshots, strips, orbit sheets, SSIM + diff, reference traces and FLIP scoring, GPU memory by category |
| Render | `render.boot_timeline` (`boot_timeline`), `render.pipeline_warm` (`pipeline_warm`), `render.memory_budget` (`memory_budget`), `render.camera_cut` (`render_camera_cut`), `render.out_start` / `render.out_progress` / `render.out_cancel` (`render_out_start` / `render_out_progress` / `render_out_cancel`), `render.out_job` (`render_out_job`), `render.sequence` (`render_sequence`), `camera.set_path` (`camera_set_path`), `camera.raycast` (`camera_raycast`) | Boot timeline, pipeline warm-up per tier and the persistent cache, memory budget and preload admission, camera cuts ([camera cuts](book/agents/camera-cuts.md)), offline fixed-dt render-out ([render-out](book/agents/render-out.md)), render jobs from a shot list or sequence ([render jobs](book/agents/render-jobs.md)), camera paths, shot sequences and screen raycasts ([camera paths](book/agents/camera-paths.md)) |
| Play & test | `play.pause` / `play.resume` (`pause` / `resume`), `play.step` (`step`), `play.set_time_scale` (`set_time_scale`), `play.inject_input` (`inject_input`), `play.wait_until` (`wait_until`), `play.expect` (`expect`), `play.get_diagnostics` (`get_diagnostics`) | Deterministic play, input injection, predicates and assertions |
| Logs & events | `logs.read` (`read_logs`), `events.list` (`list_events`), `events.read` (`read_events`), `diagnostics.crash_reports` (`crash_reports`), `feedback.capture` (`feedback_capture`), `feedback.list` (`feedback_list`), `telemetry.get_last_summary` (`telemetry_get_last_summary`), `telemetry.live` (`telemetry_live`) | Log ring and tapped engine messages, both with cursors, the local crash reports, feedback bundles, the last telemetry summary and the newest frame's live signals ([telemetry](book/agents/telemetry.md)) |
| Framework | `scripts.list`, `scripts.get`, `camera.get`, `camera.set_mode`, `settings.get`, `settings.set`, `level.get_look`, `level.set_look`, `sim.counters`, `sim.check_framerate_independence` | Presentation scripts, camera rigs, live settings, DO27 sim-bridge counters |
| Gameplay | `players.list` (`players_list`), `players.get` (`players_get`), `scene.possess` (`possess`), `save.save` (`save_game`), `save.load` (`load_game`), `save.list_slots` (`list_save_slots`) | Who is playing, what they possess, save slots and round trips — see [gameplay](book/agents/gameplay.md) |
| Terrain | `terrain.scatter` (`terrain_scatter`), `terrain.set_scatter` (`terrain_set_scatter`), `terrain.stroke` (`terrain_stroke`) | Rock / prop scatter counts and toggles — see [terrain scatter](book/agents/terrain-scatter.md); sculpt and paint brush strokes — see [terrain editing](book/agents/terrain-editing.md) |
| Renderer | `render.set_contact_shadows` (`render_set_contact_shadows`), `render.set_reflection_occlusion` (`render_set_reflection_occlusion`), `render.set_near_sun_shadow` (`render_set_near_sun_shadow`) | Screen-space contact shadows on/off — see [contact shadows](book/agents/contact-shadows.md); reflection occlusion on/off — see [reflection occlusion](book/agents/reflection-occlusion.md); near sun tile edge — see [near sun shadow](book/agents/near-sun-shadow.md) |

MCP resources (§ 3.8): `regia://project`, `regia://scene/current` (RON), `regia://types/{path}`,
`regia://assets/{id}`, `regia://logs/recent`, `regia://guide/{topic}`,
`regia://protocol/schema.json`. URIs with the scheme from before the rename still resolve, to the
same calls, for one release (see [Renaming to Regia Engine](book/user-guide/rename-regia.md)).

Entity ids are numbers; take them from `scene.query_entities`. Component and type names are the short
names `get_entity` lists (`Window`, `Transform`, `Name`). Values use the JSON shape `get_entity`
shows — note that maths types (glam `Vec3`) serialize as **arrays** (`[x, y, z]`), so `set_property`
on `translation` takes `[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]`, while *paths* use reflection field names
(`"translation.y"`).

## Discovery calls

Each line is `regia agent call <method> '<params json>' --project <dir>`; the params are the JSON-RPC `params`.

```text
agent.hello {"client": "my-script", "model": "my-model"}
agent.guide {}                                   # list topics
agent.guide {"topic": "scene"}                   # one topic's text
agent.schema {}                                  # every method, params, result, permission
project.info {}                                  # engine, app, project name and id, subsystems
types.list {"filter": "transform", "component": true}   # reflected components whose name contains "transform"
types.list {"resource": true}                    # reflected resources only
types.describe {"type": "Transform"}             # JSON Schema, docs and an example value
resources.list {}                                # resources, reflected or not
errors.explain {"code": "F0012"}                 # long-form meaning and fix
```

`types.describe` schemas describe the serialized value. Data-carrying enum variants use one tag property:
`{"Named":"a"}` or `{"Rect":{"rect":[0,0,1,1]}}`; unit variants are strings such as `"Earth"`. Tuple payloads
and tuple structs use ordered arrays; newtype variants and one-field tuple structs without serialization
skips use their inner value. Fields skipped during tuple serialization are omitted from the array. `Vec3` value schemas use three numeric array elements, as in the
wire values above; reflection property paths still use field names such as `translation.y`.

`types.describe` accepts a full type path or a unique short path. An unknown path is `F0003`
(`no reflected type …`). A short path shared by two registered types is `F0002` with `data.reason`
`ambiguous_short_type_path`; the message says `ambiguous short type path` and does not say the type
is not registered. `types.list` shows the full path that selects one type.

## Errors

Errors are JSON-RPC errors with a stable Regia Engine code in `error.data.code` and a fix in
`error.data.hint`; `errors.explain` returns the long form.

| Code | JSON-RPC | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| F0001 | -32603 | Internal error — read `logs.read` with `level: "warn"` |
| F0002 | -32602 | Missing or wrong parameters. A present optional parameter of the wrong JSON type (for example `"count": "5"` where an integer is wanted) names itself: `error.data.param` is the parameter and `error.data.expected` the type (`a string`, `a boolean`, `a non-negative integer`, `an integer`, `a number`, `an array`, `an object`). `null` still means "not given". |
| F0003 | -32001 | Entity, component, type or field not found |
| F0004 / F0005 | -32600 / -32700 | Not a text message, `jsonrpc` is not `"2.0"`, or the id is not a string, number or null / not valid JSON |
| F0006 | -32002 | No answer in time (pass `params.timeout_ms` for long operations; at most 24 hours, longer values are capped). Also answered when the app did not take the request off its queue within that time (a paused app). The request is then not run when the app drains it later (the audit log records it as `expired`), so retrying is safe |
| F0007 | -32003 | More mutating calls in a second than the project allows (default 50) |
| F0008 | -32601 | Unknown method (the message lists the available ones) |
| F0009 | -32600 | A `play.step` is already running |
| F0010 / F0011 | -32004 | Screenshot target or renderer not available |
| F0012 | -32005 | Permission denied — see [safety](book/agents/safety.md) |
| F0013 | -32004 | The engine feature the method needs is not present (the hint names it) |
| F0014 | -32602 | A `wait_until`/`expect` condition is malformed |
| F0015 | -32004 | A multi-frame capture produced no frames |
| F0016 | -32001 | The asset server is not running or the asset is unknown |
| F0017 | -32600 | A `play.hitch_report` is already running |
| F0018 | -32600 | A render-out is running (a second start, or a `play.*` clock control) |
| F0019 | -32004 | The movie format needs `ffmpeg` and none is on `PATH` |
| `too_many_pending` | -32600 | A deferred method's pending list is full (64 `play.wait_until`, 8 multi-frame captures, 2 running `seeing.reference_trace` jobs) |
| `request_too_large` | -32600 | The request would take more than 128 MiB once parsed (32 bytes per JSON value plus every string's bytes); refused before it is built, with a null id |

The UI methods also answer lowercase codes (`unknown_entity`, `not_a_list`, `bad_ease`, ...); each is listed
on its method's page and in `agent.schema`, and `errors.explain` knows every one. A mistyped method name answers
`F0008` with `data.suggestion`, the closest known name, when one is near.

## Current limits

- Screenshots cover the window, mesh-asset preview and `offscreen` targets (default 256×144; see `seeing.md`); camera-entity targets, view modes,
  overlays and pixel picking need renderer support that this build does not expose (they answer
  `F0013` rather than pretending).
- Importing, creating, editing and deleting asset **files** belongs to the editor/pipeline surface;
  the runtime serves the manifest and load state of the running app.
- No runtime undo, staged review queue or `select`/`frame`/`save_level` yet — those are editor-side.
- Android: the server listens inside the device; reach it with `adb forward tcp:<port> tcp:<port>` and read
  the endpoint with `adb shell run-as <package> cat files/agent/endpoint.json`.

## Limits (ADR-340)

At most 16 connections are open at once and requests queue in a bounded inbox; WebSocket messages over 32 MiB are
refused. A connection has 10 s to finish the WebSocket handshake (a silent socket gives its slot back), and at most 8 of
its notifications (requests without `id`) wait for the engine at once; past that it reads the next frame once the oldest
is handled. The audit log keeps at most 128 bytes of a method name and 256 bytes of the `agent.hello` `client` and
`model` (ADR-1769). The mutating-call rate limit is a sliding one-second window. A sequence holds at most 256 shots and 4096
keys per track; `render.out_start` takes at most 4096 `cuts`; `seeing.compare_images` takes PNGs of 1..=4096 pixels a
side. `replay.load` reads regular files only, at most 512 MiB, under the
allowed roots of `render.out_start` (as do `demo.inspect` and `demo.seek_plan`). Errors show project-relative paths, never the host's
absolute ones.

### Parse budget (ADR-2306)

A message under the 32 MiB cap can still parse into far more memory: `[0,0,0,...]` is two bytes of text per
32-byte JSON value. The server counts what the parse builds (32 bytes per value, the bytes of every string and key,
32 more per object entry) and stops at 128 MiB, before the rest is built. Such a request answers `request_too_large`
(JSON-RPC -32600) with a null id; the connection stays open. The largest array a method contract allows (one
million numbers) takes about 32 MiB. Split anything bigger into several calls.

```text
errors.explain {"code": "request_too_large"}     # the long form and the fix
```

### Round 2 (ADR-345)

`seeing.reference_trace` and `seeing.compare` write files, so they need the `edit_scene` permission, count against
the mutating-call rate limit, and confine `out_dir`, `a`, `b` and `map_png` to the same roots as `render.out_start`
(project root, system temp dir and `output_roots` in `.regia/agent.toml`; no `..`, no symlink out).
`replay.step` advances at most 36 000 ticks per call (`clamped: true` when it cut `ticks`) and returns at most 1000
events (`events_total`, `events_truncated`). `moments.list` pages without building the full match list.

### Method contracts (ADR-1034)

Every method has a contract, published by `agent.schema` next to its params (`agent.schema { method }` returns
one entry) and printed in the [method reference](book/reference/agent-methods.md):

- `example`: a typical call's params, valid against the schema.
- `errors`: every `data.code` the method can answer with besides the universal ones (`F0001`, `F0002`,
  `F0004`, `F0007`, `F0012`).
- `limits`: ranges, item counts and byte lengths the dispatcher checks before the handler runs. A range on an
  array param (a position, a polyline) applies to every number in it. A refused call answers `F0002` with the
  limit in `data.limit` (`{ param, kind, min, max }`) and costs no rate budget.
- `cost`: `"light"` or `"heavy"`. Heavy calls (whole-world walks, image encode or decode, multi-frame captures,
  replay loads and steps) also count against `heavy_rate_limit_per_second` in `.regia/agent.toml`
  (default 60, one a frame at 60 fps), read-only or not.

`params` must be a JSON object (or absent). An array or string param with no limit of its own holds at most
65 536 items or 1 MiB (`seeing.compare_images` PNGs may be 32 MiB, RON texts 16 MiB). The protocol-wide caps are in `agent.schema`'s top-level `limits`.

### Permission classes (ADR-3285)

Every method needs one permission class (`agent.schema` names it; `.regia/agent.toml` grants them):
`read`, `edit_scene`, `play`, `assets`, `tools`, `build`, `review`. `read_only = true` allows `read` alone.

**The rule for `read`:** a `read` method takes no output path, writes no file and changes no state another call
can observe. A method that does any of these needs the class of what it does and is `mutating` (rate-limited):

- it takes an output path (`out_dir`, `out`, `output_*`, `dest*`, `write`, `save`) or writes a file at all;
- it has a switch (`enable`, `detach`, `clear`, `log`, ...) or an `action` that starts, stops, attaches or resets
  something;
- its name says it changes something (`set_*`, `start`, `stop`, `reset`, `clear`, ...).

Switches beside the renderer's other toggles and writers of project files take `edit_scene` (their changes are
recorded in `agent.changes`); recorders and file writers that a polling client drives take `play`. Answering with
an image or a computed value is still `read` (`seeing.capture_sequence`, `xr.capture_eye`), and so is reading a log. The `security_wave2`
test of `regia_agent` runs this rule over the agent schema, so a new method that breaks it fails the build.
Editor methods are not in that schema. `regia_editor` checks the ones that change a viewport registry, the
editor selection or a panel another call reads (`state_changing_editor_methods_are_not_read`).

The name check has two named exceptions, each for one word of one method whose handler borrows the world
immutably: `spawn` in `vfx.spawn_probe` (it simulates a scratch instance, ADR-4760) and `record` in
`sequence.record_state` (the take recorder whose state it reads, ADR-5957). Every other check (output paths,
switches, writes, `mutating`) still runs on both, and any other method with those words is still refused.

Methods moved out of `read` by this rule:

| Method | Was | Now | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `audio.loopgen_render` | `read` | `play`, mutating | `wav: true` writes a WAV into `out_dir` |
| `profiler.set_capture` | `read` | `edit_scene`, mutating | turns call-tree capture on or off |
| `project.describe` | `read` | `edit_scene`, mutating | `write: true` writes `project-map.md` and `.json` (`out_dir`) |
| `render.exposure_log` | `read` | `play`, mutating | `action` starts and stops a log |
| `pacing.trace` | `read` | `play`, mutating | `log` turns per-frame logging on or off; `clear` forgets rows |
| `procgen.set_debug` | `read` | `edit_scene`, mutating | turns the debug overlays on or off |
| `ai.bt_live` | `read` | `play`, mutating | the first call attaches a recorder; `detach` removes it |
| `voice_chat.stats` | `read` | `play`, mutating | `reset` zeroes the session counters |
| `viewer.render_still` | `read` | `play`, mutating | optional `path` writes a PNG (ADR-4760) |
| `looks.render_board` | `read` | `play`, mutating | optional `path` writes a PNG (ADR-4760) |
| `editor.viewport_instance_set` | `read` | `edit_scene`, mutating | writes the instance camera, layout and show flags |
| `editor.viewport_link` | `read` | `edit_scene`, mutating | joins or leaves a camera link group |
| `editor.viewport_instance_remove` | `read` | `edit_scene`, mutating | drops the viewport registry entry |
| `editor.tests_panel_open` | `read` | `edit_scene`, mutating | replaces the editor selection |
| `editor.agent_changes_select` | `read` | `edit_scene`, mutating | sets which change the panel shows |
| `editor.tests_panel_run` | `play`, not mutating | `play`, mutating | queues a play-in-editor run |

## JSON examples in the guide

`cargo xtask agent-examples` (also run by `book-check` and `cargo xtask preflight`) reads every `json` fence in
`book/agents/*.md`, `book/user-guide/agent-protocol.md` and the bundled `agent.guide` topics, so an example an
agent copies is a call that works. A statement in a fence is a JSON-RPC request (`{ "method": .., "params": .. }`),
`method.name { params }`, a bare params object (its method is the one named in backticks between the previous
heading and the fence whose params cover most of the object's keys, the nearest mention on a tie), or a response
after `→`. A request must name a method of the current schema, declare every param, give every required param and
match each declared kind (a number where the param's description says a lone number works, `true` where it names
`true` as a value); a response's top-level keys must be named in the method's `result`. `...` or `…` stands for
elided content (as an entry, a value or an element, also quoted: `"...": "..."`), and `//` comments and trailing
commas are accepted. A fence tagged `json,ignore`, or preceded by `<!-- not-a-request -->`, is
skipped and counted; so are `editor.*` calls, which are host handlers outside the runtime schema. Findings that
cannot be fixed (the page describes behavior the code lacks) go in `docs/ci/agent-examples.toml` with a reason:
a new finding fails, and so does a row with no finding.

## Stability

The surface above is ratcheted: `cargo xtask agent-snapshot` renders every method's name,
permission class, MCP tool name, `mutating` flag, cost class, dispatcher-enforced limits, params
schema (each param's kind, required flag and structured JSON Schema shape, when it has one),
result schema and documented error codes — plus the built-in extension methods and the universal
error codes — into the checked-in `docs/api-snapshots/agent-protocol.txt` and fails when the
tables in `regia_agent` differ from it. It reads the same public tables `agent-coverage` does, so
it runs in seconds and needs no renderer; it is a step of `cargo xtask preflight` and of CI.

Each diff is classified, and the classification is what a client built against the old surface feels:

- **Breaking**: a method or param removed, a param type or shape or the result schema changed, a
  new required param, a permission, MCP tool, `mutating` or cost class changed, a limit tightened,
  an error code removed or renamed.
- **Additive**: anything else — a new method, a new optional param, a new error code, a limit
  relaxed or removed.

A breaking change is accepted only when a release fragment this branch touches (`docs/releases/*.md`)
names the method under `## Upgrade`; an additive change needs a `## New` line naming it (the match
is token-bounded: a line naming `assets.load_progress` does not document `assets.load`). The check
fails until the snapshot is refreshed, and `--update` itself refuses to write a change no touched
fragment documents — a lane that changed the agent schema always ends with two pieces of
bookkeeping: the fragment line and `cargo xtask agent-snapshot --update` (commit the refreshed file
with the code). After merging several schema-changing lanes, an integration branch resolves the
snapshot mechanically the same way (`preflight` forwards its `--base` to the ratchet, so the
fragment diff uses the same merge-base as `--changed`). The failure message of
`cargo xtask agent-snapshot --check` names the method and the exact fix. The Rust API of the engine crates
is held the same way by `cargo xtask api-snapshot` (`docs/api-snapshots/README.md`).

<!-- source: book/agents/local-transport.md -->
# Local transport (Unix socket / named pipe)

The agent protocol serves its JSON-RPC 2.0 surface over **two transports at once** (specs/23
§ 2): the loopback WebSocket listener (`ws://127.0.0.1:<random port>`) and a **local
transport** — a Unix domain socket on Linux/macOS, a named pipe on Windows. Both carry exactly
the same messages; the local transport exists for tools that prefer a filesystem path over a
TCP port (shell scripts, editor integrations, a `curl`-style probe). There is no local
transport on Android: dev builds there reach the WebSocket listener through `adb forward`.

## Where it lives

A running app with the agent feature (ADR-014) binds, beside the WebSocket listener:

- **Linux/macOS:** `<project>/.regia/agent/agent.sock` — mode 0600 inside the 0700 agent
  directory, so only the owner can connect.
- **Windows:** the named pipe `\\.\pipe\regia-agent-<pid>-<serial>` (one name per server,
  so two servers in one process never share it), created with an owner-only DACL (the current
  user, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators`, protected from inheritance — the `regia_net`
  private-file scheme, ADR-4828) as the **first instance** of its name: if another process
  already created that name, the start fails and the app keeps only its WebSocket listener
  (ADR-5878).

The address is advertised in `<project>/.regia/agent/socket`, next to `endpoint.json`, in the
same owner-only write. Cleanup only ever removes what is this app's own (ADR-5878):

- At exit the `socket` file is removed only while it names a listener this process still
  serves; another app's advertisement stays.
- Dropping the server removes the Unix socket file only while the path still holds *its*
  socket (same device and inode); a successor's socket is left alone.
- At start, a socket file nothing listens on (a crashed run's: a connect is refused) is
  replaced. A socket another app still serves is **never** unlinked: the start fails with
  `AddrInUse`, that second app runs on its WebSocket URL only, and clients reach it through
  the WebSocket fallback below. A symlink or any non-socket at the path is refused, never
  followed.
- A project path long enough that `.regia/agent/agent.sock` exceeds the platform's socket
  path limit (107 bytes on Linux, 103 on macOS) binds the socket in the account's private
  runtime directory instead (ADR-7335): `$TMPDIR/regia-agent-<key>/agent.sock` on macOS,
  `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/regia-agent-<key>/agent.sock` on Linux, where `<key>` is a hash of the agent
  directory's path (the same path on every start of that project). The directory is created
  0700, and only inside a base directory no other account can write into; the `socket` file
  advertises that address, so clients need nothing new. Without such a base directory (Linux
  with no `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`), or when even that path is too long, the app logs
  `local transport not started` and serves WebSocket only.

## The wire (ADR-5708)

Spec 23 names the transport but not its byte format; the framing is:

1. **Handshake frame:** the client's first frame must be exactly
   `{"bearer":"<token>"}` — the token from the owner-only `token` file, the counterpart of
   the WebSocket handshake's `Authorization` header — at most **256 bytes**, complete within
   **10 s in total** (each read gets only the time left, so a peer trickling bytes cannot hold
   a connection slot).
2. **Handshake answer (ADR-5878):** the server answers one frame,
   `{"authenticated":true}` — JSON-RPC frames follow — or, like a WebSocket 401,
   `{"authenticated":false}` and closes (a wrong token, a malformed, oversized or late
   handshake). The client therefore knows at connect time whether its token was taken.
3. **Frames:** a 4-byte little-endian length, then that many bytes of UTF-8 JSON — one JSON-RPC
   message per frame, the same text a WebSocket message holds. The per-frame cap is 16 MiB,
   as on the WebSocket path; an over-cap frame ends that connection only.
4. **Then the protocol is identical:** requests, notifications (bounded in flight), the
   request's own `timeout_ms` deadline, F0006 on a world that does not take the request in
   time, `render.out_progress` answers from the progress board during a render-out step, and a
   queued `render.out_cancel` or `agent.job_cancel` wakes a render-out waiting on a stalled
   output (ADR-2396).
5. **One shared budget, taken in turns (ADR-7454):** the app answers at most 64 requests a
   frame across both transports. The WebSocket inbox and the local inbox take turns, one
   answered request each, starting with the WebSocket inbox every frame, so a client that keeps
   the other transport's queue full slows a local call by at most a frame and never stops it.
   Requests the connection already answered (F0006, a progress-board poll) cost nothing and
   keep the turn.

## Connecting

`regia_agent::client::Client::connect_project` prefers the local transport when the
`socket` file is present and falls back to the WebSocket URL when the advertised listener is
dead **or refuses the token** (a stale `socket` file of a crashed app, or a live listener of
another app in the same project, does not lock clients out; a *malformed* advertisement is
refused outright — it must not choose where the bearer token goes). On Windows the client
opens the pipe for identification only (the server cannot impersonate it) and checks that the
pipe's server process is the one the name carries before it sends the token, so a pipe name
another account created first never receives it.
`Client::connect_local(address, token)` connects explicitly. `regia agent call` and
`regia mcp` go through `connect_project`, so they use the local transport automatically.

Read timeouts (`Client::set_read_timeout`) work on every local transport: the Unix socket's
receive timeout, and on Windows overlapped pipe reads bounded by a wait and cancelled on
timeout. The server's handshake deadline uses the same mechanism on both. A call the app
does not answer in time returns `ClientError::TimedOut`; the connection stays usable.

## Tests

`crates/regia_agent/tests/protocol_transport.rs` (`spec23_sec2_*`) covers the round trip, the
token refusal at connect, the WebSocket fallback past a refusing listener, the client read
timeout, the owner-only permissions, stale-file, live-socket and symlink handling, cleanup that
keeps a successor's socket and another app's advertisement, the oversized handshake and frame,
and the `connect_project` preference. The round trip, refusal, fallback, timeout and preference
tests also run on Windows against the pipe. `regia_agent::local` unit tests cover the frame
codec, the 256-byte handshake cap and the total handshake deadline (a scripted stream with a
fake clock); `regia_agent::endpoint` and `platform::pipe_rules` unit tests cover the pipe
names, the server-pid check, the connect-error classes of the accept loop, timeouts and
back-off on every host.

# Scene: finding, inspecting and editing entities

Find entities with `scene.query_entities`, read them with `scene.get_entity`, edit them with
`scene.set_property` (and friends). Several edits go through `scene.apply_edits` as one
transaction. Schemas of any component come from `types.describe`.

## Finding entities

```json
{ "name": "Rock*", "component": "Transform", "limit": 50 }
{ "component": "Transform", "near":   { "point": [0, 0, 0], "radius": 2.0 } }
{ "component": "Transform", "box":    { "min": [9, -1, -1], "max": [11, 1, 1] } }
```

`name` is a glob (`*` = any run of characters), `component` matches a short or full type name.
Spatial filters need `Transform`. Results list each entity's component short names and, when it has a
`Transform`, the translation. Take ids from here — they are stable for the entity's lifetime.

`kind` filters by [entity kind](book/agents/entity-kinds.md): a kind name, `"none"` (no kind) or `"unclassified"` (no kind and two
role families). Every row names its `kind` (or null), and `scene.get_entity` adds `kind`, `role` and `unclassified`.

## Reading and writing values

`scene.get_entity` returns every component's reflected value:

```json
{ "entity": 4294967296, "components": ["Transform"] }
→ { "components": { "Transform": { "type": "regia_scene::transform::Transform",
    "value": { "translation": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0], "rotation": [0, 0, 0, 1], "scale": [1, 1, 1] } } } }
```

Maths types serialize as arrays; other structs serialize as objects keyed by field name. Write with
`scene.set_property`, using the same shapes:

```json
{ "entity": 4294967296, "component": "Transform", "path": "translation", "value": [1.0, 5.0, -2.0] }
{ "entity": 4294967296, "component": "Transform", "path": "translation.y", "value": 5.0, "dry_run": true }
```

`path` is a dot path of **reflection field names** (it works even when the value serializes as an
array). `dry_run: true` returns `before`/`after` without applying. The response of a real edit
carries `before`, `after` and `applied: true`, and the change is stamped into `agent.changes`.

A component's field names, docs, ranges and units: `types.describe` with `{"type": "Transform"}`.

## Structural edits

```json
scene.spawn        { "name": "Agent Rock", "parent": 17, "components": { "Transform": {...} } }
scene.despawn      { "entity": 17 }
scene.duplicate    { "entity": 17, "parent": 3 }
scene.reparent     { "entity": 17, "parent": 3 }          // null detaches
scene.add_component    { "entity": 17, "component": "Marker", "value": {...} }   // value optional
scene.remove_component { "entity": 17, "component": "Marker" }
```

Only **reflected** components can be created, read or edited; `types.list` with `component: true`
lists them. `scene.despawn` is recursive: children still attached through `ChildOf` go with the
parent, detached entities survive. `scene.duplicate` copies reflected components (not the
relationship components themselves).

## Graybox shapes

`scene.spawn_primitive` spawns a parametric shape — a `Primitive` component the renderer meshes —
with a `Transform`, in one call:

```json
scene.spawn_primitive { "shape": "ramp", "params": { "size": [6.0, 1.5, 3.0] },
                        "transform": { "translation": [0.0, 0.75, -8.0], "euler_deg": [0.0, 90.0, 0.0] },
                        "name": "Loading ramp", "color": [0.6, 0.6, 0.65] }
→ { "entity": 4294967310, "shape": "ramp", "vertices": 18, "triangles": 8 }
```

`shape` is one of `cuboid`, `sphere`, `capsule`, `cylinder`, `cone`, `conical_frustum`, `plane`,
`torus`, `tetrahedron`, `ramp`, `prism`. Every shape is centered on the entity origin and about one
meter by default. `params` overrides fields of the shape by name with the JSON shapes
`scene.get_entity` shows (`types.describe` with `{"type": "PrimitiveShape"}` lists them):
`size` (`[x, y, z]`; plane `[x, z]`), `radius`, `height`, `length` (capsule middle), `resolution`,
`segments`, `caps`, `sectors`/`stacks` (sphere), `longitudes`/`latitudes` (capsule),
`minor_radius`/`major_radius` (torus), `vertices` (tetrahedron corners), `points` + `depth`
(prism outline in XY, extruded along Z). Sizes must be positive and at most 10 km, resolutions at
most 512; a bad value fails with `invalid_params` naming the field, and nothing is spawned.
`transform` takes `translation`, `rotation` (quaternion `[x, y, z, w]`) **or** `euler_deg`
(`[pitch, yaw, roll]`), and `scale` (a number or `[x, y, z]`).

To change a shape later, edit it like any component — `scene.set_property` with
`{ "component": "Primitive", "path": "shape", "value": {...} }` or `"path": "color"` — and the mesh
rebuilds on the next frame. The editor's **Create ▸ Shape** menu does the same as this method.

## Transactions

`scene.apply_edits` validates every edit first; if any of them does not validate, nothing applies:

```json
{ "edits": [
  { "op": "add_component", "entity": 17, "component": "Marker", "value": { "value": 9.0 } },
  { "op": "set_property", "entity": 17, "component": "Marker", "path": "value", "value": 4.0 },
  { "op": "spawn", "name": "Added" }
], "dry_run": false }
```

Ops: `set_property`, `add_component`, `remove_component`, `spawn`, `despawn`, `reparent`. A component
added by an earlier edit of the same transaction satisfies `set_property` validation. An edit whose
entity, or whose `reparent` or `spawn` parent, an earlier edit in the same list despawns fails
validation (`F0014`) and nothing is applied. There is no runtime undo: `dry_run: true` validates
and reports without applying. If an edit fails while it is being applied after every edit
validated, earlier edits of that call stay (`applied_all: false`, `failed_at`).

## Whole-scene snapshot

`scene.serialize` returns the whole scene as canonical RON (also served as the MCP resource
`regia://scene/current`) — useful for diffing what a session of edits changed.
Opaque resource storage is excluded (Bevy 0.20 stores resources on entities). Reflected
resource values, such as the level's layer binding, remain included so their changes stay
observable; `resources.list` also lists resources directly. Actual scene
entities with no serializable components remain included and counted, so an empty-entity
leak stays visible. Opening and closing an editor panel must not add empty scene rows (ADR-7956).

## Example calls

Example calls (`regia agent call <method> '<params json>'`; entity ids come from `scene.query_entities`):

```text
scene.serialize {}                  # { ron, entities, components }
```

<!-- source: book/agents/assets.md -->
# Assets: what the running app can load

The runtime asset surface sits on the running [`AssetServer`]: it lists the cooked manifest,
reports load state, loads assets into the app and reloads them. Importing, creating, editing and
deleting asset *files* is editor/pipeline work (specs/12) and is not part of this surface.

## Listing and describing

```json
assets.list { "query": "helmet", "kind": "CpuMesh", "folder": "khronos", "limit": 200 }
→ { "assets": [{ "path": "assets/khronos/DamagedHelmet.glb", "id": "…uuid…", "type": "regia_asset::CpuMesh" }] }
```

`query` is a case-insensitive substring of the path, `kind` of the cooked type path, `folder` a
project-relative prefix. `assets.describe` and `assets.status` take an `asset` — a project-relative
path or an id — and report its manifest entry, load state (`not_loaded`, `loading`, `loaded`,
`failed`) and the cooked file size. Only `assets.status` adds `error` when the state is `failed`.
`assets.describe` answers `state: "failed"` and has no `error` field:

```json
assets.describe { "asset": "assets/khronos/DamagedHelmet.glb" }
→ { "path": "…", "id": "…", "type": "regia_asset::CpuMesh", "state": "loaded",
    "cooked_bytes": 1834567, "cooked_file": "cooked_….bin" }
```

MCP: the same entry is readable as the resource `regia://assets/{id}`.

## Loading and reloading

```json
assets.load   { "asset": "assets/khronos/DamagedHelmet.glb" }   → { "kind": "mesh", "state": "loaded" }
assets.reload { "asset": "assets/khronos/helmet.glb" }          → { "state": "loaded" }
```

A mesh answer also carries `"mesh": { "vertices", "triangles", "skin": { "joints", "influences" } | null,
"colors", "morph_targets": [names] }` (cooked mesh format v2), so an agent can check that a skinned
character kept its skin, colours and morph targets through the cook.

## Checking a skin against its skeleton

`assets.skin_check` skins a cooked mesh with a cooked skeleton on the CPU, the way the renderer
does (palette `global · inverse_bind`, the 4 strongest influences), in the bind pose and — with a
cooked `clip` — in that clip's pose at `time` seconds:

```json
assets.skin_check { "mesh": "pilot.glb#mesh/body/primitive_0", "skeleton": "pilot.glb#skeleton/hips",
                    "clip": "pilot.glb#clip/run", "time": 0.4 }
→ { "names_match": true, "missing_joints": [], "joints": 67, "skeleton_joints": 67,
    "vertices": 18234, "bind_offset_max": 0.00002,
    "bind_bounds": { "min": [-0.4, 0.0, -0.2], "max": [0.4, 1.82, 0.3] },
    "bounds": { "min": [-0.5, 0.0, -0.4], "max": [0.5, 1.78, 0.5] }, … }
```

- `bind_offset_max` is how far bind-pose skinning moves any cooked vertex. About 0 means the mesh
  and the skeleton agree on their frame; a large value means they were cooked from different files
  or importer versions (re-cook both).
- `bounds` is the posed extent in the skeleton's object space (metres, +Y up): a walking pilot
  stays about its height tall and near the origin. A pose that blows up or lies down is a frame
  or retarget problem.
- `missing_joints` lists skin joints the skeleton lacks (at most 16); those influences are left
  out. A mesh without a skin answers `invalid_params`.
- `stored_influences` is how many influences the cooked skin keeps per vertex (4, or 8 when the
  glTF has `JOINTS_1`). `draw_influences` is how many the renderer draws: 4 by default, 8 when
  the mesh was cooked with the `skin_influences: 8` importer setting (cooked mesh v3, ADR-1622;
  [skinning](book/agents/skinning.md)). This check itself always uses the 4 strongest.

`load` decodes the cooked file into the app (mesh, texture or image — tried in that order);
`reload` re-reads cooked data, which is the hot-reload path after a cook. Both need the asset to be
cooked (`regia cook`); an unknown asset answers `F0016` with the list hint.

Loaded meshes are viewable with `seeing.screenshot` `target: "asset"` or
`seeing.contact_sheet`.

## Live reload status

In the editor and in `regia run --dev` a watcher re-cooks saved sources and reloads them in the
running app within a second (meshes, textures, materials, material graphs and instances, engine
WGSL, levels and prefabs, terrain layers and scatter, decals, VFX, audio, UI layouts).
`assets.watch_status` reports it:

```json
assets.watch_status { "limit": 2 }
→ { "watching": true, "roots": ["assets"], "debounce_ms": 120, "reloads": 7, "errors": 1,
    "last": "cook error in assets/crate.material.ron: 3:5: expected `)`",
    "recent": [{ "path": "assets/albedo.png", "kind": "texture", "ms": 95, "ok": true },
               { "path": "assets/crate.material.ron", "kind": "material", "ms": 4, "ok": false,
                 "error": "3:5: expected `)`" }] }
```

After writing a file, poll until `reloads` (or `errors`) grows, then look: `seeing.screenshot`.
A failed cook or compile keeps the previous version live, so the app never shows a broken asset.

## Texture memory and the budget

Every game preset streams material textures under a resident budget per tier
(`TextureStreaming::for_preset`: Android 256/512 MiB at a 1 K/2 K cap, Deck and Desktop Low 1 GiB
at 2 K, Desktop High 2 GiB at 4 K, Desktop Ultra 4 GiB at the authored size). A new material
uploads as much as the budget has room for, so frames match an unbudgeted renderer while memory
lasts; over the budget the least-recently-seen materials drop their top mips (a GPU copy, nothing
re-decoded) and the visible ones keep what their screen size needs. Once uploaded, the renderer
keeps no CPU copy of a texture's pixels.

```json
assets.texture_memory { "top": 3 }
→ { "frame": 912, "streaming": true, "budget_bytes": 2147483648,
    "resident_bytes": 1610612736, "streamed_bytes": 1577058304, "unstreamed_bytes": 33554432,
    "cpu_bytes": 0, "uncompressed": 212, "uncompressed_bytes": 1342177280, "tiny_uncompressed": 122,
    "uncompressed_limit": 64, "over_budget": false,
    "problems": [{ "code": "uncompressed_textures", "message": "212 uncompressed (RGBA8) material textures resident (1280 MiB, limit 64): cook PNG/JPEG sources … largest: M_Hull base_color 4096×4096 …" }],
    "wrong_platform": { "decoded": 0, "decoded_bytes": 0, "unbound": 0, "formats": [], "labels": [] },
    "textures": [{ "material_key": 4211, "name": "M_Hull", "slot": "base_color",
                   "width": 8192, "height": 8192, "resident_width": 4096, "resident_height": 4096,
                   "format": "Rgba8UnormSrgb", "compressed": false, "streamed": true,
                   "gpu_bytes": 89478485, "cpu_bytes": 0, "last_seen_frame": 912 }, …] }
```

`name` is the material's asset name (materials built by `LabMaterial::from_authored_resolved` or
`from_cooked` are named; a host names its own with `regia_render::name_material_textures`).
`budget_bytes` is `null` with streaming off. The same two problems — `texture_budget_exceeded`
and `uncompressed_textures` (more than `uncompressed_limit`, default 64, RGBA8 material textures:
the level ships PNG/JPEG instead of a cooked pak) — appear in `render.problems` and as differences
in the host checklist, naming the five largest offenders. Since v0.5.1 textures of at most 4×4
texels (placeholders) are not counted in `uncompressed`, never raise the problem and are never
named in it: `tiny_uncompressed` counts them. The limit is `TextureMemoryReport::uncompressed_limit`
(`None` = 64), so a host checking its own report can hold a level to a tighter one.

`wrong_platform` counts the block-compressed textures (material maps and terrain layer arrays)
that reached a device which cannot sample their format since the process started: BC on a phone
(decoded to RGBA8 on the CPU, 4–8× the memory and a slow load), or ASTC LDR and ETC2 on a desktop
GPU (decoded the same way; an ASTC block larger than 4×4 expands further, about 9× for 6×6, 16×
for 8×8 and 36× for 12×12). HDR ASTC, BC6H and signed EAC stay unbound. Either means the content
was cooked for another platform; `regia cook --platform
android` writes ASTC. The problem `textures_cooked_for_other_platform` appears in `render.problems`
and the host checklist while any are counted.

## Faster loads: pak environment and tools

- `REGIA_PAK_GPU_MESHES=1` at pack time stores each mesh GPU-ready (`regia_asset::gpu_mesh`, magic `FGPM`,
  layout v3). Opt-in, desktop only, never Android. A mesh with vertex colors converts and `load_mesh` returns its
  `COLOR_0` (ADR-7919); a mesh with a skin or morph targets converts too and `load_mesh` returns them (layout v3,
  ADR-10080; v1 and v2 entries still load).
  Old compact paks still load; `load_mesh_bytes` reads both forms.
- `pak_migrate <old.fpak> <new.fpak> [--raw]` (a binary of `regia_asset_pipeline`) rewrites an existing desktop pak
  with its meshes GPU-ready, every other entry byte for byte; it prints how many meshes it converted.
- `REGIA_UPLOAD_RING=0` turns off the mapped upload ring and falls back to `Vec` + `write_buffer` chunks. Output
  is identical; use it to rule the ring out when a frame hitches during streaming.
- `REGIA_PAK_VERIFY=0|force` controls the background `pak_verify` check. Until a pak passes it (first launch
  after an update) its reads copy through the file handle instead of serving views of the mapping. The terrain
  `PakTileSource` opens its own paks and follows the same rule (`pak_verify::gate_until_verified`): an unverified
  pak serves it copies until the next launch. `PakReader::read_raw` goes through the same check.
- On Windows a mounted pak cannot be opened for writing by another process (the reader withholds write sharing), so
  a patcher writing it in place gets a sharing error instead of changing bytes under the game.
- A mounted pak that is truncated or re-stamped while the game runs is detected on the next read: the log shows
  `pak changed on disk` (target `regia_asset`, with the pak path) once, and that pak is read through the file
  from then on. A cut entry then fails with `PakError::Corrupt` instead of crashing. Replace paks by rename.
- `assets.status` also reports the mounted paks and how many serve zero-copy views now:

  ```json
  assets.status { "asset": "assets/khronos/helmet.glb" }
  → { "path": "…", "id": "…", "state": "loaded", "cooked_bytes": 1834567,
      "paks": { "mounted": 2, "zero_copy": 2 } }
  ```

  `zero_copy` below `mounted` means a pak is still waiting for its first verify pass (first launch after an
  update), failed it, or changed on disk; `AssetServer::zero_copy_pak_count()` is the same count for hosts.

## Generating materials from texture sets

```json
assets.texture_sets { "folder": "assets/textures/rocks", "write": true, "recursive": false }
→ { "folder": "assets/textures/rocks", "write": true,
    "sets": [{ "name": "boulder", "folder": "…", "material_path": "…/boulder.material.ron",
               "material_exists": false, "written": true,
               "textures": { "base_color": { "path": "…", "id": "…uuid…",
                                             "settings": "(usage: Some(color))" }, … },
               "alpha_mode": "mask",
               "unreferenced": [{ "path": "…/boulder_Opacity.png",
                                  "reason": "the standard material reads alpha from the base colour map's alpha channel; …" }],
               "conflicts": [], "warnings": [] }],
    "leftovers": [{ "path": "…", "reason": "unknown_suffix" }] }
```

`assets.texture_sets` is the agent surface of `regia assets texture-sets` (spec 22 T2.14,
ADR-3320). It detects PBR texture sets — maps named `<base>_<suffix>.<ext>` grouped by folder
and base name over one shared suffix table (`BaseColor`/`Albedo`/`Diffuse`/`Color`, `Normal`/
`N`/`Nrm`/`NormalGL`/`NormalDX`, `Roughness`, `Metallic`, `AO`, `ORM`/`ARM`/`RMA`/`MRA`,
`Height`/`Displacement`, `Emissive`/`Emission`, `Opacity`/`Alpha`/`Mask`) — and generates one
`.material.ron` per set that names the set's texture ids. Without `write` (the default) nothing
is written and texture ids that have no `.meta` yet read as `null` ("new on write"). An existing
material is never touched (`material_exists`); two files claiming one slot are reported as a
conflict and neither is used.

With `write: true` the members' `.meta` settings are set so cooks agree: base colour and emissive
sRGB, other maps linear; a `_NormalDX` normal records `normal_green: directx` (flipped at cook,
never on disk); an `_RMA`/`_MRA` packed map records `orm_channel_order` (swizzled to `ORM` at
cook). An opacity map switches the material to alpha cutout. What the standard material has no
slot for is reported, never guessed: separate roughness/metallic maps (until the packed-ORM
packer lands) and the opacity map itself (the shader reads alpha from the base colour map's
alpha channel) appear in `unreferenced` with the reason.

The suffix table and the default green convention extend per project in `Regia.toml`
`[import.texture_sets]` (see [Materials, textures and import](book/user-guide/materials.md#texture-sets-a-folder-of-maps-becomes-a-material)).

Errors: `F0002` (`folder` missing/invalid or escaping the project — `data.reason`
`path_outside_project`), `F0003` (a write failed — `data.path` names the file), `F0016` (the
folder does not exist under the project).

## Generic assets: loaders, handles and load groups

A crate that owns an asset type registers an `AssetLoader` for it (`AssetAppExt::register_asset_loader`
on the app, or `AssetServer::register_loader`). `AssetServer::load::<T>(id)` and `load_path::<T>(path)`
return a reference-counted `StrongHandle<T>` at once and decode on the IO task pool, reading through the
same mounted paks and cooked cache as the mesh and texture loads. A loader loads what it depends on
through its `LoadContext` (`ctx.load::<D>(id)` returns a handle); the server records the edges both ways,
so a hot reload of a dependency reloads every asset that uses it (each reported as
`AssetReloaded { kind: Generic }`).

When the last strong handle drops, the asset unloads after a grace period counted in frames (default
120, `set_unload_grace_frames`; 0 unloads on the next frame); taking a handle again inside the grace
keeps it. Unloading drops the value and with it the handles it held, so its dependencies then run their
own grace. A per-kind CPU budget (`set_memory_budget`) unloads released assets early, oldest release
first; an asset that still has a strong handle is never evicted. A load group (`load_group`) keeps its
members loaded and is a load set named `load_group:<n>`, so `assets.load_progress` shows it beside the
hand-made sets.

```json
assets.handles { "kind": "Note", "limit": 100 }
→ { "grace_frames": 120,
    "kinds": [{ "kind": "Note", "loaded": 2, "loading": 0, "strong_handles": 2, "pending_unloads": 1,
                "pinned": 0, "cpu_bytes": 8, "gpu_bytes": 0, "budget": null }],
    "assets": [{ "id": "…uuid…", "kind": "Note", "strong": 0, "unload_in_frames": 6, "cpu_bytes": 5,
                 "gpu_bytes": 0, "cpu_data_kept": true, "dependencies": 0, "pinned": false }, …],
    "truncated": false,
    "groups": [{ "name": "load_group:0", "loaded": 1, "failed": 0, "total": 1, "fraction": 1.0,
                 "complete": true, "failures": [] }],
    "cycles": [["…uuid a…", "…uuid b…"]],
    "warnings": ["reference cycle: …uuid a…, …uuid b… hold each other and never unload by count"] }
```

- `kind` matches a loader's kind name (its asset type without the module path), case-insensitively;
  omit it for every kind. The built-in kinds are `mesh`, `texture`, `image` and `material`; they are
  listed only while they hold or load something. An unknown kind, or a built-in kind that holds nothing,
  is an `invalid_params` error that lists the known kinds.
- `pinned` marks a built-in asset a typed load (`load_mesh`, `load_texture`, `load_image`,
  `load_material`) stored: its uncounted `Handle<T>` keeps it, so it never unloads by count and keeps
  its CPU copy (`strong` counts only the counted handles beside it). A counted load
  (`load::<CpuMesh>`, ...) unloads after the grace like any generic asset (ADR-7256).
- `strong` counts live handles, including those held inside other assets and by load groups.
  `unload_in_frames` is set only for an asset with no strong handle left; it unloads when it reaches 0.
- `gpu_bytes` is the estimate a registered `PrepareAsset` returned (the step that uploads a GPU-backed
  asset); after it the CPU copy is released (`cpu_data_kept: false`, `cpu_bytes` drops) unless the load
  asked for `keep_cpu_data` (`AssetServer::load_with`).
- `groups` lists every live load group (not filtered by `kind`); `complete` is set once, when every
  member loaded or failed, and the app gets one `LoadGroupCompleted` message for it.
- `cycles` lists reference cycles among loaded assets (A loads B through its context, B loads A), each
  as its member ids in order, with one `warnings` line each. A cycle keeps its members loaded after
  every outside handle drops; break it in the loader (a weak handle, or no edge back). Not filtered by
  `kind`.
- Budgets (`AssetServer::set_memory_budget`) hold CPU plus GPU bytes per kind, so a texture whose CPU
  copy went after its upload still counts by its GPU estimate. `assets.texture_memory` stays the
  renderer's own report of the textures it uploaded itself; a texture is counted in one of the two.
- Counted built-in loads count in the `loads` block of `assets.cooked_pack` (mesh form, `textures`,
  `images_rgba8`, `pak_loads`, `cache_loads`) exactly as typed loads do, and a counted texture loaded
  from a pak that serves views keeps a view of its KTX2 bytes (no copy). A counted texture whose cooked
  file became an RGBA8 image (or back) is listed under its new kind after the hot reload; its handles
  still count it, and `load::<CookedImage>` shares the count (ADR-7284).
- A cooked model loaded with `regia_render::cooked_model::load_cooked_models_counted` shows one `mesh`
  row per part. With `AssetMeshUploads` registered its `gpu_bytes` is the upload, `cpu_bytes` 0 and
  `cpu_data_kept` false: the frame renderer draws it from the upload (`FrameRenderer::set_asset_meshes`)
  and the budget counts it once (ADR-7284).
- Errors: `F0016` when the app has no asset server. Load errors carry stable codes in their text and
  through `AssetLoadError::code`: `asset_not_found` (the manifest lists no such path), `asset_no_loader`
  (no loader for the type), `asset_type_mismatch`, `asset_io`, `asset_decode`.

The built-in mesh, texture, image and material stores keep their `Copy` slot handles (`Handle<T>`, no
reference count) for the typed loads, which pin what they load; counted loads of the same kinds go to the
same stores (ADR-7256). With the `AssetPlugin` they also send `AssetEvent<T>` messages (`Added`,
`Modified`, `Removed`, `LoadFailed`).

## Counted meshes and textures in an App (ADR-7330)

Add `regia_render::CountedMeshPlugin` next to `RenderPlugin` and `AssetPlugin`, before the first counted
load. It registers the renderer's uploaders (`CountedAssetUploads`: meshes, and KTX2 textures plus RGBA8
images) with the asset server and the runtime renderer. Then:

- `MeshRenderer::counted(server.load::<CpuMesh>(id)?, material)` draws the mesh from its GPU upload. The
  component and the extracted frame hold no vertices; `assets.handles` shows the mesh row with
  `gpu_bytes` and `cpu_bytes: 0`. Despawning the last entity that draws it lets the mesh unload after the
  grace frames.
- A material slot `MaterialImage::Asset(AssetImage::image(handle, &uploads.textures))` (or
  `AssetImage::texture` for KTX2) binds the one GPU texture of that asset, whatever number of materials
  hold it. Each slot samples it in its own color space (ADR-8610: one texture, an sRGB and a linear
  view), so one image may serve a base-color slot and a mask slot. `uploads.textures.set_srgb(id, true)`
  before the load filters the mip chain for color; the base level is exact in both views.
- A material-graph texture slot takes one too (`GraphTexture::from_asset(image, srgb)`), and
  `FoliageSway::adopt` keeps a counted map in the sway twin's graph slots (ADR-8610).
- A hot reload of a counted texture shows on the next frame in every material that binds it, without
  touching the material: `render.stats` `counted.texture_rebinds` counts the entries rebuilt, and
  `counted.textures` reports the App's counted texture table ([Skinned instancing and draw
  counters](book/agents/skinned-instancing.md)).
- A skinned `MeshRenderer` (with `SkinJoints`) on a counted mesh skins from the upload; the joints stay
  CPU (`render.stats` `mesh_cache.adopted_skinned_meshes`).
- A counted mesh with a `MeshUv1` (one entry per vertex) or a `LightmapReceiver` whose unwrap is 1:1
  with the mesh draws its second UV set. `render.get_lightmaps` reports the receivers it refuses with
  `lightmap_receiver_counted` or `lightmap_receiver_counted_pending`
  ([Lightmaps](book/agents/lightmaps.md#errors)).
- `render.stats` `mesh_cache` reports the counted meshes the renderer draws from the asset server's
  buffers apart from its own cache: `adopted_meshes`, `adopted_mesh_bytes`. The cache never evicts
  them; the asset server frees them.

- A counted mesh with a `MeshLodChain` draws every level from the upload (ADR-7428): read the chain with
  `MeshLodChain::from_cooked_asset(&server.payload_reader(), id)` (no vertex kept) and insert it next to
  the counted `MeshRenderer`. Each level's index list uploads once, shared by its colour, shadow and
  cross-fade draws: `render.stats` `counted.lod_index_uploads` counts them ([Skinned instancing and draw
  counters](book/agents/skinned-instancing.md)).

- **Visibility-buffer clusters** (ADR-7462): on a profile with the visibility buffer, a counted mesh
  draws its clusters from the upload. Give it a `MeshletSource` like any mesh: the meshlet bridge
  checks the `.fmlt` against the upload's counts and inserts it under the stand-in's key. Its vertices
  are copied into the cluster arena on the GPU, once. `render.stats` `counted.vis` reports `meshes`,
  `clusters`, `repacks` and `forward_fallbacks` (counted whole draws of the last visibility-buffer
  frame that drew forward for want of clusters), and `kept_meshlet_bytes`: the renderer keeps the
  cooked clusters of every counted mesh it admitted on the CPU, for a hot reload of the `.fmesh` alone
  (ADR-7542). A LOD or cross-fade variant draw, cluster residency, and the voxel far extension keep
  the forward path or the plain meshlets.
- Hot reload on the visibility buffer (ADR-7542): a re-import that reloads the `.fmesh` and the
  `.fmlt` in one update draws the new clusters whichever system runs first, and the bridge checks the
  `.fmlt` again whenever the mesh is uploaded again (`FrameRenderer::asset_mesh_upload_serial`), so a
  `.fmlt` that reloaded an update early is inserted when its `.fmesh` lands.

Deformers on a counted mesh (ADR-7721) draw from its upload too:
- Morph targets: the upload packs the cooked targets against the vertices it uploads
  (`AssetMeshUploads::morph_targets(id)`, the set `MorphTargets::from_cooked` builds on the CPU path);
  put it in a `MeshMorphTargets` beside the `MeshRenderer::counted`. The renderer deforms a GPU copy
  of the adopted vertex buffer; `anim.morph_weights` reports such instances in `renderer.counted`.
- The compute-skinning twin skins from the adopted vertex buffer and the four strongest influences
  the upload carries; `render.skinning` reports them in `last_frame.counted`.
- The GI probes size a counted mesh by its upload's box and bake its signed-distance brick from a GPU
  readback of its buffers, made once when the brick is first needed (`AssetMeshUploads::gi_readbacks`)
  and dropped after the bake.

Not drawn from a counted upload: a counted LOD or cross-fade variant on the compute-skinning path or
as a probe brick (they keep the vertex-shader path and are not traced), a counted emissive mesh's
probe emitters, and a lightmap unwrap that splits vertices. Load those meshes with `keep_cpu_data`.

<!-- source: book/agents/seeing.md -->
# Seeing: screenshots, strips and image comparison

Everything an agent needs to *see* results: PNG captures of the window or a mesh asset, multi-frame
strips, orbit contact sheets, and SSIM comparison with a difference image. Every result carries
`png_base64` (MCP clients get an image block automatically).

## Screenshot

```json
seeing.screenshot { "target": "window", "timeout_ms": 30000 }
→ { "width": 1280, "height": 720, "mime": "image/png", "png_base64": "..." }
```

- `target: "window"` (default) captures the primary window (`entity` selects another window).
- `target: "asset"` renders a mesh asset on the neutral preview stage:
  `{"target": "asset", "path": "assets/khronos/DamagedHelmet.glb"}`.
- `target: "offscreen"` renders headless (no window) from the extracted ECS frame
  (`Camera` + `MeshRenderer`). Optional `width` / `height` (default 256×144). Use with
  [`enable_fixed_step`](book/agents/headless-capture.md) for byte-identical lavapipe goldens.
- `calibration: "applied"` (default) captures what the player sees. `"neutral"` captures the
  frame before the player's [display calibration](book/agents/display-calibration.md), identical to a
  neutral-calibration capture. Use `"neutral"` for goldens.
- Offscreen captures include the game HUD (`hud`, default true): the runtime UI is laid out for
  the output size, not the window's. `layout` picks the HUD layout: `"auto"` (by orientation),
  `"landscape"` (16:9) or `"portrait"` (native 9:16, e.g. `width: 1080, height: 1920`). Roots
  tagged `UiVariant` show only in their layout; `SafeAreaPadding` roots are inset by the
  render-out safe area (broadcast title-safe 5 % for landscape; 12 % top / 20 % bottom / 5 % left
  / 10 % right for portrait; override with `UiOutput::safe_area`). `hud: false` omits it.
- `window_layers: true` also draws the window overlay layers over the frame, as a visible window
  shows them: the [quick draw](book/agents/quick-draw.md) 2D layer and the runtime UI.
- The editor viewport (sky, proxies, grid, gizmo, no window chrome) is
  `editor.capture_viewport`, documented on the [editor](book/agents/editor.md) page. `seeing.screenshot`
  of a running editor is the whole window, chrome included.
- `target: "camera"` renders one camera entity's view offscreen, whatever its render target or
  viewport: `{"target": "camera", "name": "SideCam"}` (the first camera with that `Name`) or
  `{"target": "camera", "entity": 4294967301}`. `width` / `height` (or `size: [w, h]`) default
  to 256×144; the HUD is off unless `hud: true`. The reply adds `camera` (the entity). A camera
  spawned this frame has no view yet: step a frame first (`screenshot_camera_not_rendered`).
- `target: "ui"` renders the runtime UI layer (the window overlay layer `ui`) alone over
  transparent black, laid out for `width` × `height` (default 1280×720) and `layout`, with no
  scene under it: every pixel the UI leaves alone has alpha 0. An app without a UI layer answers
  `screenshot_no_ui_layer`. Safe-area previews are the editor's UI designer
  (`editor.ui_designer_*`).
- `overlays` draws debug outlines over the picture of any target, after the display calibration
  and with no depth test (an outline inside a wall still shows): `"colliders"` (every
  `Collider`: box edges, sphere / capsule / cylinder / cone rings, trimesh edges, heightfield
  grid, compound children; convex hulls as their bounding box; solid green, sensors cyan),
  `"light_radii"` (point-light radius circles, spot-light cones; yellow), `"bounds"` (every
  `MeshRenderer`'s mesh box; orange) and `"grid"` (1 m, ±10 m on Y = 0). The reply adds
  `overlay_pixels`, the pixels they drew. `"selection"` and `"labels"` draw editor state: they
  answer `F0013` with reason `overlay_needs_editor`; use `editor.set_viewport { colliders,
  light_radii, bounds, labels }` and `editor.capture_viewport` in the editor. Overlays need a
  camera view to project through (`screenshot_no_view` before the first frame).
- `view_mode` needs the editor renderer's debug passes — this build answers `F0013` instead of
  pretending.

- A window the OS will not present (minimized, occluded, a locked console or a sleeping display)
  still answers `target: "window"`: a game renders the capture offscreen at the window's size, and
  the editor draws its frame into a stand-in target, so the capture shows what the window would
  show. While the OS refuses the window's surface the app steps at its hidden rate
  (`LoopControl::throttled_fps`), so a capture may take up to one hidden-rate frame longer
  (ADR-7335).
- Repeated window captures do not grow the app's memory: the readback buffer, the pixels, the PNG
  and the reply text are reused across shots of the same size (ADR-8848). The first capture's
  buffers stay until the app suspends or exits.

| Reason (`data.reason`) | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| `overlay_needs_editor` | F0013 | `overlays` names `selection` or `labels` |
| `screenshot_no_view` | F0003 | overlays before any camera was extracted |
| `screenshot_not_a_camera` | F0002 | target `camera`: `entity` has no `Camera` |
| `screenshot_camera_not_rendered` | F0003 | target `camera`: the camera has no view in the frame yet |
| `screenshot_no_ui_layer` | F0013 | target `ui`: the app draws no `ui` layer |

## Sequences and orbit sheets

```json
seeing.capture_sequence { "frames": 4, "every_n": 5, "timeout_ms": 60000 }
→ one strip image: N window screenshots taken `every_n` frames apart
seeing.contact_sheet { "path": "assets/khronos/DamagedHelmet.glb", "angles": 4 }
→ one strip image: the mesh from N orbit positions
```

Use the sequence for motion/VFX review and the contact sheet to show a model from all sides.
At most 8 sequence and sheet jobs run at once; a ninth call answers `too_many_pending`
(JSON-RPC -32600) until one finishes.

## Comparing images

```json
seeing.compare_images { "a": "<base64 png>", "b": "<base64 png>" }
→ { "ssim": 0.98, "max_channel_diff": 3, "same_size": true, "diff_png_base64": "..." }
```

SSIM per Wang et al. (IEEE TIP 2004): 1.0 = identical; flat-but-different images score low but not
zero. The classic workflow: screenshot before your edit, apply it, screenshot after, compare — the
`diff_png_base64` shows *where* pixels changed.

The images come from earlier `seeing.*` calls (take the `png_base64` values) — the comparison
itself needs no running window, so it works headless.

## Picking

`seeing.pick_entity {"x": 320, "y": 240}` returns the entity under a window pixel — once the
renderer exposes its entity-id buffer. Until then it answers `F0013`; find entities spatially with
`scene.query_entities` (`near`/`box`) instead.

## Memory

```json
seeing.memory_report { "top": 5 }
→ { "available": true, "backend": "Vulkan", "allocated_bytes": 972..., "reserved_bytes": 1476...,
    "rss_bytes": 1434..., "peak_rss_bytes": 1980..., "device_allocated_bytes": 972...,
    "staging": { "cap_bytes": 134217728, "flushes": 0, "flushed_bytes": 0, "waits": 0, "peak_pending_bytes": 2310... },
    "categories": { "terrain_height": { "bytes": 89489408, "count": 2 }, "meshes": {...}, ... },
    "labels": [ { "label": "material texture", "category": "meshes", "bytes": 201392128, "count": 36 }, ... ] }
```

Every live GPU allocation of the render device, from the backend allocator (Vulkan, D3D12), sorted
into categories by its wgpu label: `terrain_height`, `terrain_layers`, `terrain_macro`,
`terrain_masks`, `terrain_geometry`, `scatter`, `meshes` (vertex/index buffers and material
textures), `shadows` (shadow maps and their atlases; the UI glyph and VFX atlases count as `other`, a
lightmap atlas as `probes_luts`, ADR-2952), `render_targets`, `probes_luts`, `frame_data`, `other`, `unlabeled`. A
growing `unlabeled` or `other` means a new allocation needs a label (the rules are in
`regia_render::memory`). `rss_bytes` is the process resident set and `peak_rss_bytes` its peak:
Linux and Android report `VmRSS` and `VmHWM`, Windows reports the working set and peak working
set, macOS the task's resident size and `ru_maxrss`, and both are `null` on other targets and when the OS query fails. `staging` is the upload staging flush that bounds a level
load's write staging (ADR-1346, [Load memory](book/agents/load-memory.md)). On GL and Metal `available` is `false`. `device_allocated_bytes` is the whole device's
allocated size, the one figure to hold against a GPU memory cap on every backend (ADR-5860): the
allocator's live total (`allocated_bytes`) on Vulkan and D3D12, `MTLDevice.currentAllocatedSize` on Metal
(driver-internal resources included, no categories or labels), `null` on GL and WebGPU. It answers `F0011` before a render device
exists.

Budgets and the DO27 measurements: `docs/evidence/perf/memory-20261007.md`; the CLI version is
`lookdev`'s `mem_report` (load time, bytes read, RSS, GPU by category, streaming soak).

## Photosensitivity check

```json
seeing.flash_check { "dir": "captures/trailer", "fps": 30 }
seeing.flash_check { "frames": 120, "fps": 60, "every_n": 1 }
→ { "passed": false, "max_flashes": 5, "window_start_s": 1.25,
    "region": { "x": 0, "y": 0, "width": 341, "height": 256 },
    "area_fraction": 1.0, "kind": "general",
    "general_flashes": 5, "red_flashes": 0, "frames": 120 }
```

`seeing.flash_check` counts general flashes and saturated-red flashes in a sequence of sRGB frames
(WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.3.1). Pass one of two sources, plus `fps`:

- `dir`: a folder of PNG frames, read in file-name order. Subfolders are skipped. Relative paths
  stay inside the project (or the temp directory, or an `output_roots` entry).
- `frames`: capture the primary window now, `every_n` engine frames apart (default 1), and analyze
  those frames. `frames` is 2 to 600. The pixels are not kept. At most 8 sequence, sheet and flash
  jobs run at once; a ninth answers `too_many_pending`.

`fps` is the rate the sequence represents, from 1 to 480. Frame `i` is at time `i / fps`, so the
same square wave captured at 30 fps and at 60 fps gets the same verdict. A missing or out-of-range
`fps` is `fps_out_of_range`. Passing both `dir` and `frames` is `F0002`. Passing neither is
`no_frames`. An empty folder is also `no_frames`. `frames` outside 2 to 600 is
`frames_out_of_range`. More than 18000 PNGs is `too_many_frames`.

A general flash is a pair of opposing changes in relative luminance of 10% or more where the
darker image is below 0.80. A red flash is a pair of opposing transitions involving a saturated
red, using WCAG 2.2 definition note 3: at least one transition is to or from a state with
`R / (R + G + B) ≥ 0.8` on the linear channels, and each transition differs by more than 0.2
in CIE 1976 UCS chromaticity. Black has undefined chromaticity; this aid conservatively uses
`(u′, v′) = (0, 0)`. More than three flashes in any one-second period fails
when the flashing cells cover more than a quarter of any 10 degree field. The field is 341×256 px
on a 1024×768 screen; pass `reference_width`, `reference_height`, `ten_degree_width_px` and
`ten_degree_height_px` to document a different screen or viewing distance. `cell_px` (default 8,
1 to 4096) is the square the analyzer averages before it counts. A zero or oversized geometry
field is `geometry_out_of_range`. A frame side above 8192, an area above 4096×4096, or more than
2,500,000 cells is `frame_too_large`.

`passed` is false when either kind fails. `kind` is `general` or `red`. The other counts are
always in the report. `region` is the cell-aligned 10 degree window, and `area_fraction` is how
much of it was flashing in the reported second. `window_start_s` is the start of that second.

The same check offline, for a render-out or a trailer:

```text
cargo xtask flash-check captures/trailer --fps 30
cargo xtask flash-check captures/trailer --fps 30 --json
```

Exit 0 passes, exit 2 fails the thresholds, exit 1 is a usage or I/O error.

Error codes: `no_frames`, `empty_frame`, `frame_size_mismatch`, `time_not_monotonic`,
`geometry_out_of_range`, `frame_too_large`, `bad_png`, `dir_not_found`, `fps_out_of_range`,
`frames_out_of_range`, `too_many_frames`, `too_many_pending`. A capture with no renderer is
`F0011`, no primary window is `F0003`, and a capture that fails is `F0015`. `every_n` outside
1 to 3600, a wrong JSON type, or both `dir` and `frames` at once is `F0002`.

This is an aid for a release check. It is not a certification and it is not a guarantee that a
sequence is safe to watch. The balanced-pattern exception for squares under 0.1 degree is not
applied. There is no runtime limiter on engine effects yet.

<!-- source: book/agents/renderer-excellence.md -->
# Renderer excellence: reference traces and scoring

Regia Engine has a reference path tracer (`regia_pt`, `docs/specs/27-renderer-excellence.md` § 1)
that renders the same meshes, materials, lights and sky as the real-time frame, with the same
BRDF code, in physical units. It is the ground truth every real-time technique is scored
against (§ 2). Two agent methods drive it; both need a host built with `regia_agent`'s
`reference-trace` feature (otherwise they answer `F0013`).

## Trace

```json
seeing.reference_trace { "scene": "current", "width": 640, "height": 360, "spp": 1024 }
→ { "job": 1, "status": "running", "spp": 1024, "spp_done": 0, "out_dir": "/tmp/regia_pt/job-…" }
seeing.reference_trace { "job": 1, "wait": true }
→ { "job": 1, "status": "done", "spp_done": 1024, "exr": ".../reference.exr",
    "preview_png": ".../reference_preview.png", "metadata": {…}, "png_base64": "…" }
```

- `scene`: `current` (what the running app's renderer drew), or a validation scene:
  `cornell`, `cornell_room`, `furnace`.
- `source` (with `current`): `auto` (default) traces the renderer's **frame export**
  (`FrameRenderer::set_scene_export`, switched on at the first trace and left on; it is
  incremental): every mesh instance the frame drew — props, buildings, vehicle hulls, rigid or
  skinned at this frame's pose — with its cooked material (base color, packed ORM, normal,
  emissive, detail, IOR and thin transmission), the terrain the shared draw renders (heights at
  full resolution; its albedo is the shader's own when the host installed
  `regia_pt::terrain_bake::install_reference_albedo`, else the layer stack's first-order
  color), and the light the frame used: the sun after the level's sun clock, the planet's sky
  and air, the sky body and the moons. If no frame was exported yet, the extracted frame is
  drawn once offscreen to record one. `export` fails instead of drawing; `extracted` traces the
  ECS extraction (no shared-draw terrain).
- Every reply carries `scene_info` (`source`, `instances`, `triangles`, `terrain`, `sun_lux`,
  `sky`, `sky_bodies`, `stars`, `brdf_energy`, `material_clock`, `origin_offset`,
  `foliage_wind`): check that the heroes and the bodies made it in before waiting
  on a long trace. Graphs that read time, world position or wind take the runtime renderer's
  material clock, floating origin and foliage wind (a trace without a runtime renderer reports
  the origin as `[0, 0, 0]` and no clock or wind — the extracted frame alone cannot know them).
- **Airless maps** (Europa, the Moon): the sky is black with the planet's star field, the sun
  is a disc light of the planet's angular size, and each sky body (Jupiter from Europa) lights
  the scene as a disc area light with the frame's planet-shine fill (`fill_lux`, e.g. DO27's
  1600 lx) and real soft shadows.
- **Glass** (`transmission` > 0) is a thin pane: light passes straight through with the
  forward pass's weight (1 − Fresnel, base color, volume tint), and shadow rays pass it.
- Subsequent traces reuse the bottom-level BVHs of meshes they already saw, so re-tracing
  from a moved camera rebuilds only the instance level.
- `spp` 64 is a quick look; use **≥ 1024** for a reference. `seed` (default 1) makes the
  noise pattern reproducible: the same seed, scene and device give the same image bit for bit.
- `cancel: true` (with `job`) stops after the current batch and keeps what has accumulated.
- At most two traces run at once: a third start answers `too_many_pending` until one finishes.
  The app keeps the 16 most recent finished jobs; polling or comparing an older job id answers
  "no trace job" (keep the EXR paths from the finished status instead). A trace thread that
  panics ends its job as `failed` instead of leaving it `running`.
- The EXR has one layer per AOV: `beauty`, `albedo`, `normal`, `depth`, `direct` (sun, lamps
  and emissive surfaces reflected once), `indirect_diffuse` / `indirect_specular` (sky light
  and all multi-bounce light, split by the first lobe — the GI terms), `emissive`,
  `volumetric` (light from paths whose first event is in the air or fog: aerial perspective and
  fog in-scattering), `sky` (background, sky bodies and sun disc seen directly, through the
  fog in front of them), `shadow` (sun visibility at the first hit), `variance` (of the beauty
  mean) and `spp`.
- Traced since v2: the planet's air (Rayleigh + Mie, aerial perspective on everything that ends
  at a surface) and the level's height fog as media, with the runtime's parameters; sky bodies
  (Jupiter, Io) as lit discs that also light the scene with the real-time fill's illuminance —
  but with shadows; quad area lights; anisotropy, detail maps and packed ORM textures exactly as
