post stack's output pipelines and the effects' sets for that format on its first frame (ADR-7885). Tell the warm about
every such target where you create it, before the game-frame warm:

```rust
use regia_render::pipeline_warm;

// Pass the minimap camera's target key: Rgba8UnormSrgb with 4x MSAA.
fn register_minimap(target: pipeline_warm::WarmTargetKey) {
    pipeline_warm::register_warm_target(target.format, target.samples);
    // Or, with the queue at hand: queue.warm_target(target.format, target.samples).
}
```

Every frame warm that starts afterwards (`GameFrameWarm`, `FrameRenderer::warm_scene`, `warm_extracted`) renders its
warm frame into each registered target as well, twice with the frame's post stack and once without, at the target's
sample count. `VfxGpu::warm_formats` and `terrain_warm_formats` add the registered formats. A target created after the
game-frame warm ran: register it, then call `GameFrameWarm::request()` (or warm the renderer that draws into it with
`PipelineWarmQueue::warm_renderer`). Switching the window to MSAA mid-play is the same case: register
`(window format, 4)` before the warm.

The game-frame warm also builds every deferred blended and transmission variant (`lab blend`, `lab premul`,
`lab additive`, `lab transmit *`) of every forward set it made, and the GPU-driven cull pipelines, whatever the warm
frame held, so the first glass or blended draw of play compiles nothing (before, they built on a warm worker after
warm-up while the draw was skipped).

**What a late pipeline says.** Every pipeline creation carries `CreateDetail`: the target format, depth format, sample
count, the thread (`frame`, or `warm_worker` for a warm job or background build), the call site and `new_axes`, the
forward-set key axes the renderer had no set for (`first_set`, `format`, `samples`, `encode`, `double_sided`,
`sun_rt`, `studio_off`, `restir_di`). A late set with `new_axes: ["format"]` is an unregistered target; `["samples"]`
an MSAA switch; `thread: warm_worker` was compiled off the frame thread (no stall, but the warm did not cover it).

- Telemetry: the `pipeline_after_warmup` event lists `creates` with these fields; the frame summary's
  `created_after_warmup` has `sites` (per kind, label, format, samples and thread, with a count), `unnamed`
  (creations the 32-entry ring had overwritten), `frame_thread` and `warm_worker`. The counts are kept on every frame,
  so the rate-limited event loses nothing.
- Agents: `render.pipeline_warm` answers `targets: [{ format, samples }]` and `recent_pipelines: [{ label, format,
  samples, depth_format, thread, site, new_axes }]` (the newest 32 creations of the process, pipelines only).

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"render.pipeline_warm","params":{}}
```

- Bench: `do27_chase --assert-no-late-pipelines` fails the run when a pipeline is created after the warm-up frames and
  prints each one with these fields.
- Scene checks (lavapipe): `cargo test -p arena --test late_pipelines` and `cargo test -p showcase --test
  late_pipelines` warm the arena and the showcase like the game-frame warm, run 300 fixed 60 Hz steps and fail with
  these fields on any pipeline created after the warm; the arena's second test adds a registered `Rgba8UnormSrgb` 4x
  MSAA offscreen renderer created after warm-up (ADR-8122).

**TSR bind groups.** TSR's resolve builds its bind groups for both ping-pong parities of the frame's colour input and
of the views the frame hands it instead on other frames: the stochastic SSR pass returns its own input once 30
readbacks saw no glossy pixel, so a still shot of a matte area switched the resolve to a view it never bound during
warm-up (two `tsr resolve` groups about 31 frames into a still shot, the 2026-11-15 Switchbacks soak). The pass
falling asleep or waking up after warm-up now creates none (ADR-8122; `cargo test -p regia_render --test
pipeline_warm_targets tsr_creates_no_resolve_group`).

No new error codes: `render.pipeline_warm` answers `F0011` without a warm queue, as before.

## Terrain preparation

Hosts can queue `regia_terrain::prepare_terrain` before installing terrain. The existing
`render.pipeline_warm` result counts the `prepare terrain` job in the map tier, including
constructor and optional draw-pipeline compiles. Its Rust `TerrainPreparation` handle reports
success separately from terminal failure and transfers the prepared draw once. No additional
agent method is needed. See [prepare terrain pipelines before install](book/user-guide/terrain-data.md#prepare-terrain-pipelines-before-install).

## Prepare maps

A driver pipeline cache only helps on the GPU and driver that wrote it, and a game cannot ship one
for every machine, so a cold cache is compiled before play instead (ADR-8453): at first launch,
after a driver update, or after a game update that changed a map.

- `regia prepare --cache-dir <game cache> --project <dir> --scene levels/a.level.ron --scene
  levels/b.level.d` warms each level the way the game-frame warm warms it (the window formats,
  the `--profile` preset's settings when given, and every `--target <format>[xN]`, for example
  `--target rgba16fx4` for a render-to-texture camera), on the warm workers, then saves the
  cache and writes the stamp. Each level is spawned headless; each distinct `MeshSource`
  material (`.material.ron`, `.matgraph.ron`, `.matinst.ron`, with 1×1 stand-in textures) draws
  on a stand-in quad 5 m in front of the level's first camera (a default camera when it has
  none), so none is culled: pipelines depend on the vertex layout, the material's kind and graph
  and the frame's settings, not on geometry or pixels.
- Progress: one `load:<map>` line per level, then the usual JSON lines; while a map is warmed the
  `phase` is `map:<name>` (in `prepare-status.json` too).
- `--check` exits 2 when the map list changed: the stamp's unit list holds `map:<name>:<format>`
  per map and `maps:<hash>` of the names and fingerprints (a hash of each level's files and the
  material files it names). A request without `--scene` keeps the unit list older stamps hold.
- In the game: build one `regia_render::prepare::PrepareMap { name, fingerprint, frames }` per
  map from your own loader (spawn the map, run `extract_frame`, take the `ExtractedFrame`), put
  them in `PrepareRequest::maps` (and your extra targets in `PrepareRequest::targets`), and read
  `prepare::host_status(&request, &device.adapter.get_info())` before the menu: when `needed` is
  true, show a "Preparing shaders" page and run `prepare::run_on(&device, &request, |p| ...)` on
  a background thread. `HostPrepareStatus { needed, state, done, total, eta }` drives the page;
  `fraction()` is its bar.
- Packaging: `regia package --prepare-scene <level>` (repeatable) records `prepare_maps:
  [{ name, path }]` in `build_info.json`, the list the game (or its launcher) prepares.
- Agents: `render.pipeline_warm` answers `prepare: null | { state, phase, done, total, fraction,
  pipelines, skipped, error, elapsed_ms, eta_ms }` for a prepare this process ran.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"render.pipeline_warm","params":{}}
```

No new error codes. What the CLI loader does not see: content the game spawns from code, skinned
or morphed meshes, and terrain or effects a level does not carry as components; prepare those
from the game with `run_on`.

<!-- source: book/agents/low-memory-gpus.md -->
# Low-memory GPUs (agent)

How an agent checks the out-of-memory handling of a running game: whether the integrated-GPU defaults apply, whether
texture streaming caught allocation failures, and what fills GPU memory. The engine side is in
[the host checklist](book/user-guide/do27-host-checklist.md#low-memory-gpus-v0116).

## `render.memory_pressure`

Read-only, no parameters. Works without a renderer (the process-wide fields are filled; `stream` and
`integrated_limits` are `null`).

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"render.memory_pressure","params":{}}
```

```json
{
  "signals": 2, "texture_budget_steps": 1, "oom_uncaught": 0, "oom_caught": 3,
  "mips_held": false, "mip_drops": 0, "device_lost": false,
  "integrated_limits": true, "new_scene_warm": false,
  "stream": { "resident_bytes": 201326592, "budget_bytes": 201326592, "held": false, "backing_off": true },
  "categories": { "meshes": 211812352, "textures": 201326592, "virtual_texture": 0, "terrain": 157286400,
                  "staging": 33554432, "atlases": 0, "shadows": 4194304, "render_targets": 62914560, "other": 1048576 },
  "pipeline_cache_bytes": 2346284
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `signals` | Memory-pressure signals accepted since start (probe, OS, out-of-memory). |
| `texture_budget_steps` | How many times the streaming budget was halved. The first out-of-memory error steps it. |
| `oom_uncaught` | Out-of-memory errors that reached wgpu's uncaptured handler. Should stay 0. |
| `oom_caught` | Streamed texture allocations that failed and were handled (retried smaller or dropped). |
| `mips_held` | Streamed textures are held one mip lower (an error came soon after a trim; lasts 60 s). |
| `mip_drops` | How many times every streamed set gave up a level. |
| `integrated_limits` | The integrated-GPU defaults apply (384 MiB budget at most, low mips first, no new-scene warm): a desktop integrated GPU under 15,000 MiB of RAM and 8 GiB of device-local heap. |
| `new_scene_warm` | Whether a large new scene on a scene-less window would be warmed on this device. |
| `stream.backing_off` | Streaming is paused after a failed allocation (5 s, doubling to 60 s). |
| `categories` | GPU bytes per bucket at the last telemetry probe sample (`null` before one). |
| `pipeline_cache_bytes` | Size of the persistent pipeline cache (RAM). |

## Checks an agent can run

`render.memory_pressure` is a query, not a low-memory-device test. It runs headless without a
renderer: process-wide counters are returned, `integrated_limits` and `stream` are `null` without a
renderer, and `new_scene_warm` is `null` without a `GameFrameWarm` resource. `categories` does not read the
renderer; it is `null` only before the first telemetry probe sample. The handler declares no error codes
and accepts no parameters. The map-change check below can run headless; its results describe
that run's counters and do not require a low-memory device.

- **The defaults on this machine:** `integrated_limits` is `true` only on a desktop integrated GPU that is not a Steam
  Deck and is not large (16 GB of RAM or more keeps the presets; `REGIA_INTEGRATED_LIMITS=1` forces the defaults,
  `0` turns them off; `true`/`yes`/`on` and `false`/`no`/`off` work too). Then `stream.budget_bytes` is at most 402653184 (384 MiB) and `new_scene_warm` is `false` unless the game was
  started with `REGIA_SCENE_WARM=1` (or `true`, `yes`, `on`).
- **Very Low carries the cap on any RAM size** (ADR-8878): the quality tier Very Low (`render.set_profile
  {"preset":"VeryLow"}`, `--render-profile VeryLow`, Auto on a weak GPU) writes the same 384 MiB budget and lazy
  first use into its profile, so `stream.budget_bytes` is at most 402653184 at Very Low even on a 16 GB integrated
  laptop where `integrated_limits` is `false`. A discrete card at Very Low still grows the budget to a quarter of its
  VRAM, as at Desktop Low. Pair it with `render.memory_budget {"tier":"integrated_low"}` (2.5 GiB RAM, 1.5 GiB GPU
  memory).
- **A map change survives:** read `render.memory_pressure` before and after loading the next map. `device_lost` and
  `oom_uncaught` stay `false` and 0. `categories.meshes` and `categories.textures` drop after the old map is
  released and before the next one is preloaded.
- **What filled memory:** `categories` uses the same buckets as the 10 s telemetry summary (`memory.categories`) and
  the device-lost crash bundle. `seeing.memory_report` lists every label.
- **Softer textures for a minute** after `mips_held` turns `true` are expected; they sharpen when it turns `false`.

Related: `render.problems` (`vram_pressure`, `gpu_errors`), `assets.texture_memory` (per texture), `seeing.memory_report`
(per label), [telemetry](book/agents/telemetry.md).

<!-- source: book/agents/events.md -->
# Logs and engine events

Two polled streams, both with the same cursor pattern: keep the returned `next` and pass it as
`since` on the next call to read only what is new.

## Logs

```json
logs.read { "since": 0, "level": "info", "target": "regia_agent", "contains": "screenshot", "limit": 200 }
→ { "records": [{ "seq": 41, "unix_ms": 1730000000000, "level": "info",
                  "target": "regia_agent", "message": "…" }], "next": 42 }
```

`level` is a minimum (`error`…`trace`), `target` a prefix, `contains` a substring. The ring keeps a
few thousand records. MCP: recent records are also readable as the resource `regia://logs/recent`.

## Engine messages

`events.list` shows the tapped kinds; `events.read` polls them:

| Kind | What it is |
|---|---|
| `sim_event` | Routed sim events (`RoutedEvent`): the event kind and its mapped reactions (camera shake, toast, sound cue …) |
| `toast` | UI toasts raised by the event router |
| `settings` | Live `GameSettings` changes: the changed top-level field, before and after |
| `extension` | Extension life cycle (`ExtensionEvent`): `{ "Built": { "id", "phase" } }`, `{ "Failed": { "id", "code" } }`, and `Resolved`, `Enabled`, `Disabled`, `Reloaded`, `PackActivated`, `PackDeactivated`. See [extensions](book/agents/plugins.md) |
| `spacemouse` | SpaceMouse button actions (`{ event: "action", action, button }`) and hot-plug (`{ event: "connected", id, name }`, `{ event: "disconnected", id }`); desktop only. See [SpaceMouse](book/agents/spacemouse.md) |
| `procgen.run_started` | A procedural generator run started: `{ generator, entity, run_id }` (`generator` is the entity guid) |
| `procgen.run_finished` | The run ended: `{ generator, entity, run_id, ok }`; `ok: true` adds `output_hash` and `counts: { instances, entities, tables }`, `ok: false` adds the error `code` and the failing `node` (or null). Every `run_started` is followed by exactly one `run_finished` or `procgen.run_cancelled` with the same `run_id` |
| `procgen.run_cancelled` | A run was cancelled by a newer request, `procgen.cancel` or a clear |
| `procgen.bake_written` | `procgen.bake` wrote a bake: `{ generator, entity, files, cells }` (`cells` is the count of a cell re-bake, else null) |
| `procgen.cells_changed` | Resident cells of a tiled generator changed: `{ generator, entity, added, released, resident }`, cells as `[tier, i, j]` |
| `procgen.cleared` | A generator's output was removed |
| `procgen.detached` | A generator's output became level content: adds `new_root` |

Within one frame the `procgen.*` events of one generator come in run order (a cancelled run before
the run that replaced it); different generators come in entity order. See [procgen](book/agents/procgen.md).

```json
events.read { "since": 0 }
→ { "records": [{ "seq": 1, "frame": 62, "unix_ms": 1730000000620, "kind": "sim_event",
                  "data": { "kind": "sim_started", "reactions": [{ "Toast": { "text": "Sim online" } }] } }],
    "next": 1 }
```

The kinds only appear when their plugin is installed (e.g. `sim_event` needs a
`SimBridgePlugin`). Use `logs_contain`/`events_contain` conditions to wait for a message inside
`play.wait_until` (see [testing](book/agents/testing.md)).

<!-- depth-2:method-reference -->

## Call reference

Parameters, results and error codes for every method on this page. Types and defaults come from the schema and handlers; limits include the contract. Error codes are in `data.code`; names explicitly labeled `data.reason` are additional handler reasons. Every method can also return `F0001`, `F0002`, `F0004`, `F0007` and `F0012`. The server can return `F0005`, `F0006`, `request_too_large`, or `F0008` when the method is not registered; see [protocol](book/agents/protocol.md).

Unless a lower or explicit method limit is listed, the dispatcher accepts at most 65,536 items in a top-level array parameter and 1,048,576 UTF-8 bytes in a string parameter. A limit violation returns `F0002`.

The request in each fence is the call that was sent with `regia agent call`.
The line under it is the host's answer.
A second fence tagged `json,ignore` is an error answer. Large fields are elided with `...`. A fence tagged `json,ignore` is a real call on a host or plugin method that the runtime schema does not list.


### `events.list`

The engine message kinds the protocol records (see events.read).

*Read, does not mutate.*

No parameters.

Result: `{ events: [{ kind, description }] }`.

No error codes beyond the universal set.

```json
events.list {}
→ {
  "events": [
    {
      "description": "Routed sim events (regia_framework::sim_bridge::RoutedEvent): the event kind and its mapped reactions.",
      "kind": "sim_event"
    },
    {
      "description": "UI toasts raised by the event router (sim_bridge::ToastRaised).",
      "kind": "toast"
    },
    ...
  ],
  ...
}
```

Elided: `events` (array 5).

<!-- capture:events.list -->

### `events.read`

Engine messages (toasts, routed sim events, settings changes) since a cursor.

*Read, does not mutate.*

| Param | Type | Required | Default and limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `since` | number | no | Only records newer than this sequence number. |
| `limit` | number | no | Most records to return (default 200). |

Since defaults to 0 and limit to 200. Limit 0 returns no records and keeps since as next.

Result: `{ records: [{ seq, frame, unix_ms, kind, data }], next }`.

No error codes beyond the universal set.

```json
events.read {"since": 0}
→ { "next": 1, "records": [ { "data": { "Resolved": { "count": 0, "errors": 0 } }, "frame": 2, "kind": "extension", "seq": 1, "unix_ms": 1794081905233 } ] }
```

<!-- capture:events.read -->

### `logs.read`

Recent engine log records with optional filters (poll with `since`).

*Read, does not mutate.*

| Param | Type | Required | Default and limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `since` | number | no | Inclusive: only records with seq >= this value. Pass the previous `next` to resume without repeats. |
| `level` | string | no | Minimum level: error, warn, info, debug, trace. |
| `target` | string | no | Log target prefix, e.g. "regia_agent". |
| `contains` | string | no | Only records whose message contains this text. |
| `limit` | number | no | Maximum records (default 200). |

`contains` is at most 1024 bytes. `target` is at most 1024 bytes.

Omitted level, target and contains apply no filter. Omitted since returns the newest limit records; a supplied since returns the oldest unread page. Limit defaults to 200, and limit 0 with a cursor leaves the cursor unchanged.

Result: `{ records: [{ seq, unix_ms, level, target, message }], next }`.

No error codes beyond the universal set.

```json
logs.read {"since": 0, "level": "info", "target": "regia_agent", "contains": "screenshot", "limit": 200}
→ { "next": 21, "records": [] }
```

<!-- capture:logs.read -->

## Workflow: poll logs and events while a game runs

1. `events.list` once, and keep the kinds the running app actually taps.
2. `logs.read` with `since` 0 and a small `limit`. Store `next`.
3. `events.read` with `since` 0. Store that `next` separately. The two cursors are not the same sequence.
4. After the game does the thing you care about (`play.step`, or just letting it run), call each read again with its own `next` as `since`.
5. Stop when a record's `message` or `kind` is the one you wanted. A kind that is not installed never appears; that is an empty `records` list, not an error.

<!-- /depth-2:method-reference -->

<!-- source: book/agents/crash-reports.md -->
# Crash reports (`diagnostics.crash_reports`)

When a running app panics, the platform panic hook writes a self-contained crash report to
`logs://crash-<timestamp>.txt` (panic message + backtrace, build identity, OS/GPU facts, the active
level and frame count, and the last 200 log lines). Pending reports survive restarts; an opt-in
uploader (`regia_crash::CrashReporter`, umbrella `regia::crash`) can send them to a
game-configured endpoint. `https://` endpoints need `regia_crash`'s `tls` feature (ureq + rustls);
without it `https://` is refused. Plain `http://` is sent only when the host string is `localhost`
(ASCII case-insensitive) or a literal loopback IP such as `127.0.0.1` or `::1`. The name is not
resolved, so a LAN address of this machine is treated as remote, and `localhost` is treated as local
even when a resolver would return something else. Any other `http://` host leaves uploads off unless
the game sets `CrashReporter::allow_cleartext`. The uploader then sends scrubbed UTF-8, not the raw
file bytes: invalid UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD, the home directory becomes `~`, secret values become
`[redacted]`, and email addresses become `[email]`.

The agent method `diagnostics.crash_reports` (MCP tool `crash_reports`) lists and reads those
reports so you can diagnose a failure without touching the device's filesystem.

## List

Call `diagnostics.crash_reports` with no parameters:

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "diagnostics.crash_reports", "params": {} }
```

```json
{ "reports": [{ "name": "crash-2026-10-06_12-34-56.txt", "bytes": 1234, "modified_unix_ms": 1768210496000 }], "count": 1 }
```

Reports are ordered oldest first. An empty `reports` array means no bare `crash-*.txt` is pending.
The uploader removes a report after the server answers 2xx, when the path is still the file that
was sent. A final rejection (any status other than 2xx, 408, 429, or 5xx, including a 301 or a
404) renames the file to `*.rejected`. That suffix is not listed here and is not sent again. A
transport failure, 408, 429, or 5xx leaves the `crash-*.txt` for the next start.

## Read

Pass the file `name` to read one report's full text:

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "diagnostics.crash_reports", "params": { "name": "crash-2026-10-06_12-34-56.txt" } }
```

```json
{ "name": "crash-2026-10-06_12-34-56.txt", "content": "Regia Engine crash report\n…\npanic: …\nbacktrace:\n…" }
```

An unknown name answers `F0003`. The `name` is always a bare file name (path traversal is
rejected), so you can only read what `list` showed you.

## Reading a report

The report body has fixed sections. The first line of the body is `panic: <message>` for a panic,
or `<kind>: <reason>: <message>` for a device or surface loss (`device_lost` or
`surface_unavailable`). Then `location:`, `build:` (version, git hash, profile, engine), `system:`
(OS, device, RAM, CPUs, GPU), `runtime:` (frame count, active level), `backtrace:` (symbolicated
where debug info exists), and `recent logs (last 200):`. A stripped shipping binary's backtrace
shows raw addresses — resolve them with the symbols kept in `dist/<p>/symbols/` (see the packaging
guide).

## Privacy

Crash reports can contain file paths, GPU/driver strings and log text. Reading them needs only the
`read` permission, but treat their contents as user data: don't post them anywhere the project
hasn't approved. Sending is the game's choice (the uploader is opt-in and consent-gated); the agent
protocol only exposes the local copies.

## Exits that skip the exit handlers

Not every abnormal end is a crash report. Two exits end the process on purpose without running its exit handlers
(`_exit` / `TerminateProcess`), and write no `crash-*.txt`:

- **Device lost or no window surface** (ADR-276): exit code 3 or 4, with a feedback bundle that explains it.
- **A GPU worker still running at the end of a quit** (ADR-287): after the app has exited, the engine waits for its
  threads that may be inside the GPU driver (`regia-telemetry-probe`, `regia-pipeline-warm-N`,
  `regia-matgraph-N`, `regia-encode-N`, `regia-renderer-drop`, `regia-exit-renderer`,
  `regia-exit-device`). If one is still running when the budget runs out (30 s from the start of the quit,
  `REGIA_EXIT_WORKER_WAIT_MS`), the process ends with the app's own exit code, and the last log line is:

  ```text
  regia exit: 1 GPU worker(s) still running after 30000 ms: regia-matgraph-2 (in a driver call); ending the process with code 0 without process-exit handlers (ADR-287)
  ```

  `(in a driver call)` means the thread was inside a compile, an allocator report or a segment finish. This is a
  driver that did not return, not an engine crash: report it with the log and the GPU driver version. A quit that
  took long but finished logs `regia exit: waited <ms> ms for GPU worker(s) <names>` instead.

The agent connection is gone by then, so read these from the log file of the run (`logs://`) on the next launch or
from the machine.

## Android: native crash records

A native crash on Android (a SIGSEGV in the Mali or Adreno driver, a bad pointer in native code) cannot write a
minidump: Android has no crash monitor process (ADR-328). Instead the crashing process writes a small record itself,
from the signal handler, into the app's internal storage (`files/crash/pending.bin`, prepared at startup), and the
**next launch** reads it back. Every Android Regia Engine app has this; it needs no setup.

On the next launch you get, in order:

1. One warning line in logcat (tag `regia_platform`) and in `logs://`:

   ```text
   native crash record from the last run: SIGSEGV (code 1) at 0x10 on thread regia-crasher (tid 9131), record /data/user/0/<app>/files/crash/2026-10-21_17-02-11.crash.bin, report /data/user/0/<app>/files/logs/crash-2026-10-21_17-02-11-native.txt
   ```

2. A text report `logs://crash-<time>-native.txt`, which `diagnostics.crash_reports` lists and reads like any other
   report. It has the signal and code, the fault address, the thread name and id, the build identity of the run that
   crashed (version, git hash, profile, engine), and the stack.
3. With `FeedbackPlugin`, a crash bundle in the feedback folder (`feedback-<time>-crash.zip`), announced like any
   crash bundle. Its `feedback.json` `crash` object has the same keys as a desktop native crash, with
   `"minidump": null`, `"minidump_error"` saying why, `"platform": "android"` and a `"stack"` array; `log_tail.txt`
   holds the end of the crashed run's log file.

The record file is renamed to `files/crash/<time>.crash.bin`; the newest 5 are kept. A record that is cut short or
corrupt is removed and logged (`native crash record from the last run is unreadable and was removed: ...`). A
`SIGABRT` within 5 s after a panic report is the `panic = "abort"` abort: it gets no second report or bundle.

### Reading the stack

The stack is the program counter, the link register, then up to 32 return addresses from the frame-pointer chain
(the walk stops at the bound, at an address that is not a valid frame, or at the end of the chain; the report says
which). Each line names the library and the file offset in it, and, when the library is still on the device, its
virtual address:

```text
pc 0x0000007a1c2d1234 /vendor/lib64/egl/libGLES_mali.so+0x41234 (vaddr 0x52234)
#00 0x0000007b88001a40 /data/app/~~x/<app>/lib/arm64/libmain.so+0x3a1a40 (vaddr 0x3b1a40)
```

Resolve the game's frames with the unstripped library from the release's symbols:
`llvm-addr2line -fC -e libmain.so 0x3b1a40` (use the `vaddr`). A frame in a vendor driver (`libGLES_mali.so`,
`vulkan.*.so`, `libllvm-qcom.so`) cannot be symbolized by you, but the library name and the offset are what a driver bug
report needs. Code built without frame pointers ends the walk early; the PC and LR are always there.

### What is not recorded

No minidump, no other threads' stacks, no registers beyond PC/LR/SP/FP, no frame-time ring and no host fields (the
record is written inside the crashing process, with no allocation). The OS tombstone still has the full register dump:
`adb logcat -b crash` or `adb bugreport`.

### Checking it on a device

`cargo xtask android-pass --package <app id> --project <game> --crash-test` installs the app, sets the
`debug.regia.crash_test` property (`segv:8`), launches it, waits for it to die, clears the property, relaunches it,
and passes when the record line names `SIGSEGV` and the thread `regia-crasher`. With `--uninstall` it removes the
app at the end, also when the crash test fails, and `summary.txt` says `uninstall: done` only when
`pm list packages` no longer lists it. By hand:

```sh
adb shell setprop debug.regia.crash_test segv:8     # the app reads address 0x10 8 s after startup
adb shell monkey -p <app id> -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER 1
adb shell setprop debug.regia.crash_test "''"        # after it died
adb shell monkey -p <app id> -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER 1
adb logcat -d -s regia_platform | grep "native crash record"
```

Only `adb shell` or root can set a `debug.` property, so the trigger cannot be pulled by another app.

## Hang snapshots (P-08, ADR-8156)

A Linux GNU host can call `regia_crash::stack_dump::install()` once at startup,
then `write_hang_report(reason, &Settings::default())` on its watchdog thread.
The returned path is a normal pending crash report. List it and read it with
`diagnostics.crash_reports` using the calls above. Assert on the returned `content`
for `hang:`, `thread stacks:`, a worker name or an explicit outcome.
There is no new agent method or error code. Existing list/read errors are unchanged.

`capture` returns structured `StackDump` rows for every thread enumerated through
`/proc/self/task`, including its caller. Thread creation after enumeration and
thread-ID reuse are inherent snapshot races. Each row has the OS ID/name,
`is_caller`, `outcome`, and symbolized stack text. Identical stacks retain all
identities. `Captured` contains raw instruction pointers; other outcomes are
`Exited`, `NoResponse`, `WalkTimedOut`, `Busy`, `LimitReached` or `SignalError(errno)`.
A blocked signal does not produce fabricated frames. A timed-out active walker
keeps exclusive buffer ownership until it finishes, even across later captures.

Settings control maximum frames (1–256, default 96), maximum sampled threads
(default 1024), signal wait (250 ms), additional walk wait (2 s), and maximum bytes
per ELF symbol/string table (64 MiB; zero skips names). Symbol names are capped at
1024 bytes by `max_symbol_name_bytes`; parsing also caps total name bytes scanned.
Limits never drop identities.
Times are diagnostic budgets, not simulation timing. Collection is sequential,
not an atomic view of all threads. Total work can approach the thread count times
the configured waits; call it on a watchdog, not per frame. ELF names may remain
mangled. Addresses are translated through executable ELF load segments for
offline `addr2line -C -f -i`; keep the exact executable/modules. If the ELF
metadata is unavailable or exceeds the budget, `file+` labels explicitly identify
file offsets and retain the raw instruction pointer instead of guessing a symbol.

Installation reserves `SIGRTMIN + 6`; `install_with_signal` selects another
real-time signal at startup. Existing handlers are refused, not replaced. The
host coordinates process-wide signal users, must retain the sampler's code and
handler for its lifetime, and must not unload or replace them.

Requested dumps are opt-in: `install_request_handler()` reserves SIGUSR1, or
`install_request_signal(signal)` reserves SIGUSR1, SIGUSR2 or another real-time
signal. Its handler only sets a flag; a watchdog polls `take_request()` and calls
`write_hang_report` on its own thread. `request()` sets the same coalescing flag
without a signal. Occupied signals are refused. No periodic task or automatic
fatal-signal/panic capture is installed. Unwinding is
best effort and is not promised async-signal-safe by libc; a self-sample on the
calling thread cannot time out its own unwinder. This is a live-hang diagnostic,
not a reliable fatal-crash handler. Linux musl, Windows, macOS and Android return
`Unsupported`; their existing native crash mechanisms are unchanged.

Saved reports use the existing privacy scrubber, retention and opt-in upload
policy. Raw `StackDump` data is local diagnostic data and is not scrubbed until
saved. Missing logs configuration or IO failure returns an error to the host.

## Windows bare Alt (P-08)

The platform runner installs bare-Alt suppression on the primary window. A custom
menu-free winit host calls `regia_platform::alt_menu::install(&window)` on the
thread that owns the window. Other operating systems treat installation as a no-op.
`swallows_message` exposes the exact decision for portable host-policy tests.

Only `WM_SYSCOMMAND` with command `SC_KEYMENU` and no mnemonic (`lparam == 0`)
is swallowed. Alt key press/release, Alt+Space, Alt+F4, Alt+Tab and other messages
continue through the normal input/window procedure. The subclass removes itself
when the window is destroyed. Installation failure is returned to custom hosts
and logged by the runner. Agents can inspect settings with `window.get` and
exercise Alt input with `input.key`; native Windows tests must separately verify
focus and continued redraw. Synthetic input alone is not proof of Win32 delivery.

The session logs themselves are uploaded incrementally by the report outbox when the game sets
`CrashReporter::outbox`; a crash report also resends its session's log once. See
[Report outbox](book/agents/report-outbox.md) and `report.outbox_status`.

<!-- source: book/agents/feedback.md -->
# Feedback bundles (`feedback.capture`, `feedback.list`)

A feedback bundle is one `.zip` in the game's feedback folder (`user://feedback`, for example
`~/.local/share/RegiaEngine/<game>/feedback/` on Linux). On Windows it is the non-roaming
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<game>\feedback\`, so crash minidumps stay on the machine (ADR-525). The player writes one from the in-game prompt. The panic hook writes one
automatically, without a screenshot. An agent writes one with `feedback.capture`. All three
have the same parts, so a bug a player reports can be read the same way as one an agent
captures. The engine uploads nothing (see [Feedback and bug reports](book/user-guide/feedback.md)).

## Capture a bundle

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "feedback.capture",
  "params": { "category": "visual", "note": "hull flickers at the gate", "screenshot": true } }
```

`category` is `bug`, `performance`, `visual` or `other` (default `other`). With `screenshot`
true (the default) the bundle holds the next presented frame. `timeout_ms` (default 30000) is the
answer deadline; the connection waits that long plus a 5 s grace. The reply arrives once the file is
written, which is about one frame plus the PNG encode on a worker thread:

```json
{ "name": "feedback-2026-10-11_14-02-31-visual.zip",
  "path": "/home/p/.local/share/RegiaEngine/do27/feedback/feedback-2026-10-11_14-02-31-visual.zip",
  "bytes": 2481152, "category": "visual",
  "entries": ["feedback.json", "note.txt", "screenshot.png", "frame_times.csv", "hitch_report.txt",
              "system.txt", "settings.ron", "render_problems.txt", "log_tail.txt", "build_info.json",
              "host.json"] }
```

A crash bundle (`-crash.zip`) has no `screenshot.png`. It adds `crash.txt`, which holds the
panic message, location, thread and backtrace.

| Entry | What |
|---|---|
| `feedback.json` | category, note, UTC time, `map` / `position` (from the host), which parts are present, why the screenshot is missing, hitch verdict, build summary |
| `screenshot.png` | the frame when the prompt opened |
| `frame_times.csv` | the last 30 s: `t_s, frame_ms, cpu_ms, gpu_ms` and per-frame pipelines, bind groups, buffers, textures, blocking polls, inline bakes |
| `hitch_report.txt` | the `specs/27` § 2.4 report over those frames (the same code as `play.hitch_report`) |
| `system.txt` | OS and version, device, CPU model, logical CPUs, RAM, GPU + backend + driver |
| `settings.ron` | the active `GameSettings`, graphics preset included |
| `render_problems.txt` | `render.problems` at capture time |
| `log_tail.txt` | the newest 400 log records, with the home directory as `~` and secrets as `[redacted]` |
| `build_info.json` | version, git hash, profile, engine, plus the packaged `build_info.json` (glibc floor) under `package` |
| `host.json` | the game's fields (`FeedbackHost`): match id, map, player count, position |

## List and open bundles

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "feedback.list", "params": {} }
```

The reply is `{ folder, bundles: [{ name, path, bytes, modified_unix_ms, category }], count }`,
oldest first. Crash bundles are included. Pass `name` to open one. That returns each entry's
size and the parsed `feedback.json`:

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "feedback.list",
  "params": { "name": "feedback-2026-10-11_14-02-31-visual.zip" } }
```

To read the screenshot or the CSV, unzip the file at `path`. Any zip tool works, because the
entries are stored without compression.

## Checking a fix

1. Reproduce the issue, then call `feedback.capture` with `screenshot: true`.
2. Open the bundle. Read `render_problems.txt`, look at `hitch_report.txt` and the spikes in
   `frame_times.csv`, and check `settings.ron` for the preset.
3. After the fix, capture again and compare the two bundles.

Errors: without `FeedbackPlugin` both methods return `F0003` (not found). An unknown `category`
or a `name` that is not a bundle file name returns invalid params.


## Saved pipeline cache

Normal captures may include a validated `pipelines/*.fpc` from the last renderer
checkpoint. `feedback.json.pipeline_cache` names it; `pipeline_cache_missing`
explains a failed attachment. Hosts control the byte budget and can opt out.
See [Pipeline caches in feedback and packages](book/agents/pipeline-cache-harvest.md) for
capture checks, `--pipeline-cache-reference`, limits and driver compatibility.

<!-- source: book/agents/telemetry.md -->
# Telemetry (`telemetry.get_last_summary`)

The engine emits structured `tracing` events, all with targets under `regia::*`: the session
header, frame summaries, hitches, GPU errors, render problems and streaming events. They are
documented field by field in [Telemetry](book/user-guide/telemetry.md). An agent reads the newest
summary without parsing log files:

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "telemetry.get_last_summary", "params": { "session": true } }
```

<!-- not-a-request -->
```json
{ "summary": { "seq": 3, "reason": "periodic", "frames": 1187, "window_s": 10.0,
               "frame_ms": { "p50": 8.25, "p95": 9.5, "p99": 12.5, "max": 31.0, "mean": 8.4 },
               "fps_histogram": { "ge_120": 1150, "ge_90": 30, "ge_60": 7, "…": 0 },
               "cpu_ms": { "mean": 2.1, "p95": 2.6, "max": 6.0 }, "gpu_ms": { "mean": 7.6, "p95": 8.9, "max": 14.2 },
               "bound": "gpu", "gpu_pass_ms": { "forward": { "mean": 2.4, "max": 3.1 }, "…": {} },
               "textures": { "resident_bytes": 1610612736, "budget_bytes": 2147483648, "over_budget": false, "queue_depth": 0 },
               "memory": { "rss_bytes": 3221225472, "vram_allocated_bytes": 4294967296 },
               "hitches": 1, "created_after_warmup": { "pipelines": 0, "…": 0 } },
  "session": { "adapter": { "name": "NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080", "backend": "Vulkan" }, "fallbacks": [], "…": {} },
  "counts": { "frames": 3561, "summaries": 3, "hitches": 1, "hitch_events": 1, "problems_events": 0,
              "stream_events": 0, "surface_events": 0, "suppressed": 0 },
  "level": "verbose", "summary_interval_s": 10.0 }
```

- `summary` is null for the first 10 s of a session. `session` is null until the first frame
  renders, or when the `session` parameter is not set.
- An error with code `F0003` means telemetry is off: `REGIA_TELEMETRY=off`, or the app has no
  `TelemetryPlugin`.
- `level` is `normal`, `verbose` or `ship` (v0.5.1, ADR-8417; `REGIA_TELEMETRY=ship`). At `ship`,
  `session` is the allowlisted player-build header (adapter class and vendor family, RAM and VRAM
  tiers, no names or ids), `counts.hitch_events` stays 0 and `session_summary` has no `host`
  section. The field list is in [Ship level](book/user-guide/telemetry.md#ship-level).

Typical uses:

- After a scripted run (`play.wait_until`), assert `summary.frame_ms.p99` and
  `summary.hitches`.
- Check `summary.created_after_warmup.pipelines == 0`: no shader compiled mid-game.
- Check `summary.frame_scratch.growths_after_warmup == 0`: the renderer's per-frame lists stopped
  growing ([Frame list growth](book/agents/frame-scratch.md), v0.1.28).
- Read `session.fallbacks` to see why a machine looks different.
- `session_summary: true` adds the `summary.json` record as of now (frames per map, stalls, hitch
  causes, memory peaks, errors, exit state) and `summary_paths` says where the files go.

## The newest frame (`telemetry.live`, v0.1.14)

`telemetry.live` returns what telemetry saw for the newest frame, without waiting for a summary:

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "telemetry.live" }
```

```json
{ "live": { "frame": 5012, "frame_ms": 59.1, "cpu_ms": 11.8, "gpu_ms": 30.2, "bound": "cpu_bound",
            "render_scale_permille": 670, "wait_acquire_ms": 0.4, "wait_present_ms": 0.2,
            "wait_readback_ms": 0.0 },
  "thresholds": { "gpu_bound_share": 0.9, "cpu_bound_share": 0.75 } }
```

- `cpu_ms` is the renderer's `render_into` only (cull, record, submit), not the frame.
- `bound` compares `gpu_ms` with `frame_ms`: `gpu_bound` at a share of 0.9 or more, `cpu_bound`
  at 0.75 or less, `balanced` in between, `unknown` without GPU timing. `cpu_bound` means a lower
  render scale will not raise the frame rate.
- `render_scale_permille` is what the renderer drew (internal width × 1000 / output width),
  null before it drew.
- `wait_*_ms` are the main thread's waits on the GPU in the last window frame: swapchain acquire,
  present, and screenshot readbacks.
- `held` is true when the frame showed the paused-scene hold's kept image (ADR-7890): no scene pass
  ran and `gpu_ms` is the composite plus the UI. Such frames are not in the summary's `frames` or
  frame-time figures (its `held` section counts them) and never feed the hitch median; a governor
  should skip them. See [Frame pacing](book/agents/frame-pacing.md).

The summary carries the same signals over its window: `frame_bound`, `render_scale_permille`,
`wait_acquire_ms`, `wait_present_ms`, `wait_readback_ms`, `cpu_wait_on_gpu_ms` and `live`. A
steady slow frame rate is no longer a hitch (v0.1.14): `summary.hitches` counts spikes out of
the rolling median only.

For one-off hitch attribution, use `play.hitch_report`. Telemetry is the always-on version that
ships in player builds.

## Hitch truth (v0.5.1, ADR-7898)

A DO27 tester round showed three ways the hitch log misled triage. Since v0.5.1:

- **Swapchain waits are not hitches.** A frame that passes the hitch tests but spent at least half
  of its excess over the median in this frame's acquire + present wait (and is at most
  `hitch_abs_ms` over the median) counts as a present wait: `counts.present_waits` in
  `telemetry.get_last_summary` and `summary.present_waits`, not `hitches`.
- **The pacing floor.** Under a frame cap or vsync, a frame shorter than 1.5 pacing periods is never
  a hitch. `telemetry.live` returns the floor in effect:

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "telemetry.live" }
```

<!-- not-a-request -->
```json
{ "live": { "frame": 51, "frame_ms": 736.4, "cpu_ms": 0.0, "gpu_ms": 0.0, "bound": "unknown",
            "bound_reason": "no_scene", "render_scale_permille": null, "wait_acquire_ms": 0.04,
            "wait_present_ms": 0.26, "wait_readback_ms": 0.0 },
  "thresholds": { "gpu_bound_share": 0.9, "cpu_bound_share": 0.75, "hitch_floor_ms": 8.0,
                  "pacing_period_ms": 0.0, "present_wait_share": 0.5 } }
```

- **`bound: unknown` says why.** `live.bound_reason` and the summary's `bound_reason` are
  `no_gpu_timing`, `loading`, `no_scene`, `no_gpu_sample`, `hidden`, `renderer_idle`, or
  `event_wait` (null when the bound is known).
- **The hitch cause is the frame thread's.** The `regia::hitch` record's `cause` comes from the
  main and render threads only; worker spans are listed as `background_spans`. The record adds
  `unaccounted_ms`: the part of the frame interval inside no phase the engine measures. When that
  is at least half the frame the cause is `outside_frame`: the process was in the OS, a window
  change or a driver call outside the event loop, or not scheduled. `window_events` lists the
  resizes, focus and mode changes of the interval. Fields: [Telemetry](book/user-guide/telemetry.md),
  `regia::hitch`.

Typical checks: `summary.hitches` with `summary.present_waits` beside it (a vsync-bound game has
present waits, not hitches); a launch hitch whose `cause` is `outside_frame` with
`window_events.mode_changes` 1 is a fullscreen switch, not engine work.


## Stale render samples and event waits (v0.5.1)

Read `telemetry.live` after a hidden or loading interval. `live.timing` retains the source CPU/GPU
render frame IDs and reports freshness separately. `cpu_sample_ms` and `gpu_sample_ms` are null
when no fresh publication exists; the older numeric fields are zero. Inspect `cpu_absent` and
`gpu_absent` for `hidden`, `no_scene`, `renderer_idle`, `no_renderer`, `no_gpu_timing`, or `pending`.
Do not multiply the last valid renderer time by the number of update ticks.

`live.runner` reports the runner's `focused`, `occluded`, `stalled`, `surface_refused`, and
`throttle_ms`. Focus starts false until the OS reports it. `live.event_wait_ms` and
`live.phases_frame` identify the measured wait of the last completed app frame; runner state in
the live response is current. A hidden 25 ms update at a 100 ms period leaves 75 ms for waiting.
`telemetry.get_last_summary` exposes `cpu_ms.samples`, `gpu_ms.samples`, and the separate
`frame_breakdown_ms.event_wait` phase. `frame_bound.unknown_reasons` includes `hidden`,
`renderer_idle`, and `event_wait`. A dominant measured wait is a hitch cause named `event_wait`.
`thresholds.event_wait_share` is 0.5: a measured wait taking at least half the interval makes
its bound unknown; small normal redraw waits remain classifiable. These are optional additions;
tolerate their absence in older logs. No new method or error code.

Hitch records add `render_timing` and `gpu_frame_id`. A delayed hitch's `gpu_ms` is omitted when
the available readback does not match its fresh render; `top_gpu_passes` is absent then.
Elapsed update ticks alone do not establish GPU sample freshness.

<!-- source: book/agents/framework.md -->
# Framework: scripts, cameras, settings and the sim bridge

The gameplay-framework surface (`regia_framework`) is agent-readable through reflection: scripts
and their slots, camera rigs, live game settings, and the sim-bridge counters DO27's rule A1 checks.
Every call degrades gracefully — when the plugin a call reads is not installed, it answers `F0003`
with a hint naming the plugin, rather than pretending.

## Scripts

```json
scripts.list {}
→ { "scripts": [{ "type": "my_game::scripts::Door", "order": -7 }], "count": 1 }
```

`scripts.list` shows every registered script type and its execution order (from the
`ScriptRegistry`; needs `regia_framework::script::ScriptPlugin` and `register_script`).
`scripts.get` reports the script slots of one entity:

```json
{ "entity": 17 }
→ { "entity": 17, "slots": [{ "type": "my_game::scripts::Door",
     "order": -7, "started": true, "enabled": true, "running": true }] }
```

Slots attach through presentation scripts (the `KindRegistry`) or by spawning a `Scripts`
component. An entity without a `Scripts` component answers `F0003`.

## Cameras

`camera.get` reads the camera rig with the lowest entity id (or the one you name with `entity`) — its mode, yaw, pitch
and, for a chase rig, its target:

```json
camera.get {}
→ { "entity": 4294967296, "mode": "chase", "yaw": 0.0, "pitch": -0.2, "follow": "smoothed", "target": 4294967304 }
```

`camera.set_mode` switches a rig to a named mode and reports before/after:

```json
{ "mode": "overhead" }
→ { "entity": 4294967296, "before": "chase", "after": "overhead", "follow": "smoothed" }
```

`follow` (`smoothed` | `simulated`, optional on `camera.set_mode`, unchanged when omitted) picks which pose of a
predicted target the rig follows (spec 73 § 6.4, ADR-7213): the smoothed pose (the simulated pose plus the correction
offset, `NetVisualOffset`; the default) never pops on a correction; the simulated pose aims exactly at the predicted
state. A target without a correction offset has one pose. In code: `CameraRig::follow` (`CameraFollow`). An unknown
`follow` is `F0002`.

Modes: `chase`, `overhead`, `first_person`, `free` (aliases `third_person`, `top_down`,
`satellite`, `eye`, `spectator` accepted). Unknown modes are `F0002`. Needs
`regia_framework::camera::CameraPlugin` and an entity with a `CameraRig`.

## Settings

`settings.get` returns the whole `GameSettings` resource, or one reflected field via `path`:

```json
{ "path": "input.sensitivity" }
→ { "path": "input.sensitivity", "value": 1.0 }
```

`settings.set` writes one field, applies it live (frame cap → pacing, render scale and shadow quality → the render profile,
volumes → the buses, `display.resolution`, `display.fullscreen` and `display.vsync` → the primary window, see
[display settings](book/agents/display-settings.md)) and persists it to disk. `settings.get` also answers `applied.display`, what
the window and its swapchain took.
`dry_run: true` deserializes the new value and returns `{ path, before, after }` without writing, applying or persisting it:

```json
{ "path": "audio.master", "value": 0.6 }
→ { "path": "audio.master", "before": 1.0, "after": 0.6 }
```

Engine-owned paths: `graphics.preset`, `graphics.shadow_quality`, `graphics.render_scale`,
`display.resolution`, `display.fullscreen`, `display.vsync`, `display.frame_cap`, `audio.master`, `audio.music`,
`audio.sfx`, `input.sensitivity`, `input.invert_y`, `language`,
`accessibility.subtitles`, `accessibility.text_scale`. Omit `path` to see them all; the change is
announced as a `SettingsChanged` message (readable with `events.read`).

An extension's settings resource (`declare_settings`, [extensions](book/agents/plugins.md)) is reached by its extension id:
`{ "path": "dialogue.max_line_chars" }` reads one field and `{ "path": "dialogue" }` the whole value; answers add
`provider: "extension:dialogue"`. A `GameSettings` field of the same name wins. An extension settings write is live and is
saved to the user settings file under `extensions.<id>` (the RON text of the whole resource); at the next start the
saved value wins over `[extensions.settings.<id>]` of `Regia.toml` (ADR-7237). `settings.get { "path": "extensions" }`
shows what is saved.

Scene motion and the extra buses (ADR-3464) use the same methods. Further paths:
`accessibility.camera_shake_scale` (`0` to `1`), `accessibility.motion_blur` (a bool, or null to leave the
profile's bit), `accessibility.fov_override_deg` (degrees, or null for the camera's own value),
`accessibility.vibration_scale` (`0` to `1`), `accessibility.reduced_motion` (also zeros shake and head bob and
forces motion blur off), `audio.voice`, `audio.ambience`, `audio.mute_master`, `audio.mute_music`,
`audio.mute_sfx`, `audio.mute_voice`, `audio.mute_ambience`. `input.sensitivity` and `input.invert_y` apply only
when `config/input.ron` names the action in `look_actions`; otherwise the game reads them. The assist maps
(`accessibility.input_assists`, `input_assists_by_player`, `input_assists_by_gamepad`) are not reflected: set
them with `input.assists`.

## Sim bridge

`sim.counters` is the bridge instrumentation and the app clock — the raw material for DO27 rule A1
(`docs/specs/25` § 3), the frame-rate-independence check:

```json
sim.counters {}
→ { "frames": 240, "submit_input_calls": 240, "snapshot_reads": 240, "snapshot_ticks": 240,
    "events_drained": 3, "input_edges": 3, "elapsed_secs": 4.0,
    "reactions": { "vfx": 2, "vfx_unknown": 0, "decals": 2, "decals_unknown": 0, "sounds": 2,
                   "sounds_refused": 0, "announcer_lines": 1, "announcer_rejected": 0,
                   "unplaced": 0, "no_subsystem": 0 } }
```

`reactions` counts what the event router applied (`config/events.ron`): `Vfx` effects spawned and
`Decal` prefabs placed at the event's place, `SoundCue` voices started, `Announcer` lines started
or queued, and the misses: an unknown effect, prefab or cue (`*_unknown`, `sounds_refused`; a placed
cue past its range, 50 m unless the route gives `SoundCue` a `max_distance`, is refused too), a
rejected announcer line, a placed reaction of an event the sim gave no place (`unplaced`, see
`ExternalSim::event_place`) and a reaction whose subsystem is not in the app (`no_subsystem`).
Check a route: queue the event, `wait_until` the matching count rises.

`sim.check_framerate_independence` compares the sim-side tick rate of two measurement windows
taken at different frame rates and fails if they diverge beyond a tolerance (default 2 %):

```json
{ "a": { "ticks": 120, "wall_secs": 2.0 }, "b": { "ticks": 119, "wall_secs": 2.0 } }
→ { "a_rate": 60.0, "b_rate": 59.5, "ratio": 1.0084033613445378, "tolerance": 0.02, "pass": true }
```

`ratio` is `max(rate) / min(rate)`. `1.0` is a perfect match. `pass: false` means the simulation
advances faster or slower when the frame rate changes — a bug for a lockstep/rollback sim.
`sim.counters` needs `regia_framework::sim_bridge::SimBridgePlugin` (it reads `SimCounters`) and the
app clock. `sim.check_framerate_independence` does not read that plugin: it compares the two windows
in the call. With no `Time` resource it is `NOT_FOUND` (`no Time in this app`). The `sim_bridge` capability
in `agent.hello` appears when the plugin is installed.

## Threaded sim host

A game that runs its sim on `regia_framework::sim_host::ThreadedSimHost` and inserts the host's
`handle()` as a resource (`SimHostHandle`) gets three methods. Without the handle each answers
`F0003`.

`sim.host_status` reads the host's counters:

```json
sim.host_status {}
→ { "running": true, "panicked": false, "held": false, "manual": false, "tick_ns": 16666667,
    "ticks": 3600, "publishes": 3601, "curr_tick": 3600, "granted": 0, "debt_drops": 1,
    "ticks_dropped": 12, "client_waits": 0, "events_dropped": 0, "edges_dropped": 0 }
```

`ticks` counts steps since boot and `publishes` pair changes (a hold publishes one still pair);
`curr_tick` is the sim's tick in the newest frame. `debt_drops` counts times a realtime host fell
behind past its catch-up and restarted its clock, `ticks_dropped` the whole ticks skipped that way.
`client_waits` counts wakes that did not step because the presentation's frame stamp was stale.
`events_dropped` and `edges_dropped` count what the bounded event queue and input bus dropped (a
held host drops all input it is offered).

`sim.host_hold { held }` pauses (`true`) or releases (`false`) the host and answers
`{ held, was_held, status }`. A held host publishes a still pair (`prev` and `curr` the same
frame), so a screenshot of a held match is stable.

`sim.host_step { ticks? }` grants `ticks` (default 1, at most 1 000 000) more steps to a host
started with `HostPacing::Manual` and answers `{ granted, status }`; `granted` counts every grant
not stepped yet. The steps run on the host's thread: `wait_until` `curr_tick` reaches the target.
A held host keeps its grants until released.

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `F0003` | No `SimHostHandle` resource in the app. |
| `sim_host_bad_ticks` | `sim.host_step`: `ticks` is 0 or above 1 000 000. |
| `sim_host_not_manual` | `sim.host_step`: the host steps on the wall clock (`HostPacing::Realtime`). Use `sim.host_hold` to pause it. |
| `sim_host_panicked` | `sim.host_hold`, `sim.host_step`: the sim panicked on the host thread and the host stopped (`logs.read` shows the panic). |
| `sim_host_stopped` | `sim.host_hold`, `sim.host_step`: the host thread has stopped; the game must start a new host. |

`sim.host_status` also reports the lockstep, snapshot and floating-point counters (ADR-8526):

```json
sim.host_status {}
→ { ..., "lockstep": true, "fp_env_supported": true, "fp_env_reset": false, "fp_checks": 3600,
    "fp_env_changed": 0, "frames_queued": 2, "frame_stalls": 1, "frames_refused": 0,
    "catch_up_budget": 0, "catch_up_ticks": 87, "snapshots": 1, "restores": 0,
    "last_step_ns": 412000, "max_step_ns": 1930000 }
```

### Lockstep pacing

A host started with `ThreadedSimHost::start_lockstep` (`lockstep: true`) steps exact per-tick
frames that a lockstep session pushes through its `LockstepFeed`: the frame for the next tick only,
each once and in order. `frames_queued` counts frames waiting; `frame_stalls` counts wakes that
found the next tick's frame missing and waited for it; `frames_refused` counts frames refused as a
duplicate, an old tick (`frame_out_of_order` in the Rust API) or past the queue cap.
`catch_up_budget` is the ticks a wake may step while the host catches up (0 when it is at the live
edge) and `catch_up_ticks` the extra ticks stepped that way. With `HostPacing::Lockstep { tick:
None }` the host is grant-paced (`manual: true`): `sim.host_step { ticks }` grants wakes, and a wake
steps one frame (or up to the catch-up budget). `last_step_ns` and `max_step_ns` time the sim's step
call alone; they are evidence, never a pass line.

A game whose sim implements `regia_detsim::replay::DetInputSim` wraps it in
`sim_host::DetInputHost<S, F, N>` to run it on this host (ADR-10062): the adapter owns the boundary
tick, steps through `replay::advance` (the step path a replay uses) and publishes frames of type `F`
(`DetInputFrame`, `()` for none). The frame queued for host tick `t` is the `TickInputs` of the sim's
tick `t - 1`. Its snapshot body is the boundary tick and then the sim's body, under the sim's tag with
the last byte's high bit flipped (`adapter_tag`), so `sim.host_snapshot` and `sim.host_restore`
work on it and a bare sim snapshot is refused with `bad_tag`.

### Snapshots and restore

`sim.host_snapshot { tick?, include_bytes? }` takes a framed snapshot (`regia_detsim::state`) on the host
thread, between two steps, and keeps it for `sim.host_restore`:

```json
sim.host_snapshot {}
→ { "tick": 5, "size": 56, "header_hash": "9c1f0e4b7d2a6c35", "tag": "counter",
    "state_version": 1, "kept": true }
```

`sim.host_snapshot { tick }` takes it at that tick boundary instead (ADR-10062): at once when the
sim is there, `sim_host_snapshot_tick_passed` when it is past it. For a tick still ahead the call
answers `{ "tick": 120, "pending": true, "kept": false }` and keeps the request; the host thread takes
the snapshot right after that tick's step, and the next `sim.host_snapshot { tick: 120 }` returns it
(still `pending` until then). A call with another tick replaces the request.

`header_hash` is the frame's body hash (hex): two snapshots of the same state have the same hash.
The bytes are never returned unless `include_bytes: true` in a debug build (`bytes_hex`); a release
build answers `host_snapshot_bytes_disabled`.

`sim.host_restore { bytes_hex? }` (debug builds only) loads a framed snapshot on the host thread,
replaces the sim, drops queued frames up to the restored tick and republishes a still pair there;
without `bytes_hex` it loads the snapshot the last `sim.host_snapshot` kept. It answers
`{ tick, status }`. A hold stays in place. Refused bytes leave the sim unchanged.

### FP environment

The host thread puts its floating-point environment back to the IEEE default before the first step
(`fp_env_reset: true` when it started under flush-to-zero, another rounding mode or traps, as a
thread spawned by an audio library's thread can) and checks it again every `fp_check_every` steps
(every step in debug builds, 600 in release builds): `fp_checks` counts the checks and
`fp_env_changed` the ones that found foreign code had changed it. `fp_env_supported` is `false` on a
target without a guard.

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `sim_host_no_snapshots` | `sim.host_snapshot`, `sim.host_restore`: the host was started without snapshots (`ThreadedSimHost::start`, or a sim without `DetState`). |
| `sim_host_snapshot_failed` | `sim.host_snapshot`: the sim's `DetState::save` failed; the message names the det-state code. |
| `sim_host_snapshot_tick_passed` | `sim.host_snapshot { tick }`: the sim is already past that tick. |
| `sim_host_restore_failed` | `sim.host_restore`: the bytes were refused (bad frame, tag, version, hash or tick; the message names the det-state code, such as `bad_hash`). The sim is unchanged. |
| `sim_host_busy` | `sim.host_snapshot`, `sim.host_restore`: the host thread did not answer within 10 s (a long step). |
| `host_snapshot_bytes_disabled` | `sim.host_snapshot`: `include_bytes` in a release build. |
| `host_restore_disabled` | `sim.host_restore`: a release build never lets an agent replace the running sim. |
| `host_snapshot_none` | `sim.host_restore`: no `bytes_hex` and no kept snapshot. |
| `sim_host_panicked`, `sim_host_stopped` | As above. |
## Sim bridge presentation

The sim bridge (`SimBridgePlugin`) poses its entities by `SimBridgeSettings` and each kind's blend
policy (ADR-8456, [Handedness and blending](book/systems/sim-bridge.md#handedness-and-blending)).
Without the bridge both methods answer `F0003`.

`sim.bridge_settings` reads them, with the blend counters since start:

```json
sim.bridge_settings {}
→ { "handedness": "left_handed_reflect_x", "teleport_distance": 10.0, "presentation_delay_ms": 16.666667,
    "default_blend": "lerp", "kinds": { "door": "hold", "hull": "lerp", "marker": "snap" },
    "stats": { "pair_reads": 600, "single_reads": 0, "lerped": 5400, "snapped": 600, "held": 590,
               "at_curr": 12, "teleports": 2 } }
```

- `handedness`: `right_handed` (nothing converted) or `left_handed_reflect_x` (the bridge reflects
  every snapshot pose and placed event across X once: positions `x → −x`, rotations
  `(w, x, y, z) → (w, x, −y, −z)`, yaw `θ → −θ`).
- `teleport_distance`: metres a `lerp` entity may move in one tick before it snaps to the newest
  pose; `null` never snaps.
- `presentation_delay_ms`: how far behind the newest publish the presentation draws (one 60 Hz tick
  by default).
- `kinds`: every kind in the bridge's `KindRegistry` and its policy; a kind not listed uses
  `default_blend`.
- `stats`: `pair_reads` and `single_reads` count frames the sim answered with a published pair or a
  single snapshot (a single snapshot is drawn as read: nothing is blended or counted below).
  `lerped`, `snapped`, `held` (drawn at the older frame) and `at_curr` (no older pose, or the weight
  reached the newest frame) count entity poses; `teleports` counts lerped entities snapped past the
  teleport distance. A manually paced `ThreadedSimHost` always draws its newest frame (`at_curr`).

`sim.set_bridge_settings { handedness?, teleport_distance?, presentation_delay_ms?, kind?, blend?,
dry_run? }` changes them from the next frame and answers `{ before, after, applied }` in the
`sim.bridge_settings` shape. `kind` and `blend` go together and set one registered kind's policy
(`lerp`, `snap` or `hold`). With `dry_run: true` nothing changes and `after` shows the result.

```json
sim.set_bridge_settings { "kind": "door", "blend": "hold", "dry_run": true }
→ { "before": { …, "kinds": { "door": "lerp" } }, "after": { …, "kinds": { "door": "hold" } }, "applied": false }
```

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `F0003` | No sim bridge in the app. |
| `F0002` | `kind` without `blend`, or `blend` without `kind`. |
| `sim_bad_handedness` | `handedness` is not `right_handed` or `left_handed_reflect_x`. |
| `sim_bad_teleport_distance` | `teleport_distance` is negative, not finite, or not a number or `null`. |
| `sim_bad_delay` | `presentation_delay_ms` is not a number from 0 to 10 000. |
| `sim_bad_blend` | `blend` is not `lerp`, `snap` or `hold`. |
| `sim_kind_unknown` | `kind` is not in the bridge's `KindRegistry` (`sim.bridge_settings` lists them). |

# Physics: raycasts, overlaps and closest points

Query the live physics world — find what a ray hits, who is inside a volume, what is
nearest to a point. Read-only, no gameplay driven. These need
`regia_physics::PhysicsPlugin`; `agent.hello` lists the `physics` capability when it is
installed. Without it the calls return `NOT_FOUND` with a hint.

## Raycast

`physics.raycast` casts a ray in meters, world space. `direction` need not be normalized.

```json
{ "origin": [0, 5, 0], "direction": [0, -1, 0] }
→ { "hit": { "entity": 4294967296, "point": [0, 0, 0],
             "normal": [0, 1, 0], "distance": 5.0 }, "count": 1 }
```

- `max_distance` (default 100) caps the cast; `exclude_sensors` (default `true`) skips
  trigger volumes — set it to `false` to include them.
- `all: true` returns every hit sorted by distance: `{ "hits": [...], "count": N }`.
- `hit` is `null` on a miss — a good `play.expect`-free way to assert "nothing above X".

## Overlap

`physics.overlap` lists every entity whose collider intersects a query shape:

```json
{ "shape": { "kind": "sphere", "radius": 1.0 }, "position": [0, 0.5, 0] }
{ "shape": { "kind": "box", "half_extents": [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] }, "position": [0, 0.25, 0] }
{ "shape": { "kind": "capsule", "half_height": 0.9, "radius": 0.3 }, "position": [0, 1.2, 0] }
→ { "entities": [4294967296, 8589934592], "count": 2 }
```

Shape dimensions are required: `radius` for spheres, `radius` and `half_height` for capsules,
and `half_extents` for boxes. Each dimension must remain positive and finite in `f32`; missing
or zero dimensions return `invalid_params`.

Sensors are included by default (`exclude_sensors: false`); use it to check trigger
occupancy: who is standing in the volume.

## Closest point

`physics.closest_point` projects a point onto the nearest collider surface:

```json
{ "point": [0, 2, 0] }
→ { "hit": { "entity": 4294967296, "point": [0, 0, 0], "is_inside": false,
             "normal": [0, 1, 0], "distance": 2.0 } }
```

`max_distance` bounds the search (default unlimited); `hit` is `null` when nothing is
within it. `is_inside: true` means the query point was inside the shape (or on its boundary).
`normal` is the outward unit normal of the nearest surface and `distance` the signed distance to it:
positive outside, negative inside (the penetration depth), so the nearest surface point is always
`point - normal * distance` with the query point (ADR-7233). Inside a shape, `point` is the query point
itself.

## Teleport

`physics.teleport` moves a rigid body to a pose on the next fixed step without simulating the way
there (ADR-7233): the jump makes no contact and starts no CCD sweep, a kinematic body gets no
velocity from it, and interpolation does not blend across it.

```json
{ "entity": 4294967296, "position": [0, 1, 0], "rotation": [0, 0, 0, 1], "velocity": "clear" }
→ { "entity": 4294967296, "position": [0, 1, 0], "rotation": [0, 0, 0, 1], "velocity": "clear" }
```

`position` is the entity's `Transform` translation (parent-relative when it has a parent);
`rotation` defaults to the current one. `velocity` is `keep` (default: the body carries on at the
velocity it had) or `clear` (it arrives at rest). An entity that does not exist or has no
`RigidBody` answers `F0003`; a bad `velocity` name or a zero or non-finite quaternion answers
`F0002`. Verify with `play.step` then `scene.get_entity` (the `Transform` is the target) or
`physics.stats`. Game code uses `regia_physics::teleport(world, entity, pose, TeleportVelocity::Keep)`,
`commands.entity(e).teleport(pose, TeleportVelocity::Clear)` (`TeleportCommands`) or
`ScriptCtx::teleport`; scripts also receive `ScriptEvent::ContactForce { entity, other, total_force }` on
both participants when a pair's contact force crosses a collider's `contact_force_threshold`.

## Working with the results

- Entity ids interop with everything: `scene.get_entity` for components, `play.expect`
  conditions, `scene.set_property` for edits.
- Positions are the **live stepped** collider poses (the same world the character
  controller moves against), not the interpolated render transforms.
- These three calls do not set `QueryFilter::from_layer`. With `PhysicsLayers` installed,
  a collider is hidden from them only when its collision-filter bits are empty (its layer
  collides with nothing, or its index is past the layer table). The query matrix is not
  consulted: a layer that nothing may query, but that still collides with something, stays
  visible. A query that passes `from_layer` is what applies the matrix (specs/15 § 3).
- To test dynamics (settling, stacking), pause and step first: `play.pause` then
  `play.step { "frames": 120 }`, then raycast to check where things landed.

## World stats and determinism

`physics.stats` reports what the physics world is doing (no parameters):

```json
{}
→ { "bodies": 22, "dynamic": 21, "kinematic": 0, "fixed": 1,
    "awake": 0, "sleeping": 21, "ccd_bodies": 0,
    "colliders": 22, "sensors": 0, "joints": 0, "contact_pairs": 35,
    "steps": 1200, "last_step_ms": 0.08,
    "non_finite_inputs": 0,
    "solver_iterations": 4, "ccd_substeps": 1,
    "digest": "9c1e0b7d44a2f310" }
```

- `awake` / `sleeping` count dynamic bodies only. A settled pile should be all
  `sleeping`: asleep bodies cost no solver time. A pile that never sleeps is
  jittering. Check stacking with `play.step`, then `physics.stats`.
- `non_finite_inputs` counts non-finite poses, body fields, velocities, forces and
  impulses dropped at the rapier seam (ADR-1507): rapier never sees them, so one NaN
  `Transform` cannot poison a whole pile. Zero in a healthy app; a growing count means
  a script, a deserialized scene or a networked value is writing NaN or infinity. Find
  the writer, fix it at the source — the guard keeps the world alive, it does not make
  the value meaningful.
- `last_step_ms` is the wall time of the last rapier step alone. Sync and write-back are
  not included; the frame profile has those. Use it to compare scene sizes, not as a
  budget check.
- `digest` is a 64-bit hash of every body's pose, velocities and sleep flag, bit-exact,
  in 16 hex digits. Two runs of the same build with the same inputs have the same digest
  at the same `steps`. To check that a scene replays deterministically, reset or reload
  it, step the same number of frames, and compare digests. A mismatch means something
  fed different inputs, for example wall-clock time or unordered iteration in gameplay
  code.
- `solver_iterations` and `ccd_substeps` echo `PhysicsSettings`. Raise
  `solver_iterations` (default 4) for tall stacks, long chains and large mass ratios.
  Raise `ccd_substeps` (default 1) so a fast CCD body keeps the rest of its motion after
  an impact. Both are set by the game in `PhysicsSettings`; the protocol only reads them.
  A CCD body is swept against static geometry and against bodies without `ccd` where they
  end the step, not against another CCD body: two fast projectiles fired at each other can
  pass through (ADR-1387).

Without `PhysicsPlugin` the call returns `NOT_FOUND` with a hint, like the queries.
