# Animation: animator state and graph parameters

See what every animated rig is doing and drive its anim graph while the game runs. The calls
need `regia_animation::AnimationPlugin` and a rig with an `Animator`; entity ids come from
`anim.list` (or `scene.query_entities`). A rig without an animator returns `NOT_FOUND` with a
hint.

## List rigs

`anim.list` returns every animator with the same summary `anim.get_state` gives for one:

```json
{}
→ { "count": 2, "animators": [ { "entity": 4294967310, "source": "graph", "state": "Loop", ... } ] }
```

## Read one animator

`anim.get_state` reports the current state-machine state (`null` when the graph root is not a
state machine), the parameters object below, the graph's declarations
(name, type, default), the root motion of the last evaluation plus what is pending for the
character controller, and the ragdoll mode and shown physics weight. Each kind lives in its own
map. The object has one key per name: when the same name was stored as more than one kind, the
later kind in the order float, int, bool, vec2, vec3, trigger replaces the earlier one.
`Animator::set` writes the Rust value's kind and does not clear the other maps, so a float
condition still reads the float while this object can show the later kind. An explicit type that
contradicts the graph's declaration is refused; that call is below.

```json
{ "entity": 4294967310 }
→ { "entity": 4294967310, "source": "graph", "state": "Loop", "transition": null,
    "clip": null, "speed": 1.0,
    "parameters": { "Speed": { "type": "float", "value": 1.6 },
                    "Land": { "type": "trigger", "value": false } },
    "declared": [ { "name": "Speed", "type": "float", "default": 0.0 } ],
    "root_motion": { "delta": [0, 0, -0.024], "yaw": 0.0, "pending": [0, 0, -0.024],
                     "pending_seconds": 0.016 },
    "ragdoll": { "mode": "powered", "blend": 0.0, "weight": 0.0, "bodies": 11, "reacting": 0,
                 "recovering": false } }
```

`transition` is `null` unless the first state machine is mid-transition, when it is
`{ machine, from, to, progress, blend, inertial_offset }`. `blend` is `crossfade`, `inertialize`
or `inertialize_spring`. See [Inertialized transitions](book/agents/inertialization.md).
`clip` is `{ name, duration, looping, morph_tracks }` for single-clip animators. `root_motion` is `null`
until the first evaluation; `ragdoll` is `null` without a `Ragdoll` component.

## Set a parameter

`anim.set_param` writes one parameter; the graph reads it on the next frame. The type is
`type` when given, else the graph's declaration, else inferred from `value` (number → float,
boolean → bool, `[x, y]` → vec2, `[x, y, z]` → vec3). Fire a trigger with
`"type": "trigger"` (the value is ignored); it resets when a transition consumes it. Passing a
`type` that contradicts the declaration is `INVALID_PARAMS`.

```json
{ "entity": 4294967310, "name": "Speed", "value": 6.0 }
→ { "entity": 4294967310, "name": "Speed", "type": "float", "before": 1.6, "after": 6.0 }
{ "entity": 4294967310, "name": "Land", "type": "trigger" }
→ { ..., "type": "trigger", "before": false, "after": true }
```

It needs the `play` permission (it drives the running game).

## Verifying a transition

Set the parameter, wait for the state, then look:

1. `anim.set_param { entity, name: "Speed", value: 6.0 }`
2. Step or let the game run (`play.step`), then poll `anim.get_state` until `state` is
   `"Run"` (`play.wait_until` reads reflected components; `Animator` is not reflected).
3. `seeing.screenshot` to check the pose by eye.

## Ragdolls

`anim.get_state`'s `ragdoll` (and `anim.list`'s) reports the mode, the authored `blend`, the
shown physics `weight`, the built `bodies`, how many bones are `reacting` to a hit, and whether
a get-up is `recovering` (the fallen pose still easing out). Two methods drive it (both need the `play` permission):

- `anim.ragdoll_set { entity, mode?, blend?, blend_time?, strength?, tracking_time?,
  recover_snap? }` switches the mode (`kinematic` hit boxes, `powered` hit reactions, `limp`
  death, `active` motor-driven balance) and tunes it. `blend` and `strength` are 0..=1, `blend_time` >= 0, `tracking_time` > 0.
  Every field is checked before any is applied, so a refused call changes nothing; a call with
  no field is refused. Going limp keeps the animated momentum (a run carries into the fall).
  Switching from `limp` back to `kinematic` or `powered` is the get-up: the bodies re-pin to the
  animation, the rig moves (x/z and yaw) to where the root body lies when `recover_snap` is true
  (the default), and the fallen pose blends out over `blend_time`.
- `anim.ragdoll_hit { entity, joint, impulse, reaction?, recover? }` applies `impulse`
  (`[x, y, z]`, kg·m/s) to the bone nearest `joint` and raises that bone's and its children's
  physics weight to `reaction` (0..=1, default 1), decaying over `recover` seconds (> 0,
  default 1). A joint the rig's skeleton does not have is refused.

```json
{ "method": "anim.ragdoll_set", "params": { "entity": 4294967310, "mode": "limp" } }
→ { "entity": 4294967310, "mode": "limp", "blend": 0.0, "weight": 0.0, "bodies": 11,
    "reacting": 0, "recovering": false }
```

Both answer `F0003` for a missing entity or one without a `Ragdoll`, and `F0002` for a bad
value. Hits from gameplay go through `regia_framework::ragdoll::RagdollHit`, the same message
`anim.ragdoll_hit` writes. Bones with `RagdollLimits` get swing-twist joint limits centred on the
bind pose; the summary also reports `settled`, `face_up` and `frozen`, and `anim.ragdoll_settings`
sets the limits switch and the simulated-ragdoll budget (refusing a non-boolean `joint_limits` with
`ragdoll_bad_flag` and a bad `max_simulated` with `ragdoll_bad_budget`; see [character physics](book/agents/character-physics.md),
ADR-1693).

## Contact curves in `anim.clip_report` (ADR-8308)

Each clip of `anim.clip_report` lists its cooked foot-contact curves under `contact_curves`, one entry
per curve named `contact.<foot joint>`: `name`, `joint` (the foot joint), `keys` (stored keys),
`planted_share` (share of the clip's frames where the curve is at or above 0.5) and `touchdowns`
(rising edges inside the clip). An empty list means the clip has none (the source's `.meta` did not set
`contact_curves`, or no feet were found; the cook warns). No new error codes: the method's existing
errors apply. A walk cooked with contact curves shows two entries with `planted_share` near the gait's
duty factor and about one touchdown per foot per cycle:

```json
anim.clip_report { "entity": 4294967310, "clip": "walk", "compression": false }
```

The curves feed the foot planter (see [foot planting](book/agents/foot-planting.md)).

## Locomotion warp nodes

`anim.get_state` (and each `anim.list` row) has a `warps` list: one object per `StrideWarp` or `OrientationWarp`
graph node (`.animgraph.ron` v4, ADR-8540), depth first, with the node's debug path and what it did on the latest
frame. Before the first evaluation the nodes are reported at rest (ratio 1, turn 0); a single-clip animator or a
graph without warp nodes gives `[]`.

```json
"warps": [
  { "path": "root", "kind": "orientation_warp", "active": true, "delta": 0.35, "clip_heading": 0.0 },
  { "path": "root/inner", "kind": "stride_warp", "active": true, "mode": "pose", "ratio": 1.3,
    "clip_speed": 1.3, "ground_speed": 1.69, "pelvis_drop": 0.012 }
]
```

`ratio` is the smoothed ground-speed over clip-speed ratio (the clock multiplier in `rate` mode, the stride scale in
`pose` mode); `clip_speed` and `ground_speed` are m/s; `pelvis_drop` is how far `pose` mode lowered the hips
(meters); `delta` is the lower-body turn and `clip_heading` the inner root-motion heading (radians, 0 = forward,
counter-clockwise). To check a warp: set the ground-speed or heading parameter with `anim.set_param`, step with
`play.step`, then poll `anim.get_state` until `ratio` or `delta` settles.

| warning (log) | when |
|---|---|
| `animgraph_warp_no_root_motion` | a warp node's inner graph has no root motion while the warp should act (the node passes the pose); once per node and parameter |

<!-- source: book/agents/inertialization.md -->
# Inertialized transitions: author, observe, verify

Inertialized transitions are a per-transition `blend` mode of the anim-graph state machine
(`Crossfade` | `Inertialize` | `InertializeSpring`, `book/user-guide/inertialization.md`).

## Author

`editor.anim_transition` takes `blend` (default `Crossfade`). `duration` is the decay time:

```json
{"method": "editor.anim_transition", "params": {"machine": 1, "from": "Air", "to": "Land",
  "conditions": [{"Bool": {"param": "Air", "value": false}}], "duration": 0.15,
  "blend": "Inertialize"}}
→ { "index": 3, "transitions": [ { "from": "Air", "to": "Land", ..., "blend": "Inertialize" } ] }
```

Every transition in the response carries `blend`, including `"Crossfade"` (the file omits the
default). Switch an existing transition with `op: "set", index`. A layer's weight easing is the
layer's `weight_inertialize` field (seconds; edit it with `editor.anim_set_node` on the layer
node's `layers` data).

## Observe

`anim.get_state` has a `transition` object for the first state machine while a transition runs:

```json
{ "entity": 4294967310 }
→ { ..., "state": "Land",
    "transition": { "machine": "root/base", "from": "Air", "to": "Land", "progress": 0.4,
                    "blend": "inertialize", "inertial_offset": 0.21 }, ... }
```

`blend` is `crossfade`, `inertialize` or `inertialize_spring`. `inertial_offset` is the largest
joint rotation offset (radians) still added on top of the target state. It falls to 0 as the
transition settles. It can stay above 0 after a cross-fade interrupts an inertialized transition;
in that case `transition` has only `machine`, `blend` and `inertial_offset`. With no transition
running, `transition` is `null`.

In Rust and in the editor's preview, `regia_animation::debug::graph_debug` reports the same
values per machine: `NodeDebugState::StateMachine { blend, inertial_offset, .. }`. While a
transition is inertialized, the source state's node is inactive and has weight 0.

## Verify a transition

1. `anim.set_param { entity, name: "Air", value: false }`.
2. Step (`play.step`) and poll `anim.get_state` until `transition.blend == "inertialize"`, then
   until `transition` is `null` (settled after `duration`).
3. Capture frames across the switch (`seeing.screenshot` each step) and compare them by eye. An
   inertialized switch shows no single-frame jump.

The numeric proof lives in `crates/regia_animation/tests/inertialize.rs`. The test checks that
the velocity jump at the switch, including on interruption, shrinks with the frame time, while a
0.05 s cross-fade's does not. `regia_asset_pipeline`'s `inertialize_capture` example plots a
joint's angle and angular speed through walk → aim, run → land and run → death on DO27's pilot
rig, and times many characters with each mode.

<!-- source: book/agents/spring-bones.md -->
# Spring bones: hair, tails and cloth strips

Secondary motion for skinned rigs: chains of joints that lag, swing and settle after the animation has posed
the body, and are pushed out of body colliders. The calls need `regia_animation::AnimationPlugin` and a rig with
a `SpringBones` component (built from a `.spring.ron` setup, see `docs/formats/spring-ron.md`).

```rust,wrap
# use regia::prelude::*;
# use regia_core::math::{Vec3, Quat};
# use regia_scene::Transform;
# let mut commands: Commands = todo!();
# let world: &mut World = todo!();
# let app: &mut App = todo!();
# use regia_animation::{SpringBoneSetup, SpringBones};
# let rig: Entity = todo!();
let setup = SpringBoneSetup::from_ron_str(&std::fs::read_to_string("fox.glb.spring.ron")?)?;
world.entity_mut(rig).insert(SpringBones::new(setup));
```

The solver runs after the animation and any ragdoll blend, before the joint transforms and the skin palette are
written, and writes **rotations only** (bone lengths stay the animator's). It simulates in world space, so moving or
turning the rig makes a chain swing, in fixed internal steps (60 Hz by default): the result depends on how much
time passed, not on the frame rate.

## Read

`anim.spring_list` returns every rig with spring bones:

```json
{}
→ { "count": 1, "rigs": [ { "entity": 4294967310, "enabled": true, "frozen": false, "reduced": false,
      "step_hz": 60.0, "steps_last_frame": 1, "problems": [],
      "colliders": [ { "name": "head", "joint": "head" } ],
      "chains": [ { "name": "ponytail", "joints": ["tail_0", "tail_1", "tail_2"], "enabled": true,
                    "bound": true, "stiffness": 0.15, "damping": 0.1, "gravity_dir": [0, -1, 0],
                    "gravity_power": 9.81, "hit_radius": 0.02, "colliders": ["head"],
                    "positions": [ [0.0, 1.7, 0.0], [0.0, 1.62, -0.05], [0.0, 1.55, -0.1] ] } ] } ] }
```

`positions` are the chain joints in world space (empty before the first frame, while frozen or when the chain is
unbound). `problems` explains a chain that did not bind: a joint missing from the skeleton, a joint that is not a
child of the previous one, an unknown collider. `frozen` and `reduced` show the distance tier from
`AnimLodCamera`.

## Tune

`anim.spring_set` changes one chain live and keeps its simulation state:

```json
{ "entity": 4294967310, "chain": "ponytail", "stiffness": 0.4, "gravity_power": 4.0 }
```

Fields: `stiffness` (0..1: `1` keeps the animated pose, `0` is a free rope), `damping` (0..1), `gravity_power`
(m/s²), `gravity_dir`, `hit_radius` (metres) and `enabled`. Without `chain`, `enabled` switches the whole
component. Bad values return `INVALID_PARAMS` and change nothing. An entity without `SpringBones` or an unknown
`chain` is `F0003` (not found); the same goes for `anim.spring_reset`.

`anim.spring_reset` re-seeds the chains from the animated pose next frame; call it after teleporting a rig.

## Verify

Step a few frames, then `anim.spring_list` and check `positions` against where the hair should hang, or take a
screenshot (`seeing.screenshot`) and look. For collisions put a collider on the body bone, let the chain settle and
check that every `positions` entry is at least `radius + hit_radius` from the collider's surface. To prove
frame-rate independence, step the same time at two fixed deltas and compare `positions`.

## Example calls

Example calls (`regia agent call <method> '<params json>'`; entity ids come from `scene.query_entities`):

```text
anim.spring_reset {"entity": 4294967310}   # re-seed the chains from the animated pose next frame
```

<!-- source: book/agents/character-rig.md -->
# Character rigs: attach, observe, verify

Twist chains, helper joints, drivers and pose-space correctives (`.drivers.ron`,
`docs/formats/drivers-ron.md`, [user guide](book/user-guide/character-rig.md)) and skeleton profiles
(`.skelprofile.ron`).

## Attach a rig document

`anim.rig_attach { entity, ron, morphs?, dry_run? }` compiles the document against the rig's skeleton and attaches it.
Use `dry_run: true` first: it reports every unresolved joint or morph name in one error and attaches nothing.

```json
{"method": "anim.rig_attach", "params": {"entity": 4294967310, "dry_run": true, "ron": "(format_version: 1, drivers: [...])"}}
→ { "entity": 4294967310, "attached": false, "twists": ["forearm_twist"], "helpers": [], "drivers": ["elbow_bulge"],
    "correctives": [], "materials": [], "morphs": ["elbow_bulge"] }
```

`morphs` is the morph bank's names in bank order (so the weights line up with `MorphWeights`); by default the document's own
names in first-appearance order.

Parameter details: `entity` is a required integer entity id. `ron` is required string content for
`anim.rig_attach` and may be at most 16 MiB; `morphs` is an optional array of at most 1024 strings,
defaulting to the document's morph names in first-appearance order; `dry_run` is an optional boolean
(default `false`). `anim.rig_state` takes only the required `entity`. `anim.profile_check` takes the
required `entity` and requires at least one of optional string `profile` (`generic-humanoid` or
`vrm`) or optional string `ron` (at most 16 MiB); when both are present, `ron` takes precedence.

## Observe

`anim.rig_state { entity }` reports the last evaluated frame:

```json
→ { "evaluated": true,
    "twists": [{ "name": "forearm_twist", "value": 90.0 }],
    "helpers": [{ "name": "elbow_pad", "value": 100.0 }],
    "drivers": [{ "name": "elbow_bulge", "input": 100.0, "output": 1.0 }],
    "correctives": [{ "name": "elbow_crease", "activations": [1.0] }],
    "materials": { "wrinkle_elbow": 1.0 } }
```

Twist and helper values are degrees. Driver `input` is in the input's unit (degrees for joint inputs), `output` is the value
written (after the driver's `weight`). Corrective `activations` are the kernel values per example pose (1 at the example,
falling to 0 away from it).

## Verify a rig

1. `anim.rig_attach` with `dry_run: true`; fix any listed names; attach.
2. Pose the rig with `anim.set_param` (a parameter that drives a clip or a driver's `Param` input) and step (`play.step`).
3. `anim.rig_state`: a driver's `input` is the measured joint angle; its `output` should equal the curve's value there.
   A corrective's `activations` entry for a pose should read ~1 when the joints sit at that pose.
4. Capture the frame (`seeing.screenshot`) and compare the joint with and without the document (detach by respawning).

## Skeleton profiles

`anim.profile_check { entity, profile | ron }` checks the rig's skeleton against a built-in (`generic-humanoid`, `vrm`) or a
`.skelprofile.ron` text.

```json
{"method": "anim.profile_check", "params": {"entity": 4294967310, "profile": "vrm"}}
→ { "ok": false, "matched": 18, "missing_required": ["leftHand"], "missing_optional": ["leftThumbDistal", ...],
    "missing_roles": ["leftHand"], "extra_joints": ["paw"], "guessed": [], "hierarchy": [],
    "rest_pose": { "ok": false, "expected_deg": 0.0, "tolerance_deg": 10.0,
                   "arms": [{ "side": "left", "elevation_deg": 44.9 }, { "side": "right", "elevation_deg": 45.1 }] } }
```

`guessed` lists profile joints matched by the name guess rather than the name or an alias: review them. `rest_pose` is
`null` when the profile has no rule.

## Errors

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `F0002` | Missing or invalid parameters, malformed `.drivers.ron` or `.skelprofile.ron`, an unknown profile, or a profile that fails validation. |
| `F0003` | `entity` is not a skinned rig, or `anim.rig_state` is called before drivers are attached. |

These are the handler's shared protocol codes. A skeleton that simply fails to match a valid profile
is a successful `anim.profile_check` result with `ok: false`, not an error.

## Failing call

This headless lavapipe call returns the captured invalid-entity error:

```text
$ regia agent call anim.profile_check '{"entity":0,"profile":"vrm"}' --project samples/boot_probe
error: method call failed: 0 is not an entity id (-32602): {"code":"F0002","hint":"check the method's parameters in the agent guide"}
```

The numeric proof lives in `crates/regia_animation/tests/character_rig.rs`: the largest roll step along a forearm drops from
90 to 30 degrees with twist joints, and pose-space correctives reproduce their authored weights at the example pose.

<!-- source: book/agents/morph-weights.md -->
# Morph weights: blend shapes, expression layers, GPU counters

Read and set the morph (blend shape) weights of a mesh while the game runs, then check the result
with a screenshot. Weights are per target, by name (`extras.targetNames`) or by index. The renderer
deforms the mesh on the next frame.

## List morphed entities

`anim.morph_weights` without an entity lists every entity with morph weights, targets or layers,
and the renderer's morph counters for its last frame:

```json
{}
→ { "count": 1,
    "instances": [ { "entity": 4294967310, "names": ["aa", "oh", "blink"], "weights": [0, 0.4, 0],
                     "animated": true, "layers": null,
                     "targets": { "count": 3, "vertex_count": 5120, "moved_vertices": 812,
                                  "gpu_bytes": 98112, "mode": "game" } } ],
    "renderer": { "instances": 1, "drawn": 1, "dispatched": 0, "dispatched_vertices": 0,
                  "mismatched": 0, "waiting_pipeline": 0, "gpu_bytes": 101860,
                  "buffers_created": 3, "motion_instances": 0, "counted": 0 } }
```

- `dispatched` counts the instances deformed last frame (their weights changed); steady weights
  dispatch nothing.
- `mismatched` counts draws whose mesh does not have the targets' vertex count (another LOD): they
  draw undeformed.
- `waiting_pipeline` is non-zero only while the morph pass compiles in the background (the mesh
  draws undeformed meanwhile).
- `buffers_created` grows once per mesh and per instance (two more for a rigid instance: its
  motion copies), never per frame and never on a weight change.
- `motion_instances` counts the instances drawn with motion vectors last frame (ADR-2652): on a
  frame whose weights change, the velocity pass draws the instance's last and current deformation,
  so TAA and TSR reproject a morphing face from where it was. Steady weights write no motion and do
  no work. A skinned morph writes its skinning motion only, and a material graph with a vertex stage
  its own.
- `counted` counts the instances drawn last frame from a counted mesh's upload (ADR-7721): a
  `MeshRenderer::counted` with the `MorphTargets` its upload packed
  (`AssetMeshUploads::morph_targets`). Its deformed copy is a GPU copy of the adopted vertex
  buffer, so the asset keeps no CPU vertices.

`{ "entity": id }` returns the same row for one entity.

## Set weights

```json
{ "entity": 4294967310, "weights": { "blink": 1.0, "0": 0.3 } }
→ { "path": "layer", "before": { ... }, "after": { ... }, "note": "layers compose into weights at the next frame's animation apply" }
```

- On a plain mesh entity, `weights` are written into `MorphWeights` (`path: "weights"`).
- On an animated rig, or one with `MorphLayers`, they go into an override layer named `"agent"`
  (`path: "layer"`), so the animation does not overwrite them. Remove it with
  `{ "entity": id, "remove_layer": true }`.
- `weights` is an object (name or index → weight) or an array in target order. An unknown name is
  an `INVALID_PARAMS` error that lists the target names. Indices run 0..4096 (weights are stored
  densely, so an index sizes the weight list); a larger index or a longer array is `INVALID_PARAMS`.

## Expression layers

```json
{ "entity": 4294967310, "layer": "smile", "mode": "additive", "layer_weight": 0.5,
  "weight_param": "Smile", "weights": { "mouthSmile": 1.0 } }
{ "entity": 4294967310, "normalized_sets": [ { "name": "visemes", "targets": ["aa", "oh", "ee"] } ] }
{ "entity": 4294967310, "clamp": [0, 1] }
```

Layers apply in order over the animator's weights: `override` moves each weight toward the value by
the layer weight, `additive` adds `value × weight`. `weight_param` multiplies the layer weight by a
float graph parameter (set it with `anim.set_param`). Every weight is then clamped (`clamp`, default
`[0, 1]`; `null` turns it off), and each normalized set that sums past 1 is scaled to 1.

## Verify

1. `anim.set_morph_weights` on the face mesh.
2. `play.step` one frame (or wait a frame).
3. `seeing.screenshot` and compare; `anim.morph_weights` shows `dispatched: 1` for that frame.

See [Morph targets and skinned meshes](book/user-guide/morph-targets.md).

## Per-node tracks (several morphing meshes in one file)

A glTF `weights` animation channel targets a node, and that node's mesh owns the morph targets. Regia Engine
keeps the node on every imported track, so a file with two morphing meshes animated by one clip gives each
mesh its own weights.

- `anim.morph_weights { entity }` on a mesh spawned from a glTF reports `source_node` (`{ index, name }`, the
  node in the source file) and `node_driver`: what plays the per-node tracks, with its clip name and tracks.
  `node_driver.kind` is `player` (a `NodeMorphPlayer`, for models without a skeleton; it also reports `time` and
  `playing`) or `animator` (the rig's `Animator` on the entity or an ancestor).
- `anim.get_state` reports the single clip's `morph_tracks`: `[{ node: { index, name } | null, target, keys }]`.
  `node: null` is an old-style track that applies to every morph mesh of the rig.
- A mesh whose weights a per-node driver rewrites every frame takes `anim.set_morph_weights` as an override layer
  (`path: "layer"`), like an animated rig.
- Expression layers (`MorphLayers`) on a node's mesh compose over the clip's weights for that node.

Import rules (`regia_asset_pipeline::gltf_anim`): the channel's output count must be keys x the node mesh's morph
target count (x3 for cubic spline). A mismatch fails the import of that file with the channel error
`animation <name> channel <n>: morph weight output count <N> does not match <K> keys x <T> morph targets`
(cubic spline adds ` x 3 (cubic spline)`). A `weights` channel on a node without a mesh or morph targets is an
import warning (`GltfAnimationImport::warnings`) and the channel is skipped. Cooked per-node clips are the
sub-assets `<file>#nodeclip/<animation>`; clips cooked before ADR-297 load with every track unbound, so they play on
every morph mesh exactly as before (`regia upgrade-project` rewrites them at clip format v2).

## Example calls

Example calls (`regia agent call <method> '<params json>'`; entity ids come from `scene.query_entities`):

```text
anim.morph_weights {}                                               # list morphed entities
anim.set_morph_weights {"entity": 4294967310, "weights": {"blink": 1.0}}
```

<!-- source: book/agents/eyes-and-bind-poses.md -->
# Eye gaze and per-instance bind poses: drive and verify

User guide: `book/user-guide/eyes-and-bind-poses.md`. These calls need `regia_animation::AnimationPlugin` and a
rig with an `Animator` and a `SkinnedMesh`. Entity ids come from `anim.list`.

## Gaze

`anim.gaze_set` points the eyes. It creates the `Gaze` from the skeleton's eye joints by name when the rig has none
(`INVALID_PARAMS` if no `eye_l`/`eye_r`-style joints exist). `target` is `[x, y, z]` (world), an entity id, or
`null` (eyes return to rest). Optional `weight`, `convergence`, `saccade_speed`.

```json
{"method": "anim.gaze_set", "params": {"entity": 4294967310, "target": [1.0, 1.7, -2.0]}}
→ { "entity": 4294967310, "target": { "point": [1, 1.7, -2] }, "weight": 1.0, "valid": false, ... }
```

`valid` is false until the first frame solves it. Step (`play.step`) and read `anim.gaze_get`:

```json
{"method": "anim.gaze_get", "params": {"entity": 4294967310}}
→ { "target": { "point": [1, 1.7, -2] }, "valid": true, "error": 0.0004,
    "left":  { "yaw": -0.31, "pitch": 0.04, "goal_yaw": -0.31, "goal_pitch": 0.04, "saturated": false,
               "channels": { "up": 0.09, "down": 0.0, "in": 0.5, "out": 0.0 } },
    "right": { ... }, "lids": 2, "morphs": 4, "head_follow": false }
```

`error` is the worst angle (radians) between an eye's gaze and the direction to the target; it is near 0 unless the
target is outside the limits (`saturated: true`) or the eyes are still moving (`yaw` against `goal_yaw`).
`channels` are the eyelid-follow / eye-look morph weights already multiplied by `weight`.

Verify: set a target, `play.step` about 10 frames, `anim.gaze_get` until `error < 0.01`, then `seeing.screenshot` and
compare to a frame with `target: null`.

## Bind poses

```json
{"method": "anim.bind_pose_set", "params": {"entity": 4294967310, "scale": 1.15, "bone_scales": {"calf_l": 1.1}}}
→ { "overridden": true, "joints": 60, "ratio_min": 1.15, "ratio_max": 1.265,
    "changed": [ { "joint": "calf_l", "ratio": 1.265 }, ... ] }
```

`scale` multiplies every bone length, `bone_scales` the bone leading to the named joint (it multiplies `scale`).
Every factor must be greater than 0 (0 collapses the bones, a negative factor mirrors them). A rig with its own
proportions aims its eyes from where they are drawn, and gaze runs before the rig drivers and spring bones, so
twist and corrective drivers and head-rooted springs follow the gazed head.
`{"clear": true}` removes the instance data. `anim.bind_pose_get` reports `overridden`, the ratio range and the
joints that differ. A rig whose instance joint count differs from the skeleton shows `matches_skeleton: false` and is
rendered with the shared bind pose.

Verify: set a scale, `play.step`, take a screenshot, compare with `scale: 1.0`; the character is taller or longer
with the same animation and the skin stays attached (no stretched triangles, no detached limbs).

<!-- depth-2:method-reference -->

## Call reference

Parameters, results and error codes for every method on this page. Types and defaults come from the schema and handlers; limits include the contract. Error codes are in `data.code`; names explicitly labeled `data.reason` are additional handler reasons. Every method can also return `F0001`, `F0002`, `F0004`, `F0007` and `F0012`. The server can return `F0005`, `F0006`, `request_too_large`, or `F0008` when the method is not registered; see [protocol](book/agents/protocol.md).

Unless a lower or explicit method limit is listed, the dispatcher accepts at most 65,536 items in a top-level array parameter and 1,048,576 UTF-8 bytes in a string parameter. A limit violation returns `F0002`.

The request in each fence is the call that was sent with `regia agent call`.
The line under it is the host's answer.
A second fence tagged `json,ignore` is an error answer. Large fields are elided with `...`. A fence tagged `json,ignore` is a real call on a host or plugin method that the runtime schema does not list.


### `anim.bind_pose_get`

Whether a rig has its own bind pose (per-instance proportions) and how its bone lengths differ from the shared skeleton.

*Read, does not mutate.*

| Param | Type | Required | Default and limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `entity` | integer | yes | Rig entity id (from anim.list). |

Result: `{ entity, overridden, joints, matches_skeleton?, ratio_min?, ratio_max?, changed?: [{ joint, ratio }] }`.

Errors besides the universal codes: `F0003`.

```json
anim.bind_pose_get {"entity": 4294967310}
```

### `anim.gaze_set`

*Play, mutating.*

| Param | Type | Required | Default and limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `entity` | integer | yes | Rig entity id (from anim.list). |
| `target` | any | no | [x, y, z] world point, an entity id, or null (eyes return to rest). Omitted keeps the current target; a newly created gaze starts at rest. |
| `weight` | number | no | Finite blend with the animation; clamped to 0..1. Omitted keeps the current value. |
| `convergence` | number | no | Finite, clamped to 0..1: 0 = parallel eyes, 1 = each eye aims at the target. Omitted keeps the current value. |
| `saccade_speed` | number | no | Finite eye speed in radians per second; 0 = instant. Omitted keeps the current value. |

Result: `The anim.gaze_get object after the change.`.

```

```

<!-- capture:anim.gaze_set -->

## Workflow: aim the eyes, then restore the bind pose

1. Find a character with an Animator and SkinnedMesh, then call `anim.gaze_get`. `F0003` can mean a missing entity or gaze component; `anim.gaze_set` can create a gaze on a rig with recognizable eye joints.
2. `anim.gaze_set` the target position and weights, advance fixed frames with `play.step`, then read `anim.gaze_get` to check the weights and solved eye error.
3. `anim.bind_pose_get` for the joints the mesh was built with.
4. `anim.bind_pose_set` with bone_scales for the joints you mean to replace, then `anim.bind_pose_get` to confirm the changes.
5. Restore with `anim.bind_pose_set` and `clear: true`, and `anim.gaze_set` with `target: null`. Step and read both getters to confirm the shared bind pose and resting gaze.

<!-- source: book/agents/navigation.md -->
# Navigation: navmesh queries and dynamic obstacles

Inspect the navmesh and query paths without driving gameplay. `agent.hello` does not list a
navigation capability — probe with `nav.get_mesh`.

`nav.get_mesh`, `nav.add_obstacle` and `nav.remove_obstacle` need a `regia_nav::NavMesh` resource
(built with `NavMeshBuilder`). Without one they return `NOT_FOUND` (`F0003`) whose hint names
`NavMeshBuilder` and does not name `NavPlugin`.

`nav.find_path` and `nav.find_nearest` use that `NavMesh` when one is present. When the app has no
`NavMesh` and does have a `NavTileCache`, those two queries use the cache. With neither resource
they return the same `NOT_FOUND`.

Tile-cache methods (`nav.tile_cache_*`) return `data.reason` `nav_no_tile_cache` when there is no
cache. Crowd methods return `nav_no_mesh` or `nav_no_crowd` (see [navigation crowds](book/agents/navigation-crowds.md)).
Link methods prefer the cache when both resources exist (see [navigation links](book/agents/navigation-links.md)).

## Summary

`nav.get_mesh` reports the shape of the base mesh (obstacles are not reflected; every polygon has
four vertices, so `vertices` is `4 * polys`):

```json
{}
→ { "polys": 126, "vertices": 504, "regions": 1, "layers": 1, "off_mesh_links": 0,
    "bounds": { "min": [-13, -1, -13], "max": [13, 16, 13] },
    "agent": { "radius": 0.35, "height": 1.6, "max_climb": 0.5, "max_slope": 0.785 },
    "cell_size": 0.25 }
```

## Stacked surfaces

A mesh built with `NavMeshBuilder::build_layered` (more than one layer) keeps the walkable surfaces under
the top one too (ADR-8076): a tunnel floor under the ground, the ground under a bridge and each floor of
a building get polygons. `NavMeshBuilder::build` keeps the top surface only. `layers` in `nav.get_mesh` is
how many walkable layers the mesh was built from: `1` for a top-surface mesh, more where surfaces stack.
A surface needs the agent's `height` of headroom to count, so the floor under a low table stays
unwalkable, and a vertical wall through that headroom closes it, so the inside of a closed box does not
join the floor around it. Where an agent can step between a lower surface and one beside
it (the ground under a bridge and the ground next to it, a tunnel floor and its ramp), the polygons are
linked, and `nav.find_path` routes through.

On a stacked mesh `regions` counts groups of linked polygons. `nav.find_nearest` keeps the polygon
nearest in XZ, and among equally near polygons the one whose height is nearest the query point, so give
a point at the level you mean (a point in a tunnel finds the tunnel floor). A `NavTileCache` mesh has
one layer for now.

To check a level built with layers: call `nav.get_mesh` and expect `layers` above 1 when the level has
tunnels or overpasses, then `nav.find_nearest` with a point on the lower floor and a small `extents` y (say 0.5)
and expect a polygon at that floor's height.

## Layers and off-mesh links

Each walkable layer of a stacked floor is its own set of regions, contours and polygons. Bake with
`NavMeshBuilder::build_with_nav_level_cap(triangles, areas, volumes, max_nav_levels)`. A column with
more walkable levels than the setting fails the build (`invalid navmesh build input`, reason
`max_nav_levels exceeded: a column has more walkable levels than the setting`). `build_layered` still
drops surfaces past its count. Five storeys need the setting at 5 or above.

`NavAgentParams::pilot()` is the on-foot agent: radius 0.35 m, height 1.8 m, step 0.55 m.
`NavAgentParams::hover(radius)` is a hull: height is the radius plus 2 m, step 4 m. A hover bake
erodes one extra metre on each side, so a passage narrower than `2 * radius + 2` m is not on that
hull's mesh. `NavAgentParams::for_radius(radius)` keeps the pilot height and step at 1.5 m or below,
and uses the hover height with the pilot step above that.

`NavAreaCosts::passages()` sets area 60 (tunnel) to 0.75 and area 61 (flank) to 0.20. Assign it with
`NavMesh::set_area_costs`. A path of the same length prefers the tunnel. Both costs are below 1, so
the straight-line heuristic stays admissible.

Ladders and deck stairs are climb links. `pilot_layer_links` turns a `NavLayerLink` list into
bidirectional climb links for a pilot and returns nothing for any other agent, so a hull mesh does
not contain them. Each link's flags are `NavLinkFlags::PILOT` (bit 8) only, the snap radius is 0.5 m,
and the `user_id` is `0x4E414C00` plus the list index for a ladder or `0x4E415300` plus the index for
deck stairs. `NavQueryFilter::pilot()` allows the climb. `NavQueryFilter::hull()` does not. The
default filter allows every flag, so a climb that is on the mesh is usable until the filter says
otherwise. `NavQuery::locate_body` retries `find_nearest` at the body point, then 0.9 m below it,
then 1.8 m below it.

No new agent method. `nav.get_mesh` already reports `layers`. Hosts place ladders and stairs with
`nav.set_links` (kind `climb`, flag bit 8). `nav.links` and `nav.generate_links` are unchanged.

## Nearest point

`nav.find_nearest` snaps a point to the nearest walkable polygon:

```json
{ "point": [1.2, 1.0, -3.0], "extents": [2, 2, 2] }
→ { "poly": 42, "point": [1.2, 0.0, -3.0] }
```

`poly`/`point` are `null` when nothing is within `extents` (a half-extent box; default
`[2, 2, 2]`; each component must be in 0..=1000, so a negative component is refused with `F0002`). The vertical gate is strict: the same query with `y = 5.0` is 5 m above a floor at
`y = 0` and returns `{ "poly": null, "point": null }`.

## Paths

`nav.find_path` returns the smoothed waypoints (string-pulling), the polygon sequence and the
length:

```json
{ "from": [-5, 0, -5], "to": [5, 0, 5] }
→ { "path": { "waypoints": [[-5,0,-5], [0,0,0], [5,0,5]], "polys": [10, 12, 14], "length": 14.14 } }
```

`path` is `null` when either endpoint is off the mesh or no route exists (e.g. the corridor is
blocked).

## Dynamic obstacles

`nav.add_obstacle` records an axis-aligned box in the `NavObstacles` resource; `nav.remove_obstacle`
removes it (`{ "removed": false }` means a mesh is present but the id is unknown). Queries carve
the boxes on the fly, so blocked polygons are skipped by `nav.find_path` and `nav.find_nearest`,
but the stored mesh is unchanged: `nav.get_mesh` and the `nav_mesh` gizmo keep showing the base
polygons.

```json
{ "min": [-0.5, -1, -4], "max": [0.5, 2, 4] }   → { "id": 0, "obstacles": 1 }
{ "id": 0 }                                       → { "removed": true }
```

## Raycast

`nav.raycast` walks the mesh surface from `from` toward `to` (XZ; the height of `to` is ignored).
`from` snaps onto the nearest allowed polygon within `extents`; the walk then crosses polygons
through their shared edges and stops at the first edge with no neighbour (a wall) or whose
neighbour is in an area the `filter` leaves out (NM-1, ADR-8380):

```json
{ "from": [0, 0, 0], "to": [20, 0, 0] }
→ { "hit": true, "t": 0.4, "normal": [-1, 0, 0], "point": [8, 0, 0], "start": [0, 0, 0],
    "last_poly": 3, "path_polys": [0, 1, 3] }
```

`t` is the fraction of the segment from `start` (the snapped `from`) to `to` that was walked: the
wall's position when `hit`, else `1`. `normal` is the wall's unit normal in XZ, pointing back into
the walkable side (`[0, 0, 0]` when nothing was hit). `path_polys` lists every polygon crossed,
start polygon first; `last_poly` is the one the walk ended on. Off-mesh links are never taken: use
it for line-of-sight along the floor (can the agent walk straight there?), cover checks and
dash or charge abilities.

## Random points

`nav.random_point` draws seeded points. With no `center` every allowed polygon is picked in
proportion to its XZ area and the point is uniform inside it, so the points are uniform over the
walkable surface. With `center` and `radius` the points are uniform over the walkable surface
within `radius` (XZ) of `center`; `reachable_only: true` keeps only polygons connected to the
center's polygon, so islands (a rooftop, a closed room) never come up:

```json
{ "seed": 7, "count": 2, "center": [0, 0, 0], "radius": 5, "reachable_only": true }
→ { "seed": 7, "points": [{ "poly": 12, "point": [1.83, 0, -2.41] }, { "poly": 9, "point": [-3.02, 0, 0.77] }] }
```

The same `seed` (and mesh, filter and parameters) always gives the same points on every platform:
replay a wander target by storing the seed. `count` is 1..=4096 (default 1). `points` is empty
when no allowed polygon touches the circle.

## Partial paths

`nav.find_path` with `"partial": true` still answers when the goal cannot be reached: the path
then runs to the reachable polygon nearest the goal (3D distance to its closest point, ties to
the lower polygon index) and ends at that polygon's point nearest the goal. `status` says which:

```json
{ "from": [-6, 0, 0], "to": [3, 0, 0], "partial": true }
→ { "status": "partial", "path": { "waypoints": [[-6, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]], "polys": [0, 2], "length": 6 } }
```

`status` is `complete` (a reachable goal: the same path as without `partial`), `partial` (an
unreachable goal, or a goal off the mesh) or `no_start` (`path` is `null`: the start is off the
mesh). Without `partial` the answer is unchanged.

### Errors

The NM-1 queries use these `data.reason` values: `nav_no_mesh` (`F0003`: neither a `NavMesh` nor
a `NavTileCache`), `nav_bad_extents` (`F0002`: a negative `extents` component), `nav_bad_radius`
(`F0002`: a negative radius), `nav_no_start_poly` (`F0003`: `from`, or the `center` with
`reachable_only`, has no allowed polygon within `extents`).

## Working with the results

- Waypoints are world-space `[x, y, z]` on the walkable surface; entity ids from other methods
  (`scene.*`, `physics.*`) are unrelated to polygon indices.
- A wall carved as an obstacle makes `nav.find_path` return `null` across it — a good
  `play.expect`-free way to assert "no route exists".
- The stored mesh never changes when obstacles are added; rebuild it (or re-insert a new `NavMesh`) to reflect
  changed geometry.
- The builder rasterises level geometry conservatively (`cell_size`, default 0.25 m): a cell
  takes every triangle that overlaps its square, so a wall top or a plank thinner than one cell
  is in the mesh wherever it sits on the grid (since nav cell v3, ADR-8899; before it, such
  geometry could fall between cell centres, ADR-7558). A cell a triangle only partly covers
  counts as a boundary for an agent with a radius, so floor edges do not grow; a point-sized
  agent (radius 0) may stand on it. A purely vertical wall
  with no top face still records nothing in the top-surface build: give thin blockers a top, or
  carve them as obstacles.

<!-- depth-2:method-reference -->

## Call reference

Parameters, results and error codes for every method on this page. Types and defaults come from the schema and handlers; limits include the contract. Error codes are in `data.code`; names explicitly labeled `data.reason` are additional handler reasons. Every method can also return `F0001`, `F0002`, `F0004`, `F0007` and `F0012`. The server can return `F0005`, `F0006`, `request_too_large`, or `F0008` when the method is not registered; see [protocol](book/agents/protocol.md).

Unless a lower or explicit method limit is listed, the dispatcher accepts at most 65,536 items in a top-level array parameter and 1,048,576 UTF-8 bytes in a string parameter. A limit violation returns `F0002`.

The request in each fence is the call that was sent with `regia agent call`.
The line under it is the host's answer.
A second fence tagged `json,ignore` is an error answer. Large fields are elided with `...`. A fence tagged `json,ignore` is a real call on a host or plugin method that the runtime schema does not list.

### `nav.find_path`

A path between two points: smoothed waypoints, the polygon sequence and length.

*Read, does not mutate.*

| Param | Type | Required | Default and limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `from` | array | yes | Start point [x, y, z] (world space). |
| `to` | array | yes | End point [x, y, z] (world space). |
| `extents` | array | no | Half-extents [x, y, z] of the point-location box (default [2, 2, 2]). |
| `filter` | object | no | { include_flags, exclude_flags, area_costs: [[area, scale]...], exclude_areas: [area...] }, each optional (ADR-1934). |
| `partial` | boolean | no | true: an unreachable goal gives the path to the reachable point nearest it, with a status (complete, partial, no_start) (default false). |

Errors besides the universal codes: `F0003`. Filter refusals use `F0002` with `data.reason` `nav_invalid_area` or `nav_invalid_area_cost`. Omitted filter uses include_flags 65535, exclude_flags 0, no excluded areas and area scales 1; area ids are 0..=63 and area scales must be finite and positive.

```json
nav.find_path {"from": [-5, 0, -5], "to": [5, 0, 5]}
```

```

### `nav.random_point`

Seeded random points on the navmesh: area-weighted over the allowed polygons, or uniform within

*Read, does not mutate.*

| Param | Type | Required | Default and limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| `seed` | integer | no | Random seed (default 0). |
| `count` | integer | no | How many points, 1..=4096 (default 1). |
| `center` | array | no | Circle center [x, y, z]; give radius too. |
| `radius` | number | no | Circle radius in metres (>= 0, else nav_bad_radius); give center too. |
| `reachable_only` | boolean | no | Only polygons connected to the center's (default false). |
| `extents` | array | no | Half-extents [x, y, z] for snapping the center (default [2, 2, 2]). |
| `filter` | object | no | Query filter as for nav.find_path. |

`count` is from 1 to 4096.

```

|---|---|---|---|

| `to` | array | yes | End point [x, y, z] (its height is ignored). |
| `extents` | array | no | Half-extents [x, y, z] for snapping the start (default [2, 2, 2]). |
| `filter` | object | no | Query filter as for nav.find_path; a left-out area stops the ray. |
