  or v2 volume, which names none (its emitters are counted twice on High and Ultra: rebake).
- `render.emissive_lights` returns `baked`: how many of the uploaded area lights belong to emitters
  the volume holds. Those give way to the bake where it covers.
- `render.set_gi_occluders {"capsules": [{"a": [x, y, z], "b": [x, y, z], "radius": r,
  "strength": s}], "gizmos": true}` replaces the capsule occluders. `b` defaults to `a` (a sphere)
  and `strength` to 1. `"gizmos": true` also draws them as yellow wire capsules; a later call without
  it removes the drawing. `[]` clears the list. It returns `{ count, cap, dropped, gizmos,
  volume_installed, note }`. The host's own `set_gi_occluders` calls replace the agent's list, so
  use it on a paused game or one that sets none.
- Errors from `render.set_gi_occluders`: `F0002` (invalid params) for a missing `capsules` list, a
  capsule without `a` or `radius`, a point that is not three numbers, a radius ≤ 0, a strength
  outside (0, 1], or a `gizmos` value that is not a boolean. The message names the capsule index.
  `F0003` (not found) when the app has no runtime renderer.
- `render.set_gi_mode {"mode": "baked"}` forces the look and leaves the persisted
  `graphics.lighting` alone. `{"mode": "balanced"}` shows the analytic terms for a side-by-side
  comparison. `{"mode": "default"}` goes back to the default.

## Checking a bake

1. `render.get_gi_mode`: `baked.active` is `true`, `baked.error` is `null`, and `baked.scales` are
   near 1 at the look the map was baked with.
2. `seeing.screenshot` with `baked`, then with `balanced`. Shaded ground and walls should pick up
   the bounce of sunlit surfaces near them, and enclosed spaces should stay dark.
3. Compare against the path tracer's plates: shade within ±20 % is the target.
4. Emitters: on High or Ultra, `baked.emitters` is a number, not `null`, and
   `render.emissive_lights` reports `baked` > 0 in a room lit by a baked panel. Screenshot the room
   with `render.set_gi_mode {"mode": "baked"}`: it should look like Desktop Low, plus the panel's
   highlights on glossy surfaces.
5. Interiors: `baked.interior_bricks` matches the bake's interior count. Screenshot inside the room
   and just outside its walls. The room should not pick up outdoor sky, and the outer walls should
   not go dark.
6. Occluders: `play.pause`, then `render.set_gi_occluders` with a capsule over a lit patch of ground
   and `"gizmos": true`. Take a screenshot, clear with `[]`, and take another. The ground under the
   capsule should darken softly, darkest right under it.

Evidence in the repo: `crates/regia_pt/tests/baked_gi_runtime.rs` checks the following.

- The GPU lookup matches its CPU mirror.
- Per term, the bake is within the band of the path tracer's own probe at floor receivers.
- DDGI and SSGI stay off on a baked frame.
- A sunlit trench wall lights the shadowed floor.
- A sealed room stays dark (≤ 1 % of the outside ground).
- The `baked_gi_trench` golden.

`crates/regia_render/src/baked_gi.rs` and `baked_gi/occluders.rs` test the near field on the CPU
mirror:

- A v1 file looks up bit for bit as before.
- An interior brick keeps the terrain out and does not blend outward.
- An interior brick wins over an enclosing brick.
- A capsule darkens by its analytic factor, and one behind the surface does nothing.
- An empty occluder list uploads nothing.

`crates/regia_pt/tests/baked_emitters.rs` checks the emitters the bake holds (ADR-1386) on any
GPU, lavapipe included, without a golden:

- In a closed room lit by a ceiling panel, Desktop High and Ultra with a v3 volume light the room
  like the same frame without area lights, plus at most the area lights' specular. The room stays
  within the indirect light a closed room can hold over the direct light alone. The same volume
  read as v2 (no emitter list) is a full direct light brighter: the double count.
- An emissive strip added after the bake adds the same light over the bake as with no volume.
- On an open floor that a brick covers only in part, a baked lamp lights the uncovered floor
  exactly as with no volume, and the covered floor with the bake's light.
- Desktop Low, Deck and Mobile render the same bytes with and without the emitter list.

`emissive_lights.rs` tests the tagging on the CPU: only matched emitters are tagged, not one added
or moved after the bake or a unit's light; a v2 volume tags nothing; tagged lights go last over the
budget. `regia_asset` tests that a v2 file loads with no emitter list and writes back as v3.

## Screen-space AO under the bake

Where the volume lights a pixel, the SSAO counts only the occlusion its probes do not already hold,
and capsule occluders leave the SSAO's share of theirs to it. `render.set_baked_gi_ao` switches this
off for a side-by-side. See [Baked GI and screen-space AO](book/agents/baked-gi-ao.md).

Maps whose layout needs more than one portable 128 MiB binding bake as split volumes (up to four part files,
`render.get_gi_mode` `baked.volumes`): see [Split baked GI volumes](book/agents/baked-gi-split.md).

<!-- source: book/agents/emissive-lights.md -->
# Emissive lights

Emissive trim (unit lights, building and window lights, strips under a hull) lights the surfaces
right next to it. The renderer fits a few area lights to every emissive mesh and shades them in
the clustered light loop, so a strip lights the hull beside it and throws a tight pool on the
ground, the way the path tracer (and Cycles) show it. The probes and the screen-space GI only
carry a blurred share of that light; the fitted lights carry it instead, and the screen-space GI
skips the emitters' pixels so the light is not counted twice.

## What gets a light

A mesh whose material emits (`emissive` × `emissive_intensity` > 0), is lit (not `unlit`), opaque
or masked (not blended or additive), has no material graph and is rigid (no joint palette). The
fitter splits each connected emissive part into:

- **tubes** for rods and bars (thin in two directions), lit like a glowing cylinder from every side;
- **quads** (rectangles or trapezoids) for the faces of plates and rings: a closed mesh emits from
  its outside only, an open sheet of a double-sided material from both faces;
- smaller pieces when a part is curved or a quad would cover its triangles poorly.

Each light keeps the flux of the triangles it replaces. An emissive texture masks and scales the
triangles (dark texels do not emit). A one-sided face never lights what is behind it.

## Shadows: distance probes

The first time a mesh is drawn, each of its lights traces a small distance probe on the CPU
(16 × 16 directions from ten points on a quad, or five on a tube — its centre and four points
along the axis — against the scene's triangles near it): how far the light reaches in every
direction before it hits something. The forward pass
compares each receiver's distance with it, so a light on top of a hull does not light the ground
under the hull. Rays stopped right at the emitter (a frame or grille pressed against a pad) scale
the light down by that share; a face resting on other geometry is dropped (`buried`). Probes are
not re-traced when nearby geometry moves; a changed emissive color, strength or map refits.

## Cost: cached by content, new work off the frame thread (v0.1.18)

A fit is cached by the mesh's content (vertex positions, indices, the texture coordinates when the
material has an emissive map, and the material's emission), not by the `Arc` that holds it. A mesh
landed again under a new `Arc` with the same content (a damage step that re-lands the intact mesh)
reuses the fit, and on the same object (entity) its probes too: nothing is fitted or traced. Two
different objects with equal meshes share the fit and trace their own probes.

After the first frame, the fit and the probe trace of a genuinely new mesh run on a background
thread. The frame thread only hashes the mesh, copies what the fit reads and gathers the
triangles around the lights, and starts no new piece once the collection has spent 1 ms
(`EMISSIVE_FRAME_BUDGET_MS`). Until the lights land (usually a few frames), a mesh that replaced
another on the same object draws with the old mesh's lights; a mesh new to its object draws without
its lights. The first frame does everything at once, as before, so a screenshot of a freshly
loaded scene has every light. `REGIA_EMISSIVE_SYNC=1` keeps everything on the frame thread
(v0.1.17 behavior) for A/B checks.

The runtime lends each frame's emissive meshes to the renderer
(`FrameRenderer::hold_mesh_identities`), so a mesh key cannot name another mesh while its fit is
cached. A host that builds `FrameScene`s itself may skip that; the cache then checks each key's
buffers and a sampled fingerprint every frame.

## Emissive map signatures (v0.5.1, ADR-7869)

Runtime materials keep their exact content signature across unchanged frames. The cache is keyed
by the registered material generation and dynamic texture write serials; a new generation or a
successful dynamic write hashes the map once, shared by every mesh using that material. A steady
frame hashes zero map bytes. The counted unit test
`tracked_emissive_maps_hash_no_bytes_in_a_steady_frame` verifies this without timing assertions.
Hosts building `FrameScene`s can use the existing `shading_model::material_key(&Arc<CpuMaterial>)`
for the material they borrow into each `FrameMesh`; its registered ownership enables the cache.

A host supplying borrowed `LabMaterial`s directly still gets an exact full hash: their public
`LabTexture.rgba` vectors can change in place without a write epoch. That compatibility path keeps
its existing cost. `material_signature` itself also remains an exact content function, so moving
identical bytes does not change its result. Dynamic image overrides retain the fitter's existing
behavior; this change caches its `emissive_map` signature, not a new texture sampling path.

The existing `render.emissive_lights` readout remains the agent surface: unchanged content should
have zero `refits`, and changing the emission should update the fitted lights. `fit_cache.hashes`
counts geometry hashes, not map bytes; use the counted test for the zero-byte work assertion.

## Budget per quality tier

`RenderProfile::emissive_lights` / `FrameQuality::emissive_lights`: Desktop High 96, Ultra 160;
Desktop Low, Deck and both Mobile tiers 0 (off). Lights whose range does not reach the view are
culled; over the budget the brightest on screen are kept. A light's range ends where it would add
4 % of middle gray to a white surface at the frame's exposure.

## Under a baked GI volume

A baked volume (`.fgiv` v3) already holds the light of the emitters it traced. The lights of those
emitters are tagged: the forward pass leaves their light to the volume where it covers, and over
the budget they go after the other lights. Emitters the bake did not trace (added or moved after
the bake, units' lights) keep their area lights everywhere. See
[Baked GI volumes](book/agents/baked-gi.md#emitters-the-bake-holds) (ADR-1386).

## Checking it

`render.emissive_lights` reports the last frame:

```json
{ "enabled": true, "budget": 96, "meshes": 5, "fitted": 59, "in_view": 59,
  "uploaded": 59, "dropped": 0, "refits": 0, "cpu_ms": 0.03,
  "probes_traced": 0, "probes_deferred": 0, "buried": 0, "baked": 0,
  "fit_cache": { "fits_done": 5, "fits_deferred": 1, "cache_hits": 40, "probe_hits": 38,
                 "probes_traced": 61, "budget_holds": 0, "stand_ins": 3, "hashes": 45,
                 "frame_ms": 12.4, "worker_ms": 31.0, "pending": 0, "background": true,
                 "frame_budget_ms": 1.0 } }
```

`refits` is the number of mesh keys that took new content this frame (a new mesh, or a changed
emissive color, strength or map); most are served from the content cache. `fit_cache` holds
counters since the renderer started: `fits_done` (fits computed), `fits_deferred` (sent to the
background thread), `cache_hits` and `probe_hits` (new keys that reused a fit or probes),
`budget_holds` (mesh-frames whose new work waited for the frame budget), `stand_ins`
(mesh-frames drawn with the replaced mesh's lights), and the frame-thread and background
milliseconds. `cpu_ms` above `frame_budget_ms` past the first frame is a hitch worth reporting
(with `fit_cache`). `dropped` > 0 means the budget cut lights that reach the view. `baked`
counts the uploaded lights whose emitter the baked GI volume holds (0 without a v3 volume).
The 10 s telemetry summary carries the same counters per window under `emissive`.
To see the effect, take a `seeing.screenshot` with the quality's `emissive_lights` at 0 and at its
default and compare the ground and the surfaces next to the emitters.

The lookdev tool `emissive_bounce` measures it against the path tracer on a DO27 hero reference
(medians of the emitters' light in rings around them, on the ground and on the asset).

<!-- source: book/agents/display-calibration.md -->
# Display calibration (agents)

The player's display calibration (black level, gamma, HDR nits) runs after the tonemap, VFX and
UI, on the finished frame. See the [user guide](book/user-guide/display-calibration.md) for what
each value does. Guide topic: `agent.guide {"topic": "calibration"}`.

## Methods

- `render.get_calibration` returns `{ calibration, sdr_neutral, platform, platform_default,
  display, hdr_requested, persisted }`. `calibration` holds `{ black_level, gamma,
  paper_white_nits, peak_nits, min_nits }`. `platform` is `desktop`, `mobile` or `deck`.
  `display` is what the OS reports (`peak_nits` / `min_nits`, `null` when unknown).
  `persisted` is `true` when the player has saved a calibration and `null` without the settings
  plugin.
- `render.set_calibration` changes only the fields given; the others keep their value. Values
  are clamped to the player ranges. The change applies on the next frame. It is written to
  `graphics.calibration` only when `GameSettings` is already in the world; otherwise `persisted`
  is false and nothing is saved. `{"hdr": true}` requests HDR10 output only when `OutputSettings`
  is in the world. Without it, `hdr_requested` stays false, and the saved section still records
  the requested flag when `GameSettings` exists. `{"reset": true}` returns to the platform default
  and clears the saved section. Returns `{ before, after, sdr_neutral, persisted }`. Mutating;
  permission `edit_scene`.

Parameters are optional JSON numbers for `black_level`, `gamma`, `paper_white_nits`, `peak_nits` and
`min_nits`, and optional booleans for `hdr` and `reset`. Omitted fields keep their current value;
`reset` defaults to `false`. Values clamp to black level −1..=1, gamma 1.8..=2.6, paper white
80..=500 nits, peak 200..=10,000 nits, and minimum 0..=1 nit (also capped at 1% of peak).

```json
{"method": "render.set_calibration", "params": {"black_level": 0.35, "gamma": 2.3}}
```

## Screenshots and goldens

`seeing.screenshot` takes `calibration`:

- `"applied"` (default): what the player sees, with the calibration applied.
- `"neutral"`: the frame before the display stage. It is byte-identical to a capture at neutral
  calibration. **Use it for goldens and look comparisons**, so a player's or a test machine's
  calibration never leaks into a judgement of the content.

An HDR frame is captured as its SDR rendition (the black-level curve only for `"applied"`).
Offscreen captures (`target: "offscreen"`) have no display stage; `"applied"` applies the SDR
curve on the CPU, using the same function the shader mirrors.

## Typical loop

1. `render.get_calibration` to check whether the frame is neutral.
2. Compare looks with `seeing.screenshot {"calibration": "neutral"}`.
3. To preview how a dim display would be calibrated, `render.set_calibration`
   with the values `DisplayModel::solve` gives. The evidence sheet lists them in
   `docs/evidence/calibration/<date>/metrics.md`. Screenshot with `"applied"`.
4. `render.set_calibration {"reset": true}` when done.

## Example calls

Example calls (`regia agent call <method> '<params json>'`; entity ids come from `scene.query_entities`):

```text
render.get_calibration {}       # { calibration, sdr_neutral, platform, ... }
```

## Errors

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `F0002` | A `render.set_calibration` parameter has the wrong JSON type. |

## Failing call

This captured headless lavapipe call needs no physical display or colorimeter:

```text
$ regia agent call render.set_calibration '{"gamma":"dark"}' --project samples/boot_probe
error: method call failed: `gamma` must be a number (-32602): {"code":"F0002","hint":"check the method's parameters in the agent guide"}
```

<!-- source: book/agents/spacemouse.md -->
# SpaceMouse (agents)

Desktop apps read 3Dconnexion SpaceMouse devices (any number, merged into one state): on Linux
through the `spacenavd` socket when the daemon runs, otherwise (and on Windows) through raw HID. Every Regia Engine UI app (the editor, Tincal, Red-Rouge) moves its viewport camera with the same
shared function, `regia_input::spacemouse::nav::step`, so the device behaves the same in all of
them. See the [user guide](book/user-guide/spacemouse.md) for the defaults table and the Linux udev
rule. Guide topic: `agent.guide {"topic": "spacemouse"}`. Specification: `docs/specs/29-spacemouse.md`.

No hardware is needed to test: inject a state and check the camera.

With no device attached, `input.spacemouse_status` succeeds and reports `"connected": 0`
(`connected` is the number of connected devices) and a `devices` array that is empty when the
backend lists none (the other status fields describe the default merged state and configuration). Missing hardware is not an error. The handler returns `F0013`
(`unsupported`) when the SpaceMouse plugin is absent; Android also returns `F0013` because this
backend is desktop-only. Invalid injection parameters use `F0002`.

## Methods

- `input.spacemouse_status` returns `{ backend, connected, devices, state, injected_frames_left,
  config, toggles, linux_udev_rule }`. `devices` lists each device with `status` `connected`, or
  `unavailable` with a `reason` (no permission, in use by another driver), and its `source`
  (`spacenavd`, `hid` or `fake`). `state` is the merged
  sample `{ translation, rotation, buttons }`, normalised to -1..1 and before the dead zone.
  `config` is the user's `{ enabled, sensitivity, invert }`; `toggles` is `{ horizon_lock,
  dominant, object_tool }`. `linux_udev_rule` is the rule text when a Linux device is unavailable. Read-only.
- `input.spacemouse_inject` replaces the device state for `frames` frames (default 1):
  `translation [x, y, z]`, `rotation [rx, ry, rz]` (each -1..1, clamped), `buttons` (an array of
  button numbers or a bitmask). Pressing a button fires its action: 1 `view.fit_selection`,
  2 `view.home`, 3 toggles dominant-axis mode, 4 toggles horizon lock, 5 and up
  `spacemouse.button.N`. Returns `{ injected, frames, from_frame }`. Mutating; permission `play`.
- `input.spacemouse_nav_defaults` returns the fixed constants every app shares: dead zone 0.04,
  quadratic curve, orbit pan 1 orbit distance per second, zoom `exp(1.5 · v.z · dt)`, rotation
  1.5 rad/s, fly speed 1 scene scale per second, pitch limit 89°, horizon lock on, dominant axis
  off, the 2D modes (View2D pan 1 extent per second, Timeline scrub 1 span per second on `ry`,
  Step threshold 0.5 on the shaped `rz` with a 0.35 s repeat), the object tool (off, toggle
  action, 0.3 s gesture rest), the button table and the override ranges. Read-only.

Modes (`NavMode`): Orbit (default), Fly, Turntable (the Orbit delta applied to the object), View2D,
Timeline and Step. A golden table of `nav::step` inputs and outputs is checked in at
`crates/regia_input/tests/data/spacemouse_nav_golden.json`.

Frame of the values: +x right, +y up (lift the cap), +z toward the viewer (pull the cap). `rx` is
tilting the cap away from you, `ry` twisting it counter-clockwise seen from above, `rz` tilting it
left. Pushing the cap away (`translation [0, 0, -1]`) zooms in.

```json
{"method": "input.spacemouse_inject", "params": {"rotation": [0, 1, 0], "frames": 30}}
```

## Events

`events.read` records kind `spacemouse`: `{ "event": "action", "action", "button" }` for every
button press, and `{ "event": "connected" | "disconnected", "id" }` for hot-plug.

## Typical loop

1. `input.spacemouse_status` to see whether a device is present (an agent run usually has none).
2. `input.spacemouse_inject {"rotation": [0, 1, 0], "frames": 30}`, then `play.step` 30 frames (or
   wait), then `seeing.screenshot`: in an orbit viewport the camera has turned
   `30 · dt · 1.5` radians counter-clockwise around its target.
3. `input.spacemouse_inject {"buttons": [2]}` sends the camera home; `{"buttons": [1]}` frames the
   selection.

On a headless Linux run with no device, read status, inject a short rotation, advance the same
number of simulation frames, and inspect an offscreen screenshot. This checks navigation without
requiring hardware.

For example, the dispatcher's limit check (`frames` in 1..=4294967295) rejects a zero frame count
with `F0002` before the handler runs; the answer carries the `limit` it broke:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":8,"method":"input.spacemouse_inject","params":{"frames":0}}
→ {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":8,"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"`frames` must be in 1..=4294967295 (got 0)","data":{"code":"F0002","hint":"agent.schema lists each method's params and limits","limit":{"kind":"range","max":4294967295.0,"min":1.0,"param":"frames"}}}}
```

## Example calls

Example calls (`regia agent call <method> '<params json>'`; entity ids come from `scene.query_entities`):

```text
input.spacemouse_status {}        # no device in an agent run: connected is 0
input.spacemouse_nav_defaults {}   # the shared navigation constants
```

<!-- source: book/agents/render-profile.md -->
# Render profile (agents)

The render profile is the quality tier the renderer runs (`specs/13` § 3): render scale, AA,
upscaler, shadows, post. A game picks one through `RenderSettings`; without one the platform
default runs: **Mobile High on Android**, Desktop High elsewhere. Guide topic:
`agent.guide {"topic": "profile"}`.

## Methods

- `render.get_profile` returns `{ preset, tier, profile, post_enabled, platform_default, runtime_default,
  presets, profile_names, offline_presets, thermal }` (the full shape, every `profile` field included, is in
  `agent.schema`; the fields below are the ones most hosts read).
  `preset` is the preset name (`MobileLow`, `MobileHigh`, `DesktopLow`, `DesktopHigh`,
  `DesktopUltra`, `Deck`), or `null` when the game customized the quality fields. Runtime
  `temporal_upscaler` and `render_scale` choices preserve the preset and its gameplay caps
  (v0.5.1); Very Low still reports `DesktopLow`. Other quality overrides, including AA,
  can make the profile custom. `tier` (v0.7, ADR-8844) is the quality-ladder tier the profile is
  (`QualityTier::of_settings`: `VeryLow`, `Low`, `Medium`, `High`, `Ultra`, `Deck`, `MobileLow`,
  `MobileHigh`), or `null` for a profile no tier produces; it is how Very Low is told apart from
  Desktop Low, since both report `preset: "DesktopLow"`. `profile_names` lists every name
  `render.set_profile` takes (see [Profile names](#profile-names-v07)). `profile` holds
  `{ render_scale, anti_aliasing, spatial_upscaler, depth_prepass, bloom, auto_exposure,
  terrain_anisotropy, cloud_reprojection, cloud_step_percent, cloud_cone_light, mesh_lod_bias,
  mesh_lod_distance_scale, mesh_lod_shadow_scale }`. The three `mesh_lod_*` values are the mesh LOD
  tier (v0.1.20; see [Mesh LOD tiers](book/agents/mesh-lod-tiers.md)).
  `terrain_anisotropy` is the terrain's anisotropic filtering level (`TerrainBudget::anisotropy`: 0 = off, Mobile High 2,
  Desktop Low and Deck 4, Desktop High 8, Desktop Ultra 16; v0.1.8). `cloud_reprojection` is
  whether volumetric clouds march one texel in 16 per frame and reproject the rest (on for every
  preset), and `cloud_step_percent` scales the cloud view-march steps (Desktop Ultra 150, so
  64 → 96 steps; the others 100; batch v020). `cloud_cone_light` is the cone light march with
  dark edges and curl detail (Desktop High and Ultra; off on the presets without clouds;
  batch v020). See `agents/clouds.md`.
  `thermal` (batch v020) is `{ status, headroom, governor_enabled, governor_level, base_render_scale }`:
  Android's thermal status (`None` … `Shutdown`), the 10-second headroom forecast (1.0 = severe, `null`
  when the device does not report it), and the thermal governor's state. While `governor_level` is above
  0 the governor holds `profile.render_scale` below `base_render_scale`; this scale change
  preserves `preset`, so ragdoll and vehicle-FX limits continue to follow the selected tier.
  `platform_default` is the build's default preset (Mobile High on Android, Desktop High elsewhere); cooks
  and permutation lists use it. `runtime_default` (v0.2.16, ADR-3289) is what `RenderSettings::default()`
  picks on this device when the game names no preset: `Deck` on a Steam Deck (`SteamDeck=1`, as Steam sets
  it, or a Valve `Jupiter`/`Galileo` board), else the same as `platform_default`.
- `render.set_profile` switches to a preset on the next frame. It re-seeds the toggles the preset
  owns (bloom, AA, auto exposure) and keeps the rest of the post stack and the fog. `post`
  (optional boolean) turns the post stack on or off: samples that render forward-only for
  lavapipe screenshots need `"post": true` for SMAA and the SGSR upscale to run.
  `mesh_lod_distance_scale` and `mesh_lod_shadow_scale` (optional numbers, v0.1.20) override the
  preset's mesh LOD tier scales, clamped to 0.25..16 and 0.05..1; with one of them, `preset` may be
  left out. `preset` also takes the tier names of [Profile names](#profile-names-v07). The switch
  is not persisted. Returns `{ before, after }` (each with `preset` and `tier`), plus `gate` and
  `requested` (the canonical name asked for) when a preset was named. Mutating; permission
  `edit_scene`. `render.mesh_lod` prints the switch distances the scales give (see
  [Mesh LOD tiers](book/agents/mesh-lod-tiers.md)).

```json
{"method": "render.set_profile", "params": {"preset": "MobileLow", "post": true}}
```

## Profile names (v0.7)

Wherever a render profile is named (`render.set_profile`, `--render-profile`,
`REGIA_RENDER_PROFILE`, a scene's `render_profile.txt`, `Regia.toml` `[platforms.*]
render_profile`, the editor's Project Settings), the name is a `ProfileName` (ADR-7977, ADR-8844):

- a preset row: `MobileLow`, `MobileHigh`, `DesktopLow`, `DesktopHigh`, `DesktopUltra`, `Deck`,
  `Cinematic`; or
- a quality-ladder tier that has no row of its own: `VeryLow` (the integrated-GPU floor, Desktop
  Low drawn at a third with SGSR, `specs/13` § 3a) and `Medium` (Desktop High at 0.67).

Spelling is free as for presets (`VeryLow`, `very_low` and `very-low` all match); the canonical
name is what is written back. `Low`, `High` and `Ultra` stay unknown names, because those tiers
are rows already (`DesktopLow`, `DesktopHigh`, `DesktopUltra`) and no row gets a second name. A
tier applies as auto quality applies it, with the live adapter deciding the GPU levers. Very Low
gates as Desktop Low (it is never gated) and reports `preset: "DesktopLow"`, `tier: "VeryLow"`, so
water, foliage and the other systems that pick their tier by preset stay on Low's.

```json
{"method": "render.set_profile", "params": {"preset": "VeryLow"}}
```

Errors: an unknown name is `invalid_params`; its message names the bad name and lists
`profile_names`. The command-line, environment and scene-file readers (`choose_profile`,
`take_profile_arg`) report `render_profile_unknown`, `render_profile_missing_value` or
`render_profile_unreadable` as the preset readers do; every command that reads `Regia.toml`
(`regia package` among them) refuses an unknown `render_profile` with `render_profile_unknown`.

## Offline Cinematic profile (v0.2.0)

`render.set_profile {"preset": "Cinematic"}` switches to the offline profile above Desktop Ultra
(ADR-1403): every cloud texel marched every frame at full resolution with 4 stratified samples,
8192² sun cascades, the light caps at their maximum, mesh LOD toward LOD0. Android and GPU tiers
below High get their own preset instead unless `"force": true`; the result's `gate` says what ran.
`cloud_samples`, `cloud_step_percent`, `cloud_reprojection` and `cloud_max_divisor` override the
cloud march on any preset. See [Cinematic profile](book/agents/cinematic.md).

## Stochastic SSR roughness cutoff (v0.1.14)

Stochastic SSR (Desktop High and Ultra) traces reflections only on surfaces smoother than a
perceptual roughness cutoff, and fades them out over the 0.15 below it. The default is 0.55. A
higher cutoff keeps sharp reflections on rougher surfaces (wet asphalt, worn metal) and traces
more pixels.

- `render.get_sssr_cutoff` returns `{ cutoff, default, env_override, env, range, fade_band }`.
  `cutoff` is the value in effect.
- `render.set_sssr_cutoff {"cutoff": 0.7}` sets it for every renderer from the next frame,
  clamped to `range` (0.15..1); 0.55 (`default`) restores the shipped look. Not persisted. Returns
  `{ before, after, stored }`. Mutating; permission `edit_scene`.
- `REGIA_SSSR_ROUGHNESS_CUTOFF=0.7` in the environment beats the setting (read once at the
  first frame); `env_override` shows it.

To judge a value, `seeing.screenshot` the same view at two cutoffs and compare the GPU `ssr` pass
in `play.hitch_report`.

```json
{"method": "render.set_sssr_cutoff", "params": {"cutoff": 0.7}}
```

## Comparing tiers on a phone

1. `regia install-android --project <game>` installs, launches and attaches the agent
   protocol through `adb forward` (`--attach` re-attaches to a running app).
2. For each preset: `render.set_profile`, wait a second, `play.hitch_report {"seconds": 10}` for
   frame time p50/p99, and `seeing.screenshot` for the look.
3. `seeing.memory_report` gives GPU memory by category and the process RSS.

## Example calls

Example calls (`regia agent call <method> '<params json>'`; entity ids come from `scene.query_entities`):

```text
render.get_profile {}           # { preset, tier, profile, post_enabled, platform_default, runtime_default, presets, profile_names }
render.set_profile {"preset": "VeryLow"}   # after: { preset: "DesktopLow", tier: "VeryLow" }
```

## Packaged starting profile (v0.5.1, ADR-7893)

`render.get_profile.configuration` is `{ source, packaged_profile, location, error }`.
`source` is `player`, `packaged`, `detected`, or `runtime_or_host`. `packaged_profile` is the
exact profile name from `build_info.json` (a preset, or `VeryLow`/`Medium` since v0.7), or null; `location` is its desktop path or
`apk:assets/build_info.json`, and `error` is null or a diagnostic for ignored metadata.
This describes the configured starting profile; a host or `render.set_profile` can customize
the live profile afterward, which the existing `preset` and `profile` fields show.

Startup precedence is player settings > packaged profile > saved or first-launch Auto > runtime
default. An explicit `quality.detect` overrides the package for this launch; a subsequent launch
uses the package again unless the player saved a preset. `quality.get_detected.configuration`
returns the same provenance. See [Packaging](book/user-guide/packaging.md).

<!-- source: book/agents/mesh-lod-tiers.md -->
# Mesh LOD tiers (agents)

Rigid meshes with a `MeshLodChain` pick a level each frame from their projected size
(ADR-208). Since v0.1.20 the render profile has two tier knobs on top of
`mesh_lod_bias`, so the top tiers keep close-up detail:

| Preset | DO27 tier | `mesh_lod_bias` | `mesh_lod_distance_scale` | `mesh_lod_shadow_scale` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mobile Low | ULTRA LOW (candidate) | 0.5 | 1 | 0.5 |
| Mobile High | - | 0.7 | 1 | 0.5 |
| Desktop Low | LOW | 0.85 | 1 | 0.5 |
| Deck | MEDIUM | 0.8 | 1 | 0.5 |
| Desktop High | HIGH | 1 | 2 | 0.35 |
| Desktop Ultra | ULTRA / MAX | 1.15 | 6 | 0.15 |

- **Colour.** The projected size is multiplied by `mesh_lod_bias` (clamped 0.25..4, as before), then
  by `mesh_lod_distance_scale`. The product is clamped to 0.25..16. Switch distances scale
  linearly: Desktop Ultra holds every colour level 1.15 × 6 = 6.9 times as far as a bias of 1.
- **Shadows.** The shadow LOD is chosen at the colour size times `mesh_lod_shadow_scale` (clamped
  0.05..1). Below 1, shadows drop detail earlier than colour. A shadow switch distance is the colour
  one times the shadow scale. Desktop Ultra's 0.15 makes its shadow factor 6.9 × 0.15 ≈ 1, so its
  shadows select about as a bias-1 colour does; at 0.3 the unit-budget bench measured 2.3 ms more
  for 40 battle hulls at 1440p on an RTX 5080, all of it in the shadow passes.
- **Unchanged.** Distance scale 1 with shadow scale 0.5 selects exactly as before, bit for bit
  (the 8-frame dither cross-fade and the ±15 % hysteresis included).

## Methods

- `render.get_profile` returns the three values under `profile` (`mesh_lod_bias`,
  `mesh_lod_distance_scale`, `mesh_lod_shadow_scale`).
- `render.set_profile {"mesh_lod_distance_scale": 3}` overrides a scale live, clamped to its range
  (`mesh_lod_shadow_scale` likewise). `preset` is optional when a scale is given; a preset in the
  same call is applied first. The profile then reads as customized (`preset: null`). Not persisted.
- `render.mesh_lod {radius?, thresholds?, height?, fov_y?}` returns the scales in effect
  (`bias`, `distance_scale`, `shadow_scale`, `color_factor`), their clamps, and for a mesh of
  bounding radius `radius` metres with the stored screen sizes `thresholds` (LOD 0 first; default
  `[1, 0.5, 0.25, 0]`), the distances in metres where its colour and shadow LOD switch
  (`switch.color_m`, `switch.shadow_m`), for the active profile and every preset (`presets`).
  `height` defaults to the last presented window height (1080 headless), `fov_y` to 1 radian.
  Read-only.

```json
{"method": "render.mesh_lod", "params": {"radius": 6.2, "thresholds": [2.4, 0.9, 0.3, 0], "height": 1440}}
{"method": "render.set_profile", "params": {"mesh_lod_distance_scale": 4, "mesh_lod_shadow_scale": 0.25}}
```

To check a hull: read its chain's thresholds (the cooked `CookedMesh::lods` screen sizes, or the
authored `LodGroup`), call `render.mesh_lod` with its bounding radius, then fly the camera to just
inside and outside a printed distance and compare `seeing.screenshot`s.

## Authored LOD thresholds from data

An authored `Stem_LOD0`…`Stem_LODn` chain takes each level's screen size from, in this order:

1. the `_LODn` node's glTF extras, `{"lod_screen_size": 0.45}`;
2. the project's `lod_classes.toml` (next to `assets/`), by the class named in the root node's
   extras `{"lod_class": "battle"}`, else by the first `[[assign]]` glob matching the asset path;
3. the importer default (1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, …; halve at each level, ADR-7869).

From v0.5.1, LOD3 has its own interval in chains of five or more levels. Re-cook with the
upgraded importer before packaging; existing authored extras/class values stay in control.
No format migrator is needed. Inspect a five-level fallback chain with
`render.mesh_lod {"thresholds": [1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625]}` and compare the distinct
switch distances. See [glTF conventions](docs/formats/gltf-conventions.md#lod-screen-sizes-v0120-adr-260).

```toml
version = 1

[classes]
light = [0.9, 0.35, 0.12, 0.04]
battle = [1.2, 0.45, 0.16, 0.05]

[[assign]]
glob = "assets/units/light/**"
class = "light"
```

A chain that used any data must be strictly decreasing: a level that is not is set to half the
previous one, with a cook warning. Bad values (NaN, negative, above 64, a 0 before the last level),
bad classes and a class the table lacks fall back to the next source with a warning; `regia
cook` lists the table's own problems in its warnings. The file is capped at 64 KiB, 256 classes,
16 levels and 1024 rules. There is no protocol method for the table (the cook is desktop
tooling); check a result with `assets.describe` on the `#lod_group/<Stem>` sub-asset.

Format: `docs/formats/gltf-conventions.md` § LOD screen sizes. Bench:
[Performance & benches](book/user-guide/perf-benches.md#the-unit-budget-bench) (`close20` and `ultra`
layouts, and the per-tier switch-distance table).

Per object, a `ShadowLodHint` caps or floors the LOD the shadow draws use (ADR-1622):
[Shadow LOD hint](book/agents/shadow-lod-hint.md).

<!-- source: book/agents/auto-quality.md -->
# Auto quality (agents)

On a first launch the engine picks the quality tier from the GPU, can confirm it with a ~3 s probe
of the first scene after the splash (off by default since v0.1.0, ADR-173), and saves it in `GameSettings.graphics`. The full description is the
[Automatic quality detection](book/user-guide/auto-quality.md) page. Guide topic:
`agent.guide {"topic": "quality"}`.

## Methods

- `quality.get_detected` returns:
  - `setting`: `{ preset, source }`. `source` is `unset` (a first launch before detection),
    `detected` or `player`.
  - `detected`: the saved record, `null` before any detection. It holds `tier` (after the probe),
    `detected_tier` (the table's), `reason`, `rule` (the table row or `fallback`), `evidence`
    (`measured`, `by_class`, `guess` or `fallback`), `gpu`, `pci_id`, `vram_mb`, `driver`, and `probe`
    (`{ p50_ms, p95_ms, budget_ms, frames, clock, size, stepped_down, verdict, monitor_size,
    window_mode, size_mismatch }`). Since v0.5.1 `monitor_size` is the physical size of the
    monitor the window was on (null when unknown), `window_mode` the mode the host asked for
    (`windowed`, `borderless_fullscreen`, empty without a window), and `size_mismatch` is true when
    fullscreen was asked for but the probe drew smaller than the monitor (the window had left
    fullscreen or was not there yet): its numbers are not the monitor's, so it steps nothing down
    (`stepped_down` false, the preset and `tier` unchanged, no re-warm) and the probe at the monitor
    size runs from the same tier.
  - `step_down` (v0.5.1, ADR-7882): why the saved tier is below the table's pick or below `Low`,
    `null` when it is neither: `{ from, to, by, why, budget_ms, below_low }`. `by` is `probe` (the
    confirmation probe stepped down; `why` is its verdict, such as "p95 75.0 ms > 33.3 ms budget:
    Low misses 30 fps, Low → VeryLow (Desktop Low at 33 % render scale, SGSR upscale)", and
    `budget_ms` the budget it missed) or `table` (a GPU table row picked `VeryLow`; `why` is the
    detection's reason, `budget_ms` null). `below_low` is whether the tier is `VeryLow`.
  - `this_launch`: `detections` (0 when the saved preset was read), `probing`, `redetect_pending`,
    `reprobe_pending` (v0.5.1: a `size_mismatch` probe runs again on the first frame the window
    fills the monitor),
    `reason`, `verdict`, and the configuration (`enabled`, `confirm`, `target_fps`,
    `probe_seconds`).
  - `render_tier`: the tier the live `RenderSettings` match, `null` when the game customized them.
  - `probe_active` and `adapter`: the live adapter profile (name, vendor, device, class,
    `vram_mb`, limits).
  - `host`: the app's own detection when it picks its tier without `GameSettings`
    (`regia_agent::HostQualityDetection`), `null` otherwise. The Regia Forest Demo answers
    `{ tier, source, detection }` there, the same as `demo.state`'s `quality` (ADR-5131).
- `quality.detect` without `adapter` re-detects the running GPU on the next frame, like the
  options menu's Auto-detect. It replaces `graphics.preset` (even the player's), saves it, and
  runs the probe when `confirm` is on. It returns the tier and reason it computes now, plus
  `applied: "next_frame"`, `replaces` (the old `{ preset, source }`) and `probe`. Mutating;
  permission `edit_scene`.
- `quality.detect {"adapter": {...}}` is a dry run for any GPU: `{ name*, vendor, device, class,
  vram_mb, android }`, where `class` is `discrete` (default), `integrated`, `virtual`, `cpu` or
  `other`. It returns `{ tier, reason, rule, evidence, note, caps, adapter, applied: false }` and
  changes nothing.

```json
{"method": "quality.detect", "params": {"adapter": {"name": "NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070", "vendor": 4318, "vram_mb": 12282}}}
```

## Checking a launch

1. Delete the settings file (`user://settings.ron`) and launch. Detection runs on the first frame
   with a device. The confirmation probe is off by default (ADR-173). When a host opts in with
   `with_confirm(true)`, wait for it: it draws about 3–4 s of the first scene offscreen after the
   splash (`quality.get_detected` → `probe_active` false).
2. `quality.get_detected`: `setting.source` should be `detected`, and `detected.reason` should name
   the GPU and tier. `detected.probe.verdict` says whether the probe stepped down.
3. `render.get_profile` shows the preset in effect. `Medium` shows `preset: null`, because it is
   Desktop High at `render_scale` 0.67. `VeryLow` shows `preset: "DesktopLow"` with
   `render_scale` 0.333 and `spatial_upscaler` SGSR (ADR-7882): it is Low drawn cheaper, so systems
   that pick their tier by preset stay on Low's. `render_tier` in `quality.get_detected` names it.
   On Linux, on a non-AMD discrete GPU with 6 GB or more, `Low` still shows `preset: "DesktopLow"` even though it also
   turns on the terrain virtual texture (v0.1.2). `terrain.vt` should then report the texture as on,
   with `vt hit rate` near 100 %. On `Medium`, `High` and `Ultra` it reports the texture as off,
   unless the host turned it on itself or opted High in through `quality.set_terrain_vt_policy`
   ([terrain virtual texture tiers](book/agents/terrain-vt-tiers.md)).
4. `play.hitch_report {"seconds": 10}` confirms the frame time at that tier.
5. Relaunch: `this_launch.detections` must be 0, because detection runs once.
6. To check that the player's choice is kept, run `settings.set {"path": "graphics.preset",
   "value": "Ultra"}`. `quality.get_detected` then shows `source: "player"`, and a relaunch keeps
   Ultra.

## Example calls

Example calls (`regia agent call <method> '<params json>'`; entity ids come from `scene.query_entities`):

```text
quality.get_detected {}         # setting.source, detected.reason, step_down, probe_active
quality.detect {"adapter": {"name": "Intel(R) Graphics", "vendor": 32902, "device": 18132, "class": "integrated"}}
                                # dry run: the N150 class -> VeryLow (row intel_n_series)
```

### More `quality.detect` parameters

The schema (`agent.schema`) also lists these optional parameters:

- `apply` (boolean): Re-detect and replace the saved preset (default true without `adapter`).

## Minimum-spec profile explanation

`renderer.minspec_explain {"profile":"pascal"}` or `{"profile":"mobile"}` returns the named
renderer profile and two reason lists. `features` names optional wgpu features omitted from that
profile's mask; `limits` names each clamped limit field and the cap applied by the existing
minimum-spec clamp. The explanation is generated from the profile's mask and clamp, so it follows
those values directly. Unknown names return `minspec_profile_unknown` (JSON-RPC invalid params);
use the lowercase profile names `pascal` and `mobile`.

## Packaged profile provenance (v0.5.1, ADR-7893)

`quality.get_detected.configuration` reports the configured starting profile's source,
`packaged_profile`, metadata `location`, and any metadata `error`, with the same shape as
[render.get_profile](book/agents/render-profile.md#packaged-starting-profile-v051-adr-7893).
`setting` continues to describe the saved player/Auto record; it can differ from the live profile
when `configuration.source` is `packaged`. A package suppresses automatic detection, including a
saved detected preset. Player settings win; explicit `quality.detect` overrides the package for
this launch. A new launch uses the package again unless the player saved a preset.

<!-- source: book/agents/perf-overlay.md -->
# Performance overlay (agents)

The in-game performance overlay (`regia_framework::perf_overlay`, book page
[Performance overlay](book/user-guide/performance-overlay.md)) is a top-left panel. It shows FPS,
a 5 s frame-time graph, renderer CPU against GPU time, GPU passes, texture memory against its
budget, stutters, creates after warm-up, the preset, the GI mode and the resolution. Guide
topic: `agent.guide {"topic": "perf_overlay"}`.

## Methods

- `perf_overlay.get` returns `{ mode, source, host_default, setting, shown, plugin, stats,
  top_passes }`.
  - `mode` is `Off`, `Compact` or `Detailed`.
  - `source` says where the mode comes from: `override` (this protocol), `player`
    (`GameSettings.performance_overlay`, saved) or `host_default`
    (`PerformanceOverlay::default_mode`).
  - `stats` is a fresh snapshot of every value the overlay shows, read from the same engine
    sources the overlay uses: `fps`, `frame_ms`, `frame_avg_ms`, `window_frames`, `p50_ms`,
    `p99_ms`, `longest_ms`, `stutters_window`, `stutters_total`, `cpu_ms`, `gpu_ms`,
    `gpu_timing`, `gpu_passes` (`[name, ms]` pairs), `gpu_scene_ms`, `warmed_up`,
    `pipelines_after_warmup`, `bind_groups_after_warmup`, `texture_bytes`,
    `texture_budget_bytes`, `texture_streaming`, `vram_allocated_bytes`,
    `vram_reserved_bytes`, `rss_bytes`, `preset`, `gi_look`, `gi_mode`, `output`, `internal`,
    `render_scale`, `upscaler` and `overlay_cpu_us`.
  - The window statistics (`p50_ms`, `stutters_window`, …) cover the last ~5 s while the
    overlay is visible, and are 0 while it is hidden.
  - `vram_*` is filled only on the Detailed page, refreshed every 2 s off the frame thread
    (v0.1.14): null until the first report finishes, a refresh or two after Detailed opens.
  - `cpu_ms` is `FrameRenderer::render_into` only, not the frame; compare it with `frame_ms`.
    `telemetry.live` has the frame's bound class and the GPU waits.
- `perf_overlay.toggle {mode?, persist?, placement?}` changes the overlay.
  - `placement` (`{corner, offset: [x, y]}`) moves the overlay to a screen corner; see
    [Overlay placement, default font and pipeline loading](book/agents/ui-overlay-font-loading.md).
  - With no `mode`, it cycles Off → Compact → Detailed → Off.
  - `mode` is `off`, `compact`, `detailed` or `default`. `default` drops the override.
  - By default the change is a runtime override and is not saved. With `"persist": true` it is
    written as the player's setting.
  - Returns `{ before, after, note }`. Mutating; permission `play`.

```json
{"method": "perf_overlay.toggle", "params": {"mode": "detailed"}}
{"method": "perf_overlay.get"}
```

## Checking a frame

1. `perf_overlay.toggle {"mode": "detailed"}`, then `play.step 30` (or wait 5 s for a full
   window).
2. `seeing.screenshot`. The panel is in the top-left corner and the rest of the frame is
   unchanged.
3. `perf_overlay.get`: compare `stats.gpu_passes` with `play.hitch_report`'s `gpu_passes`, and
   `stats.texture_bytes` with `assets.texture_memory`. They come from the same sources.
4. `perf_overlay.toggle {"mode": "default"}` puts back the player's or host's mode.

Showing the overlay creates no pipelines and no bind groups. If `pipelines_after_warmup` is
above 0 after a toggle, the game created them, not the overlay.

<!-- source: book/agents/unit-budget.md -->
# Unit triangle budgets (agents)

DO27 has a frozen triangle table for each unit class. The bench that measures it is a test, not a protocol method:
`cargo test -p regia_render --test unit_budget --release -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1` (book page
[Performance & benches](book/user-guide/perf-benches.md#the-unit-budget-bench)). It prints one markdown row per case
and a fitted cost per 100k visible triangles for each path.

To check the same quantities in a running game, use methods that already exist:

1. `perf_overlay.toggle {"mode": "detailed"}`, then `play.step 30`.
2. `perf_overlay.get`. `stats.gpu_ms` and `stats.gpu_passes` are the frame's timestamp nodes, the same numbers
   the bench reads from `FrameRenderer::gpu_timings`. `stats.vram_allocated_bytes` is the allocator total.
3. `play.hitch_report` carries the same `gpu_passes` for the slow frames.
4. `perf_overlay.toggle {"mode": "default"}` restores the player's or host's mode.

```json
{"method": "perf_overlay.toggle", "params": {"mode": "detailed"}}
{"method": "perf_overlay.get"}
```

Reading the bench's rows:

- **visible tris** is what the colour view submits after LOD selection (shadow-only LOD draws left out). The
  visibility buffer cuts clusters further on the GPU; its row also gives the clusters drawn.
- **body LOD 0/1/2/3** counts hull bodies per level. A skinned mesh is never rewritten by `select_mesh_lods`, so
  skinned rows show every hull at LOD0.
- **geometry ms** is shadows + prepass + cull + forward: the passes that hull triangles drive. Screen-space and
  probe passes are in **GPU ms**, not here.

`perf_overlay.toggle` accepts optional `mode` (`off`, `compact`, `detailed`, or `default`; absent cycles
the modes) and `persist` (boolean, default false). It returns `F0002` for an invalid mode or non-boolean
`persist`, and `F0003` if the overlay plugin is unavailable. `perf_overlay.get` takes no
parameters and returns a snapshot even if the plugin is absent. Workflow: enable detailed mode, step a
fixed number of frames, read the overlay stats, then restore `default`.

Captured failing call (lavapipe; overlay plugin absent):

```console
$ regia agent call perf_overlay.toggle '{"mode":"invalid"}' --project samples/arena
error: method call failed: the performance overlay plugin is not installed (-32001): {"code":"F0003","hint":"add regia::DefaultPlugins (feature `ui`) or regia_framework::perf_overlay::PerfOverlayPlugin"}
```

<!-- source: book/agents/camera-cuts.md -->
# Camera cuts (agents)

A frame blends in what earlier frames left: the temporal upscaler's history (TAAU or TSR), the
froxel fog's history, the static-screen SSGI/SSR cache, cached shadow cascades and pages, and the
auto-exposure meter. Across a camera cut (cockpit to chase camera, a replay cut, menu to map)
that history belongs to another view: before cuts existed, a tenth of the old image was still
visible four frames later, with TAA off as well. Guide topic: `agent.guide {"topic": "camera_cut"}`.

After a cut the next frame is the first frame a fresh renderer would draw. Pixels match within
±2 per channel (`crates/regia_render/tests/camera_cut.rs`, Desktop High and Deck, TAA on and
off, TSR). GPU resources, pipelines and loaded meshes stay, so a cut costs no more than a first
frame: every cached shadow is redrawn once and TAA starts a new accumulation.

## Methods

- `render.camera_cut { cut?, exposure?, detection? }` requests a cut on the next frame
  (`cut`, default `true`). `exposure` is `"snap"` (default) or `"fade"`. Snap forgets the metered
  exposure: the view starts at the initial exposure and adopts its own first histogram outright,
  two frames later. Fade keeps adapting from the old view, for a deliberate eye-adaptation
  effect. `detection` configures automatic cuts: `false` turns them off (explicit cuts only),
  `true` restores the defaults, and an object `{ max_eye_jump_m, max_turn_degrees,
  max_kept_share }` is merged onto the current thresholds. Returns `{ requested, exposure,
  detection, last_cut: { frame, reason } | null, cuts, frame }`. `reason` is `requested`,
  `eye_jump`, `turn` or `scene_change`. Mutating; permission `edit_scene`. `{"cut": false}` only
  reads the state and applies any `detection` change.
  Errors: `F0003` (not found) in an app without a `RuntimeRenderer`; `F0002` (invalid params) for a
  non-boolean `cut`, an `exposure` other than `snap`/`fade`, a `detection` that is not a boolean or
  object, or a negative or non-numeric threshold. A rejected call changes nothing.

Thresholds must be nonnegative and finite as `f32`; `max_kept_share` is then clamped to 1.
An oversized threshold answers `F0002` before changing detection or requesting a cut.

```json
{"method": "render.camera_cut", "params": {}}
{"method": "render.camera_cut", "params": {"cut": false, "detection": {"max_eye_jump_m": 20}}}
```

## Automatic detection

The renderer cuts on its own, with exposure snapping, when any of these happens between two
frames of the same view:

- the eye moves more than `max_eye_jump_m` (default 50 m),
- the view direction turns more than `max_turn_degrees` (default 90°),
- the frame is a scene change: less than `max_kept_share` (default 25 %) of its objects were
  drawn last frame, *and* less than that share of last frame's objects remain. A large spawn
  into a kept scene is not a cut. Objects are compared twice, by object key and by content
  (model matrix, vertex/index counts, a few vertex positions), and both must turn over. Moving
  objects keep their keys, and a tool that rebuilds the same scene every frame under new keys
  keeps its content, so neither looks like a scene change. Objects without stable keys are
  judged on content alone.

Reflection-probe faces and render-to-texture views (mirrors, UI previews) never detect or take a
cut; a pending cut waits for the host's view. Split-screen viewports drawn by one renderer each
compare with their own last frame.

## Typical loop

1. Move the camera to a new shot (`scene.set_property` on the camera, or a level load).
2. `render.camera_cut` if the game does not cut on its own, then `seeing.screenshot`: the image
   carries nothing from the previous shot.
3. Check `last_cut` in the result of `render.camera_cut {"cut": false}` to see whether the
   renderer took a frame as a cut (an unexpected `eye_jump` from a fast vehicle means the
   threshold is too low for that game).

Game code calls `RuntimeRenderer.0.camera_cut()` (or `camera_cut_with(CutExposure::Fade)`) on
the frame of the cut, and `set_camera_cut_detection` to tune or disable detection.

<!-- source: book/agents/render-out.md -->
# Render-out (agents)

`render.out_*` renders the running scene to finished frames: any size, any frame rate, supersampled,
with the game HUD laid out for the output, to a PNG sequence or (through `ffmpeg`) to an FFV1, ProRes
4444 or DNxHR 444 movie. The clock advances by exactly one frame per rendered frame and nothing reads
a wall clock, so the same request from the same world state gives the same frame hashes
([what repeats](#what-repeats)). Guide topic:
`agent.guide {"topic": "render_out"}`. Design: ADR-267.

Frames are made as fast as they render, not in real time. A job needs a renderer (a windowed app, or
`RenderPlugin { headless: true }`) and an extracted camera and mesh, like `seeing.screenshot`
`target: "offscreen"`. Use a headless app when you can: a windowed app shares its TAA history between
the window and the output size.

## Methods

- `render.out_start { out, frames | duration_s, width?, height?, fps?, fps_den?, supersample?, format?,
  name?, hud?, layout?, cuts?, warmup_frames?, settle_frames?, calibration?, subframes?, shutter_angle?,
  bit_depth?, time_map?, aovs?, aov_format?, timings? }`
  starts a job and answers at once with
  `{ job, status, request, render_size, hud, ffmpeg }`.
  - `out` is the output directory (created). A relative path is joined to the project root: the project directory of the running game or editor or, in an app without an asset server (the headless showcase, a test app), the project directory the agent was given (`AgentSettings::project_dir`, the showcase's `--project-dir`; ADR-1561). Only an app with neither joins it to the working directory; an absolute path must lie under an allowed output root: the project root, the system temp dir, or a directory listed in `output_roots = ["/abs/path", ...]` in `.regia/agent.toml`. `..` components, NUL, a drive or UNC prefix, a device name, an absolute path under no allowed root, and a symlink leading out of every allowed root are refused with `F0002` / `invalid_params`, `data.reason = "path_outside_project"` and `data.path_reason` naming the shape (the error names the rule, not any host path; see [Request paths](book/agents/safety.md#request-paths)). `.` is the project root itself. `name` is the file stem (default `frame`).
  - `width`/`height` are the delivered size (default 1920×1080, at most 8192). `fps` is the rate
    numerator (default 30) and `fps_den` the denominator: 29.97 is `fps: 30000, fps_den: 1001`. The
    step is `fps_den / fps` seconds rounded to the nanosecond and is the same for every frame.
  - `supersample` (1..=4) renders at that many times the width and height and averages down in linear
    light; the HUD is drawn at the same density, so it matches the unsupersampled image. At most 100
    million rendered pixels.
  - `format`: `png` (default; `<name>_000000.png`, 8-bit RGBA), `ffv1` (`<name>.mkv`, lossless),
    `prores` (`<name>.mov`, ProRes 4444, 10-bit) or `dnxhr` (`<name>.mov`, DNxHR 444). The movies need
    `ffmpeg` on `PATH`; without it the call fails with `F0019` and nothing is written. `exr`
    (`<name>_000000.exr`) writes the scene-linear frame instead of the display image: see
    [Scene-linear EXR frames](#scene-linear-exr-frames-format-exr). For a deeper display image use
    `bit_depth: 16` (16-bit PNG).
  - `hud` (default true) draws the game UI; `layout` is `auto` (by orientation), `landscape` or
    `portrait`. Author one `UiRoot` per layout and tag it `UiVariant` (see the DO27 host checklist).
  - `cuts` lists frame numbers (0-based) that start with a camera cut; frame 0 always does (with `settle_frames`, the first settle frame does instead). A cut
    drops TAA/TSR history, fog history, the static-screen cache, shadow cascades (the terrain's too),
    irradiance probes and the metered exposure, as in a fresh renderer. With auto exposure on, the cut
    frame is then exposed by its own meter, not at the meter's initial EV: see
    [Exposure at a cut](#exposure-at-a-cut).
  - `warmup_frames` steps and renders that many small, undelivered frames before frame 0, so
    particle effects, spawns and streaming settle.
  - `settle_frames` (0..=`warmup_frames`, default 0) renders the last that many warm-up frames at the
    delivered size and supersampling, and the job's opening camera cut moves from frame 0 to the
    first of them, so frame 0 has that many frames of temporal history (TAA, alpha-hashed foliage, fog;
    ADR-1449). Without it frame 0 is the first frame after the cut: a one-frame still is a single
    jittered TAA sample, and foliage drawn with the hashed alpha test under TAA shows as a raw dot
    stipple. Use 16-32 for stills. Frame 0's game time is the same either way (the settle frames are
    warm-up frames); `cuts` may still list frame 0.
  - `calibration` is `neutral` (default: before the player's display calibration) or `applied`.
  - `timings` (boolean, default false): record the wall milliseconds of each delivered frame's render and
    readback in the manifest as `render_ms` (one number per delivered frame, in order; `null` when off).
    It times the one-render 8-bit path (no `subframes`, no `bit_depth` 16, no `exr`): the other paths leave
    the list empty. PNG encoding runs on the writer threads and is not in the number. The showcase
    performance table ([Showcase performance table](book/agents/showcase-perf-table.md)) reads it.
  - `subframes` (1..=64, default 1) and `shutter_angle` (degrees, more than 0 and at most 360, default
    180): motion blur. See [Motion blur](#motion-blur-subframes-and-shutter_angle).
  - `bit_depth` is 8 (default) or 16. See [16-bit frames](#16-bit-frames-bit_depth-16).
  - `time_map` scales the simulation time each frame covers (slow motion, speed ramps) while the
    output frame rate stays fixed. See [Slow motion and speed ramps](#slow-motion-and-speed-ramps-time_map).
  - `audio` (`true` or `{ sample_rate?, format?, stems?, timeline? }`) also writes a WAV mixdown of
    the master output and optional per-bus stems, rendered offline on the job's render clock (or the
    simulation clock with `timeline: "output"` or `"sim"`). See [Render-out audio](book/agents/render-out-audio.md)
    (ADR-1520, ADR-1554).
  - `aovs` (any of `"depth"`, `"id"`, `"motion"` and the material AOVs `"normal"`, `"normal_view"`,
    `"roughness"`, `"metalness"`, `"base_color"`, `"material_id"`, at most 9 entries) and `aov_format`
    (`"exr"`, the default, `"raw"`, or `"png"` / `"png16"` for the material AOVs that fit) write
    per-frame AOV files next to each frame. See
    [AOVs](#aovs-depth-ids-and-motion-vectors-aovs-aov_format) and
    [Material AOVs](#material-aovs-normal-roughness-metalness-base_color-material_id).
  `render.out_start` waits for material-graph builds already queued before it answers. If a deep queue outlasts your wait you get `F0006`, the job has still started, and asking again gets `F0018`: pass `timeout_ms`, or read the running job with `render.out_progress` (ADR-2728).
  Mutating; permission `edit_scene`. One job at a time (`F0018`). `F0009` if a `play.step` is running,
  `F0011` when the app has no renderer. Limits: `frames` or `duration_s` gives 1 to 1,000,000 frames,
  `fps` is a whole number from 1 to 1,000,000, `fps_den` from 1 to 100,000, and `fps / fps_den` is at
  most 1000, `warmup_frames` at most 10,000,
  `settle_frames` at most `warmup_frames`,
  and `name` may not contain a path separator or start with a dot.
- `render.out_progress { job?, hashes?, hashes_from? }` returns `{ job, status, frame, frames,
  fraction, game_time_s, sim_time_s, replay_from_tick, sequence_hash, camera_cuts,
  exposure_metered_cuts, out, hashes?, error?, manifest? }` (a running job also reports `phase`,
  `arming`, `warmup`, `rendering` or `closing`; `subframe`, the next subframe of the current frame; and
  `sim_step_ns` and `time_scale`, the simulation step and scale of the frame `frame`). During
  `closing` every frame is made and the app is back on its own clock, while a worker thread finishes
  the outputs (the WAVs are synced there, which can take a minute on a busy disk); the app keeps
  answering, and `status` stays `running` until every file is in place and the manifest is written. `game_time_s` is the render clock: the video time of frame `frame`
  after frame 0, `frame` steps, whatever the `time_map`. `sim_time_s` is the simulation clock: the same
  without a `time_map`, else the sum of the simulation steps before frame `frame`. `replay_from_tick`
  is the tick a replay armed with `replay.play { start: "render_out" }` started from on frame 0 (`null`
  when none was).
  `camera_cuts` counts the job's cuts; `exposure_metered_cuts` how many of them metered their frame
  (all of them with auto exposure on, none with a fixed exposure). `status` is
  `running`, `cancelling`, `done`, `cancelled` or `failed` (with `error`). With `hashes: true` it adds
  `hashes: { from, hashes: [..] }` (up to 4096 per call). The latest eight finished jobs are kept.
  Read-only. A running job also reports `warming`: `true` until the job's first render has finished (on a
  cold host that render compiles pipelines and uploads the scene; see below).
  **A poll during a long step is answered (ADR-2582).** The app answers requests between frames, and one
  step of a job can hold it for many seconds (a cold host's first render took 30 s on an RTX 5090). A poll
  of the running job that the app has not answered within 250 ms (`regia_agent::BOARD_ANSWER_AFTER`) while
  the app thread is inside a render-out step is answered by the connection from what the job published as
  the step began: the same fields as above, plus `app_busy: true` and `busy_ms` (how long the step has run).
  A poll for another job, or outside a step, waits for the app as before. The app does not run a poll
  answered this way (the audit log records it with the outcome `board`). Scoped tool tokens wait for the
  app. A waiting poll looks again every 250 ms, so a step that began after it was queued still answers it. During
  a stall long enough to fill the request queue a poll is still answered, without an audit row, and
  `render.out_cancel` still wakes a job waiting on its stalled output (ADR-2728). Polls answered from
  the board stay queued until the app drains them, marked so dispatch skips them; the skip costs no
  per-frame budget, so one draining frame clears any number of them and the cancel behind them
  dispatches at once (ADR-4894).
- `render.out_cancel { job? }` (permission `edit_scene`) stops the job at the next frame. What was written stays; a movie is
  finalized so it plays; the game clock, pause state and time scale are handed back. A job in its
  `closing` phase has no frames left to stop: it answers `{ job, status: "closing", ending }`, where
  `ending` is the status its frames ended with (`done`, `cancelled` or `failed`; the closing can still
  turn it into `failed`, so read the final status from `render.out_progress`). A finished job answers
  `{ job, status, finished: true }` with its final status. Without `job` the call means the running job,
  else the last finished one (ADR-1965).
  A cancel also reaches a job whose output is stalled (an `ffmpeg` that stopped reading, a hung disk):
  the app waits for room in a full output only until a `render.out_cancel` (or `agent.job_cancel`) is
  queued (over the WebSocket or the local transport), then keeps the frame it made, holds both clocks still for one app frame and handles the
  request. A refused or mistargeted cancel changes nothing: the frame is handed over next and is still
  frame N (ADR-2396). A movie whose `ffmpeg` still reads nothing ten seconds after its job ended is
  stopped and the job ends `failed` with what `ffmpeg` said; frame writers stuck on a hung disk are left
  to finish on their own after the same grace, and their unfinished frames are not kept.

```json
{"method": "render.out_start", "params": {"out": "/tmp/shot1", "frames": 120, "fps": 30, "width": 1080, "height": 1920, "supersample": 2, "layout": "portrait", "format": "png", "cuts": [60], "warmup_frames": 10}}
{"method": "render.out_progress", "params": {"hashes": true}}
{"method": "render.out_cancel", "params": {}}
```

Examples of the rest of the surface:

```json
{"method": "render.out_start", "params": {"out": "/tmp/clip", "duration_s": 2.5, "fps": 24, "format": "ffv1", "name": "clip"}}
{"method": "render.out_start", "params": {"out": "/tmp/pan", "frames": 240, "fps": 60, "width": 3840, "height": 2160, "subframes": 8, "shutter_angle": 180, "bit_depth": 16, "hud": false}}
{"method": "render.out_progress", "params": {"job": 3, "hashes": true, "hashes_from": 100}}
{"method": "render.out_cancel", "params": {"job": 3}}
```

### The first job of a headless host

A headless host (the showcase without `--window`, a render farm host) draws only through offscreen captures, so
nothing warms the pipelines its first render-out frame needs: that frame compiles them on the app thread, and the
app answers nothing meanwhile (30 s on the showcase scene with an RTX 5090; a poll timed out with `F0006`). The boot
warm that `render.pipeline_warm` reports does not cover it. Ask for the offscreen warm and wait for it before the
first job (ADR-1965):

```json
{"method": "render.pipeline_warm", "params": {"offscreen": {"width": 1920, "height": 1080}}}
{"method": "render.pipeline_warm", "params": {}}
```

Without the warm the first job still answers its polls during that render (`warming: true`, `app_busy: true`,
frame 0; ADR-2582), but the frame takes as long as before.

`width` and `height` are the job's render size (its size times `supersample`). The renderer moves to a thread of
its own and renders the frame there (its pipelines, the scene's uploads, the size's targets) while a stand-in holds
its place and the app keeps answering; `render.out_start` answers `F0018` until it is back. `offscreen_warm.state`
goes `running`, then `done` (`returning` for the one app frame it takes to put the renderer back) with
`offscreen_warm.last` = `{ size, ms, pipelines, renderer_back, error }`. Frames are the same with and without the
warm (two jobs in one host still repeat). A host with a window warms through its own window path and answers
`idle`. On the showcase scene under lavapipe the first job's longest wait for an answer went from 33 s to 11 s (the
second job's is 3 s). A headless host keeps no pipeline cache across launches unless `REGIA_PIPELINE_CACHE_DIR` names
one: set it so a second launch compiles less, and allow a first launch on new binaries a longer wait for
`agent.hello`.

## Errors

| Call | Condition | Code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `render.out_start` | `out` refused by the [Request paths](book/agents/safety.md#request-paths) rule | `INVALID_PARAMS` `F0002`, `data.reason` `path_outside_project`, `data.path_reason` (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start` | missing `out`; `frames`/`duration_s` absent, zero or above 1,000,000; a size, `fps`, `supersample`, `warmup_frames`, `settle_frames` (above `warmup_frames` too) or `cuts` entry out of range or of the wrong type; unknown `format`, `png_compression`, `layout` or `calibration`; `writers` outside 0..=16; a `name` that is not 1..=64 letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.` (not leading `.`) | `INVALID_PARAMS` (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start` | `fps / fps_den` above 1000 (`fps` 1001 with the default denominator, or `fps` 30000 with `fps_den` 1). `fps` 1000, and `fps` 30000 with `fps_den` 1001, stay inside the cap | `INVALID_PARAMS`: "the frame rate is above 1000 fps" (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start` | `subframes` outside 1..=64; `shutter_angle` not a number in (0, 360]; `bit_depth` not 8 or 16; `bit_depth: 16` with a movie `format` (png and raw are fine) or with `calibration: "applied"` | `INVALID_PARAMS` (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start` | `bit_depth: 16` with `hud` on (the default) in an app that has a HUD | `INVALID_PARAMS`: pass `hud: false` |
| `render.out_start` | `time_map` not an array of `{frame, scale, ease?}`; more than 4096 keys; a `frame` above 1,000,000; a `scale` outside 0..=100; an unknown `ease`; two keys on one frame | `INVALID_PARAMS` (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start` | a `time_map` so fast that one frame would run more than 64 fixed steps (`MAX_SUBSTEPS_LIMIT`). The shutter doubles the simulation time counted toward that cap, so the same `scale` hits it sooner; the cap stays 64 | `INVALID_PARAMS`: lower the peak `scale` or raise `fps` (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start`, `render.out_job` | an `aovs` entry that is not an AOV name (`depth`, `id`, `motion`, `normal`, `normal_view`, `roughness`, `metalness`, `base_color`, `material_id`) | `INVALID_PARAMS` `unknown_aov` (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start`, `render.out_job` | `aov_format` `"png"` or `"png16"` with `depth`, `id`, `motion` or `material_id` in `aovs` (they need exact values) | `INVALID_PARAMS` `aov_format_unsupported` (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start` | `aovs` not an array; `aov_format` not `"exr"`, `"raw"`, `"png"` or `"png16"`, or given without `aovs`; `aovs` with a movie `format` | `INVALID_PARAMS` (nothing is created) |
| `render.out_start` | `format: "exr"` with `bit_depth: 16` or `calibration: "applied"`; `format: "exr"` with `hud` on in an app that has a HUD | `INVALID_PARAMS` |
| `render.out_progress` | a `format: "exr"` job whose view runs without the post stack (no scene-linear frame) | the job ends `failed` with an `error` that says so |
| `render.out_start` | a job is already running, or the offscreen warm has the renderer (`render.pipeline_warm` `offscreen_warm.state` `running`) | `INVALID_REQUEST` `F0018` |
| `render.out_start` | a `play.step` is running | `INVALID_REQUEST` `F0009` |
| `render.out_start` | no `RuntimeRenderer` (add `RenderPlugin`) | `UNSUPPORTED` `F0011` |
| `render.out_start` | movie format without `ffmpeg` on `PATH` | `UNSUPPORTED` `F0019` |
| `render.out_start` | `audio` asked for and the app has no `Audio` resource; bad `audio` keys ([Render-out audio](book/agents/render-out-audio.md#errors)) | `UNSUPPORTED` `F0013`; `INVALID_PARAMS` |
| `render.out_start`, `render.out_job` | the host opened no GPU on purpose (`regia_agent::GpuDisabled`: a headless editor started with `--no-gpu`, or one that found no adapter); nothing is created and no device is opened (ADR-5180) | `UNSUPPORTED` with the host's code (`editor_headless`) |
| `render.out_progress` | no job was ever started, or `job` names no running or kept job | `NOT_FOUND` |
| `render.out_cancel` | no job was ever started, or `job` names no running or kept job | `NOT_FOUND` |

`render.out_cancel` is idempotent: cancelling a job already cancelling answers `cancelling` again, a
closing job answers `closing`, a finished one its final status, and none of them changes anything. `render.out_progress` is read-only, and `hashes_from` past the end returns an empty
window. Parsing is a pure function of the request: the same request always gives the same step, cut
list and frame count.

## Determinism and the manifest

Each frame's FNV-1a hash (of the delivered RGBA bytes) is in `render.out_progress` and, with the
request, the step in nanoseconds, the sequence hash and the exact ffmpeg arguments, in
`<name>_render_out.json` next to the output. The manifest's `schema` is `regia.render_out/2`:

- `files` is `{ "frames": [...], "audio": [...], "aov": [...] }`: the frame files (or the movie);
  the WAVs of an `audio` job, the mix and then each stem ([Render-out audio](book/agents/render-out-audio.md));
  and per AOV `{ aov, files }` with frame `i` at index `i` ([AOVs](#aovs-depth-ids-and-motion-vectors-aovs-aov_format)).
  Both lists are empty when the job wrote none. Version 1 (`ferrite.render_out/1`, up to v0.2.1) had <!-- rename-keep: history -->
  the frame list as `files` itself.
- `frame_times` has one row per delivered frame: `{ frame, game_time_ns, game_time_s, sim_time_ns,
  sim_time_s, sim_step_ns, time_scale }` (the render clock, the simulation clock, the simulation step
  the frame covers and its `time_map` scale). Without a `time_map` both clocks are equal.
- `clock` says how the frames were timed and where the app stood when the job started: `{ mode:
  "fixed_step", wall_clock: false, step_clock, job_time_origin: "zero", app_game_time_at_start_ns,
  app_sim_time_at_start_ns, app_frame_at_start, live_effects, effect_seeds, particle_clock }` (ADR-1656,
  ADR-1881, ADR-2633, ADR-2687). `live_effects` is `restored` for a job that held the world and `moved_on`
  otherwise. `effect_seeds` is `job_stream`: effects spawned without a seed during the job draw from a seed
  stream that restarts with every job. `particle_clock` is `restarted` when nothing was alive in the particle
  pool at the start, judged by the lifetimes the pool spawned, so its clock and spawn ring started over, and
  `continued` otherwise. `job_time_origin` says the job
  ran `Time::elapsed` and `Time::sim_elapsed` from zero; the `app_*` values are where the app's clocks
  stood before that. `app_sim_time_at_start_ns` tells how far the world had got. `app_frame_at_start`
  counts app updates only: a paused app runs them at its host's speed, so it differs between runs and
  says nothing about the frames.
- `game_time_s` and `sim_time_s` are the two clocks after the last delivered frame, and
  `replay_from_tick` the armed replay's start tick (`null` when none was). To encode a PNG sequence
  later, feed it to `ffmpeg` with the arguments in the manifest.

### What repeats

A job's frames, AOVs and audio are a function of three things (ADR-1881): **the world state when the
job starts**, **the request**, and the **project, settings and GPU driver**. The world state is what
the app's simulation holds: entities and their components, physics, game state, a game's random
streams, particles alive, the position of a playing shot, sequence or replay, a weather transition, and
any timeline a host runs for itself. A job does not rewind it. It continues from where the world stands
and moves it on like any other stretch of the app. One exception: a job whose `time_map` holds the world
on every frame (every key at scale 0) puts the live effects back when its frames end (below).

Nothing else reaches the frames. A job restarts all of this, so what the app did before the job does not
show:

- the wall clock, the app's frame count and how long the app has run are not read;
- `Time::elapsed` and `Time::sim_elapsed` run from zero for the job and carry on afterwards from where
  they stood plus what the job ran, so anything posed from them (the material clock's wind sway, an
  `Update` system reading `Time::elapsed`) starts at the same phase in every job;
- the fixed loop has no time banked, so the same fixed steps land on the same frames at any `fps`;
- the `regia_vfx::Weather` cloud clock and wind drift run from where the weather
  started and carry on the same way afterwards;
- every mesh and every instance of a `RuntimeScatter` field picks its LOD afresh (ADR-1881, ADR-2672), so a job
  does not inherit levels or cross-fades from where the camera was before it. A host that drives its own
  `ScatterField` calls `ScatterField::restart_lod` itself;
- ambient life's animation clock, drifts and bird flights restart when the job restarts the game clock
  (`book/agents/ambient-life.md`), and the automatic birds move back near the job's camera;
- all temporal render state restarts at the job's opening camera cut: TAA and TSR history and jitter,
  screen noise phases, fog, clouds, shadows, probes and the metered exposure.
- every frame of the job is complete (ADR-2582, `FrameRenderer::set_complete_frames`, on for the job's
  length): work the runtime renderer normally moves off the frame lands on the frame that needs it, not on
  one chosen by the CPU's or the GPU's speed. Material-graph pipelines and sky rebuilds build inline (what
  was queued before the job is waited for at its start), emissive light fits run on the frame thread,
  texture streaming uploads every set it wants in that frame without a fade, the stochastic SSR pass never
  goes dormant on a counter readback, and the GPU cull keeps submission order. On a fast card that work could
  land partway through the first job and stay for the second, so two identical jobs in one host gave different
  color frames while depth, id and motion repeated; a software rasterizer is slow enough that it always landed
  between frames.
- the history that only picks how *new* effects look (ADR-2687): effects spawned without a seed during the
  job draw from a seed stream that restarts with every job (the app's own stream carries on after the job
  where it stood); when no particle can be alive, the particle clock (the heat-haze phase) and the spawn
  ring (the slots new particles take, the blend sort's last tie-break) start over as in a new context; an
  idle `CameraShake`'s noise clock starts over; the camera director's shake seeds and the shake field's
  emit seeds start over when no shake is running or on its way.
- the particles step once per game frame, in whichever render of the frame comes first (ADR-2687). In a
  windowed app the job draws what the window stepped; when the window did not draw (minimized, occluded,
  its surface not ready) the job's render takes the step, so the job's particles do not depend on whether
  the window managed to draw.
- the effects layer's warm frames (ADR-2741): a new effects context counts as live for a few frames with
  nothing in it, so the frame builds its targets before the first effect, and each frame it is live moves
  the particle clock. A job gives it none (the app gets its own back at the end), so the first job in a
  fresh host reaches its first spawn at the same clock, and the same heat-haze phase, as every later job. A window
