  precipitation: `Σ |sky − ground| / Σ |sky|` between the sky's last row and the farthest ground
  row over 16 azimuths. 0 is seamless.
- `render.set_weather { aerial_from_tables: bool }` turns the switch on or off (with or without a
  weather change in the same call) and answers `aerial_from_tables` too. It is a runtime switch:
  `render.get_profile` still names the preset. Errors: a non-boolean answers `F0002`; an app
  without `RenderSettings` answers `F0003` and changes nothing.

```json
{ "method": "render.set_weather", "params": { "preset": "storm", "aerial_from_tables": true } }
{ "method": "render.get_weather" }
```

To check it by eye, take a screenshot with the switch off and on at the same frame; the horizon
seam on the image is `regia_render::horizon_seam::measure_horizon_seam` on a linear readback and
its sky mask. The owner's plates come from `REGIA_AERIAL_PLATES=<dir> cargo test -p regia_render
--test aerial_tables` (off | on, noon clear, noon heavy rain, sunset).

<!-- source: book/agents/weather-precipitation.md -->
# Rain, snow, wet surfaces and the wind near the ground

The [weather](book/agents/weather.md) falls, wets and blows (spec 99, ADR-1847): rain and snow drawn around the
camera, surfaces that get wet and collect snow, and a wind near the ground that foliage, grass, rain
and snow read.

All three effects are **off unless the project turns them on**, in `config/weather.ron`
([format](docs/formats/weather-ron.md)). A host that keeps a `Weather` for its clouds renders the
same frames, including a map that sits in `overcast`. `regia new` writes the file with all three on,
and an agent can turn each on for a run with the `render.set_*` methods below. Turned on, they do
nothing until a `Weather` has precipitation or wind.

## What each preset does

| Preset | `precipitation` | Temperature | What falls | What you see |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `overcast` | 0.2 | 8 °C | 2 mm/h rain | drizzle: surfaces wet, no puddles |
| `rain` | 0.35 | 9 °C | 6 mm/h rain | moderate rain, full puddles in about 85 minutes |
| `storm` | 1.0 | 10 °C | 50 mm/h rain | heavy rain, 3 km visibility, puddles in minutes |
| `snow` | 0.5 | -3 °C | 1.2 cm/h of snow | steady snow, the ground covered in about 2.5 hours |
| `blizzard` | 1.0 | -8 °C | 5 cm/h of snow | 400 m visibility, the ground covered in about 35 minutes |

Rates are `max_rate · precipitation²`. The rain preset's 6 mm/h fills puddles in about 85 minutes
from dry (near a third full after half an hour). `precipitation_kind` is `auto` by default: all snow at or
below 0 °C, all rain at or above 2.5 °C, a smooth band between. `rain`, `snow` and `sleet` force it.
During a transition the rates of the two ends blend, so a change of kind never jumps.

`render.get_weather` answers the rates in `rates` (`visibility_m` is null when nothing falls) and the
state of the config file in `config`.

## The scene wind

`SceneWind` is the wind 10 m above the ground. In `weather` mode the weather writes it every frame:
the wind at cloud height through a height profile (about 0.49 of it under a 1500 m layer), plus
deterministic gusts on the weather clock, of strength `gustiness`. The gusts stay within
`1 ± gustiness` of the mean and never reverse it, and a paused weather holds it.

| Reader | What it does with it |
|---|---|
| The renderer | the foliage wind, every frame; `off` clears it |
| Grass | the terrain wind (`TerrainWind`): heading and strength (speed / 5 m/s) of the mean, `terrain.wind` shows `weather_steered: true`; see [Terrain wind](book/agents/terrain-wind.md) |
| Rain and snow | the slant and the drift: the drops carry `velocity_m_per_s` (gusts included); `off` stills them |
| The occlusion view | its tilt, from the mean fall direction |
| Surface weather | faster drying, from the mean speed |
| VFX emitters with `wind_response` | the particle wind (ADR-2642); without a `SceneWind` the air is calm |
| The sea (`SeaWeatherPlugin`) | the swell and ocean wind, from the mean |
| The ambience bed | the wind layer's level |

Not yet following it (spec 99 § 3.3 lists them as follow-ups): cloth (`cloth.set_wind` /
`ClothSet::set_global_wind` stays the host's), the fluid and smoke simulation (`regia_fluid`), and the
far scatter impostors, which do not sway (near scatter meshes sway with the renderer's foliage wind).

- `render.scene_wind` → `{ present, mode, velocity_m_per_s, mean_m_per_s, speed_m_per_s, gust,
  surface_factor, renderer_foliage_wind }`.
- `render.set_scene_wind { mode: "weather" | "manual" | "off", wind_m_per_s? }` → `{ before, after }`.
  It creates the resource when absent. `manual` needs `wind_m_per_s`, shortened to 40 m/s.

While a `SceneWind` exists the extraction sets the renderer's foliage wind every frame, so a call to
`FrameRenderer::set_foliage_wind` is overwritten: a host sets `SceneWind` instead. `render.set_foliage_wind`
writes the resource when it exists (`SceneWind::set_explicitly`: `manual` with the value, `off` for null).
`renderer_foliage_wind` is the renderer's foliage wind, which the extraction sets from `SceneWind` every frame. Materials read it. Grass follows `TerrainWind` instead (`terrain.wind` answers `weather_steered`), so it takes the wind once (ADR-2043).

The terrain wind follows the gust-free mean only, rounded (whole degrees, 1/32 strength steps), and is
written only when that changes: gusts do not redraw the grass's cached shadows, and a `terrain.set_wind`
holds until the mean wind changes a step.

## Drawn rain and snow

Stateless GPU particles in a box around the eye: no simulation buffer, no CPU work per drop, and a
full field on the first frame after a cut.

| Tier | Rain | Snow | Splashes | Box half width / height (m) | Occlusion view |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MobileLow | 2,000 | 1,500 | 0 | 12 / 10 | off |
| MobileHigh | 6,000 | 4,000 | 256 | 12 / 10 | 256² over 32 m |
| Deck | 8,000 | 5,000 | 256 | 14 / 10 | 256² over 48 m |
| Low | 12,000 | 8,000 | 512 | 16 / 12 | 512² over 64 m |
| Medium | 24,000 | 16,000 | 1,024 | 18 / 12 | 512² over 64 m |
| High | 48,000 | 30,000 | 2,048 | 18 / 12 | 512² over 64 m |
| Ultra | 96,000 | 60,000 | 4,096 | 22 / 14 | 1024² over 96 m |

These are the counts at the heaviest rate; the drawn count follows the drops above 1 mm per unit
volume (about 9 % at 2 mm/h, 24 % at 6 mm/h).

- `render.precipitation` → `{ enabled, quality_tier, kind: { rain, snow }, rates, drawn: { rain, snow,
  splashes }, wanted: { rain, snow, splashes }, budget: { rain, snow, splashes, half_extent_m,
  height_m, resolution }, resolution, resolution_override, density_scale, max_drops, splashes,
  streak_exposure_s, occlusion: null | { size_texels,
  extent_m, origin, tilt_deg, redraws, last_redraw_frame }, fog_extinction_per_m }`. `wanted` is what
  the weather asks for now, `drawn` what the last frame's step reported (zero with the effect off or
  without air; `drawn.splashes` is zero while there is no occlusion view, since splashes draw only on the
  view's top surfaces).
- `render.set_precipitation { enabled?, density_scale?, max_drops?, splashes?, occlusion?,
  streak_exposure_s?, resolution? }` → `{ before, after }`. `resolution` is `"full"`, `"half"`,
  `"quarter"`, or null for the tier's; anything else answers `F0002` naming `resolution`.

### Resolution

Every tier draws the drops at full resolution in the frame's own pass (`budget.resolution` is
`full`). `resolution: "half"` or `"quarter"` draws them into a target of half or a quarter of the
frame's width and height in a pass of their own, which tests the scene depth in its fragment stage,
and composites that target over the frame (one bilinear sample per frame pixel). A streak thinner
than the target's pixel widens to one pixel and pays in coverage, so a smaller target shades fewer
fragments but widens and softens thin rain. `render.precipitation`'s `resolution` is the choice in
effect, `resolution_override` the run-time one (null: the tier's). The choice is a run-time setting,
not part of `config/weather.ron`; a tier's default moves only by ADR, after a device measurement
(ADR-3249 holds the lavapipe streak-survival numbers and the Pixel 6 / Fairphone 5 command).

While the effect and `visibility.couple_fog` are on, what falls thickens the air: a constant
extinction, applied wherever the frame fog is, with the fog's color. `RenderSettings::fog` is never
changed and the term exists whether the host's fog is on or not. `fog_extinction_per_m` shows it.

## Surface weather

`SurfaceWeather` is the state of exposed surfaces. In `simulated` mode the weather integrates it over
game time; in `manual` it holds what you set (a wet street with no weather clock).

- 5 mm/h wets a surface in 2.4 minutes; it dries in 30 minutes at a drying factor of 1. The factor
  rises with sun and wind and falls under cloud.
- Puddles fill only once a surface is wet, and only above 2.5 mm/h: drizzle wets and does not pool.
  Full puddles cover at most about 60 % of flat ground. Lab materials pool only with
  `WeatherResponse::puddles`; terrain may unless its layer stack says `puddles: false`, and its ruts
  and dips fill first.
- Snow accumulates at or below 0 °C (less up to 2 °C) and is kept as water equivalent, so the melt
  conserves it. Meltwater wets. 3 cm of depth hides the ground.
- `Weather::set_now` does not wet the ground at once: it gets wet at the rates above.

The response runs after the surface stage, on built-in and graph materials: porous surfaces darken
and metal keeps its albedo but gets the film, ripples stir the puddles, and snow settles on what
faces up. `WeatherResponse::NONE` keeps a material out of it.

A `.material.ron` (v5) sets the response in data, so no code is needed:

```ron
weather: (porosity: Some(0.6), wet: 1.0, snow: 0.8, puddles: true),
```

Every field is optional: `porosity: None` derives it from roughness and metallic, `wet` and `snow`
scale the effect (`0..1`, 0 keeps it out), `puddles` lets flat parts pool. No block is the default
response. A v4 file loads with the default and `regia upgrade-project` rewrites only its version;
cooked materials from earlier builds keep loading (cooked v6 reads v5 and v4). See
`docs/formats/material-v5.example.ron`.

A terrain's `.terrain.layers.ron` (v5) does the same per layer, and holds the puddle switch for the
whole stack:

```ron
LayerDesc(name: "sand", /* ... */ weather: Some((porosity: Some(0.95), snow: 1.0))),
LayerDesc(name: "road", /* ... */ weather: Some((porosity: Some(0.1), snow: 0.0))),
// ... after `layers: [...]`:
puddles: true,
```

A layer whose ORM map carries porosity in its blue channel (0 sheds a film, 1 soaks) says so with
`porosity_from_orm: true` (v5). An ORM map's blue channel is glTF metallic by default, so it is never
read as porosity without the flag; a named `porosity` wins over it:

```ron
LayerDesc(name: "cobbles", /* ... */ orm_texture: Some("cobbles_orm.png"),
    weather: Some((porosity_from_orm: true))),
```

`porosity: None` derives it from the layer's roughness, `snow` scales the cover (`0..1`; 0: a warm
road stays bare), and no block is the default response. The layers' blocks blend by their slope,
altitude and painted weights, so a sand-to-rock transition mixes the two. `puddles: false` keeps the
whole terrain to a wet film (a desert, scree). A v3 file loads with the defaults and
`regia upgrade-project` rewrites only its version. Nothing changes on a dry frame.

The Mobile tiers' lite forward path (phones) shades the same rule. It compiles its weather variant
the first time a frame is wet, snowy or has an extinction, and a dry frame draws with the pipelines
it always had. The High tier reads the occlusion view; the Low tier has none, so covered surfaces
there get wet too.

- `render.surface_weather` → `{ present, mode, wetness, puddles, snow_we_mm, snow_depth_m, snow_cover,
  ripple, rain_mm_per_h, snow_we_mm_per_h, drying_factor, frame: { wetness, puddles, snow_cover, ripple },
  terrain_variant_on, terrain_layers: [{ entity, puddles, overrides, layers: [{ name, porosity,
  porosity_from, snow }] }] }`. `terrain_layers` lists each terrain's response: `porosity_from` is
  `"layer"` where the layer names one, `"orm"` where it reads each texel's porosity from its ORM
  map's blue channel (v5 `porosity_from_orm`; `porosity` is then `null`, as there is no single
  number), and `"roughness"` where it comes from the layer's scalar roughness (a layer with an ORM
  texture shades with the texture's roughness instead; a layer that sets `porosity_from_orm` without
  an ORM texture also lands here). `overrides` is true when a layer's block differs from the
  default.
- `render.set_surface_weather { mode?, wetness?, puddles?, snow_depth_m?, snow_cover? }` → `{ before,
  after }`. It creates the resource when absent. Supplied numeric values must remain finite in `f32`
  before clamping: wetness, puddles and cover to 0..1, depth at zero. Snow water/depth conversions
  must also stay finite, including the inverse multiply used by the next simulation step; otherwise
  the call returns `invalid_params` and leaves the surface unchanged. A value given without `mode`
  keeps the mode.

## The occlusion view

A depth map of what stands between the sky and a point, looking along the mean fall direction. It
hides drops under roofs, places splashes on the top surface the rain hits, and keeps covered
surfaces dry. It lives in a tile of the local-light shadow atlas, which grows by the tile's size, so
no light loses room. It is drawn when a surface is not dry or precipitation falls, on a tier that has
one. It redraws when its snapped origin moves (an eighth of its side), its tilt bucket changes, or a
caster over its square changes bounds or pose, and holds otherwise: `redraws` counts.

- `render.surface_exposure { points: [[x, y, z], ...] }` (at most 256) → `{ ready, map_frame, points:
  [{ p, exposure, cover_y }] }`. `exposure` is 1 under open sky and 0 under cover, and `cover_y` is the
  height of the first occluder above the point (null under open sky). The first call schedules a
  one-shot copy of the tile and answers `ready: false`; a call after the next frame answers.

Errors: `F0002` for invalid parameters (the message names the field), `F0003` without a
`RuntimeRenderer`. `render.surface_exposure` answers `F0002` with `reason: "occlusion_off"` while the
frame has no view.

A bad config shows in `render.get_weather`: `config.error.code` is `weather_config_invalid` (does not
parse, an unknown field, a preset name clash, a value out of range) or `weather_config_version` (newer
than this build).

## Budgets and platforms

The budgets in spec 99 § 12 are targets until the real-card run records them in `docs/perf-log.md`:

| Where | What | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | the weather drivers and the integrator | 0.02 ms a frame |
| CPU | the precipitation prepare (one uniform, no per-drop work, no per-frame allocation) | 0.02 ms a frame |
| 5080, 1440p, Desktop High | `storm` rain (48k streaks, 2k splashes) | 0.6 ms |
| 5080, 1440p, Desktop High | `blizzard` snow (30k flakes) | 0.5 ms |
| 5080, 1440p, Desktop High | an occlusion view redraw, on the frames it redraws | 0.3 ms |
| 5080, 1440p, Desktop High | the surface response on, over lab and terrain | 0.15 ms |
| 5080, 1440p, Desktop High | the surface response present but dry | 0.02 ms |
| Pixel 6, MobileHigh | rain at 6k streaks | 1.0 ms |
| Pixel 6, MobileHigh | the surface response | 0.3 ms |

The tile costs 1 MB of atlas at 512² and 4 MB at 1024². Lavapipe measures correctness, counts and redraws, not time.

- Linux, Windows and Android aarch64 compile the same code. The draw uses no compute and no storage buffers, so it
  runs on every tier, and the shaders use no derivatives in the vertex stage and fixed loop bounds (FXC-safe).
- Android surface loss: the draw holds pipelines and a uniform, and nothing is recreated beyond what `VfxGpu` recreates.
- A tier whose shadow atlas plus the tile passes the device's texture limit has no occlusion view: drops fall through
  roofs and covered surfaces get wet there, and `render.precipitation`'s `occlusion` is null.
- A frame that goes wet for the first time compiles the terrain's weather variant once, unless the project has
  `effects.surface` on, which adds it to the pipeline warm. Going dry and wet again compiles nothing. The same
  setting has the Mobile tiers' lite forward path build its weather pipelines with its first dry frame.

## Checks you can run

```json
{ "method": "render.set_weather", "params": { "preset": "rain" } }
{ "method": "render.set_surface_weather", "params": { "mode": "simulated" } }
```

- Set `rain`, step 300 frames at 1/60 s, read `render.surface_weather`: `wetness` rose by
  `R · 5 s / (wet_mm · 3600)`, about 0.042 at 6.1 mm/h (`rain` is precipitation 0.35, and the
  rate is `50 mm/h × precipitation²` over the default `wet_mm` of 0.2). Take a screenshot.
- Set `snow` with `paused: false`, step, and watch `snow_cover` rise. A screenshot shows white on flat
  ground and not on walls.
- Put a roof over a point and compare `render.surface_exposure` under and beside it.
- Give the road layer `weather: Some((snow: 0.0))`, set `snow`, read `render.surface_weather`
  (`terrain_layers[0].layers[i].snow` is 0) and take a screenshot: the road stays dark while the
  verge whitens.
- Set `render.set_scene_wind { mode: "off" }` and read `render.scene_wind`: `renderer_foliage_wind` is
  null.
- Over grass, set `rain` and read `terrain.grass`: `report.surface_weather` is true and a screenshot
  shows darker, glossier blades; set `snow` and the blade tips whiten.
- Set `render.set_precipitation { resolution: "quarter" }` in `storm` and screenshot next to `"full"`:
  the streaks are wider and softer; `render.precipitation` answers `resolution: "quarter"`.

## Not in this page's scope

Lightning, lens drops, streaks running down walls, snow deformation, hail, regional weather, and rain
on water bodies are out of scope (spec 99 § 16). The path tracer and the baked GI stay dry, and local
lights do not light rain and snow.

<!-- source: book/agents/gltf-conventions.md -->
# glTF conventions (LOD, sockets, ORM, variants)

The cook path reads `docs/formats/gltf-conventions.md` and writes runtime payloads. No manual
remap after import. Author synthetic files the same way; do not depend on DO27 source assets.

## LOD

Name meshes `Stem_LOD0`, `Stem_LOD1`, `Stem_LOD2`, … any `_LODn` (LOD0 is the most detailed). The cook emits
one `regia_asset::LodGroup` per stem that has a chain. A lone `_LOD0` is not a group. A chain still
requires `_LOD0` plus at least one other level of the same stem; the levels stay sorted by index.

The primary mesh is the first `_LOD0` in the scene walk, or the first mesh whose name has no `_LODn`
tag. A file whose triangle meshes are all `_LODn` with `n > 0` still cooks: the lowest index present
is the primary (the first mesh of that index). That covers a file that is itself one LOD level, and
a clip file whose only mesh is the bind mesh at `_LOD2` or another level. A file that already has
`_LOD0` or an untagged mesh keeps that mesh as the primary. Generated LODs still apply only to
`_LOD0` or an untagged mesh. A file with no triangle mesh fails with `no mesh found in glTF file`.

## Sockets

An empty named `socket_<id>` becomes a `PrefabSocket` with the prefix stripped (`socket_turret`
→ `turret`). The local matrix is stored on `PrefabSocketSet` (`prefab/sockets`). The node's mesh,
if any, is not rendered.

## Collision nodes

A node named `collision_*` (`collision_<body>_<n>` hulls, or an older single `collision_hull`)
holds collision geometry. Its mesh is never rendered: the cook skips it, and so do the editor's
loaders (`load_gltf_model`, `editor.spawn_gltf_hierarchy`; ADR-1622). The rule is
`regia_asset::is_collision_node_name` (case sensitive).

Since ADR-2341 the cook also fits each proxy to a collider shape by its name: `collision_box_*`,
`collision_sphere_*`, `collision_capsule_*`, `collision_convex_*`, `collision_mesh_*` (a static
triangle mesh); any other `collision_*` name is a convex hull. The shapes are the glTF's
`collision` sub-asset; `assets.collision_report` lists them and `regia_physics::AuthoredCollision`
attaches them on spawn. See [Collision proxies](book/agents/collision-proxies.md).

## Textures

| Map | Cook |
|---|---|
| Base color | sRGB (`TextureCookUsage::ColorSrgb`) |
| Occlusion + metallic–roughness | Packed linear ORM |

ORM channels are **R** occlusion, **G** roughness, **B** metallic, **A** 255. Missing occlusion
is 255; missing metallic–roughness is roughness 255, metallic 0. The cooked material's
`orm_map` points at `texture/orm/{material index}`, not at the raw metallic–roughness image.
Source images are still cooked. Do not hide occlusion in the metallic–roughness R channel.

Images smaller than 4×4 stay `CookedImage` RGBA8 (block compression needs 4×4). Larger maps
become KTX2.

## Variants

Materials named `<slot>_Rem` and `<slot>_A52` (both required) become a `MaterialVariantSet`.
Spawn it with `PrefabInstance::new(set, "Rem")` and switch at runtime:

```rust
use regia::core::id::Guid;
use regia_asset::{AssetId, MaterialVariant, MaterialVariantSet, PrefabInstance};

fn select_variant() -> Option<PrefabInstance> {
    // The cook path emits a `MaterialVariantSet` for a slot (`hull_Rem` / `hull_A52`).
    let set = MaterialVariantSet {
        slot: "hull".into(),
        variants: vec![
            MaterialVariant { name: "Rem".into(), material: AssetId(Guid::from_u128(1)) },
            MaterialVariant { name: "A52".into(), material: AssetId(Guid::from_u128(2)) },
        ],
    };
    let mut prefab = PrefabInstance::new(set, "Rem")?;
    prefab.select("A52"); // swaps PrefabInstance.material to the A52 cooked material
    Some(prefab)
}
```

`select` returns `false` and leaves the instance unchanged when the name is missing. The
cooked `CookedStandardMaterial.authored.base.base_color` of the selected asset is the color
that changes.

<!-- source: book/agents/tunnels.md -->
# Mesh tunnels

A tunnel through a heightfield is three pieces (`regia_terrain::MeshTunnel`):

1. A `HolesMask` ellipse on the heightfield so the surface (and its collider samples) drop out
   of the bore.
2. An imported or collision-derived render mesh for the interior.
3. A trimesh collider (`ColliderShape::trimesh_from_triangles` on
   `MeshTunnel::collision_trimesh`).

```rust
use regia::physics::ColliderShape;
use regia_terrain::{CollisionProvenance, HoleEllipse, MeshTunnel, TunnelDetail};

fn build_tunnel() -> Result<(), regia_terrain::MeshTunnelError> {
    // A triangle fan for the bore (a real tunnel imports or sim-supplies these).
    let positions: Vec<[f32; 3]> = vec![[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [4.0, 0.0, 0.0], [2.0, 0.0, 3.0]];
    let indices: Vec<u32> = vec![0, 1, 2];
    let provenance = CollisionProvenance {
        source_asset: "collision_tunnel_north".into(),
        triangle_count: 1,
        note: "sim collision mesh".into(),
    };
    let tunnel = MeshTunnel::from_collision(
        &positions,
        &indices,
        HoleEllipse {
            center: [0.0, -20.0],
            radius: [5.0, 4.0],
            rotation_radians: 0.0,
        },
        TunnelDetail::default(),
        provenance,
    )?;
    // `None` when the indices are not triples into `vertices` — validated data is always `Some`.
    let shape = ColliderShape::trimesh_from_triangles(
        &tunnel.collision_vertices,
        &tunnel.collision_indices,
    );
    let _ = shape;
    Ok(())
}
```

Spawn that trimesh **and** a `ColliderShape::HeightField` cut by the same mask:
`HolesMask::cut_heights` sets the samples in (or, with a margin, next to) the hole to NaN, and
the collider removes every cell touching a NaN sample. A horizontal ray misses a flat plateau,
so the ground beside the hole has to rise across the ray.

## Cutting mouths and ramp trenches

`TerrainSharedDraw::set_holes(Some(&mask))` cuts any footprints through the drawn terrain
(ADR-088): `HoleShape::Rect`, `Polygon`, `Ellipse`, a coverage `Raster` in terrain space, or
`HoleShape::segment(from, to, width)` for an open-cut ramp (a DO27 mouth is about 20 m × 25 m).
Inside, nothing is drawn in the color, depth, velocity, decal-receiver or shadow passes, so
the cut casts no shadow while the ground around it still shades the tube below. The edge is
per pixel and fixed in world XZ at every LOD. `rendered_heights` and the `RenderedSurface`
answer NaN inside, and scatter is not drawn over it.

From the agent protocol (insert `draw.holes_handle()` as a resource first):

```json
{"method": "terrain.set_holes", "params": {"segments": [{"from": [-142.8, -286.0], "to": [-170.0, -256.0], "width_m": 20.0}]}}
```

`terrain.holes` lists the cut shapes and `pending` until the next frame applies them.

## The map's holes file (`<map>.holes.ron`)

A map's holes live in `<map>.holes.ron` next to the map (`maps/switchbacks.level.ron` →
`maps/switchbacks.holes.ron`, `regia_terrain::holes_ron_path`). The file is a serialized
`HolesMask` with a `version` (format v2, `docs/formats/terrain.md` § 5): at most 64 shapes in
all (ellipses and named holes included), rasters at most 2048 texels a side. A bare
`ron::to_string(&mask)` without the `version` field loads as version 1; a file from a newer engine
is refused. Version 2 adds named holes that gameplay opens and closes at runtime
(`terrain.set_hole`, [terrain runtime](book/agents/terrain-runtime.md)); a version 1 file loads unchanged.

```ron
(
    version: 1,
    shapes: [
        polygon(points: [(-15.0, -9.0), (14.0, -10.0), (16.0, 8.0), (0.0, 12.0), (-14.0, 9.0)]),
        rect(center: (40.0, 2.0), half_extents: (10.0, 12.5), rotation_radians: 0.7),
        ellipse((center: (-40.0, 0.0), radius: (6.0, 4.0), rotation_radians: 0.0)),
    ],
)
```

Load it and cut both the drawn terrain and the collider:

```rust,wrap
# use regia_terrain::TerrainSharedDraw;
# let draw: &mut TerrainSharedDraw = todo!();
# let map_path: &std::path::Path = todo!();
# let (mut collider_heights, spacing): (Vec<f32>, f32) = todo!();
# let sample_xz = |i: usize| [i as f32, 0.0];
let mask = regia_terrain::load_holes_ron(&regia_terrain::holes_ron_path(map_path))?;
draw.set_holes(mask.as_ref());
if let Some(mask) = &mask {
    mask.cut_heights(&mut collider_heights, spacing * 0.5, |i| sample_xz(i));
}
```

`HolesMask::to_holes_ron` writes one. From the agent protocol, `terrain.load_holes` cuts a
document on the next frame, from its text or a project path:

```json
{"method": "terrain.load_holes", "params": {"path": "maps/switchbacks.level.ron"}}
```

## What sees the holes

- **Drawing and shadows:** every pass and cascade (above).
- **Picking and engine rays:** `regia_terrain::pick_terrain(world, origin, direction, max)`
  and `raycast_with_holes` pass through a hole, like the physics heightfield: below the
  surface there is no rock, so a ray down a mouth hits nothing more of the terrain (test the
  tunnel meshes yourself). They read the mask the draw applied (`TerrainHoles`, once a draw has
  applied one) and use `Terrain::holes` only when no mask has been applied. The editor's picks call
  them, so a tunnel mesh under the
  mouth can be clicked. On the agent protocol:

  ```json
  {"method": "terrain.raycast", "params": {"origin": [0, 80, 0], "direction": [0, -1, 0]}}
  ```

  `hit` is `null` when the ray falls through the mouth; `hit.holes` counts the shapes the hit
  terrain is cut by.
- **GPU irradiance probes:** the probe rays read the draw's hole windows. A probe in a mouth is
  open interior space, not a buried probe; a ray down a mouth that runs into the ground beside
  it below the surface meets the shaft's rock wall. A new mask wakes settled probes.
- **Path tracer and the GI bake:** the shared draw's reference heightfield is NaN inside the
  holes and the tracer drops every cell touching a NaN sample (the cut is up to one cell wider
  than the drawn one). `PtHeightfield::cut_holes` cuts a heightfield you build yourself, and a
  `regia bake-gi` description takes `holes: Some("map.holes.ron")` on its terrain. A baked
  terrain-layer column over a mouth starts at the lowest rim height around it.

A bore with no local lights is black at outdoor exposure. Spawn the lights along
the mesh and an `InteriorVolume`, or an `EnclosureScene` so extraction runs
`detect_enclosure`. The shade drops sky IBL and holds the 40 lux floor at EV 8.
Fit the volume to the bore's inner faces: walls, floor and roof on a face (or up to 2 cm outside
it) shade as inside. A headlight placed exactly at the camera is fine: it lights the cone
without black (NaN) pixels.
`build_interior_lighting` traces one bounce into a probe grid (misses stay black)
and the frame takes that field plus one reflection probe. Desktop High keeps 256
of those lights; a shorter list is what a Deck profile will warn about. See
[high-end lighting](book/agents/high-end-lighting.md).

## Rays

- Into the mouth, stopping before the far end: misses terrain and walls.
- Into solid ground beside the hole: hits the heightfield.
- Down the bore through a **closed** far cap: hits the cap. The stock box helper is an open
  tube (mouth and exit both open). Add the far-end triangles when the tunnel is a dead end.
  Wind the cap so its normal faces back toward the mouth.

`physics.raycast` on the agent protocol hits the same colliders once `PhysicsPlugin` has
stepped.

### More `terrain.set_holes` parameters

The schema (`agent.schema`) also lists these optional parameters:

- `clear` (boolean): Remove every hole (with no shapes or segments).

### More `terrain.raycast` parameters

The schema (`agent.schema`) also lists these optional parameters:

- `max_distance` (number): Search distance, metres (default 10000).

<!-- source: book/agents/world-pick.md -->
# World pick: rays over terrain and layers

`world.pick` casts a ray through the rendered world and reports the nearest surface and the `MapLayer` it
belongs to. It runs on the CPU against terrain heightfields and mesh renderers
(`regia_pick::world_pick`); it needs no GPU and no window.

- Terrain is layer 0. A mesh entity takes the `MapLayer` on itself, else its nearest ancestor's, else 0.
- A ray over a terrain hole (a tunnel mouth cut by `terrain.set_holes`) passes through to what lies below.
- `origin` and `point` are local coordinates, the `GlobalTransform` frame. After a floating-origin rebase that is not world space. The terrain heightfield stays world-anchored: the march adds `OriginOffset` and subtracts it from the point it returns. A zero offset makes the two frames the same.
- Skinned meshes are cast where their joint palette draws them, not in bind pose. The default is
  four-weight linear blend. Dual-quaternion blending and an eight-influence table follow the
  skinning options the renderer resolves: the table is read only from the mesh entity, and only
  when its length matches the mesh.
- A mesh with morph targets and weights is cast in the deformed pose, using the same active
  weights the renderer applies (game mode keeps the sixteen largest). Without weights it stays
  in bind pose. Skinning then runs on that deformed mesh.
- `cull` applies to mesh triangles only. Both mesh faces count unless `cull` is `back` (front faces only). A terrain hit is only a crossing from above, whatever `cull` is.

```json
{ "method": "world.pick",
  "params": { "origin": [0, 50, 0], "direction": [0, -1, 0], "layers": [0, 1] } }
```

returns

```json
{ "hit": { "entity": 4294967301, "name": "deck", "layer": 1, "surface": "mesh",
           "point": [0, 5, 0], "normal": [0, 1, 0], "distance": 45, "triangle": 4 },
  "count": 1 }
```

`all_layers: true` returns `{ hits: [...], count }`, the nearest hit of each accepted layer, nearest first: what the
ray crosses through stacked floors. `terrain` and `meshes` switch each kind off, `max_distance` caps the ray,
`include_hidden` also tests entities whose own or inherited (hidden-ancestor) `Visibility` is `Hidden`, and `skip` lists entity ids to ignore.

From Rust:

```rust,wrap
# let world: &mut regia::prelude::World = todo!();
# let (origin, direction) = (regia_core::math::Vec3::ZERO, regia_core::math::Vec3::Z);
use regia_pick::{PickFilter, world_pick};
let ray = regia_core::math::Ray::new(origin, direction);
let hit = world_pick(&world, ray, &PickFilter::on_layers(&[1, 2]));
```

To verify a layering: `world.pick` straight down at a point over each floor, once without `layers` (the top floor) and once
per `layers: [n]`, then `terrain.holes` to confirm a mouth is cut where the ray should pass.

`origin` and `direction` are required finite 3-vectors (array or `{x,y,z}`); direction cannot be zero.
Optional filters are `layers` (u8 ids), `all_layers`, `terrain`, `meshes`, `include_hidden`, `skip`
(entity-bit ids), `max_distance` (positive distance cap; 0 is refused), and `cull` (`none` or `back`, mesh triangles only). Invalid
shapes or values return `F0002`. Workflow: cast the default ray, narrow with `layers`, then request
`all_layers: true` to inspect stacked surfaces.

Captured failing call (lavapipe; a zero direction is refused):

```console
$ regia agent call world.pick '{"origin":[0,0,0],"direction":[0,0,0]}' --project samples/arena
error: method call failed: `direction` must not be zero (-32602): {"code":"F0002","hint":"check the method's parameters in the agent guide"}
```

## A tunnel mouth

Put a tunnel's meshes on their own `MapLayer`. A ray into the mouth passes the terrain hole and hits the
tube on that layer; filtered to layer 0 it falls through the hole and hits nothing. The tunnel acceptance
scene checks this per pixel of an approach frame against a triangle oracle
(`a_pick_ray_into_the_mouth_hits_the_tube`, [Tunnel acceptance scene](book/agents/tunnel-scene.md)).

With mesh layers (`TerrainMeshLayers` on the terrain, [Terrain mesh layers](book/agents/terrain-mesh-layers.md)) the hole is cut on
its lattice triangles as drawn, and the mouth's band is terrain: a ray into the mouth hits the band (layer 0) or the
layer's chunk meshes on their own `MapLayer`, never the cut ground (`a_pick_ray_into_the_mouth_hits_the_layer`).

<!-- source: book/agents/exposure-zones.md -->
# Exposure zones

A box or a capsule that asks the eye for an EV range. The renderer samples the
zones into the frame (ADR-322): every frame `ExposureZonesPlugin` (in
`DefaultPlugins`) weighs the zones at the active camera, and the main view's auto
exposure keeps the eye inside the combined range. The math is
`regia_render::exposure_zones` (`ExposureZone`, `zone_weight`,
`combine_zones`, `adapt_ev`, `ExposureLog`, `ZoneExposure`). See the
[DO27 host checklist](book/user-guide/do27-host-checklist.md). Mesh bores stay on
[Tunnels](book/agents/tunnels.md).

## Volume

`ExposureZone` is a component. Put it on an entity that already has a
`GlobalTransform`. The shape is local, in meters:

- `ExposureZoneShape::Box { half_extents }` — half size on local X, Y and Z.
- `ExposureZoneShape::Capsule { radius, half_height }` — capsule along local Y.
  `half_height` is half the cylindrical segment. Each cap adds `radius`, so the
  total length is `2 * (half_height + radius)`.

`ev_min` and `ev_max` are the EV100 range the zone wants. A zone that wants one
exposure sets both ends equal. `blend_distance` is the width of the fade, in
meters. `adapt_up_speed` and `adapt_down_speed` are EV per second (toward a
higher EV, and toward a lower one). `priority` is an `i32`: the higher value wins
when two zones both cover the eye. The component has no serde derive, the same as
`InteriorVolume`.

The default is a 1 m box at EV 14.5, a hard edge, 2.0 EV/s up, 1.5 EV/s down,
priority 0.

## Mouth blend

Signed distance is positive outside and negative inside, in meters. The box and
the Y-aligned capsule follow Inigo Quilez's public-domain distance functions.
The blend band sits outside the surface:

```text
weight = 0    at blend_distance meters outside
weight = 1    on the surface, and everywhere inside
between       Hermite smoothstep, t * t * (3 - 2 * t)
```

A tube only a few meters across can still fade across a 25 m mouth, because the
band does not have to fit inside the bore. A blend of 0 is a hard step: weight 1
for a distance of 0 or less, otherwise 0.

A rigid transform, or a per-axis scale, keeps the box distance exact. A capsule
is exact when the local X and Z scales match. A sheared matrix is orthogonalized
first.

## One target

`combine_zones(&[(weight, &zone), ...], default)` returns an `EvTarget`.
`combine_weighted_zones` is the same for zones held by value (a reused scratch
vector).

- An empty list, or a list with nothing usable, returns the sanitized default
  range and the default speeds (2.0 EV/s up, 1.5 EV/s down).
- The highest priority with a positive finite weight wins. Lower priorities drop
  out.
- Winning weights saturate to 1. When they sum past 1 they are renormalized.
  When they sum to less than 1, the remainder is `default`. That is how one
  mouth narrows the range as the camera approaches.
- Non-finite inputs are dropped. The result is always finite.

The framework passes `ZONE_OPEN_RANGE` as the default: EV100 −2 to 15, the
default auto-exposure band. At the outer edge of the band the combined range is
that open band, and on the face it is the zone's own range.

## How the frame uses it

Each frame, after transform propagation, `sync_exposure_zones`:

1. takes the active camera: the window camera with the lowest `order` (the one
   the renderer draws first). Texture cameras are never zoned;
2. collects every zone with a positive weight at the camera's eye;
3. combines them with `ZONE_OPEN_RANGE` and calls
   `RuntimeRenderer::set_exposure_target(Some(target))`, or `None` when no zone
   covers the eye;
4. hands the frame's `Time` step to the renderer as the adaptation `dt`.

The main view's auto exposure then runs through `ZoneExposure`:

- **Metering.** The eye chases
  `clamp(metered, ev_min - compensation, ev_max - compensation)`
  (`zone_goal_ev`). `metered` is the newest histogram on its own (not the
  smoothed meter), after the auto-exposure band clamp and the bright-subject
  bias. A bright window inside a tunnel still meters, but it cannot pull the eye
  out of the range. Exposure compensation shifts the result as it does outside
  a zone. A zone may ask for an EV outside the level's auto-exposure band: its
  clamp comes after the band's.
- **Adaptation.** One `adapt_ev` step per frame with the target's speeds,
  starting from the EV the frame was about to apply, so entering a band never
  jumps. The usual luminance smoothing is not applied on top.
- **Leaving.** When the target clears, the eye keeps walking toward the
  smoothed meter at the default speeds and hands back once it is within 0.05 EV
  (`ZONE_RELEASE_TOLERANCE_EV`). From then on the frame is exposed exactly as
  without zones.
- **No zones.** With no target and nothing to hand back, the exposure is bit
  for bit the plain auto exposure. A map without zones renders the same pixels
  as before, so no golden image changed.
- **Manual exposure ignores zones.** A view with auto exposure off, or a camera
  with `exposure_ev`, is exposed at its fixed EV. The eye is dropped, so turning
  auto exposure back on starts from the meter.
- **Camera cut.** A cut that snaps exposure (`render.camera_cut`, the default)
  starts the next zone frame on its goal. A fading cut keeps adapting.
- **dt.** The host's frame step (`FrameRenderer::set_exposure_dt`, which the
  framework sets from `Time::delta_secs` every frame). A frame with no step, a
  step of 0, or a non-finite step holds the eye. The ease does not read the wall
  clock: a replay that presents the same frames with the same steps adapts the
  same way.

A host that drives `FrameRenderer` itself calls `set_exposure_target` and
`set_exposure_dt` before `render_into`.

## Adaptation

`adapt_ev(current, target, dt, up_speed, down_speed)` is one step of
`dy/dt = speed * (target - y)`:

```text
next = current + (target - current) * (1 - exp(-speed * dt))
```

`dt` is clamped to the closed interval from 0 to 0.1 seconds
(`ADAPT_DT_CAP_SECONDS`). The factor stays in 0..=1, so the step lands on the
segment between `current` and `target` and can sit on the target. Moving to a
higher EV uses the up speed, to a lower EV the down speed. A non-positive speed
holds. A non-finite argument returns `current` unchanged.

`adapt_settle_steps(gap, tolerance, speed, dt)` is how many steps bring a gap
within a tolerance: `ceil(ln(gap / tolerance) / (speed * dt))`. From sun (EV
14.5) to the tube (EV 8.5) at 1.5 EV/s and 30 fps, to within 0.05 EV, that is
96 steps (3.2 s). Back out at 2.0 EV/s it is at most 74 steps.

## Agent protocol

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `render.get_exposure` | `{ ev, goal, meter_ev, mode, adapting, settled, zone_target, zone_count, metered_luminance, logging, log_samples, zones }` |
| `render.exposure_log {"action": "start", "cap"?: n}` | `{ logging: true, cap }`, a fresh log (default cap 4096, at most 262144) |
| `render.exposure_log {"action": "stop"}` | `{ logging: false, count }`; the samples stay readable |
| `render.exposure_log {"action": "get"}` | `{ logging, count, last, samples: [{ time, ev, target }] }` |
| wait atom `{"predicate": "exposure_settled", "tolerance"?: 0.05}` | holds when `|ev - goal| <= tolerance` |

`render.exposure_log` starts and stops a log, so it needs the `play` permission and counts as a mutating call
(ADR-3285); `render.get_exposure` stays `read`.

All EVs are EV100 with exposure compensation applied. `mode` is `meter` (plain
auto exposure), `zone`, `release` (handing back) or `manual`. `goal` is what the
eye chases: the clamped meter in a zone, the smoothed meter while handing back,
the newest histogram in `meter` mode. `adapting` is true while a zone (or its
release) is more than 0.05 EV from its goal. `zone_target` is
`{ ev_min, ev_max, target_ev, adapt_up_speed, adapt_down_speed }` or `null`.
`zone_count` counts the zones with a positive weight at the eye, every priority,
and is `null` without `ExposureZonesPlugin`. Before the first frame `ev`, `goal`,
`meter_ev`, `mode` and `settled` are `null`. `zones` is the baked section list
(see [Zones from the bake](#zones-from-the-bake)): `null` when the host has not
inserted `BakedZoneList`, otherwise one object per cooked section.

The log records one sample per main-view frame, zone or not: `time` is the sum of
the frame steps since `start` (deterministic under `play.step`), `ev` the
exposure and `target` the goal. Past the cap the oldest sample drops.
`exposure_settled` fails (and a `wait_until` keeps polling) before the first
exposed frame.

Errors carry `data.reason`:

| Reason | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| `renderer_missing` | F0003 | the app has no `RuntimeRenderer` |
| `invalid_action` | F0002 | `action` is missing or not `start`, `stop` or `get` |
| `invalid_cap` | F0002 | `cap` is not an integer from 1 to 262144, or given without `start` |
| `invalid_tolerance` | wait error | `tolerance` is not a number above 0 |

## A tunnel

```rust
use regia_render::exposure_zones::{ExposureZone, ExposureZoneShape};

/// The DO27 tube: 400 m long, entered along +Z, EV 8.5 inside, a 25 m mouth.
fn tube_zone() -> ExposureZone {
    ExposureZone {
        shape: ExposureZoneShape::Box {
            half_extents: [8.0, 4.0, 200.0],
        },
        ev_min: 8.5,
        ev_max: 8.5,
        blend_distance: 25.0,
        priority: 1,
        ..ExposureZone::default()
    }
}
```

Spawn it with a `Transform` at the tube's center, rotated so local Z runs down
the bore: `commands.spawn((Transform::from_translation(center), tube_zone()))`.
A side chamber that should stay brighter is a second, smaller zone with a higher
`priority`.

The tunnel acceptance scene (`crates/regia_terrain/tests/tunnel_scene`, ADR-3257, ADR-8629) drives a
car in and out of an 80 m tube at 20 m/s (2 m a frame at 10 fps) with a zone over the tube from 15 m in
to the end cap: the cook's band for a tunnel section (EV 8.5 to 10.5, a 25 m blend; spec 121 § 5.6),
8 EV/s both ways. Starting the box inside the tube puts the portal in the blend band, so the range keeps
narrowing while the camera crosses the portal. The zone tests drive to 60 m in: the tube lit by its bake
meters inside the band for the first 40 m or so and under it beyond, where the zone holds the eye on the
band. Against the same drive without it the zone lowers the worst frame-to-frame step of the mean luma
entering the tube (14.9 against 20.2 levels) and leaves the drive's worst no higher (14.9 against 20.2;
`exposure_zone_eases_the_mouth`), and no step passes 25 (`exposure_zone_removes_the_entry_flash`). The
eye still chases the newest histogram, which is two frames old. With the default speeds (2.0 and 1.5
EV/s) this drive's entry eases by at most 1.3 levels: at 2 m a frame the roof darkens the picture in one
frame. A zone whose band does not bind (a tube that meters inside it) only makes the eye faster than the
plain meter, which can make a picture change inside the tube step harder than without the zone (27.5
against 20.2 levels at a turnaround 40 m in, ADR-8629). The scene hands the zone's target to
`FrameRenderer::set_exposure_target` with the path's frame step as `set_exposure_dt`, as
`regia_framework::exposure_zones` does with the frame's `Time`.

## Scripted drive

The acceptance drives are unit tests in `regia_render::exposure_zones`:

- `scripted_tunnel_drive_has_no_flash_or_blackout` (ADR-257): the zone math
  alone, sun EV 14.5 as the default range.
- `zoned_tunnel_drive_stays_on_the_segment_and_settles` (ADR-322): the
  renderer's eye. 30 fps for 40 s at 20 m/s through the box above. The meter
  reads EV 14.5 outside and EV 5 inside the bore. Every frame the EV stays
  between the previous EV and the goal, moves at most 0.5 EV, and never leaves
  [8.5, 14.5] (the EV 5 meter never reaches the eye). 96 frames after the portal
  it is within 0.05 EV of 8.5 and stays there to the far portal. After the far
  band it hands back to the meter at exactly EV 14.5.

The same checks against a running game: `render.exposure_log {"action":
"start"}`, drive the camera with `play.step`, then `render.exposure_log
{"action": "get"}` and assert on `samples`. From the frame the camera enters the
first blend band until the eye hands back, each `ev` lies between the previous
sample's `ev` and its own `target`, and no step exceeds 0.5 EV at 30 fps. Outside
the zones (`mode` `meter`) the frame follows the plain smoothed meter and
`target` is the newest histogram, which the smoothed value trails. `wait_until
{"predicate": "exposure_settled"}` waits for the eye to arrive.

## Log

`ExposureLog` records `(time, ev, target)` up to a cap (default 4096) and drops
the oldest sample. `to_json` writes one object:

```text
{"samples":[{"time":0.000000,"ev":14.500000,"target":14.500000}]}
```

```rust
use regia_render::{ExposureZone, ExposureZoneShape, EvRange, adapt_ev, combine_zones};
use regia_scene::GlobalTransform;

fn exposure_at_the_mouth() -> f32 {
    let zone = ExposureZone {
        shape: ExposureZoneShape::Box {
            half_extents: [8.0, 4.0, 200.0],
        },
        ev_min: 8.5,
        ev_max: 8.5,
        blend_distance: 25.0,
        priority: 1,
        ..ExposureZone::default()
    };
    // Halfway across the 25 m shell in front of the mouth at z = -200.
    let eye = [0.0_f32, 1.5, -212.5];
    let weight = zone.weight_at(&GlobalTransform::IDENTITY, eye);
    let target = combine_zones(&[(weight, &zone)], EvRange::point(14.5));
    adapt_ev(
        14.5,
        target.target_ev(),
        1.0 / 30.0,
        target.adapt_up_speed,
        target.adapt_down_speed,
    )
}
```

The post stack's exposure and tonemap settings themselves (auto exposure on or off, fixed EV, tonemap
operator, physical camera) are `render.get_exposure_settings` / `render.set_exposure_settings`: see
[Exposure and tonemap](book/agents/exposure.md).

## Zones from the bake

A cooked section (spec 121 § 5.6) is one exposure zone, one reverb zone and one interior volume.
`regia_world_geom::zones::section_volumes` reads the cooked sections and zones and returns one
`SectionVolumes` per section, in section order. It does not stop at four. The aerial composite still
packs four interior slots (the four nearest the eye). The zone list is the full bake.

`ExposureEase::step(target, dt_s)` eases toward `target` by the frame clock's `dt`. The same `dt`
sequence gives the same exposure run to run. A step of 0, or a non-finite step, holds the previous
value. The first sample, with no previous value, takes the target. There is no snap when the eye
moves a long way in one step. `ExposureEase::cut` is the explicit snap a host asks for; a drive
through a mouth does not call it.

`EaseSettings::depth_blend` defaults to on. The under-rock weight then follows a smoothstep from 3 m
to 22 m of overburden, including under a lid, so crossing a mouth does not write the interior floor
in one sample. Off, the weight is the shell's step: 0 at or below 2 m, 1 under a lid or outside an
open cut, and 0 on an open cut.

A host that has cooked a map builds the rows with `section_volumes` and inserts
`regia_agent::BakedZoneList`. `render.get_exposure` then returns `zones`, an array of
`{ section, exposure_ev, blend_m, reverb_preset, reverb_size_m, interior_center_m, interior_half_m }`.
Without the resource, `zones` is `null`. The array is not capped at four.

The acceptance drive walks each Switchbacks mouth at 2 m and a frame step of 0.25 s. The exposure
change per sample is at most 0.5 EV. The outdoor and interior floors in that test are the caller's
(11.5 and 9.0). They are not engine defaults. The Switchbacks cook has 37 sections (the plan's name
for the test says 35; the count is the cook's, spec 121 § 5.6).

<!-- source: book/agents/tunnel-scene.md -->
# Tunnel acceptance scene

A tunnel is several features that have to work as one set: a hole in the terrain, a tube and lip under it,
an interior volume, local fog, a headlight with dust, the sky and auto exposure. The tunnel acceptance
scene builds one synthetic tunnel from those pieces and drives a camera in and out of its mouth at 20 m/s,
on lavapipe, with no game content.

It is the test target `tunnel_scene` of `regia_terrain` (`crates/regia_terrain/tests/tunnel_scene/`; the
README there lists the scene and its slots).

```text
cargo test -p regia_terrain --test tunnel_scene
REGIA_DUMP_DIR=/tmp/out cargo test -p regia_terrain --test tunnel_scene -- --nocapture
```

With `REGIA_DUMP_DIR` set the run writes every frame of the path for the old behavior (the interior lit as
open sky, today's default) and for the tunnel set on, a `metrics.csv`, and `contact_sheet.png` with the old
behavior on the top row and the tunnel set on the bottom row.

## What each frame is checked for

- Mean luminance: no black frame, no frame-to-frame jump above a bound (a flash when the exposure catches up).
- No terrain pixel inside the hole's footprint (checked against an uncut control that must be flagged).
- No crack along the lip at the cut edge (checked against a lip that stops short, which must be flagged).

## The tunnel features (slots)

Exposure zones, reverb zones, a baked probe volume, interior fog, light shafts and world pick layers each
have a named slot in the scene, filled with the feature as it ships (ADR-3257; `fills.rs`). The old path
renders with every slot empty, the tunnel set with all six. One test per slot:

- `exposure_zone_eases_the_mouth`: an exposure zone over the tube (the cook's band for a tunnel section, EV
  8.5 to 10.5 with a 25 m blend) lowers the worst frame-to-frame step entering the tube against the same drive
  without it (14.9 against 20.2 levels), and the drive's worst is no higher (14.9 against 20.2). The zone tests
  drive to 60 m in, where the baked tube meters under the band; the test asserts that the zone holds the eye in
  its band there while the plain meter is under it (ADR-8629). `exposure_zone_removes_the_entry_flash` holds the
  same drive to 25 levels (14.9).
- `reverb_zone_covers_the_tube`: one tube-preset reverb zone covers every corner of the tube; the drive is
  wet inside and dry past the zone's fade.
- `probe_volume_lifts_the_tube_interior`: a baked GI volume of the tube (CPU bake in the test, well under a
  second) lights the floor 6 to 16 m in brighter than the interior shade's flat floor. The test lights the
  tube as a baked tunnel without an interior volume (it predates ADR-7975; since then the interior shade
  reads a covering baked volume too, `interior_baked_gi`).
- `interior_fog_stays_in_the_tube`: fog bounded by the interior volume (`FogVolume::interior`) leaves every
  pixel outside the interior's screen box unchanged and shows in the sunlit air under the portal.
- `light_shafts_fall_through_the_cut`: with black surfaces and the headlight off, a ray-cast oracle splits
  each pixel's air into sunlit and roof-shadowed parts; the cut and the wedge under the portal glow, the
  shadowed air does not (the `calibrated` fog sun-shadow rule; `legacy` fails it).
- `a_pick_ray_into_the_mouth_hits_the_tube`: `world_pick` rays through an approach frame hit the tube's
  meshes on their pick layer inside the cut, fall through the hole on the terrain layer, and hit the
  terrain outside it.

With `REGIA_DUMP_DIR` the slot tests also write their plates (`probe_volume_*.png`, `interior_fog_*.png`,
`shaft_*.png`).

This page is for the engine's own tests; it adds no agent-protocol method. To look at a tunnel in a running
game use `terrain.holes` and the screenshots described in [Tunnels](book/agents/tunnels.md).

<!-- source: book/agents/terrain-scatter.md -->
# Terrain scatter (rocks and props)

A map's rocks, rubble and debris come from its `.scatter.ron` (format v2,
`docs/formats/terrain.md` § 2): classes, each with weighted glTF meshes, density rules (density
map, noise, slope / altitude / layer mask, exclusion paths) and a look (tint, base blend, contact
AO, fade distances). Placement is seeded per cell, so the same file and map place the same rocks
on every client; the runtime streams 64 m tiles around the camera and hands the instances to the
frame renderer, which culls them on the GPU (frustum + Hi-Z) and draws them instanced.

## Check what is on screen

`terrain.scatter` returns the requested state and the last frame's counts:

```json
{ "enabled": true, "contact": true, "class_overrides": [],
  "report": { "installed": true, "resident": 21515, "tiles": 431, "tiles_visible": 96,
              "emitted": 4331, "per_lod": [14, 321, 3996, 0], "fading": 1779,
              "classes": [ { "name": "boulders", "enabled": true, "resident": 6120 }, … ] } }
```

`emitted` is what reached the frame before the GPU cull; `resident` is everything placed near
the camera. `installed: false` means the host has not recorded a field yet.

Instances placed by hand come from the brush, not the seed, and draw through the same field:
[painted scatter](book/agents/terrain-scatter-paint.md). `resident` and `emitted` count both.

## Toggle and compare

`terrain.set_scatter` takes any of `enabled`, `contact`, or `class` + `class_enabled` and returns
`{ before, after }`. A/B a change the way a reviewer would:

1. `seeing.screenshot` (target `"offscreen"`) → `on.png`
2. `terrain.set_scatter { "enabled": false }`, `play.step`, `seeing.screenshot` → `off.png`
3. `seeing.compare_images` on the two; set `enabled` back to `true`.

`{ "contact": false }` removes only the soft occlusion pool under each rock (the ground
darkening and dust tint); `{ "class": "gravel", "class_enabled": false }` hides one class.

`{ "class": "ferns", "class_subsurface": "foliage" }` puts the foliage subsurface profile on every
material of one class (`"off"` restores the materials the field was built with, byte for byte); plain
materials then scatter like mesh leaves wherever the render profile asks (`render.set_subsurface`, off in
every preset; [subsurface scattering](book/agents/subsurface.md), ADR-3170). A material graph does not scatter on this
path, for scatter as for any mesh, and a swaying class's materials are graphs: such a class keeps its look,
and `report.classes[].subsurface_unsupported` says `material_graph` (`null` when the class does not ask or
can scatter; the codes are in the [subsurface page](book/agents/subsurface.md)). `terrain.scatter` lists the overrides
in `foliage_subsurface` and each class's profile in `report.classes[].subsurface`. `class` needs
`class_enabled`, `class_subsurface` or both; `class_subsurface` needs `class`. A refused call changes
nothing.

`{ "class": "woodland_trees", "class_caster": { "from_lod": 1, "leaf_keep_one_in": 4 } }` and
`{ "class": "woodland_trees", "class_season": { "kind": "broadleaf" } }` set a class's lower-detail shadow casters
and its season (each `null` to clear). Both need `class`, and both are in
[Streamed forests](book/agents/scatter-forest.md).

## Far rocks as impostors

`{ "impostors": true }` turns on the octahedral impostor far field (opt-in, off by default)
where the host bound an impostor layer: rocks past their class's `fade_start` hand over to a
camera-facing card baked from the rock (no pop: the mesh dithers out across the fade band
while the card dithers in), and past `fade_end` — where nothing used to draw — cards carry
every class out to 2 km or until the rock is under a pixel. The report then shows
`"impostors": true` and `impostor_band` (meshes in the hand-over band this frame). A/B it the
same way: screenshot, `terrain.set_scatter { "impostors": false }`, `play.step`, screenshot,
`seeing.compare_images` — the difference is far rocks only. Without a layer the switch does
nothing (`report.impostors` stays false).

## Dense ground: detail limits

`{ "detail": true }` turns on the dense-scatter detail limits (opt-in, off by default; the host
supplies its `ScatterDetail` with its output height and field of view): every rock also shrinks
into the ground by its own projected size (a 5 cm pebble ends at a few tens of meters, a boulder
of the same class keeps its range; the shrink is the distance fade's, so nothing pops), classes
stream only as far as their largest rock stays above the limit, and stones under
`shadow_min_radius_m` cast no shadow-map shadow (the contact pool and contact shadows ground
them). The report shows `"detail": true` and `emitted` drops. A/B it like the other switches;
the difference is sub-pixel stones in the distance and the shadows of tiny stones.

## Host contract

The host owns the `ScatterField` and `ContactMap`. Each frame: `control.apply(&mut field,
Some(&mut contact))`, `field.update(eye)`, `contact.update(queue, &field, eye)`,
`field.collect(&view, &mut frame.meshes)`, then `control.record(&field, stats)`. The lookdev
harness (`samples/lookdev/src/scatter_shots.rs`) is the reference.

Impostors: bake once at load (`field.bake_impostors(Some(settings))`,
`ImpostorLayer::new(device, queue, &atlas)`), bind the layer with
`TerrainSharedDraw::set_impostors(Some(&layer))` before boxing the draw, call
`field.settle_streaming(eye)` at the load screen, and each frame
`control.apply_impostors(&mut field, Some(&mut layer), settings)` before `field.update(eye)`
and `layer.update(queue, &field)` after it.

Detail limits: each frame `control.apply_detail(&mut field, settings)` before
`field.update(eye)`, with `settings = ScatterDetail { reference_height_px, reference_fov_y, ..ScatterDetail::default() }`.
`cargo xtask bench-do27 -- --scatter scan --density 1,3,5,10 --detail` measures it. `REGIA_IMPOSTORS=1` turns it on in the lookdev
harnesses (`look_r2`, `do27_chase`).

`update` places tiles on the background task pool (the next ring is prefetched and stays
invisible until needed) and `collect` culls and seats tiles in parallel; both give exactly the
rocks the synchronous, serial path gives. `set_background_streaming(false)` and
`set_parallel_collect(false)` switch to those paths when a measurement needs them (a heavily
loaded machine can make the parallel path's worst frame slower than the serial one).
`terrain_lab --do27-chase --variants scatter` prints the scatter CPU per frame and the sun
shadow pages rocks dirty per cascade (`scatter-held`: a parked camera must dirty none).

Evidence: `docs/evidence/scatter-rocks/`, `docs/evidence/impostors/`.

## Shadow LOD hint

`terrain.set_scatter { "shadow_lod": { "max_lod": 1, "min_lod": 0 } }` applies a field-wide shadow LOD
hint to every scatter instance, the counterpart of `render.set_shadow_lod_hint` (which takes an entity
and so cannot reach scatter). Each instance casts from its asset's own shadow LOD (else its drawn LOD)
clamped to `min_lod..=max_lod` and to the asset's LOD chain; when that differs from the drawn LOD the
shadow moves to a shadow-only draw of it. `max_lod: null` (or missing) is no cap. `{ "shadow_lod": null }`
clears it; off is the default and leaves every frame unchanged. `terrain.scatter` reports the current
hint as `shadow_lod`.

Cluster-cast shadows (the meshlet path) do not use this hint: a cluster's shadow comes from the same
cluster DAG level the camera view selects, so a per-entity LOD cap has no coarser mesh to switch to.
`render.mesh_lod` reports what the cluster path selected.

## World-anchored grids and gameplay colliders

By default each class's cell grid starts at the map edge, so a map grown by a backdrop ring places
different rocks. `ScatterField::with_placement_origin(PlacementOrigin::World(..))` anchors the grid
at a world point instead. `terrain.scatter_colliders` bakes the gameplay colliders of a set under
either origin. See [scatter gameplay colliders](book/agents/terrain-scatter-colliders.md) (ADR-8029).

<!-- source: book/agents/contact-shadows.md -->
# Contact shadows (screen-space, sun only)

The cascaded sun shadows resolve a few centimeters per texel close to the camera and meters
far away, so small casters lose their shadow: a rock seems to float, a tire does not touch the
road, a ledge of relief has no dark underside. Contact shadows add it back from the depth
buffer. Every pixel marches toward the sun's point on screen: 48 pixels at 1440 lines and
above, proportionally fewer on smaller targets (at least 4), so the shadows cover the same
share of the screen at every resolution. A depth sample in front of the ray blocks the sun
when it is in front by more than a small bias and by less than an assumed thickness, and also
in front of the receiver's own surface continued along the march: a surface never shadows
itself, even when it faces away from the camera (inside-out meshes). The bias
grows where the depth buffer cannot be trusted to a pixel (silhouettes, ground seen at a
grazing angle), so edges do not grow dotted dark lines. The result multiplies the **sun term
only**: sky light, bounce and local lights are untouched.

It runs on Desktop Low/High/Ultra and Deck (`RenderProfile::contact_shadows`), and is off on
Mobile Low and Mobile High. It needs the depth prepass and a single-sample frame, like SSAO, and
runs only when the sun casts shadows. Lab and editor baselines (`FrameQuality::LAB`,
`FrameQuality::EDITOR`) keep it off. The shared terrain draw gets the same texture
(`SharedPassDraw::set_engine_contact_shadows`), so rocks shadow the ground and relief shadows
itself.

## Toggle and compare

`render.set_contact_shadows { "enabled": false }` returns
`{ "before": { "enabled", "active" }, "after": { … } }`. `active` is false when the profile has no
depth prepass or uses MSAA, even with `enabled: true`. A/B it like any look change:

1. `seeing.screenshot` (target `"offscreen"`) → `on.png`
2. `render.set_contact_shadows { "enabled": false }`, `play.step`, `seeing.screenshot` → `off.png`
3. `seeing.compare_images` on the two; set `enabled` back to `true`.

Look for: dark seams under rocks and props where they meet the ground, shadowed undersides of
ledges and crust plates, and the sun side of bumps lit while their lee side darkens. A shadow
that floats away from its caster, or flat ground darkening at a grazing sun, is a bug; report
the screenshot.

## Cost

One compute dispatch after SSAO, about two depth loads per pixel (each 64-pixel line strip is
loaded once into workgroup memory). `GpuTimings::contact_shadows_ms` reports it; the lookdev
chase prints it as `gpu contact shadows`. Budget: ≤ 0.3 ms at 2560×1440 on Desktop High.

From lookdev: `LOOK_R2_PROFILE=contact=0` turns it off for before/after shots of the DO27 plates.

<!-- source: book/agents/translucent-shadows.md -->
# Translucent shadows (glass, canopies, visors)

Alpha-blended and transmissive meshes cast a partial, tinted shadow instead of none. Beside each
sun cascade's opaque depth map the renderer keeps a coarser second map (half the cascade edge)
with the nearest translucent depth and the product of every translucent layer's RGB
transmittance; local-light shadows get the same pair at a quarter of the atlas edge. A surface
behind a translucent caster takes that light:

- a blended surface (`BLEND`, `PREMULTIPLIED`) lets through `1 − alpha`, untinted;
- a transmissive surface (`transmission > 0`) lets through `transmission × (1 − F0) × base color ×
  volume tint` — tinted glass casts a tinted shadow;
- a damaged pane's holes cast nothing, its cracks and crazing scatter light out of the beam;
- additive meshes and meshes with `ShadowCast::Off` cast nothing.

DO27's canopy glass (blended, alpha 0.9) therefore lets 10 % of the sun into the cockpit, as in
the Cycles references. Your own canopy still shadows the cockpit; only its refraction is off.
Opaque shadows are unchanged, and a frame without a translucent caster renders exactly as it did
without the feature. Glass is not tinted by other glass, and terrain and volumetric fog ignore
translucent casters.

## Toggle and compare

`render.set_translucent_shadows { "cascades": 0 }` turns the sun part off,
`{ "cascades": 4, "local": true }` back on (Desktop High). It returns
`{ "before": { "cascades", "local", "active_cascades" }, "after": { … } }`; `active_cascades` is
capped by the profile's sun cascades.

1. `seeing.screenshot` (target `"offscreen"`) → `on.png`
2. `render.set_translucent_shadows { "cascades": 0, "local": false }`, `play.step`,
   `seeing.screenshot` → `off.png`
3. `seeing.compare_images` on the two; restore the previous values.

Look for: cockpit and cabin interiors behind dark glass going dark, a soft tinted patch under
colored glass, holes in a shattered pane letting full sunlight through. Glass whose shadow is as
black as an opaque wall, or a bright interior behind near-black glass, is a bug; report the
screenshot.

## Tiers and cost

`RenderProfile::translucent_shadow_cascades`: Mobile Low 0, Mobile High 1, Desktop Low and Deck 2,
Desktop High and Ultra 4. `translucent_local_shadows`: on except both Mobile tiers. The maps are
allocated the first frame a translucent caster appears and redrawn each frame (glass moves with
its ship): two draws per caster per cascade. The shadow report (`shadow_cache_report`) counts
`translucent_casters`, `translucent_passes` and `translucent_draws`; the cost lands in the shadow
GPU bucket. From lookdev: `do27_chase --off translucent-shadows`, and
`HERO_NO_TRANSLUCENT_SHADOWS=1 hero_ref …`, render the before.

<!-- source: book/agents/reflection-occlusion.md -->
# Reflection occlusion (enclosed surfaces reflect the enclosure)

The sky and image-based light reach every surface's reflection unless something says they are
blocked. The AO-based specular occlusion only sees contact-scale geometry (the SSAO kernel
reaches about a meter and a tenth of the screen), so a cockpit seen through its canopy, or a room
seen through a window, mirrored the open sky: bluish streaks on surfaces that only see the
inside of the hull or the room. Reflection occlusion takes that part of the sky out.

The SSAO pass casts four short rays from each pixel through the depth buffer: the mirror
direction and three directions 30° around it. Each ray tests points out to 8 m (five on the
mirror ray, three on the others, closer together near the surface; a point seen against the sky
ends a ray as open); a point
hidden behind the depth buffer by a surface near enough to stand in its way blocks the ray (a
thin pole far in front of an open reflection does not). G of the AO texture holds the mirror
ray's result (glossy surfaces), B the four rays' (rough ones). The forward pass blends the two by
roughness and takes the smallest of three estimates as the specular visibility: the AO-based
term, this one, and the probe field's sky share. It applies once. The part of the reflection that
the enclosure blocks (beyond the contact-scale part, which stays dark) reflects the enclosure
instead: a mid-gray wall under the indirect light that reaches the surface. A surface in sun whose
mirror ray dips below the horizon keeps the environment, whose lower half already shows the
ground (a sunlit hull side over sand); in shadow (a cockpit inside its hull) the block stands. Very rough surfaces (perceptual
roughness above 0.6, fading out by 1) keep the AO-based term alone: their lobe is wider than the
rays. Glass and transmissive panes lie in front of the depth the SSAO rays saw. When
screen-space refraction is on (Desktop High, Ultra), the nearest pane traces its own mirror ray through
the refraction copy's opaque depth: sixteen steps out to 24 m, then a bisection. Where the ray
hits, the pane reflects that pixel's color from the copy: the hull beside a canopy, the cockpit
under its far pane, the ground at grazing angles. A ray that goes deep behind a nearby surface
(whose far side the screen does not show) is still blocked, as before. Panes behind the nearest one
(the far side of a canopy) keep that blocked-or-open test without a color. A miss (off screen, sky,
past the march) keeps the environment map. Before ADR-165 a hit only took the sky out, which turned a canopy over
Europa's ice black at grazing angles. Stochastic SSR still replaces the reflection of opaque
surfaces wherever its rays hit something on screen.

It runs on Desktop High and Ultra (`RenderProfile::reflection_occlusion`, with their GTAO rows of
SSAO). Desktop Low, Deck and mobile keep the AO-based specular occlusion alone; lab and editor
baselines (`FrameQuality::LAB`, `FrameQuality::EDITOR`) keep it off.

## Toggle and compare

`render.set_reflection_occlusion { "enabled": false }` returns
`{ "before": { "enabled", "active" }, "after": { … } }`. `active` is false when the profile has no
GTAO row, no depth prepass or uses MSAA, even with `enabled: true`.

1. `seeing.screenshot` (target `"offscreen"`) → `on.png`
2. `render.set_reflection_occlusion { "enabled": false }`, `play.step`, `seeing.screenshot` → `off.png`
3. `seeing.compare_images` on the two; set `enabled` back to `true`.

Look for: cockpit walls, seats and the underside of canopy frames seen through the glass, and
floors and walls of rooms seen through windows, losing their blue sky sheen. Hull tops, roofs,
glass and metals in the open must not change. A dark halo on an exterior surface next to a
foreground object, or an open reflection that darkens, is a bug; report the screenshot.

## Cost

At most fourteen extra depth loads on half of the SSAO texels (a fixed checkerboard at half
resolution on Desktop High; the blur fills the rest), inside the SSAO dispatch. `GpuTimings::ssao_ms` includes it, but the forward pass waits on the
AO texture, so compare `scene_ms` with it on and off. Budget: ≤ 0.1 ms at 2560×1440 on Desktop High.

From lookdev: `LOOK_R2_PROFILE=reflocc=0` turns it off for before/after shots.

<!-- source: book/agents/near-sun-shadow.md -->
# Near sun shadow (the first meters of the view)

The sun's cascaded shadow maps split the view on a ladder from 16 m to 4 km (ADR-061, ADR-140).
Cascade 0 covers the first 16 m, so on a 2048² map one of its texels is 1.5–2 cm wide. A hull flank
the sun grazes stretches each texel by 1/cos of the sun's angle to it. One to five meters from the
camera, a shadow edge on that flank then shows steps 4–10 cm long, which read as "garbled
letters" on the panels. A finer filter cannot remove them (the hard 2×2 compare shows the same
steps), and a 4096² cascade only halves them.

The near sun tile is a second sun view, orthographic like the cascades. It covers the first 4 m
of the view (`regia_render::NEAR_SUN_RANGE_M`) and is drawn into one square of the local
shadow atlas, the first square. On Desktop High it is 2048² with about 6 mm texels for a 60°
view; on Ultra it is 4096² with about 3 mm. Mesh receivers within that range sample it with
the cascades' receiver-plane PCSS filter. Over the last fifth of the range they blend back into
the cascades.

- **Casters.** The tile draws every sun caster whose footprint touches it and that reaches
  cascade 0 at all.
- **Terrain.** The terrain heightfield is not drawn into the atlas, so its shadow comes from
  cascade 0. Only blockers higher than the tile's topmost mesh surface over the receiver count
  there, plus 25 cm. A mesh part the tile already shadows with is never counted again at cascade
  0's coarser texels: no double shadow and no coarse fringe.
- **When it is drawn.** Nothing is drawn or sampled while no mesh lies within range of the eye.
  The tile is snapped to its own texel grid. With paged shadows it also covers a sphere a quarter wider than the 4 m slice and keeps its center until the slice's sphere leaves it, so a moving camera does not move it every frame.
  It is redrawn when its matrix moves or when cascade 0 has a dirty page.

## Toggle and compare

`render.set_near_sun_shadow { "tile": 0 }` turns it off. It returns
`{ "before": { "tile", "range_m", "active" }, "after": { … } }`. `tile` is the edge in texels
(256–8192); 0 is off.

1. Put the camera 1–3 m from a hull side that the sun grazes (sun high, vertical flank). Take a
   `seeing.screenshot` (target `"offscreen"`) and save it as `on.png`.
2. Run `render.set_near_sun_shadow { "tile": 0 }`, then `play.step`, then `seeing.screenshot`, and
   save it as `off.png`.
3. Run `seeing.compare_images` on the two. Set `tile` back to 2048 (High) or 4096 (Ultra).

**What to look for.** With the tile on, shadow edges on the flank (under intakes, ledges and
canopy frames) are straight and clean. With it off they show stair-steps. A character's feet keep
one contact shadow, not two. The far side of the 4 m range must show no seam.

**What is a bug.** A lit patch where cascade 0 shadowed the terrain over the mesh is a bug, and so
is a step at 3.2–4 m. Report the screenshot.

## Cost

When a mesh is in range, each pixel within 4 m pays a second filter: a 3×3 lookup of cascade 0
for the terrain on top of the tile's PCSS. The tile also needs one more atlas draw of the
casters over it whenever it is dirty. Measured numbers are in ADR-164.

<!-- source: book/agents/terrain-editing.md -->
# Terrain editing (sculpt and paint)

`terrain.stroke` runs one brush stroke on a terrain: the same brush core the editor's terrain
tool uses (`regia_terrain::brush`, ported from Fyrox's brush-stroke processor). Heights change
in place on the `Terrain` component; the renderer re-uploads only the dirty rectangle (the path
craters use), and the next save re-cooks only the cook tiles the stroke touched.

## One stroke

```json
{ "method": "terrain.stroke",
  "params": { "mode": "raise", "center": [120.0, -40.0], "radius": 12.0, "strength": 4.0 } }
```

| `mode` | What `strength` means | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `raise` / `lower` | meters at full brush strength | adds / subtracts, falling off to the edge |
| `flatten` | opacity 0..1 | pulls toward the height under `center` |
| `assign` | opacity 0..1 | pulls toward `value` (meters) |
| `smooth` | opacity 0..1 | pulls toward the mean of the `(2k+1)²` neighborhood (`kernel_radius` k, default 2) |
| `paint` | opacity 0..1 | raises material layer `layer`'s painted weight to 1 |

Optional: `to` or `path` (`[x, z]` points) drag the brush; `shape: "rectangle"` with `width` /
`length`; `hardness` (0 soft, 1 hard edge); `layer` (paint any mode into a layer's weight map
instead of the heights); `entity` (default: the first terrain).

With `layer` set, `strength` is a fraction of that layer's 0..=255 weight, not meters. `raise`
adds `strength × 255` at full brush strength and `lower` subtracts it. `flatten`, `assign`,
`smooth` and `paint` blend toward their target by `strength` (`assign` and `paint` scale the
target weight by 255). The same `strength` on the heightfield stays in meters, as the table says.

The reply:

```json
{ "entity": 4294967297, "mode": "raise", "target": "height", "samples": 452,
  "dirty": { "col_start": 1270, "col_end": 1295, "row_start": 1012, "row_end": 1037 },
  "cells": [[39, 31], [40, 31]], "cell_size": 32, "height_before": 212.4, "height_after": 216.4 }
```

`cells` are the 32-sample edit cells the stroke changed; a save re-cooks only the cook tiles
that hold them.

A stroke changes each sample at most once (with the strongest brush coverage it reached), so the
same call always produces the same heights, and dragging back and forth over a spot does not
pile up.

## Check it

1. `seeing.screenshot` (or `editor.capture_viewport` in the editor) → `before.png`
2. `terrain.stroke …`
3. Screenshot again → `after.png`, then compare by eye.

In the editor every stroke, from the mouse or from `terrain.stroke`, is one undo step:
`editor.undo` restores the heights bit for bit. If the brush worker dies mid-stroke, the part that landed is one
undo step too. A linked draw (`TerrainSharedDraw` with its `height_patches_handle` inserted as the
`TerrainHeightPatches` resource) gets every stroke in the next `Update`. Without an editor, only the newest 256
strokes keep an undo record.

Painted mesh instances have their own brush: [painted scatter](book/agents/terrain-scatter-paint.md). Its strokes
are undo steps too, and a sculpt re-seats what it moved.

## Painted layers

A terrain with a `TerrainPaint` component carries one 8-bit weight per material layer per
sample. Painted weight replaces the procedural slope/altitude weight in proportion to its
coverage (`TerrainLayers::blend_painted`), so an unpainted map looks exactly as before.
`paint` with `layer` that the map does not have returns an error naming the painted layer
count.
A weight map whose grid is not the heightfield's grid (one weight per heightfield sample) is
refused with an error that names both sizes, instead of painting the wrong samples.

After sculpting, `terrain.parity` ([terrain parity](book/agents/terrain-parity.md)) reports samples raised or
lowered past the map's height range, which the saved heightfield clamps.

## Noise and ramp

`noise` adds seeded value noise: `strength` is the peak offset in meters (half the samples go up,
half down), `wavelength` the feature size in meters (default 8 samples), `seed` picks the field.
The same seed, brush and path give the same heights.

```json
{ "method": "terrain.stroke",
  "params": { "mode": "noise", "center": [0.0, 0.0], "radius": 30.0, "strength": 1.5 } }
```

`ramp` cuts a straight incline from `center` to `to` (or the last `path` point). The brush width
is the ramp's width and `hardness` its shoulder; `strength` is the opacity. The heights at the two
ends are the terrain's own unless `from_height` / `to_height` (meters) are given.

```json
{ "method": "terrain.stroke",
  "params": { "mode": "ramp", "center": [-40.0, 10.0], "to": [20.0, 10.0], "radius": 4.0,
              "hardness": 0.7 } }
```

In the editor's terrain tool, `6` is Noise (each stroke draws a new seed) and `7` is Ramp: press at
the start, drag, release at the end.
