neighbours on free (ADR-353). `remove_meshlets`, a dropped mesh (`release_meshes`) and a changed mesh
return their ranges, and the next mesh reuses them. Once a streaming map is warm, inserting and
removing meshes creates no buffer. A stream that runs out of room doubles, up to a cap that is
logged once when it is hit. A mesh that does not fit past the cap draws forward until room frees up.
A stream that doubles copies its old buffer into the new one on the GPU, then uploads only the ranges
written since (ADR-7462).

## Counted meshes

A counted mesh (`MeshRenderer::counted`, drawn from its GPU upload with no CPU vertices) takes the path
too (ADR-7462). Give it a `MeshletSource`: the bridge checks the `.fmlt` against the upload's vertex and
index counts and inserts it under the stand-in's key. On its first path frame the arena takes the same
ranges as for CPU vertices. One compute pass (`vis_vertex_repack.wgsl`) then copies the upload's vertices
into a GPU-owned range that the arena's CPU copy never writes. `render.stats` `counted.vis` reports
`meshes`, `clusters`, `repacks`, `forward_fallbacks` and `kept_meshlet_bytes` ([Assets](book/agents/assets.md)).
It still draws forward with cluster residency on, as a LOD or cross-fade variant, without cooked
meshlets, or with a vertex buffer past the device's storage-binding limit (ADR-7542).

## GPU creates

The rest of the path is reused across frames too (ADR-355). Its instance and cull lists and its
shadow-cull lists only grow, by doubling, when a count passes their capacity. Its parameter
blocks are made once. Its ID, material-depth and Hi-Z targets are rebuilt only when the frame
size changes. Its bind groups are rebuilt only when a buffer or target they bind is replaced, and
its pipelines are built once per variant. A warm frame creates no GPU object through the path,
even while meshes stream in and out. It only uploads: instances, parameters and the arena ranges
written since the last frame.

`FrameRenderer::visbuffer_create_stats` (and `creates` below) counts every pipeline, bind group,
buffer and texture the path makes, with their bytes and the upload bytes. It reports a total,
the last frame, and `quiet_frames`: the run of frames, ending with the last one, that created
nothing. The blocking counter readbacks (`visbuffer_counters`) are test diagnostics and are not
counted.

## Agent method

`render.get_visbuffer` (read only) returns:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `enabled` | the profile has `visibility_buffer` on |
| `active` | the runtime renderer's last frame drew through the path (all the conditions above held) |
| `settings` | `{ lod_threshold_px, shadow_lod_threshold_px, max_clusters, occlusion, cluster_shadows, software_raster, software_raster_max_px }`, or `null` without a renderer |
| `default` | `{ setting, state }`: the dense-scene default switch (`preset` or `dense`) and why it does or does not hold the path (`applied`, `switch_off`, `preset_unmeasured`, `profile_choice`; "The dense-scene default"), or `null` without `RenderSettings` |
| `select` | `{ mode, dense, gate }`, or `null` without `RenderSettings`: `mode` is `always` or `dense`; `dense` is `{ enter_triangles, enter_instances, enter_frames, leave_frames }` under `dense`, else `null`; `gate` is `{ dense, triangles, instances, entered, left }` from the renderer (`null` without one): the last frame's counts, and how often the scene entered and left |
| `resolve` | `{ requested, single_pass, fallback, draws, materials }` from the last visibility frame's resolve, or `null` without a renderer |
| `lod_handoff` | `{ active, chained, cluster_lod }` from the mesh LOD selector's last run: chained rigid meshes it placed, and how many it left at LOD 0 for their clusters. `null` without the render plugin |
| `bridge` | the framework bridge is installed |
| `meshes` | `{ visbuffer, forward }`: distinct meshes the bridge inserted, and the other meshes drawn by `MeshRenderer` entities |
| `entities` | `{ total, visbuffer, forward, forward_reasons }` over `MeshRenderer` entities |
| `clusters_resident` | cluster records resident in the arena |
| `buffer_creates` | GPU buffers created for the arena since the renderer started |
| `arena` | `{ meshes, pending, clusters, cluster_capacity, geometry_words, geometry_capacity_words, used_bytes, free_bytes, capacity_bytes, free_ranges, growths, buffer_creates, capped }`, or `null` without a renderer |
| `load_errors` | payload loads that failed since start |
| `errors` | `[{ asset, code, message }]`: the payloads failing now |
| `last_frame` | `{ frames, instances, candidate_clusters, materials, resident_meshes, geometry_bytes, declined_meshes, receiver_instances, receiver_materials, masked_instances, masked_materials, masked_tested, sway, lod_switches, lod_history_discards, lod_history_copies, view_histories, view_history_bytes }` from the last visibility frame, or `null` (see "Masked materials", "Swaying plants", "LOD hysteresis in split screen") |
| `creates` | `{ total, last_frame, frames, quiet_frames }`, or `null` without a renderer. `total` and `last_frame` are each `{ objects, pipelines, bind_groups, buffers, buffer_bytes, textures, texture_bytes, upload_bytes }`; `objects` is pipelines + bind groups + buffers + textures |

`pending` counts meshlets inserted whose mesh has not drawn yet: they become resident at its first
visibility frame. `free_ranges` is 2 with no fragmentation (one per stream).

`render.set_visbuffer` switches the path and its knobs. Every parameter is optional, and nothing is
applied unless all of them are valid (an invalid one is an invalid-params error, `F0002`, naming it):

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `enabled` | `RenderProfile.visibility_buffer` of the active profile |
| `lod_threshold_px` | largest projected simplification error of a drawn cluster, pixels (above 0, at most 1024; default 1) |
| `shadow_lod_threshold_px` | the same for shadow clusters, shadow-map texels (above 0, at most 1024; default 1) |
| `max_clusters` | clusters each cull phase may draw. `get` and `set` store and return the integer passed (at least 1, at most 4 294 967 295; default 1 048 576). The cull capacity clamps that stored value to 1024..=16 777 216 and does not rewrite it. `dropped_clusters` counts clusters past that clamp, not past the raw number |
| `occlusion` | two-phase Hi-Z occlusion culling |
| `cluster_shadows` | instances cast as culled, LOD-cut clusters (off: through the forward shadow passes) |
| `software_raster` | clusters at most `software_raster_max_px` across rasterize in compute (off by default; see "Software raster") |
| `software_raster_max_px` | largest projected cluster diameter the software rasterizer takes: an integer from 1 to 64 pixels (default 16) |
| `select` | `always` or `dense`: `RenderProfile.visibility_path.select` (see "Dense scenes") |
| `dense_enter_triangles` | triangles at which a scene is dense, at least 1. Needs `dense` (in this call or already on) |
| `dense_enter_instances` | meshes at which a scene is dense, at least 1. Needs `dense` likewise |
| `single_pass_resolve` | `RenderProfile.visibility_path.single_pass_resolve` (see "The single-pass resolve") |
| `default` | `preset` or `dense`: `RenderSettings::visibility_default` (see "The dense-scene default"). Applied first; the other path parameters in the same call apply over it |

It returns `{ before, after, note }`, where `before` and `after` are `{ enabled, active, settings, select, single_pass_resolve, default, masked }`.
`default` (also in `render.get_visbuffer`) is `{ setting, state }`: the switch and its `default.state` code, or `null` without `RenderSettings`.
`masked` is `{ instances, materials, tested }` from the last visibility frame (see "Masked materials"), or `null` without a renderer.
`active` turns true at the first frame drawn through the path. With no parameters it changes
nothing and returns the current state twice. Without the render plugin, `enabled` is refused
(not found, `F0003`: no `RenderSettings`), and so are the knobs (no `RuntimeRenderer`).

Forward reasons (`entities.forward_reasons`): `no_meshlets` (no `MeshletSource`), `skinned`,
`morphing`, `translucent`, `graph_material`, `thin_film`, `load_error`, `meshlets_mismatch`, `sway_graph_surface`
(a sway on a surface graph of its own, see "Swaying plants"), and `path_off` (the only key while the path is off).
A lightmap receiver counts in `no_meshlets` here; `render.get_lightmaps` `receivers.{clusters, no_clusters}` says how it draws.

Payload error codes (`errors[].code`):

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `meshlets_not_cooked` | no pak and no cooked-cache file holds the asset (not cooked, or `.meta` lacks `meshlets: true`) |
| `meshlets_unreadable` | a bad cooked wrapper, another asset type, or not a meshlet blob |
| `meshlets_old_version` | cooked by another meshlet format version: run `regia cook` |
| `meshlets_invalid` | truncated, or a cluster range is out of bounds |
| `meshlets_mismatch` | cooked for other mesh data: its vertex or index count differs from the entity's mesh |

## Checking a level

1. The game turns `visibility_buffer` on in its `RenderSettings` profile, or an agent calls
   `render.set_visbuffer { enabled: true }`. Step a few frames (`play.step 3`).
2. `render.get_visbuffer`: `enabled` and `active` are `true`, `entities.visbuffer` counts the rigid
   props you expect, and `errors` is empty. `last_frame.instances` is above 0 once a camera sees
   them. `enabled` true with `active` false means a frame condition failed (no depth prepass, MSAA,
   no post stack, an unsupported device, or no meshlets yet).
3. Back the camera off past the props' first LOD switch distance. `lod_handoff.cluster_lod` equals
   the opaque chained props with meshlets (in view or not), and `last_frame.instances` does not
   drop. If `cluster_lod` is 0 while `active` is true, those props have no meshlets under their
   LOD 0 mesh key.
4. A `forward_reasons.load_error` or `meshlets_mismatch` above 0: read `errors`, recook the named
   asset, and check again (the bridge retries after the hot reload).
5. Stream the level (load and unload cells) and read `buffer_creates` before and after: it stays
   flat once the arena is warm. `capped: true` means a stream is at its cap. The log names it, and
   meshes past it draw forward.
6. While it streams, `creates.last_frame.objects` is 0 and `creates.quiet_frames` keeps rising.
   A frame with objects above 0 after warm-up is a hitch source: a list grew (a one-off, after
   which the count stays flat), or the frame size changed (new targets). If it comes back frame
   after frame, it is a bug. Report the `last_frame` counters.
7. Turn the path off: `entities.forward_reasons.path_off` equals `entities.total` and
   `arena.meshes` drops to 0 at the next frame.
8. On a profile selecting `dense`: `select.gate.triangles` and `instances` count the frame. Below the
   thresholds `active` stays false and the frame is the classic one. Spawn past them: after
   `enter_frames` frames `gate.dense` and `active` are true and `gate.entered` is 1.

## Measuring a machine

The bench prints one row per path (classic, per-material, single-pass, single-pass with the software
raster): frame time with readback, GPU stamps, the resolve's draws, the clusters drawn and the
scene's density (`tri/px`, `inst/Mpx`, `clusters/tile`; "Choosing the thresholds"). It asserts
nothing. Only a real card can decide a default. Lavapipe numbers show the paths run and their draw
counts, not their relative cost on hardware.

```sh
# RTX 5080 or RX 7900, on the machine's own Vulkan driver, 1080p and 4K:
REGIA_VIS_BENCH_SIZES=1920x1080,3840x2160 \
REGIA_VIS_BENCH_SCENES=1024x2048,4096x2048,4096x8192,16384x2048 \
REGIA_VIS_BENCH_FRAMES=60 \
cargo test --release -p regia_render --test visbuffer_dense_bench -- --ignored --nocapture
# To bracket the crossover (ADR-3149): sparse scenes and few-triangle meshes too, three
# interleaved rounds, 1080p (the floor tier), 1440p and 4K.
REGIA_VIS_BENCH_SIZES=1920x1080,2560x1440,3840x2160 \
REGIA_VIS_BENCH_SCENES=64x2048,256x2048,512x2048,1024x2048,4096x128,16384x128,4096x2048,4096x8192,16384x2048 \
REGIA_VIS_BENCH_FRAMES=60 REGIA_VIS_BENCH_ROUNDS=3 \
cargo test --release -p regia_render --test visbuffer_dense_bench -- --ignored --nocapture
```

`REGIA_VIS_BENCH_RESIDENCY=1` runs the visibility rows with cluster residency at the Desktop High budget
(`ClusterResidency::for_preset`), as the dense-scene default would ship (ADR-4906). Every visibility row runs the
LOD band. Each row ends with `lod switches N, resident X MiB (peak Y MiB, budget Z MiB)`.

The bench's `geometry` stamp spans the cull, both rasters and the Hi-Z build. For the cull alone, phase by
phase, run the ignored lib test `cull_cost` (test-only stamps around the cull passes):

```sh
REGIA_CULL_COST_SCENES=1024x2048,4096x2048,4096x8192,16384x2048 REGIA_CULL_COST_FRAMES=128 \
cargo test -p regia_render --lib cull_cost -- --ignored --nocapture
```

## Draw order

The cull lists every cluster in (instance, cluster) order on every run and adapter (ADR-2294): no slot
comes from an atomic counter. A pixel where two triangles meet at exactly the same depth therefore has
the same owner in every run and every frame, and two renderers given the same scene write the same
visibility IDs. When lists overflow the cull capacity (`max_clusters` clamped to 1024..=16 777 216),
the back-face-culled list keeps first; the counters report the rest as `dropped_clusters`.
`visbuffer::tests::cull_order` checks the order by reading
the lists back.

## Lightmap receivers

A rigid lightmap receiver ([lightmaps](book/agents/lightmaps.md)) can draw on the path: its UV2 sits beside its
clusters, and the resolve's `LIGHTMAP` variant reads its lightmap texel. A voxel-far cluster of that
receiver indexes vertices appended past the chart, so those pixels keep the probe light instead of
reading past the UV2 range. Only the materials that hold a receiver need that variant. `render.get_visbuffer` `last_frame.receiver_instances` counts the
receivers on the path, and `last_frame.receiver_materials` the materials with one: those are the ones
the per-material resolve shades through the `LIGHTMAP` variant (ADR-2689); every other material
keeps the plain pipeline. `resolve.lightmap_materials` is what the last resolve shaded that way. The single-pass
resolve has no `LIGHTMAP` variant, so a frame with a receiver falls back to the per-material resolve
(`resolve.fallback: vis_lightmap_receivers`).

## Masked materials

Alpha-tested (`ALPHA_MASK`) meshes, such as leaf cards, grass and fences, draw on the path on a device that
carries the texture table ([bindless](book/agents/bindless.md)). Their clusters rasterize with an alpha-tested pipeline that
reads each pixel's base-color alpha through the table and drops what the forward alpha test drops. One pipeline
serves every masked material, so no draw binds a material. The holes are in the depth before the occlusion
pyramid is built, so nothing seen through a leaf is culled. The resolve shades the pixels the test kept.

A masked mesh stays on the forward path, as before, when:

- the device has no texture table (`render.bindless_report` says why);
- the frame may hash its alpha test (TSR or TAAU with hashed alpha): the cluster raster tests the hard cutoff only;
- the material has hair cards or parallax.

For ECS foliage with a separate `MeshLodChain`, the ordinary chain's cluster handoff still accepts only
opaque materials. Use `DisableMeshLod` (or omit that chain) to keep the source mesh submitted while its
cluster DAG picks detail at every distance. Otherwise the ordinary chain can select a coarser forward draw.

A masked mesh casts its shadow through the forward shadow passes, which alpha-test. Masked clusters never take the
software rasterizer. A persistent instance set with a masked material draws alpha-tested on a table device, from its
first visibility frame. It casts no shadow, whatever its policy says: the cluster shadow raster has no alpha test, and a
set has no forward shadow draw. Where the set's test cannot run (no table, hair cards, parallax) it draws nothing, since
it has no forward path to stay on.

To check a level: `render.get_visbuffer` `last_frame.masked_instances` counts the masked instances on the path and
`masked_materials` their materials. `masked_tested: true` means they were alpha-tested this frame. With
`masked_instances` above 0 and `masked_tested` false, the frame did not bind the table, and the masked clusters
wrote no pixels or occluding depth. `render.set_visbuffer` returns the same counts under `before.masked` and `after.masked`. Tests and benches read
`FrameRenderer::visbuffer_counters` `masked_clusters` (a blocking readback).

To price the alpha-tested raster on a card, add `REGIA_VIS_BENCH_MASKED=1` to the `visbuffer_dense_bench` command above:
all 64 materials become masked, and each row prints its masked instances, masked clusters and `tested`.

## Swaying plants

A plant adopted with `FoliageSway::adopt` draws as clusters (spec 98 § 8d, ADR-3916). It moves the way the forward
path moves it: both call one function, `regia::foliage_sway::offset`. Nothing needs turning on beyond the path and the
scene wind (`render.set_foliage_wind`, [Foliage wind](book/agents/foliage-wind.md)).

- **Cull.** While some sway moves, an instance's bounds grow by its material's offset bound, and its clusters skip the
  normal cone test. The LOD cut does not move with the wind. In calm air the frame is byte for byte the frame of the same
  material without sway.
- **Far levels.** Voxel far levels do not sway. An instance with such levels fades its sway from 70 % of the distance
  where the first one can be selected, and is at rest from 95 %.
- **Shadows.** An opaque plant casts as swaying clusters. A masked one keeps its forward shadow draws, which alpha-test and
  sway. Both redraw their pages through the dynamic-caster class. An opaque swaying persistent set does so while it moves;
  a masked persistent set casts no shadow until the cluster shadow raster supports its alpha test.
- **Software raster.** Opaque swaying clusters take it like any other and do not crack against hardware neighbours.
  Masked clusters stay in hardware.

To check a level, read `render.get_visbuffer` `last_frame.sway`:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `instances` | swaying instances on the path |
| `materials` | their distinct materials |
| `moving` | some sway moved this frame, so the cull grew those bounds |
| `forward` | swaying meshes that stayed forward this frame, by reason; only the reasons that happened are listed |

| `forward` reason | Why the mesh stayed forward | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `graph_surface` | the sway sits on a surface graph of its own, and the resolve shades the standard surface only | adopt a plain material |
| `translucent` | the material blends, transmits, or is hair or parallax | |
| `hashed_alpha` | a masked material on a frame that hashes its alpha test | turn hashed alpha off, or accept forward |
| `no_texture_table` | a masked material on a device without the texture table | |
| `table_full` | the frame holds 256 distinct sways already (tint variants share one) | share sway values |
| `other` | skinned, morphing, a LOD cross-fade, a render override, a thin film, subsurface scattering, or no clusters | |

`entities.forward_reasons` says what the ECS bridge decided before any of this: `sway_graph_surface` is the bridge's
`graph_surface`, for an entity whose meshlets it does not insert. A persistent set has no forward path: past 256 sways it
draws at rest and counts under `table_full`.

Known limits: traced sun shadows, mesh SDFs and baked probes keep the rest pose. An adopted material on the path keeps a
second copy of its RGBA8 maps for its standard twin; cooked and shared images are not doubled.

To price the sway on a card, add `REGIA_VIS_BENCH_SWAY=1` to the `visbuffer_dense_bench` command above, with or without
`REGIA_VIS_BENCH_MASKED=1`: every material is adopted, the wind blows, and each row prints its swaying instances.

## Per-instance level range

Each instance's cull work covers only the cluster levels its distance can select. A mesh's clusters are stored
level by level. For each level the renderer keeps bounds on the level's errors and on how far its spheres reach.
The instance cull drops a level that no cluster in it could pass at the instance's distance. Clusters it drops would
fail the LOD test anyway, so the frame is the same. A near tree spends no cull work on its voxel far levels, and a
far one none on its finest levels. `visbuffer_counters` `work_items` shows the effect.

## LOD hysteresis

A cluster is drawn when its own projected error is at most the threshold and its parent's is above it. When that
error sits on the threshold, a camera move of a fraction of a pixel used to swap the whole cluster. The pass now
remembers both threshold comparisons for each cluster in each instance. While a boundary error stays inside
a band around the threshold, its stored comparison is kept. A comparison changes when the error leaves the band.
This preserves cuts that select several levels simultaneously. The first frame, a missing history and a band of zero use the hard cut.

The symmetric band half-width defaults to `LOD_HYSTERESIS_FRACTION` (one eighth) of `lod_threshold_px`. `VisBufferSettings::lod_hysteresis_px`
overrides it: `None` is that fraction, `Some(0.0)` is the hard cut, and `Some(px)` is a width in pixels. It is a
pass setting, not a field of `RenderProfile`. A still camera draws the same clusters as the hard cut, including
on the threshold, because the stored level is the level the hard cut chose. Instances near the threshold can
spend a few more cull work items once a level is stored; the drawn clusters do not change.

`render.vis_lod_hysteresis` reads and sets the band and reads how many instances changed their selected cut last frame.

| `band_px` | Effect |
|---|---|
| omitted | read the band |
| `null` | restore the fraction of the threshold |
| `0` | the hard cut |
| a positive number | that many pixels |

The result is `{ band_px, band_source, fraction, threshold_px, switches, cleared }`. `band_source` is `fraction`
or `pixels`. `switches` is last frame's count (`VisBufferStats::lod_switches`). `cleared` is false: the call
does not drop stored levels. `render.get_visbuffer` also reports `settings.lod_hysteresis_px`,
`settings.lod_hysteresis` and `last_frame.lod_switches`.

| Error | When |
|---|---|
| `vis_lod_hysteresis_bad_params` | the parameters are not an object, or `band_px` is not a number or null |
| `vis_lod_hysteresis_bad_band` | `band_px` is negative or not finite |
| `vis_lod_hysteresis_no_renderer` | the world has no `RuntimeRenderer` |

A camera cut drops the stored levels. The frame calls `VisBufferPass::clear_lod_history` from `begin_cut_frame`. An eye jump past the camera-cut
distance, an instance layout or identity change, resident geometry replacement, persistent-set changes,
a main-view frame without visibility geometry, and a replaced history buffer do the same. The draw list gives each instance its object key;
mesh/material slots and motion continuity provide additional invalidation checks. Anonymous draws retain history while their mesh/material slots and
previous-model continuity match; stable object keys distinguish replacements at an identical pose. The first stored level
after a clear is not a switch. Wind does not move the cut: the LOD spheres stay at rest.

### LOD hysteresis in split screen

Each window view keeps its own stored levels (ADR-8620). When the renderer draws another view, the
outgoing view's levels are put aside and the next view's come back, together with its cluster
visibility bits: two buffer copies each way per view change, none with one view. A view change is
therefore not a camera cut, even when the views stand far apart, and a camera cut in one view drops
that view's levels only. `render.get_visbuffer` `last_frame` reports:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lod_history_discards` | stored levels dropped since start: camera cuts, eye jumps within a view, changed instance lists, replaced buffers. A fresh view's first frame does not count |
| `lod_history_copies` | buffer copies of stored levels between views since start; stays 0 with one view |
| `view_histories` | views that own buffers for their put-aside bits or levels: 0 with one view, one per view in split screen |
| `view_history_bytes` | the GPU bytes of those buffers |

A view that has not drawn for `OCCLUSION_VIEW_RETIRE_ROUNDS` (16) rounds gives its bits, levels and
Hi-Z pyramid back on its own: `view_histories` and `view_history_bytes` drop, and so does its
`pyramid_bytes` in `render.visible_entities` (`book/agents/visibility.md`). A round ends when a
view draws a second time. Coming back, the view starts as a new one: its first phase draws no
clusters and its levels start from the hard cut.

To check split screen: hold both views still for a few frames, read `last_frame.lod_history_discards`, keep
drawing, and read it again. If it rose without a camera cut, report both readings and
`last_frame.lod_history_copies`.

Swaying persistent sets refresh shadow pages only while the visibility path and cluster shadows are on.
Shadow-off instances and masked sets contribute no dynamic shadow box. A casting set's box follows its
shadow scale and lift before adding the sway bound, so a styled moving shadow stays inside refreshed pages.

## Dense-scene acceptance

`visbuffer::tests::close` (lib tests, ADR-4906) runs one scene with every kind of instance the path takes: an opaque
rock, a masked rock, a swaying rock and a lightmap receiver, all on cooked cluster DAGs. The residency budget holds
the bases and about one mesh's fine bands. The LOD band is on. The camera cuts between two groups 297 m apart,
seven times. On every frame, including the first frame after each cut, the test checks:

- the path holds every instance in its class (`instances`, `masked_instances`, `sway_instances`,
  `receiver_instances`), and the cull and shadow lists drop no cluster;
- each rock prints: most of its body differs from the frame without it, most of its shadow is darker than the frame
  where it casts none, and its body stays close to the reference frame (a wrong material moves it far). The
  reference frames come from fresh renderers on the same device, so the test needs no golden;
- residency stays within its byte and upload budgets;
- after two cycles, a frame creates no path object, and the arena and the path's buffers keep their size.

A residency-managed receiver draws forward with its lightmap: its UV2 cannot follow the managed mesh's
non-contiguous vertices (ADR-3118). The run without residency puts the receiver on the path too. The same checks run
on the fallbacks:

| Device | What draws where |
|---|---|
| Texture table, residency | opaque, masked and swaying rocks on the path; the receiver forward |
| Texture table, no residency | every rock on the path |
| No texture table (A15 fallback) | the masked rock forward; the rest as above |
| Exactly `RESOLVE_STORAGE_BUFFERS` (11) storage buffers per stage | the path runs; the receiver forward (its variant needs 12) |
| One fewer | the classic path draws everything; no path object is created |

The resolve binds the forward view group's seven storage buffers and its own four, so the floor is 11. Before
ADR-4906 it was 10, and a device with exactly 10 failed the resolve's pipeline layout instead of falling back.

The dense-scene default (`RenderSettings::visibility_default`) stays off in every preset. With residency and the LOD
band on (`REGIA_VIS_BENCH_RESIDENCY=1`, "Measuring a machine"), an RTX 5090 and an RTX 5080 both cross over at
1.085 tri/px at 2560x1440 (bracketed), which is 3,999,744 triangles or 1,024 meshes. The path saves 22 to 28 % there.
Turning the default on is the lead's or owner's decision.

<!-- source: book/agents/texture-sets.md -->
# Texture-set census (bindless step 2)

The renderer binds one material group (group 2) per standard material today: the constants and
seven textures (base color, normal, ORM, emissive, detail, detail normal, aux) plus the sampler.
Bindless step 2 (ADR-317, refined by ADR-356) moves the constants out of that group and shares one
group between every material that samples the same seven texture views. How much that saves
depends on the content, so this census measures it on a running scene before step 2 ships.

The census only counts. It binds, draws and reorders nothing, so a frame is byte-identical with
it on or off (`census_on_and_off_draw_identical_pixels`).

## What counts as a texture set

A texture set is the seven views a material group binds, in bind order. Two materials share a set
when they bind the same GPU views:

- Untextured slots bind the renderer's fallback views, so two untextured tints share a set.
- Images shared by identity (`LabMaterial::images`, the shared texture cache) are one view, so
  materials that reference the same shared image share it.
- Two separate uploads of the same image are two views and two sets. The census reports what step
  2 would actually get, not what deduplicating identical images would add.
- A streamed material is keyed by the views it binds now (its group follows residency swaps).
- A material-graph material keeps a group of its own until step 5. It counts under
  `graph_materials` and never shares.

## Read

`render.texture_sets` (no parameters):

```json
{}
→ { "census": true,
    "resident": { "standard_materials": 3, "graph_materials": 0, "texture_sets": 2,
                  "shared_materials": 2, "largest_set": 2 },
    "pass": { "frames": 2, "opaque_draws": 4, "material_runs": 4, "texture_set_runs": 3,
              "materials": 3, "texture_sets": 2, "bind_ratio": 1.333 } }
```

- `resident` is counted when you call, whatever the switch says. `texture_sets` is the number of
  material groups step 2 would keep for the resident standard materials (against
  `standard_materials` today). `shared_materials` counts the materials whose set at least one other
  material binds, and `largest_set` is the most materials on one set.
- `pass` is the last main-view frame drawn while the census was on, and is all zero while it is
  off. The list is the frame's forward opaque draws (visible opaque and alpha-test draws, in the
  order they were collected). Visibility-buffer draws are not in it, because the resolve shades
  them (bindless step 4).
  - `material_runs`: material-group binds in that order today (one per change of material between
    consecutive draws).
  - `texture_set_runs`: the binds with groups shared by texture set and the order unchanged.
  - `texture_sets`: the floor if step 2 also sorted the draws by set.
  - `bind_ratio`: `material_runs / texture_set_runs` (1.0 when nothing would be saved).

The real pass counts can differ from `material_runs`. The draw loops group some draws by pipeline
(graph, alpha-test, double-sided) and the GPU-driven path draws instanced batches. Treat the pass
numbers as the step-2 estimate. The step-1 draw counters (ADR-316) are the measurement once both
are on the same branch.

## Switch the pass census

`render.set_texture_set_census { enabled }` turns the per-frame count on (`true`) or off (`false`,
the default). Any change of the switch restarts `frames` and the pass counts.

```json
{ "enabled": true }
→ { "before": { "census": false, … }, "after": { "census": true, … } }
```

While it is on, the cost is one pass over the opaque list and one hash lookup per draw, under the
`texture_set_census` tracing span. Hosts call `FrameRenderer::set_texture_set_census` and
`FrameRenderer::texture_set_stats` directly.

## Check it

On lookdev, vfx_lab or a DO27 map, turn the census on, let two frames draw, and read
`render.texture_sets`:

- `resident.texture_sets` close to `resident.standard_materials`: the content brings its own
  textures per material, and step 2 saves little until images are shared or packed.
- `pass.bind_ratio` well above 1, or `pass.texture_sets` far below `pass.materials`: step 2 pays.
  Record the numbers in the step-2 lane's report (ADR-356 step 2b acceptance).

## At bindless level 3

With the texture table (`REGIA_BINDLESS_LEVEL=3`, ADR-863, see
[renderer-excellence](book/agents/renderer-excellence.md) § Bindless level 3) every standard material binds the
same material group, so the opaque pass's `material_batches` in `render.get_frame_stats` is 1
whatever the census says. The census still counts by texture set: it measures what groups shared by
texture set would save on devices that cannot carry the table (tier `material_ssbo`), which is the
open question of ADR-356 step 2b.

<!-- source: book/agents/temporal-quality.md -->
# Temporal quality (agents)

The temporal upscaler (TAAU, the default `TemporalUpscaler`) blends each frame with a reprojected
history. When the history is trusted where it should not be, the image ghosts: a moving object
leaves a trail of its color on the background it uncovers, or small bright features (stars, a
moon's limb, distant lights) fade while the camera turns. `render.temporal_quality` measures this
on built-in synthetic moving-camera sequences, so an agent can check a change to the resolve, or
try other history-rejection constants, without a GPU. Guide topic:
`agent.guide {"topic": "temporal_quality"}`. Design and measurements: ADR-1151.

The numbers come from a CPU copy of `shaders/taau.wgsl` (`regia_render::taau_quality`): the
same neighborhood clip, cubic history fetch, motion test and weights. A unit test checks that its
constants match the shader source. It is a reference model, not a capture of the GPU: the history
stays in `f32`, and each scene is flat layers that translate on screen. A turning camera moves
distant layers by the same amount, and parallax is a near layer moving faster than the far one.
The GPU resolve has its own tests on the same kind of sequence (`crates/regia_render/src/taau_tests.rs`).

## Method

- `render.temporal_quality { scenario?, render_scale?, frames?, sky_motion?, tuning? }` runs one
  scenario, or all five, and returns `{ model: "cpu_reference", width, height, render_scale,
  frames, warmup, sky_motion, tuning, shipped, scenarios: [{ name, ghost_leak,
  disoccluded_pixels, rms_error, peak_ratio, frames_measured }] }`. Read-only; permission `read`;
  needs no renderer or window.
  - `scenario`: one name from the table below (default: all).
  - `render_scale`: render over output resolution, 0.25 to 1 (default 1). Below 1 the resolve
    upscales, as on the Deck (0.7) and the Desktop Low (0.75) and mobile presets.
  - `frames`: frames per sequence, 2 to 64 (default 24). The first third, at most 8, are warm-up
    and are not measured.
  - `sky_motion`: `false` reproduces the velocity pass before ADR-1151, which wrote zero motion on
    the sky.
  - `tuning`: `{ history_weight, variance_gamma, fractional_penalty, velocity_trust_px,
    velocity_reject_px, wide_motion_test }`, each optional, applied over the shipped values. The
    model only: the shader does not read them. `shipped` in the answer is `true` when the tuning
    is the shipped one.

```json
{"method": "render.temporal_quality", "params": {}}
{"method": "render.temporal_quality", "params": {"scenario": "moving_object", "render_scale": 0.67}}
{"method": "render.temporal_quality", "params": {"tuning": {"variance_gamma": 1.0}}}
```

Errors: `unknown_scenario` (the name is not one of the five; the hint lists them) and the
generic invalid-parameters code `F0002` for a value out of range or of the wrong type.

## Scenarios

| Name | What moves | What it catches |
|---|---|---|
| `parallax_pan` | The camera pans: a textured wall moves 1 px/frame, a mid-gray box in front of it 3 px/frame | Disocclusion trails behind a near object |
| `moving_object` | The box crosses the wall at 3 px/frame under a held camera | The classic moving-object trail |
| `tracked_object` | The camera follows the box (still on screen); the wall moves 3 px/frame | Trails at the edges of a tracked character |
| `bright_object` | As `parallax_pan`, with an HDR box (luminance ~3.6) over a dark wall | Bright trails and over-bright edges |
| `stars_turning` | The camera turns at 3 px/frame over a star sky (depth 1) and a ground band | Sky features fading during a turn |

The box's gray lies inside the wall's color range, so the neighborhood clip alone cannot reject
its trail: the motion test has to.

## Reading the numbers

- `ghost_leak`: the share of the foreground's color (as a fraction of the foreground-to-background
  difference) left on background the foreground uncovered in the last six frames. Its baseline is
  the same sequence resolved without the foreground, and the same statistic on background that was
  never covered is subtracted, so the ordinary softness of the accumulation and of the upscale does
  not count. About 0.02 or less is no visible trail; 0.1 is a trail you can see.
- `disoccluded_pixels`: how many uncovered pixels the leak averaged (0 for `stars_turning`, which
  has no foreground).
- `rms_error`: RMS luminance error against an unjittered 4 × 4 supersampled ground truth.
- `peak_ratio`: output over ground truth on the brightest pixels (ground-truth luminance at least
  half the frame's peak, away from the left and right 8 px, where new content enters). 1 is exact.
  A still star field reads about 0.5: the resolve's inverse-luminance blend (the firefly guard,
  Karis 2014) dims sub-pixel HDR points even at rest. Under motion the number should stay at the
  still value.

Measured on the shipped resolve (numpy port of the model, 96 × 48, 24 frames; the Rust unit tests
assert bounds around these):

| Scenario | `ghost_leak` at 1.0 | at 0.67 | `peak_ratio` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `parallax_pan` | 0.017 | 0.013 (0.104 before ADR-1151) | 1.00 |
| `moving_object` | 0.008 | 0.017 (0.151 before) | 1.00 |
| `tracked_object` | 0.013 | 0.015 (0.071 before) | 1.00 |
| `bright_object` | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.00 |
| `stars_turning` | — | — | 0.51 (0.06 with `sky_motion: false`; a still sky reads 0.50) |

## Typical loop

1. `render.temporal_quality {}` on a branch that touches `taau.wgsl` or `velocity.wgsl`, and
   compare with the numbers above. Then the same with `{"render_scale": 0.67}`.
2. To explore a change to the history rejection, pass `tuning` and compare `ghost_leak` (trails),
   `rms_error` (overall accuracy, which drops when the history is rejected too often) and
   `peak_ratio`. Only a constant that improves the model and the GPU tests belongs in the shader.
3. On the live game, confirm with `seeing.screenshot` while the camera moves (TAA history is
   per view; `render.camera_cut` drops it).

<!-- source: book/agents/upscalers.md -->
# Upscalers and quality modes (agents)

A TAA frame renders below the display size and a temporal upscaler brings it up to the display.
Regia Engine ships three upscalers: **TAAU** (the default on every preset), the **TSR**-grade upscaler and an
**FSR 3.1** port. All three run on every platform Regia Engine builds for. **DLSS** runs in builds with the
`dlss` feature and NVIDIA's SDK linked, on NVIDIA GPUs over Vulkan, when its runtime library ships with the
game (see [DLSS](#dlss)). **XeSS** runs on Windows when the `xess` feature linked the XeSS SDK and the
runtime library is present. Either vendor is refused only when that row's blockers are non-empty. The
upscaler only runs on TAA frames (`current.temporal`). Any other frame keeps the profile's AA and its spatial
upscaler.

The **quality mode** sets the render size from the display size. It uses the usual per-axis ratios:

| Mode | Ratio | Scale (permille) | 2560×1440 renders | 3840×2160 renders | Dynamic resolution range |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `native` | 1.0 | 1000 | 2560×1440 | 3840×2160 | 667–1000 |
| `quality` | 1.5 | 667 | 1707×960 | 2560×1440 | 588–667 |
| `balanced` | 1.7 | 588 | 1506×847 | 2259×1271 | 500–588 |
| `performance` | 2.0 | 500 | 1280×720 | 1920×1080 | 333–500 |
| `ultra_performance` | 3.0 | 333 | 853×480 | 1280×720 | 333 |

To get each axis, the display size is divided by the ratio and rounded to the nearest integer, with halves
rounding up. The ratio is used as an exact fraction (3/2, 17/10, ...), so the result is exact. No preset sets
a mode (`quality: null`). Without a mode the profile's own `render_scale` applies, as it always has. With a
mode, dynamic resolution moves inside the mode's range (`DynResConfig::within_quality`). At the top of that
range the frame is exactly the size in the table.

## Methods

- `render.get_upscalers` returns `{ current, upscalers, qualities, adapter, vendor_frame, reactive_mask }`.
  - `current` is `{ backend, quality, render_scale, temporal }`: the profile's built-in upscaler (`taau`, `tsr` or
    `fsr3`), the mode (`null` when the frame uses the profile field), that profile's `render_scale`,
    and whether the profile runs TAA. Setting a mode does not change `render_scale` (Desktop High
    stays `1.0`). The frame's scale is the mode's permille ÷ 1000 while `quality` is set (Performance
    `0.5`, Balanced `0.588`, Ultra Performance `0.333`) and `render_scale` while `quality` is null.
    `vendor_frame.selected` names the vendor tried before this built-in fallback.
  - `upscalers` holds one `{ backend, vendor, available, reason, blockers, unavailable_code, inputs, runtime }`
    per upscaler, in the order `taau`, `tsr`, `fsr3`, `dlss`, `xess`. `reason` is the first entry of `blockers`
    (`null` when the upscaler is available). `unavailable_code` is the one code that says what to fix (see
    [Why a vendor cannot run](#why-a-vendor-cannot-run)).
  - `inputs` is the backend's input contract (see [Input contract](#input-contract)).
  - `runtime` says where the backend's code comes from. A built-in has `{ "state": "compiled_in" }`. A
    vendor row has `{ state, env_var, library_names, found, searched, refused_relative }`: this build's
    binding state (see [Runtime states](#runtime-states)), the environment variable that names an extra
    directory, the library file names it looks for on this OS (`<version>` stands for a numeric suffix),
    the file it found (or `null`), the directories it looked in, and the variable's value if it was refused
    for being a relative path. The search only lists directories. It never loads a library and never looks
    in the working directory. The DLSS row also has `binding_built` (true when this build compiled the NGX
    sources, including the check stub),
    `sdk_version` (`none` for the stub, `check-stub` for `REGIA_DLSS_CHECK_STUB=1`, a dotted suffix such as
    `310.9.1` from `libnvidia-ngx-dlss.so.<version>` on Linux, `windows` when the file is `nvngx_dlss.dll`,
    or `unknown` when a linked build finds neither name), `code` (NGX's or the binding's last answer, see [DLSS](#dlss)) and
    the `instance_extensions` and `device_extensions` device creation added for it (the lists of the device
    the hooks made last: diagnostics only). Availability asks NGX about this device, and an empty
    requirement list means those extensions are enabled. Without the DLSS binding that ask does not
    run, and an empty recorded list is `needs_dx12_or_vulkan_extension`.
  - `resolve` says where a built-in resolve differs from the reference algorithm it ports. It is `null` on
    every row but `fsr3`, which has `{ reference, differences }`: the SDK it ports (`"AMD FidelityFX SDK
    v1.1.4, FSR 3.1 upscaler"`) and one `{ id, adr, summary }` per change to what the resolve outputs
    (for example `nearest_sample_restart`, ADR-7678). Regia Engine's FSR 3.1 is that SDK's algorithm with
    these changes, not the SDK unchanged.
  - `qualities` is the table above as `{ quality, ratio, permille, dynamic_range_permille,
    render_1440p, render_2160p }`.
  - `adapter` is `{ name, vendor, device_type, backend }` for the GPU the check looked at, or `null` when
    there is no render device.
  - `vendor_frame` is what the frame's vendor slot did: `{ selected, active, fallback, fallback_backend,
    reason, frames, fallbacks, runtime, render_range, render_preferred }`. `selected` is the vendor chosen
    (`dlss`, `xess` or `null`). `active` is true when the last TAA frame ran it. Otherwise `fallback` is the
    error code of why the built-in upscaler ran instead (see [Errors](#errors)), `fallback_backend` names that
    built-in, and `reason` is the runtime's own reason when the runtime is the cause (see [Reasons](#reasons)).
    `frames` and `fallbacks` count frames. `runtime` is the binding's state, `render_range` is `{ min, max }`,
    the render sizes the vendor accepts, and `render_preferred` is the size it asks for at the frame's mode.
    It is `null` without a runtime renderer.
  - `reactive_mask` is what fed the reactive mask on the last frame: `{ sources, present, readers, layers:
    { installed, placement, writes_mask } }`. `sources` lists the passes that wrote it (`oit`, or empty when
    the frame had none) and `present` is true when it had one. `readers` are the passes that read it (`taau`,
    `tsr`, `fsr3`, `vendor`, `frame_gen`). `layers` counts the installed translucent layers (VFX particles,
    trails, decals) and says where they draw: `after_resolve`, so they never write the mask (see
    [Particles and the reactive mask](#particles-and-the-reactive-mask)). It is `null` without a runtime
    renderer.
  - Read-only.
- `render.set_upscaler {"backend": "tsr", "quality": "quality"}` sets the upscaler, the mode, or both,
  from the next frame.
  - `backend` is `taau`, `tsr`, `fsr3`, `dlss` or `xess`. Case, `-`, `_` and spaces are ignored. A vendor
    that is available here is selected on the renderer and runs before the profile's built-in upscaler. A
    built-in clears that selection. An available vendor requires `RuntimeRenderer`; without it the call
    returns `F0003` and leaves the profile unchanged.
  - `quality` is a mode name. `"custom"` or `null` goes back to the profile's `render_scale`. Leaving
    `quality` out keeps the current mode.
  - Every parameter is checked before anything changes: a refused call changes neither field.
  - Switching upscalers drops the history of the one switched to. The switch is not persisted.
  - Returns `{ before, after, note }`. `before` and `after` are the `render.get_upscalers` state,
    including `vendor_frame`. `vendor_frame` is `null` when the app has no runtime renderer. A
    vendor this call selects is `after.vendor_frame.selected`; a built-in clears it. A
    quality-only call leaves the selection in place and still reports it.
  - Mutating; permission `edit_scene`.

```json
{"method": "render.set_upscaler", "params": {"backend": "fsr3", "quality": "performance"}}
```

- `render.reference_upscale {"filter": "edge_adaptive", "quality": "performance", "frames": 32}` runs the
  software reference upscaler on the CPU on a synthetic scene and returns its error against an 8×8
  supersampled truth. It goes through the same boundary a vendor upscaler plugs into, so it checks the
  jitter, motion-vector and reactive-mask conventions without a GPU.
  - Parameters, all optional: `filter` (`bilinear` or `edge_adaptive`), `quality` (sets the render size),
    `display` (`[w, h]`, 8 to 128), `frames` (1 to 64), `motion_px` (`[x, y]` display pixels per frame,
    -8 to 8), `motion_vectors` (`correct`, `zero` or `negated`), `reactive` (boolean), `sharpness` (0 to 1).
  - Returns `{ check, render, first_frame_rmse, final_rmse, spatial_only_rmse, accumulation_gain, note }`.
    `accumulation_gain` is `spatial_only_rmse ÷ final_rmse`: above 1 means the jitter and the history beat
    the spatial filter alone. With `motion_vectors: "negated"` or `"zero"` on a moving scene the gain drops,
    which is what a sign mistake looks like.
  - Read-only. It needs no renderer.
- `render.upscaler_jitter {"quality": "performance", "display": [2560, 1440], "frames": 8}` lists a
  Halton(2, 3) sequence whose phase count is `8 × ratio²`, rounded: 8, 18, 23, 32 and 72 frames for the
  five modes. This list repeats after `phase_count` frames. The frame's projection does not. It calls
  the same Halton on the unbounded index since the last camera cut, so frames 1 through `phase_count`
  match and the next frame of this list is index 1 while the projection uses index `phase_count + 1`.
  FSR reads the phase count only to pace lock decay.
  - Parameters, all optional: `quality` (default `quality`) or `render` (`[w, h]`, not both), `display`
    (`[w, h]`, default `[2560, 1440]`, axes 1 to 16384; `render` may not be larger), `frames` (1 to 256,
    default 8).
  - Returns `{ quality, display, render, ratio, sequence, phase_count, offsets, note }`. Each offset is
    `{ frame, halton_index, render_pixels, ndc }`. `render_pixels` is y down and is the offset the
    projection was moved by: what DLSS and XeSS are given. `ndc` is y up and is what is added to the
    projection.
  - Read-only. It needs no renderer.

```json
{"method": "render.upscaler_jitter", "params": {"quality": "ultra_performance", "frames": 72}}
```

- `render.set_vendor_upscaler {"vendor": "dlss"}` selects a vendor upscaler (`dlss`, `xess`, or `none` to
  clear it) on the runtime renderer, even where it cannot run. Unlike `render.set_upscaler` it never refuses:
  use it to check the fallback. Every TAA frame then tries the vendor. When the vendor refuses or fails, that
  frame runs the built-in upscaler, and `vendor_frame.fallback` in `render.get_upscalers` says why.
  - Returns `{ before, after, runtime, available, reason, blockers, unavailable_code, fallback_backend }`:
    `vendor_frame` before and after, the vendor's runtime state, whether it can run on this device with the
    same reasons `render.get_upscalers` lists, and the built-in upscaler that runs when it cannot. All of
    those are `null` for `none`.
  - Errors: `unknown_upscaler` for a name that is not a vendor upscaler. Without a runtime renderer, the
    `F0003` not-found error.
  - Mutating; permission `edit_scene`. Not persisted.

```json
{"method": "render.set_vendor_upscaler", "params": {"vendor": "dlss"}}
```

## Input contract

Each backend declares what it reads. The frame always passes Regia Engine's own conventions, and a backend
converts them into its own.

| Field | Values | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `depth`, `motion`, `reactive`, `transparency` | `required`, `optional`, `unused` | Whether the backend reads the input. A frame without a required input is refused |
| `motion_units` | `uv`, `render_pixels` | Units of a motion vector |
| `motion_direction` | `to_previous`, `to_current` | Regia Engine's velocity target is `previous − current` |
| `jitter_units` | `ndc`, `render_pixels` | Units of the jitter. One render pixel is 2 ÷ width in NDC, and NDC y is up |
| `jitter_sign` | `projection`, `sample` | The offset the projection moved by, or its negation |
| `vulkan_device_hook` | boolean | The runtime needs Vulkan extensions enabled at device creation |
| `max_ratio` | number | The largest display ÷ render ratio per axis |

The built-ins use Regia Engine's conventions (`uv`, `to_previous`, `ndc`, `projection`). The vendor rows use
render pixels with the same direction and sign. That is how the public integration guides describe them;
the vendor work confirms each sign against the SDK before it ships (ADR-510, ADR-1150).

A frame with [order-independent transparency](book/agents/oit.md) feeds `reactive` from its composite: the covered share of each pixel, capped at
0.9. TAAU scales its history weight by one minus the mask; TSR, FSR 3 and the vendor upscalers read it as their reactive input. Other
frames pass no mask, and each backend runs as it did.

### Particles and the reactive mask

Particles, trails and decals need no reactive mask. The frame draws its translucent layers after the
temporal resolve, into a copy of the resolve's output-sized result; the resolve itself stays next frame's
history. A particle is never in an upscaler's input or history, so smoke, sparks and fire moving over a
moving background leave no trail behind them under TAAU, TSR, FSR 3.1 or a vendor upscaler, and the
background under them is resolved as if they were not there. A mask from the particles would only lower the
history weight of that background. `reactive_mask.layers.placement` reports this (`after_resolve`) and
`reactive_mask.sources` never lists the layers.

The check is `cargo test -p regia_vfx --test reactive_upscaler`: a bright spark moving 3.7 px per frame over a
striped wall while the camera pans, through each upscaler at render scale 0.67, against the same frames
without the spark. Eight frames after the spark passes, its old footprint matches the spark-free frame
within one 8-bit level, and so does every pixel away from it (ADR-3101).

Frame generation is the one reader that sees the particles: it interpolates the presented image, and a
particle has no motion vector of its own. Its interpolator already lowers its trust in the game vector where
the mask is set. A mask from the VFX layers for frame generation is designed in ADR-3101 and not built yet;
until then a generated frame moves a particle with the surface behind it.

## Errors

| `data.error` | JSON-RPC / `data.code` | When | Also in `data` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `upscaler_unavailable` | `-32004` / `F0013` | The upscaler cannot run here: that backend's blockers are non-empty (a missing SDK link, the GPU, the API, an extension, or the runtime). DLSS and XeSS are accepted when their blockers are empty | `backend`, `reason`, `blockers` |
| `unknown_upscaler` | `-32602` / `F0002` | `backend` is not one of the five names | `backend` |
| `unknown_quality` | `-32602` / `F0002` | `quality` is not a mode name, `custom` or `null` | `quality` |
| `unknown_filter` | `-32602` / `F0002` | `render.reference_upscale`: `filter` is not `bilinear` or `edge_adaptive` | `filter` |
| `unknown_motion_vectors` | `-32602` / `F0002` | `render.reference_upscale`: `motion_vectors` is not `correct`, `zero` or `negated` | `motion_vectors` |
| `out_of_range` | `-32602` / `F0002` | A number or size is outside the range given above | `param`, `range` |

`render.reference_upscale` can also return an upscaler error code on `F0002`. These are the codes any
backend behind the boundary reports. The frame falls back to a built-in upscaler when a backend fails:

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `invalid_size` | A size is zero, or the render size is larger than the display |
| `unsupported_ratio` | The display ÷ render ratio is beyond the backend's `max_ratio` |
| `missing_input` | A required input is missing |
| `size_mismatch` | An image is not the size the frame says |
| `backend_failed` | The backend's runtime failed |
| `runtime_unavailable` | A vendor runtime is not usable (its reason is one of the runtime reasons below) |
| `render_size_out_of_range` | The render size is outside the range the vendor feature was created for |
| `invalid_jitter` | The jitter is more than half a render pixel: it was not given in NDC |
| `backend_disabled` | The backend failed 3 times in a row and stays off until it is re-enabled |

## Reasons

| Reason | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sdk_not_bundled` | This build has no runtime for the vendor's SDK (vendor features without their external SDK) |
| `needs_nvidia_adapter` | DLSS runs only on NVIDIA GPUs |
| `needs_dx12_or_vulkan` | The device runs on GL, Metal or WebGPU |
| `needs_dx12_or_vulkan_extension` | Vulkan, and this device does not enable the extensions the vendor asked for. DLSS asks NGX for this device, and an empty requirement list counts as enabled. Without that binding, an empty recorded hook list is this reason |
| `needs_hardware_adapter` | A software rasterizer such as lavapipe |
| `needs_desktop_gpu` | A mobile GPU (Adreno, Mali, PowerVR, Apple) |
| `no_render_device` | There is no render device (a headless tool, or before the first frame) |
| `runtime_not_found` | The vendor binding is built in, but its library was not found |
| `runtime_not_initialized` | The vendor binding is built in and its library was found, but no render device has started it yet |
| `runtime_reports_unsupported` | The vendor library loaded and says the feature cannot run on this GPU |
| `needs_newer_driver` | The vendor library loaded and asks for a newer GPU driver |
| `runtime_init_failed` | The vendor library was found but did not start, and neither the GPU nor the driver is why: a Vulkan or wgpu failure, or an error during init |
| `xess_needs_vulkan` | This XeSS adapter implements Vulkan; the selected device uses another API |
| `dlss_needs_vulkan` | The DLSS binding drives NGX through Vulkan only; the selected NVIDIA device runs on DX12. Pick the Vulkan adapter (`REGIA_GPU_INDEX`) |

## Why a vendor cannot run

`unavailable_code` on a `render.get_upscalers` row and on the `render.set_vendor_upscaler` result is the one
code to act on. A GPU that can never run the vendor comes first, then the runtime's state, then the device.
A device without the vendor's Vulkan extensions is what a build with no SDK looks like, so on Vulkan with no
SDK the code is `sdk_not_bundled` where `reason` is `needs_dx12_or_vulkan_extension`.

| Situation | `unavailable_code` | DLSS `runtime.code` |
|---|---|---|
| No SDK in this build (also Android and macOS, where NGX is not linked even if `DLSS_SDK` is set) | `sdk_not_bundled` | `null` (`runtime.state` is `not_bundled`; the agent does not report `not_linked`) |
| The runtime library is not there | `runtime_not_found` | `null` |
| A GPU that is not NVIDIA | `needs_nvidia_adapter` | `null` |
| An NVIDIA GPU DLSS does not support, such as a GTX 1080 | `runtime_reports_unsupported` | `feature_not_supported` (refused at device creation; measured on a GTX 1080, driver 580.173.02) or `unavailable` |
| The driver is too old | `needs_newer_driver` | `needs_newer_driver` |
| The runtime failed to start | `runtime_init_failed` | the failure's name, such as `vulkan_error` |

The DLSS row's `runtime.state` and `unavailable_code` follow the last answer NGX gave for a device in this
process: after the GTX 1080's refusal they read `reports_unsupported` and `runtime_reports_unsupported`, the
same state the frame's `vendor_frame` fell back on (ADR-4937).

Selecting a vendor that cannot run never breaks a frame. `render.set_upscaler` refuses it and changes nothing.
`render.set_vendor_upscaler` keeps the selection: every TAA frame runs the built-in upscaler, pixel for pixel
what it renders with no vendor selected, and `vendor_frame` shows `fallback`, `fallback_backend` and `reason`.

## Render size under a vendor

A vendor runtime asks for its own render sizes: the size it prefers at a display size and mode, and the
smallest and largest it accepts. While a vendor runs, the frame follows that answer instead of the mode's
fixed scale (`render_preferred`, `render_range`):

- Under a quality mode, the mode's own scale renders exactly the preferred size. Another scale, from dynamic
  resolution, multiplies the preferred size by `scale ÷ mode scale`, so a step never jumps.
- With no mode, the frame keeps the size its `render_scale` asks for.
- Either way the size stays inside `render_range`. A runtime whose smallest and largest size are equal holds
  that one size at every scale.

`DynResConfig::within_preferred` gives dynamic resolution the matching range. A frame with no vendor selected,
or a vendor that cannot run, renders the size it always did. Frames a vendor does not run (MSAA, or no TAA)
are also unchanged.

## Runtime states

| `runtime.state` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `compiled_in` | A built-in upscaler: nothing to load |
| `not_bundled` | This build has no binding for the vendor (XeSS without the `xess` feature and external SDK; DLSS without its feature and SDK) |
| `not_found` | The binding is built in, but the library was not found |
| `found` | The binding is built in and the library was found; no render device has started it yet |
| `reports_unsupported` | The library loaded and reports the feature unusable here |
| `needs_newer_driver` | The library loaded and wants a newer driver |
| `init_failed` | The library was found but did not start, and neither the GPU nor the driver is why |
| `ready` | Loaded and usable |

All codes are lowercase ASCII letters, digits and `_`, and they are stable.

## Judging an upscaler

Use the same view and the same mode for each upscaler you compare. Take a `seeing.screenshot` with each one.
For cost, read the GPU `taau` interval in `play.hitch_report`: it times the velocity pass and the upscale,
whichever upscaler runs. For motion, use the spec 27 § 2.3 chart (`regia_render/tests/taa_motion.rs`,
`do27_chase --motion`). Judge the result by eye against the reference plates, not by test counts.

## DLSS

DLSS Super Resolution runs through NVIDIA's NGX on wgpu's Vulkan backend (ADR-2002). It is off unless a game
is built with it:

The default build uses the DLSS stub: calls return `not_linked`, and it names no vendor library path.

1. Build with the `dlss` feature (`regia`, `regia_render` or `regia_dylib`) and `DLSS_SDK` set to an absolute
   path to NVIDIA's DLSS SDK checkout (v310.9.1). The SDK is never committed. Without `DLSS_SDK` the feature
   still builds, and DLSS reports `not_bundled`.
2. Ship the runtime library next to the executable: `libnvidia-ngx-dlss.so.<version>` on Linux,
   `nvngx_dlss.dll` on Windows. `REGIA_DLSS_PATH` names another directory, which must be an absolute path.
3. On an NVIDIA GPU over Vulkan, device creation then adds the extensions NGX asks for, and the first TAA
   frame with DLSS selected starts NGX. `REGIA_DLSS=0` keeps DLSS out of device creation.

Every step fails soft. A missing library, a GPU that is not NVIDIA, an old driver, a render size outside the
feature's range or an NGX error each leaves the frame on the built-in upscaler, with the reason in
`vendor_frame.fallback` and the DLSS row's `runtime.code`. After 3 failures in a row the vendor turns itself
off (`backend_disabled`) until it is selected again. The binding's codes are:

| `runtime.code` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `null` | No problem so far |
| `disabled_by_env` | `REGIA_DLSS=0` |
| `not_linked` | `DlssError` from the stub when something calls the unbound NGX API. The agent status does not use it: a build that did not link leaves `runtime.code` null and `runtime.state` `not_bundled`, including Android and macOS |
| `not_vulkan` | The device is not on Vulkan |
| `unavailable` | NGX started and reports DLSS unavailable on this GPU. A GPU NGX refuses already at device creation shows `feature_not_supported` instead (a GTX 1080 does, with the runtime present); a missing runtime can show as `unable_to_initialize_feature` |
| `needs_newer_driver` | NGX asks for a newer driver |
| `device_without_ngx_extensions` | The device (or its instance) lacks an extension NGX asks for on this device's GPU, checked per device |
| `vulkan_error`, `wgpu_error` | A Vulkan or wgpu call failed during instance or device creation (a missing Vulkan loader is `wgpu_error`) |
| `poisoned` | A previous NGX call panicked and left the NGX lock poisoned |
| `unsupported_format` | An input texture format NGX cannot take |
| an NGX failure name | `feature_not_supported`, `platform_error`, `unable_to_initialize_feature`, `invalid_parameter` (also a parent texture smaller than `render_size`, an output parent smaller than the display size, or an exposure that is not 1×1), `out_of_gpu_memory`, `denied`, `not_implemented` and the other NGX results, snake_case |

What DLSS is given:

- The frame's HDR colour, standard depth (near 0, far 1) and motion vectors at the render size. The motion is passed with a
  render-size scale, so it reaches DLSS in render pixels toward the previous frame.
- The frame's jitter, in render pixels with y down: the offset the projection was moved by.
- The reactive mask, as DLSS's current-colour bias, when the frame has one.
- The exposure, as a 1×1 texture, when the frame passes one. Creating the feature with auto exposure does not drop this texture: a size other than 1×1 still fails the call.
- A frame time of 16.667 ms on the render frame's vendor path (`UpscaleParams::new`). That path does not pass the measured frame delta, so every such frame is one sixtieth of a second.
- The quality mode the host set, or the one nearest the frame's render scale. While the live feature accepts
  the render size it keeps its mode, so dynamic resolution does not recreate it. Native is DLAA.
- A history reset on the first frame, on a camera cut and on a size change.
- A render size from DLSS's own answer (see [Render size under a vendor](#render-size-under-a-vendor)).

The reactive mask has been read through the code path only: no run has shown DLSS reading it on a GPU.

On an RTX 5090 (driver 615.71.09, SDK 310.9.1) an analytic test scene upscaled at Quality (640×360 to
960×540) has an RMSE against the supersampled native image of 0.039, where bilinear gives 0.097. At
Performance the numbers are 0.041 and 0.124. The flipped jitter sign gives 0.146 and 0.206. In the frame, at
two-thirds scale, DLSS lands 0.25 8-bit levels from the native frame on average, and TAAU lands 0.71
(`regia_render/tests/vendor_upscaler_frame.rs`). These RTX 5090 RMSE and 0.25-level figures were measured
while `FeatureFlags::REGIA.depth_inverted` was still `true`, and have not been remeasured since the flag was
corrected to `false`.

XeSS uses the optional Windows Vulkan adapter (ADR-4656). See [XeSS setup and proof](book/agents/xess.md).
The adapter consumes color, depth, motion, jitter, exposure and reset; reactive and transparency masks
are currently unused. Native maps to AA, and other quality presets map by name. Render sizes come from
XeSS because its preset ratios differ from the built-in table.

## Conformance checklist for a vendor binding

A new binding implements `VendorRuntimeApi` and `VendorEvaluate<GpuTarget>`, and must receive exactly what the
frame gives every other vendor. `regia_render/tests/vendor_conformance.rs` runs the frame's vendor slot on any
GPU with a scripted binding that records every input and upscales with a known filter. Set
`REGIA_VENDOR_CONFORMANCE` to `dlss` or `xess` to record the real binding instead.

| Item | What the binding must receive |
|---|---|
| `render_size` | The frame's render size in the frame values, the evaluate values and the inputs |
| `display_size` | The frame's display size, and an output of that size |
| `jitter_units` | The frame's NDC jitter converted by the binding's contract: render pixels, under half a pixel |
| `jitter_sign` | The offset the projection moved by, y down: `(ndc.x × width ÷ 2, −ndc.y × height ÷ 2)` |
| `motion_scale` | The render size as the factor from UV to render pixels, toward the previous frame, unjittered |
| `exposure` | Post exposure ÷ pre-exposure, in HDR colour, with no auto exposure |
| `reset` | True on the first evaluate, on a camera cut and on a new display size; false otherwise |
| `depth_convention` | Single-sample `Depth32Float` and a creation flag that says standard depth: near is smaller |
| `reactive_mask` | `R8Unorm` at the render size when the frame has one, absent otherwise |
| `transparency_mask` | Absent: no frame passes one yet |

# Frame generation (FSR 3)

Frame generation presents one interpolated frame between every two rendered frames, so the
display shows about twice the rendered frame rate. It is a WGSL port of the frame interpolation and
optical flow shaders of the AMD FidelityFX SDK v1.1.4 (MIT, the same tag as the FSR 3.1 upscaler)
with Regia Engine's own pacing on its wgpu surfaces (ADR-514, ADR-2067). No vendor binary is
involved.

It needs the cargo feature `frame-gen` (`regia/frame-gen` or `regia_render/frame-gen`), a window and a
desktop GPU (Vulkan, DX12 or Metal with compute), and it stays off until `enabled` is set. Each
rendered frame reaches the screen half a frame later than it would without it; below about 55
rendered frames per second the artifacts stay on screen longer and the pacer turns it off.

## What runs

1. The scene renders into frame generation's own image instead of the swap chain.
2. **Prepare inputs**: dilated depth and motion and the reconstructed previous depth, from the scene
   depth, the velocity target and the camera. It runs behind any upscaler, or none.
3. **Optical flow**: a luma pyramid of the presented image, a scene-change test on section
   histograms, then per level a block search, a middle-vector filter and a 2x upscale.
4. **Interpolator**: game and optical flow vector fields at the middle of the two frames, their
   inpainting pyramid, the disocclusion mask, the interpolated colour, inpainting.
5. **Present**: the generated image with the UI overlay drawn over it, then half an interval later the
   rendered image with the overlay. The overlay is never interpolated. A worker thread presents at the
   pacer's times, so the next frame starts rendering while the rendered image waits for its turn.

A camera cut, a resize (the surface is reconfigured or the scene images change size), a pause of
over half a second, a missing input, or the first tick after frame generation turns on sets the
pacer's reset. That tick presents the rendered frame only.

A scene change the histograms detect does not set that reset. Five or more of the nine luma
sections differing by more than 0.5 sets a change bit. The low four bits of that history stay set
for four rendered frames, and each of those frames forces the interpolator's frame counter back to
0, so the generated image is a copy of the current frame. The pacer still schedules both presents,
so each of those four rendered frames is shown twice.

Any error presents the rendered frame plainly, reports it in `pacing.present`, and keeps frame
generation off until it is turned off and on again.

## `render.frame_gen`

No params.

```json
{ "method": "render.frame_gen" }
```

Returns:

- `settings`: `enabled`, `hud` (`redraw`, `ui_texture` or `hud_less`), `min_base_fps`,
  `debug_tear_lines`, `debug_view`.
- `compiled`: the build has the `frame-gen` feature.
- `can_enable`: `true` once `blockers` is empty.
- `active`: generated frames are being presented now.
- `blockers`, most fundamental first:

  | Code | Meaning |
  |---|---|
  | `not_compiled` | The build lacks the cargo feature `frame-gen`. |
  | `interpolator_not_ported` | The interpolation passes are missing (no current build). |
  | `headless` | The app has no window surfaces. |
  | `needs_desktop_gpu` | The device lacks compute with storage textures or storage buffers (the passes bind 4 storage textures and 5 storage buffers per stage), or runs on GL. |

- `pacing`: `null` without the feature or without a window. Otherwise:
  - `base_fps`, `average_interval_ms`: the moving average of the rendered frame interval (eight
    frames; a hitch counts as at most twice the average).
  - `added_latency_ms`: how much later each rendered frame reaches the screen (half an interval: it
    waits behind the generated one). The interpolation's GPU time comes on top.
  - `last`: `{ kind: "generate", interval_ms }` or `{ kind: "real_only", reason }`, where
    `reason` is `disabled`, `warmup`, `reset` or `base_rate_too_low`. After the rate drops under the
    floor the reason stays `base_rate_too_low` for a hold-off of 120 rendered frames, doubling on each
    drop up to 3840: on a vsync swap chain two presents per tick halve the rendered frame rate, which
    can cross the floor by itself.
  - `present`: what the present path did since start:

    | Field | Meaning |
    |---|---|
    | `generated_presents` | Generated images presented. |
    | `real_presents` | Rendered images presented through this path. |
    | `resets` | Frames that started a new history. |
    | `acquire_failures` | Swap-chain images it could not get (that tick shows less). |
    | `fallback` | Why an enabled frame presented plainly (table below), or `null`. |
    | `last_error` | The error behind `fallback: "failed"`, or `null`. |
    | `gaps` | The spacing of the presents since frame generation started: `count`, `mean_ms`, `stddev_ms`, `max_ms` (gaps over 250 ms do not count). Even pacing has a small `stddev_ms` against `mean_ms`. |

  - `stats`: `real_frames`, `generated`, and one `skipped_*` counter per reason.
- `hud_modes`: the accepted `hud` values.
- `hud_effective`: what this build does with `hud`: `redraw` in every mode today (below).
- `optical_flow`: `block_size` (8), `search_radius` (8) and `max_levels` (7) of the estimator.

`fallback` codes:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `blocked` | A code in `blockers` applies (a device without compute, for example). |
| `multiple_windows` | More than one window is open: frame generation runs on one. |
| `multiple_views` | The window shows more than one view, or one that does not fill it. |
| `splash` | The boot splash is up. |
| `no_scene` | There is no scene to interpolate. |
| `failed` | An error stopped frame generation; turn it off and on again to retry. |

## `render.set_frame_gen`

Params, all optional:

| Param | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | boolean | Present an interpolated frame between every two rendered frames. |
| `hud` | string | `redraw` (the default: the UI overlay is drawn again over every presented frame). `ui_texture` and `hud_less` are accepted and behave as `redraw`: the overlay never enters the interpolation, so there is nothing for them to keep out. |
| `min_base_fps` | number, 10 to 240 | Below this rendered frame rate, only rendered frames are presented (default 55). |
| `debug_tear_lines` | boolean | Moving bars at the edges of generated frames, to see that they are presented and whether they tear. |
| `debug_view` | boolean | Present only generated frames, with the interpolator's surfaces in four panes: game vectors top left, optical flow vectors top right, disocclusion mask bottom left (red = visible in the previous frame, green = in the current), interpolated colour bottom right with inpainted texels in magenta. |

```json
{ "method": "render.set_frame_gen", "params": { "min_base_fps": 50 } }
{ "method": "render.set_frame_gen", "params": { "enabled": true } }
```

Returns `{ before, after }` (the settings). Every parameter is checked before anything changes.

Errors (`data.error`):

| Code | JSON-RPC | Regia Engine | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `frame_gen_unavailable` | `UNSUPPORTED` | `F0013` | `enabled: true` while `blockers` is not empty; `data.blockers` lists them. Nothing changes, including the other params of the call. |
| `unknown_hud_mode` | `INVALID_PARAMS` | `F0002` | `hud` is not one of the modes. |
| `out_of_range` | `INVALID_PARAMS` | `F0002` | `min_base_fps` is outside 10 to 240. |

A param of the wrong JSON type is `INVALID_PARAMS` (`F0002`) without a `data.error`.

## Check it worked

1. `render.frame_gen` on a build with `frame-gen`: `can_enable` is `true` and `pacing.base_fps` is
   close to the frame rate the performance overlay shows. `pacing.last.reason` is `disabled`.
2. `render.set_frame_gen { enabled: true }`, wait a second, then `render.frame_gen`: `active` is
   `true`, `pacing.last.kind` is `generate`, and `pacing.present.generated_presents` and
   `real_presents` grow together. If `active` stays `false`, read `pacing.last.reason` and
   `pacing.present.fallback`.
3. `render.set_frame_gen { debug_tear_lines: true }`: bars at the left and right edges flicker through
   colors; a capture of a real frame has none, because screenshots show the rendered frame.
4. `render.set_frame_gen { debug_view: true }` and take a screenshot: it shows the four panes.
5. Move the camera with `min_base_fps` above your frame rate: `pacing.last.reason` becomes
   `base_rate_too_low` and `generated_presents` stops growing.

## Present modes

A vsync swap chain shows every present on its own refresh, so two presents per tick would cap the
rendered frame rate at half the refresh. While frame generation runs, a vsync window uses Mailbox when
the surface offers it (it does not tear either) and goes back to the host's mode afterward;
`render.swapchain` reports the mode in effect. A surface with no Mailbox stays on vsync: a 60 Hz display
then renders at 30, under the default floor, and `pacing.last.reason` says `base_rate_too_low`.

## Conventions

These are fixed by the CPU references and their tests (`regia_render::frame_gen`):

- Motion vectors are in UV units of the render target and point from the current position to the
  previous one (`previous uv − current uv`). The frame at time `t` (0 = previous, 1 = current)
  sees a surface at `current + vector · (1 − t)`; one generated frame uses `t = 0.5`.
- Depth is standard (0 near, 1 far) with a finite far plane.
- The optical flow field has one vector per 8 × 8 block, in full-resolution pixels, pointing to
  the previous position like the game motion vectors. The GPU field equals
  `optical_flow::estimate_flow` vector for vector.
- On a camera cut or history reset, the generated frame is the rendered frame (nothing to
  interpolate from), and the pacer presents the rendered frame only.

<!-- source: book/agents/terrain-water.md -->
# Terrain water

A terrain can carry one shoreline water plane (`Terrain::water`, a `WaterPlane`). It is a flat
surface at a fixed `level` with small ripples, colored by its depth over the terrain. There is
no simulation. ADR-1237 describes the shading model.

**Where it is drawn.** The offscreen terrain renderer draws the plane when it is given one:
`render_offscreen`, `samples/terrain_lab` and its DO27 evidence shots. The look-dev harness
builds its terrain without water. In the runtime frame (`TerrainSharedDraw`), an app with
`WaterPlugin` draws the plane as a water body over the whole map at the plane's level
(ADR-1620): it shows in `water.state` with `terrain` set to this terrain, and
[water](book/agents/water.md#swell-surface-and-ray-queries) explains its look and how to add a swell to it.
The calls below read and edit the plane itself; the runtime body follows each edit on the next
frame.

## Methods

- `terrain.water { at?, time? }` reads the first terrain's plane.
  - `water`: the plane's fields, or `null` when the terrain has none.
  - `at`: up to 64 points `[[x, z], ...]` in meters. Each gets a `probes` entry:
    - `surface_height`: the rippled surface at `time` seconds (default 0).
    - `ground_height`: the terrain's sim surface (bilinear heights). Holes are not applied.
    - `depth`: `level − ground_height`. Negative on dry land.
    - `wet`: whether the plane is drawn there (`depth >= −0.05`).
    - `slope`: the bed's rise over run.
    - `shore_distance`: horizontal meters to the waterline, `depth / slope`. The slope is at
      least 0.02.
    - `foam`: the foam band's coverage before the noise mottle, 0 to 0.8.
    - `opacity_from_above`: the water's coverage seen straight down, Fresnel not included.
  - `entity`: the terrain read (the first in query order). `terrains`: how many exist.
- `terrain.set_water { water?, enabled? }` edits the first terrain's plane.
  - `water` can hold any subset of the fields below. They apply over the plane in effect, or
    over the defaults when there is none.
  - `enabled: false` removes the plane.
  - The new plane is validated before it replaces the old one. On a refusal nothing changes.
  - Returns `before` and `after`.

| Field | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `level` | World Y of the still surface, meters | 4.0 |
| `shallow_color`, `deep_color` | Body color at no depth and from `max_depth` on (linear RGB, 0..1) | teal, dark blue |
| `foam_color` | Foam color (linear RGB, 0..1) | light grey |
