# CPU budgets (`cargo xtask perf-budgets`)

`perf-budgets` runs the CPU measurements the specs' budgets rest on and says which budgets hold. `docs/perf/budgets.ron`
ties each budget to a release `cargo test` or `cargo bench` command and to the number to read from its output
([the format](book/reference/formats.md)). There are no GPU measurements here.

The command is repository tooling: it adds no engine API and no agent method. An agent runs it through the shell and reads
`--json`.

## Running it

```text
cargo xtask perf-budgets                               # everything: table on stdout, exit code 0
cargo xtask perf-budgets --filter regia_scene          # by name, spec or crate
cargo xtask perf-budgets --filter "spec 32"
cargo xtask perf-budgets --json                        # the report as JSON on stdout
cargo xtask perf-budgets --list                        # what would run; nothing is spawned
cargo xtask perf-budgets --counts-only --enforce       # the CI gate: allocation counts only
cargo xtask perf-budgets --update-baseline             # write this run's numbers into the baselines
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--filter <text>` | all | Only entries whose name, spec or crate contains the text. Nothing selected is an error, so a typo in a CI line cannot read as green. |
| `--enforce` | off | Exit 1 when an entry is over budget, regressed or not measured, or a command failed. Without it the exit code is 0 whatever was measured. |
| `--baseline <file>` | `docs/perf/budget-baseline-<host>.json` | The times to compare with; with `--counts-only`, the counts. |
| `--update-baseline` | off | Also write the measured numbers; the report still compares with the old ones. Numbers a `--filter` left out stay, and names the registry lost go. |
| `--counts-only` | off | Only the `perf-count` entries. They do not depend on the machine, and their baseline is `docs/perf/budget-counts.json`. |
| `--json` | off | The report on stdout instead of the table. Progress stays on stderr. |
| `--list` | off | Print the selected entries and exit. |
| `--tolerance <ratio>` | 1.5 | A time regressed when it is more than this many times its baseline. |
| `--count-tolerance <ratio>` | 1.0 | The same for a count; 1.0 means any growth. |
| `--host <name>` | this machine | The name in the baseline's file name. |
| `--registry <file>` | `docs/perf/budgets.ron` | Another registry. |

Each command's output is in `<target>/perf-budgets/<hash>.log`, and the last report in `<target>/perf-budgets/report.json`.

## Reading the report

The table is markdown, so a run pastes into `docs/perf-log.md`. Each `rows[]` element of the JSON has:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name`, `spec`, `package`, `stat`, `note` | From the registry. |
| `kind` | `time` (values in nanoseconds) or `count` (values per operation). |
| `budget`, `measured`, `baseline` | The numbers; `null` when absent. |
| `margin_percent` | `(budget - measured) / budget`, in percent. Negative is over budget. |
| `baseline_ratio` | `measured / baseline`. |
| `budget_verdict` | `within`, `over`, `unbudgeted` or `not_measured`. |
| `baseline_verdict` | `ok`, `regressed`, `improved`, `no_baseline` or `not_measured`. `improved` is not a failure; it says the baseline is stale. |
| `error_code`, `error` | Set when no number was read. |

The top level has `format_version`, `host`, `failed_commands` (each `command` and exit `code`) and `pass`, which is what
`--enforce` turns into the exit code.

### Error codes

| `error_code` | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `metric_missing` | The regex matched nothing, or the command did not run. | Read the log. A compile failure shows here, and the command is in `failed_commands`. |
| `metric_ambiguous` | The regex matched more than one place. | Tighten the registry's regex. |
| `metric_unreadable` | The match does not hold the statistic. | The printed line and the registry's `stat` disagree. |

## Rules for reading a number

- A time compares only with one from the same machine. `over` on a shared host at load 100 says less than `over` on the
  reference machine; the host, the load and the commit belong next to any number you quote (`docs/perf-log.md`).
- Budgets are for the reference machine their spec names, often a desktop or a min-spec class. The entry's `note` says so.
- A count compares everywhere. If a count entry regresses, an allocation really appeared, or the code path changed; update
  the baseline in the commit that means it.
- A miss is reported, not fixed here, and a budget is never widened to make a run pass (ADR-2704).

## Adding a measurement

1. Write an `#[ignore]` test that prints `perf-micro <name>: n= p50= p99= max=`, or a criterion bench. Assert that the work
   happened, never a time.
2. For a count, install a counting global allocator in that test binary and print
   `perf-count <name>: ops= allocs= bytes=` from a test whose name holds `perf_count`, so the count command stays cheap.
   Count the measuring thread only, run the work single-threaded (the multi-threaded executor moves systems between threads
   with the host's load), and assert that two rounds give the same number.
3. Add the entry to `docs/perf/budgets.ron`, run `cargo xtask perf-budgets --filter <name> --update-baseline`, and commit
   the baselines with the host and load in the message.

The counts-only enforce check is also the final step of `cargo xtask preflight`; it calls the same harness directly,
so it does not start another Cargo process or run timed measurements. A count regression makes preflight fail.

<!-- source: book/agents/gi-denoise.md -->
# GI denoise

A noisy per-pixel GI signal (a screen-space gather, a stochastic probe lookup, later a per-pixel
ray tracer) needs a spatio-temporal filter before it is shown: one sample per pixel has an error
about as large as the signal itself, and it changes every frame. `regia_render::gi_denoise`
is that filter (ADR-864). This page explains what it does, how its quality is scored, and how an
agent checks it with `seeing.gi_denoise_check`.

The filter is not yet wired into the frame: it ships as a CPU reference (`GiDenoiser`), a GPU
twin (`GiDenoiseGpu`, `shaders/gi_denoise.wgsl`) held to the reference by a test, the scores and
the regression scenarios. Feeding it the screen-space bounce is the next step.

## What the filter does

Three passes per frame, the same on the CPU and the GPU:

1. **Temporal accumulation with history validation.** Each pixel follows its motion vector into
   the previous frame and reads the history there (bilinearly). A history sample is used only if
   its depth is within `depth_tolerance` (10 %) of the pixel's, its normal within
   `normal_tolerance` (cosine 0.9), and it is on screen. Otherwise the pixel starts over: that is
   what keeps a moving object's light from smearing onto the wall it uncovers. The new sample
   blends in with weight `max(1/n, alpha_color)` for `n` frames of history (a running mean while
   young, an exponential average once settled). The first two luminance moments accumulate too.
   **Anti-lag:** per 8×8 square, the mean of this frame's input is compared with the mean of the
   reprojected history. When they differ by more than `antilag_sigma` (5) standard errors of the
   input's mean, the change is the lighting, not noise: the square takes the new frame in with at
   least the relative size of the change and its history is shortened to match. A light that
   quadruples settles in 2 frames instead of 9; on still, unchanging light the squares almost
   never fire.
2. **Variance.** A settled pixel's noise is the variance of its accumulated luminance. A pixel with
   fewer than four frames of history estimates it from its neighbours on the same surface instead.
3. **Edge-avoiding à-trous passes.** Five passes of a 5×5 kernel with tap spacing 1, 2, 4, 8 and
   16 pixels. Each tap is weighted by depth, normal and luminance; the luminance weight is scaled by
   the pixel's standard deviation, so a noisy pixel blurs wide and a converged one keeps its
   edges.

`GiDenoiser::reset` drops the history (call it on a camera cut); a resize drops it too. NaN,
infinite and negative input is treated as 0. Pixels without a surface (depth 0, NaN or infinite)
output 0.

## Scoring: the synthetic scenarios

The scores need a ground truth, so the regression tests and the agent method use deterministic
synthetic sequences (`gi_denoise::scenario`): a wall with a smooth light gradient and a hard
shadow band, a floor with a 90° crease, and a bright box in front at half the depth. The noisy
input is the truth times unit exponential noise per pixel (one path-traced bounce sample has about
this spread). Every run is bit-reproducible.

| Scenario | What moves | What it checks |
|---|---|---|
| `static` | nothing | convergence, flicker, bias, leak |
| `pan` | the camera, `pan_px` per frame | reprojection; a new column enters every frame |
| `disocclusion` | the box, `box_speed` per frame | history rejection behind the box |
| `light_step` | the light: 25 % → 100 % at `step_frame` | lag |

The scores, all relative to the truth's mean luminance:

| Score | Meaning | Good |
|---|---|---|
| `rel_rmse` (`raw_rel_rmse`) | RMS error against the truth after (before) filtering | low; `noise_reduction` = raw / filtered |
| `max_rel_rmse` | the worst scored frame | low |
| `flicker` (`raw_flicker`) | mean frame-to-frame change, read through the motion vectors | near 0 on a still view |
| `bias` | mean output / mean truth − 1 | near 0; the luminance weight makes it slightly negative |
| `edge_leak` | the box band's mean output at `box_irradiance` minus the same run at `box_irradiance / 8`, divided by the band's truth luminance | 0: no light crosses the depth edge |
| `shadow_edge_error` | mean absolute error within 2 px of a shadow edge | low; compare `raw_shadow_edge_error` |
| `disoccluded_rel_rmse` | error on pixels with no history this frame | low (spatial filter only) |
| `lag_frames` | frames after the light change until the mean is within 10 % | small |
| `mean_history` | average history length | near `max_history` on a still view |

At the default settings (64×48, one sample per pixel): `static` 1.27 → 0.076 error and 1.0 →
0.012 flicker, bias −1.5 %, leak 0; `pan` 0.14 (worst frame 0.17); disoccluded pixels 0.25;
`light_step` lag 2 frames (9 with `antilag_sigma` 0). The tests in `crates/regia_render/tests/gi_denoise.rs` hold these
with margin.

## `seeing.gi_denoise_check`

```json
{"method": "seeing.gi_denoise_check", "params": {}}
```

runs all four scenarios at the defaults. Parameters, all optional:

- `scenario`: `"static"`, `"pan"`, `"disocclusion"`, `"light_step"`, `"all"` (default), or an
  array of them.
- `settings`: any of `alpha_color`, `alpha_moments`, `max_history`, `depth_tolerance`,
  `normal_tolerance`, `atrous_iterations` (0–6), `sigma_depth`, `depth_epsilon`, `sigma_normal`,
  `sigma_luminance`, `variance_radius` (0–4), `spatial_variance_frames`,
  `history_from_first_pass`, `antilag_sigma` (0 turns anti-lag off), `antilag_block` (2–32).
  Unset fields keep the defaults; the result echoes the settings used.
- `backend`: `"cpu"` (default, the reference) or `"gpu"` (the compute twin on the app's render
  device, so the scores are the target GPU's own; it blocks on one readback per frame, so do not
  run it during a hitch measurement).
- `width` (16–512), `height` (12–512), `frames`, `warmup`, `spp` (1–64), `seed`, `pan_px`,
  `box_speed`, `step_frame`, `box_irradiance`: scenario overrides. `width × height × frames` is
  capped at 1 048 576 (the call runs on the app's thread).
- `blue_noise`: `true` draws the scenario's noise from the [spatiotemporal blue-noise
  table](book/agents/blue-noise.md) instead of the hash.

The result is `{ backend, settings, scenarios: [...], note }` with one entry per scenario carrying
the scores above.

Try a change before coding it: compare `flicker` and `lag_frames` with
`{"settings": {"alpha_color": 0.1, "alpha_moments": 0.1, "antilag_sigma": 0}}` against
`{"settings": {"antilag_sigma": 0}}` (flicker halves, lag doubles from 9 to 19 frames); with
anti-lag on, both follow the light step in 2 frames. A filter change that raises `edge_leak` above zero or `shadow_edge_error` well above
the defaults is a regression even if `rel_rmse` drops.

### Error codes

In `error.data.error_code` (the JSON-RPC error is `F0002`, invalid parameters):

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `gi_denoise_unknown_scenario` | `scenario` names no scenario |
| `gi_denoise_unknown_setting` | `settings` has a key the filter does not know |
| `gi_denoise_invalid_setting` | a setting or scenario field is out of range; the message names it |
| `gi_denoise_too_large` | `width × height × frames` above 1 048 576 |
| `gi_denoise_gpu` | `backend: "gpu"` in an app without a render device (JSON-RPC `F0003`), or the GPU run failed |

The Rust API returns the same codes from `GiDenoiseError::code()`, plus
`gi_denoise_size_mismatch` (an input buffer is not `width × height` long),
`gi_denoise_empty_frame` (a zero-sized frame).

## GPU and CPU

`GiDenoiseGpu::denoise` takes the same input as `GiDenoiser::denoise` and returns the same output.
It uploads the frame, runs the passes in one compute pass, and reads the result back (blocking);
the history stays on the GPU. It holds 160 bytes per pixel plus 16 bytes per 2×2 anti-lag
square (`GiDenoiseGpu::gpu_bytes`: input, history, temporal and the two ping-pong buffers, then
one `vec4` for each 2×2 square). A 64×48 frame is 503 808 bytes.
`crates/regia_render/tests/gi_denoise_gpu.rs` runs both on every scenario and requires the GPU
to stay within 0.1 % mean and 2 % per pixel of the CPU (the drivers' `exp` and `pow` differ in
the last bits), with identical history lengths. Those runs turn anti-lag off: it is a threshold
test, and GPU division and square root are not correctly rounded, so a square exactly at the
threshold may decide differently. A separate clean light step checks anti-lag itself.

## Path-traced check

`crates/regia_pt/tests/gi_denoise_reference.rs` feeds sixteen one-sample path-traced frames of
the Cornell box (indirect diffuse divided by the first-hit albedo) through the CPU denoiser and
compares the result with a 512-sample trace. It needs a GPU (the path tracer) and prints the raw,
plain-average and denoised errors, the bias and the flicker.

# Probe specular

Where probe light covers a surface (the Depth look's GPU-traced probes, or a map's baked GI volume:
see [Lighting option](book/agents/gi-probes.md) and [Baked GI volumes](book/agents/baked-gi.md)), the forward pass reads the
surface's indirect specular from that light at every roughness (ADR-1103):

- **A mirror** reads the probe light in the mirror direction.
- **A rough surface** reads a wide cone of probe light that leans toward the normal. At full
  roughness it meets the diffuse lookup.
- **The sky map** adds only its detail where image-based sky light is bound, such as a bright
  horizon band in a glossy floor. That detail is the ratio of the prefiltered sky to the sky's own
  smooth light in the same lobe, capped at `detail_max` (8).

Probe light sets the level and the color. A glossy floor in a canyon, a room or under a hull
therefore reflects its walls, not the open sky. Before this change, surfaces below perceptual
roughness 0.5 reflected the sky map, darkened by the probe/sky irradiance ratio, and only rougher
surfaces read the probes.

## How it reads the probes

The probes store light that is linear in direction, `L(l) = a + b·l` (L1 spherical harmonics; the
half-resolution screen lookup holds six irradiances toward ±x, ±y, ±z). For such light, the average
over any lobe is exactly `a + b·m`, where `m` is the lobe's mean vector. The engine uses a fit of
that mean vector for the GGX specular lobe (BRDF × cosine, height-correlated Smith). Its direction
moves from the mirror direction to the normal as roughness grows, and its length falls from 1 to
about 0.62. The worst error of the fitted vector against numerical integration is 0.036 (α in
[0, 1], n·v ≥ 0.1).

Energy checks, each a unit test (`regia_render::probe_specular`):

- Uniform light comes back unchanged at every roughness (white furnace).
- The rebuilt light is never negative and never more than 4× the cube's mean, which is the most a
  non-negative field can send.
- Over a pair of opposite lobes no light is made while the clamp at 0 is idle.
- The detail ratio's cap only removes light.
- The lobe's own albedo stays at or below 1 and matches the engine's GGX directional albedo.

## Settings

- `DdgiSettings::specular` and `BakedGiSettings::specular` (`regia_render::ProbeSpecular`):
  `Lobe` (the default), `RoughOnly` (the earlier look, for comparisons) or `LobeHue` (opt-in, see
  [Keeping the hue](#keeping-the-hue)). Each one applies to its own probe source and takes effect
  on the next frame. The probes themselves do not change.
- When a level installs its own baked volume, it restores the host's baked settings (`specular`
  included) when it unloads.

## Agent methods

- `render.get_probe_specular` returns
  `{ mode, ddgi, baked, detail_max, hue_floor, baked_active, ddgi_active }`. `mode` is `"lobe"`,
  `"rough_only"`, `"lobe_hue"`, or `"mixed"` when the two sources differ.
- `render.set_probe_specular {"mode": "lobe"|"rough_only"|"lobe_hue"}` sets both sources and returns
  `{ before, after, note }`. An unknown or missing `mode` is `invalid_params` (F0002). Without a
  runtime renderer the call returns `not_found` (F0003).
- `render.probe_specular_lobe {"roughness": 0.4, "n_dot_v": 0.7}` returns the fitted lobe (`lerp`,
  `length`, `fit`) and the numerically integrated one (`reference: { mean, length, albedo }`). It
  also returns their distance as `error`, which is under 0.04 over the range a frame meets. It
  needs no frame. `roughness` is perceptual, in [0, 1] (α = roughness²). `n_dot_v` is in [0, 1]
  and defaults to 1. A value out of range is `invalid_params` (F0002).
- The same method with `cube` (six `[r, g, b]` probe irradiances / π, +x, −x, +y, −y, +z, −z, each
  finite and not negative) also returns `light: { mode, radiance }`: the renderer's CPU mirror of the
  light those values give through the lobe. `mode` picks `"lobe"` (the default) or `"lobe_hue"`, and
  `direction` (`[x, y, z]`) aims the lobe's mean instead of `fit`. The GPU agrees with the mirror
  within 1e-4 of the value (`the_shader_matches_its_cpu_mirror_with_the_hue_bit`). A bad `cube`,
  `direction` or `mode`, `"rough_only"` included, is `invalid_params` (F0002). Without `cube`, `light`
  is `null`.

## Keeping the hue

`ProbeSpecular::LobeHue` (`"lobe_hue"`, opt-in, ADR-2996) changes three things about the lobe's color.
Nothing else in the frame moves, and a frame without probe light is unchanged.

- **A floor per channel.** The linear form `a + b·m` goes negative where the real light is only dim.
  Under a blue-heavy sky a mirror aimed at the nadir drove blue to 0 first and green next, which left
  a red-to-yellow spot, [202, 33, 0] on the studio sphere. In this mode each channel keeps at least
  `hue_floor` (0.2) of its mean. A floor per channel, not one scale for all of them, so a red wall
  and a green wall opposite it each keep their color at full strength. A lobe that falls below 0.9
  of its mean's luminance also takes its mean's color (fully at 0.4), its luminance kept: the channels
  of a dim lobe say little, and with the floor alone a lobe half way down read magenta.
- **The sky's detail per channel.** The ratio of the prefiltered sky to the sky's own lobe light is
  taken in each channel, not on luminance. Where probes and sky agree, the frame reads the prefilter's
  own color, which L1 light cannot hold: the near-white horizon of a gradient, a neutral ground under
  a blue sky. Each channel has the `detail_max` cap, and the ratio still fades to 1 at full roughness.
- **The ground plane in the lobe.** With `render.set_environment_ground` (or the host call
  `FrameRenderer::set_environment_ground`), traced probes hold the plane themselves: a probe ray that
  meets no surface lands on it, so the default's lobe reflects the plane too, in its L1 form. This
  mode also takes the plane into the sky's lobe and prefilter, so where the probes and the sky agree
  a mirror reads the plane's own radiance with a sharp horizon. With a baked volume, whose rays read
  the image's lower half, the probes' lobe takes what the plane hides out and puts the plane's light
  in, as the diffuse lookup does. See [Studio environment](book/agents/studio-environment.md).

The floor applies wherever the probes' lobe is read, the terrain included. The per-channel detail and
the plane apply to meshes in the forward pass. The Adreno workaround shader
(`SUN_SHADOW_PCF_ONLY`) leaves those two out and keeps the floor.

## Comparing the two looks

1. Call `play.pause`. Point the camera at a glossy surface under probe light, for example a
   polished floor in a trench or a metal hull side in shadow.
2. Call `render.set_probe_specular {"mode": "rough_only"}`, then `play.step 2` and
   `seeing.screenshot`.
3. Call `render.set_probe_specular {"mode": "lobe"}`, then `play.step 2` and `seeing.screenshot`.
   For the hue, do the same with `"lobe_hue"`: a metal sphere under a blue studio gradient is the
   clearest case. A still camera can keep the previous mode's composite (the static-screen reuse,
   ADR-2996 (8)) until the frame fix lands: move the camera a little between the screenshots.
4. Judge the pair by eye against the reference plate. For ground truth, run
   `seeing.reference_trace` and `seeing.compare` with `aov: "indirect_specular"` (guide topic
   `renderer-excellence`).

## What to look for

- **Glossy surfaces in enclosures**: a shadowed polished floor reflects the lit walls around it,
  in their color, not a darkened blue sky.
- **Mirror-like surfaces in the open**: the sky's detail (horizon band, gradient) stays, because the
  probes and the sky agree there.
- **Rough surfaces**: little change. At full roughness the lobe meets the diffuse probe lookup.
- **The default under a blue sky**: a red-to-yellow spot where a mirror reflects straight down.
  `"lobe_hue"` removes it. The default stays until the owner's look call (ADR-2996).
- **A closed room with colored walls under `"lobe_hue"`**: the lower half of a metal sphere can take
  a warm tint (the floor share lifts the walls' red and green in a lobe that sees a dark floor). The
  mode is still closer to the path tracer than the default there by FLIP and RGB error (ADR-2996).
- **Known limit**: the probes hold smooth L1 light, so a mirror under probe light shows the
  probes' smooth level times the sky's detail, not the exact image of nearby objects. Sharp
  reflections of nearby geometry come from SSR and reflection probes.

<!-- source: book/agents/hwrt.md -->
# Hardware ray tracing

Regia Engine can trace the sun's shadow per pixel (ADR-515, ADR-1149, ADR-2035). It is off in every
preset. A game or tool turns it on per profile with `RenderProfile::sun_shadow_trace`, and an
agent with `render.set_sun_shadow_trace`.

| `sun_shadow_trace` | What the frame does |
|---|---|
| `off` | The cascaded shadow map and contact shadows. Every preset's default. |
| `on` | Hardware ray queries where the device has them. Otherwise the screen-space trace. |
| `compute` | The compute BVH on any adapter. This is the reference path. It rebuilds on the CPU when a caster moves, so it is not for play. |
| `screen` | The screen-space trace on any adapter. |

What exists:

- **A probe.** At device creation the renderer checks what the adapter offers. In wgpu 30, ray
  queries are the experimental `EXPERIMENTAL_RAY_QUERY` feature, on Vulkan only, and only where
  the driver has `VK_KHR_ray_query`. The probe also records the acceleration-structure limits.
- **An opt-in.** The device asks for ray queries only when the profile says `on` before the first
  window's device is created (`regia_render::hwrt::set_device_request`; the render plugin does it
  from `RenderSettings`). Any other profile's device request is the same as before this work, and
  mesh buffers carry `BLAS_INPUT` only on a device with ray queries.
- **Acceleration-structure builds.** The frame builds one bottom-level structure (BLAS) per mesh
  from the mesh arena and a top-level structure (TLAS) from the frame's casters. It rebuilds only
  meshes that are new or changed, and only when a caster moved, appeared or left. A steady frame
  builds nothing. Input over the device's limits is refused.
- **A visibility pass** (`sun_shadow_trace` in `render.graph`). It reconstructs each pixel's world
  position from the single-sample depth and sends one ray toward the sun. It writes the texture
  contact shadows write (a pooled transient), and it runs in their place.

Each tracer writes 1 (lit) or 0 (shadowed). The frame needs a single-sample depth prepass, a sun
that casts shadows, the full forward shader and the main view. Otherwise it keeps the shadow map and
the reason says why.

## Query

`render.hwrt` takes one optional parameter, `adapters` (boolean, default false). It works without
a renderer resource, and it fails only when `adapters` is not a boolean (`invalid_params`). It
returns:

```json
{
  "probed": true,
  "requested": "on",
  "adapter": {
    "backend": "vulkan",
    "ray_query": true,
    "vertex_return": false,
    "limits": {
      "max_blas_primitive_count": 536870912,
      "max_blas_geometry_count": 16777216,
      "max_tlas_instance_count": 16777216,
      "max_acceleration_structures_per_shader_stage": 16
    }
  },
  "device_ray_query": true,
  "shadow_path": "ray_query",
  "reason": "hwrt_enabled",
  "message": "hardware ray queries are enabled on this device",
  "sun_shadows": {
    "requested": "on",
    "preset": "DesktopUltra",
    "variant": "ray_query",
    "reason": "rt_shadows_ray_query",
    "message": "sun shadows trace with hardware ray queries",
    "forward_defs": ["SUN_SHADOW_RT"],
    "trace_shader": "sun_trace_ray_query.wgsl",
    "pipeline_key_bits": 1,
    "applied": true,
    "frame": {
      "traces": 240,
      "scene_builds": 1,
      "tlas_refits": 0,
      "casters": 412,
      "triangles": 88120,
      "shared_casters": 256,
      "set_casters": 0,
      "masked_casters": 120,
      "skipped_deforming": 6,
      "skipped_masked": 0,
      "blas_built": 38,
      "blas_resident": 294,
      "instances": 412,
      "refit": false,
      "instances_moved": 0,
      "sun_maps_skipped": 0,
      "failure": null
    }
  }
}
```

(The values above are examples. Each adapter reports its own limits.)

The report describes the last render device the process created. `probed` is false before the
first device. In that case `adapter` and `reason` are null. `shadow_path` is `ray_query` only when
`reason` is `hwrt_enabled`. Otherwise it is `compute_fallback`.

| `reason` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `hwrt_enabled` | Requested, offered, and the device has it. |
| `hwrt_not_requested` | The profile did not ask for ray queries when the device was created. This is the default. |
| `hwrt_minspec_profile` | The device is clamped to a minimum-spec profile, which never has ray queries. |
| `hwrt_no_adapter_ray_query` | The adapter has no ray queries. This covers DX12, Metal, GL, and Vulkan drivers without `VK_KHR_ray_query`. |
| `hwrt_zero_accel_limits` | The adapter offers ray queries but reports an acceleration-structure limit of zero. |
| `hwrt_device_refused` | Ray queries were requested, but the created device does not have them. |

## Sun-shadow variants

`sun_shadows` describes the variant of the active profile. Once a frame has drawn the request, the
values are what that frame chose, `applied` says whether it wrote the visibility texture, and
`frame` says what it traced. Before that, `frame` is null and the values are what the profile and the
device would give.

| `variant` | Forward shader defs | Tracer | `pipeline_key_bits` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `shadow_map` | none | none | 0 |
| `ray_query` | `SUN_SHADOW_RT` | `sun_trace_ray_query.wgsl` (needs ray queries) | 1 |
| `compute_fallback` | `SUN_SHADOW_RT` | `sun_trace_bvh.wgsl` | 2 |
| `screen_trace` | none | `sun_trace_screen.wgsl` | 3 |

Under `SUN_SHADOW_RT`, opaque and masked surfaces take their sun visibility from the visibility
texture instead of the shadow map. Blended and transmissive surfaces and ghost overrides keep the
shadow map, because they are not in the depth the trace starts from. The shadow maps are drawn
while something reads them (see [Shadow maps under the trace](#shadow-maps-under-the-trace)).

`screen_trace` keeps the shadow-map forward shader, so the sun is the shadow map times the trace. A
ray that leaves the screen counts as lit. What it would have hit is the shadow map's, so nothing
goes missing, and the march adds fine contact the cascades lose, as contact shadows do but longer.

Pipelines key on the forward module, so `ray_query` and `compute_fallback` share one set of forward
pipelines, and `screen_trace` shares the shadow map's. The visibility-buffer resolve has both modules
too.

The checks run in this order. The first one that applies gives the `reason`:

| `reason` | Variant | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `rt_shadows_not_requested` | `shadow_map` | `sun_shadow_trace` is `off`. This is the default. |
| `rt_shadows_secondary_view` | `shadow_map` | A texture view or an eye. Only the main view traces. |
| `rt_shadows_no_sun` | `shadow_map` | The sun casts no shadow this frame. |
| `rt_shadows_no_depth` | `shadow_map` | No single-sample depth prepass: MSAA, or a profile without one. |
| `rt_shadows_forward_lite` | `shadow_map` | The frame draws the lite forward shader, which has no visibility texture. |
| `rt_shadows_screen_requested` | `screen_trace` | `sun_shadow_trace` is `screen`. |
| `rt_shadows_screen_fallback` | `screen_trace` | `on`, and the device has no ray queries. The top-level `reason` says why. |
| `rt_shadows_screen_shared_casters` | `screen_trace` | `on`, and the frame has a shared draw that gives the trace no casters (`SharedPassDraw::trace_casters` is `None`). Its casters would not be in the traced scene, so the frame keeps the shadow map under the screen trace rather than lose their shadows. The terrain gives a proxy, so it never takes this. |
| `rt_shadows_accel_failed` | `shadow_map` | The traced scene was refused. `frame.failure` holds its code. It stays until the request changes. |
| `rt_shadows_compute_requested` | `compute_fallback` | `sun_shadow_trace` is `compute`. |
| `rt_shadows_ray_query` | `ray_query` | `on`, and the device has ray queries. |

Before any frame, `render.hwrt` can also answer `rt_shadows_no_device`: `on` with no device yet.

## What the trace holds

The traced scene holds the frame's rigid casters with shadows on, and, since ADR-2310, three more
kinds. `frame` counts each:

- **Shared draws with a proxy** (`shared_casters`). A shared draw hands the trace coarse geometry
  through `SharedPassDraw::trace_casters`. The terrain builds a tiled grid over its whole map, one
  structure per tile, at most 2 million triangles at about 2 m spacing by default. Each vertex takes
  the lowest height within half a grid step, so the proxy never rises above the drawn ground and
  the ground does not shadow itself through it. `terrain.trace_proxy` reports it (below).
- **Persistent visibility-buffer sets** (`set_casters`), such as a static scatter. Each set keeps a
  copy of its mesh's positions for this.
- **Alpha-masked casters** (`masked_casters`, `ray_query` only). Foliage cards enter as non-opaque
  geometry. A hit is accepted for a fixed share of rays (`MASKED_COVERAGE`, one half), picked by a
  hash of the ray and the triangle. A canopy then casts a dappled shadow of about the right density,
  but no leaf shapes. The texture is not read. The compute reference still leaves them out
  (`skipped_masked`).

These still cast no traced shadow:

- skinned, morphed and vertex-animated meshes (`skipped_deforming`);
- holes cut in the terrain, which still cast as ground; relief displacement; grass; and the far
  scatter impostors.

**Moving casters refit.** When the same casters move and nothing else changes, the top level keeps
its slots and its storage. Only the moved slots are rewritten (`refit` true, `instances_moved`), no
bottom-level structure is touched, and `tlas_refits` counts the frame instead of `scene_builds`.
wgpu 30 runs every acceleration-structure update as a rebuild, so the GPU still rebuilds the top
level, but that is over instances only. A caster that appears, leaves, or changes mesh rebuilds the
scene.

The traced scene rebuilds when a caster's mesh is uploaded again. A mesh submitted with key 0 is
uploaded afresh every frame, so it rebuilds its structure every frame (`frame.scene_builds` climbs
on a still scene). Give casters stable mesh keys.

## Shadow maps under the trace

Under `ray_query` and `compute_fallback`, opaque surfaces no longer read the sun's cascades. A
frame skips drawing them, and counts it in `frame.sun_maps_skipped`, when nothing else reads them:

- no blended, transmissive, x-ray, ghost or hair surface is drawn;
- no caster is left out of the trace (skinned, morphed, vertex-animated; masked on the compute
  reference), since those still cast through the maps;
- any shared draw can take its sun from the trace alone (`SharedPassDraw::takes_traced_sun`). The
  terrain can when it draws no grass and no far impostors, which read only the cascades.

When fog, clouds or the atmosphere may run, the cascade their light shafts sample is still drawn.
The first frame after a skip redraws every cascade. A frame that skips none draws what it drew
before.

## The terrain's proxy

`terrain.trace_proxy` answers `{ settings: { spacing_m, max_triangles, tile_quads }, proxy }`.
`proxy` is null while no frame traces. Otherwise it is `{ stride, spacing_m, tiles, triangles,
tile_builds }`: samples between vertices, metres between vertices, tiles, triangles, and tile
builds so far. A height edit rebuilds only the tiles it touches.
`terrain.set_trace_proxy { spacing_m?, max_triangles?, tile_quads? }` changes the settings and
answers `{ before, after, note }`. A built proxy is rebuilt the next frame that traces. Both
methods answer `F0003` when the host inserted no `TerrainTraceProxyControl`. The host inserts
`TerrainTraceProxyControl(draw.trace_proxy_handle())` with its terrain draw. Values out of range
answer `F0002` and change nothing.

```json
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "terrain.set_trace_proxy", "params": {"spacing_m": 4.0}}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "render.set_sun_shadow_trace", "params": {"mode": "on"}}
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "render.hwrt"}
```

On a card with ray queries, `sun_shadows.reason` is `rt_shadows_ray_query` and
`sun_shadows.frame.shared_casters` equals `terrain.trace_proxy`'s `proxy.tiles`. Without ray
queries it is `rt_shadows_screen_fallback`.

## Switching it

`render.set_sun_shadow_trace {"mode": "off" | "on" | "compute" | "screen"}` sets the active
profile's knob and answers `{ before, after, note }`. It applies from the next frame. An unknown
mode is `invalid_params`, and an app without `RenderSettings` is `not_found`. A preset change
replaces the profile, which turns the knob off. `on` needs a device created with the knob already
on. Without one, the frame takes the screen-space trace and says `rt_shadows_screen_fallback`.

## Every adapter in the machine

`render.hwrt {"adapters": true}` adds an `adapters` list. Each entry has `index` (the number
`REGIA_GPU_INDEX` takes), `name`, `device_type` (`discrete`, `integrated`, `virtual`, `cpu` or
`other`), `backend`, `driver`, `driver_info`, `ray_query`, `vertex_return`, `limits`, and
`if_requested`. `if_requested` is the `hwrt_*` reason that a device on that adapter would get
from a profile that asks for ray queries. The probe creates a wgpu instance but no device, and it is not cheap, so
ask for it once and not every frame.

From a shell, `regia doctor --platform gpu` prints the same probe. A plain `regia doctor`
also prints it on Linux and Windows. Ray tracing is optional, so this section never fails the
doctor.

The builders have error codes of their own: `accel_ray_query_disabled`, `accel_missing_mesh`,
`accel_duplicate_mesh`, `accel_not_triangles`, `accel_too_many_primitives`,
`accel_too_many_instances`, `accel_custom_data_too_wide`, `accel_non_finite_transform`,
`accel_mesh_buffers` and `accel_refit_shape` (a refit asked for a scene that is not the last
build's; the frame builds instead, so it never reaches a report). Rust hosts see them as `AccelError::code()`.

## Checking a machine

1. Run `regia doctor --platform gpu`, or call `render.hwrt {"adapters": true}`. Look for an
   adapter whose `if_requested` is `hwrt_enabled`.
2. Start the game or a sample with a profile whose `sun_shadow_trace` is `on`. Call `render.hwrt`
   and read `reason` and `sun_shadows`.
3. If the reason is `hwrt_no_adapter_ray_query` on Vulkan, run `vulkaninfo | grep ray_query`. If
   that prints nothing, the driver has no ray queries.
4. To compare ray queries with the reference on that machine, run
   `cargo test -p regia_render --test hwrt_frame --test hwrt_shadow --test hwrt_shared_casters -- --nocapture`
   and `cargo test -p regia_terrain --test hwrt_terrain_casters -- --nocapture` (the terrain +
   scatter scene and the 100-frame refit). The cost measurements stay `#[ignore]`d:
   add `-- --ignored --nocapture`.

**What is a bug.** If `render.hwrt` reports `hwrt_enabled` for a process whose profile never asked,
report it, because the default device must never carry an experimental feature. The same goes for a
`sun_shadows.variant` other than `shadow_map` when `sun_shadow_trace` is `off`, or for a frame that
differs from a build without this feature while the knob is off. A mismatch between the ray-query
result and the reference in those tests is also a bug.

## Testing ray queries without a card

Lavapipe (Mesa 24.1 and later; 26.1.6 on the farm) exposes `VK_KHR_ray_query`, and wgpu gives
it `EXPERIMENTAL_RAY_QUERY`, so the ray-query path runs on a CPU. Select it and check:

```sh
export VK_ICD_FILENAMES=/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/lvp_icd.json
export VK_DRIVER_FILES=/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/lvp_icd.json   # the loader reads either name
regia doctor --platform gpu      # expect: llvmpipe ... ray queries yes

cargo test -p regia_render --test hwrt_frame --test hwrt_shadow --test hwrt_shared_casters -- --nocapture
cargo test -p regia_terrain --test hwrt_terrain_casters -- --nocapture
cargo test -p regia_render --test hwrt_ray_query_spirv   # naga to SPIR-V + spirv-val, no device
```

Each ray-query test asks `regia_test_utils::hwrt::ray_query_device()`. The gate decides from the
returned device's own features — never from `last_device_report()`, the process-wide report of
whichever device was created most recently, which a parallel sibling test can overwrite between
this device's creation and the read. It gets a device where the adapter has ray queries, and
otherwise prints `skipped: no ray queries on <adapter>` and returns, so the same command passes on
a machine without them (read the output to see which happened). `REGIA_REQUIRE_RAY_QUERIES=1`
(the `REGIA_REQUIRE_ASSETS` precedent) turns that skip into a failure: the lavapipe gate sets it,
so a Mesa older than 24.1, a lost `VK_ICD_FILENAMES`, or a wrong adapter pick fails the gate
instead of silently passing without ray-query coverage. The tests use small scenes and fixed frame
counts; none asserts on time. The `golden_hwrt_sun_pair` bless stays `#[ignore]`d until the lead
blesses it on the lavapipe reference; the `*_cost_on_this_adapter` measurements stay
`#[ignore]`d (run them on the card being measured).

## Any-hit mask

When the sun trace is already on, an alpha-masked caster takes an any-hit alpha test. There is
no profile field for it. Opaque casters skip it: on the ray-query path they are built with the
opaque geometry flag, so a hit commits without a candidate, and on the software walk a triangle
whose coverage channel is `0` (the value an unused channel had) commits the same way. A miss,
including a candidate the any-hit rejects and nothing else confirms, stays a miss.

`frame.masked_casters` is the count of those casters in the build (`render.hwrt`, the
`sun_shadows.frame` object). The ray-query build has counted them since ADR-2310. Each one
carries `MASKED_COVERAGE` (one half) in the instance custom data, packed by
`coverage_custom_data` into 8 bits. `any_hit` in `sun_trace_ray_query.wgsl` confirms the
candidate when a hash of the ray origin, the triangle and the instance falls under that byte.
Byte 255 is fully covered and accepts unconditionally; byte 0 rejects a non-opaque candidate.

The software walk (`bvh_walk.wgsl`, the compute reference and the sample-list fallback) runs
the same rule. The fraction lives in the first corner's `w` of the BVH triangle
(`ShadowBvh::build_with_coverage`). `hwrt::any_hit` is the CPU copy the walk is checked against.
A rejected candidate does not stop the walk: an opaque triangle further along the ray still
occludes.

Limit: no mask texture is bound on either tracer, so the any-hit does not fetch one. The mask
is the per-draw coverage the engine already stores. A cutout that exists only as a texture is
not read, and the shadow is a dappled field of that density, not the leaf shapes. The lit
fraction of a half-covered card is within 0.08 of one half over its footprint (1024 texels in
`tests/hwrt_anyhit_mask.rs`; a fair coin's standard deviation there is about 0.016). An opaque
card's covered texel count stays 1024.

The frame's compute build still omits masked draws until the integration patch
`sprint-hwrt-anyhit-mask-frame.patch` is applied. That patch feeds them to
`build_with_coverage`, counts them in `masked_casters`, and stops treating them as casters the
shadow map must still draw. The walk itself already accepts the coverage channel. The
ray-query frame path already includes them.

<!-- source: book/agents/frame-pipelining.md -->
# Frame pipelining

Where the frame thread's time goes, and what moves some of it off that thread (ADR-2074,
`specs/22` T2.12).

## Reading it

`render.frame_pipelining` takes no parameters and returns:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `profile` | The active profile's switch, or `null` in an app without `RenderSettings`. |
| `applied.parallel_shadow_plan` | The switch the last frame with sun pages applied. `REGIA_FRAME_PIPELINING=1` turns it on whatever the profile says. |
| `applied.on_tasks` | The last frame's page update really ran on tasks: the switch was on, with at least 256 casters and more than one cascade. Read this field to know what ran. |
| `encode_threads` | Workers that finish command buffers (`FrameRenderer::set_encode_threads`). |
| `render_thread.in_frame_loop` | Always `false`: the engine's frame loop renders on the thread that simulates. |
| `render_thread.note` | Why, and what a host that drives `FrameRenderer` itself can use. |
| `last_frame_ms` | The last frame's CPU time: `total`, `encode`, `submit`, `readback`, `shadow_plan`. |

An app without `RuntimeRenderer` gets the protocol's not-found error.

## Switching it

`render.set_frame_pipelining {"parallel_shadow_plan": true}` sets the active profile's switch from
the next frame and returns `before`, `after` and `note`. A value that is not a boolean is an
invalid-params error. `render.set_profile` replaces the profile, which turns the switch off.

`parallel_shadow_plan` projects the casters into each sun cascade and updates each cascade of the
sun page cache on its own compute-pool task, instead of all of them on the frame thread. It is off in every preset. The frames are byte-identical
either way: the update decides the same pages, and only the thread differs. Below 256 casters the
update stays on the frame thread, because spawning the tasks would cost more than they save.

A game sets it with `RenderProfile::frame_pipelining`, a host that drives the renderer itself with
`FrameQuality::frame_pipelining`.

## Measuring it

`crates/regia_render/tests/frame_pipelining_s0.rs` is the measurement behind these choices. It
prints where the frame thread's time goes from the renderer's own spans, the render targets by size,
and the frame interval with and without a render thread. The file's header has the commands. Its
numbers belong to the machine and scene they ran on. `docs/perf-log.md` holds the recorded rounds.

```text
VK_ICD_FILENAMES=/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/lvp_icd.json \
  cargo test -p regia_render --release --test frame_pipelining_s0 -- --ignored --nocapture
```

Add `REGIA_FRAME_PIPELINING=1` to measure with the switch on.

`frame_pipelining_s0_window` in the same file runs the same scene in a presenting window, inline and
on a render thread, and prints per frame the simulation thread's interval, the wait for
`RedrawRequested`, the acquire, record and present times, and the latency from the start of the
simulation to the frame's present (ADR-2798). The offscreen bench cannot see what a swapchain or a
compositor adds; this one can. On a Linux host without a display, run it under `xvfb-run -a`:

```text
xvfb-run -a -s "-screen 0 1920x1080x24" env VK_ICD_FILENAMES=/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/lvp_icd.json \
  cargo test -p regia_render --release --test frame_pipelining_s0 -- --ignored --nocapture frame_pipelining_s0_window
```

`REGIA_S0_PRESENT` (`fifo`, `mailbox`, `immediate`), `REGIA_S0_LATENCY` (the swapchain's frame
latency), `REGIA_S0_LOOP=poll` (frames from `about_to_wait`, not gated on `RedrawRequested`) and
`REGIA_S0_ENCODE` (encode threads) vary the setup. Lavapipe numbers say little about the render
thread, because its rasterizer runs inside `queue.submit`. Use a card on a real display for numbers
that decide anything.

## A render thread for a host

`regia_render::with_render_thread` runs `FrameRenderer` on a thread named `regia-render` for as long
as a closure runs, for a host that drives the renderer itself. The closure hands frames over with
`submit`, which blocks while an earlier frame waits (a channel of capacity one), and reaches the
renderer with `with_renderer`, which runs on the render thread after every frame handed over so far.
`post` queues a call the same way but does not wait for it. A host that presents to a swapchain posts
its whole frame this way (acquire, `render_into`, present), so the acquire's wait for the display falls
on the render thread. The frames are byte-identical to inline frames.

`RenderThreadSettings::queued_frames` is how many frames the channel holds while the render thread
works on another. The default 1 lets the host run furthest ahead, but a frame then reaches the display
about two frames later than inline when the render thread is the slower side. 0 makes the hand-over a
rendezvous: the next frame's simulation still overlaps this frame's recording, and the added latency is
at most one frame (measured in a window, `docs/perf-log.md`, ADR-2798).

| Error code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `render_thread_stopped` | The render thread panicked. The panic is raised again when the scope ends. |
| `render_thread_spawn_failed` | The OS refused the thread. The closure did not run. |

`RenderPlugin` does not use it: engine systems take the renderer during the simulation, which is when
this thread would hold it. ADR-2074 lists what the frame loop needs first.

## Transient aliasing

With `TransientPool::set_aliasing` on, `RenderGraph::execute` releases a transient after its last
reader, and the next transient of the same `TextureDesc` reuses its texture. `RenderGraph::alias_plan`
shows which transient gets which texture and the bytes saved, and the pool's `aliased` counter (in the
`transients` block of `render.graph`) counts the reuses.

Contents are undefined at a transient's first writer then, so that writer clears it or overwrites all
of it. The graph cannot see a writer that loads what is there or returns `Ok` without writing, and its
reader would see the earlier resource's pixels. A writer that needs last frame's contents declares its
own resource as an input. A transient read before any earlier node wrote it, or kept after the run,
keeps a texture of its own. When a node fails, its readers find no texture for what it was the first
to write, instead of another resource's pixels.

The frame itself does not run through `RenderGraph::execute` yet, so this applies to graphs a host
runs. In the frame, `aliased` stays 0.

# Lightmaps

A lightmap stores baked irradiance per texel for the static meshes of a map. `regia bake-lightmaps` lays out a
second UV set (UV2) for every mesh, bakes on the CPU or the GPU (`--gpu`), denoises, and writes a `.flmap`. At runtime the
lightmap is installed and switched on by the level that names it (`look.lightmap`) or through `render.set_lightmaps`;
without either the flag is off. Format reference: `docs/formats/lightmap.md`. What shipped for v0.3.0 (including the
automatic unwrap the cook carries and the bake density per package tier), and what is still open: `docs/specs/lightmaps.md`. Design: ADR-860, ADR-1556 (directions, bicubic
filtering, noise check, cook), ADR-1623 (the forward pass), ADR-2024 (the UV atlas, baking from a level, chart seams,
entity keys, the Lightmaps panel, the GPU baker), ADR-2107 (every path and tier), ADR-2125 (GPU tiles), ADR-2313 (levels),
ADR-2314 (denoise, block encodings), ADR-2404 (creases, stitching, automatic density).

**Reference images.** `cargo test -p regia_pt --test lightmap_quad_box` (the baked floor atlas) and `--test
lightmap_forward_quad_box` (the floor drawn as a receiver beside the red box, on the full shader and on the Mobile Low
lite shader) compare with `crates/regia_test_utils/goldens/lightmap_quad_box.png`,
`lightmap_forward_quad_box.png` and `lightmap_forward_quad_box_lite_low.png`. A missing image fails the test (ADR-3211).

**Closure status (ADR-4930).** The Mobile Low room passes the original numerical quality bars after the direct/indirect
energy correction. Derived LOW and ULTRA_LOW still miss their original seam and dark-point checks, and the corrected
Mobile Low reference frame needs owner review. No golden or threshold was changed; see
`docs/evidence/lightmaps-v030/closure-c-2026-11-09.md` for the controls and retained failures.

**The Mobile tiers against the full shader (ADR-5945).** Two tests in `lightmap_forward_quad_box` need no reference
image: `the_lite_low_frame_agrees_with_the_full_frame` draws the golden view with both shaders and holds every flat
8 x 8 window to the same mean brightness (0.5 code values) and the pair to the golden bar, and
`the_lite_tiers_draw_the_full_shaders_baked_light_on_every_material` does the same on nine receiver materials at
Mobile Low and Mobile High, metals and occlusion maps among them (1.5 code values; Mobile Low is not held on a smooth
metal, where its missing directions show). The manual study `lite_low_golden_study` (ignored; set
`REGIA_LIGHTMAP_LITE_STUDY=<dir>` for its table and plates) attributes the reference image's SSIM 0.9458: the blessed
`lightmap_forward_quad_box_lite_low.png` is the frame of the lite shader before ADR-4930, pixel for pixel, and today's
frame matches the full shader at Mobile Low's own shadow and lightmap settings in all but 48 pixels. The image still
waits for the owner's re-bless.

**Since ADR-1556 (format version 2).** The bake also stores the direction the baked light comes from per texel, so
normal maps bend it at runtime; the lookup is bicubic by default; the bake reports its noise before any filter and
can sample adaptively up to a hard cap; `.flmap` files under `assets/` cook into the pak. Versions 1 through 6 still
read; `regia upgrade-project --write` rewrites an older file at format version 7 (`LIGHTMAP_FORMAT_VERSION`).

**Since ADR-1623 the forward pass shades with it.** A *receiver* is a static mesh entity that names its entry in the
installed lightmap. It is drawn from that entry's unwrap and takes its diffuse indirect light (sky, bounce and, with
directions, the way normal maps bend it) from the lightmap instead of the probes or the flat ambient, while the flag
is on. Everything else (dynamic objects, unlisted meshes, the flag off) keeps the probe light, and a frame without
an enabled lightmap is unchanged. `render.get_lightmaps` reports `forward_pass: true` and what the last frame did.

**Since ADR-2024 (format version 3).** `regia bake-lightmaps --scene <level>` bakes a level directly and keys its
entries by entity; the UV atlas generator lays out UV2 by default; every bake measures its chart seams; and a lightmap
baked with `--direct-sun` replaces the live sun's diffuse on its receivers instead of adding to it. Versions 1 through 6 still
read; `regia upgrade-project --write` rewrites an older file at format version 7 (`LIGHTMAP_FORMAT_VERSION`).

## Shading a level with its lightmap

**Since ADR-2313 (scene format v11) the level carries it.** Bake with `--write-level` and the level names its lightmap
in `look.lightmap`; opening the level does the rest:

1. `regia bake-lightmaps --scene assets/levels/yard.level.ron --write-level` writes `assets/maps/yard.flmap` and
   rewrites the level with `look.lightmap: Some((file: "maps/yard.flmap"))` (the summary's `level_written` is `true`,
   `false` when it already named it; a `.level.d` directory or an output outside `assets/` is `lightmap_write_level`).
2. Open the level (`regia run --level`, `level.open`, the editor). The framework's `LightmapLevelPlugin` asks the renderer
   to warm the lightmap variants (`FrameRenderer::set_warm_lightmaps(true)`) as soon as the level is open (a renderer
   the host inserts later is asked on the next frame), installs the
   file (cooked from the pak or the dev cache first, else `assets/<file>`), turns lightmaps on (`enabled: Some(false)`
   loads it and keeps the probe light; `intensity` overrides the renderer's), and gives a `LightmapReceiver` to every
   drawn entity an entry was baked for, as meshes resolve: the level entity's own `MeshRenderer` is part 0, and a part
   entity with `MeshPartOf { owner, part }` (the editor's mesh resolver adds it; a host that splits models adds it
   too) is part `part`, so every part of a multi-part mesh receives. An entity that already has a receiver keeps it.
3. Check it:

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "render.get_lightmaps"}
   ```

   `level` is `{ file: "maps/yard.flmap", installed: true, error: null, error_code: null, entries: 4, keyed_entries: 4,
   attached: 4, unmatched: [], warm: true }`; `levels` lists the receivers per level:
   `[{ level: "<level guid>", current: true, lightmap: "maps/yard.flmap", receivers: 4, applied: 4, entities: [{ entity,
   guid, part, entry, applied, by_level }] }]`.

`LightmapReceiver` is reflected and saved with the level, so a level saved after its receivers were set (by the agent's
`receivers`, a host or the open itself) reopens with them. Closing the level removes the lightmap it installed, the
receivers it attached and the warm request, and puts the host's settings back. A level that names no lightmap changes
nothing. A file that is missing reports `level.error_code: "lightmap_not_found"` (the warm request stands, and the file
appearing later installs it); a file the reader refuses reports the reader's code.

The manual way, for a level that names no lightmap:

1. `regia bake-lightmaps --scene assets/levels/yard.level.ron` (or `editor.lightmap_bake`, below). It writes
   `assets/maps/yard.flmap` with one entry per static mesh part, keyed by the entity's guid.
2. `render.set_lightmaps {path: "maps/yard.flmap", enabled: true, auto_receivers: true}`. The result has `receivers_by_key`
   (entities attached) and `unmatched_keys` (entries nothing in the level matched: the entity is gone, or the entry is
   part 1 or later of a mesh source, which a `MeshRenderer` does not draw).
3. `render.get_lightmaps`: `receivers.applied` equals `receivers.receivers`, `receivers.errors` is empty. A host calls
   `regia_render::lightmap::receivers_by_key(world, &map)` and inserts a `LightmapReceiver` for each.

## Shading a map with its lightmap

1. Bake the map (`regia bake-lightmaps <map>.bake.ron`). Entries are named `instance_<k>`, `k` being the instance's
   index in the bake description.
2. In the game, give each baked static mesh entity a `LightmapReceiver { entry: "instance_<k>".into() }`
   (`regia_render::lightmap`). The entity keeps its `MeshRenderer` mesh: the engine swaps in the entry's receiver
   mesh (the same triangles, with the extra vertices a chart seam needs) and its UV2 stream, and puts the entity's
   own mesh back if the component, the entry or the lightmap goes away.
3. Install the lightmap and switch it on: `render.set_lightmaps {path: "maps/<map>.flmap", enabled: true}` (or
   `InstalledLightmap::load` and `LightmapSettings { enabled: true, .. }` from the host). An agent can attach the
   receivers in the same call: `receivers: [{entity: 4294967301, entry: "instance_0"}, ..]` (ids from
   `scene.query_entities`).
4. `render.get_lightmaps`: `receivers.applied` equals `receivers.receivers`, `receivers.errors` is empty, and
   `forward.drawn` counts the receivers in view.

What a receiver may be: a standard opaque or masked material (no material graph, not blended or transmissive),
rigid (no skin, no morph targets), drawn whole (no LOD chain or LOD cross-fade) and not a mask-decal instance. A
receiver outside that keeps the probe light and is counted in `forward.unsupported`, and so is every receiver when
the atlas is larger than the device's 2D texture limit (some mobile devices: bake with a smaller `--max-atlas` for
that tier).

**Since ADR-2107 a receiver draws on every path and tier.**

| The frame draws | A receiver draws | `forward` counts it in |
|---|---|---|
| GPU-driven batches | In the batches: one instanced draw per mesh and material, whatever entry each instance reads | `instanced` |
| The visibility buffer | As a cluster instance (the bake needs `--meshlets`): the resolve fetches its UV2 | `visbuffer` |
| The lite forward shader (Mobile tiers on a tile GPU) | From the CPU color loop with the lite shader: one bilinear fetch at Low, a second for the direction at High | `lite` |
| Anything else | From the CPU color loop with the full shader | none of them (only `drawn`) |

`drawn` is their total. A non-receiver instance sharing a receiver's mesh and material may share its batch; it keeps the
probe light. In a visibility frame with a receiver, the resolve draws all its pixels with its `LIGHTMAP` variant.

A receiver takes the visibility path only with clusters built over its unwrap, because a chart seam splits vertices and a
coarse level of the source mesh's clusters is free to cross a seam. Bake with `--meshlets`: the clusters go in the `.flmap`,
survive `regia cook`, and `apply_lightmap_receivers` hands each receiver's to the renderer while the profile has
`visibility_buffer` on (`receivers.clusters`; `forward.visbuffer` counts what the frame drew there). A receiver whose file has
none, or whose material the visibility path cannot shade, draws on the forward paths with the same light (`receivers.no_clusters`). A cooked `.fmlt` on the same entity (`MeshletSource`) is left unused
while it is a receiver, and used again when it gets its own mesh back. A host that drives the renderer itself calls
`regia_render::lightmap::receiver_meshlets(&map, entry, &receiver.vertices)` and `insert_meshlets` under the receiver mesh's
key, or `set_meshlet_builder`. Clusters that do not fit the mesh drawn (other counts or another bounding sphere: the mesh changed
since the bake) are refused the same way as none, with the warning code `lightmap_meshlets`.

**What each render profile allows.** `RenderProfile::lightmap_tier` caps `bicubic` and `directional`, and never turns on what
they turn off:

| Preset | `tier` | Lookup |
|---|---|---|
| Mobile Low | `bilinear` | One bilinear fetch. The direction section is not uploaded, which halves the GPU bytes |
| Mobile High | `directional` | One bilinear fetch for the light, one for the direction |
| Deck, every Desktop preset, Cinematic | `full` | Bicubic (four fetches) and the direction, as the settings ask |

`forward.tier` is what the last frame allowed. The lite shader lowers it too: a frame forced to the Low lite shader reads
`bilinear` whatever its preset. `render.get_forward_lite` says which shader the frame draws.

**Warming.** A frame warm (`FrameRenderer::warm_scene`, `warm_extracted`, and so `GameFrameWarm`) with a lightmap installed
builds the `LIGHTMAP` variants of every target it drew, on every path this device can draw receivers through, uploads the
lightmap and reserves its tables. Frames after it create no pipeline for a receiver. A lightmap installed after the warm has
started: call `FrameRenderer::set_warm_lightmaps(true)` at level load. Without a warm, a receiver mid-play keeps the probe
light while its variant builds in the background, and counts in `forward.fallback`. A project with no lightmap warms and
draws what it did before.

A host that drives the renderer itself calls `FrameRenderer::set_lightmap(Some(map), settings)` and
`set_lightmap_receivers(&[(object_key, entry)])`, and draws each receiver from
`regia_render::lightmap::receiver_mesh(&map, entry, &vertices, &indices)` (its `vertices`, `indices`, and `uv2` as
the mesh's second UV set).

By default the lightmap replaces the indirect diffuse term and, since ADR-4762, the indirect specular term of its receivers
(below); the sun stays live. A lightmap with `sun_direct` in
its `contents` (a `--direct-sun` bake) holds the sun's diffuse light too, so while it is enabled its receivers also drop
the live sun's diffuse term and keep only its specular, which a lightmap cannot hold. Every other surface keeps the live
sun whole, so dynamic objects stay lit and shadowed by it.

### Indirect specular on receivers

A rough floor seen at a grazing angle reflects the lit walls around it: in the v0.3.0 gallery the path tracer's floor indirect
light is about 12 % specular. A lightmap holds irradiance, not reflections, so before ADR-4762 a receiver in a level with no
image light, probes or reflection captures had no indirect specular at all and the floor read about 9 % darker than the
tracer. Now a receiver takes its indirect specular from the same baked light (`LightmapSettings::specular`, on by default):

- The directional rebalance (`E(n) = E · (1 + n · d) / max(1 + w, 1)`) is the irradiance of one radiance field that is linear
  in the direction. The specular reads that field in the GGX lobe: for linear radiance the lobe's integral is the radiance
  at the lobe's mean vector, the same lobe the probe specular reads (ADR-1103). A smooth surface sees the field toward its
  mirror direction, a rough one nearer its mean. Times the split-sum scale and bias, as every image light. Without
  directions (a `--no-directional` bake, or the Mobile Low tier, which drops them) the field is uniform: `E / π` in every
  lobe. The baked diffuse is multiplied by `1 − clamp(f0 A + B, 0, 1)`, reserving the specular
  share of the incident energy. The full shader and the lite shader (ADR-5945) also reserve the
  material's optional multi-scatter compensation from the diffuse budget and light that broad term
  from the unpartitioned bake, even without image lighting. The base GGX/diffuse lobes conserve a
  uniform white field; clearcoat and sheen retain their existing layered-material policies.
- It replaces the sky, probe and interior specular on receivers, as the lightmap already replaces their diffuse term. A local
  reflection capture (ADR-2860) keeps its share, and so does a transmissive pane's traced hit: both see the room's own
  radiance, sharper. The screen-space reflection replaces it like any environment specular. The lightmap's share takes the
  material's occlusion but not the screen-space AO or the sky-visibility estimate: the bake already darkened what the walls
  and creases hide (the diffuse term's rule, ADR-2635).
- Every preset has it: the full shader (Deck and Desktop), the visibility resolve and the lite shader (Mobile High and Low).
  The lite shader uses a view-independent lobe; Mobile Low reads it uniform. The lite shader uses the existing DFG lookup
  for this energy split and the full direct GGX/Smith/Schlick equations, including the material's optional direct
  energy compensation (ADR-4930). It shares one DFG fetch per fragment across lights and the receiver term;
  Low still reads the lightmap once and uploads no directions. Since ADR-5945 the receiver term also keeps the
  material's multi-scatter share: before it, a receiver with an authored metal material (multi-scatter is on by
  default in a `.material.ron`) drew as little as half of the full shader's baked light on the Mobile tiers. And
  its baked diffuse takes the multi-bounce form of the material's occlusion map, as the full shader's does; the
  baked reflection keeps the occlusion as it is.
- Bakes made with `--direct-sun` keep the previous environment reflection: their combined atlas cannot separate
  direct from indirect irradiance, and reconstructing from it would count the live sun's specular twice.
- `render.set_lightmaps { specular: false }` turns it off for an A/B: receivers then keep the specular of the other sources,
  which is none in a level that has none.

## Commands

```text
regia bake-lightmaps <scene> [--out FILE] [--unwrap atlas|charts] [--density T] [--padding N] [--max-atlas N]
                               [--chart-angle DEG] [--samples N] [--bounces N] [--seed N] [--direct-sun] [--no-filter]
                               [--threads N] [--min-area M2] [--instance K]... [--dry-run] [--seam-budget F] [--meshlets]
                               [--no-directional] [--max-samples N --noise-target F] [--gpu]
                               [--crease on|off] [--stitch on|off] [--auto-density on|off]
regia bake-lightmaps --scene <level> [--project DIR] [--sun ELEV,AZIM,LUX] [the same options]
regia bake-lightmaps <file.flmap> --inspect
```

- `<scene>` is a built-in (`cornell`, `furnace`, `rolling-hills`, `quad-box`) or a GI bake description (`.bake.ron`,
  the file `regia bake-gi` reads; see [Baking GI from meshes](book/agents/baked-gi-bake.md)). `quad-box` is the baker's
  reference scene: a 4 m grey floor (instance 0) with a closed 1 m red box on it (instance 1), a white sky and a low
  sun. The lightmap uses its meshes, materials
  (base color and emission), sun, sky and lights. The terrain heightfield is not lightmapped.
- `--scene <level>` bakes a level directly. Its `GiMobility::Static` mesh entities, its sun and its sky are what
  `regia bake-gi --from-scene` exports; nothing but the `.flmap` is written. `--project` names the project root (default:
  the nearest ancestor with a project manifest), `--sun` overrides the level's sun, and the default output is
  `<project>/assets/maps/<level>.flmap`. Each mesh part gets an entry `entity_<guid>_<part>` keyed by entity. The file's
  bytes do not depend on the order of the level's entities or on `--threads`.
- `LightmapSurface { density_scale, receive }` on a level's entity: `density_scale` multiplies the bake's density for it
  (above 1 for hero pieces), `receive: false` leaves it to the probes while it still shadows and bounces (the JSON lists
  it under `skipped_opted_out`). A scale that is not a number above 0 is `lightmap_scene`, with the entity in `path`.
- Every other placed mesh that is neither emissive nor unlit gets an entry named `instance_<k>`, where `k` is its index in
  the scene. Emissive meshes are lights.
- `--unwrap atlas` (the default) lays UV2 out with the UV atlas generator ([Lightmap UV atlas](book/agents/atlas.md)): low-stretch
  charts on curved meshes, packed by footprint so no space goes to a chart's empty corners. `--unwrap charts` is the
  planar generator (`--chart-angle` applies only to it). Both follow the density rules.
- `--seam-budget F` fails with `lightmap_seam_budget` when an entry's seam `p95` passes `F`, after writing the file so
  you can look at it. Without it the seams are only reported.
- `--gpu` bakes on the GPU: the same light up to float rounding, the same file format. It needs a CLI built with
  `--features lightmap-gpu`; otherwise it is `lightmap_gpu_unavailable`. A scene too large for the device is
  `lightmap_gpu_limit`: bake on the CPU. `settings.backend` says which ran.
- The GPU bake runs in tiles, one dispatch each, with at most one more queued behind it (ADR-2125). `--gpu-tile-rays N` caps a tile at
  about `N` rays (default 4194304, range 4096..=67108864). Smaller tiles hand the GPU back sooner, so an editor drawing on
  the same GPU stays responsive. `--gpu-yield-ms N` (at most 1000) waits for every tile and then leaves the GPU idle for `N` ms. There is then no
  tile queued. The
  Lightmaps panel passes `--gpu-tile-rays 1048576 --gpu-yield-ms 2`. `--gpu-memory-mib F` caps the GPU memory the bake
  holds. A larger atlas then bakes in chunks of texels that fit next to the scene. A scene that alone passes the cap is
  `lightmap_gpu_limit`. Tiles, chunks and the pause never change the file: every texel adds its samples in the same order
  (tested byte for byte).
- The tile schedule is a pure function of the scene, the settings and these options, so the same bake runs the same tiles
  on every run. The JSON's `gpu` object reports it: `adapter`, `tiles`, `chunks`, `chunk_texels`, `tile_texels`, `tile_samples`, `tile_rays`,
  `scene_bytes`, `peak_bytes`, `memory_budget_bytes`, `readbacks`, `yield_ms`, `schedule_hash` (16 hex digits, the same for the
  same tiles in the same order) and `fallback`.
- A GPU device lost mid-bake (a driver reset) ends the bake with `lightmap_gpu_device_lost`, and nothing is written.
  `--gpu-fallback` bakes on the CPU instead whenever the GPU cannot: `lightmap_gpu_unavailable`, `lightmap_gpu_device`,
  `lightmap_gpu_device_lost`, `lightmap_gpu_limit` or `lightmap_gpu`. `settings.backend` is then `cpu`, and
  `gpu.fallback` holds the GPU's `code` and `message`. Settings errors never fall back.
- `--compare REF.flmap` compares the new map with a reference of the same layout after the bake, for example a CPU bake of
  the same scene and settings. The `compare` object holds `texels` (baked in both), `coverage_mismatch`, `identical`,
  `psnr_db` (null when identical), `mse`, `peak`, `mean_rel`, `p99_rel`, `max_rel`, `psnr_floor_db` and `within_floor`.
  PSNR is `10 log10(peak² / MSE)` over the RGB irradiance of the texels both maps baked, with `peak` the reference's
  brightest channel. The GPU baker's documented tolerance against the CPU baker is `psnr_floor_db`, 40 dB
  (`regia_pt::lightmap::LIGHTMAP_GPU_PSNR_FLOOR_DB`). `crates/regia_pt/tests/lightmap_gpu.rs` holds every kind of light to
  it on lavapipe.
- `--instance K` bakes only instance `K` (repeat the flag for more). The rest of the scene still lights and shadows
  it. An instance that does not exist, or is emissive, unlit or a light, is refused with `lightmap_instance`.
- `--min-area` skips meshes with less surface than that many m². Small props (rock hints, clutter) then keep the
  probe lighting, and the atlas spends its texels on walls and set pieces. The JSON lists them under
  `skipped_small`.
- `--dry-run` lays out the atlas and prints it without baking. It is fast; use it to choose `--density`. With `--meshlets` it
  builds the clusters too, which costs seconds per mesh.
- `--inspect` reads an existing `.flmap` and prints its summary.
- `--meshlets` also builds visibility-buffer clusters over each entry's unwrap and stores them in the file, so a receiver can
  draw through the visibility buffer in a game with no meshlet builder. Off by default: it costs seconds per mesh and file size.
  The output's `meshlets` is `{ entries, clusters, levels, bytes, refused: [{ entry, code, message }] }` (`null` without the flag),
  in a dry run too. An entry the builder refuses, or whose clusters would cross a chart seam, keeps its bake and draws in the
  batches.
- Without them the command bakes on all cores (`--threads 0`) and writes `--out` (default `<scene>.flmap`).
- `--samples` is 1..=65536 and `--bounces` at most 64. Out of range is `lightmap_bake_settings` with `path` naming
  the setting, before anything is read.
- `--noise-target F` turns on adaptive sampling: a texel takes `--samples`, then more `--samples` at a time, until
  the relative standard error of its luminance is at most `F` (0.02 = 2 %) or it reaches `--max-samples` (at most
  65536). Sample `k` of a texel always uses the same random numbers, so the result is still the same for any
  `--threads`. Keep `--samples` at 16 or more: a texel whose first few samples agree by chance stops early.
- `--no-directional` leaves out the direction section (half the file; normal maps then do not change the baked
  light).
- `--direct-sun` also bakes the sun seen directly. Leave it off when the runtime sun and its shadows stay live (the
  default); turn it on for fully static lighting (low-end or mobile). A receiver of such a lightmap keeps only the live
  sun's specular.

Each prints one JSON object on stdout. Progress goes to stderr.

## Output

Bake:

```text
{
  "ok": true, "out": "bore.flmap", "bytes": 4194512, "scene": "bore.bake.ron", "density_scaled": null,
  "atlas": { "width": 1024, "height": 1024, "charts": 412, "fit_scale": 1.0, "attempts": 1,
             "chart_fill": 0.61, "rect_fill": 0.83, "degenerate_triangles": 0, "generator": "atlas" },
  "report": { "entries": 21, "texels_baked": 640000, "texels_inside": 312, "texels_dilated": 90000,
              "rays": 512000000, "triangles": 260000, "emissive_triangles": 12, "lights": 0,
              "contents": ["sky", "sun_bounce", "emissive"], "directional": true,
              "noise": { "mean": 0.031, "p95": 0.074, "max": 0.21, "mean_samples": 256.0,
                         "texels_over_target": 0 } },
  "seams": { "edges": 180, "hard_edges": 96, "p95": 0.08, "max": 0.2,
             "entries": [ { "name": "instance_0", "edges": 12, "mean": 0.02, "p95": 0.05, "max": 0.09, "worst_chart": 3,
                            "hard_edges": 8, "charts": [ { "chart": 3, "edges": 4, "mean": 0.04, "max": 0.09 }, .. ] }, .. ],
             "overlay": [ { "entry": 0, "a": [0.11, 0.2], "b": [0.11, 0.24], "world_a": [1.0, 0.0, 3.0],
                            "world_b": [1.0, 0.0, 4.0], "error": 0.2 }, .. ] },
  "coverage": { "empty": 310000, "baked": 640000, "dilated": 98000 },
  "utilization": 0.70, "exposure": 256.0,
  "entries": [ { "name": "instance_0", "instance": 0, "rect": [0, 0, 220, 96], "charts": 14, "triangles": 380,
                 "vertices": 412, "area_m2": 310.5, "texels_per_metre": 8.0 }, .. ],
  "skipped_small": [],
  "settings": { "density": 8.0, "padding": 2, "max_atlas": 4096, "chart_angle": 60.0, "min_area": 0.0,
                "instances": [], "samples": 256, "bounces": 3, "seed": 1, "direct_sun": false, "filter": true,
                "directional": true, "max_samples": 0, "noise_target": 0.0 },
  "timings": { "load": 0.4, "layout": 1.9, "bake": 38.1, "seams": 0.3, "encode_write": 0.5 },
  "seconds": 41.2
}
```

- `seams` is the chart-seam metric (`docs/formats/lightmap.md` § 2a): the relative luminance step across the edges where
  a smooth surface is cut in UV2 (two charts meeting, or one chart meeting itself along a slit), per entry and per chart; `hard_edges` are real creases, left out.
  Every pair of faces on a welded edge counts (ADR-4108): where closed blocks meet in one plane, four faces share the
  edge, and the two coplanar ones are the seam (before ADR-4108 such seams were neither measured nor stitched). `overlay` lists
  the worst edges, at most 1024, worst first, in atlas UV and in world space. The figures go in the file: `--inspect` and
  the shipping check read them. With `--seam-budget`, `seams.budget` and `seams.over_budget` are added.
- With `--scene`, `level` adds `project`, `input_hash`, `statics`, `skipped`, `skipped_by`, `skipped_entities`, `sun`,
  `sky` and `warnings`, and each entry adds `entity`, `part` and `label`.
- `atlas.fit_scale < 1` means the charts did not fit `--max-atlas` at the asked density. Every entry's
  `texels_per_metre` shows what it got. The bake then also prints a `warning:` line on stderr and lists
  `lightmap_atlas_scaled` (with `fit_scale`) in `density.warnings`.
- `density_scaled` (ADR-3121) is the same fact as a headline: `null` when every entry got the density it asked for,
  else `{ factor, requested, density, max_atlas, remedy, message }`. `factor` is `atlas.fit_scale`, `density` the
  texels per meter an entry of scale 1 got, and `remedy` what to do: raise `--max-atlas` (up to 8192) or split the
  level into smaller levels; at `--max-atlas 8192` it says to split the level or lower `--density`. The dry run has it
  too, so check it before a long bake. `editor.lightmap_status` returns the bake's JSON as `summary` (so
  `summary.density_scaled`), and the Lightmaps panel's atlas line reads "density lowered to N %: raise atlas or split
  level".
- `timings` is the wall time of each phase in seconds: `load` (the level or scene), `layout` (UV2 and the atlas),
  `bake`, `seams` and `encode_write`; a dry run has only the first two. See [Bake time at scale](#bake-time-at-scale).
- `report.texels_inside` counts texels whose hemisphere rays mostly hit back faces: the surface runs inside other
  geometry (a floor under a wall). They are refilled from their neighbours. A large count on one entry usually means
  overlapping or single-sided geometry. A texel center on a chart's border traces from just inside its triangle, so light does not come in through the joint
  it touches.
- `report.noise` is the bake's noise before the filter: the relative standard error of each baked texel's mean
  luminance (`mean`, `p95`, `max`), the samples a texel took on average, and with `--noise-target` the texels that
  reached `--max-samples` still above it. It is `null` below 2 samples. This is the check that does not depend on
  the denoiser: bake with `--no-filter` and read `p95`.
- The dry run prints `atlas`, `entries`, `contents`, `triangles`, `skipped_small` and `settings`, with
  `"dry_run": true`.

`--inspect` prints `version`, `width`, `height`, `exposure`, `density`, `padding`, `directional`, `contents`, `bake` (`samples`,
`bounces`, `seed`, `sun_toward`, `sun_illuminance`, `filtered`), `coverage`, `utilization` and `entries` (with `entity`,
`part` and `seams`).

## Errors

A failure prints `{"ok": false, "code", "path", "message"}` and exits with status 1.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `bake_scene_unknown` | `<scene>` is neither a built-in nor a `.ron` file |
| `bake_source_missing`, `bake_desc_parse`, `bake_desc_newer`, `bake_desc_invalid`, `bake_mesh_load`, `bake_manifest_mismatch` | The bake description, as for `regia bake-gi` ([Baking GI from meshes](book/agents/baked-gi-bake.md)) |
| `lightmap_scene` | The scene cannot be flattened (an instance names a missing mesh or material, a bad index), or a level's `LightmapSurface.density_scale` is not a number above 0 (`path` names the entity) |
| `export_read_failed`, `export_level_parse`, `export_mesh_missing`, `export_no_input`, `export_terrain_ambiguous`, `export_path_invalid` | `--scene`: the level, as for `level.export_bake` ([Exporting a bake from a level](book/agents/baked-gi-export.md)) |
| `lightmap_seam_budget` | An entry's chart seams pass `--seam-budget` (the file was written; `path` is the first entry), or in a shipping `regia package` `[lightmaps] seam_budget` |
