# Swapchain, HDR output and host paths (agents)

Each window's swapchain is planned from the surface capabilities, `OutputSettings` (present policy
and HDR request), the window's present mode, the backend and what the display reports about HDR
(ADR-525). `render.swapchain` reports the plan and the reasons behind it. `platform.paths` reports
where the app keeps its files on the host. Guide topic: `agent.guide {"topic": "swapchain"}`.

## `render.swapchain`

No parameters. Read-only. Returns `{ windows, count }`, one entry per live window surface, ordered by
window entity. A headless app has no window surfaces and answers `{ "windows": [], "count": 0 }`.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `window` | Window entity bits. |
| `backend` | `vulkan`, `dx12`, `metal` (wgpu backend name). |
| `size` | `[width, height]` of the configured swapchain, in pixels. |
| `format`, `color_space` | wgpu names, for example `Bgra8UnormSrgb` / `Auto` (SDR), `Rgb10a2Unorm` / `Bt2100Pq` (HDR10), `Rgba16Float` / `ExtendedSrgbLinear` (scRGB). |
| `present_mode` | What the engine asked wgpu for (may be `AutoVsync` or `AutoNoVsync`). |
| `present_mode_effective` | The concrete mode after wgpu resolves an `Auto` mode: `AutoVsync` is `FifoRelaxed`, else `Fifo`; `AutoNoVsync` is `Immediate`, else `Mailbox`, else `Fifo`. |
| `alpha_mode` | `Opaque` whenever the surface lists it. |
| `frame_latency` | Frames the CPU may queue ahead of the display (2). |
| `copy_src` | The swapchain can be read back (screenshots). |
| `requested` | `{ present: vsync / uncapped / vrr, window_present: vsync / vsync_relaxed / immediate, hdr: sdr / hdr10 / scrgb }`. |
| `hdr_active` | The configured color space is HDR. |
| `hdr_fallback` | Why an HDR request was configured as SDR: `not_offered` (the surface does not list the format and color space pair) or `display_sdr` (the display is not in an HDR mode, for example Windows HDR is off). `null` otherwise. |
| `offered` | `{ present_modes, hdr }`: what the surface lists. |
| `display` | `{ hdr_mode, peak_nits, full_frame_nits, min_nits, sdr_white_nits, bits_per_color }`. Windows reports these through DXGI for DX12 and Vulkan alike; other platforms report `null` (unknown, not "SDR"). |

```json
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "render.swapchain"}
```

### The rules (ADR-525)

- **SDR** (the default) is the first sRGB format with the `Auto` color space, as before.
- **HDR on an SDR display.** DX12 lists its HDR color spaces whether or not Windows HDR is on, and
  the desktop compositor would tone-map an HDR swapchain back down to SDR. When the display reports
  `hdr_mode: false`, an HDR request is configured as SDR with `hdr_fallback: "display_sdr"`. While
  HDR is requested, the display is read again every 120 frames, so switching Windows HDR on or off
  while the game runs reconfigures the swapchain.
- **HDR pairs** are looked up in the surface's per-format color spaces, so a format the surface lists
  only with an HDR color space is still found.
- **VRR on DX12** presents with `Immediate`: sync interval 0 with tearing allowed, which is what
  variable refresh needs on a DXGI flip-model swapchain. Without tearing support it takes `Mailbox`.
  Vulkan, on Windows too, keeps `Mailbox` first.
- **Display luminance.** When the platform reports no display luminance (desktop), the display's
  peak and minimum nits from this report fill `DisplayLuminance`, and a calibration still at its
  platform default takes them (see [Display calibration](book/agents/display-calibration.md)).

### Typical loop

1. `render.set_calibration {"hdr": true}` to request HDR10.
2. `render.swapchain`: check `hdr_active`. If it is `false`, `hdr_fallback` says why.
3. `seeing.screenshot` as usual: HDR frames are captured as their SDR rendition.

## `platform.paths`

No parameters. Read-only. Returns the app's host directories (`null` when not configured):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `os` | `std::env::consts::OS` (`linux`, `windows`, `android`, `macos`). |
| `user`, `cache`, `logs` | Host paths of `user://`, `cache://`, `logs://`. On Windows `user://` is `%APPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>` and `cache://` is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>`. |
| `crash_reports` | Where panic text reports go (`logs://`, read them with `diagnostics.crash_reports`). |
| `feedback` | The feedback folder: feedback bundles, crash bundles and native-crash minidumps. On Windows, with the standard `user://`, it is the non-roaming `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RegiaEngine\<exe>\feedback`, so dumps never sync with a roaming profile. |
| `saved_games` | The Windows `Saved Games` folder; `null` elsewhere. |
| `pipeline_cache` | `{ dir, backend, state, skipped }`. `state` is `active`, `backend_unsupported` (DX12 and Metal: wgpu 30 has no pipeline cache there, and the GPU driver keeps its own shader cache), `driver_skipped` (Intel's Windows Vulkan driver, v0.2.15, ADR-3288: the first cold compile of the Desktop High pipelines with the engine cache attached crashed inside the driver on an N150 laptop; the driver's own disk cache keeps warm launches as fast; `REGIA_PIPELINE_CACHE=1` attaches the engine cache to re-test a new driver), `no_device`, `no_directory` or `disabled` (`REGIA_PIPELINE_CACHE=0`). `skipped` is the driver rule's reason in words, `null` otherwise. |

```json
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "platform.paths"}
```

## Wayland frame callbacks

A focused window does not ask for Wayland's frame callback on any present mode, so its frames overlap as on
X11 and Windows. On `Fifo` or `FifoRelaxed` the swapchain paces the loop; with vsync off (`Immediate`, `Mailbox`)
only the frame cap does, also on a compositor that throttles frame callbacks. Every other window keeps it, because
the runner detects a hidden workspace by the missing callback (`swapchain::wants_frame_callback`, ADR-1750, amended
for the vsync-off modes by ADR-8170). The boot splash's present follows the same rule. So an unfocused Wayland window
can run at a lower rate than the same window focused, once CPU plus GPU time passes a vblank. A focused window under
a blanked panel keeps rendering.

<!-- source: book/agents/hostile-input.md -->
# Hostile input: what never crashes the game

An agent sends whatever JSON it likes, and a project holds whatever bytes its files hold. The
engine's promise for both: a bad request or a bad file ends in an error you can read, never in a
panic, a hang or an unbounded allocation. This page says what that means on the wire and how the
engine checks it.

## On the protocol

Every request gets exactly one answer: a `result`, or an `error` whose `data.code` is a stable
`F0xxx` code (`errors.explain` describes each one). Wrong types, missing fields, numbers past their
range and ids of entities that do not exist are all `F0002` (`INVALID_PARAMS`) or `F0003`
(`NOT_FOUND`), and they change nothing.

Some parameters have hard upper bounds, because a value past them would stall or exhaust the game
rather than fail:

| Method | Parameter | Accepted |
|---|---|---|
| `play.step` | `frames` | 1 to 10,000 per call |
| `play.set_time_scale` | `scale` | `0..=1000` |
| `play.inject_input` | `at_frame`, `duration_frames` | `at_frame` clamped to 10 000 000 frames ahead and to `u64::MAX / 4`; `duration_frames` clamped to 1 000 000; an omitted duration is 1 (`InputInjection::schedule` also stores at least 1) |
| `loop.set` | `max_fps` | `1..=10000`, or `null` (clears the agent cap; a profile cap applies again) |
| `loop.set` | `throttled_fps` | `1..=1000` |
| `loop.set` | `fixed_hz` | `1..=1000000000` |
| `loop.set` | `max_substeps` | `1..=64` |
| `anim.set_morph_weights` | `weights` | target indices below 4096, at most 4096 weights |
| `vfx.place_rut` | `points`, `spacing` | at most 4096 stamps; every coordinate finite in f32 |
| `players.get` | `index` | `0..=255` |

Vectors (`[x, y, z]`) for physics, navigation, picking and decals must be finite *after* conversion
to f32: `1e300` is a valid JSON number but an infinite f32, so it is `F0002`.

`scene.apply_edits` validates every edit before it applies any, and validation never changes the
world: a `dry_run` with a `despawn` edit leaves the entity in place.

```json
{ "method": "play.step", "params": { "frames": 18446744073709551615 } }
→ { "error": { "code": -32602, "message": "`frames` must be an integer in 1..=10000",
               "data": { "code": "F0002", "hint": "check the method's parameters in the agent guide" } } }
```

## On the network

A multiplayer server takes bytes from every connected peer. `regia_net`'s server refuses what it cannot decode and
tells the host (`ServerEvent::Rejected`, ADR-7892): an input bundle with a field past its cap (an over-long command
tail, more than 32 inputs) disconnects only its sender at once with `protocol_error`; other undecodable input and game
messages, including bytes left after a bundle, score malformed points until the sender is dropped with
`malformed_packet`. See [Net model (agents)](book/agents/net-model.md#hostile-input-and-input-readiness-adr-7892).

Every decode path on an authenticated link charges its sender and names it; none drops bytes for free (spec 120 § 11.2,
ADR-7984):

| Path | What is refused | Kind | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| server, input lane | an input bundle with a field past its cap | `input_too_long` | sender disconnected with `protocol_error` |
| server, input lane | a truncated or invalid bundle, bytes after it | `input_malformed` | 16 malformed points |
| server, reliable input lane | an input over 16 KiB / one that does not decode | `input_too_long` / `input_malformed` | disconnect / 16 points |
| server, either input lane | any input from a spectator (refused undecoded) | `spectator_input` | one malformed point |
| server, game lane | a game message that does not decode | `message_malformed` | 16 malformed points |
| server, any | a lane the server does not know | `unknown_lane` | 16 malformed points |
| server, sealed link | a record that authenticated but whose kind byte names no kind, or a client's `Accept`/`Deny` record | (counted in `totals.malformed`) | 16 malformed points (ADR-8666) |
| server, sealed link | a record that fails its open (forged, replayed, damaged) | (auth totals) | nothing: not provably the peer's, and it never stops a later datagram from being opened (ADR-8606, ADR-8666) |
| server runtime | a server-only message type (`ToOwner`, `Broadcast`) from a client | `server_only_message` | sender disconnected with `protocol_error` |
| server runtime, voice relay | a voice packet that does not parse (after a token of the sender's voice bucket) | `voice_malformed` | 16 malformed points |
| server runtime, voice relay | a voice control message with an unknown kind, or a block account over 256 bytes | `voice_malformed` | 16 malformed points |
| client | a server message that does not decode on the reliable stream | (client) | link ends with `protocol_error`; the client says goodbye |
| client | a server message that does not decode on the unreliable channel | (client) | dropped, `totals.malformed` + 1 |

The endpoint's kinds arrive as `ServerEvent::Rejected`; the replication runtime's (`server_only_message`,
`voice_malformed`) as `NetNode::take_rejections`, and an agent reads them in `net.status` `rejections` (`total`,
`dropped`, the newest 16 with `peer`, `kind`, `detail`, `tick`). Only traffic that authenticated as the peer's (or, on a
plain link, came from its validated address) scores it (ADR-8606). Malformed points add up per peer at each kind's
`RejectKind::malformed_weight` (16; `spectator_input` 1) and leak 4 points a second, at the endpoint and in the runtime
alike (ADR-8666); no packet or pass earns credit. At 1024 the peer leaves with `malformed_packet`: a sustained malformed
stream goes in about a second, one refusal every 4 s never accumulates. Refusal log lines share the per-peer budget of 10
a second.
Check it with `cargo test -p regia_net --test swallowed_decode` and
`cargo test -p regia_net --features voice --test swallowed_decode_runtime` (real UDP loopback, encryption required).

## In content files

The loaders of scenes (`.level.ron`, `.prefab.ron`, postcard and cooked scenes), paks (`.fpak`),
baked GI volumes (`.fgiv`) and materials (`.material.ron`) return an error for anything they cannot
use. A file that parses but describes something no bake or editor writes is handled where it is used:

- A cooked scene whose parent links form a loop spawns with one link per loop dropped, and a
  warning in the spawn result naming the entity. Prefab added children are handled the same way.
- A prefab instance that would expand past 2^20 entities and edits (nested prefabs that fan out)
  fails to spawn with `SceneSpawnError::Invalid`.
- `added_children` nested more than 64 deep is a decode error.
- A `.fgiv` whose brick counts overflow or whose origins are not finite is a layout error. A
  terrain layer without columns, or a brick with a zero count, loads; the baked GI lookup treats it
  as empty.

## How this is checked

Deterministic fuzz tests run in every gate (no nightly toolchain, no random seeds; see ADR-538):

| Test | What it feeds | Past the parse |
|---|---|---|
| `regia_agent/tests/dispatch_fuzz.rs` | every method with hostile params of every JSON type, random combinations, mutated request text | the permission check, rate limit, handler and audit record, then two frames |
| `regia_scene/tests/fuzz.rs` | mutated `.level.ron`, `.prefab.ron`, postcard and cooked scenes | spawn with the prefab baked, transform propagation, snapshot |
| `regia_asset/tests/fuzz.rs` | mutated paks, `.fgiv` v1 and v2, the full material | every pak entry read, every probe queried, the material saved, reloaded and cooked |
| `regia_test_utils/tests/loader_fuzz.rs` | mutated `.fgiv` and `.material.ron` | the renderer's baked GI lookup and material conversion |
| `regia_net/tests/fuzz.rs` `over_cap_input_tails_drop_only_their_senders` | seeded input streams of four players: valid samples, junk (unknown tags, truncated tails, stray bytes) and one over-cap command tail each | the server's refusal events, the over-cap disconnect of exactly that sender, the clean player's every tick |

Run one crate's set with `cargo test -p regia_agent --test dispatch_fuzz` (or `-p regia_scene
--test fuzz`, and so on). A failure prints the method and parameters, or the loader, that panicked.

## Review for v0.5.0 (ADR-5869)

A review of the asset and agent-protocol input paths for v0.5.0 found and fixed these; each has a test that fails on
the code before the fix:

- A mod pak's one entry may decompress to at most `ModsLimits::max_file_bytes` (1 GiB, ADR-5993), checked from the table of
  contents; mod paks are read through the file, not the mapping, so a pak rewritten in place cannot fault a read.
- The glTF checked parse refuses a node graph that is not a forest (glTF 2.0 § 3.5.3: one parent, no cycles) and
  holds the zero-filled elements of accessors without a buffer view to 16 times the file's buffer bytes (at least
  64 MiB); image headers are read first and an edge over 32768 or more than 4 GiB of RGBA8 in all is refused before
  any decode. The plant envelope loader, the scene export's source read and an animated glTF's buffers (the BVH
  retarget target, which must now be a project file) go through the same checks.
- KTX2 bytes handed to `CompressedTexture::from_ktx2`, `texture_row` or the BCn-to-ASTC transcode get the DFD guard
  the cooked texture already had; a colour LUT PNG's shape is checked before its frame buffer is allocated; the pak
  summary saturates hostile declared sizes; a chunk mount looks ids up by index (it scanned the table per id).
- Agent methods: see `platform.power_state`, `demo.record_stop`, `content.check_host`, `configurator.open_product`
  (a network or device `root` is `configurator_bad_path`) and the DCC feed's linked-folder refusal on their pages;
  the terrain file writers are `mutating`.

Every frozen content format, the net datagrams and the agent request text also have a target in the fuzz-target
registry (spec 97, ADR-1917): `regia_agent/tests/fuzz_targets.rs` fails the gate when a format has no target, and a
running dev build fuzzes one target, or a project file as the fixture, through `fuzz.targets` and `fuzz.run`. See
[Fuzzing](book/agents/fuzzing.md).

<!-- source: book/agents/determinism.md -->
# Determinism: state hashes and record/replay

A Regia Engine simulation with a fixed timestep, a seeded RNG and recorded input should give the same
state every time it runs. Two tools check that: the `sim.state_hash` / `sim.state_diff` protocol methods
for a running app, and `cargo xtask repro-check`, a record/replay stress run over 20 seeds and three
scenes (ADR-537).

## The state hash

The hash covers every reflected component of every entity, written as canonical text:

- Each value is keyed `<entity>/<Component>`, where `<entity>` is the entity's `Name`. Duplicate names
  and unnamed entities get a `#rank`. Entity ids are not part of the state. An entity reference inside a
  value prints as the referenced entity's key, so two runs that allocate different ids still hash the
  same.
- Struct fields appear in declaration order, and lists in their own order.
- **Map and set entries are sorted**, so a component holding a `HashMap` hashes the same however the
  map happens to iterate.
- Floats print in the shortest form that round-trips, which is distinct for distinct values (`0.0` and
  `-0.0` included).
- Resources are not included. The harness lets a scene add its own: the arena adds its match RNG.
- An opaque type without a reflected `Debug` contributes only its type name, so its contents are not
  hashed.

The same snapshot is what `cargo xtask shuffle-check` compares ([Schedule shuffle](book/agents/schedule-shuffle.md)).

## `sim.state_hash`

Params, all optional:

- `prefix`: only keys that start with this, for example `"hero/"`.
- `ignore`: component short names to leave out, for example `["EntityGuid"]`.
- `keys`: `true` adds a hash per key.

Read-only.

```json
{ "method": "sim.state_hash", "params": { "keys": true, "ignore": ["EntityGuid"] } }
```

Returns `{ hash, frame, entities, values, nondeterministic, keys? }`:

- `hash`: 16 hex digits.
- `frame`: the app's frame count.
- `values`: the number of keys.
- `nondeterministic`: `[{ code, source, detail }]`, what made this session not reproducible; empty when nothing did.
  An extension hot reload (`plugin.reload`) adds `{ "code": "nondeterministic_reload", "source": "<extension id>",
  "detail": "generation N" }` (ADR-9850). Hashes of a run that lists an event are not comparable with a clean run's;
  `sim.state_diff` answers the same field. A demo recorded in such a session carries `!nondeterministic_reload:<id>`
  at the end of its `build_hash`, and `demo.inspect` lists it under `nondeterministic` and in `mismatches`.
- `keys`: `{ "<entity>/<Component>": "<16 hex>" }`, only with `keys: true`.

## `sim.state_diff`

Params:

- `against` (required): the `keys` object of an earlier `sim.state_hash { keys: true }`, from this
  run or from another.
- `prefix` and `ignore`: as for `sim.state_hash`, applied to both the live snapshot and `against`.
  Filtered keys do not count as added, changed or removed.
- `limit`: how many keys each list shows, 1 to 1000 (default 50).

Read-only.

Returns `{ hash, frame, same, counts: { changed, added, removed }, changed, added, removed, truncated }`.
`changed` lists the keys whose value differs. `added` lists the keys that exist now but are missing
from `against`, and `removed` the reverse.

To check a run for determinism by hand:

1. Start two runs with the same seed and input, both on a fixed timestep with a manual clock
   (`enable_fixed_step` in the app).
2. Pause both with `play.pause` and step them to the same frame with `play.step`.
3. Call `sim.state_hash` in each run and compare the two `hash` values.
4. If they differ, call `sim.state_hash { keys: true }` in run A and pass its `keys` to
   `sim.state_diff { against }` in run B. The `changed` keys name the components to look at; the
   systems that write them are the suspects.

Errors are `INVALID_PARAMS` (`data.code` `F0002`). The message ends in a bracketed code:

| Code | Cause |
|---|---|
| `bad_prefix` | `prefix` is not a string. |
| `bad_ignore` | `ignore` is not an array of strings. |
| `bad_keys` | `keys` is not a boolean. |
| `bad_against` | `against` is missing, not an object, or one of its values is not a hex hash. |
| `bad_limit` | `limit` is not an integer from 1 to 1000. |

## The record/replay stress run

```sh
cargo xtask repro-check                       # 20 seeds × every scene, 240 frames each
cargo xtask repro-check --seeds 50 --steps 600
cargo xtask repro-check --report target/repro  # also writes target/repro.engine.md and target/repro.arena.md
```

For each scene and seed, `regia_test_utils::repro::record_replay` runs the scene twice:

1. **Record.** The scene feeds seeded input to player 0 through `InputInjection`, and
   `InputRecorder` records it. The input is a pure function of the seed and the step
   (`repro::input_noise`). The state is kept every 20 steps.
2. **Replay.** A fresh app is built from the same seed and plays the recording back with no drive. Its
   state is hashed at the same steps.

A run passes when every checkpoint matches. A failing run is reported like this (an illustration, not
a real finding):

```text
- arena_navmesh: 19 of 20 seeds replay identically (412 values hashed)
  - arena_navmesh seed 11400714819323198486: diverges by step 140: bot3/Transform, bot3/NavAgentState
    - bot3/Transform
      recorded {translation:{x:3.25,...
      replayed {translation:{x:3.2500002,...
```

The scenes:

| Scene | Where | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `physics_pile` | `regia_test_utils::repro` | 24 seeded boxes and spheres dropped into a walled pit with seeded velocities, and a character controller walking into them. |
| `character_rig` | `regia_test_utils::repro` | The schedule-shuffle smoke scene: falling boxes, the character, spring bones on a rope, a clip-driven arm with a socket. The seed moves the character's start. |
| `arena_match` | `samples/arena/tests/repro_check.rs` | The bot match with a local player: steering bots, hitscan, rockets, props, damage, scoring and the match RNG. |
| `arena_navmesh` | the same file | The same match with behaviour-tree bots on the navmesh (`regia_ai`, `regia_nav`). |

Both runs use the engine's default multi-threaded executor. A race between two systems that have no
order shows up as a divergence that comes and goes between runs. A scene that does not run exactly one
fixed step per frame is reported as an error instead of being compared.

### Your own scene

```rust,wrap
use regia_test_utils::repro::{ReproConfig, ReproScene, inject_next_frame, input_noise, record_replay};
# use regia_app::App;
# use regia_core::math::Vec3;
# fn my_level_app(_seed: u64) -> App { App::new() }

let scene = ReproScene {
    name: "my_level",
    build: my_level_app,          // fn(u64) -> App: plugins, InputRecordingPlugin, entities, fixed step
    actions: &["Move", "Fire"],   // recorded and replayed
    drive: |app, seed, step| {
        inject_next_frame(app, "Move", Vec3::new(input_noise(seed, step / 30, 0), 0.0, 0.0));
    },
    extra: None,                  // or Some(fn(&World, &mut Snapshot)) for resource state
    ignore: &["EntityGuid"],      // random or wall-clock values, not simulation state
};
let run = record_replay(&scene, 7, &ReproConfig::default());
assert!(run.is_clean(), "{run:?}");
```

Name every entity the scene spawns. Order your fixed-step systems after `InputRecordingSet`, so the
replay sees each recorded step on the same step.

## What keeps a run deterministic

These rules come from the fixes the harness motivated (ADR-537):

- **Integrate with the fixed step in `FixedUpdate`.** Use `FixedTime::step()` or `Time::delta_secs()`
  (inside `FixedUpdate` both are one step); outside it `Time::delta_secs()` is the frame delta.
  A frame can run zero or several fixed steps, so the frame delta is not the step length. A system
  that integrated with it moved differently at another frame rate. Behaviour trees, nav agents and the
  arena's bots, projectiles and match clock now use the step.
- **Give every fixed-step system an order.** Systems that touch the same data and have no edge between
  them run in thread-timing order on the multi-threaded executor. `regia_ai::AiStep` and
  `regia_nav::NavStep` name the AI and nav steps so a game can chain them; `AiPlugin` already runs
  `AiStep` after `PhysicsStep`; the arena chains input, physics, AI, nav, bots, weapons, damage and
  the match.
- **Never let a hash map's order reach state.** A despawn, spawn, list or float sum in `HashMap` order
  differs between runs, because each map gets a random hasher seed. The sim bridge now despawns vanished
  entities in sim-id order, and animation morph weights leave the evaluator in target order.
- **Read each message once.** A fresh `MessageCursor` reads the previous frame's messages a second time.
  Keep the cursor between calls. The arena's fire, explosion and death handlers now do.
- **Playback is same-step.** A recorded step's values are injected before that frame's action
  evaluation, so the replay's step `k` sees what the recording's step `k` saw. Before ADR-537 a replay
  ran one frame behind its recording.

Some residual risks are known and not yet fixed:

- Systems that spawn through `Commands` in parallel can reserve entity ids in thread order.
- The physics world inserts new bodies in entity order.

If the harness ever shows a physics divergence that comes and goes, look there first.

<!-- source: book/agents/replay-soak.md -->
# Replay soak

A replay is only useful if it lands on the same state as the run it recorded. The replay soak checks this.
It records a seeded input stream on headless scenes, replays each recording in a fresh app, and compares
state hashes at checkpoints. It does this once per compute-thread count and build profile, so it also catches
state that depends on the thread count, the optimizer or a per-process hash seed (ADR-867).

The soak is a developer tool (a command and a test helper), like the [schedule shuffle](book/agents/schedule-shuffle.md).
It is not a runtime feature, so it has no agent-protocol method: an agent runs the command and reads the
report files.

## Run it

```sh
cargo xtask replay-soak                                   # 8 seeds x 4 scenes, threads 1,2,8, debug + release
cargo xtask replay-soak --seeds 32 --steps 1800           # longer: 30 s of game time per run
cargo xtask replay-soak --scenes pile --threads 1,16 --builds release --every 1
cargo xtask replay-soak --features regia_physics/physics-cross-platform-determinism
```

On the workstation, run it through the build wrapper. Every run is one `cargo test -p regia_test_utils --test
replay_soak` process. Only the CPU is used (no GPU), so lavapipe-only machines run it too.

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--seeds N` | 8 | seeds per scene |
| `--first-seed S` | 1 | seeds run `S .. S + N` |
| `--steps N` | 600 | fixed steps per run (60 per second) |
| `--every N` | 10 | steps between checkpoints; 1 hashes every step; the last step always does |
| `--scenes a,b` | all | `smoke`, `pile`, `combat`, `crowd` |
| `--threads 1,2,8` | `1,2,8` | compute-pool sizes, one process each; `auto` keeps the default formula |
| `--builds debug,release` | both | cargo profiles, one build each (`debug`, `release` or a custom profile name) |
| `--features F` | none | cargo features for the test build |
| `--tag mac-` | empty | prefix for run labels, so files from several machines can sit in one directory |
| `--out DIR` | `target/replay-soak` | output directory |
| `--no-run` | off | merge the `run-*.json` files already in `--out`, run nothing |
| `--baseline FILE` | none | compare the reference traces with another merged `replay-soak.json` |

The command exits with 1 in any of these cases: a record trace differs between runs, a replay leaves its
recording, a run wrote no report (a build or test failure), or a baseline trace differs.

## The scenes

| Scene | What runs | Inputs |
|---|---|---|
| `smoke` | The shuffle-check scene: eight boxes, a walking character, spring bones, a clip-driven rig with a socket | `Move` and `Jump` drive the hero, `Shove` pushes `box0` |
| `pile` | 36 seeded boxes, spheres and capsules dropped into a walled bin, with collision events on | `Shove` pushes the striker sphere |
| `combat` | A turret, six seeded targets with framework `Health`, the damage step, deaths and respawns | `Aim` turns the turret, `Fire` shoots |
| `crowd` | Twelve seeded nav agents on a floor with a hole, planned with `NavQuery` and steered with ORCA avoidance (`NavPlugin`) | `Rally` sends everyone to a point that way, `Scatter` sends everyone home |

The `tally` entity carries `SoakTally`. It folds every `CollisionStarted` pair (in `pile`) and every death (in
`combat`) into a hash, in arrival order. A reordered event therefore changes the state hash, even when the
bodies end up in the same place.

The input generator is seeded (`InputStream`). Buttons alternate presses of 1 to 8 steps with releases of 3 to
40 steps. Axes hold a random value, or zero 30 % of the time, for 2 to 30 steps.

## Reading the report

`replay-soak.md` starts with the verdict, the runs (the first is the reference) and the matrix. It then has one
table row per scene and seed:

```text
| Scene | Seed | Final hash (reference) | debug-t1 | debug-t2 | release-t8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pile | 3 | `5c1f0e9a2b7d4410` | ok | ok | trace @240 |
```

- `ok`: the run's record trace equals the reference run's, and its replay equals its recording.
- `trace @S`: the record trace leaves the reference at step S. The divergence section lists the entities whose
  hash differs there. The state depends on the thread count, the build or the process.
- `replay @S`: the replay leaves its own recording at step S. The divergence section lists up to 12
  `<entity>/<Component>` values from both sides. Something in the scene is not driven by the recording: a
  wall clock, a hash order, an unordered system pair, or input applied on the wrong step.
- `missing`: the run has no result for this scene and seed.

## What to do with a divergence

1. If it is `replay @S` in every run, the scene is nondeterministic on its own. Look at the named component's
   writers: a `HashMap` iteration that spawns, despawns or emits, `Time::delta_secs()` read outside
   `FixedUpdate` in a simulation system (inside it the delta is one step), or an `Instant::now()`.
2. If it is `trace @S` only between thread counts, two systems with no ordering race on the named
   entities. Engine steps have sets to order against: `PhysicsStep`, `NavStep`, `AiStep`, `DamageSet` and
   `InputRecordingSet`. `cargo xtask shuffle-check --ambiguities` lists the candidate pairs. Add the edge, and add a test that
   fails without it.
3. If it is `trace @S` only between builds, look for float code whose result depends on optimization. Also look
   for a type-registry or `TypeId` order used as a tie-break.
4. Rerun with `--every 1 --seeds 1 --first-seed S --scenes X` to get the exact step.

## Across machines

Run on each machine with its own tag, copy the run files into one directory, and merge them:

```sh
cargo xtask replay-soak --tag mac- --builds release --threads 1,4      # on the Mac
cargo xtask replay-soak --no-run --out merged/                         # after copying run-*.json there
cargo xtask replay-soak --baseline linux/replay-soak.json              # or compare against another merge
```

Different CPUs and OSes may round floats differently. In that case, a `trace` divergence between machines is
expected unless the build enables `regia_physics/physics-cross-platform-determinism`.

## Report formats

`run-<label>.json` (`format: "regia-replay-soak-run"`, `version: 1`) is written by one test process:

```json
{
  "format": "regia-replay-soak-run", "version": 1,
  "label": "release-t8", "build": "release", "threads_requested": 8, "threads": 8,
  "os": "linux", "arch": "x86_64", "steps": 600, "every": 10,
  "runs": [
    {"scene": "combat", "seed": 1, "entities": 8, "values": 31, "active_inputs": 702,
      "record": [{"step": 10, "hash": "9a0c…", "entities": {"tally": "17be…", "turret": "40d2…"}}],
      "replay": [{"step": 10, "hash": "9a0c…"}],
      "replay_divergence": null}
  ]
}
```

A `replay_divergence` is `{"step": S, "differing": [{"key", "record", "replay"}]}`. Values longer than 400
characters are cut and end in `...`. Hashes are 16 lowercase hex digits. `threads_requested: null` means the
default formula.

`replay-soak.json` (`format: "regia-replay-soak"`, `version: 1`) is the merged report. It has these fields:

- `configs[]`: `label`, `build`, `threads`, `os`, `arch`. The first entry is the reference.
- `reference`, `steps`, `every` and `pass`.
- `cells[]`: `scene`, `seed`, `reference_trace[]` (`step`, `hash`), `final_hash`, and `results[]` with one entry per
  run. Each result has `label`, `present`, `matches_reference`, `first_divergent_step`, `divergent_entities`,
  `replay_matches` and `replay_divergence`.
- `problems[]`.
- `baseline`: `path`, `reference`, `compared`, `missing` and `mismatches[]` (`scene`, `seed`, `step`).

## Playback timing

`InputRecordingPlugin` injects recorded step k's values in `PreUpdate`, before `InputSet::Evaluation`, for the
frame that runs step k. Step k of a replay therefore sees what step k of the recording saw, triggers and phases
included, and playback ends on the last recorded frame. Before ADR-867, the values landed one frame later, and
every replay ran one step behind its recording. Exact replays need at least one fixed step per frame;
`enable_fixed_step` runs exactly one.

## In your own tests

```rust,wrap
use regia_test_utils::replay_soak::{SoakConfig, SoakScene, soak_seed};
# use regia_app::App;
# use regia_input::ActionKind;
# fn build_my_app(_seed: u64) -> App { App::new() }

let scene = SoakScene {
    name: "mine",
    build: build_my_app,
    actions: &[("Move", ActionKind::Axis2D)],
    components: &[], // or only the gameplay components: &["Transform", "Health", "Pawn"]
};
let report = soak_seed(&scene, 7, &SoakConfig { steps: 600, every: 10 });
assert!(report.replay_matches(), "{:?}", report.replay_divergence);
```

`build` must return an app that runs one fixed step per update. It must also have `InputPlugin` with those
actions, `InputRecordingPlugin`, and gameplay ordered `.after(InputRecordingSet)`. Name every entity: the
snapshot keys entities by `Name`. If the app holds asset handles or render state whose ids come from process-wide
counters, list the gameplay components in `components`. Two apps in one process otherwise differ in those ids.
`samples/arena/tests/replay_soak.rs` does this for the arena.

<!-- source: book/agents/memory.md -->
# Memory per subsystem (agent)

How an agent sees where a running game's memory goes, CPU heap and GPU side by side, for each engine subsystem, and how
it checks that a level can be loaded and unloaded many times without leaving memory behind (ADR-539).

## Heap tracking

The CPU numbers come from `regia_core::memory`. When the host installs the tagging allocator, every heap allocation
counts against the subsystem the allocating thread is working for, and is freed against the same one:

```rust
#[global_allocator]
static ALLOC: regia_core::memory::TaggingAllocator = regia_core::memory::TaggingAllocator::system();
```

It costs a 16-byte header (or the alignment, when that is larger) and a few atomic adds per allocation. Use it in
dev builds, tests and soaks, not in a shipped game. Without it the heap numbers are `null` and `heap.hint` says why.
`regia_app::Diagnostics::allocated_bytes` is filled from the same ledger.

The engine opens a scope at these entry points: level spawn and unload (`scene`), asset loads (`assets`), the
physics step (`physics`), the audio drain (`audio`) and the frame render (`render`). Game code can open its own:

```rust,wrap
use regia_core::memory::{self, Subsystem};

let _mem = memory::enter(Subsystem::Gameplay); // until `_mem` drops, this thread's allocations are gameplay's
```

Scopes nest, and the innermost one wins. Work outside every scope counts as `unscoped`. That includes host code,
start-up, the standard library, and tasks on worker pools, because a scope belongs to the thread that opened it.

GPU bytes come from the wgpu allocator report (Vulkan and D3D12; `null` on GL and Metal), grouped by label. Terrain
and scatter data count as `terrain`, VFX and particle buffers as `vfx`, UI and glyph textures as `ui`, and everything
else as `render`.

## `memory.report`

Read-only. `top` (default 10, max 200) sets how many of the largest GPU allocations to list.

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"memory.report","params":{"top":3}}
```

```json
{
  "heap": { "tracked": true, "live_bytes": 412090368, "peak_bytes": 530579456, "hint": null },
  "gpu": { "available": true, "backend": "Vulkan", "allocated_bytes": 1610612736, "reserved_bytes": 2147483648 },
  "process": { "rss_bytes": 1932735283, "rss_peak_bytes": 2040109465 },
  "ecs": { "entities": 18342, "archetypes": 211, "components": 486 },
  "subsystems": [
    { "name": "unscoped", "heap_bytes": 96468992, "heap_peak_bytes": 120586240, "heap_allocations": 40211, "gpu_bytes": 0 },
    { "name": "scene", "heap_bytes": 25165824, "heap_peak_bytes": 31457280, "heap_allocations": 9120, "gpu_bytes": 0 },
    { "name": "assets", "heap_bytes": 201326592, "heap_peak_bytes": 268435456, "heap_allocations": 3310, "gpu_bytes": 0 },
    { "name": "render", "heap_bytes": 67108864, "heap_peak_bytes": 75497472, "heap_allocations": 12007, "gpu_bytes": 1258291200 },
    { "name": "terrain", "heap_bytes": 0, "heap_peak_bytes": 0, "heap_allocations": 0, "gpu_bytes": 335544320 }
  ],
  "owners": [
    { "name": "render.shader_modules", "subsystem": "render", "heap_bytes": 9437184, "heap_peak_bytes": 11534336, "heap_allocations": 52110 },
    { "name": "render.frame", "subsystem": "render", "heap_bytes": 4194304, "heap_peak_bytes": 6291456, "heap_allocations": 3012 }
  ],
  "top_gpu": [
    { "label": "material texture (streamed)", "subsystem": "render", "category": "meshes", "bytes": 402653184, "count": 311 }
  ],
  "since_mark": null
}
```

Every subsystem is listed in a fixed order: `unscoped`, `scene`, `assets`, `render`, `terrain`, `physics`, `audio`,
`animation`, `navigation`, `ui`, `vfx`, `telemetry`, `agent`, `gameplay`. The example above shows only the first five.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `heap.tracked` | Whether the tagging allocator is installed. When it is `false`, every heap field is `null`. |
| `heap.live_bytes`, `heap.peak_bytes` | Heap bytes held now, and the highest value seen. Allocator headers are not counted. |
| `gpu` | The allocator report's totals; `null` before a render device exists. |
| `process` | Resident set now and at its peak. Linux and Android use `VmRSS` and `VmHWM`. Windows uses the working set and peak working set. macOS uses the task's resident size and `ru_maxrss` (ADR-5860). `null` on other targets and when the OS query fails. |
| `ecs` | Spawned entities, archetypes, and registered components. |
| `subsystems[].heap_bytes` | Live heap bytes the subsystem allocated and has not freed. |
| `subsystems[].heap_allocations` | Live allocations of the subsystem. |
| `subsystems[].gpu_bytes` | GPU bytes whose label maps to the subsystem; `null` without an allocator report. |
| `owners` | The named owners (above), largest live heap first: `name`, `subsystem`, `heap_bytes`, `heap_peak_bytes`, `heap_allocations`. Their bytes are also in their subsystem's row. Empty when the heap is not tracked or no owner was entered. |
| `top_gpu` | The largest GPU labels: bytes, allocation count, subsystem and the finer `seeing.memory_report` category. |
| `since_mark` | The change since the last `memory.mark` (below); `null` before one. |
| `assets_by_type` | Per asset type (`mesh`, `image`, `texture`, `material`): `type`, `loaded` (assets loaded now) and `bytes` (the heap blocks their decoded payloads hold; a texture from a mapped pak counts its payload length). Counted when asked, never per frame. With the tagging allocator they add up to the `assets` subsystem's growth over the loads within 64 KiB plus 2 %: the rest is the asset server's own maps (ADR-9740). `null` without an asset server. |

### Named owners inside a subsystem

A subsystem row says which part of the engine holds bytes; an owner row says what inside it does (ADR-3351). An owner
is a `static` declared next to the code that allocates, entered like a scope:

```rust,wrap
use regia_core::memory::{self, MemoryOwner, Subsystem};

static LEVEL_CACHE: MemoryOwner = MemoryOwner::new(Subsystem::Gameplay, "gameplay.level_cache");
let _mem = memory::enter_owner(&LEVEL_CACHE); // gameplay's bytes, and the owner's row
```

An owner's bytes count in its subsystem too, so the subsystem totals do not change. A plain `memory::enter` of another
subsystem inside an owner scope clears the owner (an asset load started by renderer code is the asset subsystem's);
one of the owner's own subsystem keeps it. The innermost owner wins. At most 63 owners get a row (the first ones
entered in the process); later ones count in their subsystem only.

The renderer names its start-up and idle holders (`regia_render::heap_owners`):

| Owner | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `render.plugin` | What `RenderPlugin::build` allocates: resources, schedules, type registrations. |
| `render.device` | The wgpu instance, adapter and device. |
| `render.shader_modules` | WGSL composition: the per-thread composer over the engine library, its cached imports, and the composed modules the shader modules keep. |
| `render.pipelines` | Render and compute pipeline objects and their backend compile. |
| `render.pipeline_cache` | The persistent pipeline cache's file payload, load and save. |
| `render.atmosphere_luts` | The sky and atmosphere tables (transmittance, multiple scattering, sky view, aerial perspective). |
| `render.blue_noise` | The spatiotemporal blue-noise texture (only with the knob on). |
| `render.color_luts` | Level LUTs, post-volume LUTs and the color-vision LUT. |
| `render.cloud_noise` | Cloud noise volumes and the curl field. |
| `render.extract` | The frame description extracted from the ECS each frame. |
| `render.upload_queue` | The background upload queue. |
| `render.frame` | The frame renderer's own state outside every owner above (texture views and windows). |

## `memory.mark`

Read-only, no parameters. Records the heap ledger, the entity count and the GPU total as a baseline, and replaces any
earlier mark. Later `memory.report` answers carry `since_mark`:

```json
{ "heap_bytes": 1048576, "largest": "assets",
  "subsystems": { "assets": { "heap_bytes": 1048576, "heap_allocations": 12 } },
  "gpu_bytes": 0, "entities": 0 }
```

`subsystems` lists only the subsystems that changed, `owners` only the named owners that changed. `largest` names the
subsystem that gained the most heap bytes.
`gpu_bytes` is `null` when either side had no allocator report.

## Checks an agent can run

- **A level unloads cleanly:** load the level once and unload it, so caches settle. Call `memory.mark`. Then load and
  unload it five times and call `memory.report`. `since_mark.entities` is 0. `since_mark.heap_bytes` stays within a
  few KiB and does not grow with each extra round. If it does grow, `since_mark.largest` names the subsystem holding
  the memory.
- **What fills the GPU, by owner:** compare `subsystems[].gpu_bytes` for `terrain` and `render`, then read `top_gpu`
  for the labels.
- **Heap not tracked:** when `heap.tracked` is `false`, read `heap.hint` and use `process.rss_bytes` for the total.
- **What inside the renderer holds the heap:** read `owners` (largest first). The `render` row minus the sum of the
  `render.*` owners is what the renderer allocated outside every owner; start-up work outside every scope is still
  `unscoped`.

## The soak test

`crates/regia_scene/tests/level_leak_soak.rs` runs 1000 load/unload cycles of a 64-entity level under the tagging
allocator. Each cycle parses the level from RON, opens it, runs a frame, unloads it, drops its data from the
`LevelLibrary` and runs another frame. The heap and the `scene` subsystem are sampled after every unload and judged
with `regia_core::memory::LeakCheck`. The first 100 cycles are skipped. Then the peak of the last 100 cycles may
exceed the peak of the first 100 measured cycles by at most 8 KiB. One 16-byte allocation kept per cycle would add
12.8 KB and fail. A control run of 300 more cycles leaks 64 bytes per cycle on purpose and must fail the same check.

## Telemetry

The 10 s `regia::frame_summary` record carries the same numbers in `memory.subsystems`:
`heap_tracked`, `heap_live_bytes`, `heap_peak_bytes`, and `by_subsystem: { <name>: { heap_bytes, gpu_bytes } }`.
GPU bytes there come from the last telemetry probe sample, so they can be up to 10 s old. See
[Telemetry](book/agents/telemetry.md).

<!-- source: book/agents/startup-assets.md -->
# Startup asset work (cook skip, stamps, batched model loads)

What a dev start costs before the first frame, and how to check it. Design: ADR-530. Spec:
`docs/specs/12-assets.md` § 6.

## The cook before a dev run

`regia run`, `regia preview`, the editor's content panel and the live cooker cook the project
incrementally first. A glTF/GLB, image (PNG, JPEG, TGA, BMP, DDS, EXR, HDR, SVG, PSD), channel-pack recipe (`.texpack.ron`) or audio (WAV, OGG, FLAC, MP3) source is skipped **without running its importer** when
none of the files that importer reads changed since its last cook:

- the source and its `.meta`;
- for a `.gltf`, the buffers and images it references by URI and their `.meta` overrides;
- for a glTF, the project's `lod_classes.toml`;
- the platform, the importer version, and the build of the cooker. A rebuilt or updated engine imports
  everything once.

The source also needs its outputs still in the cooked cache. Other importers (material graphs, atlases,
tilemaps, scatter, baked GI, terrain) import and then compare their cache key, as before.

A file whose size and modification time match its last hash is not read again. A file modified less than
2 s before it was hashed is read again on the next cook.

## Checking it

Run the cook and read its summary line (stderr):

```text
$ regia cook --project game
cook: 0 cooked, 412 skipped, 0 errors, 0 non-cookable files skipped (38.0 ms; 412 skipped without import, 0.0 MiB hashed)
```

- On an unchanged project, `skipped without import` should equal `skipped` minus the sources of other
  importers. A glTF or PNG that is imported on every run points at an input that changes each time,
  such as a generator rewriting a `.meta` or a sidecar.
- `MiB hashed` is 0 when every input is older than 2 s and unchanged.
- Hosts read the same counts from `CookReport::imports_skipped` and `CookReport::hashed_bytes`.

To force a full import, run `regia cook --clean`. That is also the fix after a tool rewrote a file with
the same size and a restored modification time (`touch -r`, `cp -p` of other bytes). The keys and stamps
are a cache in `.regia/assetdb/cook-inputs-<platform>.bin`, and deleting that file is safe.

## Loading cooked models

`regia_render::cooked_model::load_cooked_models(&mut server, &gltf_ids)` loads several cooked glTFs in
one batch:

- the part lists and materials load through the server;
- then every mesh and every distinct texture decode together on the compute pool;
- each texture is read once, and a texture several models share is decoded once.

`load_cooked_model` is the one-model case. Meshes and textures loaded this way show `"state": "loaded"`
in `assets.status`, which reports where their bytes came from (they are marked with
`AssetServer::note_external_load`). They are not held in `AssetServer::textures()` / `images()`.

To measure a map load, use `pak_load_bench load --paks DIR` (sample `lookdev`). It prints
`PAK_LOAD {json}`, where `cpu_load_ms` is the batched load. For the boot side, use
`render.boot_timeline` ([instant load](book/agents/instant-load.md)).

To retain authored LODs above zero and select generated index levels without rebuilding tangents,
use the additive [all-LOD cooked model loader](book/agents/cooked-model-all-lods.md). It loads compact and
GPU-ready meshes (`REGIA_PAK_GPU_MESHES=1` desktop paks are its fast path) and shares GPU image
identities across the batch; this legacy loader keeps its behavior.

<!-- source: book/agents/frame-scratch.md -->
# Frame list growth (`summary.frame_scratch`, v0.1.28)

The renderer builds its per-frame lists (lights, shadow casters, shadow jobs, the GPU cull's
instances, the storage-object upload) in buffers it keeps between frames (ADR-385). A list that
needs more room than it held reallocates once; that is a *growth*. Once a scene and its camera
path settle, every list fits and the growth count stops rising: the steady frame allocates none
of those lists.

Read it from the frame summary (`telemetry.get_last_summary`, see [Telemetry](book/agents/telemetry.md)):

```json
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "telemetry.get_last_summary" }
```

```json
{ "summary": { "…": 0,
               "frame_scratch": { "growths": 0, "growths_after_warmup": 0, "total": 61 } } }
```

- `growths`: growths during the summary window (main view and texture views together).
- `growths_after_warmup`: the part of `growths` after the warm-up frames.
- `total`: growths since the renderer was created.

Typical uses:

- After a scripted run (`play.wait_until`) on a settled level, assert
  `summary.frame_scratch.growths_after_warmup == 0`. A non-zero value on a held camera means a
  list outgrew its buffer every few frames: something the frame builds keeps getting larger.
- A level load, a camera cut onto a denser view or a larger crowd grows the lists once; the next
  window goes back to 0.

What is counted, and what is not:

| Counted (one reusable buffer each) | Not counted |
|---|---|
| uploaded local lights, the light and shadow-tile records, GI probe records, the draw list | a buffer created for a new mesh or material |
| the joint palette, per-mesh skin spans, glass index, changed object uniforms | wgpu's own command recording |
| opaque, blended, shadow and translucent draw indices; cascade splits | caster lists of pages rebuilt this frame (they are kept and shared while the page holds) |
| caster bounds and cascade masks, caster footprints per cascade, page and atlas casters | the emissive light collection, the post stack |
| shadow jobs, GPU-cull instances and slots, storage-object bytes and their draw map | |
| the GPU culler's sort order, cull spheres, batch commands, and the instanced shadow and depth lists | |
| the velocity pass's sort keys, instances, skinned palettes and batched draws | |
| the stream pass's material order and the in-scene material map | |

Hosts and tests read the same numbers from Rust with `FrameRenderer::frame_scratch_stats()`
(`FrameScratchStats { growths, last_frame_growths, frames }`). The renderer's own tests
(`crates/regia_render/tests/frame_scratch.rs`) draw a scene with a held and an orbiting camera
and assert that no steady frame grows a list.

<!-- source: book/agents/render-robustness.md -->
# Degenerate cameras and NaN guards

What the renderer does with inputs that would otherwise turn a frame into NaN, and the log lines that
tell you it happened (ADR-869). None of this has an agent method of its own: you see it in
`seeing.screenshot` output and in the log (`logs.read`).

## Cameras the frame repairs

Before any matrix is built, `FrameRenderer::render_into` checks the frame's camera and renders a
repaired copy when one of these is true. The first repair in a process logs one warning
(`unusable camera (eye … target … fov_y … near … far …); rendering with …`).

| Input | Rendered as |
|---|---|
| `far = f32::INFINITY` | far 100 km (`view_math::INFINITE_FAR_STANDIN`); depth is standard Z, not reverse-Z |
| `far` NaN, `−∞` or not beyond `near` | `near × 10⁴` |
| `far` beyond 1e9 m | 1e9 m (`view_math::MAX_FAR`) |
| `near` NaN, infinite, zero or negative | 0.1 m |
| `near` below 1 µm or above 1000 km | clamped to that range |
| `fov_y` NaN | π/4 |
| `fov_y` outside (1e-4, π − 1e-4) | clamped to that range |
| eye NaN or infinite | the origin |
| target NaN or infinite, or on the eye | one meter ahead along −Z |

A camera looking exactly along the up axis (straight down at a map, straight up at the sky) is not a
repair: the view keeps its direction and takes −Z as screen up looking down (+Z looking up), the
picture a camera pitched to the pole from −Z would show. The same holds for a sun at the zenith in
the sun cascades. Before this, all of these drew a black or garbage frame.

## Camera fields the 3D frame does not draw yet

They log one warning the first time an extracted camera uses them, and the view still renders:

- `Camera::orthographic` / `ortho_size`: the frame draws the camera in perspective with `fov_y`.
  Picking (`screen_ray`) already uses parallel rays for it, so picks and pixels disagree.
- `ClearMode::Color(c)`: the frame clears as for `ClearMode::Skybox`.
- `Camera::hdr` and `Camera::msaa_override`: not read; the render profile decides.

## History that cannot be poisoned

Four passes carry results from frame to frame. Each replaces a NaN or infinite value before storing
it, so one bad pixel or probe recovers on the next frame instead of staying for good:

- the GPU probe volume (DDGI) irradiance and distance moments (a bad probe restarts from black);
- the cloud reconstruction (a bad texel restarts as clear sky);
- the froxel fog integration (a bad froxel is clear air);
- the auto-exposure average (a non-finite meter reading is skipped).

TAA, TSR, FSR 3 and stochastic SSR already guarded their histories.

## Checking a scene

- A black frame with a camera straight up or down, or with an infinite far plane, is no longer
  expected. If you see one, capture it and read the log for the warning above.
- A render graph built with `RenderGraph` reports a dependency cycle or a resource written by two
  nodes through `RenderGraph::try_compile`; `compile` logs the same error and runs what it can.
